Far Cry Primal is an open world, story driven, FPS game set on pre-historic time (10,000 BC). You play as Takkar, a Wenja (some kind of a tribe) warrior that is trying to conquer the Land of Oros for his people. Conflict starts when Takkar found out that Oros is conquered by Udam (cannibal tribe) in the north and by Izila (Sun worshipper) in the south. Far Cry Primal introduces several new features and an entirely new story 'pattern' compared to its predecessors. You are no longer a badass rambo-like warrior or a teenager stranded in an island or a remote area. The main new feature is the taming capability. Along the journey, Takkar was introduced to his skills as a Beast Master, capable to tame dangerous predators and even ride it after you have reached a certain level. In short, Far Cry Primal is a fresh new idea in the Far Cry series that offers the same gameplay pattern but with new environment, features, and challenges.
First off, I'm going to talk about the good things. It still has the same gameplay pattern as other Far Cry series - you still have to conquer 'radio towers' (now called bonfires) and enemy encampments while completing your journey in the main story at the same time. It still have the same epic graphics like Far Cry 4 but the story pattern is completely new. Hunting has become a major element in Far Cry Primal since you have to craft everything instead of purchasing it directly from a store. Takkar also has Assassin's Creeds' Eagle Vision that can track animal tracks, blood scents, and enemy heat signatures. This is vital in helping you hunt for animals, especially rare animals. If you love hunting games, Far Cry Primal might not be as realistic as an actual hunting game but it's satisfying enough for me. You will also progress faster compared to previous Far Cry because you'll get permanent XP boost if you rescued a lot of other Wenja (remember the impromptu events). The combat system is obviously very different, there were no guns yet so you only have clubs, throwing shards, several different 'bombs', bows, and spears. You can't butcher the whole base from afar with a .50 cal sniper rifle again, you have to come up close for most of the combat - even the long bow only give you so much attack distance. Their effort to create their own pre-historic language is also worth mentioning, I always respect game developers that pay a lot of attention to details in their games.
Now, the bad things. The content is a lot less compared to Far Cry 4 in order to make it 'makes sense'. But come on, the throwing shards, grappling hooks, animal taming, animal riding, and a ton of other features already don't make sense in the first place. The 'radio tower' part is also much shorter, you won't need to climb anything. Simply kill several enemies, shoot a fire arrow and boom, you're done. No more parkour-ing to the top of a tall tower. Map is also smaller-ish (I'm no expert in measuring virtual stuff) but it's adequate. They really should have put more features in the game. Now, the story. I somehow feel it's much less engaging and very short. As you see from my gameplay, I finished this game only in 23 hours. That 23 hours already gave me a TON of time to fool around completing the side quests, crafting everything, complete my beast collection, and building my village. IMHO, this is the reason a lot of people harshly dismissed this game as a Far Cry 4 re-skin with less content. The short story, little amount of weapon choice, and the less content disappointed them. The main beast taming feature simply couldn't make it up to the amount of lost content. To make it clear, the specific 'lost content' for me is the long and beautifully written story, fighting arena, flying, lots of weapon choices, engaging story, capability to make choices that will affect the outcome of the story, etc.
But, I still personally love the Far Cry series. I don't really care much about the less content, it's still 23 hours of fun for me. As I said in my thesis, it's a fresh new idea. An entirely different age, a different combat system, different story 'taste' and basically, as long as it's a Far Cry series, I don't care about the reviews - I want to play it. As an analogy, same thing goes for the PAYDAY 2 DLCs, the weapons may be useless and all but as long as it's something new, I want it, regardless of the mostly negative review. I'm not saying this game is 'bad but buy it', it's good and it's worth it, but don't expect to have the same experience as the previous Far Cry series. If you're looking for a very long gameplay, go for Far Cry 4, but if you don't mind the bad things that I mentioned, this game is heavily recommended.

Alan's Wake American Nightmare is the pseudo follow-up/se to the well received Alan Wake. It is a 3rd person shooter which controls exactly the same as the first game. American Nightmare improves drastically on one of the few low points of the original Alan Wake, the combat. A.N. adds several new weapons and enemy types. These additions would have been welcome earlier, since it grew tiresome using the same 4 weapons in Alan Wake and fighting the same enemies over the 10 hours the game took to beat. However, I could see how the weaponry might not have fit in that atmosphere. The variations in the enemy types help keep the combat fresh as you continue through the estimated 3-4 hour campaign.
The real standout in Alan Wake, the story, really takes a backseat in American Nightmare to the improved combat. While it will catch your attention at the beginning, I eventually found myself just wanting it to be over. Most of that I believe is due to the Groundhog Day esque nature of this installment, where you will be going through some of the same areas and events multiple times. It just fails to really engross you all the way through like Alan Wake did.
Speaking of the environments, they are a nice change of pace from the Pacific Northwest. The events take place in Night Springs, Arizona, a fictional town which is the setting of an in-game TV show. You will be running around through some desert landscape for a few hours, but this game is shorter so it doesn't wear out its welcome like the forest did.
The graphics have seen a slight improvement from the previous game, with the character animation looking much better, but still not stellar. The sound is also fantastic once again, with some great soundtrack moments during some battles.
I would recommend American Nightmare to fans of the original Alan Wake for two reasons. If you liked the combat, which some did, you will love the additions to the weaponry and enemies. If you liked the story, which most did, you will be interested in finding out what happens next to our protagonist. If you have not played Alan Wake, I would recommend picking that up before trying out American Nightmare. There are too many spoilers for the events of the first game, and it would ruin the experience.
Grade: B-

Lethal League is a competative baseball/dodgeball hybrid that supports up to four players in one match. With each strike of the ball, the speed is doubled, sometimes even quadrupled (and in serious cases, maxed at one million). Maybe you and a few friends sit on the couch and hit the ball back and forth a few times. Maybe it's you and a stranger online. Regardless, every hit and dodge are anxiety and adrenaline riddled. With more than four friends who've enjoyed this game with me, we've never experienced any rage or upsetting losses, only awe at how insane it is to bunt the ball at such ridiculous speeds and then pelt it right back at the poor soul who bashed it towards you in the first place. Each character has a special ability that makes the matches all that much more interesting once they've filled their blue bar. Beware Dice and Candy Man. There's also an interesting secret character which you can play as in local matches; I'll let you google the code for yourself.
My friends and I give this game a 10/10 for competative shenanigans and I give it a 9/10 for the minor network bugs.
Worth the price, but I'm glad I snagged it on the humblebundle for a buck.

Greyfox is a story about a woman who 'takes control' of her life and moves to a new town. There she meets a rather interesting woman who gives her the power to make decisions. Depending on the decisions you make, determines how the story ends.
The game is built upon the idea of taknig a look at 4 different people's lives that could be viewed on the surface as kind of bad. There is a good little bit of detail in this one town game that changes based on which life you are exploring. While some of the assets are stock, it really doesn't make much of a difference, the stories are interesting enough that you don't really notice them unless you really care about that sort of thing.
The Achievements are pretty easy to get, and seeing the different endings is actually interesting. The music is pretty good, but depending on how long you play could get irritating. Most importantly, the dialogue in the game is pretty good. You can tell the authors put some thought into the game.
I would recommend it if you have time for a short 2 hour game to explore, unless you aren't interested in the concept. There are no battles, do don't get your hopes up. This is not a traditional RPG Maker game.
One tiny gripe is the devs couldn't figure out how to make F12 not reset the game to the title screen. No screenshots for you. :/
Overall for the price tag it carries, it's worth getting and playing.
For an RPG Maker game definite 6/10

Re;Birth2 is a fun game and a worthy installment of the Neptunia franchise...on Vita. On PC, it's buggier than a big bug bugging out in a dune buggy:
-General performance issues causes inconsistent framerate that can tank from 60 to 9 FPS when the game loads during a dungeon.
-CG scenes are potentially hobbled by lagging audio and skipping video. Currently, I have not been able to fix this.
-Enabling select DLC (I've found the Additional Content Packs and Histoire's Rescue Plans to be hassle-free) may cause scripting errors.
-Crashes are not frequent, but can happen at critical moments where saving is not possible.
-The game may not load on start-up, prompting a trip to Task Manager to end the process. Also, it may simply cut the knot and crash every time instead.
-The game may suddenly stop recognizing controller inputs.
-Memory leaks, ho!
-If you're unlucky, you will always crash past a certain event in the plot, usually after the prologue. I had this issue for a long time, which eventually went away for no apparent reason.
-Some artwork has not been upscaled for HD resolutions, resulting in pixelation of otherwise terrific backgrounds and artwork.
-The sound mixing is awful. Dungeon music is too quiet, world map BGM is far too loud, and effects are always leaning on the extreme ends of the scale from "pen drop" to "Linkin Park concert".
And those potentially aren't the last of the issues that exist.
The game has been patched in June, but resulted in even more problems cropping up. As a result, the patch was undone a day later. The devs have remained quiet since then, and with the release of Re;Birth3, it is unlikely Re;Birth2 will ever be fixed.
I was able to soldier on through all the issues and fully complete the game on all my avaliable free time over the course of two months. It's still got the irreverent charm the series is known for, with addicting gameplay and a short-but-sweet length that compels you to come back and get all nine endings. But as a Vita owner, I have to question if it was really worth my patience.
Re;Birth2 as a game is great. Re;Birth2 as a PC port is simply dreadful.
This review will be updated should patches come out.
P.S. I've spent around 10 of my 75 hours simply finding solutions to fix my issues. On a side note, Re;Birth2 has repeatedly caused my computer to overheat and automatically shut down to avoid damage to internal systems. This is likely an issue relegated to myself, however.

Simple in concept, complex in it's strategy, Slay the Spire will have you sweating in later battles as difficulty ramps up, and every decision effects the outcome of each battle. (Lets Play Video Review.)
The game allows you to build your deck each run, and every card can potentially play off one another. Whether you prefer an offensive, defensive, or mixture of the two; every style of play is viable with the right planning, choices and little luck too. The art style may appear simplistic, or rough even, but you will be shocked at how quickly you are sucked in and forget the art entirely as the masterfully crafted gameplay takes stage front and center. With cards, relics, potions and buffs all in play the strategic possibilities are near endless. Every run starts on the level one map, with multiple branching routes to choose from. On these routes are enemies, merchants, campfires (where you can rest or upgrade a card), encounters and mini bosses. These routes all lead to the boss battle which upon completing will start you out on the next "level" map. There is a save option where you can leave and come back to where you left off for longer runs. This game is worth the price, and with multiple updates already implemented, seems to have a long life ahead. Have fun and good luck on your next run.

This game is intended for mature gamers.  Violence, skimpy outfits, provocative dialogue, and a few "sex scenes" (you don't really see anything but it's clear what's going on) make it inappropriate for kids.  If you want a kids' game, get Final Fantasy or Spongebob.
The first three Saints Row games played a lot like GTA 3 or 4.  This one is... different.  You can still run around a small city (it's a "digital simulation" version of the Steelport city from Saints Row 3) and you can still steal cars and mug people.  You can still buy new outfits and upgrade your guns.  You can even customize your character.  And there are still some activities and side missions you can do to earn bonus XP (called Respect in the Saints Row games) and money.  That's where the similarity to the other SR and GTA games ends.
Your character is the same boss of the Saints gang from SR 2 and 3, but now you're President of the USA.  Your gang lieutentants from the old games make up your cabinet and staff.  But that doesn't last long, since an alien invasion kidnaps you and half of your gang and then blows up the planet.  You and your friends are trapped in a computer simulation that is supposed to represent each person's worst nightmare.  So when you accept a mission to rescue your friend, expect it to get a little bit weird.  Most of the game is played in a simulated version of Steelport city, but it's like the Saints gang never existed.  And instead of rival Syndicate gang forces, you have to compete against the alien invaders.  You don't buy property in this one, and you don't have cribs to store your cars and guns.  You can "buy" stores by doing a little mini-game to unlock each one.  You can't buy anything from a store until you do that.  Instead of the old cribs, you can steal a car and store it instantly in your digital garage.  Same for planes and helicopters.  Most of the vehicles can be modified just like in SR3.  In place of the regular cribs, you eventually get a space ship in the "real world" which your crew stole from the aliens.  Much like the ships from the movie "the Matrix" this is where you will hookup into the simulated world and fight the aliens.  You can also talk to (and "romance") your crew.  They don't say anything useful unless your current mission specifically tells you to go find them, but the romance options are a little funny.
Oh yeah, and you get SUPERHERO POWERS in this game.  you can jump high, fly (well, glide anyway), run super fast, and you get energy blasts, telekinesis, super-stomp, and elemental aura powers.  Certain enemies have shields and you can only hurt them by first removing the shield.  Shields can be removed by your super powers, or some of them by killing a robotic orb (called a CID) that hovers around the enemy.
The plot for this game is absolutely ridiculous.  It's a ripoff of The Matrix and a few other movies.  Mildly funny, but not great, in terms of the dialogue and stuff.  The simulation world you play in is not very big; it's just like the Steelport from SR3.  So although you can just run around the city doing whatever you want, which makes it an open-world game, the world is tiny.  My personal opinion:  not worth more than two bucks.  Saints Row 2 and 3 were both more fun than this, and less crazy.  Maybe this game would be more fun if you play co-op online, which I didn't bother to do.

Unlike FTL, there is clearly a good choice at the events, for example, 90% of the time you will take additional 150g in exchange for a curse. Unless you know you won't have time to spend it.
The real dillemas come from picking an early "average" card which will be lackluster late game, but that will make the early game easier. Also rest or upgrade is a hard choice at times, because you know that on the "ideal" run, you never rest and only heal by beating the boss, but that means avoiding most "normal" fights to conserve health.
Also, you might have an idea of what is the perfect deck for your run, but the random cards you get push you to another style. And you need to adapt.
All in all, great game. Hopefully it will get more variety of enemies, itens and cards.

This is the best game I have played this year, despite the game being early access as of posting this review.
I was doubting that there would ever be released a game that I would enjoy as much as Dream Quest, but here it is. Slay the spire does not simply copy the fantastic formula for roguelike deckbuilders established by Dream Quest, it also improves it. And it has nice aesthethics to boot!
The deckbuilding process is ruthless, as you are never allowed to go back. Your decision to take or not take a card is final, and you have to deal with the consequences. Having a plan is essential.
The combat is purely strategical, since you will know your enemies' every move before they perform them. The balance between attacking and blocking makes it feel like you are actually in a battle, not just playing cards.
I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of roguelikes and/or deckbuilders, turn-based strategy games in general or Dream Quest in particular.

A variation on Rampage Knight's theme (not Rogue Legacy, as everyone in the reviews section seems to think?), best played coop.
It's a plenty worthwhile game, it feels unfairly hard at first, and I was a little miffed about spending like 10s chopping away at goblins in the first level. But this is mostly because the game has a combat logic that emphasizes crowd control over picking off one or two enemies. There's no "roll", but jump serves largely the same purpose. So you end up manuevering around the field, herding enemies into a group and take turns dealing out damage with your coop friends. This difficulty gets even worse in later levels, but the challenge is overcomable with good teamwork and instincts about when to engage and not.
The randomization is pretty similar to Rampage Knights (you pick up armor, pets, consumables, weapons with stats and procs, etc), but there are definite balance issues. If you get the wizard staff as the starter weapon, your basic attacks apply a burning effect to enemies, and attack in a cone (instead of just straight ahead), AND you get a teleport instead of "dodge". If this sounds overpowered, it's because it is. A lot of things feel this way; some items make things ludicrously easy, others are worthless. Some talent tree slots are obviously useful, some are completely inane. It doesn't make the game feel unfair, per se, but you sure get the feeling that it wasn't very tightly designed.
Which is alright, but worse than that is easily the controls themselves. Feathering the basic attack button randomly decides to pop off your cooldown-based special attack (despite the special attack having its own button). You have to stop moving to perform most actions (which is a real pain when you just want to dodge, but have to stop moving to do it). Blocking USUALLY locks your character's facing, but for the first couple seconds you can get turned the wrong way - all in all there's just too many things which make the game feel like it's not really obeying your commands as much as its own whims.
A nice little microcosm of this weird control scheme is how it handles dialogue. Entering dialog with any character freezes you, and you have to constantly hit the "use" button to continue the dialog - the very same button that chooses your responses. So even just asking a vendor to pay $20 for a random item requires 5-6 rolls of dialog, and if you just mash the "use" key, you'll more often than not accidentally use the default response of "no", and end up having to start all over. Most games let you skip dialog with any key, so you can just flail around until the dialog is at the point where you make a decision. Or, i dunno, just not have rolls and rolls of dialog for simple things? The game plays up this thin veneer of having a story, but we all know it doesn't. Your choices are "buy it or not", and they're not lore-critical. Is it too much to ask for more concise systems?
The game has rough edges, and doesn't feel like it was competently designed. This is exactly the kind of game that couldn't have been playtested well before release, and whose designers didn't learn any lessons from games who carefully balanced disparate stats like attackspeed / damage / crit chance / range.
So why am I still recommending this, despite spending three paragraphs describing why I don't like it? Because that's all the bad stuff I could think of. Everything else is great and just like it should be - you won't be bothered by anything else. It's not perfect, I doubt anyone will think back fondly to their time with this game in 10 years. But it fills the role of a challenging coop experience that was worth playing once a month with friends on a couch.

I tend to look twice before I buy a game made with RPG Maker, since the production value can vary greatly from experience. This title was a bit of a special case though, since it played more like a linear novel than a traditional RPG.
First of all there are no combat scenes, and by extension, no level ups to speak of. There is an inventory of sorts, but what you get is mostly linear to the plot progression. The game play lasts around two hours or so and there is a lot of talking involved, if visual novels are not your cup of tea, this won’t fare much better for you.
If you’re willing to look past the strange design choices, or the mediocre range of sprites used, you’ll probably get to enjoy the storyline as I did; which was a decent mix between the slice-of-life and supernatural genres.
Lastly, I regret to say that the game has zero replay value beyond the different endings, but it was memorable for the duration, no matter how short it was. I would recommend this to others, though only if you have nothing else to play on your backlog.

The absolute best aspect of XCOM is the sense that there’s never enough time or resources to do everything that needs to be done. Do you pull a trooper off of active duty to undergo psionic training or do you keep him out in the field where he can get better at his core skills? Do you spend your budget producing satellites to help locate UFOs or do you spend that same money producing interceptors to be sure you can shoot down the few UFOs you do locate? Every moment of XCOM is defined by these either/or decisions where every move involves some sort of sacrifice or compromise. When you combine that with the overall tone of the game, which emphasizes a DEFCON style countdown to a complete alien takeover, the whole experience is fantastically tense and engaging

When i first played this game, I had just finished watching The Walking Dead, and i thought i would look for an entertaining zombie game. I had heard the name Dying Light, and i knew it was a zombie game, so i downloaded it. I really didnt expect to have this much fun with it.
Graphics: Simply put, the game is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. The atmosphere, the debris, the dust gliding through the air. Everything looks very beautiful. While there are occasional lighting bugs, i can say with confidence that they are rare, and do not effect the game whatsoever.
Gameplay: A lot of games try to go for parkour in their game, because its "cool". Mirrors Edge comes to mind, and that game was fun. But then i remember games like Brink, that completely tanked, because the parkour just wasnt well done or well implemented. But this game does it fantastically. When running from rooftop to rooftop, it feels natural and extremely fun. And when you start leveling up, thats when you can really take advantage of the beautiful city that was created.
DLC: So The Following basically removes the free running aspect, and replaces it with cars. Normally, i wouldnt like it, since the free running was so well done. But i have to say, they really worked to make the car mechanic feel extremely good. It honestly doesnt feel like a DLC Mechanic. I can't say much for the DLC story, besides i dont like the ending
All in all, a great game, and i would reccomend this game to anyone

A short bit of DLC that hit the spot.  This is not a long game, this is not an Alan Wake 2.  It is a small adventure to burn through in a long night.  The original Alan Wake game had some issues, combat and running could be a pain, some elements were left over from previous builds, somethings just didn't work right together.  American Nightmare delivers a tighter experience.  Combat is given a boost with new enemies and new weapons, and running away is now an option.  Ammo and weapons stay with you, while there's many ammo depots with infinite ammo around, this at least means when you find a weapon you like you're not going to lose it for the next scene or segment.  Driving is gone.  The darkness don't talk nearly as much, they still say a few things, but gone are the long winded reciting the rules of the park.
The story is not for everyone, be warned, it is groundhog day over three maps, and its "style" is prevelant, there's a scene you'll see more than once where a song is playing over a satellite falling from space into an oil pump and then it all explodes.  It is a style I'm fond of, and really enjoyed here.  To me, it feels like more of Barry and his Little Monsters moment of covering himself in christmas and flood lights to battle the darkness.  Fun, silly, with a few touches of creepy.

The ultra short version is that it's a reskin of a reskin of a reskin.  In terms of controls, mechanics, missions, collect-a-thons, and playstyle its the same as any other FarCry game.  That may be good for you, that may be bad.  Frankly the "10,000 BCE" thing does nothing for the game, or the franchise, and it seems unclear whether one is meant to realize you're playing on literally the same map (Kyrat) as FarCry 4.  There's no music, everything is in subtitles, the missions are hum-drum at best, and the "clear bases, take towers, kill animals" mantra of FarCry seems - oddly enough - remarkably out of place in this prehistoric setting.  I guess what I'm saying is... there's so very little here that's new... and what is, isn't worth paying attention to.

A very enjoyable game with a simple concept, but deceptively complex, challenging and overall satisfying.
It borrows elements obviously from the collectible card game genre, but supplements it in a rogue-like package, reminiscent of Darkest Dungeon or Binding of Isaac, with replayable elements and singular dungeon runs.
The dungeon plays out like a draft-mode in a typical card game, with each encounter rewarding you with gold and a choice of cards to add to your deck, which grows over the course of the dungeon.  The addition of relics, vendors, and puzzles/other encounters make planning important, with encounters requiring strategy.
Definitely recommend this game if it looks interesting to you.

Older gamers that didn't know Quake was still played today, rejoice.
Younger gamers that may want to try their hands at something difficult yet fun, welcome. We need you blood; come and quench our thirst. Well, actually, the way Quake Live is made, chances are new players will get to play between themselves and mid-skilled players mostly so I guess I'll have to wait for you to escalate the skill cliff. But please do so!
So what is Quake Live? Some might say this is a Free To Play version of Quake 3 Arena. There is some truth to that and this is how QL was identified since its inception yet there is more to it. Q3A had mods, QL tries to incorporate them into the main game instead. Q3A had a large community running plenty of servers, QL has servers ran exclusively by id software with the option for subscribers to spawn their own customized using this infrastructure. Q3A had a one time payment, QL generates its revenues through a subscription system. It's worth noting that despite being Free To Play, QL is not Pay To Win (and it's a shame that both expressions have almost become synonymous today).
You might still wonder why you should play QL if you have Q3A. Well the main argument is kinda lame but I'm afraid it is true nonetheless : QL is overwhelmingly more populated than any other Quake at the moment. But there are reasons for that! For starters, it's easy to get into. You press the "install" button, you start the game, you create your account then you click on "Play Now" and you're set. You won't be told you don't have the right mod installed or you lack a specific version of a map. It's easy (but you can still spend some time tweaking your config if you want to). The same argument can be made about the default gameplay itself and this is where things get somewhat controversial. Purists say the recent changes made to make the game more welcoming to newcomers are a travesty. While I agree that the new default settings are inferior for us experienced players, I'm still open to the idea that new players will have it easier and have more fun that way. You can be sure I will still be there in the servers running the classic settings, waiting for the courageous survivors who defied the default ruleset and want some more. In any case, QL is still very unforgiving, given your opponents catch on your mistakes. The best thing we can hope for is a larger playerbase which will allow tighter skillmatching and a better experience overall for everyone.
For those who don't know Quake 3 Arena or Quake in general, the above paragraph is probably kinda meaningless. Let me list some important aspects of Q3A/QL which make it a good game :
- Fast paced. Well, I guess if you like taking it slow and camping in bushes with your sniper riffle in other games it's cool for you, but you're missing out on something!
- Simple rules. Anybody can understand the objectives very fast. You know you have to kill more than you die in a duel. It's nothing hard to conceptualize.
- Diversity in the weapons. Yep. It's not all a thousand variations of machine-guns, handguns and rifles. Unreal Tournament is arguably superior to Quake in this field but it's still worth noting.
- Vertical gameplay. It may sound kinda stupid but this axis is a lot more in the typical map design of an Arena Shooter like Quake and it's a lot more fun this way.
- Great movement system. Easy to use (WASD), hard to master (and it's so satisfying to fly around the map at high speed).
- Gameplay depth. This one doesn't necessarily apply to every gametype but it is the most important point in my opinion. The game is old yet there's still room to improve for EVERY player. If you think Quake is all about shooting down enemies without thinking, you couldn't be more wrong. Sure, aim is part of the game, but you need to deal twice as much damage as your enemy if he has twice your health/armor because he controls the map better...
tl;dr It's a good game and with the recent changes everybody should be able to get some kills and fun. Let's just hope you can have fun without winning every match, because we can't all be winners and chances are against newbies in that field.

This is a game with a lot of potential, but I feel the game is way too repetitive. There are only five levels in this game, and once you go through the same level two or three times, you've seen all the level has to offer. Sure, there may be a door on the top instead of the bottom due to procedural generation, but it's very easy to get sick of going through the same level over and over and over and over again.
The first level is fairly easy once you power up your blacksmith, but the problem is you have to keep repeating the level even if you die on level two or three. I guess this is what some people want though, right? I mean, this is what Rogue Legacy does. I just feel the game could have been way better if it had more levels and didn't reset you back to the goblin castle and forest every time you die. The game just doesn't feel satisfying. Instead of using procedural generation to augment content, the developers used procedural generation as a replacement for content. I mean, there's only five levels and dying and being pushed back to the same level you've already seen countless times feels punishing not difficult. This game would have been SOOOOOO much better if it was built like Castle Crashers instead of Rogue Legacy.
Difficult vs punishing:
Before you pick this up. I STRONGLY suggest you think about whether this game is your thing or not. Remember, this game only has FIVE levels and once you beat a level two or three times, it's pretty repetitive. I have way more time invested in the game than what it says. I play offline with my friend and I guess Steam doesn't track that.

There's not really that much to be said besides that. It's another Tropico, and it looks and feels very much like its predecessor. You build a city, you find out if you'll win the election, and then you win the game.

Though nothing can compare to the original Company of Heroes Saga, CoH2 does its job of bringing in the WW2 RTS for its second installment. Be warned however that Company of Heroes 2 differs quite a lot from its predecessor in terms of play style and over all feel. In Company of Heroes 2 you change up the Command Trees for Command"ERS" Abilities. The points you earn slaughtering your enemies and or capturing points is instantly spent on a predetermined skill list as dictated by your Commander choice at the beginning of each match. Though there are quite a few Commanders to pick from, most are similar in their given abilities and just appear at different tiers. Unfortunately as mentioned in other reviews, this game does have a shop in which you can purchase certain Commanders outright with USD or whatever your curency. (I for one just did the digital upgrade and don't see myself purchasing many additional Commanders) I also felt that the Commander's abilities were lack luster and gimmicky. Another thing to note on is that during the "winter" maps you have to micro manage your soldiers near fires or else they can, and will become Reichsicles.
Being a fairly competent CoH 1 player I felt that the combat and flow of each match was very familiar and still very much enjoyable. Overall I would give this game a HUGE thumbs up and would recommend it to any RTS fan or CoH veteran. Is the game different from CoH1? Sure, but I do not agree that it is not worth a playthrough especially if you were a fan of the original game.
Overall Feel - 10/10 - It felt like I was playing a new installment of the franchise and the new levels are enjoyable!

Single Player - 8/10 - Not much of a genre changing attempt here as most RTS campaigns are highly scripted events.
I hope this little review gives people a positive spin on the immense atmosphere of "ITS A FAIL GAYME!!!!" and gives you as a returning or new player to the Company of Heroes franchise a better idea of what to expect going into this game.

I ask the question, what is a mystery game with no mystery?
The answer is Greyfox.
Okay, let's break this down one point at a time.
GAMEPLAY:
You spend the entire game walking around trying to find out how to progress the story, usually by doing menial busy work, like buying grapes... really? Grapes?
I would talk about all the different gameplay mechanics in this section, but there is literally nothing on display here.
Not a thing.
STORY (SPOILERS):
When you fall asleep in this quiet suburban retirement town, you are met with an enigmatic woman who beckons you to gaze into a nearby mirror. Turns out, you're old now, if this is part of some strange dream or not is never explained. One might think that the ambiguity is intentional, to leave such a thing up for debate or discussion. Mind you, the game never beckons the question, so does it really matter? Probably not.
You step into the shoes of four of the town's old timers, each one leading a different life and having thier own internal struggles. You might, for a second, think this to be an interesting affair, right? Not a chance.
The characters you step into the roles of are really uninteresting, and the main character doesn't learn anything between here experiences, causing her to still ask stupid questions like "What's going on?" and "Why am I old?"
By the end of each miniature storyline, you are asked if you want to kill the character you've taken control of, or let them live the rest of thier (probably dwindling) days.
This choice is just there for an arbitrary good/bad/neutral ending system.
My point is, the story is lack lustre and not interesting in the slightest. None of the characters really grabbed me, and the main plot points were predictable.
SOUNDTRACK:
Drab, unappealing, worth muting.
Not much else to say here.
VISUALS:
The artstyle is... inconsistent.
It's a mix between standard RPG Maker assets and visuals that, one could assume, were made by the developer. If the entire game was just one or the other, the game would look.. better? I mean, better isn't saying much, but it's saying
You can tell the developer just traced over stock photos to create the "art" for the game. Tip for the future: Get an artist, it'll help set the tone of your game visually and keep the artstyle consistent.
WRITING:
Weak attempts at comedy and drama, and a distinct lack of knowledge of adult concepts, like moving out of town, or finding a place to live. If those topics were handled better, the writing would've been that much more bearable. As it is right now, I wouldn't recommend or commemorate this game for its writing.
FINAL VERDICT:
A lack of mystery, weak writing, a flimsy story, unimpressive visuals, and a drab soundtrack leaves this game with nothing to offer, even for the CDN$1.00 price tag.

Ever since I saw the movie "Cave of Forgotten Dreams" where Werner Herzog takes the viewer on a rare trip into a cave found recently in France that contains 30,000 year old cave paintings, I have wanted to experience what it may have been like in the stone age, when the labyrinth of this world was barely known and where animals were the biggest threat to your welfare. Far Cry Primal seems to have captured it better than any game before it and with a familiar interface.
Far Cry elements are obvious, the familiar stealth-o-meter is there as is the grappling hook (eventually), you ride animals instead of driving vehicles, capture and light bonfires instead of capturing and deactivating transmitters on radio towers. You will hunt and skin animals just as before but a lot more and your quarry is bigger, less familiar, teeth longer.
You eventually become a beastmaster where you tame all sorts of predators to work for you. You will command an owl to do reconnaisance, call in a cave bear to unleash remote death by claw and you may even send in a badger to do tasks under the noses of the enemy. You will have a living arsenal to command and pet.
The languages spoken feel real and you will think you can speak them since they are open captioned. There are friendly  and unfriendly tribes and as you capture prisoners, some will work for you and teach you their secrets and technology.
It appears that it used the same map as Far Cry 4, hard to tell from the ground but in map mode it is obvious. This did not bother me, rather it served as a reminder of the many hostories of the same land we live on now. The Flora and Fauna are quite different than in FC4 and far more plentiful and dangerous.
The Dunia engine runs well on modest machines but give it some horsepower and it becomes nearly photographic.
All in all it is a worthy and important addition to the Far Cry story and I will finish this like I have everything else in the series. And if you, dear reader, are human you should rent and see the movie "Cave of Forgotten Dreams".

Older gamers that didn't know Quake was still played today, rejoice.
Younger gamers that may want to try their hands at something difficult yet fun, welcome. We need you blood; come and quench our thirst. Well, actually, the way Quake Live is made, chances are new players will get to play between themselves and mid-skilled players mostly so I guess I'll have to wait for you to escalate the skill cliff. But please do so!
So what is Quake Live? Some might say this is a Free To Play version of Quake 3 Arena. There is some truth to that and this is how QL was identified since its inception yet there is more to it. Q3A had mods, QL tries to incorporate them into the main game instead. Q3A had a large community running plenty of servers, QL has servers ran exclusively by id software with the option for subscribers to spawn their own customized using this infrastructure. Q3A had a one time payment, QL generates its revenues through a subscription system. It's worth noting that despite being Free To Play, QL is not Pay To Win (and it's a shame that both expressions have almost become synonymous today).
You might still wonder why you should play QL if you have Q3A. Well the main argument is kinda lame but I'm afraid it is true nonetheless : QL is overwhelmingly more populated than any other Quake at the moment. But there are reasons for that! For starters, it's easy to get into. You press the "install" button, you start the game, you create your account then you click on "Play Now" and you're set. You won't be told you don't have the right mod installed or you lack a specific version of a map. It's easy (but you can still spend some time tweaking your config if you want to). The same argument can be made about the default gameplay itself and this is where things get somewhat controversial. Purists say the recent changes made to make the game more welcoming to newcomers are a travesty. While I agree that the new default settings are inferior for us experienced players, I'm still open to the idea that new players will have it easier and have more fun that way. You can be sure I will still be there in the servers running the classic settings, waiting for the courageous survivors who defied the default ruleset and want some more. In any case, QL is still very unforgiving, given your opponents catch on your mistakes. The best thing we can hope for is a larger playerbase which will allow tighter skillmatching and a better experience overall for everyone.
For those who don't know Quake 3 Arena or Quake in general, the above paragraph is probably kinda meaningless. Let me list some important aspects of Q3A/QL which make it a good game :
- Fast paced. Well, I guess if you like taking it slow and camping in bushes with your sniper riffle in other games it's cool for you, but you're missing out on something!
- Simple rules. Anybody can understand the objectives very fast. You know you have to kill more than you die in a duel. It's nothing hard to conceptualize.
- Diversity in the weapons. Yep. It's not all a thousand variations of machine-guns, handguns and rifles. Unreal Tournament is arguably superior to Quake in this field but it's still worth noting.
- Vertical gameplay. It may sound kinda stupid but this axis is a lot more in the typical map design of an Arena Shooter like Quake and it's a lot more fun this way.
- Great movement system. Easy to use (WASD), hard to master (and it's so satisfying to fly around the map at high speed).
- Gameplay depth. This one doesn't necessarily apply to every gametype but it is the most important point in my opinion. The game is old yet there's still room to improve for EVERY player. If you think Quake is all about shooting down enemies without thinking, you couldn't be more wrong. Sure, aim is part of the game, but you need to deal twice as much damage as your enemy if he has twice your health/armor because he controls the map better...
tl;dr It's a good game and with the recent changes everybody should be able to get some kills and fun. Let's just hope you can have fun without winning every match, because we can't all be winners and chances are against newbies in that field.

is a single player card game with roguelike elements – this means that every run is procedurally generated and you only have one life to complete the game (just like
,
, among others). The most impressive aspect of this game is that, even though there’s a lot of RNG involved, everything is very balanced. Also, this is one of the best Early Access games you can find, and it’s already playable (and beatable) and I haven’t found any bugs yet.
During your journey through three major areas, you’ll find about 50 different enemies, 200 unique cards and 100 special items. The navigation through the map works in a similar way as
, and you can choose what is the best path according to your needs at the moment. You can clearly see where are the monsters encounters, elite monsters fights, merchants, treasures, a campire for resting or upgrading your cards, and an unknown spot that can result in any of these encounters or can take you to a unique ‘risk vs reward’ choice you need to make – these ones usually grants great buffs or terrible curses.
The mechanic that sets apart Slay the Spire from other single player deckbuild games is the discard mechanic, that works in a different way than usual – at the end of your turn, you can’t keep the unused cards in your hand; all remaining cards are discarded. But don’t be afraid, this is actually a good thing, since when you don’t have more cards to draw, your discard pile becomes your draw pile. Also, this takes the player out of his/her comfort zone as he/she needs to be creative about what the next move will be. It’s worth mentioning that after every fight, you can choose another card (from randomly generated options) to include in your deck, and on some events, you can delete unwanted cards from your deck.
Developed by the indie studio
for two years before entering Early Access,
is a joy to play, and can even please players that are not used to card games and/or roguelikes. I believe that the price asked is very fair, since the game is already very polished, replayable, beautiful, and fun. Since its random nature and procedurally generated content, this is one of those games you can play forever.

Like a sequel granted with its expectations, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation lives up it's name  by giving us more lore, more content, more
than its older sister counterpart.
Being more shy and diligent than her older sister, Re;birth 2 brings a more serious story comparing to the adventure hero archetype of the first series. There are more Chirper Events, more systematic built, more progressive than the first game, but in the end, both games have the same line of heroic quest, saving Gamindustri. (Btw, you get to have 4 people on the field at the same time. 4 People, how cool is that!?)
However, contrasting its older sister, there is a bad ending, (although you will not encounter it simply) and we need to replay the game at least once (and work harder) to experience the full extent of the contents the game brings. Some research or experiments may be needed to fulfill this requirement, simply playing the game wasn't enough.
The only thing that doesn't fit in is that the Chirper Events occur doesn't match the hassle and busy mood the game proposed. Other than that, there are too many Chirper Events piling up on a certain point that we may get tired of reading it through. Blanc, Vert and Rom might enjoy this, but I'm pretty sure NepNep & Ram doesn't, since they prefer to smash and bust the concrete of those buildings with evil intentions.
Comparing to the first game, some of the map designs were unoriginal. But most of it feels like having its own backstory from its design, like epic, ya know. It's maps were more structured than the first game.
Music is a blast! (If you aren't comparing with the first game, mood is different, less action, more atmospheric) The music were refined as if it was designed for an older action gamer audience, its composed of more structured roots than its randomness.
Characters design and progression were original, pretty well set and preserved from the first game. Nothing much to say here other than the game adds more beloved characters to vanquish the monsters with!
This review may sound critical, but the game is awesome as much as the first game, like sisters, both have different sets of cognition, and I love both of them. (But NepNep is still the best.) If you enjoy the first series and gameplay style, you will truly enjoy the second.

Sasha Baren Cohen starred in the 2012 movie, The Dictator.
Tropico 4, is basically stepping into the life of General Admiral Aladeen.
You play as one dictator from a variety of historical/fictional south american dictators, and set out to create an Tropical Island paradise as you see fit. The game is a sort of mix between the tried and true city building simulator genre made popular by sim city, and strategy games such as Civilization. This is unique, and puts tropico a step higher than other city simulators. The game is also inviting to history buffs as well. Taking place during the cold war, elements such as Military coups, juntas, nuclear proliferation, taiwan's independence, the bikini atoll testing, Nixon, and other people and events are mentioned. The game is quite charming overall, you'll be laughing at several political pundits, witty humor, absurdity of your advisors, and the caracterization of certain ideologies.
But let's cut to the quick.
Tropico is as follows
City sim with heavy political elements
You must juggle relations, and policies, as well as an army and a budget
graphics are decent
The sound is incredible
Lovely  soundtrack, with great voice acting.
Small spanish grammatical errors
The gameplay is fluid, full of replay value, and fun.
9/10 would reccomend.

Lethal League is a 2D unique fighting game that has several similarities to other fighting games and even non-fighters. and has a unique gameplay style consisting of a single dodgeball that can be comboed. Other than that gameplay mechanic, the game itself is quite similar to Super Smash Bros. since the character moveset functions identical to it and the percentage/launch speed goes to the ball instead of the player, and the Stock/Time mechanic is still there, but instead uses rounds similar to other fighting games like Mortal Kombat or Street Fighter. The game has a special bar that functions like the PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale one since it increases while doing direct hits. The small but varied roster consists of iconic characters with there own unique gameplay styles and special moves. Maps are all very similar but have different height and width, but no real stage hazards. The soundtrack is a love/hate thing and is really just based on your taste of music. The art-style is nothing special and unique, but combined with the soundtrack, it feels like playing a fighting game based off of Jet Set Radio. However, the lack of content in this game is not really worth the price considering the low ammount of characters, stages, and things to unlock in this game. Overall, this is a peculiar but decent indie fighting game that should be bought when on sale, because of it being a bit overpriced for what it's worth.
Verdict: 7/10 "...a peculiar but decent indie fighting game that should be bought when on sale..."

A simple premise, a very fun game. Lethal League puts you in control of one of multiple fun characters, playing a mix of dodgeball / squash against others. Each character has its own style and personality, making it fun to test them out. Also, special moves provide you with flashy high-powered attacks, sure to impress (or more accurately depress, if successful) your buddies.
As a personal opinion, the game is best played locally against friends, something which will likely result in a lot of fun & mayhem. There is of course the option to play on public servers, but it can take a while to find a match, especially with a good connection (with lag and connection issues being commonly reported problems).

Though nothing can compare to the original Company of Heroes Saga, CoH2 does its job of bringing in the WW2 RTS for its second installment. Be warned however that Company of Heroes 2 differs quite a lot from its predecessor in terms of play style and over all feel. In Company of Heroes 2 you change up the Command Trees for Command"ERS" Abilities. The points you earn slaughtering your enemies and or capturing points is instantly spent on a predetermined skill list as dictated by your Commander choice at the beginning of each match. Though there are quite a few Commanders to pick from, most are similar in their given abilities and just appear at different tiers. Unfortunately as mentioned in other reviews, this game does have a shop in which you can purchase certain Commanders outright with USD or whatever your curency. (I for one just did the digital upgrade and don't see myself purchasing many additional Commanders) I also felt that the Commander's abilities were lack luster and gimmicky. Another thing to note on is that during the "winter" maps you have to micro manage your soldiers near fires or else they can, and will become Reichsicles.
Being a fairly competent CoH 1 player I felt that the combat and flow of each match was very familiar and still very much enjoyable. Overall I would give this game a HUGE thumbs up and would recommend it to any RTS fan or CoH veteran. Is the game different from CoH1? Sure, but I do not agree that it is not worth a playthrough especially if you were a fan of the original game.

Multiplayer - 10/10 - Not a surprise here. Every match I played was different and enjoyable.
Single Player - 8/10 - Not much of a genre changing attempt here as most RTS campaigns are highly scripted events.
I hope this little review gives people a positive spin on the immense atmosphere of "ITS A FAIL GAYME!!!!" and gives you as a returning or new player to the Company of Heroes franchise a better idea of what to expect going into this game.

Here are some things that I love about
:
Gameplay -
is a war game, plain and simple. There are about six classes to choose from in each of the respective four armies, and playable Heroes such as Luke Skywalker and Boba Fett are available. This title also allows players to engage in vehicular combat, even hosting maps for dogfights in space against two rivalling fleets. Described earlier, there are several game modes similar to that of the
games, though
has a unique game mode known as Assault, where Heroes from both the Good and Evil spectrums of the Star Wars films battle against each other. Overall, the game balances very well between aerial and ground combat, and evolves into a truly unique experience over multiplayer; unfortunately, the company that originally hosted the dedicated servers for
, GameSpy is no longer operational, so other means of multiplayer are required on the PC port.
Game Modes - In Campaign Mode, you mirror the Star Wars trilogy while playing as this group of soldiers as they influence the structure of the story that fans of only the movies know and love; this concept is similar to
in which the character Kyle Katarn is the one who was said to steal the Death Star plans for the Rebellion. Unlike the other Star Wars games such as
and
,
maintains a focus on a specific group of Stormtroopers-rather than a single individual-infamously known by fans of the extended universe as the 501st, or Vader’s Fist. The Campaign introduces gameplay unique to the rest of the game in that it is objective-based, contrary to the usual skirmishes. For example, instead of a player dropping into a battlefield without an pretense as to what to do and why they’re fighting, the player is briefed on the purpose of the mission beforehand to perform a specific task such as protecting a Command Post for a given amount of time, or to locate a driver for a downed AT-AT that requires services.
Galactic Conquest Mode is a change of pace, as players strategically maneuver battleships across a large map in an attempt to overtake all territories. This game mode features out-of-battle unit purchasing as well as upgrades that allow the player to determine how they want to progress in an all-out war  against a rivaling army; the opposing force depends on which era of the Star Wars universe you are in, and pits either the CIS against Clone Troopers or the Empire versus the Rebellion.
Don’t want to worry about progressing through the story in Campaign Mode or strategically planning your way through Galactic Conquest? Give Instant Action Mode a go! Skirmish is exactly what it sounds like: you pick the game mode you want to play-between Conquest, Hunt, 1- and 2-Flag CTF, Space Assault, Assault, and Space 1-Flag CTF-and go from there. There are various settings for each, as well as playable Jedi/Heroes.
Class System - Like
, this title has multiple unique classes that operate differently. Every class has their own unique appearance, primary and secondary weapons, statistics, and secondary equipment. For example, the Engineer class is much quicker due to his primary weapon being a shotgun. This class has a low rate of fire and a quick land speed, and is meant to splice into or repair vehicles with their Fusioncutters; it is played like a support class in most instances, but can easily clear singular enemies without a problem. The Engineer is also equipped with Detpacks-which are detonated remotely-and health and ammo dispensers.
TL:DR - I had planned to write about weapon similarities between this game and the movies, as well as other topics, but if I had to talk about everything that is good about this game I would be typing for days. As you can tell from the above quote and through each of the screenshots, the
series does not look as polished in comparison to modern titles. However, this is just one of those games that stands the test of time with its amazing feel and fanatical impression. If you are a Star Wars fan, this title should
be passed up; if you are a
fan, this installment to the series will not be forgotten. Thanks for reading.

I DO recommend Far Cry Primal, but only with a bundled set of disclaimers, caveats, and concessions. Let's cover those first...
1) Ubisoft/Uplay. An understandable dealbreaker for many gamers. You have to be signed in to Uplay and Steam to play, even though Uplay is a useless ghost town everyone hates. But Ubisoft doesn't care. Because they're Ubisoft. Being THE WORST is just what they do. Sometimes I try to imagine what the Ubi offices must be like, and when I do, I always envision a bunch of unregistered sex offenders sitting around in cubicles chomping their own sun dried feces.
"Yo, bro, you wanna bite of my mookie stick?"
"Naw, bro, I got a peanut allergy, I best chomp my own."
So, instead of drowning this collection of human detritus in the nearest bathtub or waterlogged old tire, you have to give them $60. Assuming you possess a human soul, this will make you feel dirty. #foreverunclean
2) The core game, played on default settings, is just another crummy, shallow, hand hold-y Far Cry game. If you've played one, you've played them all. The spear and the dingo won't change that.
3) Technical issues abound. From what I can surmise, Primal inherited some pretty massive frame rate and memory leak problems from Far Cry 4. My rig overpowers Primal by miles, and yet there have been many times when I could only play for half an hour, before crippling frame rate issues forced me to restart. Sometimes I'd make it all the way to a couple of hours, but most of those forced resets landed in the 45 to 75 minute zone. Ubisoft was, of course, too busy a'chompin' to offer any tangible assistance, despite my requests for help. Luckily, I was saved by a kid on youtube, who had posted a video about how to tweak the problems away in the .ini and nvidia control panel. That was a complicated hassle in its own right, but I was lucky enough to have a set up very similar to the one in the video, and in the end, it did fix my issues. Completely. There's no gaurantee that's going to work for you, but, hey, feel free to utter a prayer to whatever gods you worship and take the leap, if you're feeling frisky.
And now you say, ok, Third, I get it, and I'm still potentially willing to navigate this circus of failure if there's a fun game on the other side of it, where I get to run around as a cave man!
And I say to you, excelsior!! For those that survive the many trials of the feces chompers can find something very special at the end of their stinky, half broken rainbow.
In Survival Mode (which was added post launch), with almost all of the interface turned off, Far Cry Primal becomes a fascinating and unique experience. It's just you and the wilderness.
You have to eat, and sleep and stay warm. It's survival-light, really, but that's the correct setting for what's going on here. Unlike many of the true survival games, where survival mechanics overwhelm everything else, Primal's realism has a much lighter touch. The food and shelter considerations only add to the organic feeling of being there, among the Wenja (your tribe), without ever hijacking the experience.
Organic. In almost every circumstance, organic is what Primal does best. The combat, for example. In a game with a spear, a club, and a bow, the combat is never going to be the centerpiece. And it's not. Fighting feels functional, at best. I find that accurate. You're a bunch of primitive hunter/gatherers, not ice age warlords, and the combat reflects the fact that you're using primitive hunting tools to engage in warfare, at the times where warfare happens. The big game changer of interpersonal conflict is not a grand contraption like a massive rocket launcher, or the guidance lens for an orbital laser array, but, simply, fire. Good old fire. It's what keeps the wolves at bay.
In this case, literally. All of the conflict in Primal takes place on a steep incline. A couple of wandering tribesmen are easily dispatched with a few jabs of your spear. Encounter a little pack of fussy dingos and they are likewise fodder. In these types of fights, the game can seem too easy. But add just a few more tribesmen, or substitute a trio of wolves for those three dingos, and you've gone from academic to intense. Add a village. Meet the wolves at night, in unfamiliar terrain, far from the nearest campfire. Now we're all the way to overwhelming, and we haven't even reached the game's true leviathans: big animals. You don't want to make them angry. A wooly rhino or a bear will come down on you like an angry mountain. I've never been killed faster than that time I thought it would be a good idea to shoot an arrow at a moose. The hooves were real. It was like being the floor at Riverdance.
Luckily, most of the animals are only hostile if you mistreat them, and most predators can be tamed, assuming you can isolate them from their pointy friends, and you've been keeping up with the homework at wild kingdom charm school. The taming is a lot of fun, if vaguely reminiscent of pokemon. Tougher animals need to be worn down before you bait them, but once you get them interested in the free snack, it tends to go pretty well. A lot of the joy in Primal comes from these furry friends. They're fun to pet. And since you've got the interface turned off, they're also vital to exploring safely, as their growls and yelps provide a kind of sketchy biological radar. It's another great example of how beautifully organic the experience of playing Primal can be. Correctly optioned, you're never looking for an icon, or following a trail of magic waypoint lights. You're being there, in the forest, scanning foliage for danger, listening to your companion for clues, listening to the myriad calls of the wild around you, deciphering what feels like a breathing world on its own terms, in its own language. It's a wonderful, unique experience.
There is a story, and it's a fairly simple one, befitting of the simple cave folk it concerns. There are a few named NPCs, and what they lack in numbers they make up for in sheer lunacy, most of the time. Without spoiling the game's scripted moments, I will simply say that they are a fairly memorable group of people, with similarly memorable interactions. There are collectibles to stalk, and rare beasts with different pet skills, better pet stats, or, just finer pelts. Your village can be upgraded and expanded as you find and recruit more Wenja. Aside from a few NPCs, they don't really interact, but they're fun to watch in an ant farm kind of way; the villagers without real speaking parts get up to all kinds of domestic shenannigans as they pursue their daily lives. And there is the owl, your friend and totem, who would be useless in the default game, had we not agreed to kill that interface and play survival mode. In our version of the game, where no icon pops up in your HUD to inform you of nearby people, quests, and locations, the owl, with his flight and keen eyesight, is an invaluable scouting tool. (And a lot of fun to inhabit and fly.)
I feel as though I've said almost everything that needs saying here, so I'll close with a few notes on killing the interface, because you probably want most of it turned off, but not all of it...
Leave your health bar on. If you turn your pet's health bar off, you can still tell when it's injured because you will have an option to heal it. Your health bar has no in-world equivalent, so if you turn it off, you have no idea when to heal yourself. Leave the environmental prompts on. If you don't, you'll spend ridiculous amounts of time on simple things like looting or trying to align for grapple throws. And finally, leave the thing on that tells you what you're picking up. You kind of need to know what resources you're accumulating, and even if you didn't need to know, it's still silly to suggest that you wouldn't know what you're putting in your own bag.
***A quick thanks/credit to my friend Matt, who coined "unregistered sex offender".

Slay the Spire is a turn-based card-collecting roguelike dungeon crawler, at least that's how I'd describe it.  Essentially you pick 1 of the available classes to start out in your adventure, with a basic deck of cards to get you going.  You then plunge into the depths of a dungeon, and will encounter monsters, Elite monsters, loot chests, randomized scenarios, merchants, campfires, and Boss monsters as you plug along, surviving as long as you can and collecting more cards and relics.  Between each "room" you have a map to view the tree of each series of floors, and you can plan your way through and choose between forks in the paths to either get some treasure, see a merchant, avoid/fight an Elite, etc.
Combat is simple, straight-forward, and user friendly - The game is 100% turn-based, so you have plenty of time to plan your moves to be as efficient as you can, and there are numerous buffs and debuffs that can be on you or the enemy - all of which can be hovered over to see their effects, which is super handy (non of that "what the ♥♥♥♥ is this green toxic buff on me what is it what's it doing????"♥♥♥♥♥♥you see in some games).  You take turns using cards to peform various actions, and you can see your enemies' "intent" for their turn, allowing you to prepare for an incoming attack or debuff.  Combat and the game ends when you die, if you survive and defeat the enemy; you continue.
There are several types of cards, I won't go into too much detail since it'd take 3 paragraphs to explain, but you got different skills you can use, attack cards, defense cards, and some situational cards.  There is a LOT of variety in cards, with some making a huge difference in how you want to build your deck.  Notes on the Store Page say more cards and things will be added, I'm really excited about this.
In terms of aesthetics; the game is quite pleasing to the eye.  The art is pretty, the characters and enemies look cool, the in-game sounds are accurate and high-quality, the music is catchy, and there's a decent amount of spell/card effects, so that when you do something cool, it actually looks cool (no visually dull combat here).
I picked up this game and immediately played it for 2-3 hours; I made it through 2 Bosses on my first run, died almost instantly on my second run, then completed the game (sorta?  You don't really "beat" roguelikes, there's still LOTS to do, I just made it through enough bosses to uhhhhh, do some spoiler-y stuff) on my third run.  I will definitely be playing this a lot more, especially if more content and classes are added.
This game is very well polished for an Early Access title; I found absolutely no bugs, and didn't experience a single crash.  The developer is obviously very competent.  It's also a very cheap game for the fun it offers.  I'm only 2-3 hours in, and I already consider my $15.99 purchase completely worth it.
I wish there were more games as good as this one!  Just need to get those other classes and more cards added ;)

If you invested more than 100 hours into the first Re;Birth and want to continue playing something exactly similar, get this one. Otherwise play something else.
Re;Birth2 reuses very much things from the Re;Birth 1. New Characters are few and the old ones have remained the same. They look, sound and even their moveset has remained exactly same. Of course characters are unlocked in a different order, so fighting in the early part of the game feels a bit different. However, most of the areas are new. Most new stuff is in music and voice acting (duh). New  music tracks are nice, but they are inaudible or will drown under every other sound because of  botched up sound levels. Unlike Re;Birth1, this one isn't fully voice acted and perhaps 10% of scenes are missing sound. Because of high reuse, Re;Birth2 doesn't really feel like a new game after Re;Birth1.
Re;Birth2 has its stand-alone issues and annoyances. Some game-design choises are really hard to understand. The biggest problem of the game is bad scripting and it is worsened by a very awful english translation. When the first game was absolutely nonsense and therefore great, this one is clichéd growthstory of timid a girl into the role of world savior. Also making piracy focus of the story doesn't really work. This is especially because without humour the topic turns easily into preaching. Good side of the script are new side characters. However making only fun of character's one-dimensional personality doesn't work on the fifth or sixth encounter.
Interesting feature of the game is that it has 4 unique endings. Two of those endings change storyline of the last chapter and one adds extra chapters. This means there is maybe 20 hours of (alternative/additional/hidden) game content.
However there are some huge issues considering the endgame and those chapters. First of them is that there isn't even a single hint in the game about how to obtain those endings. Because of that the player is forced to seek answers from the internet which is always negative thing for a game.
Second problem is forced NG+. In order to be able to view next ending, the game has to be completed again. Only inventory, character lvls and plans are carried over. This  means that all of the characters have to be recruited again and effectively most of the late game characters become useless. Also several hours of gameplay is required to reach areas already visited. In worst case you might want some material for a plan from some late area but are playing NG+.
In Re;Birth2 case NG+ doesn't add anything to the new to the game, it is only forced running through of underleveled enemies and it gets tedious. Second time might be manageable, but fourth forced playthrough is really a task... I watched quite much tv while playing Re;Birth2
In addition one really weird thing in Re;Birth2 is clothing. In Re;Birth1 vanity items were a huge feature; literally several hundreds pieces of clothing to make your girls prettier/original looking. In Re;Birth2 those same pieces of clothing cost 50 times more. With the price of a single hairpin you could often decent new weapons, armors and accessories for the whole party. And outfits... they cost more than final weapons of the main game.
About the DLC: The stuff in those is very very late game related (everything else is done related). Consider buing those only after you have played 100 hours or more and still want to start grinding exp.

Saints Row IV marks the point where the devs of the series decided to stop pretending at being a serious Crime Drama (ala Saints Row I and II), and instead embraced the absurdity of Saints Row III. The leader of the saints is the president, and his first year in office is the same year that the Earth is invaded and destroyed by aliens. What ensues is a vague parody of The Matrix, of The Matrix had been written by the Waynes brothers. But don't get me wrong! That's a good thing!
Saints Row IV is definitely a fun game for when you just want to speed through the city like a freight train, leap over a bank of buildings, punch a tank in the face, and curbstomp a few aliens. The physics and controls are almost identical to those seen in the last game, with the only real difference being the newly added science fiction elements and the fact that you basically have super powers. It's a great sandbox game with a so-so storyline, and it does deliver the occasional laugh (though many of the gags will have you rolling your eyes instead). The controls are a little awkward when you're speeding along at a hundred miles an hour or leaping across half a city block, but your powers generally allow you a fairly significant margine of error - so unlike in the previous games, you won't find yourself quickly overwhelmed when you're outgunned and outnumbered by law enforcement or rival gangs. At worst, you can always take to the skies or sprint away like a cheetah to buy yourself some time to regroup.
Story-wise, the game's not bad. It's all built on a fairly one-note joke, but it's an enjoyably shallow story ("Oh no, aliens!"). For long time fans of the series, there are a lot of enjoyably satisfying nods - a lot of familiar faces return from the previous installments, and a lot of story elements from the earlier games are revisited as well. Sure a few characters are insultingly sidelined, but it's still impressive to see how many of the old characters they managed to cram into the game (especially if you get the story DLCs). Even some of the dead characters from previous games show up (because it's all a virtual simulation, after all), and that leads to some pretty entertaining conversations between your allies.
But now for the down side. The game is great, but it gets old after a while. You start off overpowered, which is certainly fun, but you just get more powerful from there. Don't expect to ever be seriously challenged, especially after you've unlocked half or more of the power upgrades. Great for when you just want to stomp all over some badguys, but not great when you're trying to finish a twenty-hour game and things start getting incredibly repetitive after the first five hours. This is exacerbated by the fact that, unlike the previous games, there's really only one enemy "gang". In previous games there were always two or three themed gangs to mix things up with. In Saints Row IV there's only really one gang - the aliens. Get used to fighting them, because you'll be doing it the entire game (with the very occasional cameo from some other generic gangsters, mostly in the form of recycled skins from Saints Row III).
To that same extent, you still have a lot of game elements that were great in Saints Row III (customizable cars, customizable weapons, customizable gangs), but that are largely rendered pointless in Saints Row IV. Sure you can carjack a sweet sports car, pimp it out with a royal purple paint job and gold rims, and then speed down the streets at a hundred miles an hour - but why bother, when you can already run at a hundred miles an hour? Why bother pimping out your assault rifle when you can punch a guy through a building, or shoot explodo-beams from your eyes?
The story is entertaining, but it suffers from rapid tonal shifts. While I do appreciate the callbacks to Saints Row I and II, for example, there are entire story segments dedicated to re-exploring some of those grimdark stories - in the middle of a game about fighting aliens with your digital super powers. It's great to revisit the past of characters like Benjamin King and Johnny Gat, but those are characters who had bloody backstories that were spelled out in the first two games. It feels very strange when you suddenly go from shooting dubstep rays to agonizing over how this guy was shanked in prison, or that guy's girlfriend got tragically murdered by his archrival. And, like all the Saints Row games, there's a LOT of filler. You'll get about fifty or sixty missions throughout the game, but the vast majority of them are just time-wasting filler missions - races, time challenges, shoot'em up survival missions, and so on.
So, would I recommend the game? Heck yeah! But you need to be sure you know what you're getting into. This is not a gritty crime drama (despite the occasional grimdark moment) or even a Grand Theft Auto knock-off. At this point, it's basically Crackdown but with a rude sense of humor. If you're looking for something immersive and well-written with streamlined controls and cutting-edge graphics, then take a pass on Saints Row IV. But if you just want to have some fun, then throw on your shutter shades, queue up the dubstep, and give Saints Row IV a try!
