Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a spin-off/sequel to Alan Wake. A heads-up about the game and this review, Alan Wake's American Nightmare takes place after Alan Wake, and has spoilers for the first game. It really shouldn't be played until after the first game, and as such with this review I am going to be comparing it a lot to the first game, and will drop a few spoilers.
Alan Wake's American Nightmare takes place in Arizona, in a fictional town known as Night Springs. However, as we find out early on, Night Springs is not actually a solid place, but rather rather more like an illusion brought to life by the Darkness, and a town that can appear anywhere, just tonight it happens to be in Arizona. When we last saw Alan Wake, he was trapped in the Dark Place, and in American Nightmare he still hasn't quite escaped. Instead, he appears where the darkness goes, and in this case he has written himself into reality as a the hero to an episode of the TV series from the first game, Night Springs. He's done so to combat Mr. Scratch, who's called as such as trying to say his real name comes out like scratching noises. Mr. Scratch is Alan's doppelganger, who was seen briefly towards the end of Alan Wake. He's come into reality since, after Alan's disappearance, rumors of the author who went missing into the night has spread, and these rumors have taken on the form of Mr. Scratch, a psychopathic killer who wears Alan's face.
American Nightmare is even more focused on combat than the original game was, but the combat has seen a lot of improvements. It feels much more solid and fast-paced, on-top of the fact the enemy variety this time is much larger and weirder. There are even more guns, and they manage to feel more varied than the original game as well. This is all backed with still impressive lighting effects, and an overall sleeker look to keep up with the more sci-fi tones this game has.
However, with the improved combat comes a step-down of a lot of the charm the original game had. There's no full-on exploration sequences this time around, and the atmosphere is not nearly as immersive this time either.
Basically, there's a throw-up between improvements and downgrades. For one, the levels are now no longer linear, instead being more hub-like small open-worlds that you can explore, and generally are fun to as well. There are find-able manuscript pages, televisions, and radios like the first game, but they're more spread-out. There are also guns to unlock, and side-areas to explore just to really explore them. This is a welcome change of pace, especially for a much more combat-composed game.
On the other hand, the story is not nearly as interesting. Alan Wake spends most of the narrative chasing down Mr. Scratch, and interacting with a few different chicks that Mr. Scratch has managed to swoon. However, the story in AWAN really doesn't go much further than where Alan Wake ended off, and more elaborates on the ending of the first game rather than move past it, and as such really feels more like filler and sort of lacks climax, conclusion, or really any huge developments.
However, Mr. Scratch is a very enjoyable villain. He makes more of an impact than the antagonists of the first game, being deliciously psychopathic and charismatic, and dealing in twisted acts with a child-like glee. The televisions you can find with him are definitely one of the highlights of the game.
But then, in probably the biggest flaw for the game, and something really stupid, is that in the game's story you go through its three 'hub' stages three times each. The excuse is that Alan Wake is stuck in a time-loop, and time keeps on resetting itself so he has to start from the beginning again until he can break the cycle. What this means for gameplay is that there really are only three levels in the game, and each one is repeated three times. They do change things up, areas not previously available open up and different events happen each visit, but it still is a bizarre design decision.
Made even more bizarre by the game's wave-based horde-like mode. This mode is actually a lot more enjoyable than I thought it would be, and honestly may be more fun than the game's actual campaign. It's very frantic, tense, with an addicting risk-and-reward system to try and get high-scores in the mode's five different stages. And this is where it gets bizarre, as the 5 stages in this mode are completely different than the stages in the main game, hell some of the stages are actually larger than the main game's stages. On-top of this, you can actually see the Horde-mode stages in the background of the main story, and see the main story's stages in the background of the Horde Mode stages. Why these five other locations weren't added to the game's story to help keep things more varied is completely lost on me.
But the game's Horde Mode, known as Arcade Mode, is completely worth taking part in. It's inclusion is surprising, but not nearly as surprising as how well-executed it actually is.
For an arcade-like shooter, Alan Wake's American Nightmare is not bad at all for a spin-off. It's fun, fairly tightly made, and has some fun content to delve in. However, it also as a spin-off feels it misses the mark of what people loved about Alan Wake in several ways, and focuses on the elements that were less enjoyable. Given here, they definitely have been improved, but it strikes as an odd decision.
If you liked Alan Wake and want more of it, this is and isn't it. In some ways it retains the charms of the original game, but also doesn't quite have everything that made the original game charming. It is more fun strictly gameplay-wise than Alan Wake, but then it is arguable if that actually makes it more enjoyable overall as it misses what made the first game really enjoyable in many ways.
Basically, I cut it like this; The new stuff they introduce is well-done and appreciated, such as the open-world levels, Mr. Scratch as an antagonist, and the surprisingly fun Arcade Mode. The game focuses on combat, which was not the first game's strong point, but it pulls it off much better here, with better mechanics and a larger enemy selection. However, elements like down-time exploration moments, much of the atmosphere, and the narrative are mostly missing or much more limited. And the game is plagued by one big problem, repeating levels, which is made bizarre as the Arcade Mode has completely different levels the devs could of used that are even tied-in with the stories' locations.
But it's an enjoyable little romp, and an interesting spin-off that does expand more on the world of Alan Wake, while also improving over it in some ways. It isn't quite as good, but is enjoyable in its own way. If you like exploration, the locations are fun with multiple landmarks and sections. The music is still appropriate and moody, with a few-stand-out tracks. The voicing gets hammier, but it works with the sort of hammier tone of the game (being modeled after a parody of Twilight Zone and all).
Alan Wake's American Nightmare is not the sequel fans may clamor for, but is an enjoyable arcade spin-off.

Excellent game. It has replay value and will take some time to finish.
The story and protagonist can be a little cheesy and predictable at times, but it's certainly not bad overall. The game is lots of fun and is visually pleasing. 8/10 and worth it. The developers put a lot of effort into this game. Below is a more detailed review of the pros and cons.
Pros:
- Zombies: Lots of zombies that get tougher as you get stronger. Until later levels, you will always be wary of the threat a horde of zombies can pose.
- Story: there's a story here. Yay! It's not the deepest, but it will keep you motivated to keep going.
- Characters: there are a variety of characters with their own quirks in the game.
- Missions: lots of side missions encouraging you to explore the map of Harran. The map is vast and while it can take time to get from A to B, you will find it's actually fun to take a detour to get to the airdrop before the bad guys can.
- Gameplay: parkour to the core. There is a grappling hook that can help you get around, but leaping from rooftop to rooftop, kicking zombies off high places (THIS IS HARRAN!!!!) and dodging attacks is quite satisfying. You always have to be aware of your surroundings so you can escape or use it to your advantage.
- Level up!: You have three main skills: Agility, Strength and Survivor. There is a fourth one (Legend...wait for it...dary!) that unlocks when you max one of the others out. They help you slay zombies faster, dodge attacks, run longer, climb faster, regen health and generally be a better parkour badass. You can even be more stealthy by using zombie guts to camouflage yourself and take the zombies out one-by-one without alerting the horde.
- Crafting: Yes, you get to make your own melee weapons and augment them with different elemental effects. Who knew a battery and some power cables could electrocute zombies to death...
Cons:
- Optimisation: The original game wasn't as bad, but after the Enhanced Edition update, my GTX970 and core i7 2600 seem to be taking strain. When there are lots of zombies on the screen, even with everything set to its lowest, I expect the FPS to drop below 60, and it does. The game performs poorly on linux, so I had to install it on windows to be able to play it.
- Some glitches. The zombies sometimes stay stuck in a mannequin-like pose and don't attack for a bit. They're easy to kill, so I shouldn't complain, but stationary zombies are not undead. They're just dead.
- Skills: even though you can max out the skills, you'll find your strength skill shooting up quickly while agility is lagging a bit. Expect to be able to carve through hordes while running short of breath when trying to beat Rais's men to the air drop. Secondly, not all skills are valuable and you have no choice but to invest in a skill under a specific tree when you level up. There is no levelling up a skill, such as camouflage, to level 5 so you have to invest the next point in something you may never use. This creates characters that are all the same when all levels are maxed out.
- Being bitten: pretty early on in the game, you're bitten by a zombie which means you need Antizin to stop from turning. Problem is, your character never actually "needs" Antizin until crucial, scripted moments when he gets seizures. For some reason he never thinks to bring any antizin along while he is swinging around the city. You go from being Spiderman's zombie slaying clone, swinging from building to building, carving zombies in two to suddenly unable to effectively swing your weapon because "plot". It is frustrating investing in all those skills but never being able to use them when the story main storyline demands it.
- The Following: Enhanced Edition is a little pricey.
Cons aside, it's definitely a decent game. Grab it on sale, if possible.

This game has a lot of interesting ideas. It plays like an action RPG, and the worker-empire you build as you do lifeskills is cool and it really helped pull me into the game in the beginning. Unfortunately, the publisher has become increasingly grasping and desperate with the addition of more and more PTW mechanics.
I played through the main quest on a few characters, so I definitely got a few dozen hours out of this game before I quit. Why do I not recommend it then? Because a game like this, if it's good, can provide hundreds of hours of enjoyment without making you feel like you are constantly being nickel-and-dimed. As a publisher, when you optimize for revenue too much, your game ends up constantly taking players out of the experience by reminding them that they can reach for their wallet to make the boring parts less boring. Then, as a designer you have less incentive to make the boring parts less boring through actual game design. And that is what this game is: a boring grindy slog, and this is coming from someone who normally enjoys very grindy games.
Apart from the awful monetization, I can't fail to mention the gear upgrade system. Not only is it heavily dependent on RNG, but your gear will
when an upgrade fails. This means potentially dozens of hours where you not only fail to progress, but can actually end up weaker than when you started. This is unfun, and the reddit community has proven in several cases that many items have hidden stats that the player has no way of knowing, and it is often very counter intuitive. Imagine deciding you wanted to play a very offensive build, so you invest hundreds of hours getting high level (not even BiS) gear for your build and then finding out that defense items with no attack stats mentioned would have given you more offense than what you chose, being functionally better in every way. You would have chosen that gear in the beginning if you knew but now it's too late and you're stuck with that you have.
When people say the upgrade system is terrible in this game, they are not exaggerating, it really is that bad. The upgrade system is an evil nightmare, but if not for the monetization I would have persisted by saving up money and buying my upgrades from the market, even though the cost of high items on there is pretty massive.
The monetization is just so bad that I will never touch another game from Kakao the publisher or Pearl Abyss the developer. I can't trust companies that have so little regard for the experience of their users that they would release something like this. Even if they suddenly released a paid game with no microtransactions, I would expect them to shoehorn it in later after people have bought it, because, as I said, they have no regard for the user experience. They are the worst kind of game designers.
Edit: Thanks for the response Serenity. The unfortunate truth is that these concerns are in no way fresh news to Kakao or Pearl Abyss. Rather than listening, the most offputting aspects of the game have continued to get worse, even in patches as recent as this month with the addition of the ability to speed up workers by paying 20 pearls. Even removing that at this point is too little too late, because I have no confidence in the people making the decisions for this game. Their philosophy towards gaming and mine are too different.

One of the best, zombie-apocalpse game in Steam. An awesome blend of FPS and action w/ an addition of creepy, gore and horror. The Following - Enhanced Edition is two games: Dying Light and Dying Light: The Following. This edition fixed all the glitches from the original Dying Light game with added content such as an outfit pack and weapon pack. It's a single player game, but can be played multi-player via online up to four players.
-Shortcut Review-
A great, spiritual successor to the Dead Island series. Much improved on graphics, mechanics and playability. Storyline is short, but the sidequests, repeatable quests, and parkour challenges makes this game quite enjoyable. It's quite fun to play with others, however, it may take awhile for someone to join your game. Although playing against the Hunter is very hard, the gameplay is tolerable once skills are high and weapons are highest grade (orange). May remind you that parkour is the key to survival - will give you the urgency to climb and jump building to building in other, zombie apocalypse games.
-Full Review (Somewhat Spoiler free)-
The beginning is very challenging because it takes some time to get used to the parkour skills: one must find a place on the wall to grip, use crosshair to aim n press button to jump while holding on to the grab button and having aim in place with gamepad stick. Player will follow a level-up system that upgrades perks and abilities. This is forgiveable because the start is an (epilogue) or tutorial and acts as part of the storyline. Also, the game also gives some useful hints to evading zombies early on.
At first, it's somewhat difficult to find weapons and can be tough to defend with them because the weapons are the lowest-grade. They have a high breakability and also low attack power to kill zombies. They also require materials to repair them if found. As for the items like gauze and alcohol to make medkits, they are pretty easy to find and don't require much scavenging. I think it's great that there's no "overcumberance" when reaching the max capacity in storage bag. It just simply doesn't allow the player to gather anymore items. There's too many games out there with this nuisance.
The characters are likeable, even though, they're created in a cliche way. We have a typical, rugged mercinary, a naive, yet brillant engineer, his athletic and♥♥♥♥♥kicking of an older sister, a clueless leader, and a ruthless, dellusional villan. The voice actor, Roger Craig Smith (RE series), does a wonderful job with Kyle Crane - he keeps his character relatable with the audience by a running occurance whether he is doing right or wrong in his actions. Unfortunately, the writers made the character to be just another, war hero with vanilla morals. All of these characters are complimented by each other because they have to survive against a higher power and the undead. See how where this is going?
Overall, this game easily makes you forget about the horrors from Dead Island, literatly. Techland learned their mistakes from the DI franchise, regrouped their tactics and created one, badass of a game with this one. You can get it for a great discount on sale (Summer and Holiday sales) at $15, even though, this game deserves to be paid in full price. Thanks for reading!

-WARNING: THIS GAME MAY HAVE GAMEBREAKING PERFORMANCE ISSUES FOR YOUR MACHINE. RESEARCH ACCORDINGLY BEFORE PURCHASING-
The sequel to Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth1, but this time with Nepgear, Sister and Sister candidate to Neptune, as the protagonist.  The mechanics are very similar to the original game, but are different enough to feel fresh. Many characters that were included in Re;birth1 are back, along with several new characters.
Pros
Lots of improvements over the original, and you can still have a personal army of waifus.
-Loads of new characters, while still keeping (most) of the originals. (21+ characters if all are unlocked)
-More (English) voice acting than the original
-For most characters, voice acting quality is good (You will know the bad ones)
-More endings than the original
-Dungeon plans are simpler than the original (Original has giant webs of plans that make missing certain events easy.)
-Combat is very similar to the original, but provides enough to feel fresh
-Progression difficulty spikes are toned down a bit (In the original, you'd often have the grind heavily to fight the next boss, notably (Spoilers) Black Heart around chapter 2
.
-Story is trying to be a bit more serious, and even side characters are given a bit more lore
-4 characters to a party opens up a lot more strategies
-Dungeons feel larger, and the change dungeon plans give a lot more depth
-You find interesting items more often (original often gave boring items from treasures)
-Quest rewards are more interesting.
-You can gain little extra rewards through the use of "Stella's Dungeon", an unlockable in-game feature.
Cons
Mostly minor, except for performance problems. I'm mostly listing little pet peeves.
-PERFORMANCE PROBLEMS
-Odd technical glitches (World Map volume is incredibly loud for example)
-While most of the voice acting is good, bordering great, certain voice-acted characters are immersion breaking and downright cringy. (Dogoo and Killachines being the worst)
-Early on, it is very easy to get locked into a single party composition and not use other characters.
-Outfits for the sisters are fairly dull (So far, I can only get them from the shop, and they are just city-colored reskins of the default)
-Bosses are heavily recycled ((spoiler) An early boss, Underling, is recycled a painful amount of times. If memory serves, I've fought her at least 8 times, with little variety)
-Almost all the outfits obtainable require New Game+ items
-Many random information events give very little knowledge to the player, and are practically carpet bombed on you after some major events and at the beginnings of new chapters (You may have to spend 5-10 minutes going through them all, some of which are major character events)
Neutral
Things I feel people could feel one way or the other about
-Story is apparently an alternate-dimension side story...?
-(SPOILERS) Ending requirements are difficult to prepare for without prior knowledge.
--Conquest requires Nepgear to have a Lily Rank of 7 or less with all characters (Except Oracles?), and for all characters to be recruited before the last chapter (no prior warning).
--Normal ending can even be difficult to get if you have the requirements for another ending, which may require a New Game+ to get. (Normal ending is anticlimactic as sin.)
-Share management is a bit different from the original. Quests give more.
-Colosseum battles are harder
Overall a good game, but has a few frustrations, my biggest being the ending requirements (prior knowledge is required to avoid a forced New Game+).

I've been playing BDO off and on since it came to NA. Recently, I switched over to Steam after a long break away from the game. Currently in a love hate relationship with it, I've been back and forth with the idea of a positive or negative review. I've seen a lot of people making negative reviews but they only complain about the anti-cheat software. I've seen a lot of people make positive reviews but only drool over the combat gameplay. I'll try to be a bit more... fair. Grab a cup of coffee and prepare to read a long♥♥♥♥♥review.
Black Desert Online is a very unique MMORPG. It's character customization is among the best I've ever seen, only surpassed by the likes of a heavily modded Skyrim. It's combat style brings some new and refreshing mechanics, steering away from that boring "Tab 1, 2, 3, 4 DON'T STAND IN♥♥♥♥♥♥, 5, 6, 7 style of combat that many MMORPG's are built around. It also provides your typical professions you'd find in most other MMO's, fishing, "blacksmithing", farming, and some professions that don't exist in many other MMO's such as trading and hunting.
The ability to do all the professions AND without going to a trainer or being limited on how many you can learn at one time makes them a welcomed design. However, doing them is very different than you would typically do them in other games. In this, you instead hire workers, invest in nodes that surround major cities and towns, and send your workers to gather resources, then tell your workers to make an item. From merchant wagons to fishing boats, from armors and weapons, to refined materials or even trade crates. The options are almost limitless. You can even help your workers by gathering things yourself.
The combat system is very fun and unique, offering the ability to put most skills on a very small, very limited action bar, or to press button combos to activate skills. The animations that come with this combat is also very well done. The graphics are also among the best you'll find in an MMO, unfortunately they come at a price. Even on high end systems, FPS can and will drop into the low 20's in major cities, mostly due to over population of other players, the option to hide other players in said cities/towns would be a very welcome option. Sometimes you can't even find an NPC because so many players are surrounding it. Graphical "pop in" is also another major issue and kills some of the immersion when flora and shadows is just popping into frame as you approach. Despite some of these flaws, it looks fantastic, and it is, to an extent. However, with every positive this game has, there's a major negative that comes with it.
While BDO has appeared to perfect some areas of the genre, other areas, it miserably failed. PvP is one of those. Yes, I know, the hardcore PvP buttboys will hate what I'm about to say here, but it's true, and it just about ruins the whole game. Once you pass level 49 and hit level 50, you enter a permanent "flagged for PvP" state, where, you can and WILL be attacked at anytime, in any place outside of cities and towns, by other players. You have a choice when you hit level 49 whether or not you want to hit level 50. There is one MAJOR problem with this. Listen up devs, you need to be aware, because quite frankly, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you choose to stay at level 49, you miss out on a substantial amount of the games content. Areas you just can't go to because the enemy levels are too high, despite having an excellent gear score, you wont be able to compete much. Due to the level gap, your accuracy falls off, making it near impossible to fight in areas of a higher level. Also, awakening weapons/skills you can't access until level 56. Which brings an entire new page of extremely powerful abilities and a unique weapon that you'll never be able to use if you don't want to be forced into extremely unbalanced PvP.
That's the biggest problem with PvP. There is ZERO balance, yet they force you into it. People just one level higher, or with +10-20 AP/DP more can easily defeat you. Skill holds no place and only gear and level play a role in how "good" you are in PvP. PvP should have remained only in battlefields, and guild wars, or at the very least given us an actual PvP toggle that completely eliminates PvP for those of us not interested. Yet it's every where and prevents PvE content access. Not only that, but other players will harass and attack to prevent you access to certain quest areas, grind spots, resource nodes and even towns and cities.
Another massively huge failure is the "Marketplace" (auction house). The Marketplace was designed around preventing gold selling and real money trading, which is nice, but losing 35% of every sale, forcing users to buy the cheapest item, and a RNG bid mechanic that prevents users from buying anything until that bid is over... it's an absolute mess and it sucks. Let's touch on it a bit. The bid mechanic. So, when an item is placed on the market, it's up for bid by anyone. If 10,000 people bid on it, then RNG kicks in and says, one person can buy it. It's not a, "who offers the most money", but a "Whoever RNG decides is worthy". Also, forcing users to buy the cheapest. The biggest issue with this is, if 100 people are trying to buy the same "cheapest" item, then it comes down to who can click buy and mash the spacebar the fastest so you get it first. It's so impossibly difficult to buy popular things, such as Memory Fragments,  off the market because of this.
I do also have a huge issue with their "not-so-micro-transactions" and it's just that, not so micro. $40 for a non account bound, single character outfit does little more than showcase the "Asian Greed" we see in so many games coming out of Asia. It shows they care more about money than their product or customers.
My current review score will be negative for the time being. When the devs change a few mechanics, I will definitely give this a thumbs up.

TLDR, message to the devs.
Devs, why restrict your player base by forcing a mode that, according to polls and studies, only a rather small minority of players want to take part in? You may be happy with a million players, and you'd probably do quite well for yourselves. What if you had 2 million? 3 million? 5 million? You know why games like EVE Online has such a small playerbase? Because they force PvP. Some of the best, and most successful MMORPG's in the industry have optional PvP and in no way force it, nor lock PvE content behind it. World of Warcraft, Guild Wars 2, FF-XIV and many more, All MMORPG's that have a massive multi-million fan base, they all also don't force PvP. There's no reason to lock PvE content behind PvP, and no reason we can't have PvE servers, or at least an actual PvP toggle. Until you stop forcing PvP, and stop locking PvE content behind PvP, my score for this game will be negative.

Step 4:
Step 5: If the person who's item is up for grabs didn't go in with your all in, keep doing all in's until you get him to play your matching hand.

First impressions of this game looked promising, but expectations fall short and it turns out to be disappointing in terms of hype the creators of this game made it looked like in their description.
I’ve played many times both Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy VI, completed them several times as well, and to say that Greyfox is inspired in their style... seems a bit boastful in my opinion
Story
Your story begin at the controls of an unnamed female protagonist who just decides to up and leave, quits the job that she claims makes her miserable and moves to the small town of Greyfox, whose population mainly consists of old grumpy people. After doing a bit of exploring around town, talking to the residents, you come across a mysterious woman who talks about seeing life through someone else’s eyes, then she vanishes. Not thinking any further of this, you head to your room at the inn to turn in for the night.
As you wake up, you find yourself in a strange place with that mysterious lady. Your “heroine” is suddenly all wrinkled up and confuse about what happened to her. The mysterious lady will then ask you how you feel about old age, one of the main theme this game keep bringing up. Depending on your answer, you will taking be at the control of some of the resident of Greyfox, seeing what they see and deciding of their fates.
Design
As you will quickly notice, this game is pretty basic when it comes to a RPG maker spawn. A few element look like customized assets but there’s not too many of them. The town itself is small, but beautiful. Greyfox is the only area where you’ll be traveling into, aside for the little street map that precedes you entering the town, you’re boxed in there.
UI are kept to a minimum with only an inventory box, and an option to save and quit the game. There also a window to keep track of your cash, but given how little use it has through the game, its almost useless.
While this game is fairly short and easy to complete, it does offer multiple endings. Your actions throughout the game’s course will dictate which ending you will be getting. Seeing all the endings will require 3 playthroughs. Before you claim that it will be a daunting task to accomplish, just note you can see it all and obtain all the achievements in less than 2 hours. Your first run of the game might take you longer if you chose to fully explore and interact with everyone and everything, but after that, you can just go for the story triggers and finish this game in about 30 minutes or less.
As the author mentioned on the kickstarter page for this project, the concept inspiration came from their own life, living in a “retirement” town similar to what depicted in the game. What disappoints me is that this game could have been a great thing, it seem full of potential,  it touches on topics not often bought up in video games, but alas after playing through multiples times to get all the achievement, it felt lackluster.  The characters may have been inspired by real-life people, but here they felt generic and lacking depth. Each character could had a much deeper story, more events to unravel. Instead we just get treated to a point and click visual novel.
Gameplay
Greyfox is your non-combat flavor of RPG. So no random battles, grinding, dungeons or challenging boss battles. Instead you take control of four different town residents and guide them through their “tough” choice. By tough choice, i mean a decision between yes and no more oft than not. Do you put your avatar out of their misery by killing them off or do you let Father Time take care of it for you. Certainly brings a question of morality but given how bland and shallow they are scripted, you barely get any attachment to any of them. If killing them off meant to bring a shock value of any kind, it missed its mark by a long shot.
You can interact with just about any object found in the game which is good to see that a lot effort went into making this possible. If you’re looking to get all the achievement, you will need to check everywhere for hidden stuff. Some items found make getting some achievements impossible to attain unless you get them. Overall this might prolong the duration of your first run of the game, but ultimately  it acts like filler to give you something else to do in this short game rather than always going from point A to point B.
The effort put in this project is real, but somehow, it feels more like a PSA to raise awareness on how many seniors people can have it difficult in their old age, rather than a video game. It does a good job at this. Most people probably know an old scrooge who hates and is hated by everyone around him, or that crazy cat lady who just seems even crazier when she’s off her meds.
Final Thoughts
Regardless of what ending you get, it all seems like it was all a dream. The good ending sees you waking up in your bedroom to the sound of a blaring alarm clock. The bad ending sees you locked in the loony bin, perhaps because killing all these people in your dream snapped your sanity last straw. The so-so ending finds you in therapy with a psychiatrist who believes you imagined everything and the town of Greyfox might just be a figment of your vivid imagination and ups the dosage of your medication.
Regardless of its brevity, Greyfox did entertain me for a little while, if you like a short story game that doesn’t require to much thinking to get through, then you’d probably like this game. You don’t need to be a hardcore completionist to get all the achievements, a few might be a bit cryptic at first, but just in case you’re stumped you can always check out the guide in the community section.
With this in mind, I give this game a final rating of 6/10

Was on the fence about collecting this title for some time. Did the usual; waited for a sale to come around after all episodes were available. What to say?
As an avid reader of the books it is a very faithful recreation of the world of GoT. Many reviewers pointed out that there seems to be a 'parade of cruelty' to the game. This is a fair point - Characters you grow to care about are often killed with very little warning and your just left sitting there going "Jesus... this is brutal...".
This is keeping with the books (I do not watch the show on HBO as it feels more like thinly veiled murder porn than is my liking) AS far as telltale games go this is a very good one (I am slowly collecting then as and when they come on sale).
If you like the books, You will like this game. The voice acting is perfect. the settings are exactly as I had pictured them in my mind when reading the books and all the characters really ring true to the GoT universe. I really loved this game and played one episode at a time over the space of a week. The pacing was good and the different environments were challenging and beautifully rendered.
I have developed a real interest in the Foresters, The struggle against the Whitehill house is life and death for them and brutal, frustrating, an involving. If you can pick this series up on sale it is well worth getting and I would not hesitate to recommend it to anyone who has an interest in GoT or even other telltale type games. As ever I would advise that you wait till the season is complete and available before purchasing; mainly to avoid that anticipation/completion cycle which often leaves players waiting for the next instalment while simultaneously giving them time to vent their collective spleens about things in the completed episode that they really didn't like.
It is a really enjoyable story which has some really great highs which are often peppered with some crushing lows. When you get a chance to take revenge on a character that has slighted you it can be tempting to take it there and then. despite the clamour that your choices don't really matter, I would not agree. The over all plot points do need to link up from one episode to the next but you do make choices that will pre-empt  or cause things to happen in different orders.These choices will no doubt become much more important in season 2; Saving one main character to sacrifice another will have definite ramifications that can only be borne out in the subsequent seasons. I am being purposely vague here as I do not want to spoil it for you!!
I would recommend this game to anyone.

Slay the Spire’ is an addictive, challenging, and gratifying game that combines the best of “deckbuilding” and “roguelikes” into one tight package.
It's the perfect example of “easy to learn, hard to master”. You’ll enter the Spire as a neophyte pawing at cards and items that confuse and overwhelm you. Only by learning, adapting, and risking it all can you ascend to the peak as a master.
You will hate your enemies. You will hate your deck. You will hate this game. But for those brief moments of strategic glory, for the serendipitous card draws and satisfying combos, you will come back.
The Spire calls and you must answer.

I absolutely love this game, it has base building and turn based combat with your soldiers falling into four combat classes. When they earn promotions you can give them new skills in their specific skill trees and they even earn a nickname as they advance. The dlc adds two more specialised classes and a few new mission arcs to playthrough which can increase the replay value, though because the battles are randomised and so are the soldiers it does already have good replay value. If you want a real challenge you can play Iron Man mode, in which you only get one save slot, preventing you from reloading when things inevitably go belly up. It's a great game and well worth picking up.

Long story short. It's a revamped version of an old classic game. Not quite as complex, nor as unforgiving, but some decent solid turned based strategy. Class system gives a decent variety to your gameplay style as well. If you want a decent game to occupy your time and have some replayability if you want to do everything, this one will not disappoint. Especially since it's currently on a massive sale. I'd advise on picking up Enemy Within at the same time. It's the same game essentially except for numerous additions are made to a playthrough.

I feel like I need to start this review by stating that I don't normally enjoy RPGs, turn based games, or deckbuilders. I am a total FPS fan girl. With that being said, when asked to review this game my initial thought was 'Alright, so I'll stream it for about a half hour. People can see what it is about & then I can uninstall it and never play it again.' 30 hours of gameplay & 19% achievements unlocked later and I can't put this game down! There is this odd, hard to explain appeal to it. As you progress through the floors and sometimes narrowly escape permadeath, the euphoria you feel after slaying a boss with just 1hp left to your name blends perfectly with the fear & anxiety as you realize you must face your next challenger with minimal hp to depend on. Slay the Spire's aesthetics help transport you into this magically, terrifiying battle. The background music is pleasing, while not overbearing. Sometimes you almost forget it is there. The character "lines" are these adorable sound bites that you can't help but begin to anticipate joyfully. The art style is beautiful, full of understated details. I don't want to spoil anything for anyone as discovering just what this game was all about was part of the enjoyment. I will say that the developers have done an excellent job at creating something new & entertaining. This is not the type of game you will play for a bit & grow bored of!

EDIT: Finishing the game with Conquest Ending, completely changes my view on the game...
Being an RPG, this game is pretty average based on other more mainstream RPGs we have today. The game shines more so however in the characters.
If your a pretty big anime fan, or fluent gamer, this game is filled with references to popular animes, and video game-related products. The entire concept of the Hyperdimension series is four goddesses; representing an old cancelled Sega console (The Sega Neptune), Xbox, Playstation and the Nintendo Wii, which ironically enough are engaged in a war coincidentally called "The Console War"(sound familiar?). And this game in particular focuses on the goddess's younger sisters. Which represent the "portable" versions of what the CPUs represent, such as the Nintendo DS, PS Vita, and the Sega Game Gear. Aside from the obvious references, there are a plethora more that are hidden and can be found if you know your someone who in the past has played nintendo, xbox, playstation or any other video game platform aside from steam.
All in all, in order to enjoy the game to it's fullest, you need to be able to recognize a bunch of the references it has. And since the game was developed as a monument to console gamers and anime fans alike, simply buying the game without any past experiences on playing on game consoles or anime shows can make the game seem pretty stale like your average moe cheesy RPG. So in other words, if you watch anime, and have played other gaming platforms, you'll find it that you can relate to this game quite a lot.
This sequel retains much details from the previous games and basically the same graphics. It is however, much much more darker should take the conquest ending path. I would explain it, but doing so would tarnish the feels that come with it.
Watching the conquest ending nearly brought tears to my eyes, and I wouldn't recommend skipping through it as it's like basically spitting on a good book.

I like this game better than the first. I think it's the protagonist, and the sisters. It's not because Nepgear's Japanese voice is Yui Horie, a famous singer and anime character voice in Japan.
Nepgear is probably the most boring character in the series, but as a protagonist, it works. Chrono of Chrono Trigger really isn't that interesting, but that doesn't matter as much because the player is the one that makes him interesting. The same I feel goes with Nepgear. You actually feel like you are Nepgear. This is unlike the first game, where I felt like I was just along for the ride with Neptune. That being said, if you own both games, load up the first game after playing this one for a while. There are many enhancement in the UI. It's a very nice touch that they probably didn't need, but did anyways. Playing 4 characters instead of 3 is also nice, especially how large your party can get

I've seen a lot of negative reviews for this game. Not Far Cry enough? I beg to differ. You're still running around a lush open world, murdering your enemies like a righteous badass; it just so happens that your living in 10,000 BC this time around. So, no massive arsenal of machine guns and rocket launchers and the like. Instead you're rocking (heh heh puns) a more primitive arsenal. Your spear is your best friend in the wilds, functioning both as a face-jabber and a long range projectile. You've also got clubs for more personal encounters (which can also be thrown) and of course, a trusty bow. Any weapon you throw can be retrieved, plus you can craft more weapons on the go - which means foraging for resources and supplies is now an important part of your life.
Oh yeah, you can also tame wild beasts, which is good since pretty much everything wants to kill you and make you its lunch. Once tamed, said beast becomes sort of like a 'familiar' in the sense that you can call and dismiss it at will. There is a pretty good variety of beasts to tame and each has its own specialties and abilities. Plus, you've got your very own spirit animal - the trusty owl which can be used to scout the surrounding area, mark enemies, attack from above and even drop bombs on unsuspecting foes.
Seriously... what's not to love? If you're a Far Cry fan I implore you to at least give it a chance. Hell, even if you've never played a Far Cry game in your life I still recommend you give it a go!

Game of Thrones is a Telltale 'adventure' game set in the fantasy world created for the television series based on George R. R. Martin's fantasy series of the same name. The gameplay and style of the game are the same as previous Telltale games, so there's no traditional point-and-click style adventuring here; instead the game plays like a choose-your-own adventure style TV show, allowing interation through scripted quicktime events and conversation choices.
The game is made up six episodes, but now that all six have been released they are bundled into one on Steam, so buying the game gets you all six to play through from start to finish.
Graphics in Game of Thrones are surprisingly variable in quality. Unlike other Telltale Games that I've seen (the Walking Dead and the Wolf Among Us), which had consistently good graphics and sets throughout, Game of Thrones has some great graphics and some exceedingly poor sections. A few times the game cuts to wide-open vistas which are obviously just static two-dimensional backgrounds, like poorly made Hollywood sets, and sometimes the character models look particularly bad as well, such as the seemingly pasted-on winter clothing of the Night's Watch.
Facial models are mainly very good, though, with cameo appearances from characters made famous in the TV series looking very much like the actors that portray them, and the new characters mostly being very well modelled and animated indeed.
Sound is fantastic, from the theme song music (which I personally don't like, but which is reproduced faithfully here) to the atmospheric music and sounds that are played throughout the game. Sounds, too, are very well done; there's nothing to complain about here.
Every line in the game's script is spoken, too, and the voice actors are obvious professionals. I'm not sure whether the cameos from characters in the TV show are played in the game by the actors from the show, but if not then they do an excellent job of mimicry. You'll recognise the Imp, John Snow, Ramsay Snow, and more, both by their character models and the excellent voicework.
Game of Thrones plays like the other Telltale adventure games I've played. Each episode is like an episode of the TV show, with some parts giving way control to you to make a decision or perform an action, which might affect what happens next in the story. But the game is more action than adventure; traditional point-and-click adventure game fans won't find any joy here. Almost all of the player actions in the game limited to timed quicktime sequences and conversation choices, with very occasional walking sequences where you're free to look around, but even those don't offer any puzzle solving or complicated choices.
Most of the time the character you're playing will respond in tune with the general response type or action you've selected, but a few times I found myself cursing the game because a two-word action I selected didn't correspond very closely with what the character did or said in response to selecting it. So beware: if you don't interpret something exactly the way the game designers intended, you'll end up with some surprising actions occurring in response!
Pros:
+ character faces and voices are excellent, including stars from the TV show
+ the new characters are mostly well developed, to the point that I actually cared about what happened to some of them
+ the plot is consistent with the world we're familiar with from the TV show (if not necessarily the books)
Cons:
- inconsistent graphics quality
- not as much choice and control over the plot as I'd like; some events are foregone no matter what you do
- inclusion of characters from the TV show necessarily limits plot choices (the game can't let you kill the queen, for example)
- results are not always obvious from player selections
- like other Telltale games, it's not really what I'd call an 'adventure' game; it's more action like a slow-moving Dragon's Lair, with some conversation choices added in
I don't think Game of Thrones is as good as the other Telltale 'adventure' games that I've played, but I still enjoyed it enough to play through all six episodes once, and the characters were interesting and developed enough that I cared what happened to them.
I'm not a fan of the Martin books and I'm not as into the TV show as many people are, so perhaps I'm not really the game's target audience. But I liked Game of Thrones enough to look forward to the sequel, which is apparently coming out later this year.
Recommended if you're a fan, or you've played the other Telltale games and you know what you're getting into. Otherwise, if you're a traditional adventure game fan, I'd recommend you play something else instead.

There's a special place in my heart for the Tropico series.  I still consider the first Tropico one of the best gaming experiences of my life.  Unfortunately, none of the sequels have significantly evolved past the design of the original - and indeed, the challenge has largely regressed.
My primary issues with Tropico are:
1.  Every game plays out quite similarly.  You'll end up building the same buildings (Tenement, Church, Clinic, etc), in around the same order every game.  The primary mechanism of differentiation is via your economy:  will you farm, mine, industrialize, and/or suck tourists dry.  Regardless of what you choose...
2.  You'll swim in money, triviliazing one of the central "goals" of sims which is maintaining a balanced economy.  Esp. in Tropico 3 and 4, it's far too easy to make money and just build whatever you want.  Where's the challenge?
3.  There's little incentive to be a militant dictator, regardless of how they've marketed the game.
What do I love about Tropico?
1.  The setting.
2.  That every citizen is modeled.
3.  That you will be rewarded for efficient city-planning.
4.  It's playful ambience.
If you asked me what my favorite city-builder was, I'd be hard-pressed to decide between Tropico (any version, except 2) or Sim City (my personal favorite was Sim City 4).  I like the crunchiness and difficulty of Sim City, but the atmosphere and relaxation of Tropico.

Ok So BDO in a nutshell: After the First 3 Hours you figure out everything is menial labor. At The 10 Hour mark you find out it's not so bad with references to the ingame cash shop. 50 Hours in you start to realize just what a gem that poor first impression was hiding of a game.
That's my experience at the moment, Allow me to explains some things:
Q:What is BDO?
A:A Unique MMORPG with Survival/Crafting Elements. Simply Put it's Archeage done right without the bad management and poor community spirit.
Q:Why did I flip my review on it's head?
A:Because I finally started to invest enough time in the game to actually have it be fun.
Also Allow me to list some pros/cons
Pros:
+The World is your osyter and you are set free to do as you like; although there is a storyline this is largely optional and you will level whether you take up a trade or actually engage in combat (which tbh I would be surprised if you didn't do both)
+The game has a unique system where you can own an entire village of (instanced) houses (only 5 for personal use at a time) withg Different functions and forms. Many of the "Higher End" Crafting Agendas find themselves passing through housing a number of times.
3. The Game isn't free; But it is designed to be played with a minimal investment: I am standing before you having spend a total of 19.99 on this game as a whole, the only reason I spent the extra $10 was because I wanted some minor cosmetic things which you'd be surprised what coupons they give rookies - it almost is easier to buy more than you need every time. I plan to invest a small amount more depending on how long I stay - Tbh I could justify $10/month for that Unlimited Dye Pack (Merv's Palette they call it).
+ The Game is designed to be played solo - but with a overall community feel: While you can play the game completely alone - you will always have the community both helping and hindering your progress as you play; I mean this in more than a Kill Stealing Issue; The Marketplace Prices are set via Min/Max based on Supply and Demand. There's also several balancing features in place that make it more lucreative to work alone - but with the overall goal in mind.
+One of THE Best Guild Systems in the Genre: You actually have 2 Kinds of guilds: Clans, Which are kinda like "Pre-guilds" and don't have  a setup cost or any advantages other than being able to talk to people and reserve a name and Guilds, which I might add full guilds CAN be operated by just 1 person (it won't get very far with the PvP Tho)
+The Combat System is Action Oriented - So it plays out like a fighting game in 3d with MMORPG Mechanics. Additionally the Movement System is very parkour-esqese.
Now to the Cons:
-There is absolutely NO fast Travel in this game: You either walk it yourself (by mount or on foot) r or use their unique system to login an alt while your character automatically travels in the background. That said this is ideal for those who feel Fast Travel is kinda cheaty and unrealistic (which it is).
-There are no (instanced) dungeons from what I can tell, there's only a huge world map and I've only been to a tiny region or two of it. Underground Places do exist but technically they're part of the world map itself.
-Mobs respawn QUICKLY; This would normally be a pro; but with the amount of effort you put into killing mobs they respawn as soon as you finish looting the group - you will NEVER run out of enemies.
-The game isn't exactly an easy one to learn; Even with video tutorials and a wiki there's information about this game even Google Can't find.
And the Last Part is neutral
+/- The Game is designed to take your damn time and eat it up like candy; If this is your ideal lifestyle then this game is for you' If you can't deal with a longterm or high level investment of time you might want to give it a pass (why are you looking for MMORPGS if you have no time?!)

Don't let the screenshots or art style put you off. This is actually a very funny game. The combat system and levels might show its Vita origins, but that doesn't make this game any less enjoyable. The silly humour and semi constant 4th wall breaking are whaat makes Neptunia Rebirth shine. I'd personally recommend playing it with japanese audio, especially because a chunk of the jokes and references aren't carried over in the English localization.
Combat wise expect a system that is based on positioning. Different weapons/attacks have their own aoe cone/circle/rectangle, and enemies within these can be attacked. There is also an overdrive style mechanic called hdd mode, and the usual buff/debuff spells.
The share system adds a level of strategy to picking up side quests. For some of the optional content (and not just that) players must keep an eye not only on the rewards, but also who gains from you completing a specific quest.
On a whole if the art style doesn't put you off I'd highly recommend picking up this very amusing rpg.

After how epic the first game was i had come to expect a lot from this one, the sequel. The difference in this one is that you are using the younger sisters of the charecters from the first game. Those sisters got put into a trap and you(as Nepgear) have embarked on a quest to get them back. In the mean time game industry is being plagued with piracy and cheats breaking the economy.
So what to say about this then, well firstly the storyline is shorter then the first game, with 1 playthrough i took 23 hours to finish the original campaign, this took 18 hours. That being said the first game had two endings, i believe this has six or seven each with their own requirements. Beyond that the whole of the roster from the first game make a stand(apart from peachy and plutia as far as i know) but you have to earn them instead of them just being thrown at you as part of the campaign, there are a few graphical changes to the recurring charecters as well and a few more combo ex skills for our protagonists.
Generally the formula hasnt changed much, some will like that while others will not, pretty much all of the features from the first game return in addition there is a new charecter by the name of stella which you can throw into dungeons and she will give you all the crap she finds, she works in real time even if you arent playing the game so for example if you send her off for 12 hours and then sleep for a day when you launch the game she will be done searching whatever she is doing, a neat feature but not amazing. There appears to be more plan content however as for clothing it could just be me but it seems like there is less of that.
The general banter and stupidity between the charecters is still there also which is great as it is just as hilarious as the first game, its still dubbed and subbed so you get to pick what you like more. A small issue is that there are a few areas which didnt get dubbed, this isnt the end of the world and it doesnt effect the storyline or quality
A minor issue that i would like to point out is that there is a cache issue with the game and it turns into a problem, basically the game will crash when you try to enter a dungeon, seems quite game breaking, well whatever it is there is a simple solution, change the shortcut that steam uses to the exe in the game directory, no clue what its about and you would think that this is the link that is already being used.
The game runs at 60fps 99% of the time(you can push it higher in an ini file easily) anyways when you break the enemy defence the game will drop to 30fps for about half a second, sometimes you will notice it sometimes you will not, i have no clue why that happens, it something that i would like fixed however it really isnt gamebreaking.
In the end i still think that the first game was better, i believe that is because i like the personalities of that game a little better however this is a worthy sequel to that game without a doubt, there are many hours of fun in this game, if you like anime, rpgs, jrpgs, hack n slash or comedy in general the hyperdimension series is one hell of a buy.

There's a special place in my heart for the Tropico series.  I still consider the first Tropico one of the best gaming experiences of my life.  Unfortunately, none of the sequels have significantly evolved past the design of the original - and indeed, the challenge has largely regressed.
My primary issues with Tropico are:
1.  Every game plays out quite similarly.  You'll end up building the same buildings (Tenement, Church, Clinic, etc), in around the same order every game.  The primary mechanism of differentiation is via your economy:  will you farm, mine, industrialize, and/or suck tourists dry.  Regardless of what you choose...
2.  You'll swim in money, triviliazing one of the central "goals" of sims which is maintaining a balanced economy.  Esp. in Tropico 3 and 4, it's far too easy to make money and just build whatever you want.  Where's the challenge?
3.  There's little incentive to be a militant dictator, regardless of how they've marketed the game.
What do I love about Tropico?
1.  The setting.
2.  That every citizen is modeled.
3.  That you will be rewarded for efficient city-planning.
4.  It's playful ambience.
If you asked me what my favorite city-builder was, I'd be hard-pressed to decide between Tropico (any version, except 2) or Sim City (my personal favorite was Sim City 4).  I like the crunchiness and difficulty of Sim City, but the atmosphere and relaxation of Tropico.

Quick Review -
Tropico 4 is the best entry in the Tropico franchise so far. If you are not fimiliar with Tropico, here's s short rundown:
> You are El Presidente
> You are the newest ruler of Tropico Islands
> Build♥♥♥♥♥♥
> Juggle your nation's relationship with the Capatilist United States and the Communist USSR.
> $$$
With a great map editor that can be used to share your creations with the world, and about 100 hours of content and endless replayability, this game is 100% worth the current $20 asking price. If you ever wanted to play Sim City on a tropical island and get to chose wether to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥bag control freak or a man of the people, try this game for sure.
There is plenty of game modes. Like I mentioned before, there's a map editor where you can change the entire layout of of pre-made island. You can raise mountains to the exact pixel you wish, create rivers of gold deposits to fill your wallet with cash, and best of all, add any kind of settings you want. The island is your canvas. You can be as artistic as you want. Want a forest here? Go for it. Feel like ruling an island full of nothing volcanic ash and a few ancient ruins? Your funeral. Do as you please, you are El Presidente!
The commentary of your island's growth (or demise, if you are THAT guy) is done by Penultimo, your most trustworthy advisor (and your only advisor) and Sunny Smiles, a hippie with a really bad dental problem... perhaps they should have added "dentist office" as a building option. It is witty, creative, and sometimes downright made my laugh. The humour in this game is very much to my liking. Every joke is either a really good one, or one that is so cheesy it still makes you smile. The person who represents the United States introduces himself as such: " Good day, El Presidente. I am Senetor Nick Richards. I am not a crook!"
On the negative side, the music - while good - gets repetitive after a while. You hear the same 5 songs over and over. I actually had to look for a mod to add more tracks in it, just to be disappointed there is none as of yet. At least the songs are really catchy and upbeat, otherwise this would practically ruin the experience.
The only other problem I have with the game is the lack of ways to appeal to the enviromentalist and militarist factions. The damn hippies whine everytime you cut down a few trees... even when it is to build a wind turbine. They just seem to hate everything you do, especially if it makes you money. Open a mine in the middle of a craig? Well screw you, we're not voting for you in the next election. What's that? You built a garbage dump on a distant valley to reduce polution in the streets? Impeche El Presidente for trying to accomidate our desires.
Overall, great game. Final Verdict: 9/10 for City Builder fans, 7.5/10 for others.

As a long-time player of many western/american designed MMORPG's, I will admit I was jaded before jumping into BDO. My perceptions of the differences between NA and Korean derived titles of this nature made me very wary of the value I'd get in the game at all. For example, although almost all NA MMO's have done away with subscriptions the pay-to-win/item shop and pay-wall designs coming from other countries turned me off. So, here I was jumping into BDO... Why?
This game hooked me for an intense 7-10 days of playtime, then I quit. Once I saw how broken some of the mechanics in the game were, it really shocked me to understand what kind of pay-farm I was participating in. I won't knock the developers - they need to make money, right? I just could only go so far before the clear need to slowly grind OR pay for boost items while in a poorly written facade of a fantasy world overtook my enjoyment for discovery and supply-chain management in game.
Try it today, and form your own opinion!

Let me start off by saying that Black Desert Online is not an inherently bad game. I believe some people may find it to be a great game, and this review is meant to inform them as well. Here are some things to know before you buy.
Be aware that although this game is not neccessarily pay to win, it does have a upfront in-game paywall. In order to be competitive, you need to spend about $40 USD in game to get pets, which are essential to grinding and leveling up life skills.
Leaving your game running in the background when you are not playing will give you a significant financial advantage. This advantage is so large that if you intend to be competitive (buy the best gear), I would consider it a neccessity. Most players leave their game running 24/7.
The marketplace doesn't work very well. The entire game is balanced so that long time players will get a boost over newer players, and this extends to the markets as well. If you are a new player you will not be able to compete financially with older players.
There is no end game PVE. Their are no raids or dungeons, the most you can do is fight the world boss every once in a while with the whole server, or grind high level mobs.
Cosmetic items are prohibitively expensive. If you are like the RP aspects of the game this is worth pointing out. As of writing this, clothing costs between $22 and $35 each, and house furniture costs between $11 and $25, not including floors and wallpaper. While these will not neccessarily improve combat, but if you like RP, its seriously going to cost you.
Lastly, creating and leveling up alts will give you a decent overall boost. While this will not matter to most people, if you RP and only want to use one character, it will be to your detriment.
With all these factors under my consideration, I cannot recommend the game to people who intend to RP and who only do PVE.

"Greyfox" is a brief interactive short story that can be played out over the course of an hour or two. The game deals with issues of mortality and ethical values, which you explore as you play as a young woman who up and leaves her current life in order to start anew in the town of Greyfox.
This title falls very short in terms of storytelling, which is unfortunate because the gameplay is nearly non-existent. The moment you start the game you are thrust into your character's life with essentially zero backstory. The only other thing you will learn about your character will depend on the ending you wind up with, which will depend on the major decisions you make during the game.
So, the majority of time you will play through the present day events of four elderly people. As with your own character, you will learn very little of these people. You will guide them through their current circumstances and in the end make a life or death choice. The huge problem with this game is that there is so little character development that when you come to this final choice, you really don't care which outcome you choose. There are other games out there, such as "To The Moon", which do a much better job at creating an emotional link between the characters and yourself. "Greyfox" just doesn't have the same effect.

Greyfox is another game that has been added to the RPG Maker Library. For the most part, this game isn't really that bad. You play as a 35 year old lady who is going into an early retirement. She moves to a town called Greyfox, named accordingly because of the giant, gray fox statue in the middle of the city.
The enviroment offers lots of interactable objects, but with an RPG game with no combat, it's all about the story. You stumble upon a woman with magical powers. Suddenly you find yourself inhabiting the bodies of other townspeople at crucial moments in their lives. It could use some work and some originality, but overall this game is pretty fun for just a cents. If you're really into RPG games the $2 full price is fine, but if your just looking for something to occupy you for a few hours wait until it's on sale.

Slay the Spire is a fantastic game that combines some fo the best elements of turn-based RPGs and deck-building card game with some roguelike elements thrown in.  The art is fantastic, the gameplay is dynamic and interesting, and the overall "mouth-feel" of the game is very satisfying.  I highly recomend this game.

If you're new to this genre: Deckbuilding roguelikes are great. You gain power as you progress up the spire by adding and removing cards from your deck, and then you use your deck to fight monsters, sometimes cycling through all the cards several times in a fight. You can try and build combo decks, once you have played a few times you'll be able to anticipate what cards you might find in shops or as monster loot in future and influence your deck in that way. The monster variety is good and the game is always a challenge.
If you have played Dream Quest / Monster Slayers before: This game is not just a clone. It's new and different. You can have encounters where you fight multiple enemies, you can use consumable items during fights, you manage your resources differently in fights, and the monsters are fairer and have less RNG - you can see what they are going to do on their turn before they do it. I'm not even sure the monsters use a deck of cards to decide what to do. Also navigating the overworld is pretty simple, leaving you to focus on what matters.
Either way, you will enjoy this game.

Here is what I like about this game:
Beautiful graphics.
Freerunning mechanics allow you to reach any point on the map with relative ease once you get used to the controls. Entertaining way of getting around too.
Many fun ways to kill zombies, and a variety of zombie types to encounter (some more annoying than others)
Fun skills to acquire over the course of the game which steadily give you more and more abilities including drop-kicking zombies, vaulting over zombies, covering yourself in viscera to blend in with zombies.
Two whole campaigns,
Drop in/drop out cooperative play, multiplayer competetive mode against a zombie player, and a cooperative survival minicampaign called Bozak Horde.
Great variety in weapons to choose from for zombie killing.
Drive a custom buggy around with entertaining weapons and gadgets.
Things I dislike about this game:
The community can be very toxic. Ex: Forums have many trolls, cheaters are rampant, and many players are fond of exploiting mechanics in the game.
PvP can seem unbalanced at times, and very competetive.
Overall, I very much enjoyed this game while I still played it. I enjoyed the leveling up, the weapons, the campaign, the graphics. Over time I improved my skills and found myself dying less to zombies, I found some fun weapons, did plenty of quests. Although, I don't recommend playing with random players before completing the game or leveling up a bit. They tend to spoil the experience of the game in my opinion. When I first tried Be the Zombie mode (unintentionally as a player invaded my game) it was a very fresh and exciting experience, and a bit scary because I didn't know the capabilities of the Night Hunter. Although, the more time I spent around players, the less entertaining Be the Zombie became for me.
Overall rating: 8/10

FINAL VERDICT: Buy it on sale, it's worth it for an intense story, lovely style, and stays rather true to the Game of Thrones atmosphere of utter hopelessness.
I see a lot of "no" with reviews for this game and honestly, I understand all of their complaints (about 90% of these are with the ending which... yeah, okay) ... that being said, I still recommend it. It is visually appealing, it's an interesting story, and I honestly think it has a great lesson: Sometimes, nothing you do or plan will matter and ultimately you will fail.
I didn't say it was a "happy" lesson, now did I?
Look, if you like Game of Thrones, if you like stylistic visuals, and if you like story games then you will likely enjoy this one. It's engaging, you get wrapped up in it, and like any good Game of Thrones arc, most of the people you care for die. The ending is a cliffhanger, but honestly, I love Telltale and I would have bought the sequel either way. Do your decisions matter immensely? Well... that will really be seen if they are able to make season 2.
They can't ALL be Tales from the Borderlands, but this one got me emotional, engaged, sweating the fate of my characters and it entertained me. In the end, isn't that the point? I'll be buying season 2 if they can make it.

I have mixed feelings -- but overall I really enjoyed this game. Having the actual voice actors from the show was a nice touch, and being able to interact with main POV characters from the ASOIAF books was fun. I feel like TellTale did a wonderful job with their research and the lore, which made everything so much more enjoyable.
I also felt really attached to the characters when all was said & done. It was hard to watch people die and make decisions about who would live and who would die. I enjoyed the different story lines, and had a lot of fun.
That being said: interacting with main POV characters from the series felt weird at times. For example, being given the option to try to hurt a character that is included in the books & movies feels pointless, since I know that (very important) character will go on to live anyways.
I also felt frustrated a lot of the time. Even when I thought I had acted wisely or diplomatically, I felt as though the game was unfairly punishing me for no reason -- bad♥♥♥♥♥♥just keeps happening; it doesnt matter whether you are a diplomat or a defiant rebel.
But I'm still dying to know what will happen next. If you love Game of Thrones & GRRM's work, and don't mind a game that is heavy on story, I would highly recommend.

While going through my Que, a game in the JRPG Bundle was listed.  I have a history with RPG Maker games, and checked out its page.  I don't like seeing many of the harsh reviews people have because of poor writing or the way some people use their RPG Maker games as a sort of "fan-fiction," ripping off ideas from other media instead of being completely creative and fresh.
That being said, I noticed that I could buy the one game for 49 cents on sale, or buy 4 games in this bundle for the same price.  Honestly, who could complain about such a cheap game?  So I bought it and the same day played the smallest game on the list, Greyfox RPG.
First off, I couldn't call this a JRPG for anything, and I could barely call it an RPG in the sense I am familiar with RPGs.  (Although, in the sense of you playing the role of a person, this IS an RPG.)  It is just like the description says.  You move to a town called Greyfox where you meet a mysterious woman and you get to live the lives of 4 old people in the town.  You decide what happens at the end of their lives, and can possibly solve a mystery or two along the way.  I have only played through once so far, getting the "bad" ending, but I liked its premise.  I played a Psychological-Horror type game with RPG Maker when I was a lot younger, and appreciated the use of the program for story-telling, rather than a traditional "kill enemies and level-up" RPG game.
There are a few little secrets to find, a little bit of humor, and many "What exactly is going on here?" moments that make you feel like you're in the main character's shoes. If you're new to this genre: Deckbuilding roguelikes are great. You gain power as you progress up the spire by adding and removing cards from your deck, and then you use your deck to fight monsters, sometimes cycling through all the cards several times in a fight. You can try and build combo decks, once you have played a few times you'll be able to anticipate what cards you might find in shops or as monster loot in future and influence your deck in that way. The monster variety is good and the game is always a challenge.
If you have played Dream Quest / Monster Slayers before: This game is not just a clone. It's new and different. You can have encounters where you fight multiple enemies, you can use consumable items during fights, you manage your resources differently in fights, and the monsters are fairer and have less RNG - you can see what they are going to do on their turn before they do it. I'm not even sure the monsters use a deck of cards to decide what to do. Also navigating the overworld is pretty simple, leaving you to focus on what matters.
Either way, you will enjoy this game.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is something of a sequel to the original Alan Wake. From what I understand it's the continuation of the story and was intended to be either released episodically or as a stop gap between the first and second game. Sadly there isn't any news on a second game coming so far, beyond the 'to be continued' that you get at the end credits.
Anyway, the game itself is pretty good. It hasn't lost any of the voice acting or nice little bits. The Alan Wake series is one of the few games that actually makes me want to collect the collectibles,, which in this cases are manuscript pages that can be read. Each page reveals more of the world so The player can understand the world more.
This title is a lot more combat orientated that the original with more varied enemies and tougher ones at that. Not to worry though your arsenal can be upgraded through weapons cases that are unlocked by finding the aforementioned collectibles. 3 gets you an smg, 10 a magnum and so on.
I'd recommend this game, it's actually worth it's asking price, though replayability is low. There is a arcade mode that can make the game last a bit longer. Be aware that you really do need to like plot heavy games to really enjoy this title.

While still enjoyable, and certainly worth the price if on sale Game of Thrones is without a doubt the weakest of Telltale's most recent efforts, sitting comfortably behind The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us. I would also like to point out this is the first time I've been able to put down a Telltale game for long periods, I finished episode 6 two weeks after episode 5 when I usually knock out an episode a day back to back due to being engrossed. Take from that what you will.
Telltale have changed their usual format with Game of Thrones, you don't play the role of one person, you play many and I feel this hurt the immersion, I didn't feel truly connected to any of the characters as you are swapped between them so regularly, although some were definitely more likeable than others. I guess it makes sense, and follows the format of the TV show but still, I don't think it translated very well into the game.
Another big complaint I have was the bizarre choice of graphical filters and effects used throughout the game, all edges appear blurred and jagged regardless of settings and there's no way to correct this as it's an artistic choice made by the devs (supposedly to make it look like an oil painting), one that completely butchers the visual fidelity. At first I thought something was simply wrong with my game, but after researching further I discovered this is 100% intended and I couldn't disagree more with the overall aesthetic of the game. Telltale aren't known for their technical prowess, but at least their games usually look clean, and that's just not the case with Game of Thrones, the overall look reminds me of playing a game at a non native resolution. The technical issues didn't stop there either, the game crashed to desktop many times when first starting the game, sometimes taking 3 - 4 attempts before it would open correctly, thankfully this never happened during gameplay. I would just like to point out this has never been an issue with any other Telltale game and I'm certainly not alone, many people have reported the exact same issue with no solution. On top of these extra problems the usual Telltale engine issues are of course present, so don't expect any improvements on that front.
While this review may seem negative I would still recommend it, it's definitely the weakest, recent Telltale offering but it's still a solid game, especially at 66% off and if you enjoyed their recent work you will most likely enjoy it as well, but I'd be surprised if you don't feel the lack of Telltale magic because it's just not there, or at least it's spread too thin.
