This is one of the most minimally interactive games I've ever seen.
It has all the drawbacks of every TellTale adventure game.  As usual, you're presented with choices.  But you don't have enough information to make a meaningful judgment about which choice is best or what the mechanical consequences might be, or if you'll have the opportunity to change your mind later.  There's a time limit, so by the time you're done reading all the choices, you don't have any time left to think about your decision.  It's very stressful at first, and then you realize that none of your choices mattered anyway, because you're going to be going through the exact same sequence of scenes no matter what.  End then at that point, you realize that nothing you do in the game matters at all, and there is literally no reason why this is a video game and not just an animated miniseries.
This particular game is even less interactive than other TellTale games.  In Wolf Among Us, at least you got to investigate crime scenes from time to time, even if the outcome was always the same.  There's nothing like that here.  Just meaningless TellTale choices and the occasional combat scene composed of a series of quicktime/Simon Says events.
The only thing I'd praise this game for is the cool-looking hand-painted art style.  The character models look pretty appealing, and it's neat to see the cast members from the show sculpted in 3D.

Your character is controlled by the usual Keys (W,A,S,D) & the mouse & the key binbdings can be customised.
Most of the maps are not real big & most of the weapons are able to shot from one side all the way to the other. ATM there are at least 1 of the weapons in the game that are OverPowered but you are able to choose from 2 types of pistols & 3 or 4 types of rifles from M16 through to a Shotgun.
There is no real way of boosting health back up once you have lost it other than dying & respawning at full health again. When killed there is basically NO drawback as everything in the game is FREE & available to ALL players ALL the time.

(ATM I am not sure if you are able to MUTE individual players which is maybe something they will do in the future)
In summing up I really can't recommend that ANYONE take the time to download this game as it is very much dying ATM due to a FAST growing number of HACKERS that basically wreck the game for 15 minutes for everyone else by 1 shoting other players which doesn't give you a chance as most of the weapons in the game take several shots to kill another player with so you always loose to trying to face off with them.
Maybe if the developers do something about the lack of in the game then the game would be a whole lot better, but with the hackers, the lack of much to do ingame & the repetitiveness I think they might have a HUGE task infront of them that they just may not be able to complete.

I think you're supposed to play this game with friends.
I don't have any of those so I played it by myself. Big mistake.
Srsly tho, I think this game could be fun and chaotic if you had some people to play it with. I couldn't find a multiplayer match, and wasn't about to go searching for someone to play it with on a forum or anything so I stuck with single player. I couldn't beat the first level of the story mode. I tried. I tried different characters, slightly different strategies, no luck. I managed to reach the boss on my most recent playthrough, died pretty quick, and then closed the game for the final time.
Part of the factor could be that I'm not the best at bullet hell type games. But I don't think being able to die in one hit is doing me any favours either. In a game where the screen can be covered in bullets, dying in one hit just doesn't seem fair. The game doesn't really try to help you out much, either. Powerups and extra lives can be destroyed by your bullets, and are often far behind enemy lines so there's a good chance they're gonna get shot in the process of getting to them. It also felt like a lot of the characters just sucked in general. I stuck with the 13th Legion or whatever because it was the only character that could sustain more than one hit and could also output a barrage of bullets at once.
There's a good chance you'll be screwed over by the level progression system. After the first level, you're given three random choices of where you go next, and the different pictures shown will mean different things. Either a weapon place, a perk upgrade, or some sort of shootout. Sometimes you won't get the choice of an upgrade level unless it's really early on in which case you won't be able to afford upgrades. There's also a chance you'll get levels with extra challenges, where if you don't accept the handicap of having a bigger hitbox, being slowed, or some sort of other debuff, you'll have to fight a stronger enemy. It's just kind of annoying because there's no sort of reward to balance out this challenge. I've had situations where I've progressed up to the point of one of these levels without losing a life, and then slowly my lives all drain on this one stage since it's almost impossibly difficult.
I have no idea how the hell the other boss fights work, but the first one felt like something I would never be able to defeat so I didn't bother trying to get back to it. It was basically a giant tank on tracks with a claw that would fire out and kill you. The claw was huge, probably about a fifth of the screen, and you also have to avoid being run over by the tank and the slew of little guys that are also after you. Even when I managed to defeat all the smaller enemies and then focus on just the boss, the damage I delivered was so little, that I never even got him to halfway before dying myself. I don't really understand how the weapons work in this game. At the point of me fighting the boss, my 13th Legion guy had the Samurai Warbanner equipped. It was the most expensive weapon I could get for him at the time but my damage dealt still felt pretty weak. The only change I noticed was that I could run into enemies to kill them now. Not much help when you're gonna get shot getting that close.
I don't feel like this game explains enough. They tell you the controls for the characters, show you the different weapons you can get for them, but don't bother explaining how you can use these things to your advantage. It's not the worst thing, I've ever played, but it wasn't good enough to hold my attention for long.
I will add, I did enjoy the music. The Western pixel artstyle was cool and unique, but my only gripe with it was that the orange bullets blended in to the general brownness of the setting a bit too much.
If you have a friend to play this with, either locally or online, then maybe try it out on a sale. If you're just looking for something to play by yourself then I would suggest looking elsewhere.

I am a huge Game of Thrones fan. I have read all the books and love the show. When this was announced I was so excited as a telltale game set in the Game of Thrones world sounded like a perfect fit. Unfortunately I was completely wrong.
The first episode captured the right feeling, but as we got to the end of the season the biggest flaw of the game started to show, your choices do not matter in a game about choices. Telltale seem to believe that to make this authentic, everything has to go wrong. Although this is true in the show, it all happens for a reason. There is no reason for most of the mindless abuse that the game throws at you. Characters die before you even get a chance to care about them and there is almost always no way to prevent their deaths.
These new characters from House Forrester seem interesting until you realise why. They are incredibly similar to the characters from House Stark. There is a girl out of her league in Kings Landing (basically Sansa), a young boy trying to be lord over a castle (Bran/Robb) and an honourable outcast who goes to the wall (Jon). The only character who truly interested me was Asher as he was a unique character and very well written.
The character's we knew from the show initially made you start to care about the characters from the game. However, their inclusion, especially Ramsay Bolton's, as the antagonists made you realise you can't win as nothing can really change.
The obvious set up for a sequel was also incredibly frustrating. It caused the ending to be unsatisfying as there was barely any payoff to any of my decisions and some things I had done seemed completely pointless (including one playable character's entire storyline).
I so wanted to enjoy telltale's Game of Thrones but I cannot recommend to even the biggest Game of Thrones fan.

This game is big. With two large cites that are both very different, and the DLC adding a very large countryside to explore in your car there's a lot to do.
There's not much to say about the story. Its pretty much your standard zombie apocalypse story, but the guy who created the main villain was playing Bioshock while he wrote it so Rais (The game's big bad) is basically a crazy version of Andrew Ryan if he was in a zombie apocalypse.
So the main story is a bit meh, but the side quests are all interesting. You meet characters who are fun, and add levity to the main story's darker parts. All in all the story of the whole game is okay. If you want your zombie story play the main quest. If you want to have something more fun make sure you do the side quests.
This is where Dying Light shines. The gameplay is solid. Early game you apend most of your time running from rooftop to rooftop. Never letting your feet touch the ground because as soon as they do you're likely to get killed. Later it becomes more about keeping your momentum as you run through the city. Fighting stays mostly the same throughout. Though you get more powerful, and once you're a ways in the basic zombies don't pose a threat. Even the special ones are easily dealt with once you have the right gear. It can get repeitive, but if you're playing with a friend it won't really ever get old, and if your friend is easily scared by horror games it makes night sections really fun. So the gameplay is good, but best with a friend.
I can only kind of speak on this part. I don't have all the DLC, but most of it is just skins and weapons. The Bozak Horde is just parkour challenges, and a new weapon. So I didn't bother with those. (Though it seems that when my brother bought the game all the DLC came with it. Which is a bit annoying to me as its kind of rude to the people who played it as the DLC was coming out.)
However The Following is good. It has an interesting story, and the ending is alright. The main part is the gameplay. Where its more of the same, but now you can drive around in a car. It changes traversal a lot, and it makes night time really fun. Racing around the country side with volitiles right on your tail. Every turn is a chance for you to overshoot slowing down and letting them catch you. There are hazards on the roads that you have to learn to deal with, (Like water or acid where the best solution is to not touch the wheel, and just gun it through them.) and overall its a good time.
This game has surprisingly good boss fights. However I didn't go into it expecting good boss fights, so that does help it. The final boss is just a QTE, which looks cool, but completely ignores the gameplay that made it fun, and the bosses aren't exactly creative, but they are well put together. (except for the aforementioned QTE.) Overall they're good enough for a game where most of your time is spent running around killing hordes. (The final boss of the Following is actually pretty good, and more creative than the others. It still isn't the best boss fight I've ever played, but it was good.)
Its a good game. Get it, and The Following DLC. (The other DLC is up to you.) Play it with a friend and just have fun.

There are many free-world role playing FPS out there, with different themes, franchise and all. Well, Saint Row IV here has made it more than explicite that they are different, and you better be accepting of chaoctic fun if you want to know why.
Early in game, they have made it apparent that a major part of the game takes place in a Matrix-like setting, where you enter a simulation while exploiting their glitches to attain super powers. But no, you are not Neo, and you are not Superman. You normally don't act alone, because you are the leader of the Saints, and being a gang leader means you lead your brothers and sisters into war. Also, you'll still be carrying around the promised gigantic diIdo, and you won't find any superheros who will do that unless you are in Japan.
While, like many free-world FPS, there are quests and side-quests and all, there is pretty much one single objective of the game: destory the world. Do that while you team up with your best pal in co-op while you laugh your way through those parodies, vulgarities and adult humors. Though you should be reminded that this is afterall a colored battle between blue (with purple) and red, so if you are an advocate of political correctness or against the idea of a bunch of purple gang representing the entire Earth, you shouldn't even be here looking at games.

I want to give this game a positive rating. I really, really want to. But I just can't, because I know that no matter what my rating is the outcome will be the same.
That sums this game up. I love Telltale games. I love Game of Thrones. This series started out amazingly, but by about half way through it turned into an outright depressing affair. Because in this game, your choices really do not matter. Not at all. Whenever you think you might win, in comes Ramsey Snow with his cloak of "Nothing bad can happen to me or else this game will no longer be canon" and the story takes a turn for the worst. This was fine the first time, but when it happens again and again...I reached a point in the fourth fifth episode when I was really struggling to go on. No matter what I did, the good guys die and the bad guys win. Even if the arrival at that outcome makes no sense whatsoever, that was what happened. Again, and again, and again.
I know that this is Game of Thrones, and people will die. But even in Game of Thrones, there is hope that someone might survive. In Telltale's game, nobody wins. Your choices do not matter, and no matter what you do there is no winning in this game. This is a shame, because it started as a masterpiece and had the potential to remain one. This game was an emotional rollercoaster, but once I arrived at the end (which is a set-up for a 2nd season, in case you were wondering), it really began to hit me how disappointing this game was.
In conclusion, this is by no means a bad game. However, it is by all means a disappointing one.

Like a good sequel should,
Lethal League doesn’t ignore the formula of fast, fluid gameplay that has made the series famous, but introduces a unique new premise, unprecedented player personalization, and sweeping changes that breathe new life into the multiplayer experience. It’s over-the-top and at times unnecessarily complex, but serves both current and next-generation consoles with ambitious new ideas and tremendous replay value.
Despite sharing a name with one of
Lethal League best-known characters, Ghosts takes place in an entirely new Call of Duty universe set in the not-too-distant future. In a genre overwrought with antiquated Russian conflicts and ambiguous Middle Eastern terrorist threats, Ghosts takes on a refreshingly unique premise in which the threat comes not from the east, but the south: a federation of oil-rich South American nations rises to take over the hemisphere, pushing north and coming to blows with the U.S.
The prelude establishes a harrowing vision of a United States homeland that's broken but not beaten – not quite Red Dawn, but not Fallout 3, either. It’s a space not often explored by modern shooters, and its mood is heightened by missions set in a besieged Santa Monica and the wasted remains of San Diego, to the tune of an excellent, somber score from David Buckley (The Town, Metal Gear Solid 4). But ultimately, time on the poignant homefront is short lived as the story goes behind enemy lines in Caracas, the Andes mountains, and other exotic locales.
Those might lack to familiarity, but the variety of environments keeps the campaign fresh, not only in terms of visuals, but in gameplay as well. Instead of just fighting waves of enemies through a linear stage at ground level, you’ll find yourself rappelling down skyscrapers, flying helicopters, having firefights in space, commanding tanks, scuba diving through shipwrecks, playing as a dog, and evading shark attacks. Each requires new strategy, acute situational awareness, and – in the case of the space and water missions – special consideration for verticality and physics.
Of course, it wouldn’t be a Call of Duty game without elaborate setpieces, fierce shootouts, and tense stealth missions, and Ghosts delivers some of the most memorable experiences in the series. I felt genuine dread as the ground and buildings collapsed around me during orbital weapons strikes, the zero-gravity spectacle of the Federation’s space station ambush is awe-inspiring, and bursting through a highrise window as the entire building crumbles during the Federation Day mission is exhilarating.
But like previous CoDs, the story of Ghosts struggles to remain in focus amidst the fray of explosive cinematic moments and relentless firefights. Narrated loading sequences with stylized story animations push the campaign forward, but only last for one or two minutes before launching back into the action. It’s there, on the front lines, that much of the plot progression is presented and oftentimes lost.
It's by no means an achievement in dramatic storytelling — it's more about dumb fun — and it lacks the player-choice element introduced with Call of Duty: Black Ops II, but when given time to breathe Ghosts actually offers some interesting human drama. The story centers around two brothers, Logan and Hesh, their father Elias, and yes, their dog Reilly as they fight the Federation as part of the battered remnants of the U.S. military, and later as the elite Ghosts squad. The family ties, specifically the relationship between Logan and Hesh, made me care about the protagonists in a series that's habitually made its characters a dispensable commodity. The voice acting is decent overall, though there are periodic moments of cringe-worthy dialog, like one superfluous moment when Elias reveals he’s a member of the Ghosts. And then there’s Riley. Though the subject of many a meme at this point, Riley not only acts as a useful tool for recon and silently dispatching enemies, but is integral to several dramatic sequences, saving your character on more than one occasion.
The story stumbles in the second act when it strays away from the more evocative character focus in favor of a long stretch of back-to-back missions driven almost exclusively by guns-blazing combat. While not poorly done, this visually arresting, action-packed, but ultimately hollow middle stands in stark contrast to the effective first and final acts. On the bright side, that padded out my play time to roughly 10 hours, making this campaign one of the longest CoD single-player experiences.
The Verdict
Lethal League isn't a reinvention of the franchise, but proves there's still room for innovation within its existing formula. Though at the risk of overcomplicating things at times, its robust multiplayer gameplay, surprisingly fun co-op modes, and lengthy, challenging, and varied campaign makes
Lethal League one of the best Call of Duty games to date.

First time I have done an actual review
Pros :
The Graphics
The game is stunning. Like holy sh*t the graphics are so nice (can get laggy in towns though)
The combat
The combat is very smooth allowing you to quickly combo multiple abilities together and also allow for a players skill to be shown.  The lack of gear (to an extent, sometimes the other persons gear just simply outclasses yours in every way so even if you are skilled at pvp you will still lose, but its an mmo, thats to be expected) can be made up by out playing the other person in combat.
The character creation
BDO has one of the most in depth character creators out there.  Honestly though, no one is playing this game for the character creator
The number of the things to do is absurd
There are so many things in this game to do
Cons
Trading
BDO has a very "interesting" version of trading.  In most MMO's if you need a boat (yes, I'm talking about the epheria sailboat and the absurd number of logs I need for it)  you could ask your friend to also cut down trees and then give you the logs he got, but the only way for you to give something like logs to a friend in BDO is to put it on the marketplace and hope you buy it (which you probably won't)
Some items can only be bought with irl money
Now keep in mind, these items aren't game breaking or anything, none of them provide any extra attack damage or defense but the camo's hide your name in the world meaning you pretty much always have the first attack onto a person outside of the safe zones and it is also harder to track you in pvp.  Most of the paid items can be bought off the market place with in game currency however which is quite nice.
Very overwhelming / bad tutorial
The second you get into the game, you get bombarded with notifications about stuff going on the market, people failing enhancements, and other crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥that you don't care about.  Just do what I did and go into game settings and disable all of that.  Also the tutorial teaches you merely a fraction of what you'll do in this game.  After the tutorial, it seems like its just kill quest after kill quest after kill quest and it gets quite boring, but trust me it gets better once you start understanding everything and realize theres more than just killing everything

Neutral
"Too much grinding"
I've read a few of the other reviews and a lot of them have complained about grinding and how its to much, but who is forcing you to grind.  There is other stuff to do than just non stop grinding, sure grinding is the fastest way to level up but again, no one is forcing you to do it.
RNG
Rng plays a pretty big role in BDO and is really annoying when you fail an enhance, espicially on accescories, because you lose the item if it fails.  Also once you get to the higher levels of enhancement (+18/tri) if the enhancement fails, the item reverts back to +16 or pri which just means youve gotta spend a lot of money to get it back to what it once was, but I never really cared since I was always very careful when upgrading stuff.  I've never had good luck so I just hoard materials until I have enough so that I have about a 90% success rate, but I can see why its really annoying to some people.
Lots of AFK hours needed
I mean yes, afking for fishing or something is something I would reccommend but you don't need to.  The way that I look at it is that people are going to find a way to use bots to level up this stuff, so kakao just made it so that everyone could do it without a bot meaning that theres no point to bot.

This looked like it was going to be a fun little game, but I am completely underwhelmed. On a foundational level, A Fistful of Gun actually is a good game. All of the nuts and bolts that go into a solid shmup are present, but the developer decided that a classic formula should be needlessly complicated. There are a ton of characters to choose from, but there's something horribly wrong with all of them: Their movement is slow, their range of attack sucks, or their unique control scheme ranges from overly complex to nigh-unplayable. No matter which of the eleven characters the player chooses, he's hobbled in some crucial fashion. As a result, you have a game that would have been fun, were it not for a hackneyed attempt at balance or novelty (I can't tell which concern was at the forefront, but it scarcely matters since attempts at addressing either were clearly in vain).
That might have been perfectly fine, were this game not challenging enough without the need to handicap the player. You'll be subjected to some rather dense fire as you progress, and the stages are filled with environmental hazards in addition to enemy sprites. There were times when I honestly had no clue what hit, exploded, or in some other fashion killed me. Story Mode is even more difficult. It all adds up to an experience that's more frustrating than it is enjoyable. The player just feels robbed of a good time, having wandered into an unforgiving arena shooter while hamstrung by a character roster that offers a whole lot of nothing. I can tell a lot of good intentions went into this game, but paying $13 for this is a ludicrous proposition.

The 7.1 experience deep in the forests with giant cats taking down goats, random NPCs battling it out or epic fights of the fauna is just fantastic.  Wait until you see a sabretooth cat taking down a small mammoth!  Or cave bears fighting.  Eagles swooping down and flying away with a boar in their talons.
I really like "no guns".   I also found the bow to be the most challenging and interesting of the weapons in the other games in the franchise.   Yes you can approach every camp and get to high ground and pick off unsuspecting foes just like previous games, but the bow means you have to get in closer.
I am an admitted completionist and like to clear a map of all objectives.  I am about 60 hours in and only 50% of the way through the main storyline.   I guess if you want to rush through and not explore the amazing world the game isn't that long.  The amount of stuff to discover off-narrative is unbelievable.  This isn't a rushed expansion pack but a whole new game.  The complaints about "cut and paste" missions are true for the side quests, but the main quests are not.  I do wish it was required to do more sub-quests before the main plot progressed.
Being a completionist, I did wind up with all the perks and a bit of a formulaic approach to enemies.  I try not to go back to what works, but it is too tempting.   I wish there were more scaling of difficulty.   The owl is great for tagging bad guys, but it also makes things much too easy.   Same with the mounts, they are so powerful you can command them to attack and not do anything but hide in the flora.  They scare off any wandering creatures so you are virtually invincible when they are present.  And once you have the most powerful, there is absolutely no reason to use anything but.  It could have been amazing to have to use specific creatures for specific reasons.   They do have ratings for stealth, strength, speed - but they are almost irrelevant.  A massive rare cave bear is a poor choice for every reason than a sabretooth cat.  A sleek white wolf is slower and just as stealthy.  Huge opportunity miss here to add new game dynamics and have beast mastery fundamentally change the experience.
The language(s) are "proto-European" and completely convincing, consistent and immersive.  The character models are getting so convincing a real performance is possible.
It doesn't have the incredible, memorable characters like Vaas or Pagan Min but the facial close ups almost tell the stories without subtitles!
This is hands-down the best looking game I've ever played.  Can't wait to see Dunia version 3.
I do wish there was more story, more variety in animals (although there are a lot), more weapons and MORE.
I'm afraid the "good" not "great" reviews will mean the end of the experience but I find the game just short of classic.  Developers should be proud.  I hope there is a Primal 2.
p.s. Uplay sucks big time and you are forced to run it every launch and it stays resident after play.  Boo.

Now I am sure that most of you will skip over this review, and for good reason, I have only played the game for just over 5 hours as of writing. I personally love how the game builds up tension and immersion, while still being fun to play (for the most part, I don't think I will return to the "Water Hazard" Chapter for a while), but there are a few issues, which effect my gaming experience quite a lot. What drew me to write a review for this otherwise great game, was the chapter "Highway 17". *Potential Spoilers ahead for those who haven't currently reached this chapter.*
When the chapter started, I had a feeling that I would not like "Highway 17" due to one gameplay aspect, the dune buggy. Traversing through the beach, getting to the area in which the rocket launcher is obtained was quite easy, however, it seems that Valve didn't prepare for a player as clumsy as I am to drive the buggy into water. This made the rest of the chapter, after the rocket launcher, unavailable to progress on. The buggy could not be driven out of the water, and the player has no chance of pushing it out, unless you have a bunch of grenades to get it onto land. This combined, with the lack of a save file reversing my idiotic mistake resulted in me quitting for a while. Infact, the only way I managed to reverse this was from the knowledge of a console command from a steam friend of mine. I am sure that this may have happened to other people less fortunate and without any knowledge of commands, so I'm putting it out there, if you have any reason to restart it, then use the command "map d2_coast_02".
Despite this issue, I have been able to enjoy the game very much, which was a surprise to me, as prior to this I haven't had many fps experiences. This judgement may be biased in some way, due to the summer sales discount, but I can confirm that this game is worth the purchase, just don't be as mindless as I am :P

According to the ending credits,
was created in a program called ‘
’—a program from which
derives nearly all of its assets. It’s a lazily-designed, glorified point-and-click game dressed up as a proper role-playing game that provides a mere semblance of an actual narrative concept. The game tells the story of the residents of Greyfox—a small town inhabited mostly by the elderly and named after the big stone statue of a fox in the centre of the little village. Everyone in town seems to openly aggressive towards the player, which the game is quick to point out is as a result of their age. For some reason.
Throughout the game’s short story—I saw all three endings in under two hours—age seems to be the primary theme, though none of the endings have anything to do with this. Honestly, the entire plot is a meandering, disjointed mess with no proper focus and excessive use of ex machinas do drive the proceedings. The decisions you make essentially come down to either killing a person or not killing them, with the only impact being different ending cinematics. Maybe
could win a short story contest hosted by a primary school, but as a game it’s just a frustrating mess.
In regards to gameplay,
does initially start out with a mildly interesting element of exploration. You’re presented with the eponymous town and encouraged to just explore, which is fun for a few minutes, until you realise the map is approximately the size of the average grocery store, and is filled with random NPCs who yell at you for talking to them. The game completely fails to capitalise on the sense of discovery it almost establishes, instead railroading you down a ludicrously linear corridor of short, hastily written dialogue which relies heavily on exposition. The gameplay itself is about as organic and enjoyable as checking items of a shopping list—talk to someone, then go to a specific building and click on a specific item and then go back and talk to the same person. It’s a rinse and repeat formula from which next to no enjoyment could be derived.
There’s not much else to say about
, because there’s very little to say in the first place. It’s a tiny game with no proper story or gameplay that’s really best avoided. Some may appreciate its focus on emotion, but it is no more than a short and lacklustre experience.

Good squad-based tactics game. It has a cutsy presentation (good or bad, depending on your preference) but the mechnically it's quite involved.
The major gimmick is the dice, which are influenced by your gear selection. The dice are allocated to each character at the beginning of the turn, based on inititive order including 'hero' enemy types, and each dice provides a small but sometimes extremely significant edge to some aspect of that character's performance. This is where much of the strategy of the game comes into play, as you need to trade off which character needs that specific buff this turn, and which hero might be able to do without. Especially once enemy powers comes into play, as you may start picking to deny enemy abilities rather than to enable your own powers. More than anything else, it's this aspect that makes the game not really casual (at least at higher difficulties) as doing the cost/benefit analysis here can be agonizing. This especially gets challenging as activation order becomes extremely important as more hero units are on the board.
Since all of the character power comes from gear, there's no issue of respeccing (just swap out gear). This is quite convenient and allows you to experiment a lot with different builds, but the downside is that a lot of the characters feel somewhat same-y. The only real distinction between two characters using the same set of gear are the character-specific support skills; for many characters this is becomes almost a non-factor (though with a few very significant exceptions - couple of characters are practically defined by their support abilities).
The game does feel somewhat unpolished in some areas (I noticed at least one misspelling) and the storyline is entirely forgettable, but it's a great mechnical tactics game.

Played the game a second time (and at higher difficulty) and it's a great game, and no need to know anything about the tabletop game.
I - SUMMARY
Details will follow, but to summarize first:
- At first it looks like a casual game for kids, BUT play one or two hours is enough to realize it's a game with a depth and a mood that could fully satisfy many adults.
- Greatest aspect is combats that have a nice depth, a fair diversity, and are based on a system avoiding routine and automatic playing.
- Second greatest aspect is party building. It is very special because it's based on equipping party and party composition selected among a roster. Also it's useful and fun (but not mandatory) to redo the party building each time you'll start a series of missions and prepare a party for it.
- Equipment seems simple but it's rather deep and complex and it is linked to party building.
- The writing is ok, but it is surprisingly interesting, and it is easy to read.
- The graphics are pretty good if the style isn't a problem for you.
- It lacks of polishing on some details like some points of the UI but overall this is good stuff.
- Secondary missions have a too short story, and should have been more secondary quests.
Overall a great Tactic RPG focused on combats and party building, both with a very original approach.
II - GREATEST ASPECT, THE COMBATS
Combat system use two original designs not coming from the tabletop:
- There's a mix of an initiative system and a system that allows you to choose the order you play your characters. It avoids most often play the full party before there's any enemy reaction, and choose character order adds choices and depth.
- There's dices coming from tabletop but unlike in tabletop, at beginning of each turn you throw them all and set yourself a dice result to each character. This is increasing the tactical depth, and it force think at each turn.
Those two combats mechanisms provide:
- Quite a lot of depth to each turn.
- A lot of control on the random aspects.
- Make impossible to quickly rush each turn.
- So avoids routine which is the classical main curse of turn based combats.
Moreover combats have other qualities:
- A fairly good diversity of missions types.
- A pretty good design and diversity of each combat.
- The difficulty progression along the campaign is very well done, nowadays even many AAA games aren't as polished on that aspect.
II - SECOND GREATEST ASPECT, THE PARTY BUILDING
Party building isn't based on pure character progression, the characters don't really level up so you don't have skills and attributes to choose for each level up. Instead each character in roster is unique, and their equipment provide:
- Characteristics increase, health, speed, attack power, armor, damages bonus (armor, jewel, weapon, special, consumables)
- Provide one or two base attack types and many with a specific AOE (weapon)
- Provide special skills either passive or active, those skills are different for each item and each character that can use the equipment (armor, jewel, weapon).
- Provide dices results that will influence the chance of those result to happen (armor, jewel, weapon, special, consumables).
- Each equipment item is unique except for consumables, but there's a progression so some items will make obsolete some older items.
The result is the party building is a complex choice of characters from roster that you put in party, from 2 to 10 characters to choose among up to 15. For each character you need choose the equipments they'll use, knowing that there are many conflicts between characters because any equipment is unique. And you need choose from 2 to 5 consumable types depending of party bag size.
It's a special party building, but if you like party building then there's a lot to enjoy with this game because it's complex and before each quest that is a series of missions you can redesign your party.
III - PRETTY GOOD, EQUIPMENTS
There's only 4 slots per character, plus up to 5 or 6 slots for party consumables, but there's still a nice depth:
- Your party is up to 10 characters which is meaning 40 slots, no single character RPG can challenge that from far.
- All items but consumables are uniques which is pretty cool, and many are adapted to each character, knowing that final roster size is 15.
- As items are uniques and most are adapted to each character, equipping characters of party is quite more complex than just pick best equipment that can wear each character in party.
IV - SURPRISINGLY INTERESTING WRITING
I can's say that the writing is great because it's a standard story and standard characters. But it is surprisingly interesting, it captures well the attention, it is easy to read, and it builds well the curiosity. Not sure why it worked so well even for a second play, what I quoted is:
- There are touches of gentle humor, and myself I enjoyed.
- I found most characters sympathetic, despite it's nothing very deep or original.
- The story brings well interrogations and suspense elements to increase player curiosity to know "what's next".
- One aspect is lacking a bit, the secondary missions tend have a too short story, and should have been more secondary quests with a real story.
V - SOME DETAILS NOT FULLY POLISHED
Since about 10 years, some indie games target an AAA polishing level for many aspects like UI, controls design, controls customization level, rules clarity, in game documentation, more.
Despite it's a game with a production level quite higher than many indie games, and with many aspects quite polished, it has also some polishing weaknesses, I quoted mainly:
- UI is overall good but has some weaknesses, overall it's quite playable anyway by learning a few shortcut, use mouse mainly, and disable option to request confirmations.
- It is missing a few more shortcuts and some more handy mouse interactions.
- Drag & Drop is a burdening mouse usage and nowadays a bit obsolete and replaced with click to pick something, move it, click again to drop it. The game UI implements it a few time but it's not consistent and not always possible.
- There's only 3 profiles and for each only 3 saves slots, it's usable but a pointless limit.
- You can't customize the keyboard keys and mouse buttons (probably not the gamepad buttons too).
- Despite a large part of the game is in 3D (not the UI) and characters have nice 3D graphics, the characters equipment isn't shown on the 3D characters. Ok with the large amount of unique items and the number of characters this would be a lot of work, but it's clearly a lacking aspect anyway, not really breaking the fun, but it would be great and fitting well the game design to have it.
- Combats graphic animations are ok, but it's nothing spectacular nor even noteworthy.
- On Mac the fullscreen mode let Menubar and Dock popup in game when mouse goes on top and bottom borders.
- It seems that first creation profile for a game newly installed on a computer can still cause a problem with a game stopped on a "please wait" message. Try again eventually in window mode not fullscreen and after even for new profiles it seems solve the problem. At least it happened to me in September 2017.
VI - CONCLUSION
It's already in the beginning of the review that starts with the summary, I copy/paste: Overall a great Tactic RPG focused on combats and party building both with a very original approach.
EDIT: Update after to have finish a second full play only at Veteran difficulty and did all secondary missions available, and there's plenty. Again, a lot of fun, again. It's a different challenge level, and Veteran difficulty shows more clearly that some heroes and setup are stronger in general. But there's still a lot of possibilities to experiment many different approaches. This game is a bit more for players that like experiement than those focused on optimization, great game overall but more food for the first category of players.

- THE REPETITION. Its so incredibly repetative that i have no desire to focus 70% of the time playing.
- Throughout the game there are a total of 3 moments when there would be "battle music" of some kind to add to the "epicness" of the situation and 2 out of 3 of the songs were terrible. Now I am sure that most of you will skip over this review, and for good reason, I have only played the game for just over 5 hours as of writing. I personally love how the game builds up tension and immersion, while still being fun to play (for the most part, I don't think I will return to the "Water Hazard" Chapter for a while), but there are a few issues, which effect my gaming experience quite a lot. What drew me to write a review for this otherwise great game, was the chapter "Highway 17". *Potential Spoilers ahead for those who haven't currently reached this chapter.*
When the chapter started, I had a feeling that I would not like "Highway 17" due to one gameplay aspect, the dune buggy. Traversing through the beach, getting to the area in which the rocket launcher is obtained was quite easy, however, it seems that Valve didn't prepare for a player as clumsy as I am to drive the buggy into water. This made the rest of the chapter, after the rocket launcher, unavailable to progress on. The buggy could not be driven out of the water, and the player has no chance of pushing it out, unless you have a bunch of grenades to get it onto land. This combined, with the lack of a save file reversing my idiotic mistake resulted in me quitting for a while. Infact, the only way I managed to reverse this was from the knowledge of a console command from a steam friend of mine. I am sure that this may have happened to other people less fortunate and without any knowledge of commands, so I'm putting it out there, if you have any reason to restart it, then use the command "map d2_coast_02".
Despite this issue, I have been able to enjoy the game very much, which was a surprise to me, as prior to this I haven't had many fps experiences. This judgement may be biased in some way, due to the summer sales discount, but I can confirm that this game is worth the purchase, just don't be as mindless as I am :P

It is hard for me to recommend Company of Heroes 2, even though it pains me not to, because I love the RTS experience Relic created in 2006 to universal acclaim with the original Company of Heroes. To this day, I maintain that the original Company of Heroes offers the best RTS experience in existence, and that qualification comes even as a huge RTS fan, playing most RTS titles available from the days of original Command & Conquer and Warcraft up through now. Although the core game of Company of Heroes 2 remains the same as the original, and so in many ways offers an unparalleled RTS experience, the menagerie of DLC offered has ruined the experience. Because of this, CoH2 is less balanced and fun than the original. On top of that, the other benefits offered in this sequel are minimal compared to the original, with many aspects actually receiving a downgrade. The end result is something I can only recommend if you are a die-hard Company of Heroes fan -- all other types of players I recommend skipping the sequel to the legendary groundbreaking game.
First off, the DLC offerings for this game is truly a mess, and the model Sega has employed seems to over-leverage -- and as a result -- kill a fan base. To explain: I am not a fan of DLC in general, although I can tolerate it when done correctly. Unfortunately Sega seems to have resorted to deceptive tactics, as it *appears* this game only has three DLC packs available for it on the Steam product page. The reality is much different -- in truth there are dozens and dozens of DLC packs, costing hundreds of dollars if all bought outright, but they are "hidden" on Steam and you can't view the product info page on them unless you are in-game or have a direct URL. My only theory as to why Sega has hidden all these DLC packs is that they want to control prospective customer's perceptions when they view the product page for this game. i.e. new players might be scared off when viewing the CoH2 product page on Steam, if they saw along with the main game dozens and dozens of DLC, along with a "ADD ALL DLC TO CART" button that has a price tag of HUNDREDS of dollars on it. The reaction might naturally be "Wow, this game requires a huge investment in time and money to get enjoyment out of it, I'm just going to skip it altogether". And honestly, that reaction is an accurate assessment of the investment required for enjoyment out of this game. On top of that, the value offered by some of the DLC packs is very questionable (coming in at $4 per commander, more on that below). As the various DLC offerings give players additional abilities in multiplayer matches, many have accused the whole DLC model as "pay to win", and they aren't wrong. The end result is that I've boycotted all DLC for this game outright. Without any DLC, CoH2 really has a dearth of content when compared to CoH1, and that is just unacceptable.
As far as other "improvements" expected in a good sequel, there aren't many. Most "improvements" really seem more like side-steps in most ways, not something which advance the game or RTS genre. The snow environment is neat, but the blizzard game mechanic offers novelty at best and is usually more or less just annoying when it happens. The Russians offer a new and refreshing perspective, but since they replaced the Americans & British, the swap is a wash when compared to CoH1. What's more, the expansions in CoH1 actually offer a total of 4 factions, which offers much more needed diversity of gameplay compared to anything Relic attempts to come up with its DLC commanders -- and even though the various commanders are cool, accessing them will require purchasing a boatload of individual DLC packs. What's worse is that the commander trees are gone and now you just get new commander abilities as the game progresses.  Relic keeps making new Commanders to offer more variety, but at the the end of the day, there are still only 2 factions in CoH2, while its predecessor has 4. That is reason enough to stick with CoH1.
Honestly, I think the biggest improvement has come in the graphics department, which is sad to say, since the graphics are only slightly improved more than 6 years after the original game was released. The improvement isn’t obvious either, as it comes mostly in the form of improved effects and scaling. More units are possible on screen (as squad sizes are always at least 4 in size, up from the CoH1's minimum squad size of 2), and the effect fidelity on explosions has been greatly improved. As impressive as CoH1's artillery barrages were, CoH2 has upped the ante, and the largest types of artillery are truly earth-shattering which cause awe that can jolt you away from all the intense close quarters combat that usually takes place otherwise.
There is little else offered in terms of straight-away “improvements” in this sequel. For example, although I think the automatch process has seen improvements (as it requires less time and effort to "play now" compared the original), custom games are now only accessible between friends.... this essentially means that all online matches are now Victory Point -- meaning there is effectively no way to play Annihilation mode online. That's a huge problem because the tone and shape of Victory Point style games is drastically different than Annihilation. As a player who enjoyed playing Annihilation mode about 90% of the time on the original game, this glaring omission alone is a deal breaker, not even considering all the other problems in this game.
If you're a fan of the original Company of Heroes, you are likely to be sorely disappointed with its sucessor. On the other hand, if you're new to Company of Heroes 2, even though the core gameplay experience remains unchanged, you might go with the logic of just “jumping to the sequel” as it will probably offer more improvements that you won’t be biased against not having played the original. But in reality, there really isn't much here that you can't get on the original. Furthermore, if you want to get a "complete" experience in CoH2, buying all the DLC out there would cost you hundreds of dollars more than the original. That coupled with the facts that you have four factions in CoH1 while only two in CoH2, and a lack of online Annihilation mode in the sequel, all leads to a clear conclusion: Company of Heroes 2 is overall an inferior experience compared to its predecessor, even when judged in the same light 6 years later. As a result, I cannot recommend this game.

Don't let the graphics fool you, this game is good and fun.
The gameplay is simple but pretty involved.  The bulk of your strategy will rely on mixing and matching equipment which are semi-randomly dropped from the missions you complete, equipping them to characters, and then selecting the right characters for a mission.  At a tactical level, the game can be a bit slow (dice assignment is time consuming and large maps with tons of enemies take a lot of time to get through) but is overall very rewarding.
Elements that detracted from the game include nearly everything left to random chance and not being able to save in the middle of a multi-map mission.  Battlefield control is kind of wonky; threat is well implemented but monsters can still run past your frontline without anything to stop or slow them down.  Also, there's no way to influence initiative that I could see.  Non-HP consumables seemed pretty useless... but I say that in almost every game I play so whatever.
The UI is adequate but could use a lot of polish to improve quality of life.  I would have liked to see an item-centric screen that lets me quickly see who can equip it and what the differences are.  Being able to adjust characters on the character... bar? on the bottom of the screen.  Saving consumable selection between missions.  Relatively small changes that could have improved my experience by quite a bit.

Les fourmis constituent la famille des Formicidae (ou formicidés en français) et, avec les guêpes et les abeilles, sont classées dans l’ordre des hyménoptères, sous-ordre des Apocrites. Ces insectes eusociaux forment des colonies, appelées fourmilières, parfois extrêmement complexes, contenant de quelques dizaines à plusieurs millions d’individus. Certaines espèces forment des supercolonies à plusieurs centaines de millions d’individus. Les termites, parfois appelés fourmis blanches pour leur ressemblance formelle et comportementale, sont de l’ordre des dictyoptères (sous-ordre des isoptères) mais ne sont pas de proches parents.
Les sociétés des fourmis ont une division du travail (polyéthisme d'âge et de caste), une communication entre individus et une capacité à résoudre des problèmes complexes. Ces analogies avec les sociétés humaines ont depuis longtemps été une source d'inspiration et le sujet d'études scientifiques.
En 2013, plus de 12 000 espèces ont été répertoriées1,2 mais il en reste probablement des milliers encore à découvrir. Famille cosmopolite (elle a colonisé toutes les régions terrestres à l'exception du Groenland et de l'Antarctique), elle atteint une grande densité dans les milieux tropicaux et néotropicaux3. Bien que les fourmis représentent moins d'un pour cent des espèces d'insectes, la masse de la myrmécofaune4 excède le poids de l'humanité et cette masse conjuguée à celle des termites représente le tiers de la biomasse animale de la forêt amazonienne.
Bref, malgré ses graphismes plutôt sympathiques, ce jeu est merdique.

Was a very nice tactical game.  85% rating IMO.

Pros:
Nice fluffy graphics
No randomness in combat actions.  You know exactly how much damage you'll do per atatck, and to whom.  Randomness instead based on initiative order each round and on distribution of dice rolled for each PC and major enemy.  You'll then know if your turn is going to be good or bad and prepare accordingly.  No 5 misses in a row at 95% chance XCom style.
Some nice customisation options for each character, be it weapons (AOE vs. single target armour piercing), armour (Heavy vs. faster), Amulet (Different active and passive abilities, including AOE party buffs within a small area), Misc (Extra HP?  Extra ARM?  Extra speed?  Auto enemy pushes?  Auto damage on nearby enemies?  Choose wisely - especially as some more powerful items are more likely to give you bad dice results.)
Cons:
A couple of missions I had to go to the forum as no idea what to do next.  I believe the mission text beign patched so you actually know how to find the missing villagers in one mission.
A couple of missions (Haunted House) dragged as had to loop back around a very mazey set of corridors.
Some options and characters did seem plain superior to others, but I think that's true of almost every game out there.  And finding the dirty combos is part of the fun of these games, right?
Shallow story - not an issue for me personally as I just need a little bit of narrative garnish between massive killing sprees.  But, be warned, Baldurs Gate 2 this ain't...
Item and equipment list gets cluttered.  Would be nice if you could bin certain items so they are not selectable (Maybe with option to search the bin if required) as no need to select from tier 1 weapons when up to tier 3.

Disappointing flight models. Even on 'Veteran' difficulty... It shouldn't really be advertised as being advanced.
I had sort of suspected that this would just be the helicopter parts of Arma, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, and to be fair its a little more than that. The flight models are more realistic than Arma, but they just still aren't that good.
You're able to make violent changes to the collective without any consequences. In a real helicopter, ANY change to the collective requires changes to the other controls.
In an out-of-ground-effect hover, the chopper behaves ok at first, collective needs to be higher than in forward flight, it wants to yaw and drift so you need to compensate, but you can then raise and drop the collective very quickly and ascend/descend as if on a ladder, with virtually no risk of a vortex ring state.
The cyclic and pedal response is far too instantaneous to be believable, the sheer speed at which you can change direction and attitude removes any illusion of weight and inertia. It never feels like a heavy vehicle hanging under a rotor system, but more like a go-kart driving on an invisible 'track in the sky'.
Although I've not spent much time looking, it seems that the cockpits and avionics are also very simplistic and startup procedures are not very authentic.
It kind of feels like an Arma 2 mod, rather than something thats supposed to be a flight simulator. Oh and the music is apalling.
As a game, its quite pretty, seems fun enough and would be interesting to flight enthusiasts, but as a simulator it's quite poor. If realism is important to you then DCS UH-1 is an infinitely better choice

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation is a sequel to the game industry parodying Hyperdimension Neptunia Re-, ahh the heck with it. It's a sequel to the game of the same name except change 2 to 1 and remove Sisters Generation from the title. Honestly, what were the creators thinking when they made that name?
Anyway, this game picks up three years after the events of the first game where you must once again tackle the foes of Gamindustri (no, not EA). This time around, however you aren't played as the voluptuous CPU Goddesses. You're playing their sisters, Nepgear, Uni, Rom and Ram. You'll see your characters grow from the start of the game to full fledged goddesses right before you eyes before you're done with this game!
Anyway, let's do a list of positive and negatives about the game when comparing it not only to it's predacessor but to the JRPG genre alltogether.
|||Positive|||
- There are a lot more plans to make than the first game. I mean a
more.
- There are less boobs in your face throughout the game. It's sorta your call on this, but less disraction = good imo.
- More characters are given full sprites instead of just a little picture box.
- The developers realized that the first game made you grind, so to remedy that but keep the RPG vibe, they made a plan which gives you a ton more EXP whenever you would normally earn it.
- We see characters using long range attacks instead of close range melee attacks.
- Vert's bust is still unmatched
- Uni is best CPU Candidate.
|||Negative|||
- Game crashes a lot more. There are instances where the game will just freeze entirely, like during transformations.
- Game looks, acts, and plays mostly like the first game with nearly no changes that are big.
- Game is infinitely shorter, with only a total of 5 chapters.
- There are a lot less references to pop culture in this game than in the first one. Bad!
- You don't get access to EXE attacks (bar 1-2 characters) until near the end of the game.
- No Peashy or Plutia
- Characters don't even seem to remember the events of the previous game. Meeting people they've seen before and acting like they've never heard of them.
- Gathering materials for plans is still a pain. Why do I need to farm this enemy a hundred times only for it to drop an item 1/10th of the time? And I have to get 5 of the item??? WHAT!?
- Chest Piece processors are gone except for specific ones. Anything you can buy (bar Devil) and the ones you get from story progression have no central/chest part. I spent hours looking for Flame C only to find out there wasn't one.
- This game is loud as heck. It's a lot louder than it's first game. You can put the volume down to 5 % and it still is loud.
Overall, it's alright. It's not as good as it's predecessor but it's solid. Pick it up if it's on sale and beat it.

Easily the best Company Of Heroes mod I've ever played; I can say that because I've played four different mods including this one.
Actual modern tanks and vehicles, such as the Abrams and four variants of the infamous Stryker (one of my guilty pleasures), are included and as available as they probably would be if this was a standalone COH game.
Alas, at this time of this review, Modern Combat still needs serious gameplay tweaks, mainly to artillery, vehicle combat, and the differences between the US Army and the Marines; the Chinese PLA could also use some TLC for most of their units too. I for one also hope for new voice acting for all three factions (who use the voices of the original game's Americans).
Regardless, the other COH mods I've played are hardpressed to compare to this one. A sequel, totally converted from Company Of Heroes 2 and including an Insurgent faction, would not be amiss.
As always, don't take my word for it - if you've got Company Of Heroes 1, try out Modern Combat and decide for yourself.

When Telltale's GoT was announced I was intrigued but also concerned how effectively the writer's would be able to build a credible story within Westeros.  Conceptually I was impressed by the introduction of a minor house as the focus of the story and by the development of the characters who belong to it.
From what seems to be a strong foundation the telling of the story itself falls short.  It's sad to try and "namedrop" principles from the franchise to float a nonexistent story but it's almost worse when storytelling suffers as result of their introduction.  The overwhelming gravity of plot armour destroyed much of the suspense and uncertainty that should have been one of the pleasures of the story.
George R. R. Martin writes a good dead guy. He takes us on a final first person journey with them to advance the story.  Telltale writer's do it reasonably well but they aren't Martin.  They do it with hamfists that feel like satire.  House Forrester drops like wheat under their unmerciful hand.  Where Martin kills character's for the story or to elicit a response from his readers they seem to try and do it in improbable volume because Martin does it.
Maybe I wanted a happier ending or wanted what felt like a greater degree of control.  Maybe someone is laughing at me and in their best XCOM voice is screaming, "That's Game of Thones Baby!!!".  I enjoyed the experience and struggled to bring the Forresters to their best possible ending.  For all intents and purposes I think I failed.  While it was am enjoyable storytelling experience it failed to deliver an illusion of free choice which is necessary for a great interactive experience.  A fair pass if not a glowing review.

When starting up
for the first time I was greeted with retro style pixel graphics combined with the dusty zest of an old Western movie. I grabbed my controller and jumped right in, since there was no tutorial, and promptly died. The game is a top down shooter that is very much like a bullet hell game. Shots are flying every which way as you run around killing bad guys and picking up the gold left behind. Despite being horrible at this sort of game I still found it fun and enjoyable, albeit frustrating. It’s a good game to pick up every now and again, especially to play with friends.
There is a story to the game but I won’t lie, I didn’t pay too much attention to it. From what I gathered there is a rich railroad baron named Cayton Boon and he’s making life miserable so a group of sharp shooters are after him. I am unsure if all of the characters know each or not, due to me not being very good at the game I didn’t progress very far in the story. There are currently three acts to the story and a fourth act coming shortly.
Where the game truly shines is arcade mode which I enjoyed a lot more than the story mode. You progress through short levels and at the end of each you can upgrade your character, making their shots hit harder or giving them protection from fire. You can also play with a friend go for versus mode, or even hop online to play with others. The game offers a fun experience alone but is even better with others. Whatever mode you play, you have the choice between eleven unique characters. You can use a controller or your mouse and keyboard though I preferred the controller. Each character offers a different play style, some use guns, others use bombs and one is actually a whole regiment of soldiers that loses a soldier with every hit. I loved the variety, however the game has no tutorial or training mode so the only way to learn is through trial and error.
The game has a decent user interface, but sometimes the text can be a bit tiny, such as when you’re selecting an upgrade in arcade mode. The graphics are great, it’s like a pixelated spaghetti Western in all of its cheesy glory. However, sometimes with all the action going on at the screen at once it can become a chaotic mess and disorienting, however that’s what most bullet hell games seem like to me. The music is very fitting of the game, has a great Western vibe to it and brings the package together well. You can buy the soundtrack separately if you like.
While a good game the price seems a bit high for what it currently offers. However, if you find this on sale or in a bundle then go for it. If you enjoy bullet hell style games or top down shooters this should be a fun experience for you.

Having played the original version way back when, I can happily say the full release is a hell of an improvement on what was already an amazing game. Fistful of Gun is one of those great arcadey games that work best in short bursts solo, or when playing along with a friend, either on a couch, or across the net with voice chat.
The game's a blast solo, sure, but the real chaos starts when friends start joining in, and mixing/matching the nearly dozen characters to see what mayhem can occur. With three people, suddenly kinves, bullets, and rockets are flying everywhere, all the players are screaming obscenities, and a half the challenge is trying to remember which projectiles you need to dodge. It's a difficult game, but not due to controls or unfair spikes, more that it's just shy of being a bullet hell at the later levels.
Pick it up, grab some friends and controllers, and you'll be laughing for days about just how silly fun the game is.

What I enjoyed about the game was it's positively preposterous plot, the colorful cast of characters, and their entertainingly eccentric encounters with one another. The game is full of wacky and zany comedy that constantly breaks the fourth wall and sometimes borders on the, "oh my god just shut up", line of nonsensical nonsense.
I'll be frank here. This is a very niche game that only people with a high tolerance for overly cute moe girl high jinks can really enjoy. As that is basically all there really is to the game. If you're looking for exciting and challenging gameplay or a deep and rich story with complex character development and well-written dialog... this is not anything like that.
But if all you want for a while is to play a light-hearted and colorful game that in no way takes its self serious at all, then that is exactly what you're going to get with this title.
Do I recommend this game to everyone? Heck no! But to the small audience that does enjoy what I've come to call, "Moe Girl Games", then yes I will recommend it to them.

Super Dungeon Tactics starts out as a fun little game, but then it goes downhill. Sometimes the GUI at the bottom of the screen pops up in your way. The biggest flaw, though, is that the deeper you get into the game, the cheaper it feels.The game also requires ridiculous amounts of clicking at times.
Furthermore, the difficulty levels (of which there are 6) are very poorly designed. Once you get into the game a ways, you will come to realize Normal mode is what most games would call hard mode. In the game's late levels, the game is ridiculously difficult even on the lowest difficulty levels (easy and casual). This of course strongly implies that the developers don't understand basic English words like easy, normal, hard, and casual...
Because of all this, the game becomes more of a chore than something fun to play. This is particularly true when you enter the bounty missions and challenge levels. The first challenge level in the game is quite stupid, even on casual mode! It feels like they just spammed a ton of strong enemies and called it a level. Sounds like the kind of level you'd get from a kid playing Super Mario Maker with absolutely no knoweldge of game design, doesn't it?
The devs obviously need to read up on game design, especially on the psychology of video games. Difficulty for the sake of difficulty is not the secret to good games. The book "Glued to Games - How Video Games Draw us in and Hold us Spellbound" is a very good one on the subject.
There are much better games than this, like Final Fantasy Tactics Advance, which is years old now. It's usually not a good sign when a years old game kicks your butt...

One of the best games I've ever played.
The game features two core gameplay elements. The first is managing your covert base and troops, which includes researching new equipment, building and upgrading facilities, customizing individual soldiers, using your aerial troops to defend against UFOs, and responding to alien threats.
The second gameplay element is the combat, which takes place during the main story missions, and when you respond to an alien attack on a certain area. The combat is turn-based and requires a great deal of strategical thinking. You'll need to utilize the abilities possessed by the 4-6 soldiers you control to eliminate the alien threat, save civilians, or complete a story objective.
Then there's the permadeath, which will actually♥♥♥♥♥♥you off to a great extent since you'll be constantly customizing, upgrading, and winning battles with your soldiers. If you make a huge mistake, watching them die for good is the most agonzing feeling, so much so, that winning a difficult battle without any losses can be very rewarding and a huge relief. It's funny, since the characters barely even talk save for a few military phrases here and there, and they have zero backstory. However, this allows room for you, the player, to formulate your own story for your troops. This system also forces you to cycle different soldiers in and out and to recruit and upgrade new troops to replace those that died again and again and again.
Overall, you will get many, many hours of enjoyment out of this game if you're into the whole base management and turn-based RTS genre. It is extremely fun, rewarding, and requires strategy in almost every aspect.

What I like about this game:
-Game play is fast while maintaing satisfying depth and variety (dice assignment has a lot to do with this)
-Is not too grindy, rather (as of right now) it feels just grindy enough
-Invokes feel of Super Dungeon Explore (SDE) Board game
-Pays homage to the 16 bit titles of yesteryear with its numerous nods JRPG tropes
-I'm left feeling excited about new content and DLC
This game is really gratifying. As many other reviewers have pointed out, there are some areas that really need polishing. That said, the devs seem quite responsive to user input, and they release patches on the regular. I've only played the board game on which this is based (Super Dungeon Explore, or SDE) in Arcade Mode. While this title is not a direct port of the board game, the game has captured the feel of SDE admirably. The story is lite, but compared to SDE - which has no story or character growth (SDE: Legends not withstanding) - anything is a welcome addition.
For my part, the quirks of interface and unpolished aspects are tolerable, and I remain confident that they will be addressed in time - i'd certainly not dissuade folks from getting this game on account of its issues if they are otherwise interested in it.
So - if you like tactics, JRPGs, cutesy anime, engaging game play, and fun in general - Super Dungeon Tactics is certainly worth it.

I agree with most that this game is short, and that it had the potential to do much more than it did with the unique plot. I, however, found this game to be very enjoyable. It had dark themes as well as some much appreciated crude humor (case in point: an achievement for getting "teabagged"). For an RPG maker game, it was put together very well. Hell you even get to drive a car and interact with a McDonalds drive thru (although its named Makku{?} in the game)!

I think this game has a lot of potential:  it has interesting and colorful graphics, the world itself is inspiring and the characters are endearing. However, they have a LONG ways to go. The game play is turn based, and I assumed this day in age that would mean something akin to "Dragon Age: Origins". Instead, I was presented with clunky mechanics and an abundance of confirmations for, seemingly, every single move. Also, the cut scenes are fun, but it doesn't feel like I am in the world. Cut scenes are fine, but I would like to see my third person characters actually walk around, interact with stuff, include some funny animation, etc. The reading sequences are exhausting. My suggestions:  1.) keep it turn based, but speed up the game play 2.) Include animations of the characters actually running to their move positions in battles sequences. 3.) Don't make it an option:  make the enemies all move simultaneously to speed up the gameplay. 4.) Show the characters enter and exit scenes to make the narrative feel more cohesive. 5.) The dialogue has potential, but needs some more punchy lines, perhaps a note could be taken from "Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars" for SNES. 6.) Don't have people right click the characters and then have to select a move with a left click 7.) Immediately ground your players by showing the world and where the characters are beyond the map in the intitial intro scene 8.) Add more sound effects to dialogue scenes:  no need to upgrade the animation, the simplicity is part of the charm, but it needs to be sold more.  Good luck creators and folks! I would not purchase this game for a few more updates.

This game has two big issues.
The first and most obvious is the casting. Because JRPGs are not games in the proper sense of the word, a JRPG sinks or swims on the quality of its main cast as charismatic characters, and this game has no single character I could root for. Neptunia's formula was an "Abbot&Costello" thing, and without Neptune to act as the Costello to everyone else's abbot, you end up with a cast of:
1) Awkward teen.
2) Wangsty teen.
3) Unsufferable brats.
4) Muggle supporting cast.
Not only none of them have enough redeeming quailties to hold the narrative's weight, as a formula, the team isn't funny, period. The comedy was stale, and Neptune arrived much too late to rescue the act.
Now, for the second problem. While the previous Neptunia game was already a "Nintendo Power game" (i.e a game you forcefully require an internet guide to finish to completion, because the Japanese are stuck in the 80's and they still think it's cool to "earn your fun" and trial-and-error everything, but back to the point...), there's a big difference between a game withholding bells and whistles without a guide, and the game denying you ACTUAL CONTENT without a guide, and unless you do a -very specific- set of things you can easily miss out, the game denies you the last two chapters, which is BS and sapped me of any enthusiasm to even try a replay.
I really hope Rebirth 3 does better than this.
TL;DR: Don't waste your time and money here, the series follows no continuity so you can go straight for Rebirth 3 and you'll have missed nothing.

Hard to write a Review for this but ill do my best.
I saw a trailer for this game and thought It looked like a decent RPG game, so i put it on my wish list, then the summer sales happened and I got this, at 75% off it was a steal, and it was an amazing game.
There are very few games out there, that hook me in, and actually make me feel "I wanna get all the achievements"
I played this game many many times, to see all the endings since it was tired to the Achievements (conquest ending the worse, and made me feel like I was stabbed in the heart So depressing ><)
But lets talk about the game.
It takes place 3 years after the first one, Though by the intro I dont think you need to play the first, since it seems the first ended on a cliffhanger
You play as Nepgear, in the world of Gameindustri You fight along side your friends IF and Compa, in a effort to Save your sister, and the other captured sisters from the other nations.
The game has alot of References, since its all around well Gaming, the 4 nations represent Sega, Nintendo, Playstaion and X box there is alot of minior details, such as outfits, NPCS quests mobs, all sorts, that goes back to the olden days of gaming.
All the Sisters, are known as CPU's or "Goddess" and all can transform, there detail form usually represents the console that they are, Such as the Leanboc (Xbox) her transformation matches the X box console through its evolution.
Combat is pretty good as well, each character having a wide "Circle" they can move in, and then you combo attack Later on in the game, you earn "Exe" which unlock a devastating special attack (Caves black label is my fave.)
Overall I love the charaters Vert the Leanbox CPU Cave, And nepgear are among my faves The story is good too with alot of references, fourth wall breaking jokes and more.  Having said that also, the game is from japen, so some scenes might seem alittle strange For example, one of the Main Villians wanting to Marry two of the Youngest Sisters, and i mean young!  And there is a groping scene where our party gets attacked by goodogs.  And of course there is the Hot springs scene too.
Voice acting is top notice, but the characters avatar, doesnt lip sync well, And there is a huge lack of cutscenes Due to the game starting on psVita i believe most Cutsences are in Pictures, with "Jiggle" around
There is also a mini game "Stellas dungeon" where you send a npc off, to dungeon crawl, dungeons you done before to find you gear, and treasures but at later stages it gets super hard (specially the last when the floor 1000 boss can crit for 9999 damage!)
Another Aspect of the game is the "Plans" part, this will allow you to make certain things, if you have the Materials such as Weapons, Armor, Outfits for the girls, Bonous to xp, credit drop weaker monsters.
