I hope you're not like me and bought this thinking "Super Dungeon Tactics? A grid based turn battle system?  Huh...I wonder if it's like Final Fantasy Tactics?"  Don't wonder any longer because it isn't.  I'm quite sure the game developers didn't spend any time looking over that game's shoulder or they would have got some pointers on how to get gamers more invested in the characters they played.  I could comment on how cartoony the charaters are, but Final Fantasy Tactics was the same (only their cartoony characters were capable of treachery and betrayal, making the overall mood of the game dark and oppressive).  However, this game is far more light-hearted and not nearly as deep but the playable characters  ... just show up ... they can be quirky but nothing draws you to them.
I played the game with medium difficulty, shrugging off that it was nothing like FFT - yet I still had one major issue with it.
In a turn based game, having a large opposing force is not challenging - it is boring.  Waiting for twenty enemy units to complete their turns made me feel like I should be folding clothes in another room while the enemy did his thing.
And...the enemy also has spawners.  With a turn-based game, this is very bad.  While carefully chipping away at the enemies already on the map, the spawner can summon a sizeable army within six turns or so - giving them many attacks in succession that can easily kill a tanky character that was at full health while you still struggle to take down a heavily armored enemy with your small team.  Enemy spawners are not unheard of in tactical games but I would hope if the game sets you up to fight an army in turn based combat, you get to have an army too.   Unfortunately, just about the time where playable characters start arriving in twos and threes, the game starts to limit your access to them.  Meaning, your overall team chilling back at the guild hall could be sizable but you only get to utilize a scant few of them at a time depending on the mission.
Dull story, dull characters, extremely boring waits while swarms of enemies move in one at a time to slaughter your poor overwelmed heroes.  Yawn...delete.

The game does an adequate job of providing tactical, turn-based play. However:
-'Creating a Guild of Heroes' is a bit of an embellishment.
There's less of creating a guild, more of following mobile-esque story missions which add new characters to your pool. The bounty missions do a good job of providing loot, but they're limited. I don't see how there would be much replayability after you go through the story line once.
-It fails to adequately explain its mechanics.
Why are enemies getting buffed when I select dice? How does equipment affect my dice rolls? At what darkness level do spawners release spawns?
-The UI is tedious and woefully inefficient.
Before the start of a mission, if I haven't selected any consumables, I need to leave the mission select screen, go back to the main guild screen, go to the item select screen, select consumables, then go back to the main guild screen and then back to the mission select screen. The same situation if I haven't selected heroes. Additionally, once I go through that menu dance, if I click on a new mission, or even the same mission, my item/hero selections disappear and I have to do it all over again. Simply saving the last item/hero loadout, with a button to change the loadout right on the mission select screen would save a lot of clicks and minimize some frustration.
During combat, the lack of hotkeys or even a hotbar is frustrating. Given the relatively few number of actions available per character, the actions I can take should simply just display near the bottom of the screen; I shouldn't have to keep clicking a character to click the end turn button.
-There is no feedback to the player after the completion of a mission.
In the event that you get loot during a battle, the excitement of discovering what, exactly, that loot was is left to the player to figure out--by going through the many guild hall menus. A relatively simple solution would be to show exactly what those items acquired are at the end of a successfully completed mission, and, even better, an opportunity to have that item immediately equipped.
Again, the most critical element, the tactical gameplay, is solid, however, everything leading up to and away from that gameplay is a headache. With some common-sense quality of life UI changes and a more detailed explanation of its systems, this could potentially be a game worth playing.

Okay, I'm updating the review now to reflect my thoughts after sinking another few hours into this charming little game.  Please see the bottom of this review for the old one, and the comments section for my main criticisms and feedback.
Short review - This would be a lot of fun in multiplayer (I've only played single player), and it would eliminate the grinding feel somewhat.  It also appears to be balanced towards multi, rather than solo, which needs addressed.
It takes a few hours for your character to start becoming viable, and the ranged weapons really are a lot better than the melee if you are solo.  The bows with their backwards jumping missile attack are way overpowered, making them the best weapon to use if you want to survive a while between deaths.  It is actually more like the other weapons are all under powered.
The lack of solid dodging ability really makes the game suffer, but again this may be negated in multi as someone will be helping you fight.  The grinding aspect of the game really was making me not want to play, but the charming visuals kept me coming back.  Now I'm a higher level the game is still one long grind, but it is becoming much more fun now I'm not moving at a snail's pace and I can actually take and deal a bit of damage.
Your mileage may vary on this one, so I'm recommending it as a maybe, rather than a full yes.  If the solo balance is fixed, and a decent dodge / block added, it will definitely be a full yes.  Try the demo if there is one.

The Game as such manages to capture the spirit and idea of the Game of Thrones, but really it is a pale picture. The story itself lends a lot from the actual song of ice and fire, mimicking Sansa's predicament and the Stark's situation in the North. While cleverly intervined with the rest of the GoT universe, it would have been nice to actually see places and parts of the world we have not see yet, something more innovative.
That said there are mostly points of criticism:
- the story is very linear and does hardly differ depending on what choices you make. there really is only one decision which shapes one chapter, but really, the end of the whole story is so fatalistic that it makes no fun to replay the game, because in the end nothing you did before matters and your characters could as well all died earlier
- the violence is even worse than the series, but does not manage to shock it is more boring and creates "oh, come on really?"-moments.
- the graphics are very low quality. While they try to hide that fact behind an imitation of "comic" style still texture details are very low res, as is the sharpness of the figures. the worst thing with that is that it is all pre rendered (looks like done with Poser) and therefore there should be a lot power to do better. furthermore most figures look the same, hardly any variation here.
All in all the game is not really worth replaying, although there are some moments of suspense. It is a filler until the next GoT season, but really nothing more.

This is a complicated game to give a score to. The story stage-setting (we'll see how it develops) and the world & environments are amazing - been a long time since I saw anything that good. The skill-tree progression is also good. Usually in these types of games you put a few points in an initial skills which you'll then abandon more or less (except for passives) once you get higher-tiered skills. In this case (at least so far) further branches simply improve upon base skills, which is a lovely concept - however, it also gets VERY repetitive as you don't get to try out anything new. They also separate class levels so if you want to get to a higher level faster you could just ignore putting points in skills and just improve the class. The idea of devotions (which I'm still not quite sure how it will turn out) is also interested. The skills (at least for the class I'm doing) are also pretty good. Usually a game has 3 branches of skills with something like 10-15 skills/branch, only a fraction of which are actually useful. In addition to improving on base skills, the base skills themselves are incredibly useful. The dual-classing is also interesting allowing you to experiment - say having a wizard that doesn't die as soon as a monster farts in their general direction.
My main gripe with this game is that it's just too damn easy. I started at normal for while I play one of these games once in a while I have no illusions that I'm good at them - I died all the time when I played torchlight 2 (and that was on normal). Except for "champion monsters" there's really no challenge. I'm playing as a wizard (or arcanist in this game) and 1-2 hits of the base skill they die. And I'm not just talking about the first type of monsters too. I've died ONCE in 3 hours (hell, I don't even lose any health most of the time). I checked "veteran" which is supposed to increase the difficulty level - can't say I noticed much difference. I'd like to increase the difficulty, but the developers locked that option - you get a higher difficulty only once you finished it once. It's a good idea actually - allow you to keep challenging higher once you finished it - something Torchlight 2 does not allow, where the Game+ mode on Normal simply wasn't enough for me to care. But in order for the idea to work, the normal difficulty needs to be challenging, and it really isn't.
So, in summation - interesting stage-setting, wonderful word & gameplay mechanics - it's just too easy.
I would not recommend this at full price, at what I got it at, which is a 50% sale, it's just about worth it, because it's still an interesting game.

30$ plus 30 more to fix the game with an expansion is way too much for a unfair three years old unpredictable tactic RPG.
Here the long version
This game has ENORMOUS game design flaws that makes this TACTIC RPG unpredicatable, the encounter system forces you into extreme caution and creates boring gameplay. Also, this game's UI and engine are super buggy. Most of the problems can be fixed by a 30$ expansion, but the bugs aren't patched in the regular game.
First of, the difficulty is artificial. This game is not hard if you know what you're doing, but RNG makes it unpredictable. Sometimes you miss 95% shots. It happens and is not inhenrently bad game design. What is bad game design is when you cannot prepare in a tactic RPG. Sometimes enemies just spawn next to you and uses overwatch, which means your first priority is to kill that enemy because he prevents you from repositionning safely. But when that enemy dies, he explodes into a poison cloud on one of your unit that you could not move without getting shot and killed. There are plenty of those unpredictable situations that makes the game smiply unfair instead of difficult.
The way you encounter enemies is also very flawed. Since you are very vulnerable to aliens because there is very little full cover (at least in Enemy Unknown), you advance very, very slowly, which creates boring missions. If you don't move slowly, you encounter several alien groups in one turn and they simply kill you. Sometimes alien run into you during their turns, at which point they are given another turn to reposition because aliens do not have good enough AI to move from cover to cover in the fog of war. This si not a huge problem, but it still creates this impression that the game is cheating you. Sometimes, during the aliens' turn, multiple groups of them walks in your line of sight. This creates situations in which you are at a clear disadvantage only because of the game's RNG.
The UI is extremely buggy and lacking. First of, you cannot know what your soldiers are able to shoot before moving. This forces you to take moves without knowing what follow ups are possible afterwards. The lack of indication on your line of sight (and the aliens' line of sight) makes it that you have to GUESS in a TACTIC RPG, which is exactly what you are trying to prevent in this genre of games. You cannot take the less risky move if the game lacks a UI that indicates what the safest move is. Sometimes, parts of the UI don't load, which leaves you waiting 10 seconds for the max distance of a soldier's move to load. When you shoot a rocket or a smoke grenade, the game shows you a sphere to indicate the range of the explosion. That sphere is lying. The range is actually a bit smaller than what it shows you, which can result in you wasting ressources because of the terrible UI.
This game has a weird way to show the results of its RNG calculations into the engine. Sometimes, you miss, then the game shows you shooting into the alien's shoulder three times and tells you you missed. Sometimes you shoot trough ally soldiers or walls, without breaking the walls, etc.
I think the worst about this game is how most of these UI problems are fixed through the game's expansion, Enemy Within. The 30$ patch provides other gameplay elements, but, most importantly, it fixes issues with the original game. For exemple, rockets indicators now changes to red everthing that will be damaged by the explosion. This is nice, sure, but these changes were not patched into the regular game. This basically makes Enemy Within a paid patch and renders this game alone a TERRIBLE value proposition.

It really shouldn't be surprising, though. After all, Relic is no longer what it was after the death of THQ, having been sold to Sega during CoH2's development along with the loss of most of the staff. What you have here is a hack-job cash-in on what Sega purchashed. Too bad, really.

No experience gained from battles, no money to buy items for healing and the like. These are not necessarily bad, but just makes the game not for me, not my style. This game has a lot of things that are different from what people might consider a "normal" Tactical RPG. It has the normal mechanics, and then it has some strange ones. Turn based fights, with squares, which is par for the course, but the weapons and armor decide your level, abilities and the dice that are rolled at the start of every round. The side of the die decies what each character gets as a buff or debuff for that round. This is an interesting mechanic, coupled with everything else.
I had a bit of fun at first, but after I got out of the tutorial and into the game, doing a few missions, it struck me hard. Not getting experience or any type of money for completing the missions, just isnt for me. You get story or bounty missions, and what you earn in those bounty missions, is items such as gear or useable items like healing sodas. Some people will probably like this, as while it seems different and difficult, it is VERY simple and straight forward. You should not have a steep learning curve here, and after a few battles you will get how to play the battles to best survive.
All this being said, I prefer a more typical RPG, where you gain experience to gan levels, and the levels increase your stats. For this reason, I just can't play the game, but I CAN recommend this game to ANYONE that is willing to play a tactical RPG, with some cute graphics and humor, with different game mechanics than the normal tactical RPG.

All together I give it a 9/10!

Would recommend but only if you've played the first Re;Birth game beforehand.

So this is being review by someone who has never played the board game and at around 1.5 hours of gameplay time. The time I feel many people choose to keep or refund their games. Here are my personal impressions:
TL:DR
This is a nice little turn based rpg. You are builing up a guild, thus having a bunch of hero's to choose from. Each with their unique play style. These are you basic archetypes: barbarian, mage, rouge, ranger, etc. The graphics are not amazing, but the art sytle agrees with how it is implemented and its humor imo. As other have said, the music is repetitive. I have not found it annoying yet, but I have not played it for more than 1.5 hours at time of review.
My rant:
Gameplay:
I really am enjoying the gameplay. The best thing i can relate the combat to is XCOM EU/XCOM2, only with reguards to actual combat. There is no meta strategy that I have come across yet. However, this is like xcom-light, since there is no percentage hit calculation. You will always hit your enemy. Many people will perfer this to xcom's rng demons ( i like them, but also enjoying this as well).
From what I can tell, each hero gets an action and a movement, in any order. An action can be an attack, or an environment interaction. Consuming an item is a free action. Die are used, but only to give buffs/debuffs to your heros at the begining of each turn. This helps keep the combat a bit different every turn imo. Other reviews have said that the game does a good job of making your heros feel strong, by throwing waves of enemies at you and watching your guild mates crush them, which i fully agree with. This is not to say the game is a cake walk. Under harder difficulties, one wrong move will spell disaster for your heroes.
Another positive point is that there is no lvling for your heros. Yes, I said that this is a GOOD thing, imo. You see them get stronger purely based on items/equipment. This means the heros you may not use often will not get left behind as you will aquire loot for them even if they are not in your party. This allows you to change party comp between missions at will without worrying about not lvling your favorites.
So, it is obvious I like this game, but I will point out some flaws that I believe people should know before purchasing:
* Everything is done purely using the mouse. No key mapping at all. They have said they looking in to fixing this in a patch, but it shouldnt have been an issue. You are builing a pc game.... you should be able to use a keyboard. Unless it was initially intented to be a mobile game.... i digress.
* I can tell that the story will not be something that will pull you through the game. It is kinda interesting and a bit funny ish... The combat is enough for me to enjoy it for the price, but I know others may need a well written plot, which I do not see this as being anything other than building up a guild to accomplish harder and harder missions.
* Every hero is predesigned. You cannot change appearance, sex, hair, etc. The only thing you can change is their name. Not an issue for me, but I know some people hate this.
* My largerst complaint in this game, which I have seen this problem occur more frequently over time, is that new items and gear do not look any different! I hate this with a passion. So i finished the first non-into/tutorial mission. During the fight I saw that an enemy dropped an orange weapon! :) I went to my guild hall to look and it was a bad♥♥♥♥♥looking bow for my ranger. Much more intimidating than her current twig-bow. I equipped it and...... still looks like a twig bow. Same with armor. Come on devs! You have only 2 appearnce changing item slots! ( there is also accessory as well as some diamond type item, which seems to boost archetype stats, like my dwarf has the 8-bit guardian which increased defense die stuff) Let us see those bad♥♥♥♥♥items on our heros. Since we dont have lvling in the game, items are the only way to see growth, and I want to SEE it, not just look at stat increases. I know it is based off a board game, and you dont change the mini for every item, but use the video game medium to do things you couldnt do on the tabletop.
Rant over...
So, I will definitly be finishing the game over the next few months. I think it is worth the price and a really fun little tbsrpg. Small problems aside, if you really enjoy tbsrpg combat and the thoughts of building up a guild, then this is a good game for you. I will update review with info on more features as they present themselves.

Review:
Today’s review was still selected by automaton thanks to the folks at steamholic, and this time, though I had seen ads for this game before, and have actually seen a few recommendations for this one, I can safely say that I had yet to really see enough to know what Fistful of Gun was before I opened it up, so this really is a first impressions review in most senses of the word.  That being said, I will make the statement that the first fifteen minutes I spent in this game, i spent playing around with the steam controller configurations, because the submitted ones didn't seem to work right.  This, of course, is to an extent how it should be, as one of the key interesting factors of this top-down 8 bit bullet hell shooter is that each of the 11 characters you can play with actually uses a completely different set of controls, for aiming, firing and reloading, and as a result each character adds a new dynamic to the gameplay.
Structurally the game is fairly simplistic.  Due to standard western plot device number thirteen, you are out to kill a railroad baron that apparently is also a jerk.  Your goal is to take your gun and/or guns and travel through twelve different levels killing western villains who try to shoot at you.  Between the different levels and learning the new weapon for the new character, the game has a surprisingly high replay value, and that's notwithstanding the multiplayer modes (which I was unable to play during my sample)  The graphics are beautiful even if the colors are rather samey (typical old west browns and the like.  And the character models are fantastically detailed for being sprites.  I have a fondness for the old 8-bit styles, and this game plays faithfully to the traditional styles of gaming while being a fresh take on the western genre.  All in all, a solid game, worth every penny you want to put into it.  If you pick it up, you may see me online at some point.
Game’s Fate: Kept, and played.  Will have to work out the odd control schemes, but after that, this game is totally worth the time
Buy/No Buy: I won’t deny I am a big fan of basically all the Devolver games, but this one in particular is especially worth it.  Buy Buy Buy

Welcome to the Wild West! A Fistful Of Gun is a fast-paced top-down shooter with rogue-like elements separated into 2 main modes: Arcade and Story. There's 11 different characters to choose from, each of them comes with unique controls and their own fighting system. The game has full controller support but for some characters you have to switch to keyboard & mouse, otherwise the game won't let you play them. When you start up the western action for the first time, you most likely begin with Arcade Mode that lets you pick all of those characters. Which is nice for practice purposes but can be terrible if your first choice is one of the guys with very odd controls. I have to admit I rage-quitted the game after two short runs of Arcade because I thought there's something wrong with the Steam Controller bindings (I'm using a template from the community). The character 'Noah' was the reason for it though. He's on the very left of the character select screen and why would you not start from the left?
Well, obviously I gave the game another shot after checking the discussions and finding that other cowboys play very differently. I didn't regret starting it again because I found myself getting addicted to this little gem. Let me know tell you more about the main modes:
: You can select any character and start on a warm-up map. The goal is to clear the screen to get to the next one and reach the highest score. The maps and enemies are randomized but get significantly more difficult over the time. After you cleared a screen, the game gives you the option to choose among 5 random upgrades to make yourself stronger. One shot or hit of an enemy kills you and takes a life (in form of a card). You start with five hearts but a horse - that you can either steal from an enemy or get through an upgrade - or an armor upgrade take 1 bullet instead of you which basically means an extra life. Arcade can be played in single-player, local and online multiplayer.
: Unlike Arcade mode, you can only pick one of the three already unlocked wranglers to start your journey with. The goal is to reach the 3rd chapter and kill the railroad baron Clayton Boon, the reason for all our troubles along the way. Each chapter ends with a unique boss fight and is 14 miles (= 14 screens) away from the start. Just as in the other mode, the enemies, type of maps and events are randomized, although you decide which direction you want to continue on. But keep in mind: There is no going back. Coins that you collect can be spent on several things such as new weapons, upgrades, playing cards (very important to increase the amount of your lives).  Unfortunately the story can only be played alone or in local co-op and there is no support for playing it online.

It has many of the same problems as Titan's Quest, but also many of the triumphs.
Fundamentally speaking, this is Titan's Quest with a total conversion ontop of it.  All the system are going to be familiar with some tweaks.  Classes work the same way (except the skill tree is horizontal instead of vertical), and there's a secondary progression system to EXP.
I haven't played TQ in a while, so I can't specifically compare, but it feels like this game isn't quite so endlessly long as Titan's Quest felt for me  (which made it daunting to want to play through more than once), but the bosses in Grim Dawn feel so underplayed, the whole game feels like it's one act of TQ.
Now this is all well and good, except for many of the new things Grim Dawn brings to the table.
The existence of Scrap and Dynamite serve such a sporatic use, and drop in such a specific manner, that it adds deliberate farming to the game to accomplish certain tasks.  While this already exists in how one would find the upgrade materials, they have a more specific use.  Crafting components would fall into this capacity if it weren't for that the core component that drops from certain enemies should never need to be farmed.
There's also an additon of a Faction system and Bounties to support this.  This system undercuts the game in two different manners:  First, the faction system is straight out of an MMO, and requires time spent simply to raise these values.  You will find literally zero use out of the factions without this;  Second, there are mutually exclusive factions, and without looking up these factions, you can have no real concept of the value of choosing one over another.  Lastly, the bounty system requires faction to even unlock.  The entire system is daft at best.
Then, we have the problem of leveling.   Monsters appear to level with you for large portions of the game, and so the gear they drop, which has level restrictions, will frequently be well outside of your level to equip (Most recent drop I got was +6 levels), leaving to a very neutered gear experience.
The elements of the game offer some kind of replayability, but in a forced manner instead of an organic one.
Beyond that, you're getting largely the TQ experience without it being rooted in any kind of historical context.
Fundamentally, I'm not recommending the game because it feels like it tacked on game elements to TQ that detract from the overall experience.

Ant War: Domination is like a clicker game combined with some strategy. You take the lead of an ant colony and must build up your army until you take over the world. You’ll need to breed ants, get food, and build up your army so that you can defend yourself from the world.
To manage your ants, you must set what percentage of each type you'll have doing that job. Gathering food and having a decent army are all pretty important. The more you grow your colony, the tougher your opponents will become.
The problem with Ant War is that is all you do. You set what percentage of each type do each job and then just watch, sometimes interacting when it comes to doing battle. Sometimes, even if you're able to win a battle, the game will still suggest you run away. The goal is so exceptionally high that it's not something you'll just complete in a few hours.
I cannot recommend Ant War: Domination at all, and I'd rather recommend you find a game that actually lets you interact a bit more. The constant "Like us on Facebook!" ads also get exceptionally annoying whenever you level up, and really do make it feel like a flash game (perhaps because it was one).
If you liked Diablo II or Titan's Quest you owe it to yourself to check this one out!

This game is what seems to be a mildly successful first attempt at someone using an RPG maker engine. Overall, however, I feel I must give it a 2/10
[MILD SPOLERS BELOW]
Graphically, I'd say it sits comfortably at a 4/10. While utilizing mostly RTP assets, there are cases where the creator clearly made something somewhat custom. However some effort in finding more reasonable face graphics would not have gone arwy.
Audio is a 5/10, though again it seemed to be mostly RTP. For the most part well placed, there were a couple incidents where changing the music would have given the scene more depth and intensity.
Programming is where the game starts to trip over itself and has me giving it a 2/10. Glitches were present both graphically and situationally.
Story/Interactions is the make or break in this case and I'm afraid the game broke hard at a 1/10. The general premise of the story, which is 'girl spends one day in the lives of some elderly person and choses their fate', is a very interesting one with a lot of potential, however this is where a lot of the shortcomings lie. While initially giving off an 'always sometimes monsters' feel in the beginning, it's quickly made apparent that you have a very small amount of game impacting choice. Most of the time I felt Iwas running blind with no direction, and the main 'antagonist'[if we can call her that?] has less personality going for her than a silent protagonist.
Of the four people's who's lives you take part in, I feel as though the depth and effort put into them were horribly skewed. On one hand, you have a hallucinating woman with too many cats where you can have some measure of choice in their fate, and a decent amount of development in who she is; on the other you play a nurse before randomly popping into a kitchen with a grumpy and slightly sexist man who you can then poison. In the latter example, you never even learn his name or the story. It felt as though it was thrown together in just a small handful of minutes and I still don't understand how supposedly poisoning a man in a fever dream before death made an impact in real life?
IN CLOSING

Having completed one playthrough of this game, I found it to be charming and fairly thought-provoking. It starts out fairly average, leaving the player to feel as if they are simply going about their character's normal life... which they are. Little will you know until later on how ironic the character's comment, "I am taking control of my life" is, in consideration of what happens next.
It doesn't take long to finish the game, but the different outcomes you can get for different, vital choices in the game encourage more than one playthrough, at least if you're curious how fate can happen differently. Overall it's pretty straightfoward though, and you get to experience life through the eyes of different people and become responsible for their fate... literally.
My favorite thing about the game is that the antagonist isn't painted in black and white; she isn't necessarily evil, even if she denies responsibility for any of the tragedies that happened (even if she is a direct influence and she is responsible for placing you in a position where you can make potentially bad choices). However, it could be argued that she is simply trying to enhance your knowledge and your perception on life... even if her reasons for doing this are unclear.
Either way, it's definitely worth a playthrough or two. Especially if you're in a mildly sadistic mood.

To those not aware, this is an adaption of Ninja Division's very fun Super Dungeon Explore board/miniatures game. I wanted to get this review in quickly since there doesn't seem to be a whole lot said about the quality of the game in the current (all-positive) reviews:
First of all, there are notably low-quality aspects of the game right off the bat. Rough edges, if you will. There are interface oddities that make em think this was really meant to be a mobile game. There are some exceptionally ugly icons. The soundtrack, while cute in short bursts, becomes monotonous in minutes. Etcetera.
Second of all, if you're here because of the brand, please know that this is not a true recreation of Super Dungeon Explore. It has its own systems, it simplifies combat dramatically, and it's very quest-oriented in a way that the board game never could be. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as the game plays very smoothly and quickly, but please don't go into this expecting a faithful recreation of a game you already love.
Finally, though, the game plays very well. Specifically it walks the fine line of making your character feel "overpowered" as they mow down anemies with weapons and magic, while also making the game challenging by throwing hordes of enemies at you. I'm enjoying it quite a lot.
PROs:
++Fast tactical combat
+RPG mechanics
+Source material
+Quick "rounds"
CONs:
-Poor visual quality
-Mobile-style controls
-The music
-JRPG tropes, everywhere
If it appears interesting in the trailers, I would encourage anyone to try it. That said, feels beta-quality in a lot of regards, so a $20 price tag may feel like a lot for the end result.

So, I have to say guys that when the game first started I immediately thought “This is definitely a Far Cry Game” Meaning that yes, I was immediately sucked in to the visuals of the game. The developers did a wonderful job conveying the experience of being a caveman armed with nothing but a spear, fighting for survival when literally everything in the world is in a kill or be killed state. However, there ARE certain drawbacks in attempting to convey such a primitive time in such a format.
Mainly is the lack of meaningful technology. You’re a CAVE MAN. Which means the equivalent of what they had to work with was “Here’s your rock. Here’s your sharp stick. Go nuts.” Unfortunately, the length of the game requires a certain amount of variety in weaponry or else it would get boring VERY quickly. They attempted to stave that boredom off by introducing the Bow and Arrow, “Stink bombs”, and magical sharp rocks in order to try and flesh out your weapon set. And for a while, it works… but in the end the boredom and repetitiveness of the fetch quests and needless grinding wear on you and will definitely take their toll. Couple that with their re-using NPCs for minor quests gives the game a shallower feeling than it should otherwise have.
TONS of repetitive fetch-quests, rescue missions, and gathering of crafting materials artificially pad this game in a very uninventive and extremely iterative fashion. Ubisoft did nothing to innovate in this game and it clearly shows here as after 20 hours of play, the senseless grinding got to be too much and I found myself drifting away and my desire to go back and play more slowly grew less and less frequent until it finally stopped completely, leaving the game un-finished.

Very fun game to play with friends.  There are a lot of weapons to choose from each with various unique abilities.  Gameplay can get a little repetitive sometimes, but I think with a lot of roguelikes out there that is to be expected since you are replaying the entire game over and over again with each death.  The developers also seem to be pretty responsive to criticism and updates, and that is very nice to see.
A few changes I would like seeing:
1.  I think this game would suit 4 people even better than just 2.  I see no reason that you wouldn't be able to add 2 extra players to this game.  The graphics interface for 2 people ends at the middle of the screen from the left side, so it's not even like they'd have to find room for player 3 and 4.  They could extend it to the right.
2.  I sorta liked the goblin castle music during early access.  It seemed sorta goofy and funny.  When I started it up yesterday I noticed it had changed to a more upbeat serious tone.  I hope we might get a feature to customize music for levels if possible, but I know that's a bit to ask for.
3.  Increase player speed.  We walk too slow to effectively dodge enemy attacks.  It's not impossible to dodge them as it is, but being faster would be a huge quality-of-life upgrade and make you feel more in control of your character rather than just losing because of the player's low speed restriction.  I think a lot of people who play this game probably feel the same way.
Other things I think of to balance the game a bit more might be to slow down the attack speed of the trees in act 2.  Those guys are not fun to fight at all.  And also decrease damage taken to zero when holding up a shield.  There is no reason to hold up your shield when you think you might be hit because you'd almost always rather dodge the attack instead.  This makes the sword and shield quite underpowered weapons compared to the other ones in my opinion.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who's looking for fun co-op games with one other friend, and I hope the developers take my suggestions into account for future updates.

Lost Castle is a fast paced, cartoonish, rogue-like game. I would describe it as a combination of Rogue Legacy, Castle Crashers, and Binding of Isaac. If you like any of these three games, you'll find something to like in Lost Castle.
Learning the basics of the game is pretty easy, but after the first few screens you'll find the difficulty ramping up quickly. The bosses especially are tough, but they're a lot of fun and there's a lot of enemy variety. I played for a few hours, and I managed to get to the third chapter (the game has permadeath). There are different classes to unlock, and you can earn experience to spend after you die. So the game becomes easier on subsequent runs... I could imagine this game becoming very addictive.
The art style is clean and cartoonish, and the music and sound effects are solid. The game clearly has high production value, and I didn't notice any bugs when I was playing it.
Overall, if you enjoy rogue-likes, or side-scrolling action RPGs, you'll probably like Lost Castle.

Over 36 hours and still haven't completed it on easy. This is a great game, until a few things start getting to you:
1. It's all random. Doesn't matter how well you do, there is no way of being good enough/powerful enough to complete it if you have even one stroke of bad luck. the only thing that matters is how lucky you are.
2. Literally cheating. Okay, you may not call this cheating. But it's not like when you blame the game and it is clearly you that was at fault. The final boss may be just about to die, and let out 15 or so blasts at once, completely randomly (it doesn't always happen). The only possible way to protect yourself from that would be to cloak immediately. But if you don't have cloak, or don't have it recharged at that second, or the reflexes of The Flash, you are instantly dead. Game over. 1-3 hours. Gone.
3. All punishment, no reward. How do you unlock ships that aren't aweful? Beat the boss. How do you realistically have a chance of beating  the boss? Use ships that aren't aweful. Before, you could find the things to get the new ships, but I imagine that was removed because they literally never happened for most people. Me included. The punishment comes in because each time you loose, after hours of playing, you get NOTHING out of it. Nothing to help you next time- UNLESS you beat the boss and unlocked a new ship (or managed to unlock the few poor ships that don't require that).
4. Skill is essential, but barely helps. If you are terrible at the game, you will never beat it. You need to be good at it to have a SLIGHT chance.
5. That is all on EASY.
But what's good?
1. The game! Though I couldn't recommend it, it is a fantastic game. I like the difficulty- TO AN EXTENT. I like it not being easy, a struggle, just nowhere near this difficult by default.
2. Gameplay. Very fun, great mechanics, weapons, systems, all sorts.
3. Graphics. Lovely pixel art, except the backdrops, personally I am not much of a fan, they could have been a lot better if they weren't like a pixel brush painting. Difficult to explain, but doesn't detract.
4. Sound. Soundtrack is great, very fitting and no sounds seem out of place or re used.
But the bottom line is this becomes torture. Trying for hours just to get destroyed, with no kind of progression. If the easy mode was a bit more forgiving, so we can unlock new, better ships, we could then go on to try harder difficulties with pleasure. I'd love this game so much if that were the case. But it isnt. Don't buy it unless it is on sale or you really want it.
EDIT: Finally won with the first ship. I was crushed when I realised that doesn't get you another ship anymore.
EDIT 2: I have beat the game multiple times now, which leads to my next downfall of this game.
6. Tactics. You can only beat the game with one of a few methods of playing. For example, without cloaking, you cannot defend yourself from the final boss very well, but, the 'cheating' I mentioned before, the 15 or so lasers let out at once, they are a death sentence without cloaking. They will either kill you outright or damage you enough to lead to your death. This is one way it forces you to play in one very specific way.

Ok so it may seem that I am coming right out the gate with all the negatives but I did enoy this game and I'm going to justify it. Even though you repeat the same 3 levels 3 times over, which at first disappointed me, but near the end I felt they handled it the best they could, with each time you play that level it was a different experience because the characters sort of knew what was going on and helped speed the process of completing the level. Everytime you went back they completed some of the tasks that you had to complete yourself the time before. The graphics are beautiful just like in the original but this time it didn't have as many post card type scenes to look at. Gameplay and combat are the same from the original with Alan Wake not being the most agile guy in video games but it felt right for the context of the Alan Wake universe. Manuscripts this time around serve more of a unlock system rather than just a piece of additional pieces of information about the story, if you collect enough manuscripts you can open weapon boxes that are laid out around the environment which give you more powerful guns to help you proceed a little faster through that game (ex. SMG's, Assualt Rifles, and Hunting Rifles). They also added a few more enemy types that are very welcomed, nothing worse than fighting the same enemies over and over again.
Aside from the story mode, they have Arcade Mode, this is like a horde mode that you defeat the Taken until the sun comes up (10 minutes), it was fun but I do feel like it was a missed opportunity for co-op or multiplayer, which it weird because usually I'm the one that doesn't want multiplayer in story driven games like Assassin's Creed and Mass Effect. But in this case it would've been nice, especially since you only play it to get the highest score on the leaderboards.
That's pretty much it without spoiling the game, I do recommend it for people who like Alan Wake or for people who never played it before, it is a good game with a couple disappointments here and there but nonetheless a great game to play for a few hours.

A fantastic addition to the series! They take a lot of the strengths from the first game and keep them in place, but they also take a bunch of the weaknesses as well and greatly improve them. In comparison, this game is much easier than Alan Wake but I had so much fun playing it the difficulty nerf didn't really bother me. Finally there is a larger selection of weapons, but to be honest my favorites ended up being the standard issue 9mm pistol, and the crossbow, together they got the job done clean and quickly. If you are familiar with the predecessor to this game, the flash bangs and flare gun have been nerfed as well, but with a decent amount of balance. Ammo conservation isn't nearly as pertinent in this edition with the abundant and refilling ammo caches in each zone. Exploring isn't nearly as nerve racking or dangerous as well, which is a bit of a letdown.
********ATTENTION: POSSIBLE SPOILERS AHEAD********
The story of this game is solid, but also unoriginal. The whole idea of a repeating day has been done a lot, but it somewhat fits in with the setting of Night Springs that the game presents. Still not 100% sure if this is just another episode, or if it actually happened. Either way, the change of setting is very welcomed and the new enemies are a nice addition. I do enjoy the idea of dealing with a doppelganger though, and Mr Scratch pulls it off VERY well, I actually really like the guy.
********END OF POSSIBLE SPOILERS********
As for rating, on an enjoyment level I would give this game a solid 8.5 / 10 if you are just in it for how fun the game is. If you want to be a stickler and rate the actual level of design and originality in the game, it would have to be a 7 / 10. Either way, this is still a damn good game, especially if you played Alan Wake.

The game is a very mixed bag, but if you can get it on sale, it's worth it. You play as an unnamed young woman who moves to a town called Greyfox, where pretty much everyone is unpleasant or upset with life.
After performing some tasks (and a few degrading ones), she is brought into an alternate dimension by a mysterious woman and is told to judge four people. The player controls four different people, each with their own issues and motivations and must ultimately decide their fate through their actions.
This essentially amounts to the video game equivalent of a short story collection with a wrap around story to tie it together. Despite being made in RPG maker, there's no fighting to speak of. Instead, it is more of an adventure game without any real puzzles. The stories are all pretty interesting and have some pretty intense decisions to make. they are fairly well written, too, and play nicely off of stereotypes to subvert expectations.
That being said, the main protagonist is incredibly underwritten. Her only traits are that she hates her job and wants to take control of her life. There's no past, no hidden motivation or personality traits at all, just her apparently wanting to make her life better. It feels like at the end, the protagonist (and consequently the player) was supposed to learn something a la It's a Wonderful Life or Five People You Meet in Heaven, but it feels more abrupt than anything.
Still, I got this game when it was on sale for 20 cents and that's more than a fair asking price. It's not life changing or extremely well made, but it's good enough to warrant checking out at a price drop. If you love collecting achievments, the game is very sort which means it won't take very long to get all of them either (it took me less than an hour and a half to play through to the end).

Needs a loli class/body type. Aside from that, it's a good game with many things to do (many).
Combat is a big step forward over other action MMOs like TERA. You don't even need to press 1-0 keys to use your skills; instead you execute them in combos using a few buttons (and clicks), which makes it perfectly playable even with a controller (except for chat off course). Every single skill looks, and feels,  great (in my opinion). You can create some badass looking combos here.
Character customization is great for the most part. There are some limitation in color selections (hair, eyes and skin) and hair styles. Also, while face have a lot of things to edit, body is way more limited in options. In the case of Tamer class, there are less options for face and body, compared to the other classes.
Graphically, it's just beautiful; Enemies, NPCs, objects, trees, grass, rocks, everything has a great amount of detail. Hell, you can see your character sweating after running for some time, or after you used your wepon and/or skills; or how she/he and the terrain get wet with the rain. Minor details that make the game feel more alive and satisfying to watch.
The world in Black Desert Online is a big and seamless map without instanced places (exept for housing), so you can literally wander without restriction and go anywhere.
About the storyline, it's.... good, i think. It's not the best main scenario story and things could be better explained, but it's not bad (at least you don't start the game as a prisioner).
The ONLY thing i do not like is that, once you watch a cutscene, you will never be able to do it again with a different character. Also, there are steps in quests which get skipped automatically, without even asking you. Personally, this is something that should be changed, maybe adding an option to display/skip the stuff we already watched if we want.
I really like this game (more than i thought). I bought it just to see if my PC was able to run it (since it's not a high end machine; maybe not even medium end); and to see how bad it could be, since i usually end up getting bored with most MMOs i play after some hours (except for FFXIV and TERA, those are the only two MMOs i love) but, at the end, things resulted totally different. Now i regret myself for not buying one of the packages instead of just the base game (because there's no way to upgrade in the Steam version).

Let's keep it short, I wasted enough time on this already playing the whole damn thing.
So again it's striking me as to how long Telltale keeps their engine around while pushing out yet another licensed story from a franchise I care about. The animations are weak and figures pop in and out of scenes so bloody obvious it's getting annoying. Yet, I do like the tone and atmosphere of the game, especially the art style.
The 4 storylines are not in your favor and you can see it. George R. R. Martin hasn't delayed his book for no reason, because it takes time to accomplish something truely unique. This is just a game about NPCs, even if they're a noble family. Nobody cares about NPCs and that's why this game is not a worthy addition to the lore, if it is even considered such.
The only really good thing about this game was we combat scenes with Asher Forrester in the later game. Kept me excited, yet the other parts, the politics, were so boring on the other side that it's just a small patch on the otherwise patchwork.
Please, consider fast forwarding in your future games, even if you don't get to tell the story you intend to deliver. It's sometimes easier, especially when the bloody game crashes after a false save and I have to relive certain scenes over and over again just before I try a rewind on the chapter.
My final statement: if you are really thirsty for Game of Thrones, you'll get your Valar Morghulis. If you are a fan of good storytelling, even from Telltale, you'd be better off without this game.

Well another TellTale game completed, and I liked it.
For those who played a Telltale game, you know what to expect with this one in terms of game play. But for new players let me sum it up for you. Its a typical point and click advernture where you go from set to set interacting with the various items and environment to progress the story along. There also be quick time events doing actions scenes. You'll also be presented with choices that can have a ranging effect whether other characters will trust your character to even if a character live or die.  The choices are the strong point to a Telltale game. Some you may find easy to go with but others will leave you just scratching your head and wondering if you did the right thing.
End of the day this is your standard Telltale game set in the Game of Throne universe. The major characters make an appearance and you do interact with them. The game start on the 9th episode of the 3rd season (I'll say Red Wedding to avoid spoilers), so if you haven't seen up to that part, you may want to. If you seen further well let just say that knowing what happen at the end, may not help you with the current problem you're faced with. You play as various people associated with the minor house of Forrester. They never appear in the tv, but are canon to the book series.
I only had 2 problems with this game. The first was the art style. They went with a cell shading oil painting style. At time its good, but it just make some of the scenes feel low quality when playing at 1080p. I often felt like I was playing the game on a low setting when looking at some scenes. As for my second problem. Well Game of Thrones is filled with 2 things: Violence and Sexual Content. The violence is here but none of nudity and sex that I've come to expect from a typical episode.
All things negative aside, I still enjoyed this game and would recommend it to any Game of Throne fan. Also "Iron From Ice!"
You'll get it when you play the game.

This is a very simple game, reminiscent of an idle game, except you have to click "Go" rather than wait for things to scroll.   The game mostly consists of clicking go, with short bursts of splitting your colony between four different tasks, moving to a new location to encounter different events, and buying things from a store using a rare currency you might encounter.  Events can vary a lot, ranging from free food, to battles with roaming critters or people.
Unfortunately the control you have over these events is very small.  It's expected that they be random, but the game doesn't even tell you what some of them do.  My ant colony had been poisoned multiple times while I was in the house, with no visible effect.  Weather changes at random, there's a temperature gauge, being indoors lets you avoid weather, but...I have no idea what any of the weather does.  Many locations are listed as being good for something, but I have failed to notice any of those areas coming through on thei rpromise.
Battles also happen as random events, the idea being that you have to assign a certain number of ants as soldiers in order to overcome an area's encounters.  It seems like the stats of encounters just goes up if you assign more soldiers, though, resulting in a roughly even chance of victory regardless of how many soldiers you assign.  Battles consist solely of either hitting the attack button repeatedly (sometimes 50+ times) or deciding to retreat.  There's an auto-battle button, but auto-battling includes the retreat option, there's no feature that simply automates hitting the attack button.  And the AI will almost always choose to retreat.  Even when the chance of taking damage is miniscule, or even absolutely zero, the AI may decide that the battle isn't worth it and it'd rather lose the standardized 0.5% of your ants for running away.
Your other ant jobs aren't much more useful.  None of them are really transparent as far as numbers are concerned, and they seem to operate off of certain plateaus that change sometimes, but without a discernable reason.  The worst part is that the effectiveness of every job is dwarfed besides the bonuses you can get from the gem shop (which thankfully doesn't take real world cash, despite what the name might imply).  Harvesters are the only job that you'll really need any amount of ants in, but that job is also rather pointless in appearance when compared to the random food events.
Overall, the game obscures all of the necessary information to play it, and seemingly does so because if you saw any of the games inner mechanics you'd be appalled at how broken and ridiculous they are.  The makers of this game aren't just Anarchists, they're pratically criminals, creating games like this to make a cheap buck off of people who don't know any better.  I would not recommend this game under any circumstances.

I am an absolutely massive fan of Alan Wake; it's one of my favourite games of all time, I've finished it countless times on the Xbox 360, and I have a blast every time I play it. With that said, I found this standalone sequel to be rather disappointing in comparison to the brilliant first game; bear in mind that I do not think this is a bad game, it just falls rather falt and disappoints after the first game.
Alan Wake's American Nightmare is intended to play out as an episode of the fictional TV show called Night Springs, and is narrated by Lloyd Floyd, who provides an interesting narration to the story.The game has Alan Wake trapped in a sparse desert area, and who must find a way to escape the recurring nightmare he is stuck in.
And that leads to my first problem with the game; because Alan is stuck in a nightmare which repeats itself, you are forced to endure the same hour of gameplay THREE TIMES in a row until you finish this game. The exact same missions and locations, repeated three times. The first time is fun, the second time is kinda uninteresting, and the third time is downright boring and repetitive. This is a lazy way to repeat locations in a game, and it also reflects the poor writing skill of the writers.
The story is rather weird and disjointed. Throughout the entire game, you do a lot of things for unexplained reasons which aren't apparrently clear when you do them or even at the end of the game. The whole story is weird and quirky, but not in a good way, as it barely makes sense. The characters, apart from Alan and the absolutely BRILLIANT Mr Scratch, are boring and are just as quirky as the story itself. However, I found the live action cut scenes rather good, which was a surprise for me.
The gameplay is exactly the same as the first game, except that you can use new weapons like sub machine guns and nail guns. That's it. Zero changes made to the gameplay.
There's also a survival mode, which is actually quite fun. It's intense, challenging, and a fun way to compete on the leaderboards with your friends. I found this mode better than the campaign to be honest.
Overall, this is certainly not a bad game; it merely fails to innovate, and doesn't capture me the way the first game did. I still love Alan Wake, but this game disappointed me quite a bit. If you don't mind an extremely repetitive story, even with the game's shining parts, then pick t up for $3 on sale. 6 / 10.

Greyfox is a short point-and-click (without the click) adventure game. You take on the role of a young woman who is fed up with life in the big city and decides to move to a sleepy little town called Greyfox. However, shortly after arrival, you find yourself learning more about certain members of the community than you ever thought possible.
The plot is simple but creative. You take on the lives of some of the townsfolk, granting you the ability to make a critical decision for each of the four residents you play as. I really like the concept, and the fact that there multiple endings depending on your choices, but I feel like they definitely could have taken it a step further. Only one of the four characters gives you an additional decision, although it has no bearing on the ending. It would have been nice to expand range of influence you have over more minor decisions and see those choices reflected in the ending. The endings, too, leave something to be desired. They consist of very short cutscenes that briefly depict how your decisions ultimately affected you. While you do get a snippet about each of the characters you played as, I think it would have been more interesting to have a couple of additional cutscenes from their perspectives or that of their familes/friends/townsfolk.
The graphics aren’t the super high quality stuff that many of the top video games feature, but it’s certainly not a drawback. The town of Greyfox is cute and set up with consideration that encourages – and sometimes demands – careful exploration of your surroundings. I personally found the controls a little bizarre, using the arrow keys/enter after being so used to WASD/mouse, but it’s not a big deal.
The alternate endings provide at least three iterations of the game – more if you missed certain achievements. However, once you’ve played through all the possibilities (~2 hours, maybe more if you’re struggling to nab those last couple achievements and you’re determined not to look it up), you’re probably not going to play it again.
It’s an interesting premise and perfect if you don’t have the time to get sucked into a really involved game. I bought it on sale for $0.19, and for 2 hours of entertainment, I think it was worth it. I personally wouldn’t spend $5 on it, though.

Well, I just finished the game, and I have to say, I think it's one of the best FarCrys yet.  The reviews so far are all over the place, and some people I normally agree with hate it, and others love it. Shoot, there's even some apathy.  I had a great time in the game, and it felt like a good length.   Maybe the game's format just wasn't what I needed at the time, but I still haven't finished FarCry 3, whereas I powered through 4 and Primal. The map feels like a great size, although I wish the snowy areas and tundra were expanded on, as well as marshier marshes and maybe some other terrain as well.  Love the sequoia style fir trees.  The game has some of the best ambient lighting I've ever seen, especially at night with the moon out and distant fires lit throughout the land casting their cozy glow.
The combat needs a tad bit of fleshing - if melee is a focus, blocking and dodging should also be options.  Swinging and powerswinging is nice, and the autoaim is enjoyable for the most part.  Even if you're not a great counterstike player, you can still nail those satifying headshots with a spear atop a sprinting sabrecat, and those are some great moments.  There is much repetition - indeed, I could save a lot of words if I simply agreed with someone else that said it was FarCry 3 with a Caveman skin, just like 4 was 3 with an alpine skin.  There's a lot of fetch and kill quests, but the characters are great and some of the dialogue you get makes the grinding seem less grindy.  The owl is a treat, and the one thing that really changed, I felt.  No longer are you restricted to binoculars. I remember a lot of speclation about what, exactly, one would climb in this game, and the answer is naught.  Cliffs, to be sure, but you actually light bonfires instead of climbing towers.  The bonfires are like small, small forts, though some of the endgame enemies (midgame?) like the yellow shield fellas with flaming clubs, can still make them a challege.  As always, and more so than ever, pulling off a stealth takeover on a fort is a feat.
In any case, I'm just rambling with no sense of focus.
TL;DR -  Is FarCry 3 with Cavemen. Beautiful atmospherics, fun quests and dialogue, but similar game.  Uncover the map 'n' kill stuff.  Very fun at base level - just running and hunting is a treat.  Fetch quests are omnipresent. Owl is great.
PS: URKI!!! He's back - only he could pull off a trailer-trash caveman that, even though speaking a primitive dialect with powerful, dignified-sounding words, still sounds like he just rolled out of a double-wide in lower Alabama.  Amazing.

Look, Telltale games have a lot of problems. They're riddled with bugs. My game was
crashing on more-than-capable hardware at less-than-stellar settings. Achievements didn't pop. Load times were often ridiculous. Some animations were wonky. This lack of polish is kind of unforgivable for a developer this successful.
Furthermore, there's a little truth to all of the regular "not a game" whining from the so-called hardcore crowd. The limited interactivity of the Quick Time Event-style action sequences gets old, and while dialogue trees give the illusion that you're playing a significant part in crafting the narrative, any application of critical thinking allows one to recognize that all branching panths inevitably lead to many of the same outcomes. Most of the personalizations you can make to the story are pretty thin illusions.
But, you know what? The plot here was still ultimately more engrossing than half of what I've encountered in my experience playing games. Twists made sense, deaths felt significant, and I found myself growing to care about and root for the members of the Forrester household (who spend most of the season's six episodes getting their asses handed to them).
Season one of
was a beautiful, novel experience that appeared to move the medium in a positive direction. And while I'll gladly continue to pick up Telltale games that offer more of the same, I do find myself wishing they'd shake things up a bit and try to up the degree to which your choices affect the narrative.
Or, you know... I'd also settle for less bugs.

Star Wars Battlefront II takes you on a journey through the start of the Clone Wars all the way to the events at the end of episode 5 through the eyes of the legendary 501st Clones. In the story mode, you will capture objectives, whipe out enemy forces, and take out objectives usually with a limited garrison of reinforcements.
SWBF2 has three main game modes; Story Mode, Galactic Conquest, and Instant Action. Story Mode should need no explaination.
Galactic Conquest is a strategy style game where you play as one of four factions; The Empire, the Rebel Alliance, the Republic, or the Confederacy. Depending on who you choose to conquor the galaxy with, you will fight their rivals of the era. So if you choose to side with the Confederacy, you will be fighting against the Republic and vice versa, for example. In this mode your objective is to capture about 13 planets and have them under your control, with the enemy having the same goal. There is space and planetary combat, and each battle will reward you with credits. You use these credits to recruit new classes such as engineers and assassins, or to buy special bonuses to use against your opponent in a battle.
In instant action all you need to do is pick one of several match types being the standard Team Death Match style game mode, two versions of capture the flag, hunt, assault, and space battles. There is a wide variety of maps to choose from, and both eras are available. TDM is self explainatory. 1-flag CTF and 2-flag CTF are the capture the flag modes available. In 1-flag CTF you must steal one flag from the middle of the map before the enemy does and then take it to their goal to score for your team. In 2-flag CTF you steal the enemy's flag and take it to your goal to score. In hunt, only available on certain maps, you play as specific creatures native to that world. So on Naboo you can play as Gungans, or on Geonosis you can play as the Geonosians. Basically a twist to the standard TDM. Space Battles are regular fights, in space, with an objective to either shoot down every fighter in sight or destroy the enemy ship from both the outside and the inside. Assault is the biggest game mode, playable only on Mos Eisley. In this mode it is the heroes vs. the villains. Play characters such as Yoda, Han Solo, or even Mace Windu for the heroes; otherwise destroy the forces of good with Bobba Fett, Darth Maul, or even the Emperor himself.
This game has a lot of replay value, and despite the mid-PS2 era graphics has aged very well. While some missions in story mode frustrate, the game is worth a 9.6 out of 10, with my own bias being 10/10.

Game of Thrones is my favourite TV show of the last five years, and possibly of all time. I'm also a big fan of Telltale's recent games including The Walking Dead, A Wolf Among Us and Tales From The Borderlands. Combine those two elements together and the end result is a fantastic game that I thoroughly enjoyed from start to finish.
The story focuses on two houses that haven't appeared in the TV show. The Forresters are an ally of House Stark in Northern Westeros. Their home, Ironrath, is surrounded by a massive forest whose trees produce especially strong wood, which they use to craft weapons and shields for King's Landing and the Knight's Watch.
The game runs parallel to seasons 3 and 4 and references key events such as the red wedding, purple wedding, liberation of Meereen and battle of Castle Black. When the Forresters lose the protection of the Starks, their long time rival House Whitehill attempts to seize control of Ironrath, with the support of the Boltons and the Lannisters.
Gameplay is exactly what you'd expect if you've played any of Telltale's previous games. Its basically like watching an 11 hour season of the TV show, while making dialogue choices, performing QTE based combat, and occasionally making tough decisions that will have a massive impact on how the story plays out, who lives and who dies.
There aren't any puzzles to solve, and there's no meaningful way to interact with the environment. The rare sections where you can walk around are pretty pointless, because you're always confined to a really small area. I would like Telltale to try to expand this side of the gameplay in future games, especially having recently played Life Is Strange. Dontnod showed that its possible to do it without hurting the pacing of the story.
The player controls several members of House Forrester in different locations around the world, and each character's scenes have their own unique tone. The scenes in Ironrath, as Lord Forrester, felt most like Game of Thrones. There's a constant sense of unease, as if anyone could die at any time if you make the wrong choice. My favourite scenes were in King's Landing, as Mira Forrester, getting involved in the politics and the scheming, trying to secure an alliance with Margaery and Tyrion, even getting into a verbal dual with Cersei. Meanwhile Ashur's scenes in Meereen feel a bit more light hearted, and there's plenty of combat to break up the dialogue. And Gared's quest has an interesting sense of mystery.
Voice acting is top quality. All the major characters - Cersei, Tyrion, Margaery, Daenerys, Jon and Ramsey - are voiced by the actors who play them on TV, while the rest of the cast who performed the Forresters, Whitehills, and other support characters, all did a great job. The biggest compliment that I can give to the writing is that I now care about the Forresters, and hate the Whitehills, as much as any character in the TV show.
If you're a fan of Game of Thrones, this is an obvious purchase. The opportunity to interact with major characters while meeting new ones is so much fun. However, if you've never watched the TV show, or read the books, I imagine you'd find the story of the game a little hard to follow.

Brutal good arcade-style fun. If I ever scratch "build a MAME cabinet" off of my bucket list, this game will find a home on it.
It reminds me of the old Capcom game Gun.Smoke but way more frantic. There's usually plenty of enemies on screen and one hit knocks you dead unless you manage to commandeer one of their horses. Gameplay is mostly just "shoot enemies and don't get shot" but there's a large variety of maps and some have unique environmental hazards. On Arcade mode you conquer these maps one-by-one and get a power-up as a reward for clearing each map; "Story" mode makes things more interesting.
In story mode after you complete a map you'll be given the choice of which direction to go, the layout being randomized each time. Each of the directions has an icon that hints to what kind of map or event will take place there. You can collect gold to gamble on cards to earn extra lives, buy weapon upgrades from a gun dealer, or pay your way out of a tricky situation. There are unique events that can occur to keep things interesting and there's "neutral" maps filled with non-combatants. You can murder these people and take their loot, but you may regret choosing to become an outlaw if you run into the sheriff down the road.
Difficulty ranges from challenging to brutal. One map you may find yourself fighting a dozen outlaws, on another a large horde of angry chickens. There's a whopping 11 playable characters to choose from and rather than just being simple skins they have their own unique playstyle. What really surprised me is that they even control differently. Some you may find more suited to a keyboard/mouse (Abel- revolver with six rounds) so you can aim more precisely while others play better with a controller (Two-feather can fire in four directions with the A/B/X/Y buttons or the I/J/K/L keys). It changes things drastically because depending on their weapon you either have to make every shot count or can fire carelessly but have to have to be more precise with your movement.
It really nails the arcade style. Graphically speaking it has a low-res pixel aesthetic for sprites, but everything else reminds me of early 90s arcade games. Using voice samples in the menus, the sort of lo-fi sound effects, and the game-over screen in story mode where the villain appears on screen mockingly to coerce another precious quarter from your pocket. One of the samples used in the soundtrack sounds straight out of Turtles in Time.
All around it's a fun, challenging, diverse and charming game.

It's Sim City (one of the good ones) set in a Cold War Banana Republic.
Some actual Pluses and Minuses:
+Not the 2013 SimCity Reboot, but the roads still curve, so it's got EA's offerings beat
+A decent sense of pseudo-political humor and self-parody
+A LONG Campaign that will last dozens of hours and poses some interesting, and ocassionallly bizzare, scenarios
+Interesting Faction and Foreign systems that's integral for things like Elections, Foreign Aid, etc
+Many viable economic paths, from growing subsistence and cash crops to Industry and Tourism
+Things like Education, which could have been phoned in, actually matter and create difficult dilemnas on how to best proceed
-Less of a Sandbox than the best SimCity games
-A bit much for genre newbies to leap into, though far from terrible
-The ocassional random event (read "natural disaster") that serves to disrupt the usual flow
I haven't got enough experience with Tropico 3 to compare the two, but the above are my impressions of 4 as it sits with a Strategy/Simulation veteran.
Conclusion: Great for fans of the genre, especially those who want something other than a conventional modern city-builder, and worth investigating for Simulation newbies if only because while a bit dense at points, this is no Paradox game, and ruling over an island nation is quite enjoyable.

Over 36 hours and still haven't completed it on easy. This is a great game, until a few things start getting to you:
1. It's all random. Doesn't matter how well you do, there is no way of being good enough/powerful enough to complete it if you have even one stroke of bad luck. the only thing that matters is how lucky you are.
2. Literally cheating. Okay, you may not call this cheating. But it's not like when you blame the game and it is clearly you that was at fault. The final boss may be just about to die, and let out 15 or so blasts at once, completely randomly (it doesn't always happen). The only possible way to protect yourself from that would be to cloak immediately. But if you don't have cloak, or don't have it recharged at that second, or the reflexes of The Flash, you are instantly dead. Game over. 1-3 hours. Gone.
3. All punishment, no reward. How do you unlock ships that aren't aweful? Beat the boss. How do you realistically have a chance of beating  the boss? Use ships that aren't aweful. Before, you could find the things to get the new ships, but I imagine that was removed because they literally never happened for most people. Me included. The punishment comes in because each time you loose, after hours of playing, you get NOTHING out of it. Nothing to help you next time- UNLESS you beat the boss and unlocked a new ship (or managed to unlock the few poor ships that don't require that).
4. Skill is essential, but barely helps. If you are terrible at the game, you will never beat it. You need to be good at it to have a SLIGHT chance.
5. That is all on EASY.
But what's good?
1. The game! Though I couldn't recommend it, it is a fantastic game. I like the difficulty- TO AN EXTENT. I like it not being easy, a struggle, just nowhere near this difficult by default.
2. Gameplay. Very fun, great mechanics, weapons, systems, all sorts.
3. Graphics. Lovely pixel art, except the backdrops, personally I am not much of a fan, they could have been a lot better if they weren't like a pixel brush painting. Difficult to explain, but doesn't detract.
4. Sound. Soundtrack is great, very fitting and no sounds seem out of place or re used.
But the bottom line is this becomes torture. Trying for hours just to get destroyed, with no kind of progression. If the easy mode was a bit more forgiving, so we can unlock new, better ships, we could then go on to try harder difficulties with pleasure. I'd love this game so much if that were the case. But it isnt. Don't buy it unless it is on sale or you really want it.
EDIT: Finally won with the first ship. I was crushed when I realised that doesn't get you another ship anymore.
EDIT 2: I have beat the game multiple times now, which leads to my next downfall of this game.
6. Tactics. You can only beat the game with one of a few methods of playing. For example, without cloaking, you cannot defend yourself from the final boss very well, but, the 'cheating' I mentioned before, the 15 or so lasers let out at once, they are a death sentence without cloaking. They will either kill you outright or damage you enough to lead to your death. This is one way it forces you to play in one very specific way.

You know that sort of game that's from a genre you don't care about, but you give it a shot anyway and you're really glad you did? A Fistful of Gun is exactly that.
Extremely well polished, from interface to art design, AFoG takes you into a mock-Wild West flick full of arcade action. Whereas almost all such shooters restrict you to one control scheme -- indeed, some build the whole game around it --, AFoG allows you to select from a variety of such schemes, and also wildly varying weapons which directly affect gameplay.
Co-op is a great way to play. The various scenarios you will be playing in have varying gimmicks, and are slightly randomly generated. The scenery affects the action nicely, and the existence of power-ups also spices things up. So it has the usual shooter props, plus several great additions of its own.
The arcade mode is the main attraction, but the story mode makes for a great break, and it's quite different. It adds random events between stages and allows you a limited choice of your next stage, counting down the days until the last shootout.
AFoG is a perfect example of evolutionary, rather than revolutionary, gameplay. It consists of taking something established and old, and polishing it until it shines. And AFoG gleams indeed.
