There are some games that are just plain fun for a variety of reasons. Maybe because the developers have made a fun experience. Maybe because you've got good friends to play with on multiplayer. Or perhaps just because it makes you laugh. This game doesn't mave multiplayer, but two out of three isn't bad.
Politics is often describes as dirty, and as a ruler of a carribeian island with a population of between fifty and four hundred, you will learn this fast. As a minor power, many, more powerful nations will have demands. The Chinese want help stablizing the economy, and they request seven thousand dollars to help. Russia has a new plan to assist a neighbouring country, and want you to export some iron. Do this, and they promise to give more favourable trade prices further down the road. Europe wants lumber, and will give you plans to build a lumber mill if you don't have one and cash if you do. The American ambassador tells you that if you don't export some coffe fast, then he cannot gaurantee that there won't be any "accidents" and you may or may not end up with a cruise missile from a warship hitting your palace. So he thinks you should get on that... right now. Or else.
Of course, you'll be laughing at vaugely worded threats, requests for help, and the "new plans" that Russia wants to share with you. And why? Because the game never takes itself seriously for a moment! Be it the new weapons... sorry "pipe factory" that just so happens to sell pipes so good that if you used a chemical reaction you could propel a small metal slug at great speed, or the snide comments made by your military commite/general when discussing the intellectuals talking about the new burlesque house and how the head of the faction "Mistress" Pineapple has a new show at 10pm, you will find yourself enthralled by the clever, well voiced people each with seperate agendas.
Make a military dictatorship where you control everything, and anyone who protests is shot on the streets! Make a communist utopia where the burgoize bankers are kicked out and there is food for all and free high quiality housing with air conditioning! Make your radio and TV stations broadcast propaganda 24/7, or give the people a voice for their concerns! Be the dictator you want to be, with traits, costume, and policies that reflect who you are.
Though the game has a steep learning curve, which can be problemactic, and you will find yourself having to find new sources of money in a changing world, the game is helpful by allowing you to have tutorial messages turned on or off where party leaders talk to you about problems they face. Be it the Communists complaining about low wages or poor housing and Capatalists demanding a police force to reduce crime, or the Militarists wanting new facilities and Intellectuals wanting a new highschool so that Penultimo stops spelling his name with eight mistakes, they will keep you abreast of problems you are facing with clear reports, and recommendations on what to do.
The UI is easy to use, and finding information about your island is easy, with an almanac telling you about all your people, the needs being met, your economy strenth, to even food consumed and how much more is needed, it is all there to find, in easy to understand numbers and charts. Map overlays showing resources, crop conditions, liberty, crime, and disaster danger zones are all there, ready to provide needed information at a few clicks.
This game is fun, funny, and easy to play, but hard to master. Buy it now.

This review comes after I, first, played Megadimension Neptunia for the PS4.  It would seem that the Neptunia series is one of the few that can claim the sequels to represent improvements over each other.  Which is good - and by no means is Re;Birth1 a bad game.
The core Neptunia games are turn based tactics games.  Battles all play out in arena form with movement taking place within a restricted radius (as opposed to a fixed grid).  All weapons have an area of effect that can potentially reach multiple enemies (this works both ways), and attacks can be built into combos with each class of attack having a different overall purpose.
The gameplay is, overall, solid.  There are some odd difficulty spikes at times (or... for whatever reason everything was suddenly hitting like a truck compared to where I just was in the plot), but nothing an RPG-familiar gamer is going to be completely unprepared for.  Everything is fairly intuitive and min/max style gameplay is available, yet unnecessary to advance.
If you are simply looking to try Neptunia to see what it is all about, I would actually recommend Megadimension Neptunia VII.  It represents, in my opinion, a number of refinements and improvements over what was already a good system and has some better "NewGame+" features.  These are games that can be played out of order without being totally lost.
So... What makes Neptunia ... Neptunia?
If it isn't already obvious, the entire universe is a metaphor for the videogame industry - consoles, games, publishers, developers, etc.  The game is loaded with both blatant and obscure references to games, hardware, and the history of the industry.
The plot, at least thus far, centers around the character "Neptune."  Neptunia has its origins in Sega, and Neptune was the code-name for a console that was all of the hardware of the Genesis and its add-ons (the 32X and Mega CD) into one package.  It was cancelled because it would launch practically alongside the Sega Saturn (wait... there was a console between the Genesis and Dreamcast?).  I will abstain from a review of Sega's console marketing strategies, or complete lack thereof...
The care-free personality of Neptune is, precisely, what makes the Neptunia series work, in my estimation.  Her frequent video game references don't work unless she is allowed to break the fourth wall and to see herself as being in a game.  Yet, it is written in a very tasteful manner.  She is both random/delusional, and measured/wise at the same time.  It's a game that doesn't take itself too seriously - and Neptune's character is how the developers say "we know you've been here, before and you know what's going to happen - just have fun with it."
And that is what Neptunia is about.  It's a parody, tribute, and celebration of the history of videogames and the culture around them.  That is the core of Neptunia.
The bad for Re;Birth1 ?
The English voice acting is... English voice-acting.  Neptune is great, Compa is great, Vert is good, IF is good, flip a coin for everyone else and chalk up 'minion 43' to being one of the programmers who lost a bet.  That... and some of the scenes which actually get voice-acting are kind of random.  A few key plot events are ignored while a few scenes of idle banter get full attention.
The "shares" system is a little wonky and, while not crucial to the central game, does play a role in the True Ending and some item development requirements.  It's a zero-sum game representing the console wars and each system's share of the market and quests will deplete shares from one system while rewarding them to another... so it can lead to repeating certain quests a few times in order to get shares where they need to be for an item's requirments or whatever.  It's a neat idea... but not exactly fun.
Why no complaints on gameplay?
I could list them... but the way Neptunia is designed, most of these are optional elements of the gameplay.  There are various settings you can unlock which make the game easier, or harder.  You can choose whether or not to use the plethora of healing and buffing items in the game.  You can buff the enemies so that the guard break system does play a more important role.
In the end, it's a game that has fun being a game about games.

The very first word you will probably come up with while playing this game is - Stylish. So far, I've really enjoyed it, both Story and Arcade mode (sadly said, Multiplayer part is already dead even though game wasn't released long ago; so if you are up for coop'ing with other players or in contrary playing versus them, - you better find yourself a regular partner).
To start from a good side, AFoG got really loveable graphics (aside from being just stylish) and represents, if I can call it so, a rather difficult light bullet hell example where you die from 1 shot with nice western touch and fast paced gameplay, even within the Story mode. You start in a town, progressing further by choosing a side to go to [marked with an icon to show the nature of the next encounter], sometimes it may be a saloon or a graveyard, other time it's just vast prairies where you can shoot/smash/exterminate bad guys. Long story short, a lot of things to do, with a similar basis. If you start a fight with civilians, prepare yourself for consequences of getting a "Wanted status" along with some stars, though you can later atone your sins by shooting some more bandits while carrying a heavy pig around (not literally, ouch).
Arcade mode, on the other hand, is also a pack of different areas, but without any background story, so you will only need to kill everyone present while picking power-ups and sometimes fullfilling some other [meaningless] tasks, like rescuing those in need of help or moving wagonets from the bottom to the up of the screen. I couldn't play Versus mode, unfortunately, since there was no one else online besides me.
You can choose from a roster of 11 different "heroes", most with unique gameplay-changing abilities. However, Devs could add not only biography and a list of available weapon looks for each of these, but also some kind of more throughout guide. Of course, it's rather easier to figure on your own, but I'd prefer if "fast paced" thingy wouldn't also apply to How-to element of the game and figuring basics.
Also, some characters may perhaps need rebalance. For example, there is a chinese guy who launches infinite amount of small and big rockets, which takes
long time to set off and you just need to run around evading projectiles while waiting for some of them to hit enemies. Moreover, there is a unit which looks like a troop with square formation, it moves rather slowly (you can boost the speed for a short amount of time with your right click - banner), but it won't die unless all of the soldiers die, which seems a bit cheating.
During my playthoughs, I haven't met any critical or even small issues worth of mentioning. Nevertheless, once in a Story mode I wasn't able to progress past the level and thus lost the game. It was a night themed sneak map with a projector to avoid, but I finished up facing a bandit, who raised the alarm. Briefly, these bandits were simply unkillable no matter how much lead I made them "eat".
Summing up, I can confidently say that Fistful of Gun is an enjoyable experience, which may be worth both your money [better pick it on sale though] and time, but since it's mostly short sessioned game with lots of deaths, try to consider finding a friend to play with or you can throw it pretty soon.

A Fistful of Gun is the most fun I've had with a top down shooter in quite a while.  The action is fast paced and nearly non-stop, and the old west visuals and music are pure awesome.  It has a bit of a retro feel to it as well, like a game Capcom could've developed for arcades in the '90s.
The gameplay is a mixture of top down shooter and bullet hell, but it isn't the typical shooter, so it might not appeal to those who want to dive straight into the action and feel like an invincible gunslinger. Going in guns blazing will quickly lead to your death.   Unlike most top down shooters, you have to take the time to learn how to play; memorize patterns, learn the controls, and use your reflexes.
You start out with a choice of 3 characters in story mode, and you can unlock 8 more.  The characters all play a bit differently from each other, which is great, but the controls can be frustrating:   Some characters use keyboard & mouse, while others use a gamepad.  For now I'm looking at mastering the controls for each character as part of the challenge - it's not hard to learn anyway - but I can't help feel that full gamepad support for all characters would make the game better.
Pros:
+ Fun, action-packed top down shooting.
+ Great music and sound effects.
+ Awesome pixel graphics with a old west theme.
+ Loads of fun to play with a friend, and almost any game that can be played local and online co-op earns a bonus point from me.
Cons:
- Can be a little repetitive.
- Controls need to be streamlined.
- The price seems a bit steep.  In my opinion, they should lower it to $10.00 USD.

Background: I played a lot with Terror From The Deep back then, then replayed it and again. Also I have played a lot with the free UFO Alien Invasion. Since most is said by others I will focus on what I feel as improvement or disadvantage compared to these. The game is pretty cool, I really loved it, and recommending it. Please consider this review as ideas for improvement.
------------------------------------------------
I feel the game is well done and a lot of time was put into balancing it (with the exception of Impossible difficulty). So I recommend it. Low number of bugs, nice visuals, immersive. The sad thing if you loved the original game, that all it's descendants are missing things:
- XCOM is streamlined, oversimplified and lots of the individual choices are taken away; but well balanced, professional in all sense
- the free UFO Alien Invasion is permanently unfinished: lots of original ideas, lot of the features from the original, but indestructible environment, outdated graphics, pet project feel
So if you are a hardcore fan, this is bad news, since none of descendants has reached the level-of-depth of the original game. But still really fun.
The game design feels insecure sometimes, I hear the voice of the designers in my head back in 2011/2012:
So I feel that many elements of the game was removed, because of the fear that turn-based strategy is a past thing. In 2012 this was only hoped that the genre is still profitable. So my guess as being a (non-game) developer myself and seeing projects from inside, that they turned down features that seemed "too brainy" or "slow", because they weren't sure the market really existed for this kind of game (if you read interviews the creators, they
surprised that the game got that huge following.
On the other hand, if you replay either UFO or Terror From The Deep you will be surprised how feature-rich was the original game compared to XCOM: EU/EW! For instance: take explosives:
Or just motion scanners, torches in dark environments, really postponable urgent needs (like alien base assaults), multiple types of hybrid planes.
I loved the...
On the other hand so many things are missing, that made a lot of sense in the original. If you haven't played the original this list will be an eye-opener:
These could lead to very different play styles depending on your needs or on the environment. For example, on harder difficulties you would bring lots of explosives and play it very heavy handed. Or use different weapons for long range attacks.
Also UFO Alien Invasion (the freegame) had some cool features, like personal flame-throwers, close-range weapons - heavy weapons that were more accurate, but had no burst capacities... Or were powerful but inaccurate like grenade launchers...
So you COULD have the choice in these games between long-range fighting, close quarter heavy damage, area-of-effect, etc.
Maybe XCOM 3 will give you these choices. I see that XCOM 2 is going in the right direction (the rebellion idea is very-very good!). But all-in-all, a really nice game, nice challenge. Just puzzling that older games could have lot more features and depth to them.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is an interesting title. A psuedo-sequel/spin-off/expansion to the psychological thriller "Alan Wake," American Nightmare is both familiar and different from it's parent. It's familiar in the sense that the core of the gameplay remains the same: you still use light to burn away protective darkness to make enemies vulnerable. Light is your ally, your friend. What's changed however, is the setting, your abilities, and the nature of the areas you'll traverse.
American Nightmare is set in the American Southwest—Arizona, to be exact—outside a fictional city known as Night Springs. Unlike Alan Wake, which presented the player with mostly clear point A-to-B setpieces, American Nightmare follows a more open route. Although each of the areas you'll explore isn't exactly large (the developers are clearly feeling the crunch of being restricted by XBA's size limit), you're free to roam them as you please while you accomplish your objectives, and it's usually in your best interest to do so—provided occasional darkness attacks don't prove to muc for you.
Fortuitously, however, Alan Wake is no longer the out-of-shape writer with a limited weapon selection he was before. In American Nightmare, he's changed himself to a more contemporary action-hero, with far more agility and skill than last we saw him. You'll find your arsenal expanded as well: sawn-off shotguns, Uzi's, Magnums, crossbows, even nail guns ... All will be needed. It's not an awe-inspiring set, but as you make your way through the game unlocking new weapons on the way to the final showdown, you'll definitely find some favorites.
The story is short (and involves a time loop, to save space once again) so you'll get used to seeing the same scenes in the basic game. Fortunately, there's more to American Nightmare.
Those weapons you unlock in the main game (via finding manuscript pages)? Once you've unlocked them, you can find them in Alan Wake's other mode: Arcade. Here you're tasked with lasting ten minutes on one of several maps, using whatever you can scrounge from nearby. The generic maps aren't too challenging, but once you've beaten a few, you'll unlock a new mode that ramps the difficulty up to eleven and probably past that becomes quite intense. Trying to use your flares and flashlight to hold the horde of enemies back while frantically reloading is a blast.
From the standpoint of a newcomer, this title could be hit or miss. I recommend it, but Alan Wake seems to be a polarizing cup of tea for many. If you're a fan of action-survival modes (CoD Zombies, Gears Horde, Resident Evil Mercenaries) than American Nightmare is worth grabbing for the Arcade alone. Otherwise, I'd recommend watching a few videos first and seeing if the gameplay style appeals to you. For me, it does.
Pros:
—Clever enemy design
—Unique Light-based combat
—Exhilrating Arcade mode
—Excellent soundtrack courtest of "Old Gods of Asgard" (AKA Poets of the Fall)
—Genuine psychotically eerie villain, even if he is a ham
Cons:
—Repetitive Environments
—Limited types of enemies, even if they are clever
—A little too much focus on conventional weapons over the light based ones
—I did miss the more powerful flashlights from the original title.
Recommendation: Buy it if you're a fan of the genre or a fan of Alan Wake, watch first otherwise. Definitely fun though.

I own this game quite a while, occasionally taking free flights in Seattle and i must admit - level of detail in envelopment is far beyond for any flight simulator game even today. There is probably thousand of different models for buildings, not only for landmark, but any major building have it's own model and detailed texturing. Those also all collision enabled, meaning you can crash or land on. Even trees are crashable 3D models. You can even land and get out of your bird and start playing ARMAII in Seattle. Or in normal ARMAII maps - if you own it in Steam.
I was so looking forward to start playing single player campaign, imagining limitless country of fun with all goodness above combining with full range of civil helicopter's activities, starting with simple taxi missions and ending with sling load operation and search-and-rescue mission using FLIR (thermal vision camera).
To my very disappointment there is - as we russians say - one spoon of♥♥♥♥♥♥in barrel of honey. And it's flying itself. I'm not IRL pilot so i can't explain things in the right worlds, but i own (and fly almost daily) DCS UH-1 and X-Plane 10 with some payware helos, so i guess i know that is right and that is wrong. And TKOH helicopters are behaves wrong. More of that - they all share same dynamics, just with different coefficients. For example all of them have same speed. It's not like i didn't notice that playing free flights, i just thought i could deal with slow response, overreacting titling and nonexistent transition on lightest bird in campaign.
Turns out what with adding more power by coefficients thing only becomes worse, so heaviest copter not only overreacting inputs (but still slow) but tends to get lift with smallest lateral movement and suddenly drop it then you manage to get steady. Combined with oversaturated (remember - we have add power) tendency for forward movement (you need a several degrees of back pitch to hold it in place) makes most docile and presumable easy to hover craft unmanageable. So on second container in 7th mission of campaign i ragequit.
Speaking of campaign - in 7 (+2 sidemissions) missions i did, there was only two civilian missions. Three if you count whale seeing mission, but single engine helo without emergency water landing equipment not sounds like civilian job for me here. And there is more of such nonsense. Why two-engine helicopters goes down after one failed? Yeah we have two turbine for fancier look. Why we need rope insertion on flat roof in heavy wind, especially after i perfectly landed before mission marker even appears.
Concluding, i wouldn't recommend this game to any flight sim enthusiast. Despite perfect envelopment flying itself is unbearably broken and won't be fixed because of 3rd party component BI have to rely here.

Some have criticised FC:P for the 'lack of story' but as someone who enjoyed the Far Cry formula since FC2, I think I prefer it that way.
While I think Vass, Pagan, et al, are great characters, what keeps me coming back to the Far Cry series is the core game-play.  It's more than immersive - it transports me to another place (especially when I remove the HUD elements). It doesn't just allow for emergent game play - it encourages it. If anything, I find the 'story' elements often intrude on what is otherwise an almost zen like experience for me.
I understand that some may find it repetitive; I have certainly lost interest in Assassin's Creed, (and other Ubisoft products) which are in many ways very similar, but there is something about the Far Cry series that really has me hooked.
Steam controller works well, and there are a couple of good community configs, but I wish there was an official profile for the game.
Edit: The Final Boss Fights.
I won't change my recommendation because I absolutely loved Far Cry Primal, but the boss fight against Batari is a nightmare, and not in a good way.
I had played through the 'meat and vegetables' of the entire game: the side missions, defeating the villages, taming all the beasts etc (things that other might find grindy, but I love). I was taking my time, and really enjoying it till i was ready to end it and take down the two main bosses.
The first time I was defeated after a long battle. It was pretty grindy, so I left it for the night came back the next day, only to die again after getting Batari down to 1%. I must have hit her a dozen times with my mighty two handed club when she had hardly any health left, but she kept on coming, seemingly unharmed...
And I just didn't have the desire to go back again. I must be two missions off completing the entire thing, but I doubt now that I'll finish it.
It's such a shame. I love the Far Cry formula. I love taking each village, one by one; I love the emergent gameplay and the way the game allows you to play it your way. And UBI have shown they have the capacity to make really interesting side missions. So I can't understand why they insist on making these tedious boss fights.
It's not that they're all that difficult per se. They're just not fun.

Poker Night at the Inventory is a great game for non-Poker players to learn the game.  It can be a little daunting, but playing around with three loveable characters and Tycho can really help one learn the game.  It's got a brief tutorial, but most of what you'll learn is obtained through trial and error.
The TF2 bonus items are pretty sweet, and for a lot of people, it's the reason they picked up the game.
My only real quarrel with Poker Night is the achievements.  Whoever assigned those needs to be dragged out in the street, tarred, then feathered.  Over half of the achievements are entirely luck based (specifically winning a hand with a particular hand of cards, requiring you to first get that hand, and then pray to whatever supernatural influence you prefer that nobody else has a better one.)
For one particular example, the Straight Flush achievement has a 1-in-Thousands chance (specific number depends on who you ask it seems), and that's assuming you play every hand to the end without folding, no matter the risk.  Needless to say, seeking this achievement *will* cost you a lot of tourneys, not to mention a lot of wasted time and wear on your mouse in clicking through everything.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who wants to learn Texas Hold 'Em, enjoys getting TF2 items, and is NOT fussed about achievements.

A short, but highly replayable and entertaining multi-directional shoot-em-up in the tradition of Smash TV.  Great fun for a few bouts with friends now and then, but only buy solo if you're really into this type of game.
In a Fistful of Gun you can get together with a few trigger-happy friends to play with guns, get drunk, break stuff, and blow up angry chickens with dynamite all without the real-life consequences!  You choose from one of 11 different characters to run through random levels of retro gunslinging action, grabbing as many gold nuggets, power-ups and alcoholic boosts along the way as you can.
One of the biggest draws of the game is the multiplayer aspect, with high-score progress designed to track a full posse of players.  This is emphasized even further by the unforgiving gameplay, which can cause the 'continue' screen to pop up rather often in solo mode.  Even though bullets are too scarce in many stages to push this into bullet-hell territory, between the heat-seeking farm animals of doom, stray crates of dynamite, and of course a horde of guntoting baddies, you WILL die.  Simply completing the relatively short single-player story mode (which is truthfully about as story-less as a story mode can be) might take some practice.
Of course, once a playthrough ends, the secondary hook of Fistful of Gun may very well entice you into another round;  Each of the eleven different characters to choose from features a different gun, which is actually an entirely new control scheme and shooting style.  One gunslinger fires large shotgun blasts, but only in the direction you're currently running and limited to a single shot in each barrel, while another wields a 6-shooter that can be quickly fired in any direction, but requires joystick flicking and a lengthy reload period after you empty the chamber.  Each of the guns requires you to learn a new set of skills, so perfecting them all could provide a very lengthy challenge.
All in all, Fistful of Gun is a fun, difficult game reminiscent of old school shooters, but with modern features added to boost entertainment and replayability.  If you're buying it purely for solo play, you might want to wait for a decent sale or be certain you enjoy this type of game - a short Story Mode, and a highly replayable but somewhat repetitive Arcade Mode designed around high scores might leave you feeling that the experience was a bit lacking. However, if you love retro shoot-em-ups or have a few friends to play with, A Fistful of Gun could be a blast.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is essentially an all action (similar to Resident Evil) 'sort-of' continuation of the original Alan Wake storyline. It follows the "stuck in nightmare world" idea, and most of your time is spent blasting away enemies in (the same) three stages. Repeat that three times and that's all there is to American Nightmare. Not much.
American Nightmare completely lacks the psychological aspect of 'psychological thriller,' that the original Alan Wake was barely able to pull off (similar to Silent Hill). Besides sharing the same name, the two titles have little in common. American Nightmare is simply Alan Wake, reduced to a basic shoot-em-up arcade style games with little-to-no story set in three repeated stages.
Also worth mentioning is that if you're looking for some resolution to the ending of the original Alan Wake, you won't find it here.

Exploring it, though, is a smooth, epic-feeling experience that regularly demands long treks through enemy territory to get to the next boss or quest objective, and just about every path is scattered with both big combat engagements and dungeons to dip into for an extra boss fight and bonus loot.
Grim Dawn unfortunately never recaptures the promising pathos of the opening cutscene, but it slathers the grittiness around in text boxes and often laughable voice acting like old crunchy peanut butter on otherwise savory fresh bread.
More often than not, the gear's not even useful, being either vendor junk or limited by huge stat restrictions, and I found myself accidentally picking it up in my click-trance even when I meant not to. That thus leads to one of Grim Dawn's few real downsides: the perpetual trips back to town to sell it all off. At least you got a free portal and dont rely on a portal scroll, like Diablo.
Grim Dawn delievers a sincer old-style hack-and-slash experience so purely and so satisfyingly, and its hybrid class system makes each new jaunt a little different. More than once it found me playing more then 1 hour, and my appreciation for any game that manages to do that is top notch.

As a fan of The Song of Ice and Fire first and the HBO Series next I also have to say I am a fan of Telltale games specially The Walking Dead series.
I had a lot of expectations for this game and they were met somehow while at the same time not quite so.
First thing first, I liked the game overall. It contains the basic dynamics of any Telltale games and so you are pretty safe playing them if you had played previous games. That being said I think they overused their "QTE" implementation on this as there are quite a number of fights in the whole game (GoT right?). Mostly the ones involving button mashing as a test of strength were often used and didn't properly work. I don't quite get the idea of having to button mash one button and at the very end hit another one. I would often hit the wrong button and the game would just ignore my mistake.
The story is moderately fleshed out specially given we are talking about a House that was almost non-existing in the original books and was never mentioned in the show. I mean, of course Margaery handmaidens wouldn't have received much notice at all but introducing such a strong character like Mira as her personal handmaiden was a bit too much.
Also, the Forresters acquired quite an importance in the game as being the singlemost producer's of Ironwood articles yet their existence was nonetheless absent from the book and series. True, some fitting was required to produce this game in a unique way (meaning, not having to repeat what the show already did) but it takes a bit of a suspence of belief  inside the lore of the books/series to play this one.
Overall the characters were likable and well animated and voice acted. I do have some issue's with Talia's animations as her emotions were just so...fake it was a pain to watch. Her emotions switched so abruptly that she seemed like a puppet being grossly manipulated into changing without a normal human response of grading from one emotion to the next.
The apperance of the shows characters, and their actors voicing them, should have been a plus. Some are, specially as they can imprint the same range of emotions through voice acting alone in their virtual counterparts. Some though, are just horrible. Ramsay Snow's character was bizzare in animation form. And the actor Iwan Rheon couldn't imprint the same madness and psychopaty to the character by voice alone. He is much more of a method actor and needs his body to imprint that feeling and Telltale dropped the ball when it came to that.
Tyrion Lannister was sort of okay although he looks like a bloated potato in virtual form. Peter Dinklage manages to salvage him singlehandedly by sheer acting brilliance but it was a damn close call. Cersei Lannister looks....sort of okay I think. Luckily she didn't have more proeminance as I was not sure Lena Hadley could hold her own on voice acting alone.
Daenerys Targaryen was a bit of a deception. The animation is pretty dead on but either because I wasn't liking her much at this phase of the story and her smugness or because Emilia Clarke just forgot how she was suppose to portray her emotions but the acting seemed cold and distant and flat on emotions.
Jon Snow also had a disfigured animation but Kit Harrington managed to come through and salvage the character.
Now Margaery Tyrell was weird and bizarre. The animation was ridiculous. Her squinting her eyes seemed like the animator had a bad hangover when he was creating that. Natalie Dormer managed to imprint her touch on the character, as much as she does in GoT, but somehow it didn't seem she was taking it much seriously.
Now, the major dissapointment to me is the graphics. What in the f***ing hell was that? That waterpaint finish on the background which sometimes happened on the foreground as well. It seemed like a three year old was asked to come in and do the finishing touches on all the artwork. That is completely ridiculous and detracted a lot from the overall experience of the game. Constantly my immersion was completely shattered because I started paying attention to the freaking objects on the background instead of listening to the conversations. I was expecting a lot more from Telltale on this front as their previous games were fantastic. But it seems the need to rush thins in order to get the game out in the market completely screwed this.

The random weapons seem to have more negative "enchantment" than they used to.

The new stage (in the middle) is, on average, more difficult than the other stages were and have become. That is except for maybe the last stage, sometimes.

To describe it one sentence:
A Fistful of Gun is an extremely addicting, fast paced, Western-themed pixelized bullet hell with single player arcade, versus, and story modes as well as online/co-op arcade.
Now for a more in-depth review (:
To start off the game, you've got (like I said before) 4 different options:
-Arcade
You're automatically thrown into the action. Shoot as many bandits (or whatever else is thrown at you) as you can. However, you only have 3 lives, so use them wisely. It starts off easy, only a few people coming at you at once. You clear the level assuming the next will only be slightly harder, but suddenly you're being bombarded with enemies on horseback, pigs running around, tnt exploding everywhere, and all your lives are gone. It gets real difficult, real fast, so keep that in mind.
-Story
I haven't played much of the story mode, but from what I've experienced it's nothing like the arcade. It seems to have a slower, gradually increasing pace rather than suddenly spiking in difficulty.
-Versus
Play against a friend!
-Online
Much like classic arcade, but you can play with friends. If you're going to try out this mode, I reccomend getting a group of your friends together to play, as there isn't much of a player base online at any given time.
Character Selection:
You've got 11 completely different, yet equally fun characters to chose from. Each one has a different playstyle, appealing to pretty much everything. You've got a guy that shoots rockets, an archer, an army regiment, a sniper, and many more. I started out playing The 13th (the regiment) as it's easy to play, and I'd reccomend that character for beginners.
Overall, it's a great game and I'm definitely going to be playing it more.
Thanks for reading!

This game is part of one of my favourite single player series. If you have played and enjoyed the likes of UFO: Enemy Unknown or X-COM: Apocalypse then...you probably already own this game.
If you enjoy strategy games in general and somehow don't own this then it comes highly recommended. It has depth in the overall game as you build your base, establish a team and make sure they're kitted out well through research.
The story is ok if not spectacular but it's main purpose is to guide you through from a bunch of 4 rookies with standard issue assault rifles towards a crack team of highly-armoured and lethal soldiers with fun mind powers at their disposal.
And the real fun comes when your Skyranger touches down for each mission and you control each of your squad members as they scour the well-designed maps looking for enemies, or saving civilians, or searching for a VIP to escort.
The enemies are great and imaginative; the graphics are good even by today's standards (this game is now over 3 years old); and the sound/music is atmospheric and add to the overall feel of the game.
The only downside is that the campaign doesn't actually take that long to finish, although it has great longevity through addons, mods or even just playing again on different difficulties and tinkering with the settings. And the AI isn't the best as you have to walk through the mission waiting to "trigger" the enemies, whereupon they spring into action and chase you down.
Overall it is an excellent game. Buy it in one of the many Steam sales and you'll have chance to get excellent value for money ahead of XCOM 2 in a few months!

I came to XCOM a little late--after all my friends had played and recommended it, I knew I wouldn't dislike the game. I'm glad I gave it a chance because this is one of the few single-player games I've finished and thouroughly enjoyed.
This game is definitely about adaptation; you must constantly be aware of positioning, how skills interplay with one another, and learning (painfully) what does and doesn't work against certain alien types.
The story isn't terribly engrossing. You progress through the story by researching alien technology and integrating it into your own arsenal. What makes it so much fun is naming all the characters after your friends, and then trying like hell not to get them killed. Thank god for the save/reload function, as I used it far more often than I probably should have.
I enjoy turn-based games, and this one doesn't have a ridiculously high learning curve--anyone can play on normal and with some basic trial-and-error, figure out a way to beat the game. However, the one thing I didn't understand at the beginning, and wish I would have known earlier on is: BUILD SATTELITES. BUILD UPLINKS. Finished? BUILD SOME MORE.
If you enjoy tactical, turn-based games, and you haven't given XCOM a try, I highly recommended it. Blow up a few friends, it's great fun.

So CoH2....
I'm a huge fan and long time player of the CoH franchise. They such fantastic RTS games to play and a testamant to the longevity of the orignal which still plays like a modern game should.
I have thoroughly enjoyed the sequel and I believe it has improved on it's predecessor in a multitude of ways.
Graphically it is better looking which for the most part should be expected from a newer game.
Gameplay is more or less the same which is positive given how rock solid it was in the original. Units feel very similar to control, movements are smooth and reactions are generally fairly quick.
The improved vehicle control is fantastic and tanks etc feel much easier to use (the addition of a reverse option is great).
Balance is far from perfect but I've yet to feel (as a top 100 2v2 player) that there are combinations/units that are genuinely overpowered nor uncounterable. In any case good players will make them seem this way.
The multiplayer maps are feel fairly well designed, the introduction of the winter and summer versions of the same maps gives a great way to subtly change these maps and make them play different.
The variety of commanders are fantastic and the option to purchase more, I think, is one of the better ways to handle DLC. There are more than enough free commanders for a player to find one (or more) they enjoy using (and be competitive) without being forced to buy the DLC. The skins are totally optional, which never existed in CoH 1 so you're not being charged for something you previously got for free. Should you decide to purchase them though, they are not expensive.
There are lots of players online as well, giving you a good chance of finding a game quickly.
However, the campaign is fairly shallow. The missions don't seem as involved as the original nor as challenging. There can also be problems with lag online with the matchmaking system sometimes making some poor matches.
If you've played CoH 1 and enjoyed it then I cannot see why you wouldn't also enjoy CoH 2. It modernises elements of the original while keeping the core of the game intact. Given it's now available for alot less than it's orignal selling price it's definately worth the money.

It's a simple game, but I enjoyed it.  It's definitely not an RPG, though.  It's more like a VN that just happens to be made in RPG maker.
I thought the concept was interesting.  Each "section" of the game was emotionally effective in its own way, though the one I found the most effective was the nurse's story.  I would've loved for each section to be longer and explore the characters more thoroughly, but the amount of content included is fine for a five dollar game.
One final thing I want to point out is the attention to detail.  I was really impressed by how pretty much every item on the map had a description when you examined it.  In fact, while I was playing, the only object I came across without a description was a palm tree, and it turned out that it was related to an easter egg. Most of the descriptions were unique (even the descriptions for mundane things like different houseplants), and some of them were humorous.  I played this game for way longer than you would if you were just rushing through the story, because I wanted to examine everything.
Please don't compare this game with ace of spades etc. This game is a unique and awesome it is it's own game. I just want everyone to know this.

I was a little hesitant about buying this game.  I love the time period and the rawness of using more simplistic weaponry, but I was concerned about some of the negative reviews the game was getting. I decided to take the risk and buy it, and I'm so glad I did.
Firstly, the game looks beautiful.  The lighting as you creep through dense jungle through rays of light is just astonishing. As is the volumetric fog and the atmosphere it creates.  The different biomes really do breathe life into the map in a way similar to Skyrim.  I just don't get the irony of all the people who bought Far cry 5 and are complaining that the game is like a far cry game.  The simplistic weapons really add to the crafting system and make the survival element of the game more real than just walking around the map to complete a story.  There's more UI customization in this game than previous ones.  I 've chosen to get rid of all the clutter.  I turned off The minimap, game hints, enemy tagging etc in favour of realism.  The game now feels more like a more advanced stone age Skyrim than a Far Cry game.  Another patch is in the making already to add a survival mode with features such as permadeath and other options, so support is ongoing.
My advice to anyone thinking buying the game, is to ignore negative comments and trust your instincts as I did.  If the nature of the game appeals to you, the simple weapons, the survival elements and the time period, then go for it. I'm sure you won't be disappointed.

This review comes after I, first, played Megadimension Neptunia for the PS4.  It would seem that the Neptunia series is one of the few that can claim the sequels to represent improvements over each other.  Which is good - and by no means is Re;Birth1 a bad game.
The core Neptunia games are turn based tactics games.  Battles all play out in arena form with movement taking place within a restricted radius (as opposed to a fixed grid).  All weapons have an area of effect that can potentially reach multiple enemies (this works both ways), and attacks can be built into combos with each class of attack having a different overall purpose.
The gameplay is, overall, solid.  There are some odd difficulty spikes at times (or... for whatever reason everything was suddenly hitting like a truck compared to where I just was in the plot), but nothing an RPG-familiar gamer is going to be completely unprepared for.  Everything is fairly intuitive and min/max style gameplay is available, yet unnecessary to advance.
If you are simply looking to try Neptunia to see what it is all about, I would actually recommend Megadimension Neptunia VII.  It represents, in my opinion, a number of refinements and improvements over what was already a good system and has some better "NewGame+" features.  These are games that can be played out of order without being totally lost.
So... What makes Neptunia ... Neptunia?
If it isn't already obvious, the entire universe is a metaphor for the videogame industry - consoles, games, publishers, developers, etc.  The game is loaded with both blatant and obscure references to games, hardware, and the history of the industry.
The plot, at least thus far, centers around the character "Neptune."  Neptunia has its origins in Sega, and Neptune was the code-name for a console that was all of the hardware of the Genesis and its add-ons (the 32X and Mega CD) into one package.  It was cancelled because it would launch practically alongside the Sega Saturn (wait... there was a console between the Genesis and Dreamcast?).  I will abstain from a review of Sega's console marketing strategies, or complete lack thereof...
The care-free personality of Neptune is, precisely, what makes the Neptunia series work, in my estimation.  Her frequent video game references don't work unless she is allowed to break the fourth wall and to see herself as being in a game.  Yet, it is written in a very tasteful manner.  She is both random/delusional, and measured/wise at the same time.  It's a game that doesn't take itself too seriously - and Neptune's character is how the developers say "we know you've been here, before and you know what's going to happen - just have fun with it."
And that is what Neptunia is about.  It's a parody, tribute, and celebration of the history of videogames and the culture around them.  That is the core of Neptunia.
The bad for Re;Birth1 ?
The English voice acting is... English voice-acting.  Neptune is great, Compa is great, Vert is good, IF is good, flip a coin for everyone else and chalk up 'minion 43' to being one of the programmers who lost a bet.  That... and some of the scenes which actually get voice-acting are kind of random.  A few key plot events are ignored while a few scenes of idle banter get full attention.
The "shares" system is a little wonky and, while not crucial to the central game, does play a role in the True Ending and some item development requirements.  It's a zero-sum game representing the console wars and each system's share of the market and quests will deplete shares from one system while rewarding them to another... so it can lead to repeating certain quests a few times in order to get shares where they need to be for an item's requirments or whatever.  It's a neat idea... but not exactly fun.
Why no complaints on gameplay?
I could list them... but the way Neptunia is designed, most of these are optional elements of the gameplay.  There are various settings you can unlock which make the game easier, or harder.  You can choose whether or not to use the plethora of healing and buffing items in the game.  You can buff the enemies so that the guard break system does play a more important role.
In the end, it's a game that has fun being a game about games.

Welcome to the Wild Wild West, stranger! Do you have what it takes to survive in these rough times? You are here to crush Clayton Boon and his Railroad company. But be aware, rumors say that he made a deal with the devil to kill everybody who is dumb or brave enough to enter his eyesight. Be prepared for a spaghetti western full of evil freaks, not-so-evil freaks, whiskey and - of course - bullets. And horses. And...bullets.
A Fistful of gun offers (very) fast top-down arcade that demands quick eyes and fingers, name it western bullet hell. Choose one of 11 different psychos, each with a unique playstyle, to release the western town from Boons mercyless grasp. Picking your favourite Psycho might rely on your prefered playstyle: Hide, Kill and Hide again? Choose Zeke, The sniper. Unleash a bulletstorm to saw through hordes of enemies? Choose Duke, the man with the chain gun. To do this, you can choose either arcade, story mode or multiplayer via web or local co-op. Story starts with only 3 psychos available since the others need to be unlocked whilst playing. Moving screen by screen you`ll reach Boons hitmen and finally Boon himself whilst collecting gold, finding power ups, alcohol or even finishing some quests. Arcade let`s you pick all available “heroes”, offering a more “endless” feeling with the chance to set your own personal highscore, that can be compared worldwide. Multiplayer is fun to play, works great and makes the game much more enjoyable.
Soundwise not much to say here: typical wild west soundtrack mixed with the sounds of exploding bombs, srcatching bullets and running horses. I like it!
Graphics might not be everybodys cup of tea but, again, I love it. Wonderfully crafted pixel art that already offers the charm of a 90s classic. Flashy colours, lots of small details and a nice sense of (dark) humour add to the “spaghetti western”-feeling I mentioned earlier.
Let`s add some negative points here before I valuate. The controls of some playable characters work great with a 360 controller - but not that great whilst playing via keyboard. Vice versa, too. They have to be great because A Fistful of gun can be hard sometimes, even too hard for people who recently started to play. Due to the fact that dying in story mode means starting from the beginning it tends to become repetitive after a while, although not worn off. That said I hope for more active “psychos” for multiplayer. This is not a real negative argument against the game itself but, hands down, A Fistful of Gun is best played in a pack of players, laughing out loud, dying even louder. I hope for a small future discount to attract a wider playerbase.
So, enough explanatory banter! A Fistful of Gun offers hours of fun (and anger), binding you for at least 1-2 hours daily, not to mention if played with friends. Thus said, Multiplayer is highly recommended since the Singleplayer starts to get repetitive unless you try to beat some High Scores.

I played Tropico 3 after a friend recommended it and loved it, Tropico 4 is in many ways a very similar game to three, I picked up the collectors edition however for a bargain £4 on sale. This includes all the DLC which really sets it apart from Tropico three - especially the 'modern times' DLC which gives you HUGE skyscrapers, and there's nothing like a central business district full of shiny modern buildings surrounded by shanty towns. The people need something to look up to, you see. One of my favourite things about 4 though is the addition of labour camps, no longer must you be content with boring old public executions for your political opponents and other poor sods, now you can work them to death for the greater good. Better still, ever notice how when people get old they get lazy? Some people call it retirement, but really these people just feed off el presidentes generousity. Thankfully, now you can just chuck these sorts in a camp and squeeze 30 years more good labour out of them! I once threw a man in a labour camp for living in a shack by my palace, and many many years later found the same man - he had lived to 138! This is older than anyone has ever lived in real life, therefore I concluded that labour camps must be good for your health - maybe Kim Jong-Un's got the right idea after all.
All in all this a brilliant game, although after a while you do tend to forget you're not actually a dictator......

I came to XCOM a little late--after all my friends had played and recommended it, I knew I wouldn't dislike the game. I'm glad I gave it a chance because this is one of the few single-player games I've finished and thouroughly enjoyed.
This game is definitely about adaptation; you must constantly be aware of positioning, how skills interplay with one another, and learning (painfully) what does and doesn't work against certain alien types.
The story isn't terribly engrossing. You progress through the story by researching alien technology and integrating it into your own arsenal. What makes it so much fun is naming all the characters after your friends, and then trying like hell not to get them killed. Thank god for the save/reload function, as I used it far more often than I probably should have.
I enjoy turn-based games, and this one doesn't have a ridiculously high learning curve--anyone can play on normal and with some basic trial-and-error, figure out a way to beat the game. However, the one thing I didn't understand at the beginning, and wish I would have known earlier on is: BUILD SATTELITES. BUILD UPLINKS. Finished? BUILD SOME MORE.
If you enjoy tactical, turn-based games, and you haven't given XCOM a try, I highly recommended it. Blow up a few friends, it's great fun.

American Nightmare is a stand alone expansion to Alan Wake from Remedy Entertainment. Originally an Xbox live title this has made its way over to the PC with a few tweaks.
Graphics are not powerhouse hungry but its not going to make you vomit in disgust at its admitadly bland pallet. As this game is set mostly in the desert with minimal indoor environmets this game is no stranger to the colour brown. The PC version does look better than its console sibling with AA options and a HD texture pack.
The gameplay is very similar to the main game with a familar over the shoulder third person camera with a reasonable FOV. Ok its a very console orientated FOV and this game does play better with a gamepad than a keyboard and mouse although you want cry and bang your head on the desk if you dont have a gamepad. So I would recommend plugging in a pad and scooting your chair back a tad for a more comforatable experience. The weapons have a nice feel to them, the traditional pistol, rifle and shotgun are back with interesting additions such as the nail gun. There is enough variety of weapons around and plenty of ammo to keep gameplay fresh.
The flashlight returns to burn off the "Darkness" which acts as a shield to enemies making them imune to bullets. But like in the main game the enemies are vunerable to all forms of lights, whether this is car headlights, flares or the sun.
The game lets face it is not very long. The story mode takes about 3/4 hours to complete but considering this started out as an xbox live arcade expansion this is not a bad thing. Especially when the game costs less than a pint. New to American Nightmare is an arcade mode. This is basically a horde mode escape the zombies make it till dawn affair. It has a couple of achievements and map unlocks but single player means its not something you are going to come back to.
So should you buy it? Have you played Alan Wake? If not go pick that up. Its not expensive, has a great story in the style of Stephen King novels. This game is a bit of an oddball rounding off the story that a lot of people expected from the main game. If you have played the base game, then deffinately pick this up. Although a little repeptive in the story it provides a better finish to the story you got so into in the previous incarnation.

A friend gave me this game. I had never played a roguelike before and I'm not much of a strategy buff so I didn't really think I'd enjoy it this much. I also thought the top down pixel graphics made the game look fairly uninteresting.
I'm really glad it proved me completely wrong. I totally got sucked into this game right away. It's really immersive and addicting. The soundtrack really adds a lot. I think I like it even more than the VVVVVV soundtrack. Playing is a rush, and when I die I just want to start over again rather than rage.
The pause mechanic is really great and lets me think things over and micromanage. I don't like rushing to make decisions so that's why I don't like RTS games but there is no time limit here. You can also save and quit and pick up your progress whenever you want which is great.
I ended up getting pretty good at the game a lot faster than I thought I would. The different ship unlocks and upgrades, plus the random encounters give this a ton of replay value. This game will also make you pretty ruthless, so forget about roleplaying Jean Luc Picard. You'll never survive unless you're outright viscious and greedy. There are not really any moral consequences though, but at one point it did guilt trip me pretty damn hard (not going to give spoilers)
Long term strategy is key, so you'll find yourself limping from sector to sector only to die close to the end because you were unprepared for the more powerful enemies later on. It has a lot to do with luck, which is a bit frustrating. But the game is not too difficult on Easy.
TL;DR This game is great, buy it.

The clue was in the title all along and I just failed to see it.
It's like the studio and creative minds behind this disaster were so stoked with the idea of having Superman and Batman fight each other, they couldn't have a coherent thought after to come up with any form of a story. So they let Zack Snyder make a movie to satisfy the 10 year old in him.
Major spoilers ahead!
I thought there were 3 very strong, compelling ideas from the trailers, but the movie failed to delivery on them
1. Batman's aggression towards Superman. 3/4th of this movie is dedicated to this. In fact Batman wants to KILL Superman. And finally, when the moment arrives, Batman stops because his mother's first name is the same as Superman's mother's. And so they become the best of friends. Just like that.
2. People of earth's distrust of Superman, due to the events from the first movie. This too runs through most of the movie, with Superman trying to earn some brownie points by saving a few people. The fact that there is a public hearing against him, indicates that people are not buying it. But in the end, after his supposed death, why does he a get a military/hero style funeral? Why is the country mourning? Did I miss something? Especially since there is confusion on what happened during the hearing.
3. The public hearing: This should have been a really powerful scene. If Superman were to concede, then he'd be answerable to the people and he would not get to be the hero we know he is. The same, if he did not concede. I was giddy with anticipation when this scene started and was immensely disappointed when the Senator starts mumbling. Zack Snyder took the path of least resistance.
- - - - - -
I guess after the writer's gave up on the main ideas, they didn't care about smaller plot points
- Superman has no remorse for the destruction he caused in the first movie. In the big fight he smashes Batman through a building causing the building to collapse. Ditto for Doomsday, smashes him in to a power plant of some sort. He is not even thinking about anyone's safety.
- Just like in the first movie, there is an apocalypse level destruction. Superman himself contributes to some of it. Thousands are probably killed, but superman only saves Lois Lane
- Superman threatens Batman that he can easily kill Batman, twice. Sounds like a bully to me
- Batman STEALING from Lex Luthor so HE gets to exact revenge on Superman
- Batman uses guns, not to intimidate, but actually kill. He even dreams of gun battles.
- The govt. has Zod's body and the ship for 2 years. Luthor comes up with the idea that since the ship has a bio-metric security, he can use Zod's body to gain access. It did not cross anyone else's mind
- One alien craft/tech is lying in the Indian Ocean for 2 years. No nation/military has claimed it. Local fishermen are freely swimming to it and breaking away pieces
- The all powerful Kryptonian key has no security what so ever. Anyone can use it. Even Lex Luthor. It only unlocks EVERYTHING, why should it be secure?
- Kryptonians have banned the technology to create Doomsday. It's so dangerous, they decide not to remove it from the system but keep it, with so minimum security that it can be enabled with a simple voice command by a non-Kryptonian.
- There is no compelling reason behind Lex Luthor's hatred towards Superman. How does he stand to gain or lose?
- There is no villain, purpose, motive or problem to solve in the story. Doomsday appears so that Zack Snyder can once again have a city-leveling battle.
- Why is Doomsday angry with Superman? Since he is made from Zod & Luthor's genes, does anger/hatred towards someone pass through genes?
- When Batman steals the Kryptonite, it would have spoiled whatever Luthor had planned, but Luthor just eggs Superman to fight Batman like they were in cahoots. How does Luthor know what Batman has planned? How does he know about the battle royale. Has he read the comic?
- Why is Batman not suspicious of the other meta beings? Why does he think they are friendly and will help? And against what? Why does he think he will need their help? How come Luthor is in on this?
- Why does Luthor have well designed logos for each meta human?
- Why was wonder woman so concerned with being exposed? According to the photo, she had already revealed herself, in FULL COSTUME. So why the secrecy? And why come out of hiding when she sees lightening coming from the dome? She did not feel the need when world was practically getting destroyed in the first movie.
- Why does Luthor introduce Bruce Wayne and Clark Kent to each other? BW is a billionaire, but CK? Why would anyone care about him?
- Superman stops the car chase. Literally allowing the bad guys to escape. He may not like Batman's methods, but he couldn't figure out if Batman's giving a chase, he's after bad guys?!
- In the midst of deafening destruction Superman can hear Lois Lane. But his mother...his hearing, speed, x-ray vision...he doesn't even give it a shot. And of course Batman finds her in a jiffy because he is...
... the list goes on...but IMDb has a word limit...
I can't believe such a high profile movie had no thought put behind it. Amateur hour. A total disservice to a 75 year legacy and to the fans. I hope the remaining DC movies are scrapped or they finally pulls their socks up.

Bought this game since it was on sale. I usually like games with rouge-like elements and a good challenge, but this game was just plain frustrating. Everytime I used a melee weapon I found it impossible to not eventually take a hit every time I went into a fight, due to the large abudance of enemies that swarm you with both close-range and long-range attacks. Ranged weapons are quite obviously king in this game. If you are ever able to, just use the bow. I've tried to play around stat bonuses on armor for certain weapon types, and it worked well enough to get me to the boss, but the only weapon that I ever got to see the next level with was the bow (which I was then immediately stricken down my a swarm of spiders and tentacles with long ranged attacks. The shotgun is useless. You'd think it work well since it's a ranged weapon like the bow, but don't let it fool you. The shotgun only works a little bit out of melee range.
I understand that dying a lot is probably something that the game was developed around, and it has a Rogue Legacy-esque upgrade system where you can unlock new upgrades and stat bonuses everytime you die in exchange for souls that enemies sometimes drop. The problem that the game is very tedious and frustrating before getting these bonuses. The combat is nothing special, you get 2 attacks based on the weapon, and a seemingly random special move based on the weapon type. Your character moves slow unless you get armor that lets you move faster and that makes it more difficult to dodge incoming attacks.
I got this game for about $5, and nothing about it really makes me want to keep playing after about an hour of playtime. I would not reccomend.

A Fistful of Gun is a nice indie game set in the Old West with a ton of characters to play as and, surprisingly, a wide variety of “control schemes” for said characters (something I had never seen before in a videogame).
After trying a few, I found myself playing mostly with Abel using a controller. It was quite a thrill, specially since pushing the right analog stick as fast as I could kind of resembles reloading a hand gun and it certainly adds to the fun.  The soundtrack is fine, it doesn’t become repetitive and it fits its theme and purpose of the game quite well, but it’s also not too catchy. I wish the multiplayer wasn’t as dead as it seems to be now, because I would have liked to try it out. The artwork is really good and I’m really digging the pixelated style. However, it is true that sometimes there are too many things on screen and all also kind of similar looking, so it can be frustrating not to know where your character is at some points.
I still haven’t managed to beat the story mode, but I really like how each stage seems to be randomly generated, which really adds to the replayability of the game as you never know which event may show up. One thing that bothered me at first is that there is almost no explanation of what anything is and you kind of have to guess it all. Like… the aces. It took me a while to figure out that they were meant to represent the available lives of my character. Or figuring out who was friendly or not. Or what alcohol does or if there is any way not to die after setting yourself on fire (besides going to the next stage). Maybe a small tutorial or a really small "west encyclopedia" on the menu would be good, although it is not too bad, since after a few playthroughs you start to get what everything is, more or less.
I would definitely recommend this game if you liked some rogue-like games like Risk of Rain or the Binding of Isaac. Although A Fistful of Gun has another approach to the genre, the randomly generated levels, the stage after stage formula and trying to reach the final boss, etc. are some really attractive things that a Fistful of Gun shares with these games. One thing that  is missing though is more “upgrades” to further increase that rogue-like experience of the games I mentioned. You can buy a new gun or upgrade your character, but that is not something that always happens. (I've been killed many times without seeing a single upgrade, sadly)
Besides all this, the game is a lot of fun, the random events are quite diverse and the achievements (which can be quite funny) and cards are just the icing on the cake.  So to sum up, this game is definitely a yes. I’ll see you in the multiplayer, once Fistful of Gun becomes more popular. Until then, keep your revolvers ready and no shooting until the coin hits the floor!
Disclaimer: I received this game for free for reviewing purposes.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is the 2nd game in the Alan Wake franchise. Although it is a standalone product on Steam, it plays more like an expansion pack to Alan Wake than a direct sequel. The story is shorter and far less compelling, but the action, gameplay, and graphics are all beefed up a bit and actually a lot more fun than Alan Wake.
* Low price tag, the game is $10 base and frequently goes for $5 during Steam sales.
* Rather than walking down a hallway with the occasional monster (which is the original Alan Wake in a nutshell), American Nightmare features a more open-world. That being said, the game-world is incredibly small and features only three locales: a rest stop, an observatory, and drive-in theatre.
* The arcade mode, which is supposed to be one of the main draws of this game, is flat and not fun. It's very similar to Resident Evil's "Mercenaries" mode, where you simply run around and try to kill monsters in combos. However, Resident Evil somehow manages to be more fun and feel faster-paced.
* Some art objects were taken directly from the original Alan Wake and stand out.
* Being from Arizona, where the game is set, there were way too many noticeable errors. We don't have license plates on the front of our cars. There are Saguaro Cactuses in our deserts. There are not tall deciduous trees. I understand the location is a fictional town created in Alan's head, but I really don't care. I choose to be outraged!
American Nightmare is short and sweet, and fixes almost everything that was wrong with the original Alan Wake. Since most people buy both games together, I kept this review short. However, if you have to pick one of the two, I would definitely tell you to get American Nightmare. Keep in mind, though, that American Nightmare does NOT compare to many other AAA shooter titles - it is fairly generic and won't offer you a revolutionary experience.

With a great scenery and beautiful graphics, Dying Light is easily the best looking zombie game out there. The story of Dying Light is really generic, but the characters and the protagonist make up for that. Dying Light has a decent sized city to play in and gives you a new city to play in further into the game. Free running over the roofs and many obstacles in the city of Harran feels awesome and really smooth. Combat could use a bit more depth but has some really smooth dodging mechanics to keep it fun, and make it challenging at times. There's also a nice upgrading/crafting system for your weapons and creating fun gadgets like Throwing stars and Fireworks. Leveling is really fun aswell, you have 3 different skill tree's which you level up at the same time and some really nice skills to unlock. The game is pretty overwhelming when you start out, you're gradually introduced to the UI elements but it'll probably be confusing for the first few hours. You'll want to fiddle with the settings to reduce the noise that it creates.
In those first hours you’ll be exploring the different aspects of the game such as the combat, node/worker system, crafting, upgrading gear and so on. Note that this takes some effort on your side as it's easy to miss some of the in-game guides/tutorials that explain those parts of the game.
BDO features various paths where you can progress in, you'll gain XP as in other MMO's and gain combat skill points, but there are other features such as contribution points, used for (but not limited to) the craft parts of the game and energy points (used to execute a variety of actions such as crafting, hiring new workers, talking in server chat)
It'll be no surprise that XP and combat points can be gained by beating up mobs. I think the look and feel of the combat is by far the best quality of the game. I've mainly played as a berserker and it was very refreshing being able to beat up mobs using the shortcut/hotkey system (shift + LMB, or -> + RMB etc.) instead of the typical MMO's 1-2-3 button mashing. It features combos and pretty visceral animations. Note that your mileage may vary here if you play another class.
Quests rarely sparked my interest and following the main quest quickly falls into the pattern of "introduce mob type -> kill them -> kill different variations of them -> kill boss -> introduce to new mob type". The solo bosses that I've encountered had no interest mechanics going for them aside from some frontal attacks that you can evade to avoid being stunned etc.
The problem however is that if you play on the XP boosted servers, despite following the quests & doing the side quests you'll out level the quests and mobs & nothing is really a challenge until you reach level 50-51. I didn't mind since I had fun trying out the combos and enjoyed the playstyle of berserker until then, after which it turned into grinding packs of mobs.
Aside from your typical XP bar, you also gain contribution points by doing the side quests (or handing in side products gained by crafting). These points can be used to invest in nodes, or housing in a town. Nodes are thing such as farms or mines to which you can assign workers that will gather materials for you.
The workers and the materials they gather need a place to stay, and this is where the towns housing comes in. You can buy houses at towns, again by using contribution points, and assign them as storage to expand your warehouse capacity, or lodging so you can hire more workers.
This was a promising interesting system that for me fell flat around the same time I reached level 50. By then I had unlocked the nodes around the first two towns and had workers (26 or 27 of em) assigned to most of them.
All in all it seemed like a complex system but it turns out to be bait for a simple grind you have to go through, maxing out workers seems like a tedious process with little complexity/challenge to it.
On top of that, workers will only finish their current task (you can queue tasks), if you go offline, so to get the most out of it you’ll have to keep the game running.
I’ve only explored cooking, processing and fishing in BDO. The materials you gain from the worker nodes can be sold directly on the marketplace. You can also use them as ingredients for the various crafting systems so it earns you more if you have the appropriate skill.
While crafting is mostly AFK friendly, the time you can go AFK depends on your inventory space, weight limits, durability of the tools etc.
Gear is probably best gained by buying it from the marketplace. Note that the marketplace has fixed prices which I suppose is based on supply/demand, you can only list items for the price range that the game sets for you. I’ve had no fun interacting with the market what so ever, popular items are sold instantly so you’ll either sit there & hoping you can snipe items, or use the pre-order system. A buy/order system such as you can find in Eve wouldn’t hurt it in my opinion.
Gear is typically chosen based on their set bonus, and you upgrade them using black stones to enchant it. Each successful enchant increases the defense or attack stats the item has and it becomes progressively harder to enchant the item. If the enchantment fails, you gain fail stacks, which increase the chance of success of your next attempt. Failure also lowers the max durability of an item, forcing you to repair it after too many failed attempts by using either the same base item or memory fragments (expensive!). This is a RNG game where you have to build up the fail stacks by enchanting other items, switch to alts, etc, I didn’t like it all.
Since P2W seems mentioned a lot I tend to agree that it favours people that buy items from their cash shop. Pets can be bought from other players through the market, but you’ll have no chance at that when you start out, so you best buy them from the shop. Pets have various skills, but most importantly, auto loots stuff for you. Considering the quests progress towards “kill 100 of mob type X”, you’ll have a lot of manual looting to do, so these pets are very handy to have.
Other cash shop items are increasing inventory space (not really needed), weight limits (probably very handy, as while you increase inventory slots, the weight limit does not), costumes which give bonuses to crafting or things like stamina, xp gain, jump height. Items that increase the max durability you can repair with a fragment or item, outfits that allow you to craft stuff from your warehouse instead of your inventory and value packs.
Value packs increase your weight & inventory limits, more xp and 30% increase in money you gain from the marketplace (so to negate the taxes I suppose). It’s basically a subscription as value packs last 7 or 30 days.
You can argument that these are all convenience stats but I find it all adds up rather fast and it’s pretty pricey to get the items, so for me another downside to this game.
The game features good combat animation but falls short in that category when it comes to challenge and boring mechanics. The other aspects of the game hide behind a thin veil of complexity which was fun to explore and discover, but once you look past that you’ll see it’s grinding all the way. If you’re fine with grinding and the playstyle that that offers, you’ll have good fun with the game, otherwise I fear the discouragement of slow progress will push you towards the cash shop, or in my case, stopped playing.
