I played Diablo III and was one of the people who got bored. I picked this up because a) people claimed "it's what Diablo III should have been" and b) my friend helped sell it with the game's skill progression.
I am somebody who likes RPG's with a lot of character progression options and a fairly open approach to how I build my character, their stats, their skills, their profession and so on. I didn't like the options Diablo III gave me, but I am finding Grim Dawn gives me plenty in this respect, for me to develop my own play style and experiment. My main character, a battle mage, for example, has had their skills redone over and over to try different things. I started out with a big 2h weapon hailing down icey boulders down onto my enemies. But my current build, I am running in full heavy armour, am moderately tanky, I have a 1h and a tome, I can charge at my enemies, smash their zombie faces in with my hammer, thanks to Cadence. Or...fire a massive Death Ray and obliterate them, but to a big detriment to my mana. And my Occultist on the other hand, Bloody Pox is just...nasty, instant Ebola that spreads...and spreads to anything that touches the infected and you just watch a chain reaction of bodies - given my Occultist is also a gunslinger, I don't even have to get close to just watch stuff drop. But if I wanted, I could go for a heavier build of an Occultist, give them heavy armour and a scythe and problem mix them with a Soldier build to reap the benefits and could live a Dark Knight fantasy or something.
The reality is, there's a lot you can do to mould your own playstyle. First you have your stats:
Physique -> Benefits heavy stuff, can mean for tankier stuff
Cunning -> More beneficial to physical damage, but think of it as being beneficial to more dextrous builds
Spirit -> Magic orientated.
How you balance your stats can help benefit the build you want and also certain items will have a minimal stat requirement. So if you want that massive heavy axe, you need the physique to use it.
Then you have your class. In fact, you have two at level 10. You can combine them to create a new class. For example, my Battlemage was created by combining Soldier and Arcanist. You get full access to their full spectrum of skills, so there's no Major/Minor system going with the classes combos. So you can choose which sides to invest in more or go for something more balanced. In the builds you add points to the skills you want and level them up. Going back to the Battle Mage, at one point I was mostly invested in Trozan's Sky Shard, which helped crush enemies, but has a recast, so I'd go in melee and then drop sky shards intermittantly. Now that i have a charge from soldier, I can run in and still spam Cadence, but I've replaced Sky Shard with Albrecht's Aether Ray, which is now fully upgraded and incredibly deadly. So my melee now is a back up, rather than my primary approach, because Aether Ray uses a LOT of mana to sustain.
Then comes the next bit. Devotion. For every Shrine you purify in the game, you gain Devotion points, which allows you to gain stats and passive skills from the stars. You can go for stuff that gives your fire based attacks more damage, for example. Or something that gives your pets more "oomph", there's a number of choices and as you invest more into Devotion, more trees will unlock.
And finally. The last point of customisation. Gear. Gear doesn't just boost base stats, it can also boost things like "Fire Damage" or "Frost Damage" it can also provide extra levels to skills (and push them over cap), like +1 to All Arcanist Skills or +3 to Cadence. As examples. So loot you pick up and use can hugely benefit your builds. In additions, you can get passive and active skills from gear too. I have an item that grants me a skill called "Demon's Breath", which is a nice instant cast AoE I can throw in between attacks. You will also get materials you can put into an item's slot to add or upgrade stats on it.
So as you can see, when I say there's a lot of options for building your character and customising your playstyle, I am not kidding.
Now what about the rest. Graphics are decent. Gameplay is enjoyable and the game is challenging, I'd recommend using the "Veteran" option in your settings, it gives you more formidable foes, but can give you more of a payoff as result. I'd recommend getting the Crucible DLC for two reasons: it's a good way to get any new characters kick started in the game if you don't want to keep going through the initial 10 or 20 level grind with the game's story. And the second is that it helps you test your build, the more you can survive the crucible, the stronger your build.
I feel like it created a better atmosphere than Diablo III. I am somebody who has ended up getting bored of games that focus so much on the undead, but this game helps me care again. You are literally the last of mankind and the war has already been lost and humanity hasn't stood well against the force known as "aetherials". It's a dark fantasy settings, with a distinctive Wild West feel to it. So not just zombies and dark things, you'll be fighting molotov throwing, gunslinging cowboy bandits. Given it is a post apocalypse, some of the gear you can get feels thrown together. In terms of its post apocalyptic wild west sides of things, maybe think of Wasteland.
The story and lore is interesting and there's a number of things to pick on along the way. But the game is not heavily story focused as an APRG, but still has enough to keep you invested an interested.
All in all, a great game. But for me, the biggest selling point, the level of customisation I can go to in my character builds. It offers a replayability for me, to play the game with all sorts of builds and with the option to easily skip dialogue and run through story related stuff quickly and with the help from The Crucible, it doesn't making it so monotonous to keep restarting over on a new character for a new build.

TLFU: 4/10 Some of the worst, most ill conceived controls I have ever seen in any game, ever.
This is not a bad game as far as most production levels go. Sound, music, voices, graphics, and presentation value are a 10/10. One thing I like about the game is how it pays homage to spaghetti westerns which are some of my favorite movies. What I don't like is that the game can have crazy difficulty spikes because of all games that share one thing in common that makes them "NES hard": the controls. I am no slouch in the skills department though, as I have beaten some tough games in quick fashion. Like Risk of Rain. I beat that in 2-3 hours. I even beat House of Dead Ninjas in under 2 hours despite its awful loose slippery controls. There are some even tougher that I have beaten, but then I have seen some people in the forums say they blew through this game's story fast and that it was too easy. I feel like I am missing something yet I know exactly how to play the game. Enemy bullets are a real problem, especially when there are twenty guys on screen, they all have three-way spread shot, and they all fire at once, covering all available screen space with fire that is impossible to avoid. It is screens like this that stop a long story or arcade run dead in its tracks, draining every single life that I haven't lost up until then on one screen.
Upgrades - are offered at random, so if you are 7 screens in on arcade mode and it has yet to offer you a dmg increase, you are in big trouble. That is one aspect of the game that could use a fix big time, if nothing else. The option screen is a mess too. It at first looks like foreign language until I messed around some and finally figured out how to remap my controller buttons. The option screen absolutely needs to be more clear and friendly and there is no ifs ands or buts about that. What irks me most is in my opinion poorly concieved control schemes for most of the guys. So here are the characters and reasons why I hate most of them because the control design in this game is horrible.
- Noah: Best gun imo but it is offset by the fact that he moves too fast, like he is flying around the screen like a plane in a shmup with too sensitive of controls. If he is slowed down then enemy projectiles will need to be slowed down some also on later stages. As it is, their projectiles are way too fast the deeper you get, eventually coming to a screen where all bad guys have spread and their bullets reach you almost instantly, making dodging bullets a pipe dream. Also his default buttons for both barrels are A and B, which is the worst combo that it could have been because it basically eliminates being able to fire both barrels at once unless you keep your thumb at a uncomfortable angle. I had to remap my controller to make barrels one and two buttons X and A.
- Two Feather: You fire up/down/left/right with the four buttons on the controller and that is actually fine, but you can only fire one arrow at a time and you can only fire in 4 directions. You can fire repeatedly, but not instantly. There is a delay, which is enough to negate him as being even close to as useful compared to a guy like Noah. Besides, I don't want to mash fire for every single arrow in a shoot-em-up twin stick styled game
- Billy: Has a good gun, but you have to press whichever button on screen above his head that is showing (X Y A or B), otherwise the gun will just click and another button lights up. The problem with that is you have to keep your eyes on your character the whole time to see what to press instead of being able to keep your eyes on the game. Also, his buttons get messed up from when I had to rebind them for Noah so if I want to play him, I would have to go back into the options and re-rebind the controls.
- Pablo: This guy is alright, not much complaint for him, other than when you are on the spread of death screen, it is tough to lay bombs and kill guys when you can't dodge the screen filling spread gunfire.
- Abel: Another worthless character. You have to flick the right thumb stick in the direction you want to fire, one flick for each shot, and he is highly innacurate until you can get accuracy upgrades which come at pure random so you can be stuck with♥♥♥♥♥accuracy for a long time. The big problem is after you fire 6 bullets you have to flick the right stick six more times to reload before you can fire again. This pause in gameplay creates a window for enemies to quickly fill the screen with bullets. And with that much thumbstick flicking it quickly wore my thumb down.
- Virgil: Has some kind of weird musket gun that you fire once with right trigger then you have to reload it by pumping left trigger 5 times. You can fire it after any number of pumps but the less pumps means the less bullets comes out which is bad news when the screen is filled with bad dudes.
- Duke: His minigun can mow lawn but the problem is that when things get tough in later areas and enemy projectile speed gets to a level where bullets reach you near instantly, you are going to die because he moves extremely slow while firing.
- Tao: Hate him. He can fire small or large rockets. You can lay multiple rockets, but the problem is that the little rockets take 2+ seconds to take off, which can maybe be accomodated for and honed by some players, but just still imo sucks. The bigger rockets are one of the dumbest things I have ever seen, as they sit there for what seems like ten seconds before they fire. By then enemies are long gone and it's 2016 already.
- Zeke: You L-click to throw knives and R-click to reload them and can carry like 7. Again, having to reload each individual shot in a single shot weapon in a game where enemies don't have to and can fire a unlimited barrage of screen filling spread fire at you make this guy less desirable.
- The 13th: I like this one. Moves slow but you can R-click to zoom around, pop off a shot, then move again. The problem is that it's a squad of guys making you a much bigger target for the screen filling gunfire and they drop like flies. Still, a much better choice than other guys.
Keep in mind this is all single player. Someone just told me in the forums that they got the highest score on their server with a combination of Duke and Tao, so maybe the characters become less useless if you combine them. I don't know because my review is based off of SP experience. I would play online, but not enough people own the game and online is a ghost town.

Lethal League is a what you get when you cross a fighting game with dodgeball in all the best ways.  Players jockey to control a small ball, hitting it around the screen in an attempt to knock out eachother.  Every hit on the ball speeds it up, and it quickly moves from an easy to predict slow moving projectile to a streak that bounces around the screen, ricocheting off ceiling, walls, and floor to take out players.
This simple set up leads to an exciting and incredibly fun game.  Unlike most fighting games, there are no long lists of special moves to learn and memorize (each character has slightly differnt angles they will hit the ball at, and a special move that can be powered up during play and used, but no difficult button combos are required for any moves).  This makes the game very intuitive and easy for players to jump in and start playing, even if you are not into fighters.  However, the interplay between player and their specials does lead to a suprising amount of depth in the combat, and learning the timing to intercept balls as they come off of other players at higher speeds will take practice.
If I had any criticisms for the game, it would be that the simplicity of it can be a double edged sword.  Games can start feeling repetative during long play sessions.  Game options can extend this a bit, but in the end most feel gimicky and I find myself losing interest after 30-60 minutes.  However, that being said, I still find myself coming back to this game to get in a few quick rounds against friends when we don't have time for a long playsession, or to finish out a night of gaming.  And that is where the game shines imho, quick bursts of action and excitement when I don't have the time to spend hours playing.
This games perfectly fills a niche in my gaming library.  It is well worth the price (and worth getting a few extra copies for your friends as well).  An unreserved thumbs up from me.

So I finally decided to write a review for Grim Dawn. After 400 hours it deserves one.
So a little background about myself. I have been playing action RPG's for a very long time. I grew up playing Diablo 2 for 10 years.
So i would like to say that i have over 10k hours invested into that game.  I have also put a few thousand into Diablo 3.  I never played titan quest back when it came out unfortunetly.
Played through Torchlight(not on steam). And also some of Torchlight 2. I havent been able to get into Path of Exile though.
The three big ARPG's right now are Diablo 3, PoE and Grim Dawn. So comparisions will be made between the three.
Ill break down key points about the game.
Graphics: The mood and tone of the game are represented well by the graphics. It deserves its name of "Grim" Dawn Textures are good and so is the lighting. But its nothing too crazy that the lower-end systems out there cant handle the game.
Now the animations are definately not as polished as they could be. Compared to Diablo 3 or even PoE. Comparing PoE or grim dawn to Diablo in that regard isnt too fair because both of these other games are made by indie devs.
With all that being said the lack of super high quality animations does not detract from the enjoyment of the game for me personally.
I run a I7-4790k and a GTX 1070 and i get around 200 frames in some areas and others a lot less. The engine itself is the cause of this im sure, but the only time that happens is when theres a ton of enemies on screen and effects
start going of like the fourth of july. It can be a little frustrating to deal with but any game that has a lot of effects can in certain circumstances have bad performance.
Content: You get 4 acts to play through and many dungeons and secret areas to explore. a full playthrough on normal will probably take you 15-25 hours. This game is less random than diablo and PoE but what you get instead is a
hand-crafted world full of secrets and mystery. I have 400 hours and there are so many secrets im still finding them and rediscovering old ones. A fifth act will be coming in the expansion thats planned.
You will get your moneys worth if you pick this game up and play it through just a few times. Espically so if you get it on sale.
End Game: This is where Grim Dawn lacks a bit compared to Diablo 3 and PoE. As of right now there are 3 end game dungeons you can explore and fight through, and hopefully not die.
The third one which is a 4-5 layer dungeon was added free a few weeks ago. GG Crate. <3 The other "end game" activity is farming up enough reputation of the various factions to hunt down nemesis enemies.
Nemesis enemies are extremely tough bosses that spawn randomly throughout the world and will drop awesome loot. Only the strong need apply. Other than that "end game" is kind of bare. Its more like diablo 2 in that regard.
I spend a lot of time making new builds to see if i can push them into ultimate difficulty and complete the dungeons etc. Hopefully they will bring something in to help with this lack of "end game" in the expansion.
*hint hint*
Gameplay: The combat feels tight and responsive, you never feel like you out of control of your character under normal circumstances. Every now and then♥♥♥♥♥♥happens but its only happened to me honestly a handful of times in 400 hours.
The camera is zoomable both in and out from the default spot and full 360 degree rotation is enabled. I love this camera so much that other ARPGS that dont have it makes me upset haha.
The combat isnt as "fast and hectic" as diablo or PoE but that doesnt mean the game is slow or dull. Its all relative. Once you get into the higher levels challenge dungeons and other areas will make you♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself with how tense
the game can be. With the way they have built the classes and items you will be able to find a playstyle that fits you for sure. As fast or as slow as you want.
Sound: Metal clanks, blood spills. The dying breathe of your enemies escape their lips, cursing you as they evaporate into a pink mist. You can hear giant hulking brutes breathing off in the distance, skeletons shambling around the corner and so on. So the sound scape is good and positional audio cues are there to help you out. Sound is very good. Not award winning but does its job and does it very well
Itemization/stats: This is a very important aspect for any RPG and i would dare to say more so for any ARPG. ARPG's revolve around the gameplay loop of: Kill enemies, aquire loot, kill stronger enemies, aquire better loot.
Once you nail that and make that as fun as possible thats when good ARPG's are born.
You have your standard item rarities in Grim Dawn: Common Items(white), Magic items (yellow), Rare Items(Green), Epic Items(blue) and Legendary items(Purple). Legendary items only drop when youre level 50+.
As standard you are looking for epic and legendary gear but they way they have set up the stats on items in this game is well thought out. In some cases, rare, green items can be best in slot for certain builds.
Thats something youll never see in diablo 3. The rate at which you find gear in this game is also very fair. it makes playing solo very doable and with the itemization as good as it is you can get to end game without no-lifing the game.
Thats not to say the items and stats are perfect but the pros definately outweigh the cons.
This has been a big factor for the enjoyement of the game for me. The robust item and stats paired with a dual class system means you can make and try builds to your hearts content.
Fun factor: The game is a blast to play once you sink your teeth into it. I wont lie at first i was kind of bored with the game but once i got past blood grove the game "clicked" for me. Milage may vary on that. BUT because i said that if you feel that same way i did back then give it a full chance and push yourself to do at least one whole playthrough. Look up some builds online and find something you think youll like
A lot of builds start becoming fun and viable around level 30-40+ it seems to me. Skills and gear starts to fall into play and synergies start forming.
I cant recommened this game enough to people. I love it to death. It has its faults but if what i described doesnt bother you then youll find youll love the game too.
*disclaimer i did not talk about every aspect of this game in this review only stuff i felt was important. There are many other little things and systems that make Grim Dawn greater than the sum of its parts.
Thanks for reading! Any questions or comments feel free to post them! :)

I saw this game on the front page of Steam and being a sucker for westerns I just had to try it out, and boy am I glad I did. As for the gameplay, it is quite fun and generally controls quite well, except for a few of the characters which can be a bit awkward at least on KB+mouse. I think the biggest selling point of the game is it's eleven unique characters, which each have a very different style and are all fun to play; chances are you will find at least one character you enjoy playing. You can play either story, arcade, or versus mode. Story is single player, and has some rogue-like elements, it's actually something like Binding of Issac in that you have to get through X number of squares to reach a boss, and you have to defeat a number of bosses before you reach the final boss, picking up and buying powerups along the way. As you'd probably expect, the story is about as simple as it gets, it is a standard western revenge plot: the head of a railroad company has wronged you and now you are out for blood. Personally I think most of the replayability lies in the arcade mode, where you must clear out as many of the randomized areas you can either by yourself, with friends, or online. As long as there continues to be an online community I think this mode could have some lasting appeal. As for versus mode, I honestly haven't played it yet, though it seems like it could easily fall prey to unbalanced characters.
The art style in this game is fantastic, pixel graphics have been done to death at this point but the visuals of this game manage to capture the aesthetic of spaghetti westerns very well, and considering how rare western games are, even in the realm of indie games, I think the style really holds its own. As for the music, from what I've heard I'm not too impressed honestly, just seems like a bit of a mish-mash between retro game music and Ennio Morricone, but it really doesn't have a style all its own like in say Luckslinger, another indie western-themed game, in any case this isn't that big of a deal.
My Verdict: For a little over the price of a movie, I think you'll probably get your value and then some out of this game, especially if you enjoy westerns or top down shooters.

Each "battle" takes place on a map that's similar to the ones used in TRPG's like Final Fantasy Tactics. And like RPG's, you can level up your guys (by increasing their rank - Sergeant, Lieutenant, etc.) to give them improved skills, like increasing the effectiveness of using Med Packs, or giving Snipers a bonus to their Aim if they're shooting at someone that's at a lower elevation.
Your home base is where you'll spend your time when you're not out hunting down aliens. It's a 4-level building, built below ground. You'll start out with only a couple buildings on the first level. You'll have to pay to excavate the rest of your home base, as well as pay for whatever buildings you decide to build.
Even if you play the game on the easiest mode, this game will still prove to be a little bit of a challenge w/o using cheats.  Which is one thing I liked. It's not "we'll let you walk all over us back and forth" easy, but it wasn't "We can 2-shot you blindfolded from a mile away" difficult.

Here are a few items that I enjoyed and found compelling about
:
Story - As explained,
is centered around a young woman who is relieving herself from work for the final time to retire in a the remote town of
. The player discovers secrets within the community, as well as between its members, in a well-written adventure that spans over several periods; the dialogue and themes are fluid and interlock appropriately. This title has multiple endings and subsequent consequences depending on what the player decides to do throughout its advancement.

Hidden Content - From its side objectives to its references, unlike many Indie titles,
composition is established on subtlety. Because of this, exploration is highly encouraged; the game only takes about an hour to complete the story entirely while interacting with most things in the world, but there is so much more to unearth in the relationships between the various people and timelines.
Dialogue -
, since there are no complex mechanics other than its sense of choice, heavily relies on spoken and written word. In a sense, there is a purpose and comment for and from each non-player character in this title which really entices the player to inquire from others within the world to not only progress, but to also simply enjoy what is said. As stated previously and emphasized by the opening quote,
empowers the player when it should and shuts them down when applicable; it has some powerful writing, which compliments the playstyle well. It is humorous, fun, grim, and intelligent at the points it is necessary to be.
TL:DR - Beginning this title, I was skeptical with the story hook. However, it did not take long for the lore to engulf my entirety, as I interacted with nearly everything I could with glee simply to see what text would appear from either the author or the individual being spoken to. This title is extremely cheap but easy to finish totally, and is generally fun and thought-provoking throughout. I would highly recommend this title for those who enjoy story-based games as well as simple roleplaying games with choice-related elements. Thanks for reading.

Compelling overhead twin-stick shooter with multiple classes, satisfying firearms, a deep and varied skills tree, and a versatile drone buddy with its own helpful abilities and skills. On the graphics side, dynamic animations, lots of bloody alien monster gore, explosions and flames. I know lots of twin-stick fans see no online co-op in this, and then dismiss Solstice Chronicles: MIA out of hand -- just imho, I think you're missing out on something special that's trying some truly unique things in the category. :)
While the single player campaign isn't Shakespeare,  missions are connected by interesting cutscenes with fairly decent voiceover work. My favorite mission has to be that one that takes place on a moving train, but there are also several memorable boss enemies.
Survival mode drops you in a large, open map with multiple objectives. While the single player maps largely use hallways, tunnels, nooks and crannies, the Survial map's openness means you need to stay on the run and always be trying to avoid getting swarmed over.
When a timer runs down, you get an opportunity to evacuate ('use' key to get a blue path to that point) or if you stick around, the evac aircraft drops in supplies to help you. You only earn skills tree points in Survival if you successfully evac.
I've enjoyed the game very much on keyboard/mouse. All keys are rebindable. The crosshair is always "on screen," turning from white to red when you're firing. If you enjoyed Helldivers on kb/mouse, what I've found is that holding RMB down lets me aim precisely and keep pointed in certain directions as I do in Helldivers. Colorful lines denote the firing cone radius of each weapon, and there's a skill available to narrow that radius, if you prefer.
Solstice Chronicles: MIA's four classes include:
I've enjoyed trying the different classes, and different available skills. We're pushing for a true 'respect' system, but it is at the least fun to try different builds, and I think this in itself helps give the game some replayability value.
I've enjoyed using all the firearms, which include a pistol, shotguns, assault rifle, energy rifle, submachine gun, light machine gun.
All classes can also pick up "Brutal" weapons in-game. These are high damage, temporary weapons that only last as long as the ammo they have, and so can't be reloaded. An available passive skill increases the amount of ammo a Brutal weapon has. Examples include the spinning minigun and the autocannon.
One of the unique features of the game is the threat meter. This results in a game  where the pacing can often ebb and flow throughout the course of a mission or a Survival mode session. You have to keep an eye on how the enemy spawns respond to your effectiveness, and also the impacts of the Drone using its Taunt mode, or its bombs.
Also using certain skills may trigger introduction of certain tougher enemies, so really the game is often quite unpredictable from one session to the next.
The drone buddy takes a while to get the hang of using, but is such a lifesaver at times, and its four tactical skill-set has its own skills upgrade tree. The drone tactical skills include:
LIke anyone, i think online co-op -- perhaps at least two-player in Survival mode -- would add a lot to it, but the Fig crowdfunding  fell well short of the stretch goal that would have ensured that feature's addition. What's there now is still plenty fun, and local co-op is supported. I'm having a blast so far, and I don't feel like online co-op's absence is a dealbreaker.
imho what the game needs now is more -- more single player mission maps, more Survival maps, maybe some sort of procedurally generated levels mode that could add more long-term replayability.
The drone abilities, and some of the class skills add a lot of unique flavor and tactics to the game, and I think any twin-stick  shooter fan should at least give Solstice Chronicles: MIA a try; or at least wishlist it and wait for a sale. :)
I may be biased or naive because this is the first game I ever backed on the Fig crowd funding site -- I want it to succeed. It's a little rough around the edges, but the devs communicate frequently at forums, it's gotten updated a few times since release already. I think it'll get even more fun over time. :)

This is a game I really wanted to love. The genre of high quality top-down shooters is underserved, and when I saw this I picked it up immediately. Unfortunately, while the gameplay is decent, the game doesn't seem finished and I ran into numerous bugs (not the kind you shoot!) and technical problems that ultimately made the experience frustrating. First, the good parts:
The core gameplay is solid - shooting and melee are satisfying, if a bit clunky, and there are enough enemy types to keep things interesting. The use of the drone is pretty cool but takes some experimentation to figure out (the game is short on explanation). Resources are limited, so you have to weigh your options carefully. "Do I shoot this group or use a grenade or bash through them to save ammo?" Enemies usually just keep coming (the spawn mechanics are a bit hard to understand), so you either keep moving or spend a lot of time bashing/wasting ammo. The guns are fun though, and theres enough variety to let you experiment, particularly with heavy weapons. The customization options with skill points are decent.
Unfortunately, this brings us to the bad parts.
GRAPHICS GLITCHES EVERYWHERE. Before I say more, I would like to note that I have a several year old gaming laptop and I was forced to run on low graphics to mitigate the FPS lag. Even so, I still had FPS trouble at times. Beyond this, however, I ran into missing textures and enemies teleporting through objects. One level was so bad I was running around half the time in empty space. This is something I might expect from a beta or EA, not a released game. Hopefully these glitches get fixed.
Beyond the graphics, the controls can be a bit clunky and the AI is terrible. All the enemies on the map just run towards you without avoiding obstacles. Trying to throw grenades and use skills precisely is tough and not intuitive. If you're not extremely careful they get thrown in random directions and distances, wasting valuable supplies. And, if you die (by a mis-thrown grenade for instance) and have to restart at a checkpoint, all the gates you've opened are now closed. This means you can't backtrack for ammo/guns or escape an onslaught of enemies. I ended up having to restart multiple levels because I couldn't continue. Maybe this is by design, but what's the point of a checkpoint if you have to restart anyways?
Overall, I'm very disappointed. With some patches and optimization, this could be a very fun game. At the moment, I can't recommend it :(

A solo game with the lore that followed Red Solstice, this gem is somewhat short but sweet.  With giblets and bullets flying I was never in short supply of action.  Here's a rundown of the pro/cons:
Pros
Near flawless xbox 360 controller support, seamlessly swap between gamepad or mouse.
A funny drone sidekick with a story that follows "Grunt".
Deeper skilltree development than Red Solstice, mouseover them to see details if using a controller.
Strol Virus afflicted bosses, fully voiced and wicked tough, they'll have you running a lot to stay alive.
Great selection of abilities and weapons that can be customized and swapped each mission with upgradable levels.
Multi-playthrough friendly having an assortment of marine classes.
Lighting, graphics and sound all felt good, and provided an adequately creepy monster squashing experience.
Cons:
Very, very, very short.  Completed it in 4 hours.
Currently no online multiplayer. solo experience or local co-op only but possible in the future.
Occasionally found myself unable to shoot enemies at different heights, had to reload a checkpoint to fight a boss that suddenly disappeared - needs bug fixing polish.
Heavy weapons are no longer built into classes (flamethrower exception) - can't start with a minigun or autocannon.
20$ price point for a game this short with no multiplayer is a bit rough, maybe wait for a discount or expansion.
Overall:
8/10 damn good fun splatting swarms of infected mobs.

As much as I enjoy Game of Thrones and A Song of Ice and Fire, I can't, in good conscience, recommend Telltale's take on the franchise. Mainly because I find it to be an unfinished product with an unsatisfying conclusion with a cliffhanger.
The illusion of choice you're given in these games was, unfortunately, to be expected. Wanting wildly different branching paths that reward multiple playthroughs is apparently a utopic wish, because the game has a set linear path in the end, and as much as Telltale may want you to think otherwise, the game doesn't offer different experiences with different choices.
Sure, you'll get a different response and some minor changes may occur, but in the end, things are still going to stay the same. I honestly think that Telltale should at the very least advertise the game the way it truly is: a linear story with a few ultimately meaningless choices set in a rich universe with some good characters and twists, but incomplete.
Having some famous TV characters show up in the game was a neat touch, but knowing that the game is set in HBO's Seasons 3 and 4, with the show having finished Season 5 with 6 coming in a few months, people who have watched the series will undoubtedly realize that some of these characters have literal plot armor, which further diminishes your "choice" in the matter when dealing with them.
The finale didn't feel like a finale, it felt like the prelude to the actual finale. Instead, we're told we have to wait for Season 2. I'm okay with having a few loose ends to keep the story going after the season's story arc's over and done with, but that's the problem, it never felt resolved.
And I know Telltale can do better. The Walking Dead's Season 1 was perfect, you had both closure, and loose ends that allowed the story to carry onto Season 2. Game of Thrones simply has you waiting for Season 2 to find the closure you should have had in Season 1, and that I can't accept.

First and foremost, this is a great game and I recommend it to anyone who is either a fan of the Farcry series (post Farcry 2) and/or is interested in the theme of this game. I would not however, recommend it for those who enjoyed previous Farcry games purely for their gunplay, explosives, and so on.
I am writing this as of patch 2, about 3 weeks after launch, and I am still encountering a number of bugs. Specifically:
* The cutscene audio frequently goes out of sync, usually the audio goes ahead of whats on the screen
* The recap segments have spoiled elements of the story for me a few times, showing me things that hadn't happened yet
* When I try to close the program normally, it occasionally comes up with a Windows "This program has crashed" error screen
* Some of the objects and people you need to interact with are extremely picky about where you need to stand in order to activate them. The worst example of this was when I needed to speak to a person who was tied to the ground, and I had to jump into the air and talk to him mid-air in order for the interact prompt to appear. Normally you just need to circle the person or object a few times until you find the very tiny, invisible sweet spot. This was an issue with Farcry 3 and 4, and so I can see that this is still not fixed.
Lastly I wanted to comment on the story. I'm a little dissappointed with it so far. I'm 20 hours in and I still don't really feel like I'm part of this vast, epic struggle as was the case in previous Farcry titles. That isn't necessarily a problem, but coming from a long time series fan it is a little bit of a let down. However, the gameplay and environment is engaging enough to keep me entertained, though not quite as enthralled as I had hoped for.

I played Diablo III and was one of the people who got bored. I picked this up because a) people claimed "it's what Diablo III should have been" and b) my friend helped sell it with the game's skill progression.
I am somebody who likes RPG's with a lot of character progression options and a fairly open approach to how I build my character, their stats, their skills, their profession and so on. I didn't like the options Diablo III gave me, but I am finding Grim Dawn gives me plenty in this respect, for me to develop my own play style and experiment. My main character, a battle mage, for example, has had their skills redone over and over to try different things. I started out with a big 2h weapon hailing down icey boulders down onto my enemies. But my current build, I am running in full heavy armour, am moderately tanky, I have a 1h and a tome, I can charge at my enemies, smash their zombie faces in with my hammer, thanks to Cadence. Or...fire a massive Death Ray and obliterate them, but to a big detriment to my mana. And my Occultist on the other hand, Bloody Pox is just...nasty, instant Ebola that spreads...and spreads to anything that touches the infected and you just watch a chain reaction of bodies - given my Occultist is also a gunslinger, I don't even have to get close to just watch stuff drop. But if I wanted, I could go for a heavier build of an Occultist, give them heavy armour and a scythe and problem mix them with a Soldier build to reap the benefits and could live a Dark Knight fantasy or something.
The reality is, there's a lot you can do to mould your own playstyle. First you have your stats:
Physique -> Benefits heavy stuff, can mean for tankier stuff
Cunning -> More beneficial to physical damage, but think of it as being beneficial to more dextrous builds
Spirit -> Magic orientated.
How you balance your stats can help benefit the build you want and also certain items will have a minimal stat requirement. So if you want that massive heavy axe, you need the physique to use it.
Then you have your class. In fact, you have two at level 10. You can combine them to create a new class. For example, my Battlemage was created by combining Soldier and Arcanist. You get full access to their full spectrum of skills, so there's no Major/Minor system going with the classes combos. So you can choose which sides to invest in more or go for something more balanced. In the builds you add points to the skills you want and level them up. Going back to the Battle Mage, at one point I was mostly invested in Trozan's Sky Shard, which helped crush enemies, but has a recast, so I'd go in melee and then drop sky shards intermittantly. Now that i have a charge from soldier, I can run in and still spam Cadence, but I've replaced Sky Shard with Albrecht's Aether Ray, which is now fully upgraded and incredibly deadly. So my melee now is a back up, rather than my primary approach, because Aether Ray uses a LOT of mana to sustain.
Then comes the next bit. Devotion. For every Shrine you purify in the game, you gain Devotion points, which allows you to gain stats and passive skills from the stars. You can go for stuff that gives your fire based attacks more damage, for example. Or something that gives your pets more "oomph", there's a number of choices and as you invest more into Devotion, more trees will unlock.
And finally. The last point of customisation. Gear. Gear doesn't just boost base stats, it can also boost things like "Fire Damage" or "Frost Damage" it can also provide extra levels to skills (and push them over cap), like +1 to All Arcanist Skills or +3 to Cadence. As examples. So loot you pick up and use can hugely benefit your builds. In additions, you can get passive and active skills from gear too. I have an item that grants me a skill called "Demon's Breath", which is a nice instant cast AoE I can throw in between attacks. You will also get materials you can put into an item's slot to add or upgrade stats on it.
So as you can see, when I say there's a lot of options for building your character and customising your playstyle, I am not kidding.
Now what about the rest. Graphics are decent. Gameplay is enjoyable and the game is challenging, I'd recommend using the "Veteran" option in your settings, it gives you more formidable foes, but can give you more of a payoff as result. I'd recommend getting the Crucible DLC for two reasons: it's a good way to get any new characters kick started in the game if you don't want to keep going through the initial 10 or 20 level grind with the game's story. And the second is that it helps you test your build, the more you can survive the crucible, the stronger your build.
I feel like it created a better atmosphere than Diablo III. I am somebody who has ended up getting bored of games that focus so much on the undead, but this game helps me care again. You are literally the last of mankind and the war has already been lost and humanity hasn't stood well against the force known as "aetherials". It's a dark fantasy settings, with a distinctive Wild West feel to it. So not just zombies and dark things, you'll be fighting molotov throwing, gunslinging cowboy bandits. Given it is a post apocalypse, some of the gear you can get feels thrown together. In terms of its post apocalyptic wild west sides of things, maybe think of Wasteland.
The story and lore is interesting and there's a number of things to pick on along the way. But the game is not heavily story focused as an APRG, but still has enough to keep you invested an interested.
All in all, a great game. But for me, the biggest selling point, the level of customisation I can go to in my character builds. It offers a replayability for me, to play the game with all sorts of builds and with the option to easily skip dialogue and run through story related stuff quickly and with the help from The Crucible, it doesn't making it so monotonous to keep restarting over on a new character for a new build.

So I finally decided to write a review for Grim Dawn. After 400 hours it deserves one.
So a little background about myself. I have been playing action RPG's for a very long time. I grew up playing Diablo 2 for 10 years.
So i would like to say that i have over 10k hours invested into that game.  I have also put a few thousand into Diablo 3.  I never played titan quest back when it came out unfortunetly.
Played through Torchlight(not on steam). And also some of Torchlight 2. I havent been able to get into Path of Exile though.
The three big ARPG's right now are Diablo 3, PoE and Grim Dawn. So comparisions will be made between the three.
Ill break down key points about the game.
Graphics: The mood and tone of the game are represented well by the graphics. It deserves its name of "Grim" Dawn Textures are good and so is the lighting. But its nothing too crazy that the lower-end systems out there cant handle the game.
Now the animations are definately not as polished as they could be. Compared to Diablo 3 or even PoE. Comparing PoE or grim dawn to Diablo in that regard isnt too fair because both of these other games are made by indie devs.
With all that being said the lack of super high quality animations does not detract from the enjoyment of the game for me personally.
I run a I7-4790k and a GTX 1070 and i get around 200 frames in some areas and others a lot less. The engine itself is the cause of this im sure, but the only time that happens is when theres a ton of enemies on screen and effects
start going of like the fourth of july. It can be a little frustrating to deal with but any game that has a lot of effects can in certain circumstances have bad performance.
Content: You get 4 acts to play through and many dungeons and secret areas to explore. a full playthrough on normal will probably take you 15-25 hours. This game is less random than diablo and PoE but what you get instead is a
hand-crafted world full of secrets and mystery. I have 400 hours and there are so many secrets im still finding them and rediscovering old ones. A fifth act will be coming in the expansion thats planned.
You will get your moneys worth if you pick this game up and play it through just a few times. Espically so if you get it on sale.
End Game: This is where Grim Dawn lacks a bit compared to Diablo 3 and PoE. As of right now there are 3 end game dungeons you can explore and fight through, and hopefully not die.
The third one which is a 4-5 layer dungeon was added free a few weeks ago. GG Crate. <3 The other "end game" activity is farming up enough reputation of the various factions to hunt down nemesis enemies.
Nemesis enemies are extremely tough bosses that spawn randomly throughout the world and will drop awesome loot. Only the strong need apply. Other than that "end game" is kind of bare. Its more like diablo 2 in that regard.
I spend a lot of time making new builds to see if i can push them into ultimate difficulty and complete the dungeons etc. Hopefully they will bring something in to help with this lack of "end game" in the expansion.
*hint hint*
Gameplay: The combat feels tight and responsive, you never feel like you out of control of your character under normal circumstances. Every now and then♥♥♥♥♥♥happens but its only happened to me honestly a handful of times in 400 hours.
The camera is zoomable both in and out from the default spot and full 360 degree rotation is enabled. I love this camera so much that other ARPGS that dont have it makes me upset haha.
The combat isnt as "fast and hectic" as diablo or PoE but that doesnt mean the game is slow or dull. Its all relative. Once you get into the higher levels challenge dungeons and other areas will make you♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself with how tense
the game can be. With the way they have built the classes and items you will be able to find a playstyle that fits you for sure. As fast or as slow as you want.
Sound: Metal clanks, blood spills. The dying breathe of your enemies escape their lips, cursing you as they evaporate into a pink mist. You can hear giant hulking brutes breathing off in the distance, skeletons shambling around the corner and so on. So the sound scape is good and positional audio cues are there to help you out. Sound is very good. Not award winning but does its job and does it very well
Itemization/stats: This is a very important aspect for any RPG and i would dare to say more so for any ARPG. ARPG's revolve around the gameplay loop of: Kill enemies, aquire loot, kill stronger enemies, aquire better loot.
Once you nail that and make that as fun as possible thats when good ARPG's are born.
You have your standard item rarities in Grim Dawn: Common Items(white), Magic items (yellow), Rare Items(Green), Epic Items(blue) and Legendary items(Purple). Legendary items only drop when youre level 50+.
As standard you are looking for epic and legendary gear but they way they have set up the stats on items in this game is well thought out. In some cases, rare, green items can be best in slot for certain builds.
Thats something youll never see in diablo 3. The rate at which you find gear in this game is also very fair. it makes playing solo very doable and with the itemization as good as it is you can get to end game without no-lifing the game.
Thats not to say the items and stats are perfect but the pros definately outweigh the cons.
This has been a big factor for the enjoyement of the game for me. The robust item and stats paired with a dual class system means you can make and try builds to your hearts content.
Fun factor: The game is a blast to play once you sink your teeth into it. I wont lie at first i was kind of bored with the game but once i got past blood grove the game "clicked" for me. Milage may vary on that. BUT because i said that if you feel that same way i did back then give it a full chance and push yourself to do at least one whole playthrough. Look up some builds online and find something you think youll like
A lot of builds start becoming fun and viable around level 30-40+ it seems to me. Skills and gear starts to fall into play and synergies start forming.
I cant recommened this game enough to people. I love it to death. It has its faults but if what i described doesnt bother you then youll find youll love the game too.
*disclaimer i did not talk about every aspect of this game in this review only stuff i felt was important. There are many other little things and systems that make Grim Dawn greater than the sum of its parts.
Thanks for reading! Any questions or comments feel free to post them! :)

Have you ever wondered what it would be like for superheroes (or beings with superpowers) to play various sports? Perhaps dodgeball? Or baseball? No doubt they would take things to a new extreme, with smashes that break the laws of physics and reaction speeds at mere fractions of milliseconds.
Lethal League is a little like that. Imagine Super Smash Brothers but on PC and instead of fighting, you're essentially playing dodgeball in a fairly small arena. Things can get real chaotic, but boy is it fun!
Lethal League combines sport, with a highly competitive and slightly strategic game that requires you to have good timing, or a good understanding of angles. This does not mean it's a math or physics game. It simply means Lethal League has an extremely high skill ceiling whilst having a very low barrier to entry. Anyone can pick this up with their friends or play vs bots and have a really great time, and those with the best reaction times can duke it out for the top spots.
Your goal is to eliminate all your opponents, by hitting the ball into them. The standard game mode allows you to
which puts it in your colour and makes it pass through you (so that you don't hit yourself). You can also disable ball tagging for a much more challenging experience. Each time you hit the ball, it goes a little faster. You can hit it up or down depending on whether you are in the air or on the ground. If you smash a ball (air hit) the ball speed is doubled. Now this is where the real fun comes in. If you manage to get 3 or more smashes in, the ball speed is going to ramp up so fast that it quickly becomes a blur of lines in various angles. This is where a knowledge of angles can help you to overcome your opponent.
The maximum speed seems to be capped at 1 million. As you break through known speed limits, your hits gradually have a longer delay but the ball speed is so fast that it becomes ALMOST impossible to react to it. You're likely going to struggle with this until you learn the timing windows for various hits, and it is oh so satisfying to counter a ball ping-ponging across the room at over 100,000 (whatever the speed measurement is) into your opponent.
You can also bunt the ball in various directions, temporarily slowing it down and allowing you to regain control and possibly change its direction. This is used in combination with regular hits to quickly rack up speed or pull off an unexpectedly fast smash, because bunting a ball reduces the delay on a hit (even the insanely fast ones that require 2-4 seconds of delay) to almost nothing.
There are 6 characters to choose from and each of them have distinct strengths and weaknesses. Some of them can jump higher than others, some can jump off walls indefinitely etc. This alone would make it fun, however the devs decided this is not enough so they added special abilities. Where do I even begin? Special abilities can drastically change the course of a match in an instant! By hitting the ball you gain charges of your special meter. At 4 charges you can use the ability by double tapping the regular hitting button. Each character has their own unique move that you'll discover on your own, and it adds so much more fun to the game along with previously mentioned elements.
The visual style of this game is unique, but still quite simple. Characters have some lovely color variations and stages are fairly well designed.
I absolutely love the music in this game, as well as the other assorted sounds in the game. When you break the sound barrier, the hit sounds are so impactful and sound like rockets or small bombs going off.
Running at 60 FPS is pretty much required to be able to learn your timings properly. The first time I ran the game, it had some very weird frame drops that may have been an issue on my side, but it initially turned me off from the game. However subsequent play sessions did not have that issue, so it must have been some other unrelated issue. The game is very lightweight and runs flawlessly.
I would have liked to see more characters in the game, as 6 is hardly a roster of characters compared to other games in this kind of genre. I mean not even the Scout from TF2? That's an iconic character that would have been perfect here.
Lethal League is the type of game you can pick up at any time and play with friends. Even as a solo player, you'll find that the bots are quite challenging, and there's enough single player content to keep you interested for even a couple days. The gamplay is fun and rewarding, and is definitely worth checking out if you're interested in a fun, fast, sport-action game.

Fistful of Gun is a top down arcade shooter that's best enjoyed with friends online or off, though it does support single player as well. It features quick round gameplay, a varied skill ceiling and some eye catching pixel art.
The premise is pretty simple. Pick from a large variety of characters, who all play very different from one another go out and shoot a bunch of stuff and dudes as the title would suggest. There are 2 main modes with a single and multiplayer variant to them. Arcade mode has you going round to round clearing the screen and at the end of the round you get to pick from an assortment of randomly generated upgrades. In story mode you can play either as a hero, or a bandit. As a hero you'll avoid innocent NPCs while shooting out the baddies. You'll get upgrades if you can find a store keep, or if you're lucky from barrels and crates. While if you play a bandit, you'll be doing similar except you'll be shooting every one, innocents be damned, and collect all the bounty from from your massacres. The balance to playing the bandit is, every one will shoot you on sight, and store keeps are rarer, as they tend to fear and run from you.
The game's flow is pretty fast paced, some rounds only taking seconds to complete, though there will be a variety different events that may take more time. The game also runs on a limited continue system, and it's very possible to get a game over in your first few runs. It plays a lot more like an arcade classic than a modern game. Permanent gameovers, no quick save or loads, and a limited life counter are rarities in this age of gaming. Because of this, the game does benefit from faster paced style of gameplay, but that also means the game is short, can be potentially repetitive to some.
The game is a lot of fun, but there are some issues I take with it. Though the character selection is fantastic, and I love how each character are so drastically different from one another the game can feel a bit samey after an hour or two. Even with the character variety you will be shooting and dodging over and over again, with only a handful of random events that help mix things up. To be fair, the game does help alleviate some of the monotony not just with character selection, but also with game mode variety as well. The game's controls can also be an issue at times. Some characters just play better on the keyboard and mouse, while some better on the gamepad, this is mostly due to the huge degree of divergence in the characters' play style. Though this is certainly something to be admired about the game, it also does require the player to have an encumbrance of hardware ready at hand to fully enjoy the game to it's max potential. Also be aware, during our time with the game, we also ran into some bugs as well, some gamebreaking, but since the writing of this review, I have noticed dozens upon dozens of updates. It's very possible they're patched out.
Overall A fist full of Gun is a really interesting top down arcade shooter. It's not perfect, and can be repetitive for some, but it does have a lot of potential, especially if the continue to support the game with more maps, and events, as that's what I think is lacking the most.
Pros:
- Great Pixel Art
- Excellent variety in character selection
- Variable skill ceiling
- Very fun with friends online and off
Cons:
- Lacks variety in events
- Requires both keyboard and gamepad to be enjoyed appropriately
- Some re balancing required

Greyfox is a game that looks good but ultimately fails to deliver much and certainly isn't what it's store page claims. When it says "style of Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy", it means the art, and I still question that. The game is nothing like those.
You are a young woman who is excited to move to a town called Greyfox to start a new chapter of her life. When she gets there she meets a few grumpy and a few odd characters, including a strange woman. When she goes to sleep, she meets that woman in a dream. The woman asks her about being old and inserts her into the bodies of 4 different elderly residents.
The store page claims that you enter at crucial moments in their lives, which is somewhat true. What isn't true is that you make important choices. The one choice you make in each is to kill the person or not, except in one where you can kill someone else.
Now these people are not great people, to be sure. One is a rude miser, another murdered her husband, another considers murdering her husband (though the end of that arc made me wonder if it was real or not) and the last is a Crazy Cat Lady that sees Santa Clause everywhere without her meds. My problem is that there is no chance to help these people be better or at least help the people around them, like the silly Chris Rock movie "Down to Earth."
I think the game wanted to make a statement about being old and dying or something but all it really is asking is if you want to be a murderer or not. Even the good ending isn't the least bit satisfying. All I did was not murder people. Wow, what an achievement. Everything stayed the same!
The only good thing about this game is that afterwards you read a few newspaper clippings. If you killed someone, there is a story about it. If not, you get a story about that person's peaceful death some time later. They could have done something cool with this concept, but they didn't. I want the game described on the store page, but this isn't it.

A Fistful of Gun is a fun cowboy shooter where each character plays very uniquely.
The game is hard but rewarding. The game shines when playing multiplayer, because you can choose a wide variety of characters to maximize your effectiveness in battle. Each character plays interestingly and uniquely. As far as the fact that they even control differently. One character requires that you press the correct key or controller button, corresponding to the next revolver bullet, another can only be played with the mouse, and can teleport to wherever you click.
Although many of these characters can be fun, I feel like there are some obvious choices over others.
The game is very strategic if you want it to be. You have to think on your feet, and can use cover cleverly.
There are a few fun game modes to choose from. Arcade being the most entertaining in my personal opinion. Each screen you clear of enemies will grant you the chance to choose 1 random upgrade for you character. It gets pretty satisfying once you've racked quite a few upgrades up.
Story mode also has an entertaining system where once you've cleared a screen, you can choose which direction you'd like to go to next, which determines what next battlefield you will fight on, or could give you an extra life. There are a few other fun mechanics in place, as well a bit of dialogue.
There's also a versus mode which pits you against your friends.
Overall it's a cool game with some really fun mechanics!

Greyfox is a short, depressing anthology about growing old and miserable with a few interesting tales and thankfully no preachy attitude. It’s worth its price if you are into fanfic style stories.
Made by a group of enthusiastic young artists, Greyfox is an anthology made on the popular RPG Maker game engine, about the concept of growing old and how most people feel about their aging.
These tales are told through the eyes of an energetic young woman who moves to the titular town, Greyfox, with the hopes of starting a new, exciting life there. But she soon finds out the town is full of grumpy old people, and with a help of an unexplained mystic, she manages to take control of four of them.
The scenarios after that try to tell you how not to grow miserable by your old age, further emphasised with the option to give a verdict on the lives you intrude on. This message is not always easy to spot under the clunky dialogues, but it is there.
Don’t expect detailed and complex stories; unless you get lost, the entire game can be finished in about 30-45 minutes– 60-70, if you want to see all endings. Still, it’s cheap, and gives as much entertainment as one would expect for this price.

So, i played Red Solstice before and i tried this one not specially hyped about the change in gameplay, but i was happily surprised by this game
The game is overall good for me, good graphics, fluid gameplay, the first missions of story mode used as a tutorial in disguise but still with enough difficulties to be called missions. made it run on high definition without fps drop or graphic anomaly
We have 4 classes, each with it's own mecanics : Assault (good melee and shooter), Demolition (heavy use of skills), Hellfire (Tank and crowd control), and Terminator (Powerful but decrease suit integrity with each used skills)
Having played Red Soltice i know that the Hellfire is the one i play the best among them but each one has its goods and bads
When you choose your class you can then evolve your suit, getting new skills and bonuses, making you stronger and able to take on bigger challenges
The story mode is quite good except for one thing in my opinion : the scenario needs you to have played Red Solstice to really understand the threat you face and

Also, in survival mode, you gain level and keep weapons only if you evacuate, never forget that or you may never get to evolve your suit, leading to frustration and rage quit (this mecanic is similar in Red Solstice)
but i'm a little disappointed about 2 things :
- in Survival mode we have access to only 1 map. I really hope that other maps will come in the future.
- no online coop, at least not for now. but from what i heard they'll do it in the future, so let's give them time to do it

Gameplay is reasoanbly accomplished.  The effects, animations, how zoomed in it is, scale - everything sells the experience.  I've played 10 hours, mainly on survival, and it's a great loop of trying to get out alive to keep your loot and unlock xp.  The loot and xp is quite well designed and there are several different character/classes (suits) to play as which have very different possibilities and approaches.  Weapons upgrade by use - which I quite like too - and something like the SMG doesn't get better at shooting, instead allowing quicker movement and skill command speed (an officers weapon) which is a nice twist on simply the DMG number going up.
All of that gives me a reason to play one more run (completing survival can take an hour) - and the gameplay is good enough that I want it.  This is something I missed in Alien Swarm- and am pleased to have it here.
Desperately needs a bit of polish elsewhere - but the GAME is here.  Just need to polish the story, add more survival maps and put an online coop in to go with the excellent local coop (played at least 5 hours of that and it's great - you get a lot of player slots so your buddy can have their own character and enjoy levelling them up).
I think the main game should be the survival mode - it's got the gameplay to go the distance I think.
Nevertheless - it has problems.  When there's lots of enemies on screen there's a lot of noise - probably too much.  The UI in game is rather busy and some of the mechanics are a little hard to appreciate.  Perhaps released a little too soon - I still recommend if you like this sort of genre.

Having loved CoH the first version I thought I would take advantage of the free play weekend.
As many others may have done, we have eagerly awaited a sequel to what in many people’s minds was, and still is a brilliant game. Brilliant, I thought, I can try for CoH2 for free. Oddly I was reminded of the days of old when we would buy a PC magazine with a CD attached, we  could go home and install it, play the game demo, and away you go you would either want more or you would leave it. Anyway, I digress.
I downloaded the game etc etc. Clicked start and was immediately struck by the superficiality and lack of real depth. We are hit with a simple cinematic (perhaps this is a stripped Steam version I may need correction here) and bang we are in, no real atmosphere or scene was set in contrast to the quasi story personalised as in the original CoH. To immerse yourself fully you have to have some prior knowledge of this conflict to really appreciate the fundamental change in tactic that goes hand in hand that is required by the player to understand this expansion. In sum sacrifice is the mode of the day.  As another reviewer aptly summarises; the days of CoH allowing for an individual approach to gameplay such as defend, or inch by inch ground gains are gone in this release, hence the flavour of individual gameplay so loved in the original is overbearingly crushed by the mechanics of this expansion. Whilst trying to capture the spirit of expendability synonymous with the military approach of the time, little consideration was (supposedly) given to impact this may have on gameplay when transposing this approach to a RTS platform.
However, at $16.99 on steam free play weekend you would think it would be a steal, considering the relative time between its release and now right? Wrong, very wrong. Please do not get caught by this as it is as close to a legal scam as you will get. Yes, I mean DLC, and there is lots of it.
I'm sorry, even at the budget price of $17 there is no way I am touching this game, even with the deep affection I have for the first one. I really feel Sega and Relic are hoping to cash in on an emotional attachment that many of us have for the first game. One reviewer mentioned a bait and switch scam, which I have to agree with as that is what I might feel caught by if I buy into this DLC horror.

Lost Castle is a side scrolling beat-em-up and RPG hybrid with roguelike features. It’s inspired by Castle crashers. It has roguelike elements and every time you play a different dungeon is presented to you. The game is in Early access, so there’s a few glitches etc. but not a big deal. The game is fully playable. The developers are pretty active which means the glitches should be fixed very soon.
Lost Castle feature cartoon-like graphics and art-style. The graphics are very sharp and pleasing to the eyes. The characters are cute and kept reminding me of Scribblenauts characters for some reason. There are not many graphics settings in the game, the only one available is the resolution adjustment option and full screen option. The game ran smooth for me throughout my gameplay with it with over 60 FPS.
The music in this game is very neat. I really liked the creepy type of music this game features. There could’ve been more tracks though. Sound options have separate music and sound adjustment options.
The game has fully re-bindable keys for both keyboard and controller. The mouse works in-game menus and the upgrades page. The controls felt really responsive. A controller is highly recommended for this game though I had no problem with keyboard as well.
The story is about demons and other evil creatures have come to the Castle Harwood and your character is a treasure hunter trying to get rid of the evil in the Castle and in the way loot some treasure. Your character gets kidnapped by these evil elves who throw you into the dungeon. That’s where you start every time you die. You’re given a random looking character with a random weapon. Depending on the weapon you’re given you get different normal, heavy and super attacks. The dungeon is also randomly created. There’s 5 levels from what I can tell (didn’t progress through the later levels) and every time you die you start at the first dungeon cell. Each time you clear a screen a door opens and you’re given a chest with some random items in it. The chests also upgrade from wood to silver to gold and so on as you progress through level. Along the way you can also find a dodgy salesman every once in a while who will sell you a random thing for some coins. This can be an apple or a very nice weapon.
There’s a lot of different types of weapons, bows, dual welded swords, long heavy swords, shotgun, fireballs, sword and shield combo etc. Every weapon has their own stats and abilities, for example the bow and arrow has a super attack which shoots an electrocuted arrow which passes through enemies. The fireball weapon lets you teleport if you use the heavy attack or a crystal spawns and shoots fireballs at all nearby enemies with the super attack button. Some weapons have dash or evade or teleportation abilities instead of heavy attacks. You can also find companions who follow you and shoot at enemies and other upgrades like a percentage chance to electrocute enemy etc. Armor pickups can not only alter the stats they can change the look of your treasure hunter entirely with different themes and cosmetics.
You gain souls by killing enemies, these souls can be used to get upgrades and unlocks after you die. You start off pretty weak but as you gain levels and get additional bonuses using these souls you get better and better. Though as you get upgrades the other upgrades become expensive and if you cannot afford to buy one your souls will be sacrificed. One of the upgrades does let you keep a certain percentage of your souls though.
There’s a lot of enemy variety. Skeletons, goblins, spiders, slime creatures. The game has some hilarious mechanics too like unknown potions which can either be good or bad. One of the potions has you pooping everywhere which reduces your move speed for a short time. Other funny things like you slipping off your recently eaten banana’s peel, making your vulnerable to enemies, or chest falling on your head and other such things. Plenty of bosses in the game as well. Consumable items include apples, bananas, finger lickin’ good chicken (yes, there’s a reference to KFC in the game as well) all of which restore some of your HP. Throwable weapons includes daggers, bombs etc. Potions are there as well and usually random which can either poison you, make you fart uncontrollably, restore health and many other things. So it’s always a gamble using these potions.

Man was I hyped for this Game! A fan of Telltale since "The Walking Dead" as well as huge fan of both the books and the series of GoT, I really looked forward to it.
Based on my experience with Telltale Games I was expecting a really great story, where I would have to make difficult decisions, being immersed into the story and really get to life it with all the characters. Being within the GoT Realm as a huge bonus on top.
But, sadly, I have to say - this has fallen really short on much of what I expected.
Biggest let down is what made the other TT games so great - the impact fo the decisions you make.
I once felt that my decision actually had an impact on the story, but apart from that, nothing you do really makes much of a difference. Or feels like it does.  Hence, it was a nice interactive "movie" to "play", but nothing more. It does look like there is a 2nd Season around, but I am not yet sure if I buy, and for which price. Most likely only if it's in some kind of sale.
Pro:
- I do love the art style, going into a different directions than the TT games I played so far - it really fits the world I think
- The story was nicely done, and one could expect a similar story happening in the original stories of Mr. Martin himself. Perhaps not as sophisticated, but still - a good story
Con:
- The decisions you have to make seldom feel important or impactful - and neither do they actually have a big impact. At one point you'll have to decide who survives, but that's pretty much it in regards to heavy impact. Granted, there might be a couple that will play out differently depending on your choice, but within the whole presentation it really never fells like it.
- The Game does not feel polished at all. Eye and mouth movements seem of at times, there are some potentially buggy scenes (Encountered one myself, but was fixed with a save reload), and the art styles sometimes really clashes with the animated scenes.
- Worse, the expressions on faces do change within a conversation seemingly without any correlation to what you said before, will say now, and how conversations with the same person played out eralier in the game. There are smiles, where noone said anything funny or nice at all. There are weird looks, even though your character just said something cheerful and the response tells you it worked - not those looks though.
- implementing known characters from the books and the series was a really nice touch, but in the end they overdid it, adding to the feeling that your decisions won't matter much.
Would I recommend it?
Well, if you are TT and GoT fan - give it a try for sure. If you are neither, this game won't change your mind.
If you get it in a sale, you'll get a nice story of roughly 10-12 hours.

Star Raiders seem to be an interesting reimagining of an old classic, but ended up with horrible controls that makes the game virtually unplayable, wasting a decent engine and a good license.
(For the record, I am one of those PC kids who NEVER played the original, okay?)
The intro is quite lame, it's just some static comic-book type panels about how the cabal of friends, including Ruiz, that's you, the geek, joined Atar Academy in order to work your way into the Star Raiders squadron on the Solaris carrier in the war against the Zylons.
Your ship has three modes: turret (heavy shields and weapons, don't move much), as well as assault and attack (I still can't figure out which mode is better for what, and there's no manual).  In the intro/tutorial you can only use a single mode and it's only later you get to choose the modes. (Why does this reminds me so much of Robotech, i.e. fighter, guardian, and robot modes?) Somehow you have to upgrade the weapons individually in each mode too.
The graphics are a bit sparse but workable, and it's compatible with modern high-res screens (no problem setting it to 1680x1050). It's annoying though to get prompted with legend of onscreen HUD every time one starts the mission.
So far this sounds cool, but that changed when you're in the cockpit.
I have a MS XB360 controller, which is like *the* standard, so I use it when I can. I cannot get it to control the ship at all. The ship ONLY reacted to mouse and keyboard. I also cannot adjust the sensitivity, and to loop I have to keep moving the mouse (including taking it off the desk), which is ridiculous.
I managed to complete the tutorial missions by spamming the sky with missiles and I seriously doubt I could drive the fighter with any precision in an actual dogfight, when I have no problem playing games that require such precisions, but then those work with gamepad. This one doesn't.
All in all, don't bother buying this, unless you want to spend a while figuring out how to get your gamepad to work, and maybe you still won't enjoy it.
