This is a shooter quite like no other. The Wild West themed bullet circus is utterly insane and enjoyable. All the mechanics of the game feel finely tuned and precise: dodging bullets and sending them back feels so intuitive you should never have to stand there and bleed. The levels and areas are all varied and peppered with details and events such as carrying a giant explosive piñata, robbing banks, dodging rolling crates and so on. The structure of the game has these different level types shuffled around and enemy placement is randomized, but this only one small part of what keeps the action fun and exciting throughout.
The playable characters are a definite highlight of the game. While most games might settle for differentiating characters by stats or looks alone, the colorful cast of a Fistul also has different styles based around the actual input and control of the character: you have a shotgun toting teacher whose two barrels need to be reloaded individually,  the wanted outlaw Billy who wields twin revolvers that only fire when the highlighted chamber is pressed, Bomberman fans will feel right at home playing as Pablo the demo daredevil and this is barely scratching the surface. Each character feels vastly different from the next and they all come with some alternative weapons that can be picked up in the game. Mastering each gunslinger bit by bit feels immensely satisfying and the only problem is deciding which one is your huckleberry.
However, strong characters would be wasted if they didn't have some clever enemies to go up against and Fistful delivers on this front as well. Machine gun wagons, rabid bears, magic arrows, among others, are all a great match up against the heroes of Fistful. However, even the more standard gunslinging enemies keep things interesting as they will move about the map, flank you, set of explosives, and shoot behind cover. To help out against the overwhelming amount of bullets, the game also has powerups in the form of different whiskey that can give you a chance to ignore a bullet or make one of your own explode. Even with powerups though, you will need to hone your skills to keep your continues from running dry.
This shooter has a sure sense of style. The narrowing wide screen, red tones throughout, panning shots, acid wild west colors, arcade font and voice over, and old west monologues all come together nicely to bring out a sense of the legendary west. The soundtrack also does a fantastic piece of Morricone inspired tunes. The chants, whistling and marching drums go along nicely with the rest of the aesthetics.
The local and online co-op are both fun experiences and each mode available is pure hectic fun. However, the 9 player local co-op is really more for laughs than ever actually accomplishing anything in the game. That being said playing in a group as The Magnificent Seven or going at it on your lonesome like The Man with No Name, there is a good time to be had. The story and arcade modes, aside from cutscenes and a definite ending, differ between some shuffled around mechanics and events (such as how upgrades work and taking peyote). Aside from unlocking characters in story mode, there are also safes that have a chance to drop new locations that get shuffled into the gameplay mix. The versus mode is a great way to let your friends know that this living room ain't big enough for the 2-9 of you. The different modes, unlocks, and urge to be better all go a long way in replay value.
As far as pure arcade madness goes, A Fistful of Gun has no equal.  The top down shooting action, whether alone or in co-op, is frantic, adrenaline fueled, and challenging.

"101 hours in and he's not recommending it? What's this guy smoking?"
I know, I know. But despite all the memes, I really don't think this game is worth thirty bucks - much less the extra fifteen they try to squeeze out of you via DLC.
Story:
The story is as bland, light-hearted, and generic as they come. It's your standard, run-of-the-mill "save the world" plot, but its unique writing is a large factor in this series's popularity. Unfortunately, it's also a double-edged sword. As you probably know already, this game breaks the fourth wall fairly often, with characters constantly coming up with excuses to make reference to the fact that they're in a game. This, however, gets old. Fast. Especially when you realize that half these references were never in the original Japanese to begin with.
It also makes fun of several tropes often found in anime, but forgets that it's also shamelessly playing them straight. For example, Noire is occasionally ridiculed in-game as being a tsundere (or at least, what that word's definition has morphed into), but that doesn't change the fact that she is one. Same thing for Older Brother and Younger Brother - their existence serves to make fun of male characters who obsess over boobs, but they themselves are male characters that obsess over boobs (something we don't need, since we have the player for that). News flash: pointing out your own stupidity doesn't change the fact that you're stupid.
Where the writing isn't annoying, it's lazy. Who are these six people and why do they know Neptune? Oh, they're from another dimension, so no biggie. This will never again be questioned or even mentioned. Uh-oh, we're in a pickle! It's okay, we just need a Shares ex machina. (The game itself makes fun of this, but still - it happens.)
But Kazoo, you argue, all that is just the game being silly and light-hearted! Can't you just have some fun for once in your life? Well, let me ask you this: would you eat candy - the same candy - for every meal for an entire week? You'd get sick of it, right? The problem with this game's story is that it's too one-note; it refuses to take itself seriously. There aren't really any dramatic tonal shifts, so the stakes never seem to be very high. It's hard to take interest in a story that's the same all the way through.
Assets:
Many JRPGs reuse enemy sprites at some point because they just didn't have the time, money, or creativity to come up with more. Oftentimes, that's understandable - when it's a rare occurrence, at least. In Neptunia, recycling of sprites is the norm. There are dozens of Dogoo enemies with only three different sprites between them. You'll fight the same orange flower in dungeon after dungeon, with maybe a new coat of paint to tell the difference. Giant dragons? Well, every last one of them looks exactly the same - they aren't even recolored. Even the (non-main-character) bosses are reused! I posit that once you finish Chapter 2, you'll have seen almost every significant enemy sprite the game has to offer.
And it's not just enemy sprites. It's dungeons, too. Now, reusing dungeon textures isn't as bad a problem as reusing enemy sprites, but reusing dungeon LAYOUTS is even worse. Every last cave dungeon in the game is exactly the same, with only a few minor differences. Every last forest dungeon in the game is exactly the same, with only a few minor differences - and so on and so forth. Out of the 36 dungeons in the game, there are only (off the top of my head) nine different ones. Coupled with the recycled enemy sprites, this is GRUELING. It eliminates the fun of exploring a new dungeon. How can I get excited about it when I already know what it will be before I even enter?
Gameplay:
But this is a JRPG. The most important part about it is the gameplay. And to the game's credit, it has solid battle mechanics that seem mundane at first, but quickly become complex and interesting once you get slaughtered in the Colosseum for the first time. It's easy to understand, but it has aspects to it that make the more hardcore JRPG players salivate. You don't have to be good at JRPGs to have fun playing this game.
Unfortunately, you collide - hard - into a brick wall near the endgame. Maybe I just suck at it, but I am convinced that certain parts of the game's later content (lookin' at you, Zeca Ruins 2) are designed to be impossible (or at least prohibitively hard) unless you buy the DLC. Which I didn't do, 'cause paid DLC is an evil concept that never deserved to exist in the first place. So if I'm getting slaughtered effortlessly by trash mobs at level 99, why should I feel the need to get Nepgear to level 99 too? Why should I feel the need to NG+ again and get Rom and Ram? Granted, I'm only talking about non-story dungeons here, but still.
Perhaps it'd be easier on me if I bought better weapons for my characters. But with said weapons ranging from one to five million credits each, I'd have a lot of grinding in my future. A ridiculous amount, really, even by JRPG standards. And since this is an enormous price increase from the next tier down, the message is abundantly clear: either you fork over more cash, or you waste days on end trying to save up for a better weapon that will only MARGINALLY increase your chances of surviving an ordinary battle.
After 101 hours of Neptunia, I'm looking back and wishing I could have them back. I really wanted to like this game - the range of character customization options is insane, the character designs are cute and full of life, the battle system is fun - but the story and the world are unbelievably boring. The cherry on top? The translator is incompetent at best and infuriating at worst. Don't buy this game. Not for thirty bucks. If it goes on sale, maybe - but personally, I'd recommend you take your business elsewhere altogether.

Basic review and opinion: Amamzing game, with clever and fast paced action keeping you on your toes at all times during the game. As well the amount of ships and layouts to unlock make it so that you have so much to keep playing for. Personally I have put many hours into trying to get a single ship, and the payout is glorious when you finally do it. 8/10 Highly Recommended.
Frustration level: To say that this game is frustrating at times is a very large understatement, as at times it has made me want to throw my laptop across the room. This game is very rage inducing, but not because of something that IT did, most, if not all rage and frustration are from player mistakes. Yes it was a missle that killed you, but it was your fault for not repairing your ship in a shop. This game will force feed you humble pie, as you will begin to realize that it was not RNG or Bad luck that got you killed, but your own mistakes.
Gameplay (Mostly the combat and first impressions of mine): This game will look very bland and slow paced from a viewers perspective, having to wait for lasers to fire and watching as they only take a small block of health from the enemy each shot. However from a players POV the game is much faster paced, as not only do you have to keep track of so many systems and crew, but you also will have to send crew all around the ship to repair and activate weapons/shields/etc. The game takes a little while to get into, as for veteran players will feel bored with the beginning grind in the first sectors, while new players will feel like they are drowning in things they have to memorize and do. However once you reach about sector 4 or 5 the game picks up drastically, as the real race begins: Your ship is now running out of the fuel you had in the beginning and you are running into battles with much tougher ships, and you feel as though your next jump could be your last with every click of the mouse. This caught me by surprise my first playthrough, and I got horribly murdered by a massive enemy, and I sat back in my chair wondering what the heck happened. The other large part of the game is the Risk/Reward evaluation that you have to do at every choice. Some are obvious, turn over a crew member or attack the ship. But ones like the giant space spider station will always have random results, sometimes you get some scrap and useful items, other times your crew will die and you are left missing a person. This type of thing overshadows the entire game, making you feel cheated at times.
But with all those things put together with an amazing soundtrack this game is a wonderful thing to pick up for something to do, and you will not be dissapointed. Unless you hate roguelikes or risk/reward situations, in that case avoid this game like the plague, as most of the game is Risk/Reward. Well worth the money, and even more so when it goes on sale.

When a sequel is released, there are a couple of different options you can take.  It can be a sequel in name only, be loosely connected on the first title, or be a direct sequel, and a few other options.  Hyperdimension Neptunia is a little bit of one and two, in that you have to play the first to understand anything as the game sure doesn't take the time to introduce you to everyone again('If you're playing this, you've played the first' is the logic) and pretty much everything's changed, as the game takes place in another dimension, so every event that you remember in the first game goes out the window.  Some facts are still the same though, such as characters and personalities.  Since this game is trying to be a sequel, it's only fair that we look at it as a sequel, with comparisons to the first game.  The 'feel' of the game is the same, so graphics, sounds, those are pretty much the exact same, this will be more focused on the differences in gameplay and story.
So the story feels a little shorter in this one, but there's more to it as well.  Characters are introduced earlier and have much more time to get their personality fleshed out..  Although one-dimensional characters are always one-dimensional.  The well-written nature has only been improved.  In fact, there are optional characters that you can scoop up along the story that have no story presence, but plenty of optional scenes that showcase their own personality.  It's a good solution from the previous game in where you suddenly got 6 characters who have a total of 9 lines.  This way you have all your characters show their personality and quirks.  However, characters unlocked through special means that also aren't related to the story still get shunned.  It was a bit of a shocker when my party almost doubled in size in the span of a few hours of gameplay.
The plot could be described as "Team Rocket is trying to destroy the world, and Jesse&James try to ruin your day, every day."  The Jesse&James in this game are fought about 10 times as you two have to be at the same area, so you always run into each other.  Pretty much every part of the story involves them somehow.  They're pretty bothersome, but needed to move the story along.
Later in the game, depending on certain objectives that you complete(Possible to achieve without realizing it, but unlikely) you can branch out the story conclusions, and one of them is just heart-wrenching.  The feels felt like I was watching Clannad, but everyone dies instead of just having sad stories with happy endings.  Just sadness and feels in this ending.  The basic plot isn't better or worse, just different.
Gameplay hasn't changed much.  Battle system is the same, but has the addition of a fourth character, so fights are even easier.  As long as you kill every monster you see, you’ll have a hard time losing a fight.  The 'use Ram to get perks' is still there, with one important perk added: Exp and gold gotten when you use the ‘destroy enemy’ perk.  Otherwise, the enemy dies and you get nothing.  Conversely, the jumping star perk(2x jump height) is used for nothing at all, except to look at Uni’s underwear for a tenth of a second longer;  Feels like they improved it while leaving the old stuff there. Also, unlocking tougher dungeons follows more of a path this time, as opposed to extra bosses being all over the place and level 100 monsters in basic upgraded areas;  General improvements all-around in that area, although relying on hidden items to give plans to upgrade dungeons dungeons is a terrible idea, as the low chance of it appearing means that you HAVE to read a walkthrough to continue to upgrade dungeons.  Next to no chance of bumbling into it.
... Of course, there are still 10,000 hats for you to get, but the amount of unique/reference costumes seems to have gone down in favor of recolors.
One of the new things introduced was Stella's Dungeon.  This little game is best described as an idle game.  You give Stella some equipment and send her off to a dungeon.  After some real-time has passed, she comes back and if she beat the dungeon, she gives you cool loot and keeps everything.  If she fails, you keep the stuff you found but lose all your current equipment.  Pretty cute idea on a little bit of extra farming and some bonus equipment, but the problem is actually that it takes too long.  I downloaded the DLC which made the dungeons take half the time needed and Stella doesn't lose equipment upon failure.  Even with this, it still took almost a week and a half to do all of her dungeons.  Without the DLC, it'll take about a month.  Sure, it's an idle game designed as a little coffee break, but it should at least be timed so that by the time you're super powerful and done everything, it still doesn't take two weeks just to finish it.  Good idea, ultimately pointless.  If you want the achievement, just get the DLC.

I'm generally a fan of Telltale games, despite knowing that the choices never REALLY matter. But here, that fact was far too bare. The game hands you a bunch of choices that seem important, but are rendered irrelevant shortly thereafter. Do that enough times, and it stops being credible. As opposed to Telltale's "The Walking Dead," which presents choices mainly of moral substance, many of GoT's choices are ostensibly strategic. Both games are supposed to make you wonder "Did I make the right choice?", but the transparency of the lack of consequences to strategic choices leaves you frustrated, while moral decisions stick with you. My point is that even if you like Telltale's other recent games, you may be disappointed by this one, even though it has basically the same formula, and even if you love Game of Thrones.

American Nightmare is a slight step down from its first game.  The story felt slightly shorter than AW and the whole time travel idea is a sloppy excuse to recycle the maps and characters.
The Goods:  The graphics are as good as AW if not better, as well as better optimization.  Just about all of the mechanics from AW are there, save from a few small things.  The UI has the same information as AW, but it looks different.  For example, the health bar in American Nightmare is a proper bar where AW had a bit that surrounded a compass.  You can also turn off the UI in American Nightmare, however the visual cues aren't as present.  Other than the story mode there is an arcade survival minigame that the first game lacks.
The Not-So-Goods:  The game was lacking in real character develpment.  There was a time travel plot device that recycled all of the maps.  There is a character known as Mr. Scratch that is one of the worst additions to a sequel.  Overall sloppy story.  There is no real mention to Alice other than the end of the game.  The subtlety of the visuals in AW are not present in American Nightmare.  While the weapons are much more varied than AW, it feels like the nailgun for instance is just a rapid fire pistol with lacking damage.  You cannot drain the Taken's darkness from them by simply pointing their flashlight at it.  You must boost it as well.
I give this game a 6/10 for its lacking story.  However, most of what makes AW great is present in this one.  The score is so low because the decisions Remedy made to the game are slightly sloppy.

This is a remake of 1993 XCOM UFO Defense which is very well done yet lacks some strategic depth of the original.
The good:
- in many things, the game tries to stay very close to the original
- more alient types, including heavily armored robots
- all aliens and your soldiers have new special abilities
- more weapon types, including shotguns
- great music, some tracks remind Deus Ex Human Revolution
- great graphics
- the story is accompanied with many cutscenes and voiced comments from your staff, which helps build drama
- great detailed tutorial
- mind control requires the target to be in sight (no more mind controls at the very first turn)
- you can research additional upgrades to weapons and other things in the Foundry building
The so-so:
- 2 action points instead of 50-70 like in the original, soldiers normally just walk once and shoot once. This takes away some depth yet makes you camp less
- can only take 6 soldiers in a mission instead of 14 -> faster turns but fewer tactical options
- night missions have the same visibility as daytime ones, no flares -> easier, but micromanaging flares was fun and night missions used to be real challenge
- a strange cover system: when a mob is behind an edge of a wall, it still can be shot at, yet with a high penalty. Most battlefields are filled with tree logs, groups of stones, stairs-like elevation levels which makes the battles mostly about running from cover to cover and staying on Overwatch
- critical hits are important -> more randomness
- soldiers have no stats (which grew from "usage"), instead the game randomly assigns them to specializations (sniper, heavy, assault, support). Specializations offer a few special abilities though
- after getting max rank ("Colonel"), soldiers won't improve anymore (only psi abilities, if they have psionic powers), which doesn't let you train super-ninzas and forces you to send new soldiers to let them train as well
- a few new types of missions which are heavily scripted and linear, usually with a turn limit
- can only build facilities in one base, no storage limit, no ammo -> less micromanagement but feels too casual
- mobs' facing doesn't play any role: they see equally well all around them, and attacks from behind don't inflict more damage (though usually a mob won't have a covering object behind it and will be considered "flanked")
- no arctic/desert/jungle maps but many varied urban maps
- a soldier can take just 1 extra item (e.g.1 grenade) in addition to main weapon and pistol
The bad:
- most battles are scripted and not randomly generated. Enemies appear when you pass trigger tiles and take a free move to get behind cover right after they appeared. Some fall directly from above (out of thin air) behind your troops, switching to Overwatch and pinning all your soldiers down. Some will run very close to you, all while you're waiting for their animation to finish. This takes away much strategic feeling as all your battle plans are trampled by script. Worse, it makes playing on higher difficulty or iron man mode pointless, as it feels unfair to lose when you didn't know in advance a scripted situation
- camera always tries to zoom in on the next selected soldiers which is very annoying if you want to keep camera zoomed out for a tactical overwiev
- camera sometimes fails to correctly detect the tile under the cursor -> it may take many attempts to open a door with V key (and rotate the camera for that a lot), or sometimes the solder will run to a wrong tile which is on a different floor and visually behind the one you wish to go to
- if a soldier sees an enemy during movement he doesn't stop and can even lose sight of the enemy by the end of the move (it was the same in the original XCOM but there you could walk tile-by-tile, and in JA2 soldiers stopped when seeing a new enemy)
- no base defense missions
- although everything is destructible you can't shoot at objects, except if your weapon misses an alien and hits an object instead, or you throw a grenade or fire a rocket launcher

Before we begin it must be said that I have had close contact with the developer throughout production. He is very open and talkative with his fans and took a lot of my pre-release feedback to heart. As a fan I find this refreshing, but also know that because of this it is my duty to disclose that to anyone reading this review.
Fistful of Gun is a rampaging, fast paced shooter full of over the top art, unhealthy levels of alcoholism and thirteen people who can inexplicably all ride the same horse at the same time. It makes no sense, its story is threadbare and the entire game is unbalanced to the point where a newbie can steamroll skilled players just by using an OP character... and I love every minute of it.
Fistful provides an unparalleled level of co-op support for all kinds of play styles. Every single 'gunslinger' has two methods of control, rebind-able keys and a unique weapon with a series of incomprehensible alternate gun pickups to shake things up. You may choose to play with a controller, mouse, keyboard or keyboard and mouse- you may choose to play single player, co-op, verses, online, offline- through a randomly generated and hectic campaign... Fistful is all about choice. Which is great to me.
The only downsides I could think to add is more down to the theme than anything else. The wild west is great, but it likely doesn't provide many options for enemy variety, or map settings. I personally would have liked more missions taking place in a town or tavern just to shake the game up a bit. They exist in story mode, but are not found in arcade (which I consider to be the meat of the game). Overall though what is presented is very solid and there are often a lot of surprises (such as bears) which you will love to find out (not like bears) and others which you will have less positive feelings for (mothertrucking bears).
Overall Fistful of Gun is a solid arcade shooter with many surprises to be had. The sound and music is great, the art style is unique and hilarious and overall I personally think it is worth your time.

A small fun shooter about killing sheriffs, mexicans, indians and other spaghettiwestern minorities, in both single-player and multi-player (9 players!!). As you can see from the screenshot it's beatifully crafted, the western theme is well represented in both graphic and music (inspired to Morricone), and it's hard to not fall in love with it.
You can choose between 11 characters, everyone with a special perk, a unique weapon and a strange mechanics. They can require a controller/mouse only, though, so better be prepared with both. My favorite is "The 13th", a freaking entire regiment.
There are actually three different modes: Arcade, Story and versus. On the official FAQ they're explained pretty well, so i'm gonna paste the description here:
Story mode (Single only) - The structure of this mode uses the arcade action gameplay and has a dialog system over it with branching options based on choices, most interactions in story mode are encountering traders, different gangs, assisting with quests, bartering for goods and perks, having tense shootouts, doing some bank robberies, assassinations, pushing wagons full of money through Indian territory, stealth missions and getting really smashed on peyote. There are a few more but that covers the basics of it. The over arching goal is to stop the train baron Boon in his tracks through several boss battles. As all the other modes, this one is built procedurally so sometimes the story may be in a different order to the last play-through.
Arcade mode (Single and Multi) - Smash through waves of enemies and shoot outlaws to reach the highscore board at the end, you will gain skills and perks at the end of each round and occasionally encounter merchants who sell you weapons, offer you bounties or challenge you to a game of cards.
Versus mode (Single and Multi) - Similar base mechanics to previous modes, versus mode would be best described as competitive co-op, where one person holds the Sheriff badge, and only he is the one who gains skills and perks at the end of each round, the catch is other players can shoot the badge from him and kill each other, its a delicate balance between shooting each other and shooting the bandits. The last person standing with the sheriff badge is the winner. everyone else can take a walk.
The games works well, with a steady framerate of 120 fps (GTX 970) and until now i had no connection issues with the multiplayer modes.
Be aware: It's extremely fast paced, hard in single, but extremely fun online.
P.S. Played offline on the laptop too, so hours doesn't count.

Note: This reviewer has 500+ hours on an alternative account
Dying Light is the third edition to Techlands Zombie Killing games, and manages to incorporate some familiar, and improved features from Dead Island 1 and Riptide, with a few weak points here and there.
You have your weapon crafting and repairing system, similar to how Dead Island Riptide handled it, but this time, you're able to have increased stats from weapon mods which effect how much damage your weapon does, or even the speed and critical rate, which is nice to have once you learn how it works.
Weapon Quantity has been increased too, with more unique variants of weapons, and base weapons when compared to Dead Island or even Riptide, with the rest being DLC weapons that have their models and textures locked away until you purchase the dlc, which isn't bad, but the Bozak Horde DLC is a bit questionable, but we'll get to that later.
The graphics and animation are a major step up from Dead Island 1 & Riptide, with more fluid animations, more animations in general, and proper god rays and beautiful textures that are nice to look at.
Low-Tier gaming rigs should avoid playing the game on ultra, anything with, let's say a 550ti can run the game on high settings or more.
The weakest point of the game, cardboard box tier character interest, and an annoying QTA sequence that'll happen to you makes it a bit frustrating to get through, there's some interesting characters here and there, just not enough of them.
One of the earliest DLC's done with Dying Light, you're able to be invaded by Night Hunters controlled by other players, or do it yourself!
You can turn this off or have certain conditions before it happens, It's pretty fun and hilarious to surprise friends with.
Mostly used for its weapons, The Bozak Horde offers a short story alone or with your friends, with the story being mostly forgettable, and the final boss being poorly implemented.
The Following offers and entirely new world, rivaling that of the main game itself, with places to explore, side quests to do, and an all new
to ride in, so you can mow zombies over and get to places faster.
Sadly, It's exclusive to the DLC Worldspace, but the main game is cramped enough and meant for parkour so it's reasonable.
Dying Light is a pretty decent zombie killing game, one of the underrated games that came out in 2015, It's fun alone, and even more enjoyable with friends.

is a superb 2D side scroller beat ‘em up which features some dungeon crawlers mechanics, as well as randomly generated dungeons.
The game begins when a wizard tries to use magic to become powerful enough to rule the world. He finds out that something has gone terribly wrong and ends up opening a portal to Devildom, the demon realm. You play as one of the treasure hunters that venture into Castle Harwood, where the portal appeared, in search of riches.
As soon as you start playing you’ll be captured by goblins and taken to the Goblin prison tower. This is the first zone out of 4 different zones. The overall enemy variety is pretty good, ranging from giant goblins, armored knights, archers, mages and drummers that make nearby enemies go berserk. There are also unique boss fights. Killing a boss causes new items to spawn and lets you proceed to the next zone.
The levels are divided into rooms that sometimes have more than one exit, allowing you to choose from various paths after killing all the enemies. By clearing a room you’ll spawn a chest that can contain food, gold, weapons, armor pieces, potions or even fragments that grant you passive bonuses. Be advised that potions have random properties, they can either give you strength or they can poison you.
Food is used to heal you for differing amounts of HP. One funny thing I found is that when you eat a banana it will leave the banana peel on the floor and if someone walks over it, they will slip and fall on the ground. There are also traps scattered around the dungeons such as falling objects or spikes.
As you play you’ll collect gold and souls. Gold can be used in the dungeons to buy random items from merchants. Souls are one of the core elements of the game. After you die, you can spend them to buy permanent upgrades to all characters or to unlock more characters. The twist is that the souls that you don’t spend will be lost, so you’ll start each run with zero souls. You’ll also be able to free NPCs from the cells such as the Blacksmith, the Thief and the Pharmacist. These NPCs give you different benefits during your run. As with your heroes’ stats, you can also increase the benefits that they give you by spending souls.
There are various different types of characters, and at the start of each run you’ll be assigned a random one. I’ve played as a knight (slow but powerfull), as a rogue (low damage but fast), as an archer and as a mage. However, even if your character starts with these abilities, if you pick up another type of weapon, their abilities will change accordingly.
One minor complaint that I have is the fact that you are only presented with a description of an item before picking it up. After it is on your inventory there is no way to check what each item does. Maybe having an actual inventory to check this would be good.
Lost Castle is a blast. I’m not usually a fan of beat ‘em ups but Lost Castle manages to capture the best elements of other games and turn them into an amazing experience. It is easy to play but difficult to beat and it offers a lot of replayability. It is a shame that it doesn’t have online co-op at the moment but hopefully that, along with more content, will become available before the final release. If you enjoy beat ‘em ups, roguelikes/roguelites, dungeon crawlers or side scrollers in general, do yourself a favour and check this game out!

I'm a big fan of Telltale's games, especially The Wolf Among Us, but this title leaves me with mixed feelings.
1. The game feels like Game of Thrones. The music is good, and the voice actors from the show reprise their roles in this game (including everyone's favorite, Iwan Rheon). The voice actors for the new characters also do a solid job.
2. The story is interesting, and manages to tie the new characters into the show universe without feeling hamfisted. You'll meet major characters and be at major events, but it always feels natural. They don't try to shoehorn the new characters into anything, you're simply playing as side characters who have a story of their own to tell (think of it as an Expanded Universe sort of thing). How future installments play out remains to be seen, but the game is being made in partnership with HBO, so I don't forsee any issues.
3. If you're expecting the same sort of brutal violence and disregard for the lives of likable characters, then your expectations will be met. This game doesn't pull punches, and it definitely earns its "Mature" rating.
1. The game is ugly. And I mean real ugly. They use the same sort of basic art style that you see in The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us and Tales from the Borderlands, except they didn't apply the cel-shaded look you see in those games. Instead, they chose to use a sort of muddy, water-color type of filter and it just looks bad most of the time. Also, even with anti-aliasing and high settings turned on, the graphics are awful. Trees and other background props are blurry, flat textures that look like they belong on a PS2.
2. The game is full of bugs. Texture pop-ins are frequent, or they fail to load at all, resulting in characters who have black voids for eyes or faces. It's not uncommon to see entire characters pop into a scene, in the T-pose, before jerking into whatever position they're actually supposed to be in. And near the very end of the game, I encountered a bug where half the letters in lines of text wouldn't appear. They wouldn't show up in dialog choices, and they didn't even appear at the end where the game shows you what choices you'd made. It was like I was playing Hangman and trying to piece together the sentences.
3. The QTEs are a nightmare. In previous games the QTEs never gave you a lot of time to react, but in this game they're split second. If you don't hit the key the
it pops up on screen, you'll end up with a spear in your gut or a knife in your throat. It's utterly ridiculous just how quickly this game expects you to react. The autosaves are generous, so if you mess up it puts you right back to where you were, but I frequently found myself replaying the same sequence over and over until I'd actually memorized each button in the sequence. This isn't supposed to be a Megaman game where you learn the boss patterns in a fight.
4. The game runs like pure garbage in full screen for some reason. I had to play the game in windowed mode to get it to run smoothly, otherwise the framerate would plummet.
The ending is unresolved. I see
of people on here complaining about the game ending on a cliffhanger, and I'm not sure why. Telltale has stated before that they intended for this game to have multiple seasons as they continue to work with HBO. Maybe it's because the game title doesn't explicitly say "Season 1" or something (which would remedy the confusion). Ending on a cliffhanger isn't a negative to me, since the show does the exact same thing every season. At least a second season of this game is guaranteed, whereas GRRM still has no idea when he'll even be done with The Winds of Winter, let alone the final book.
As a Game of Thrones fan, I enjoyed this game, but it's full of too many issues to overlook. The story, voice acting and music all make this feel like an authentic Game of Thrones experience, but on a technical level, this game is inexcusably lazy. Any sort of immersion you may experience can and will be broken repeatedly. This game feels like a huge step backwards for Telltale, and I honestly have a hard time recommending this game. I only paid $5 for this during the Christmas sale, and I'm fine with that. If the standard price of the game was $5, or even $10, I could recommend it, but $30 is way too much for a broken game.

Original Review from 2014:
Company of Heroes 2 is a visually polished but poorly executed sequel to the fantastic Company of Heroes and it's expansions Opposing Fronts and Tales of Valor. Post release Relic have added a variety of free maps - all of which (less than 5 maps) bring to the total maps to between a third to half as many as the original game. They have also released one or two free commanders to offset the growing number of purchase-only commanders. Steam workshop is offsetting the lack of maps but these cannot currently be used in multiplayer.
Pros :
Excellent graphical representation of WWII Russia. Excellent upgrade over the original graphically.
Excellent new truesight system, meaning units only detect others where they realistically would be able to see. This makes games far more tactically involved.
Very good new abilities for unit command. Reverse orders a vehicle to reverse to the given location. Vault orders infantry to climb over small obstacles such as fences or walls.
Vehicles can now be abandoned and captured and repaired by the enemy. Semi-realistically this adds a sensation of risk to any "Tank Rush" as if you are unfortunate they could soon be used against you.
Weather effects are excellent (when they are present). The blizzard system is a genuine difficulty to be overcome on the battlefield. It is not just fluff - it represents a key component to successful strategy.
Cons:
Far less maps than the original game.
Removed server browser - Matchmaking only ruins the multiplayer experience.
Removed any multiplayer game except 500 point Victory Point (King of the Hill) gameplay.
Violent connection problems. Chronic disconnects.
Serious balance issues with the purchase only commanders. They can be countered but only if you know what you are very innovative with existing armies.
Relic shows little to no interest at fixing any of the above issues and keeps promoting new purchasable content while not fixing the existing serious design flaws with this game.
Unrealistic ice mechanics. In cold weather rivers will freeze and allow vehicles to drive over them. Mines, explosives etc will sink these into the river, instantly destroying them. This is possible on shallow areas of rivers, small inlets etc where water depth is 1-4 feet. You cannot sink a 12ft Tiger I into 2ft of water.
Terrible lack of new unit control. COH2 has added emphasis on Tank Destroyers which the original game lacked (featuring only the Marder). These tank destroyers lack a turret and turn slowly, making them vulnerable being rushed from the sides. If you order a tank destroyer to face an enemy vehicle it will fire at it while it is visible. If it then withdraws into cover the tank destroyer will auto attack anything it can see, meaning it will turn a full 180 degrees to fire at anything, even infantry, allowing it to be flanked easily by the enemy armor. There is no way to prevent this happening.
Overall I do reccomend this game, sadly just because it has no good competition anywhere. The original COH has been ruined substantially by the sale of THQ intellectual assets as Relic recently touted that they updated the original. What this did was fix some small issues relating to the tracking of stats and so forth while totally destroying the matchmaking game. As of writing you literally cannot reliably (90%+ failure rate) connect to an online game.
If you are able to look past the fact that this game has glaring issues such as the inability to play any form of multiplayer other than 500 point King of the Hill, the relatively limited maps, the chronic disconnects caused by the matchmaking system and indeed the matchmaking system itself then you will find at the core a very good game. The armies are balanced but challenging, the mechanics for vehicle versus vehicle combat are sound, the (Stock) commander abilities are balanced and historically relevant.

Are you ready for a super cute, fairly challenging JRPG packed with cliches, bad jokes and pop culture references? No? Then F&!$ off.
Using an identical system to Re;Birth1, navigating this game will be like riding a bicycle if you've played any other Hypdimension Neptunia game. The combat, lily rank, remake and game dev systems are identical. If you haven't, it'll be pretty easy to pick up. Join CPU Candidate Nepgear on her journey to rescue the CPUs, and save Gamindustri once again from the evils of game piracy, low shares and ultimate destruction!
Admittedly, Nepgear is nowhere near as likeable as Neptune. She has probably the most unimaginative and cliched personality they could (not) think of. But making returning appearances are all of the developer characters, with the same endearing (and annoying) personalities, delivering the same hit and miss humour as before. Overall, the story and characters have passable writing and decent pacing, even if it is nothing new and has definitely been done before. Most notably in its prequel. But who doesn't like a game in which a SEGA takes (extremely valid) potshots at the PlayStation, XBOX and Wii?
But let's get down to the actual bad. This is a functional PC port, but it has problems and lots of them. Where Re;Birth1 ran like hot butter for me, Re;Birth2 had problems right from the off. Memory leaks, unreliable framerates, occasional UI lockups, screen tearing, buggy text wrapping and eventual crashes that sometimes required the task manager to shut down plague the port. I was able to complete the game with these issues, as none of them actually managed to break the game. But it was at times aggravating, nonetheless.
Ultimately, I'm giving it a 7 out of 10. It's a good JRPG, for those that are interested in the genre and don't mind a completely female cast. Without the technical issues I would give it a 7.5, maybe an 8. Hopefully Idea Factory, Compile Heart, and Felistella do something about these issues in future patches.

I get a chill down the spine just thinking about the words of House Forrester and some of the epic moments they were used in during this game.
I use the term game in a loose sense though. 'Game of Thrones: A Telltale Game Series' is more of an interactive movie than a traditional game, where you watch the drama unfold and are prompted to make dialogue choices during conversations or complete quick-time events during action sequences. These sequences are however interspersed with small RPG like gameplay sections where you can walk around in a small area to interact with objects/people and obtain some lore related information or extra conversations or complete a mini-quest before moving into the next sequence of the story.
While this may not be everyone's style of gameplay it definitely does work for this title and you find yourself being pulled headlong into a tale of honour, intrigue and betrayal from within a few moments of the game starting. Most importantly, this story, the characters and the lore holds true to the Game of Thrones world and playing this game is almost the equivalent of being sucked into the show/books through the screen.
Unfortunately, for a game that is all about your choices, they seem to have little apparent impact on how this season of the story plays out. That said, by the end (without any spoilers) the game looks to be in a position where your choices will likely have a noticeable impact during the next season.
This leads to the other downside to this game. It is designed to be a series of seasons, each released in chapters, so you'll be left with a fair amount of loose ends at the end of this season that will require an unknown number of seasons to be purchased and potentially quite a while of waiting time before you can see the whole story played  out to the end.
On the technical side, the graphics are pretty good but I found that occasionally things could look a bit fuzzy around the edges of faces and the like, though nothing that ruined the immersion. The voice acting is fantastic and thankfully includes having the actual actors from the show voicing their respective characters. The game also auto-saves as you go through so you rarely have to replay much if you fail a quick-time but you can use the built in rewind feature if you do wish to go back and redo a section (or several) of the game.
The only bug I encountered during the entire game was that the quick-time events didn't always acknowledge the mouse input but simply using the keyboard instead worked fine (this may or may not have been fixed since I played it).
So final judgement? I found this game to be beautifully designed and a brilliant addition to the Game of Thrones world. If you are a fan of the show or even the books* then this is definitely something you want to give a go. If you haven't seen the show or read the books you may find yourself a bit confused, at least at the beginning, as it follows off from a particular event in the show/books before expanding out into its own original story and does assume some familiarity with certain characters and events. Even so, if you are a fan of fantasy/medieval games then you will probably enjoy this game. I highly recommend it.
*For the record, I have seen all the TV episodes and read all the books.

The original plan for this review involved an FBI interrogation, complaints about the "streets being awash in Nep-Nep", and a man in a black & pink fur-coat with matching boots. Oh and he's wearing a Hatsune Miku shirt. Plan #2 was a written account, of a failed attempt at doing a co-operative video review, between an ordinary gamer critic and fur-coat guy (aka the anime waifu warrior). Plan #3 was inspired by one beer, an existential crisis, and I had just finished watching the David Cronenberg movie "eXistenZ".
Yikes.
So instead of all that nonsense, you're going to be reading a straight review of Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation. Can you feel the irony? As it burns through your skull?
Gamindustri is in trouble once again. Our heroines of the previous game, the CPUs, have been captured by an obviously evil woman who is dressed appropriately provocatively evil. Compa and IF arrive to make the daring rescue, but only succeed in helping NepGear. GeGe is as unlike Neptunia (NepNep or Nepu-Nepu) as you can imagine. Her personality can be summed up as "Um...I...I need to become stronger!", she actually takes her job as CPU Candidate seriously, and doesn't feel the need to break the 4th wall at every opportunity (which at times is detrimental to this game). She will eventually team up with Uni, Rom, Ram, Cave, 5pb, and nearly everyone else with a unique portrait. Their mission? Save Gamindustri from pirates....or was it piracy...hm. I think this game takes place in an ever-so-slightly different dimension than the previous title. Why? Because Gamindustri is a vast and complicated multiverse...or Idea Factory just loves writing stuff that makes no sense.
Let's throw all that out the window and focus on what's most important: Underling and her plot to do bad things. She dresses like a rat, wields a pipe, and refers to chicks as broads. How is that villain-quality? She teams up with an actual rat, that fantasizes over Compa. This is all just an exercise in absoludicrosity. It feels like half the game, is spent chasing her around, attempting to stop her Team Rocket BS. Along the way Ge-Ge meets the other CPU Candidates. They don't get along very well, which leads to arguments, boss-fights, and kids...well..acting like kids. Ram & Rom have a combined age of what...10? Decades of JRPG-playing has forced me to accept that as normal but still...jeeze.
Most of the unlockable characters and endings require share-manipulation. This feature from the previous game is more fleshed-out, but not really improved. The first play-through is liable to produce headaches, until you get smart and just use the colosseum to get the shares you want. However, while you can and probably should make constant saves at critical points, in order to get every ending in one play-through, NG+ is required in order to get everything (plans for additional dungeons mostly).
One of the most welcome features in a JRPG (or any genre) is New Game+. Nep2 delivers a quality NG+ experience. Between the option to fast-forward through the plot, and the strength to one-shot everything, it doesn't take long to get to the specific chapter you need. However, if you spent a lot of time unlocking everyone in your last play-through um oops? Yeah you have to unlock them again. This means you have to go back to the Colosseum for more share-shenanigans. There really should have been a simpler option. This can be especially frustrating if all of your favorite characters, are the unlockables. Plus when you run around the dungeons, you have to stare at the backside of the same chara-ack! Oh gosh! I mean their back, because dungeons are explored in 3rd-person.
Fanservice. Neptunia 1 had less, this game has more. Neptunia 2 also has more kids. It's not a good combination. There are a couple scenes -- one of which that shows up in every NG+ -- that just make me uncomfortable. In the end it's all supposed to be semi-innocent humor, but...I don't know. Some of the other scenes also play it a bit too close to "It's like one of my Japanese animes." Sure, Nep1 was moe, but Nep2 is like...moe cubed? I could just be overly-defensive. Back when I played through No More Heroes, I realized I was sitting in a chair that looked exactly like Travis Touchdown's. That's the kind of meta-nonsense that'll mess with your head something fierce.
The dungeons are still lousy. In fact, some are even copy-pasted from the prequel. I've given up dwelling on this aspect, because it might as well be a part of Neptunia's design. The dungeons serve their purpose: there are monsters to grind on, goodies to collect, and an object to touch that triggers plot-advancement. I'm not going to bother asking for anything more. I've got other RPGs I could play if I want dungeons with atmosphere, puzzles, depth, and whatever else. Stella's Dungeons...well...I hope to all that is everything that they're improved in subsequent games, because they're terrible.
Stella doesn't have an understanding of self-preservation. While you're out saving Gamindustri, she's going on excursions of her own. It's something of a rogue-like, as Stella loses everything if she dies in a dungeon. In order for her to survive, you have to send her out on short, incremental visits, so that she can acquire better equipment. But I, you, and hopefully everyone else bought the DLC that strips the massive penalties for death. Now Stella's minigame exists to say "What? You want 100% achievement completion now? Kiss my♥♥♥♥♥and wait!"
Also while fingers are being pointed at the localization, I have to wonder about what happened to Nep-Nep. She's become a caricature of herself. In Nep1 she was already a caricature so....Now she's something of a try-hard*, and her wackiness is less endearing as a result. Maybe it's that alternate-dimension at work. It would explain why (spoilers!) Iffy x Vert is no longer a thing. Also, as I mentioned way back, NepGear plays it a bit too on the nose. She's the heroine trying to become stronger, make a lot of friends, and say "Goodness!". Most of her best moments involve her pairing with someone else. That's fine, but a large chunk of the game is just Nepgear, Compa, and IF. Compa is the only one who comes remotely close to not playing the "straight-woman".
Altogether, Neptunia Re;Birth2 is a textbook sequel. In a way it comes off as semi-cynical, like being forced to buy new college textbooks because they're the "latest edition". However it does share all of the qualities that made the previous game work, and it includes some nice improvements (4-character parties!). It's addictive, fun, has some laughs, and is a solid entry in a franchise I suspect that we'll see a LOT more of in the future.
*Yes, I am the pot calling the kettle plaid.

I've been playing this for a while now, and I though I should leave a review.
Grim Dawn is a Diablo-esque ARPG that started as a kickstarter project by two of the creators of Titan Quest. It slowly evolved into what you see today, after some years in development. Worth noting, the devs are still working on it everyday and there is an expansion coming soon™ that will introduce an expanded world with new areas, missions, gear, constelation, and the most important, two completely new classes: Inquisitor and Necromancer(!).
Pros:
+Dual class sistem that provides a lot of combinations (the base, vanilla game offers 20(!) possible combinations).
+Every class feels unique and has distinct skills to fit to every playstyle.
+In adition to classes, there is a devotion system (with constelations) to further customize your character.
+Tons of loot.
+A good story that will differ slightly on every playthrough (pay atention to the dialogues!!!).
+Great soundtrack that perfectly fits the theme and atmosphere.
+Not only does the game look beautiful (with a lot of detail), the game is also very well optimized. (Note: If you're looking to play with a friend, I'd recommend making sure your Rig is above minimum specs, as the FPS will surely drop if there's too many particles).
+Huge map, with lots of details and secrets.
+Very friendly comunity.
+Lots of replayability.
+Good Crafting system.
+Lots of factions with a good reputation system.
+If by any chance you're a fan of Lovecraft, one of the enemy factions (Cult of Ch'thon, obviously) is heavily inspired by his work.
+Well balanced, with a lot of potential to experiment different builds.
+Official mod support (you can get them on Nexus Mods. I'd recommend Aetherial Reshade, as it greatly enhances the visuals, making the game look better most of the time).
Cons
-Such a huge variety builds can be a bit overwhelming at first.
So, what are you waiting for? Even at full price, this game is well worth it, as it has the potential to offer countless hours of fun. Highly rocommended.

After a mere 18 hours, I am compelled to write a review. Keep in mind, I have never felt compelled to write a review for any game, on or off of Steam, ever. Grim Dawn, however, has blown me away.
I've loved ARPGs since I was a child- FATE was the first PC game I played all the way through. Within the last few years, there has been a surge of mediocre-at-best ARPGs released. I've been searching for one that would pull me into its world the way an RPG is supposed to, one that had a satisfying quest pool and adequete character customization/skill tree. Grim Dawn has taken all of these and amplified it to over 9000.
The skill tree and character customization is seemingly unlimited. Each character gets two classes, giving players the ability to mix and match different skills to create some REALLY awesome combinations. On top of the class skill tree, there's an entire sky of constellations of upgrades and abilities to gain in exchange for restoring the land's shrines.
The story has an interesting plot with fluid development and relevant quests and dialogue. In my opinion, this is a quality that many ARPGs sorely lack. Grim Dawn has impressed me in every aspect.
If you're looking for an ARPG that competes with the old school Diablo, Grim Dawn is the game for you.

Dark Heritage: Guardians of Hope certainly isn't as bad as all of the reviews make it out to be.  Granted, it's not the best game Artifex Mundi has published on Steam, but I found myself engaged and willing enough to keep at it instead of bored and rushing through just to 100% so I could move on.  Now don't get me wrong, the FMV cut scenes and characters felt pretty out of place, and the story itself was lackluster at best, but let's be honest with ourselves; how many HOGs ACTUALLY have a good, compelling story?  The premise was sufficient to prop up the gameplay, and that's all I'm really asking for.
I play these games on Expert, because Easy is usually way too much hand holding in a genre that makes it easy enough to steer you in the right direction if one is stuck, so this may not apply to Easy playthroughs.  The game isn't a cakewalk.  There's a lot of gathering and backtracking, but I enjoy that aspect of the genre.  HOGs that are too linear end up losing my focus way too fast.  Also, the game's logic wasn't crazy out there with item placements.  Sure, there are a few things locked away in odd places, but it's not so egregious that it pulled me out of the experience as many other HOGs tend to do.  The puzzles were also a bit of a challenge, but not so much of one that it drove me to look up the solutions elsewhere.  And once I figured them out, I felt pretty proud of myself for having stuck with it. Even more, the hidden object scenes were well-translated and nicely composed with nothing so obscured that I had to pull up a walkthrough to locate any deceptively hidden items. HOGs will always earn brownie points with me for that.
On the flipside, the artwork is nothing to write home about, and it's clear the game was stretched from a 4:3 to 16:9 aspect ratio to make it "widescreen," but it's not like other older AM titles haven't done the same (Enigmatis 1 is a good example). Music-wise, I was pleasantly surprised.  The soundtrack features lots of haunting piano melodies that made the lesser qualities of the game a bit more bearable.
Ultimately, Dark Heritage has some good things going for it on the gameplay side, but is a bit dated and campy on the presentation end of things.  If you're more of an adventure gamer like me, you might find the game pretty enjoyable, as long as you temper your expectations going in.   But if you demand gorgeous artwork and a good story to go along with it, well...there are plenty of other HOGs on Steam, though to find one with both won't be quite as easy as some claim.

Secondly, the gameplay you know and love from Alan Wake isn't here anymore. Where Alan Wake used to make you scavenge for ammo, always making you count your bullets and making you panic whenever combat starts; American Nightmare shoves ammo down your throat, combat is easy (especially if you've played the previous game) and the game plays less with the fear of darkness. Should you get this game if you haven't played Alan Wake? No. Should you get it if you have? Definitely... but don't expect another game of equal quality.

This is a remake of 1993 XCOM UFO Defense which is very well done yet lacks some strategic depth of the original.
The good:
- in many things, the game tries to stay very close to the original
- more alient types, including heavily armored robots
- all aliens and your soldiers have new special abilities
- more weapon types, including shotguns
- great music, some tracks remind Deus Ex Human Revolution
- great graphics
- the story is accompanied with many cutscenes and voiced comments from your staff, which helps build drama
- great detailed tutorial
- mind control requires the target to be in sight (no more mind controls at the very first turn)
- you can research additional upgrades to weapons and other things in the Foundry building
The so-so:
- 2 action points instead of 50-70 like in the original, soldiers normally just walk once and shoot once. This takes away some depth yet makes you camp less
- can only take 6 soldiers in a mission instead of 14 -> faster turns but fewer tactical options
- night missions have the same visibility as daytime ones, no flares -> easier, but micromanaging flares was fun and night missions used to be real challenge
- a strange cover system: when a mob is behind an edge of a wall, it still can be shot at, yet with a high penalty. Most battlefields are filled with tree logs, groups of stones, stairs-like elevation levels which makes the battles mostly about running from cover to cover and staying on Overwatch
- critical hits are important -> more randomness
- soldiers have no stats (which grew from "usage"), instead the game randomly assigns them to specializations (sniper, heavy, assault, support). Specializations offer a few special abilities though
- after getting max rank ("Colonel"), soldiers won't improve anymore (only psi abilities, if they have psionic powers), which doesn't let you train super-ninzas and forces you to send new soldiers to let them train as well
- a few new types of missions which are heavily scripted and linear, usually with a turn limit
- can only build facilities in one base, no storage limit, no ammo -> less micromanagement but feels too casual
- mobs' facing doesn't play any role: they see equally well all around them, and attacks from behind don't inflict more damage (though usually a mob won't have a covering object behind it and will be considered "flanked")
- no arctic/desert/jungle maps but many varied urban maps
- a soldier can take just 1 extra item (e.g.1 grenade) in addition to main weapon and pistol
The bad:
- most battles are scripted and not randomly generated. Enemies appear when you pass trigger tiles and take a free move to get behind cover right after they appeared. Some fall directly from above (out of thin air) behind your troops, switching to Overwatch and pinning all your soldiers down. Some will run very close to you, all while you're waiting for their animation to finish. This takes away much strategic feeling as all your battle plans are trampled by script. Worse, it makes playing on higher difficulty or iron man mode pointless, as it feels unfair to lose when you didn't know in advance a scripted situation
- camera always tries to zoom in on the next selected soldiers which is very annoying if you want to keep camera zoomed out for a tactical overwiev
- camera sometimes fails to correctly detect the tile under the cursor -> it may take many attempts to open a door with V key (and rotate the camera for that a lot), or sometimes the solder will run to a wrong tile which is on a different floor and visually behind the one you wish to go to
- if a soldier sees an enemy during movement he doesn't stop and can even lose sight of the enemy by the end of the move (it was the same in the original XCOM but there you could walk tile-by-tile, and in JA2 soldiers stopped when seeing a new enemy)
- no base defense missions
- although everything is destructible you can't shoot at objects, except if your weapon misses an alien and hits an object instead, or you throw a grenade or fire a rocket launcher

Generally speaking, American Nightmare is like a less-intense version of its predecessor- it's done in the style of a Twilight Zone episode, narrator & all, instead of the Stephen King/H.P. Lovecraft style of Alan Wake- though it still maintains the original's feel (and can get intensely dark) in the little extras, should you decide to go for things like the video recordings.

Hello gang,
I am a Fig backer, that was able to partake in testing various aspects of Solstice Chronicles: MIA. In no way, shape or form did I receive this game for free or get payed financially to write this review, and also I am not an employee of IRONWARD. I am a simply man with simply needs. A video game to use as an escape from the soul crushing reality I call life! So, now that's out of the way, let's begin!
Do you find yourself wanting to be a space marine that shoots foreign creatures in the face to save humanity? Then look no further! If you are fans of the movie 'Aliens' or games like 'HELLDIVERS', then this is the game for you.
Now a brief backstory to the game.
The game itself takes place on Mars where these mega storms called 'Red solstice' are slowly killing the planet due to terraforming. The worst storm has yet to show its face, but it's quickly creeping up. However if that wasn't bad enough, the STROL virus has now come to Mars because corporations are wieners. Now if you haven't played the first game which is called 'The Red solstice', that's OK. This game stands on its own, with nods to the original.
So, what is STROL?
Think of the T-Virus from Resident Evil, but it did a pound of cocaine. People turning into creatures from hell and others that...look like a bus hit their face. Not only do you have the virus, a giant storm that will tear the planet apart, evil corporations...but you have terrorists too which got the ball rolling in this hellscape.
Why can't we just go back to Earth?
Well that's already overrun by the STROL virus. So the only option you have now is to grab your rifle, nut up and shoot anything that doesn't look human. Solstice Chronicles: MIA is a top-down shooter that plays like HELLDIVERS. However, a more in-depth tech tree, a unique threat system and no heavy support makes this game stand out. You will be finding yourself fighting with the bare minimum against odds that not ever god could think you might have a chance to make it by! Good thing you have plenty of butt hair left from that explosion. Oh, did I mention that you can play as 4 different classes? Well, do you want to know more?
Assault is your run of the mill badass. He shoots stuff, and it dies. The more he shoots, the more damage he does. Sometimes he will get so angry he hits things with a giant blade. Maybe you don't like shooting stuff. Maybe you prefer burning? Maybe exploding everything that makes Michael Bay get a freedom boner? Or you like to be the odd ball with all the science guns? Well don't worry! We have the Hellfire, Demolitions and Terminator too!!
What if singleplayer is too boring for me?
Well don't worry my friend! Survival mode has you pitted facing endless amounts of waves...that is if you miss the dropship. Most of the time you will Evac at wave 16 which is a good 45 minutes of play, but be careful. If you die, you will lose all gear that you have gotten from that match. Good thing this is a video game and you can revive! Run out of your nine lives, and its game over, man!
Now please note. At the start of the game you will not have multiplayer. Only local (as in you have to use the same computer, so party like its 1994!), because of budget issues and all that crap. If it makes enough, you bet this will have Multiplayer! Till then, sit tight and pray you make it to the ground while you shake, rattle and roll in the express elevator to hell!

LOST CASTLE:
~~~~~~~~~~~

The Earl of Harwood Castle wants to own the entire Kingdom . . . No, “THE WORLD,” summoning demons.  Well, his dark magic has a slight . . . should we say, complication. He managed to open the portal of “Devildom” and had the misfortune of meeting one of the demons itself! Misfortune for one is the fortune of the other. Demons took over the castle and brought valuable treasures from “Devildom” to store in it. WOW, as you are one of the finest treasure hunters in the Kingdom, it is an occasion not to be missed.
Lost Castle is a beat-em-up / rogue like type of game. You will take control of opportunistic treasure hunters who will fight a horde of demons and their minions through randomised dungeons.  You will start the game in the castle surroundings but quickly be taken prisoner by the goblins - this is basically a tutorial. Then you will appear in your prison cell at the goblins’ tower; luckily for you the door will be open.  Check out the other cells and meet the gate keeper. When you are ready he will open the gate for you.
This game is extremely good for an early access. As you fight your way through the dungeon, dispatching your enemies, you will earn souls, coins and other items by doing so. Also, make sure to destroy buckets, barrels etc within the level as they sometimes have items hidden in them. When you eliminate all foe in the level, you will earn a reward - a treasure chest full of goodies!
If you encounter the adversity of dying, don’t worry, you will respawn back in your prison cell with a totally new hero with an entirely new weapon (great fun)!  Before respawning, you will be able to use the collected souls at the Soul Sacrifice ability tree to strengthen your new hero.
Great content here, plenty of enemies, over 100 weapons (with they own special moves) and armour. 50 plus items and 30 plus potions. Just one little anecdote for you . . . I was fighting the first boss, I was in strife moving all around him to avoid his bombardment so in this case the essence is moving fast. Well, I had one item left, a potion with unknown effect (they are all a mystery, by the way). I used it, and the effect was . . .  A gastric attack! My hero needed to find a toilet, farting and pooing every few steps. Potions have a passive effect but this one was a death sentence for my hero!
In this version, you can play single player and local co-op mode. I believe you will have a multiplayer mode in the final release.
The graphics are well done and fun. The gameplay and the controls are good. Plenty of re-playability.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Single player and local co-cop
-	100’s of items, weapons and armour
-	Randomize dungeons and hero
-	Great re-playability
-	Good price point
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No multiplayer as yet
Lost Castle is a little gem in the making!
9/10

Telltale Games does it again! Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series works like every other Telltale Games (The Walking Dead, Borderlands etc.) What you get is an interactive story set in the GOT-universe. It follows the TV-series, but focuses on House Forrester, rulers of Ironrath, whose members, including the five playable characters, attempt to save their family and themselves after ending up on the losing side of the War of the Five Kings. The game includes settings, characters and voice actors from the novels and TV series. It takes place between the end of season 3 and the start of season 5.
The game is pretty simple. I would say it's like the TV-series but it's you (the player) who choose how you want the story to progress. You choose what your main character says and makes their decisions based on what you think is right or wrong. It's not much to do than follow the interactive "movie" and do what you think is right. You also have quick-time events where you need to press different buttons when they show up on the screen. Quick-time events often occurs in combat and thrilling situations where you dodge by pressing wasd (shown on screen) and attack by clicking with your cursor on the target (it is also shown where you have to click). Bow and arrow and crossbows are also used but I feel the aiming is a bit clunky.
The game is divided into  6 chapters, where I think the 3 first chapters are the weakest. It feels like a proper GOT-season where the first episodes are for character development while the last episodes are more action packed. There is a lot of talking, so be prepared for that! I love the games made by Telltale and I have played quite a few. I am also a big fan of the Song of Ice and Fire, I really am. But this story was a bit over the top. You might enjoy it if you are a true emotional masochist, because plainly put it is a story of downfall of a single Westerosi house. Nothing more, nothing less. Things get from bad to worse. People die. Physical and psychological torture goes rampant in every chapter. Every turn of the plot is teeming with helplessness and despair. And no, it does not get better. Ever. Basically all that the player is left with are grim choices, which of the characters are going to be butchered next; are they going to be hit in the face a little or a lot; and how much they are going to be humiliated morally. Sometimes you don’t get to choose at all, but they still pass away in the most horrible ways. No matter what you do, everything just goes to hell anyway, leaving you with the feelings of helplessness, anger and frustration throughout the game. You can guess the ending. It’s stark (pun intended), despite all expectations to see at least a glimmer of hope. Oh, and there is a huge cliffhanger at the end, so don't expect the feeling of resolution and relief that should be there once you finish the game.
Some of the script solutions made by the Telltale writers are also very questionable. SPOILERS AHEAD.
All too often you can feel the characters are being deliberately cornered so they would HAVE to make the tough choices in the next chapter.
The controls are crappy. The mouse cursor moves with a delay, which makes it difficult to select the right answer within the limited timeframe. Moreover, the time starts running out BEFORE the other character finishes speaking. There were so many times I had to reload the game because I selected the wrong answer due to the floating cursor. The controls in the fighting scenes are hard to grasp too. Sometimes the fight just goes on, and sometimes you are required to press a random key at random moments. Sometimes pressing a key before the icon on the screen disappears fails to produce any results. I just don’t get it. The system has to be more precise. Or is it made to frustrate players like everything else in the game? It could be considered a great success then.
I guess the only thing that was really nice were the familiar and memorable voices of the characters from the TV series performed by the same actors. Applause for that.
My overall impression of the game was very mediocre. The controls have been poor in all the games of Telltale, but the writing has been mostly good or great. Still you can’t keep beating the dead horse of dark worlds, tough moral choices and bad endings. It gets predictable and boring. I doubt that making the scripts even darker and hopeless – like they did with Game of Thrones – is the right path.

This is a bit of a difficult game for me to review. The big question is "Did I like it?" And the answer is, yes and no. It brings very mixed feelings. I still checked Recommend but I've got caveats.
First of all the writing and acting and story are all good. There's one plot line that I don't think is all that great, but that's personal preference. I'm not really sold on some big mystic secret that is never mentioned by anyone in the books or show yet tons of people know about and just doesn't seem all that hard to find despite still being hidden.
And the other weakness of the story is how it fits in with the plot of the books and show. A few of the major characters do show up here, but they feel a bit odd surrounded by none of their supporting characters and instead being with a bunch of new people you've never seen before. Why is Danny with some new sellsword instead of Daario? Who's this Frostfinger guy with Jon basically filling in for Ser Alliser Thorne? And if Mira is so close to Margaery, why does she never show up in the show or books?  It's a companion story, but it feels like there is a disconnect.
But other than that I thought the story was rather good. The problem is I'm not sure it works as a game. Especially as a Telltale game. The biggest problem with Telltale games is the lack of any real control. Yes you can make some choices which has some impact, particularly if certain characters live or not. But in the end it still just feels like you have no real power. And this story in particular repeatedly beats you over the head with your powerlessness and lack of choice. It's true to the source material in that, but it's not exactly fun to play, for me at least. And by making powerlessness a major theme it highlights the weakness of the Telltale formula. I enjoyed the hell out of Season 1 of The Walking Dead, and Season 2 is pretty good too if not quite as good as the first, and the Wolf Among Us is also great. But here I'm just not sure it works.
I did actually enjoy the story to an extent, but it also leaves a bad taste in my mouth. As a game it feels more like all this bad stuff is happening to me. Which isn't exactly fun to go through. Especially if there isn't a rewarding pay-off, which I don't feel there is. Maybe it's intended for a future season. If you're a fan of the book series and TV series and can enjoy being made to feel powerless, then I'd actually recommend this one as much as I've criticized it. Your mileage will vary.
