Many mixed feelings whilst playing this game and most of them were positive because of the games uniqueness compared to the generic mmos we're used to see. It's not a ''do the main quest'' type of game to reach the level cap, there are many ways you could progress in this game and you can set your own goals for the game. Professions actually feel enjoyable to do since the progression is fun and you can progress in whichever profession you want to without any restrictions. Game has alot to offer as an mmo but as you play it out for some time you realise that it gets repetetive and not as fun which is obviously normal for any game. The gear progression is really stale and daily rewards make it seem useless to continue generating any form of wealth since the rewards are generally 5 - 10mil in items. Just to clarify the daily rewards are based off of my 20 days played. Cash shop items are not a necessity but some of them feel too important to stray away from buying them, for example one of the few items you are most likely gonna buy is pets. Pets are your companions that pick up your loot for you. It may sound like its not a big deal but in reality I myself have bought 4 pets just so I can enjoy the combat without constantly stopping every 15 seconds just to pick up the loot. Some pets have special abilities to them which are somewhat useful but not exactly a thing you should look for when you buy them since their priority job is just to pick up the loot.
Combat in this game is amazing in a way but stale at the same time. whilst you level up your character to soft cap you are presented with set abilities that are the ones you are gonna use to level up your account toward the awakened abilities. After you have leveled to soft cap, you have a new quest line to learn awakened abilities that are in general 10x times better than your default abilities. After you finish the quest line and learn the awakened abilities u can throw the default skills to the trash bin since they are weak as hell and almost never used useless unless they provide the necessary mobility or cc for pvp, because in pvm you most likely wont use them at all because the awakened ones are just that much better in terms of dps, which is really dissapointing because as flashy as the awakened abilities are there are just not as many and the combat becomes really stale once you repeat a specific rotation of abilities for hundreds of times.
This game is not pay to win and I have a strong feeling in my gut that it might just become that when the game loses its popularity. Currently there are convenience tools that are given to you in the cash shop, but some of the things like I mentioned previously are almost a must buy. Weight limitations are so low that it almost feels as if the devs made sure that players will get frustrated with the weight system and ultimately lead their customers into buying additional weight just so they could finally play the game without so many restrictions that the game gives you as a player who is not willing to pay for these convenience items.
Gearing in this game is one of the worst things I've ever seen combined with the utmost terrible market system that the devs gave the players to deal with. Most of the problems lie in the rng part of the game where u have to invest all of your wealth into gear progression that is nothing but luck and a little bit of skill in terms of using your failstacks correctly. I have never been as disgusted with a market system like this one. You are very lucky to buy your needed enchanting items within 10 minutes.
Grinding in this game is aswell very linear and it is indeed very boring because u have nothing else to farm but specific mobs for the next 3 months and the worst part about it is the ammount of people killing the same mobs as you do at the same time. There is always someone there with you no matter what who ruins or you ruin their clear rotation which will usually lead to open world pvp, which is completly gear reliant.
I do not hate this game, infact I do really enjoy playing this game but I might honestly slow down because of the repetetive content that is constantly recycled in this game. It is a shame that there are aspects of the game that make it really boring and unsatisfying but you have to realise that there is much more to it in this game. If you are a new player I highly suggest to take it really slow because u might burn out really quick with this game and come to this negative conclusion like I did.
All in all this game gave me something to do for some time and I enjoyed it a lot and will enjoy in the future aswell but not as much.
This game is worth the 10€ and maybe even a little more if you are truly enjoying this game.

This game was an honest shock for me as to how well it was put together. Dead Island was a special game as well but it did indeed fall short. Very buggy, awkward character development but was still enjoyable being the first Borderlands/Zombie game. Dying Light really improved on all the aspects Techland was trying to create with the original. Honestly I am happy they got away from Deep Silver. Considering the shambles that Dead Island 2 is in at the moment.
The graphics have improved, animations are cleaner, characters are easier to connect with and sound design is pretty nice as well. My biggest clap is to the RPG elements of the game. All quests are mostly voiced and give you some characters to mess around with. They have a pretty good variety as well. The skill trees are pretty diverse give you some different ways to focus at first.
Overall it is a great game and I totally recommend it. Awesome with friends.
Things that could still use some work. Mostly story development. Although much better it still sometimes feels a little empty. In the sense as I didn't always feel the drive to get to the end all the time. Again, it wasn't bad but I still think it's one of Techlands improvement points. The animations are much better yes, but characters can also feel a bit static in the face when in conversation. I'm sure Dying Light 2 will have heavily improved face works which will immerse the emotions the game trys to convey. Also at times it seems the game doesn't always respond or connect in combat at times. It's not really bad but sometimes it just doesn't seem to work correctly. That's being very picky.
One thing I would like to see in Dying Light 2 is creating your own character and gender picks. It would be a huge step for Techland but that would be awesome to have.
Again, love the game, it's near perfect. Just has a few things the sequel can perfect. PLAY IT!

I enjoy HO games as a method of relaxation when I'm not playing more adventurous, action games. But this game is not good. It's incredibly frustrating and not well done.
The game tries to integrate full-motion cutscenes; however, to reduce overhead when it comes to different languages, the majority of the cutscenes involve you staring VERY CLOSELY into the eyes of the person that you're talking to. This is not creative, emotive, or compelling. The eyes say nothing. They have no emotion in them at all. "Just keep looking into the camera. Yeah, that's it. Okay, we're done." When the video switches to a full face mode, the expression on the people's faces is one of being in a drugged, nearly catatonic state. So, whenever one of these idiotic cutscenes appear, I need to look away from my screen because of how annoying and unnecessary those segments are (until the cutscene acheivement appears, then I skip every horrid one of them!)
Some of the puzzles and item locations are borderline idiotic. Oh, you need to find salt in one of the HO games? That's easy. Pick up that 9mm pistol and SHOOT the bag of salt that you see there! Yes, this is an actual solution. One can always find a box of matches in the bottom of a potted plant, of course! And for some reason the artists have an infatuation with spiders and insects. Just about every HO game featured spiders or insects in them, not necessarily as part of the selections either - just to be there.
The game was clearly desigend for people who still have 4:3 monitors; but rather than place a border on each side of the screen to allow the game to be played in a proper 4:3 aspect ratio, they decided instead to run the game in stretch-o-vision to fill out a 16:9 screen. This is not a full-screen/windowed issue either because if you turn off the fullscreen function, the game plays in a stretch-o-vision, 16:9 window! This is clearly evident when you select an item during an HO segment and its width suddenly shrinks by about 25%. Someone decided that this was a good idea. Someone is dumb.
The Hint section also glitched out on me at one point where it kept focusing on the spot between the book and the map in the lower left corner. The map did not indicate where I had to go either. So I had to go around to every area until I finally found a trigger that told me what I needed to do. So, you can add "glitchy" to the ever-growing list of things that are bad about this game.
The game is also not friendly for those with mild colorblindness. There is one section where you have to rotate stained glass in four sections in a type of color-matching game. Two of the lighter colors were so close in hue in that I needed to use the red lens of a pair of 3D glasses to be able to differentiate the two. The devs couldn't have chosen a bright yellow for one of them. No, no, they both needed to be close to a neutral white. This was an inexcusable design choice.
And the final "battle" again the bad guy (who turns out to be not a surprise at all) was lame. He fades out. That's it. No drama, no anguish, not even a Darth Vader NO-O-O-O-O-O-O-O-O!!!
Obviously, this is not a good game. There are plenty of HO games that are worth playing to kill a few hours. This is not one of those.
Play this again in expert mode just for the achievement? Nothappening. And, seriously, what the hell is it with all of the spiders in every HO scene?!

First - Ignore my hour count in case low hours puts you off. I've been without internet for 2 weeks and found very few of my main games available, so I conveniantly had this installed and replaced my usual D3 with it for the past 2 weeks.
So, first: Is it like D3? Yes, yes it is. Similarly playstyle, quest style, level style, fights, mobs, etc etc etc. There are a few differences, but by the by it holds up well directly comparing both on just a "is it good" scale.
Break it down, however, and things start to fall apart for me. The gameplay and story is decent, definitely worth a shot! Very smooth and fun, can be fast paced (if you don't focus too much on the map like me) and the skill variation is incredible!
So, skills, I want to talk about this seperately. There are a lot of them, but each can be "augmented" in ways. So, you have a fire skill, but there may (it is fixed) be an upgrade to give it an area lightning affect. So you can adopt skills in different ways, if they suit one playstyle over another. On top of this! The "Devotion" tree allows you to invest in 'star signs' [basically]. These give you bonuses to stats, as well as possibly granting you a "skill". These "skills" are unique as they are (all) CHANCE skills.. So, for example, chance on it, chance on crit, chance on being hit, etc... These "skills" will then proc on that chance.. The best bit, is that you attach them to your actual class skills.. So I have a missile skill that is attached with a thunder storm, and on hit has a chance of summoning a swhirling vortex of lightning! It's awesome :D But there are a lot of different ways to mix up your build and I think this massive variation really gives itself an amazing feeling and something to aim for.....
That said.... If you are like me and you aim for that end... You aim for that ultimate goal... And you fall in love with that one character deeply... Then prepare to be disappointed, sad to say. It can take a while to get to max level, but that's by the by.. The MASSIVE problem, for me personally, is that there is pretty much no end game content [as of now]. There are 3 dungeons, that's it, and even then it can take 15 minutes to get TO the dungeon, and then a good hour, maybe 2, to finish.. This is not a viable game option for me due to my lifestyle unfortunately, so this sort of thing is out of the question.
Additionally, to get to the higher difficulties (something I enjoy) you have to complete the game... Fine! Lets do this :D Oh, it only unlocks Elite and not Master as well.. Oh, okay, well that's fine I guess I'll go about completing it again (but this time run through it) *sigh*.. Now I've only got an hour into my new runthrough when I started feeling a little bored for 3 reasons: 1) I hate having to run a story just to run it again knowingly.. It's boring to me.. 2) I purposefully adventured and unlocked 100% of the ENTIRE map on my first run through simply so that I could see where I was aiming! This progress is NOT carried over to your new run through (really made me sad). 3) I decided to make a rogue character, just for something fresh whilst also starting on Elite and completing Elite THAT way rather than doing it with the same character... OH BUT WAIT!! You unlock difficulties seperately for each character... Well that's me out: I quit now.
Awesome game, highly recommended, but do not expect end game.. This game is about rerolling one character over and over into new builds, rather than having a seperate alt entirely... Complete the game 3 times JUST to get end game? God please don't make me... But to have to do it ANOTHER 3 times for an alt rogue, and ANOTHER for an alt warrior... Sod that!!

Alan Wake's American Nightmare  was an improvement in every area over Alan Wake.  While Alan Wake was tedious and clumsy in movement, American Nightmare  was fluid and fast moving.  American Nightmare took away the lack of ammo element of the game and replaced it with more, faster enemies; a move that made gameplay fun and exhilirating.  The story in American Nightmare was well done with better paced voice acting all around.  In contrast, the original Alan Wake's voice segments were long and tedious.  Manuscript pages were now fun and relevant to find due to a game mechanic that tred the pages to next tier weaponry.  In Alan Wake, I found hunting the pages to be little reward for an often tedious treasure hunt (tedious due to the sloggy feel of Alan Wake in the first game).
I fully recommend the American Nightmare, although a short story style game (less hours), its much more enjoyable in every way than the tedious (unrecommended) Alan Wake.

This game is an evolution of Titan Quest. The most important improvement is the *feel* to the combat. It's hard to pinpoint, but there was just something off with Titan Quest combat. Attacks and spells did not feel impactful, muted sound effects, etc. By contract, Grim Dawn combat is very fluid and satisfying.
It also continues the excellent system of dual class selection with some expansions like the constellation and more build variety within a class.
Unfortunately, it is also a big step back in terms of the world design and story. Colors are a lot more muted and the world / dungeons feels much more same-y compared to TQ. It feels like it is more influenced by D2 grimdark style. Unfortunately the worldbuilding is just not as good as, say, Path of Exile, or even Diablo 2 in my opinion.
In the end, I would recommend to pick this up during the sale. If you were a fan of Titan Quest this is a no brainer. Highly recommended for most arpg fans as well.

I love this game, I hope they plan to implement multiplayer in the future. The gameplay follows the Far Cry formula; open world fps, random events, except unlike 3 there isn't much character development. There are, from what i can tell, three factions; "Sun Walkers," "Udam," and your own, the "Wenja." The story isn't very immersive, the game instead centers its selling point around being based in the stoneage and having you be the "Beast Master." The landmarks aren't geographically correct and they aren't in the correct time period. (I.E. Stonehenge is from 3000-2000 B.C. not 12,000 B.C. and it's in southern England, not central Europe) The Udam is the only faction that visually seems to be set earlier in the human evolution. I have run across female fighters in the Wenja and Sun Walker factions and there are female main characters who play a bigger role than maintaining the cave and expanding their mental capacity by smashing rocks together, so I like that the game seems to be balancing real world social issues too but i would have liked having the choice to play as a woman since the story isn't central to the game. I like the Beast Master feature and it was implemented well, but to the same point I dislike it because it isn't accurate of the time period. I would have liked seeing less animals being tamable, instead just the wolf and it's variations and maybe the Yak as the ridable animal. I was hoping to see a more realistic game because I am an agressive proponent to evolution and antiabrahamic ideas in general, although it is based in the stoneage so I suppose i should be satisfied. 7/10 Needs multiplayer, to be more accurate to the time period and a better story. Even though this game uses the Source Engine, this is not a Valve-made game. It's an indie game, and is very different than any other Source Engine game I've ever played.
In fact, Double Action: Boogaloo looks, and plays, A LOT like Max Payne and Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne (perhaps closer to MP2 graphically). Although the graphics are somewhat lacking, that isn't the point of Double Action: Boogaloo.
I've pondered, in the past, how someone could implement a 'Bullet Time' element in an online game while still having a substantial balance within the game. Double Action: Boogaloo has made that pondering cease, because they've done it damn near perfectly. Sliding, jumping, shooting, punching, dove-exploding fun!
If this game was remade with cutting-edge modern graphics, tuned up animations and tighter controls, Double Action would easily become a AAA title. The gameplay is incredible, and should totally serve as inspiration, if nothing else.

Lost Castle is a game that currently in version 0.06. They’re calling that beta access, and for the way it plays I’d honestly say that it’s damn near ready for release aside from the occasional bug and… it still have some memory/duplication things which can cause the game to either lock or drag your system down. There’s some technical things behind that, but I don’t know enough about raw game design to get into it, I just know that it involves the engine, the particles/projectiles, and something that happens when you accept an item that can cause it to replicate indefinitely. Like I said, most devs would consider it’s current version an EARLY alpha.
Let’s talk about the gameplay. The raw gameplay, what they’re attempting to achieve, works. It works well. In my opinion, it takes a lot of its aesthetic choices from something similar to Castle Crashers with a slightly more serious twist. Not much more serious, but still more serious as the game progresses. And it’s a good look for the game. It’s a fun aesthetic. Things are colorful. You’re colorful, the enemies match the color tone of the levels which are usually… not vibrant, but they pop. The (oh god I’m sorry art majors if I misuse this) shades they use are bright. Not bright enough to be distracting, but bright enough to give everything a bit of a light-hearted feeling.
I was talking about the gameplay, sorry. It’s simplistic, but not in a bad way. There are controls or mechanics that I wish the game itself had, but remember, version 0.06. The fact that things work well at this stage says a lot about the skill of the developers. You have a character who finds themselves in a dungeon. Pretty stereotypical as far as beginnings go. You begin with a random low-tier starting weapon and can unlock the ability to find other, higher-tier items early on. Each weapon type has it’s own unique moveset, and there are I believe six different weapon types in total: Sword and Board, Greatsword, Dual Swords, Bows, Shotguns (Muskets, whatever), and Staves.
Each weapon type comes with its own set of strengths and weaknesses and they’re varied enough to suit individual preferences, which is surprising provided that each weapon has 3 moves. Total. Basic, Alternate, and Special. Basic is your swing, the button you mash to kill the things. Alternate varies between weapons. It can be a charged swing, a shield block, a piercing shot, etc. Then there’s the specials. Specials are shared across most weapon types. You obviously can’t perform a spear charge with a bow, or summon a crystal with a sword, but many of the special abilities are shared between weapons. Each weapon has a type, which in turn dictates its special ability. Again, these are varied enough that even in their current state that each weapon can provide players with enough variety to find at least one to suit them. I’m partial to frenzy myself, but I also enjoy being directly in my enemy’s face, or chasing the enemy ranged units down shouting, “FIGHT ME!”
It claims to be a rougelike, meaning simply that progress is reset each time you die and you always begin at the beginning and attempt to reach the end. It’s closer in its current state to a rogue-lite since it allows you to make upgrades to your adventurers after each death, and the upgrades themselves are permanent. This may change in the future; the developers could implement a true roguelike mode whenever more content is implemented, but for now the rogue-like aspect is appreciated. The game itself still has a decent chance of failure, which to me makes it more fun. A game without a failure state is just… dull. Uninteresting to me.
As you progress through the levels, you can discover various items for your character. These include new weapons, new armor, consumables, passive stat upgrades in the form of crystals, and items that add modifiers to both your character and your attacks. There’s a whole lot of potential here, especially considering EVERYTHING STACKS. Traditionally speaking, this has created problems as more content and modifiers are added, but for now you can freeze, burn, poison, knock down, set enemies ablaze, and others I’m sure I’m missing all simultaneously. You’d think this would make the game incredibly easy, but the enemies actually scale well between levels.
The aforementioned upgrades aren’t necessary to complete the game, but let me tell you without any defensive upgrades by the third or fourth level you’d better be damn good at avoiding attacks otherwise you risk losing a third of your max health from a decently strong mob. There are some brief invulnerability frames after taking damage, but they last approximately half a second, so they’re enough for you to not get stun locked and that’s about it.
Speaking of, hit detection is a bit peculiar. I’m not saying it’s terrible, you stand near the thing and swing your weapon you’ll usually hit the thing, but you can tell that they’re still working out the hit/hurt boxes for the game. You’ll definitely be confused a few times because some attacks are larger than they seem and some you can practically stand in and not be damaged.
The soundtrack matches the game very well, but simultaneously it’s incredibly repetitive and not at all memorable. I played it today and I can’t remember a single background track from it. Again, as content is added, I’m anticipating more songs, but at the moment the soundtrack is far and away the weakest aspect to this …beta? Who the ♥♥♥♥ releases a game at sub .1 as a beta?
I have high hopes for this game, it has a lot of potential. Don’t misunderstand me, it’s definitely not for everyone, especially if you dislike losing, and as a beta it still has its fair share of issues. However, there’s a lot that the developers can do with the rogue-lite system, more weapons and items to add, more levels, branching advancement paths, new room types, environmental effects, and even secret content. This game is far from complete but if you’re looking for something cheap that’s challenging but fairly enjoyable, then I’d suggest picking this up. The devs deserve the money. They’ve made a damn good open sub-beta-but-not-an-alpha.

It's fun and quirky, but does not seem to present itself as a serious game. The reviews here made me take the plunge without looking too much into it because everyone seemed to like it, but they never seem to really specify why they like it. The game generally suffers from poor production quality. Perhaps the design studio was on a very low budget, but the whole game seems like a poor attempt at being a castle crashers, rogue-like mix.
I really haven't played the game enough to comment on the gameplay because the other factors contributed to such a bad taste in my mouth after playing the game for such a short amount of time that I could not give it another try. The main turn-offs for me are as follows: Intro to the game and the story as a whole, grammar issues everywhere, and art style.
First off, the story is just silly. I can't tell if it was actually trying to be funny or not and this is simply due to the terrible grammar in this game. It seems that all of the text in the game has been translated from another language using Google Translate alone and no spell-checking. I can't understand the story, but it seems to be just as encapsulating as most other roguelikes: you must be continuously sent off to your peril in order to claim more demons' souls and defeat a big bad guy that some magic person accidentally unleashed from its hellish depths who is now wreaking havoc on everyone in the land. It actually almost seems like a really cheap and horrible copy of the story to Demons' Souls (but no one knows that story anyway). This combination of horrible story and even worse story-telling leads to a laughable atmosphere that does not make you feel like you are playing a game that takes itself seriously.
The only thing that makes these points worse is the super lazy art style. They went for repetition wherever they could place it with a lack of depth. It looks like a flash game that you would find online really. This alone made the game feel stale to me. No effort in story, no effort in art.
The cherry on top is just how HORRENDOUSLY ugly I find the character design. This might not be as big of a factor for anyone else and this will probably make me sound silly or childish, but this character design makes me almost as angry as when I see Gnomoria on the front page: A game which I am absolutely certain would sell more if the image they used to advertise the game wasn't that of the ugliest piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥anyone could fathom. The problem with this game is the opposite of Gnomoria: the ugly characters aren't on the front page, but plague the entirety of the game with their stupid neckless, head-in-front-of-shoulders design. This is almost every character and it is annoying.
Normally I would keep such comments regarding the art style of a game out of a review and leave the judging to the individual interested in the game, but I state this here in this review because, first of all, I had no clue how bad it was until after I bought the game, and also, because it is not simply the art style, but the lack of ingenuity with said style that leads me to believe the artist(s) that developed this game are lazy.
Now, I don't know why I didn't understand how bad the graphics would be, but I think it ought to be pointed out: I checked out the screenshots and thought it looked cool, but when it was loaded up in full-screen it looked so ugly to me.
Okay, so this game has some critical failures that make me unable to recommend the game, but there are some redeeming factors. The game is challenging, it seems like it would take some real skill to become good at the game. It is kind of a cool system to have each weapon have its own unique moveset, just like the Souls games, but I personally find this mechanic unpleasant here as if you grow to like one weapon a lot, the only way to play with it again is to find it again, which appears to be random. Though the "talents" system, akin to Rogue Legacy's upgrades system, is quite bland, it is at least present and offers greater replay value. The abilities and different weapons did not seem too varied, and neither did the armor, but at least you have a decent pool of options, and of course I wasn't very far into the game anyway.
This game is good if you're looking for a lightweight game you can enjoy with a friend. At the time of writing this, the game is about 400mb. If you don't expect your games (or their developers) to be incredibly serious and you're looking for a fun, kind of quirky, castle-crashers-esque rogue-like, then give it a shot. If you're looking for the next big rogue-like with innovating mechanics, move along.

It's ok, I guess. I love Game of Thrones but this game is just as every other game about GoT: Dull, boring and average or below average. I trusted that TellTale could make a decend GoT game after I played Wolf Amongst Us which was a masterpiece. This on the other hand... is not. It's average.
It certainly has some GoT-ish aspects. Voice actors from the show are used poorly and the overall "you choose what happens in the game" feel is gone. When those major characters from the show are all the time messing around, you know that anything significant can't happen. The whole game feels just like playground for children. Only the last episode gave you the feel that your actions can made something important to happen, but otherwise I didn't feel the freedom of choice. It felt like whatever you do will make you lose in some way. It has the GoT-ish feeling that everyone can die, but only sometimes. Sometimes you just know that something is not going to happen. Only the ending was really surprising.
The story as a whole was a kinda messy and confusing. The whole point of the story ended up very lamely and the possibility of 2nd season was way too obvious. It feels like Telltale is only milking from GoT's popularity by doing this kind of games.
Other telltale's games are fine, good or amazing but this is so far the worst of them. I really wanted to like this game but it's just not possible. The game could have been better and I hope that season 2 does something better. This game is not worth its price but if you catch it from a sale, it's certainly nice to play trough. Just don't expect it to be amazing because it feels like it's a bad fanfiction.

Tower wars is an online competitive hybrid tower defense game built in the source engine. Games are fairly fast and there are ranked and unranked modes, offline maps, 2v2 and 3v3 modes as well as the full set of steam features, achievements, stats, leaderboards and whatnot. The players are tasked with constructing and upgrading a tower maze while also launching attacks comprised of a mix of the games units. The graphics and sound are solid and the gameplay is quite tight, like most TD games the rounds start slowly but once it gets going it becomes a rather hectic back and forth. Tower wars offers a fresh take on the genre and the multitude of modes offer an excellent amount of replayability.
-everything works smoothly and there is plenty of content to keep you busy
-the maps offer a good layout for constructing mazes which I like. TD games with no maze building really miss the chance to add an extra element to their gameplay
-games are nice and competitive
-matches are kind of about slowly gaining an advantage and this can be easily gauged by the upgrades on your gold mines. Opponent got a full lvl3 mine while you are just upgrading from lvl2? You're boned friend
As far as tower defense games Tower Wars's competitive nature separates it from it's peers and it offers a fun and interesting take on the genre. Fans of slower, more thoughtful TD's might not find it to their liking but in my opinion it's well worth the asking price and fans of competitive strategy or TD heads will most likely get a kick out of it.

I would recommend Telltale's Game of Thrones, but it isn't without fault. If you're a fan of the TV show, you're bound to enjoy it. If you enjoy Telltale's particular brand of 'choice' oriented interactive storytelling, then you will more than likely get a lot out of this one too. It features some of Telltale's best narrative decisions, but also some of its clunkiest. In none more so than this one are the failings of Telltale's narrative and visual structure most obvious. Thier game engine lacks the power to emulate the cinematic world of the TV show, and they seem unable to show character emotion without obvious closeups of faces, and distorted expressions. Dialogue choices suffer from 'Mass Effect Syndrome', in which you're given truncated dialogue options that sometimes only vaguely represent what you're character is saying, sometimes with a completely different emotional emphasis than you were expecting.
The game spirals outward from the TV series' infamous third season finale, but largely refuses to stray much from the template of the original. The Forresters are very much analogous to the Starks, trying to keep thier house afloat with enemies cropping up in all directions. Rodrick resembles Robb, Gared follows a similar arc to Jon, and Mira is much like Sansa (although to Telltale's credit, Mira is a much more sympathetic and likeable character than Sansa). Luckily they do take these initial similarities in different directions in later episodes. The game is at its best when it is doing unexpected things, and one of these is just how many women exist in this world, both in speaking and background roles. A particular highlight is Beskha, best friend to exiled Forrester son Asher, who features prominently throughout his storyline but is never reduced to a one-dimensional character or (thank goodness) a romantic interest. Several popular characters from the TV show make appearances, but are thankfully used sparingly, as thier performances are mostly quite wooden, presumably because the actors aren't used to voice work. Only Lena Headey's Cersei really comes off as sinister as her TV counterpart, possibly in part because her character model is also the only one that doesn't look like it came off a creepy waxwork parade.
Despite these flaws it isn't a bad game. The characters are generally engaging, and while the villains are fairly one dimensional, you do end up rooting for the scrappy underdogs against the relentless parade of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The later episodes in particular feature plenty of exciting actions, and heart wrenching decision making. My biggest complaint however, is that the finale features absolutely no closure for any of the story. Season 2 was recently announced, and will pick up where this one left off. Unlike The Walking Dead, which was a surprise hit at the time and so actually finished its initial story in the first game, Telltale have no qualms setting us up to buy a second game next year in order to find out what has become of these characters. If they had advertised it as such (as 'Season One' from the beginning) perhaps this would be less irritating, but this is the only Telltale game I have played which so clearly doesn't have an ending yet. How are we to know that the second season will finish the story? Perhaps the games are now planned to go as long as the TV series? It seems disingenuous to do such a thing so blatantly, but perhaps many people don't feel the same way, and will happily pay for a second season. I will probably wait for a sale price at the end of next season.

If I were to put all the hours into how long I've played Half Life 2, on top of what Steam shows, before I even used Steam and on my Xbox-360, there would surely be over one-hundred twenty hours (give or take) in just Half Life 2 alone. Why? It does everything right in what a FPS game needs. Many nuanced details, simple but oddly rewarding little puzzles as you pass through the many environments, the environments themselves, all strung together as you see just about everything City 17 has to offer. Between run down slums, abandoned industrial parks, a country side with spits of run down buildings in the distance, radiated rivers, giant bug infested shores, head crabs and zombies coming out of the wood work all along the way and a physics engine which even today rivals modern gaming. On top of all that, the story which goes almost untold from the silent protaganist, Gordan Freeman, who in all honesty is about as lost to the happenings of the world as the player is. Only slivers of clues and a very indirect method of story telling always seems to provide just enough to keep people coming back for more.
Edit: Weapon variety. You eventually have something suited for every situation you find yourself in, assuming you've explored the environment and scrounged around for ammo. A fast firing SMG, the trusty little pistol, laser guided rockets, the loud and certainly power Combine Assault Rifle and some other rather unique weapons to the Half Life universe. Such as ant-lion lure, a Zero-Point Energy Field Manipulator AKA the Gravity Gun and of course a crow bar used for everything but it's intended use. Weapon variety is one of the things that keeps this game fresh like a jar of unusually old pickles with a sweet crunchy taste that have undeniably aged well in their, what can only be known as, a secret goo.
These days, the graphics are clearly aging, but retain a certain quality that is undeniable. Though a few bugs and glitches still exist in the game, at this point, you would have to try to cause a glitch to happen. But all in all, this is one of the most polished games you can run across from the mid 2000's, along with it's two following episodes. Along with that, the only way you wouldn't be able to play Half Life 2 on it's top graphics is if you PC is from 2007 or has spam bursting out of the hard disk drive and spilling across your motherboard.
I honestly can't give any good negative to this game. It was a sublime experience back when it released and to this day, remains so. The gameplay remains smooth as can be and continues being one of those gems many other developers can only dream of. If there is a downside to this game, the only one I can really bring out is the AI is plain and simply old. It's not bad and can be challenging enough, but to any vertern FPS gamer of this modern day, it will come across as a little dumb, but that said, the AI won't hold back just how good Half Life 2 is.
So did I have fun? You can bet your bottom dollar I had fun. Will you? Of course! You can typically get all the Half Life games for dirt cheap most of the time and when it's on sale, you can get them for just under $5(USD). I guarentee, it's one of the best purchases you'll make in gaming for a long time to come.
P.S.: I'm wearing rose colored glasses when it comes to this game, so my opinion is cleary biased.

First - Ignore my hour count in case low hours puts you off. I've been without internet for 2 weeks and found very few of my main games available, so I conveniantly had this installed and replaced my usual D3 with it for the past 2 weeks.
So, first: Is it like D3? Yes, yes it is. Similarly playstyle, quest style, level style, fights, mobs, etc etc etc. There are a few differences, but by the by it holds up well directly comparing both on just a "is it good" scale.
Break it down, however, and things start to fall apart for me. The gameplay and story is decent, definitely worth a shot! Very smooth and fun, can be fast paced (if you don't focus too much on the map like me) and the skill variation is incredible!
So, skills, I want to talk about this seperately. There are a lot of them, but each can be "augmented" in ways. So, you have a fire skill, but there may (it is fixed) be an upgrade to give it an area lightning affect. So you can adopt skills in different ways, if they suit one playstyle over another. On top of this! The "Devotion" tree allows you to invest in 'star signs' [basically]. These give you bonuses to stats, as well as possibly granting you a "skill". These "skills" are unique as they are (all) CHANCE skills.. So, for example, chance on it, chance on crit, chance on being hit, etc... These "skills" will then proc on that chance.. The best bit, is that you attach them to your actual class skills.. So I have a missile skill that is attached with a thunder storm, and on hit has a chance of summoning a swhirling vortex of lightning! It's awesome :D But there are a lot of different ways to mix up your build and I think this massive variation really gives itself an amazing feeling and something to aim for.....
That said.... If you are like me and you aim for that end... You aim for that ultimate goal... And you fall in love with that one character deeply... Then prepare to be disappointed, sad to say. It can take a while to get to max level, but that's by the by.. The MASSIVE problem, for me personally, is that there is pretty much no end game content [as of now]. There are 3 dungeons, that's it, and even then it can take 15 minutes to get TO the dungeon, and then a good hour, maybe 2, to finish.. This is not a viable game option for me due to my lifestyle unfortunately, so this sort of thing is out of the question.
Additionally, to get to the higher difficulties (something I enjoy) you have to complete the game... Fine! Lets do this :D Oh, it only unlocks Elite and not Master as well.. Oh, okay, well that's fine I guess I'll go about completing it again (but this time run through it) *sigh*.. Now I've only got an hour into my new runthrough when I started feeling a little bored for 3 reasons: 1) I hate having to run a story just to run it again knowingly.. It's boring to me.. 2) I purposefully adventured and unlocked 100% of the ENTIRE map on my first run through simply so that I could see where I was aiming! This progress is NOT carried over to your new run through (really made me sad). 3) I decided to make a rogue character, just for something fresh whilst also starting on Elite and completing Elite THAT way rather than doing it with the same character... OH BUT WAIT!! You unlock difficulties seperately for each character... Well that's me out: I quit now.
Awesome game, highly recommended, but do not expect end game.. This game is about rerolling one character over and over into new builds, rather than having a seperate alt entirely... Complete the game 3 times JUST to get end game? God please don't make me... But to have to do it ANOTHER 3 times for an alt rogue, and ANOTHER for an alt warrior... Sod that!!

This game is an evolution of Titan Quest. The most important improvement is the *feel* to the combat. It's hard to pinpoint, but there was just something off with Titan Quest combat. Attacks and spells did not feel impactful, muted sound effects, etc. By contract, Grim Dawn combat is very fluid and satisfying.
It also continues the excellent system of dual class selection with some expansions like the constellation and more build variety within a class.
Unfortunately, it is also a big step back in terms of the world design and story. Colors are a lot more muted and the world / dungeons feels much more same-y compared to TQ. It feels like it is more influenced by D2 grimdark style. Unfortunately the worldbuilding is just not as good as, say, Path of Exile, or even Diablo 2 in my opinion.
In the end, I would recommend to pick this up during the sale. If you were a fan of Titan Quest this is a no brainer. Highly recommended for most arpg fans as well.

This version of the game is very unpolished, and it's very possible that you'll encounter a game-breaking bug partway through.  In my case, it was the gear puzzle in the widow's house.  The gears will not spin at all, even when placed in the correct places.  Yes, I could use the skip button, but this would prevent me from getting the Steam Achievement for 100% completion.
The 2D graphics are much better than they are in the mobile version of the game, and the desktop interface makes multi-step item discovery a little easier.  However, the live action cutscenes fall straight into the uncanny valley.  The post-production editing is terrible with nauseating filters applied.  The scenes were filmed with Polish actors and then dubbed over by Voxworks.  Extreme closeups on the speakers' eyes and forehead obscure this fact for most of the game, but when we do get to see lips moving, it's clear that they didn't even TRY to make the dubbing match.  (And no, there isn't any Polish audio available.  English is your only option.  Not that it's a problem.  The dub is good enough that you probably won't even notice that it's all done by two people.)
I can only describe the story with a backhanded compliment: "It isn't as poorly written as it initially seems to be."  The protagonist and her mentor often seem to behave in an illogical manner, but much of this is foreshadowing.  It's actually a plot point that the heroine is so "pure-hearted" that her first thought upon seeing a firearm is to use it to
for a hidden object sequence rather than, oh, I don't know, take it with her to shoot or at least threaten the "Evil Master" who keeps pushing people in the ocean, burning towns and their firefighters to death, and probably even
There is one thing that I really like about the game:  The soundtrack is fantastic.  I won't claim that it never gets repetitive (it can if you're stuck on the same screen for too long), but it's very atmospheric and complements the gameplay well.  I would pay more for a standalone copy of the soundtrack than I would for this version the game.  At least I know that I'd be able to play a soundtrack all the way through.
TL;DR Don't buy until the bugs are patched.  Even then, it's probably only worth it on a deep discount.  If you really want to try it, try it on mobile.

Game Mechanics:
The game focuses on logic puzzles and hidden-object-scenes, however finding interactable areas or items can be tricky, due to a very small cursor change. In and of itself every overworld area therefore becomes a sort of hidden-object-scene in and of itself, but without any kind of indication what you are looking for. Lastly, items that need to be combined with certain elements in an area can be relatively unclear and the overall gamme seems unfocused.
Plot:
The plot seems an uninspired attempt at a contemporary fantasy mystery, but doesn't feel very gratifying to progress through or even complete. The characters are flat and lifeless and don't really add anything at all.
Presentation:
The game uses live-action cutscenes, which interrupt the normal aesthetic flow of the game. It also uses a sort of game-engine/live-action-hybrid style, which seems stilted, as CGI-elements don't move or react naturally and the overlay of characters make them stand out like a sore thumb.
Completion:
If you do decide to get this game, completion shouldn't be too difficult, but I'd recommend against getting it in the first place.

Just like the original game, the writing in this is absolutely top notch.  The story delves even deeper into the dizzying ramifications of being able to fictionalize and alter reality as Alan has learned to do, even while at the same time saying that trying to understand those ramifications could drive a person crazy.  And even more than the original game, it doesn't just present these ideas as part of the storyline, it actively uses them as part of the gameplay as Alan works to change and effect everything around him in order to defeat his new nemesis Mr. Scratch and work out a solution to his situation that leaves things better rather than worse off.
And speaking of new nemesis Mr. Scratch, ho-lee
is he a good villain.  Major props have to be given to both Iikka Villi and Matthew Porretta for pulling double duty, combining their powers to be the body and voice of both Alan and Mr. Scratch.  They both do an amazing job, especially with Scratch, who really pulls off the affably evil part well.
Where
was very linear, leading you from point A to point B,
is much more open world, which I really liked.  Though you are boxed in to a single area for each section (not by invisible walls, but by justified, actual in-game impediments), you are given complete freedom to roam through most of that area at will, picking up whatever clues or pages or other items you find along the way.  I do hope that if they ever get around to making another game, it tends more toward this setup than what was essentially a platformer in 3D.
I had some control issues with the first game, but those were mostly cleared up here, leading to a much smoother gameplay experience, which enhanced my enjoyment of the overall game to a great degree.
Wow, I kinda thought I'd have something for this section, but I guess I don't.  There
a point early in the game that I thought I was going to have a fit, when it immediately shuffled me right off to the second level without giving me a choice to continue roaming around the first and finding all the pages and whatnot, but eventually they not only let me go back to the first section to finish all that up, they did it with such a neat twist that I felt bad for having been ready to badmouth the game at all.
It's not a perfect game, by any means, I'm not going to say that.  It's really just that what problems it has are so small that they're not really worth mentioning or even remembering.
The creators have said that they do want to make
at some point, but as far as I'm concerned they already have, and this is it.  I went into
with the preconception that it was just going to be a rinky-dink little addendum, probably with little to no real bearing on the main game storyline at all.  Just a step above a regular bit of DLC at best.  Instead what I got was a fully realized game with a complete and awesome storyline that compliments and continues the storyline of the first game while also setting things up perfectly for the third installment.
And I really wish Remedy would come out with a third
already.  I would give them
.

The best thing that can be said about Dark Heritage is that it is at least better than many hidden object games. Still, the unengaging storyline, questionable acting performance, and the lack of challenge won’t rank it high in the Artifex Mundi portfolio.
Dark Heritage: Guardians of Hope feels like wasted potential: it looks good and the individual parts are working, but the end product is just not engaging at all.
The story about chasing around some Dark Master on a derelict island in hopes of preventing him from getting a powerful artefact isn’t bad on its own, but it just cannot build a good atmosphere—in large parts due to the inclusion of live actors who do nothing but stare emotionlessly into the camera.
On the technical side, it looks good, and that’s about it. Game time is spent mostly with backtracking, as the entire area is open from the start, and it is easy to forget some arbitrary item from the beginning a dozen screens later. The hidden object scenes and the puzzles exist, but neither offer any challenge whatsoever. I wouldn’t say the game is tiresome though, it’s just almost insultingly easy.

Far Cry Primal is a beautifully designed game, with a stunning environment and fantastic audio. The game play is solid and enjoyable and loaded with features. Its biggest flaw is the lack of incentive to use all the pets, skills, and features in the game because of the lack of content. The content that exists starts to get monotonous by the finish because of the copy and paste programming used to fill it up. Here is an analogy to sum up Far Cry Primal.
One of the top restaurants in the world wants to make a great dessert. They hire some of the top pastry chefs to work on it. But the restaurant is impatient and wants to start selling the dessert before the chefs have time to finish. One chef insists it is great the way it is, and the customers won't notice whats missing. When the first customers order it, they are in awe when it is brought to the table. It's one of the most beautiful desserts they have ever seen. When they taste it, it has almost no sugar. When they ask about it, the chefs say that they will add more later for an extra charge.

Dark Heritage: Gaurdians of Hope is a hidden object adventure published by Artifex Mundi, a company that is quickly becoming a household name. Like many of their other publications, the story to this game is easily forgettable, yet drawing enough to keep the player interested.
Pros:
-Beautiful scenery
-Story IS quite interesting for what it is
-Comfortable hidden object scenarios (not too easy, not too hard)
-Fitting music
-Lots of locations
-Lots of mini games
-This game isn't short and has another side story unlocked in the end which ensures a good few hours of gameplay.
Cons:
-As mentioned, very forgettable storyline. For me personally, I forgot what I was doing prior to each launch and would have to abuse the hint button until I had an idea of what my objective was once again.
-This game uses real actors, yet the camera constantly stays zoomed to their eyes and the actors were very one-dimensional and boring.
-Final "fight" scene is just....dull. Like they had to TRY to reach this level of dull.
-Story seems as though it never truly gets told during gameplay.
With that said, as much as I hate to say this on a review meant to give positive feedback, I would not recommend buying this game full price, but it should definitely be grabbed while on sale as it is very beautiful and fun to play.

I've never written a review for a game but this is one I have strong feelings about.
Do you like fetch quests, pointless hunts, and saving the same person? Then get in line for Far Cry: Primal! The game where you can taste the copy and paste.
Yet again Ubisoft has treated it’s audience to an a,ss blast to the past that has left me unfulfilled and a little ashamed.
The first few hours were fun and full real "badass" moments as I plunged my spear into generic cave man #2’s face or burned a forest down to keep the wolves at bay, but the more I played the more I felt there was a glitch in the matrix and I was going in circles. The experience of this game is like being the security camera monitor in any heist movie ever; where the thief’s have looped the footage and its the same thing over and over and over. Save this random, collect this animal, find these carfting items and save the random person again. The story has all the drama and complexity of a dirty puddle and all builds to a climax as satisfying as a sandpaper hand-job. In fact I’m not even sure if I finished, I never saw credits? But I couldn’t do anything else after the mission so I  suppose I have. Then Ubisoft had Uplay throw acid in my face and was all like "Consoles? What consoles? Can’t you see that we really pushed for graphical performance on every platform?” I commend Ubisoft on using a real cave man dialect, but can't they just admit that we are in the animus and it can just translate it for us. I didn't mind reading subtitles but when I read the subtitle and the character is still letting out emotional grunts it really breaks up the any emotional investment in any of the dialogue. Someone was talking about killing children and I just sat there thinking I get it, he's bad and Adam Jensen is cross about it. Let me skip to the next line and maybe I won't skip the next game!

Far Cry Primal is a great game. People say its repeatative, go here, get that, but its not. Sure you have to travel, but for different reasons. In my four hours so far, ive already saved a hunter, helped a crazed warrior burn corpses, escape a freak's cave filled with leopards and urine, gone on 3 acid trips, hunted a bear, and created a village. And you know what, I regret nothing. I havent even scratch the games surface yet, and im already having tons of fun.
Hunting is amazing. To track an animal, then hunt it down, or, even better, have my recently tamed bear wipe it out by tackling it and biting its throat. Visuals are outstanding from affar, fur gets a litle funky up close, but thats understandable.
People say the characters arent interesting because they dont speak english. I find that a lie. I have met a fearful gatherer, who wants to be more than she is, a crazed shaman who loved getting me high as the sky, a insane warrior who loved to burn corpses, and a elderly hunter who thinks i look like a mammoth. Not to mention the one armed psycho who peed on me.
I dont follow all the hate for this game, yes its not perfect, but its a long way from a thumbs down. Id rate it a personal 8.8/10 Its good, the only downfall I see, is getting my damn population count to 40. Other than that, Far Cry Primal has taken me to a time i never thought I'd see, and I wouldnt trade that for the world.

Lost Castle is an amazing rouge like game where demons and other monsters are summoned to your land you its your job to fire yourself out a cannon an infinite amount of times until you or they die. Having only played FTL and binding of isaac I cant say if its the best rouge like game but its certainly worth your time if you like rouge likes. The price is easily worth it, You can be a warrior, mage or acher and each class has their own unqiue weapons to use along with spells and potions to give you a boost in damage, make you faster or even transform into a werewolf and take revenege on  everyone not fortunate enough to be a werewolf. When you die all the souls you have collected from your downed enemies can be used to give you a permantent boost in damage, hp, crit or better starting gear.
PROS:
+ Balls cheap
+ Cute art style and music
+ Lots of variations on gear, weapons and spells.
+ LOCAL co op
+ Multiplayer to be added
+ Combat flows with basic attacks, heavy attacks and specials all tied to the weapon you have.
CONS:
- Small spelling errors but nothing major
- Needs a NG+ mode
- Cant save progress in current area and continue after exiting
- Cant back track to buy items you saw but didnt have enough money at the time.
All in all its a great game for a great price and i recommend it!

Switching between different characters to give you different perspectives on events like in the books, and to let you explore different parts of Westeros (and Essos) was an interesting idea, to be sure.  I think it was a mistake, though - Telltale games don't really let you affect much plot-wise with your decisions, so they work best when you can at least empathize with your character.  That becomes much harder to do when you're given so many different perspectives, some of which are short-lived, and odds are you'll find you dislike at least one of the characters and want to just get their chapters over with.
That said, there's a lot of good points to the game.  Some very good voice acting, as with all Telltale games.  The writing is solid, if not inspired, and it's easy to like some of the characters.  The games a bit buggy at parts - at one point I spared the life of an enemy, only to have the next chapter tell me that I'd killed him - but that's just a bit annoying...   Not a dealbreaker.
What made me a touch angry, though?  The game tells me that I can play this to determine the fate of House Forrester.  This is a bald-faced lie - everything is left on a cliffhanger, so that they can get those sweet, sweet sequel bucks.  In fact, by episode five I was starting to wonder how a couple of plot threads would relate to the central dilemma of the game, and surprise...  They don't.  At least until the next six episodes.
This is particularly bad in that the villains of the piece continually go out of their way to hurt and humiliate the characters you're supposed to care about.  I'm sure that the writing team approached plenty of scenes thinking "what can these guys say or do that would be the most horrible in this context?"  I kind of assumed this was setting things up for their eventual comeuppance to be that much more satisfying.  Hah, no - all that grovelling and humiliation comes with no payoff whatsoever.
I was left with a distinct feeling of "Why the hell did I bother with all this?"  Maybe I just lack the masochistic streak that Telltale was expecting me to have.  If I have to be railroaded into your plot with little to no control, at least make sure the rails lead to a satisfying destination.
If you're cool with that, you'll probably really like this game.  Personally, I would have rather had a proper ending, with the main plot threads resolved and a satisfying payoff for all the horrible events that took place.  Really, guys, it IS possible to have an ending with a decent story resolution, AND follow it up with a sequel.  Plenty of books and movies manage it.  You just have to try a bit harder.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is more an expansion of some sort to the original game than a proper sequel.
While the gameplay is exactly the same as Alan Wake, this downloadble title makes two little mistakes:
1) Pumping up the action a bit too much for a game that is supposed to be some kind of survival horror: in American Nightmare your weapons do a lot more damage and refilling your ammo and throwable weapons becomes a trivial affair. Suffice to say, running from enemies doesn't have much sense anymore. The more variability with the Taken does so little to makes things harder, unfortunately
2) The game is basically about three distinct locations that you have to visit thrice each. While I kind of expect to revisit levels in roleplaying and open world games, I don't like doing so in action adventures and horror titles. While this design is perfect, storywise, it can't help but to feel annoying and tiresome
The new arcade mode is basically a hold the line mode against endless waves of Taken and nothing more. It's a quest to unlock all the available maps and reaching the highest score possible
Therefore I consider Alan Wake's American Nightmare a weaker expansion for the original game, but quite fair, given its price

The first problem I have encountered is pretty minor, but it's a problem nonetheless and that's the sound quality. When characters talk, it sounds very clippy, almost blown out to the point that it grates on my ears (this is the Japanese audio, I haven't tried the English audio). I tried adjusting the volume on my headset but there was no improvement in the quality (this could be a problem on my end but I doubt it).
The second annoyance I encountered was with the translation of text not matching the speech (Japanese audio, English subtitles) which probably has to do with the fact that they didn't want to write two seperate translations for the Japanese audio and English audio to both be accurate. This creates a problem when listening to the Japanese audio though because there are entire sentences said by the characters that just get left completely out of the translation.
I could just be nit-picking because I've been playing/reading the Grisaia series and Steins;Gate recently, as they have superb translations and dialogue that's for the most part faithfully translated but those are the reasons I won't be continuing this game and this review is aimed at people who would find fault in areas similar to the ones I've mentioned. So now that I've got over a hundred hours logged on the game I figured I'd leave a review. It's not the best mmo out there, but it's definitely worth the price. A lot of people complain about the in games purchases system, which is annoying, but the game is at least in no way pay-to-win. The combat element takes a little while to adjust to (you need to memorize a new key combination for every skill) but actually ends up being a lot more fun and engaging than the standard "press this number on the hotbar to do this" system. My main complaint with the game is the way boss fights are set up. If you're looking for an mmo with complex boss raids and exciting dungeons, then keep looking. BDO has arguably the most anticlimactic boss system of any game I've ever played, which was disappointing since dungeons and raids are generally my favorite part of mmo's. However, the graphics are great, the world is enormous, and there are a great deal of activities to take part in outside of questing and grinding. For only being ten dollars, the game still manages to put out an impressive amount of enjoyable content.

I found this really interesting game on YouTube, and it looked appealing. So I waited for a good sale, bought it, and just had a blast. When I first saw this game, I thought it was your average fighting game that you could land all the sweet combos with friends. But Lethal League is so much more than just a fighting game. With the only way to blast fighters out of the arena using a ball that is consitantly gaining speed, bouncing, flying, and who knows what in any direction, this game adds an intense factor in trying to stay alive.
I remember when I had three friends over and we all had out own wired controllers, so I suggested we played Lethal League. I had already been playing a lot of it, and they had never played in their life. Now, when I thought playing alone was fun, I never accounted having friends to play with. But when more people joined the game, it becomes hilariously joyous, with a lot of tense moments of only two people left and the ball being at over 1000 speed, some people figuring out new attacks, or people getting that three-hit wipeout, mostly on accident.
All in all, Lethal League is a sweat-inducing and creative game, bringing a fresh idea to the fighting game genre, and one that works incredibly well. The multiplayer works great, hit detection is fine, the characters are interesting, and the gameplay is just plain awesome.

People dislike the simplicity of this game; however, I recognize the art in its simplicity. You play as a gritty, Before Common Era, character and this game does so extremely well. The "fun" of the game isnt just the regular run-and-gun gameplay mechanics. You actually have to struggle making your own weapons, your own ammo, and hunting for sustinance like the era of the game dipicted here. I find the game to be a satisfying fictional depiction of the olden times before cell phones and lead ballistics. Yes, many missions invole infiltration, killing everyone, and taking over; yet so did the missions of the BC era. This game goes against the point-and-shoot cliche and dives deeper into the development of early man. The bad rep people are giving this title is the result of dissatisfaction for the status quo. I've found this game well optimized, its mission clear, and its delivery unique and earning of the surtitle "Primal." It runs extremelty well on a modest gaming computer like my own, and I've found it to be an intelligently articulate piece of artwork that I will gladly see from start to finish. Do not knock it until you've tried it.

I'm having qualms about the fact that good players get boosters to help them win as opposed to having powerups on the map like there was in Specialists, but hey, it's a spiritual successor to Specialists, that's more than enough reason to check it out.

Dark Heritage: GoH is the kind of game that makes me wish there was a neutral recommendation. It's not necessarily bad, but it isn't exactly good, either.
First of all, this is
a $10 game, so do yourself a favor and stay away unless it's on sale. I personally got this in part of a Artifex Mundi (the developer) bundle, so I don't have an issue with pulling 5 hours for pocket change, but there is no way I'd tell anyone to spend full price on this.
That said, let's talk about the game itself. "Meh," seems like a good place to begin. More importantly,
.
Dark Heritage combines the challenges of Myst with the fun of an I Spy book. If that sounds underwhelming to you, then I'd probably walk away right now, because what you see is what you get. The art's neat, and the puzzles are interesting. Unfortunately I found most of the hidden object challenges to be a little easier than I would have liked.
The gameplay was enjoyable. The story, on the other hand, was just painful. The plot of this game is probably one of the worst I've ever heard in my life - it's confusing and poorly written, the voice acting is garbage, the video actors are laughable, and the ending made me smack my head so hard I saw stars.
All in all, Dark Heritage isn't anything special, but it's still entertaining if you're into casual puzzle games. The achievements are easy to unlock, the art is pleasant, and if you opt to wait for a sale, I expect you'll feel like you got your money's worth.

This game is just downright bad. I, a self-declared completionist, actually uninstalled it about 1/3rd of the way through because I just couldn't take it. Here's the breakdown:
+ Graphics: I'm not sure what everyone's complaining about. The graphics are actually pretty high quality. The cut scenes with video are not really my taste, but they're well integrated otherwise. Nothing to compain about here. That is, however, where the positive aspects end.
- Music: repetitive. Sooooo repetitive.
- HO scenes & games: either entirely too easy or way too complicated. Example: so if I have a crowbar, a hammer and a knife, I have to use the *knife* to get a boulder out of the hole in a tree? And break off the blade while doing it? Really?? And I need piece A to open a box to find piece B which opens another box to find piece C which completes a puzzle that I have to shift three pieces in to solve? Really??
- Story: The story is completely contrived and ridiculously cheesy (some strange cult on an island, a kidnapped professor), but somehow I'm not allowed to actually work towards the cult and the professor plotline because I absolutely *have* to help every NPC I meet along the way. Because reasons. Plus laughable, pseudo-cryptic, pseudo-esoteric mumbo jumbo from a talking red-winged blackbird with an incongruously gravelly voice. No real plotline to make it exciting or make me want to play, plus weird, ridiculous, pseudo-creepy stuff (I can see the developers now with a storyboard: "Creepy things: spooky castle high on a geologically-improbable spire of rock, cemetary, tomb, abandoned mine, random skeleton in the ferry office"). I wish I could say the kitsch was amusing, but it's not.
- Price: Dude, I can get 10 beers at the late night store for that and have more hours of fun than I did with this game. Hurrah for Steam sales.
Constructive conclusion: I'm a big fan of HOGA games, and of Artifex Mundi. Try one of their in-house titles instead. I recommend the Enigmatis series highly.

For example they even use the M3 scout car and M5 half track the americans did from the first game as historical lend lease vehicles (but not the bren or shermans which they had more of). They have the katusha rocket truck. But its just the calliope sherman attack mount on a truck rather then tank. Perhaps most damning are soviet infantry. They come in big groups like the Americans. Conscripts have Oorah just like Fire up. Small differences that they have molotovs and not frag grenades. While both have sticky bomb anti tank grenades that have a high chance of damaging vehicle engines. Some of the units do not make ANY sense. With the announcement of Tropico 5 coming out later this year (with our favorite dictator playing a part reminiscent of one of our favorite pirates) I decided to re-play Tropico 4 with some of the enhancements and DLC packages that were recently on sale. Tropico 4 happens to be my favorite city/country building game, and hides so much depth but has plenty of accessibility for people just coming to the genre. Not to mention the atmosphere is absolutely addicting.
Seriously, I love the music. I'll talk about everything else in a bit, but the atmosphere that the music and voice acting creates for the game definitely gives it soul. Mariachi music blaring from my computer and the horns of the industrial sector of my city convince me that what I've created has substance. The voice acting of the international leaders and constant radio broadcasts are comical and at the same time engrossing. I love hearing praise and snide remarks from political group leaders letting me know exactly how my choices are affecting the lives of the population.
This helps with the depth of the game, because without the comical side, Tropico could be very intimidating. Every person on your island has their own set of statistics and meters that feed into a larger pool of political powers on your island. Those powers make up a balance that you have to cater to if you want to keep order in your slice of the world. Every time you enter your "Almanac" which houses the statistics of the island and the world you can get lost. It is time consuming, but having visible data makes the weight of your decisions heavier and the results more compelling.
You'll like this game if: You want the challenge of playing the US off the USSR in a nuclear standoff while smuggling illegal goods internationally and running the worlds best resort location. Also if you always wanted your own Penultimo. (PENULTIMO GO COUNT MY MONEY AGAIN!)

In 'Greyfox' you play as a young lady that is leaving her job and starting anew in a retirement town called Greyfox. There is no real context as to why you are leaving the city/town that you live in, or why you would leave everything to go somewhere that you have no work or anyplace to live. Instead it is explained to you that you are going to rely on the kindness of others. Once in Greyfox you met a mysterious woman who puts you in the bodies/lives of residents of Greyfox.
I have to say that the game is not "bad" but there really isn't anything that makes it memorable. The town of Greyfox itself is very small and often you find that most of it is closed off, making the world seem even smaller. Time spent with the four people whose lives you take over is so brief that many will have no interest in the outcome of their decisions which are basically just "do or do not" choices. The dialog goes from uninspired to poor attempts at bathroom humor. And while the story's premise is good, the execution is really just not there. That leaves the game feeling rushed and incomplete.
Now comes the big question, "Is this game worth my time, and more importantly is it worth my money?" I would say the game itself is worth your time as long as you are comfortable with not expecting too much. You will likely only spend an hour with the game before completing it, and with little replay value the time investment is not a huge loss if you hate the game. Being worth the cost, well that depends on of you are buying it on sale or not. With the game going under a quarter in sales, you really aren't losing anything by giving it a runthrough (like it or hate it). At full price 'Greyfox' just doesn't carry enough value for me to recommend it.

Pros:
— Captures the essence of the GoT universe. Not bad as far as fanfiction goes, even if it is based on another fanfiction (TV series).
— Keeps you interested in the story and leaves you wanting to play more after completing each episode.
— Great voice acting, as usual; acceptable visuals and facial gestures.
— You get to play as different characters in various settings: Ironrath, The Wall and Beyond, King's Landing, Essos and Mereen.
— Characters from the TV series do more than mere cameos (except for Jon Snow).
Cons:
— As usual, Telltale gives you only the illusion of choice: no matter what you do, the plot unfolds in pretty much the same way.
— Episode format sucks. If you're gonna play a Telltale game, I recommend you wait until all episodes have been released.
— The story has no closure, leaves you hanging until the next season. (A subjective con, I know, but I personally hate it when they do that.)
All in all, a very decent and enjoyable game. Maybe not as good as, say, The Walking Dead Season 1, but still worth it.
