So another year, and we have another Far Cry, but without guns!?
Yes, Far Cry Primal takes a dive into time and brings us to 10,000 BCE, and with it comes a package of interesting details. First and foremost the wildlife as this is one of the reasons people want this title.
The wildlife in Far Cry Primal is based upon the Wildlife from 10,000 BCE - however even though the game is set in Europe we are getting quite a lot of Central American wildlife and to those that actually care this will bother them. It features the formidable Sabre-tooth Tiger among Cave Lions, and even Cave Bears, and all of the carnivorous animals are in fact tamable, so during your time in Oros you can have companions.
We have a simple but contextually appropriate story where you play Takkar - beast master of Oros from the Wenja tribe. Having been nearly (or so it seems) eliminated by Ull of Udam, Takkar must find the remaining members of his tribe and restore them to their former glory whilst eliminating the problem of why they were culled. The three tribes simply cannot co-exist and kill each-other on sight. The Wenja are a spiritual people and they love to party, the Izila who are prestigious and believe everybody is under them, and the Udam who are dying out due to what we can assume hygiene issues and disease. Takkar must eradicate both of these tribes.
The land of Oros is beautiful, diverse and easily scalable. It features a simulated Aurora Borealis, many locations of diverse vertical height and it's rather big for what's perceived as an expansion. Primal is a fully featured game, it borrows many elements from previous Far Cry games and many game-play mechanics are nearly identical to the previous release in the franchise.
For many people there will be problems with having no co-op available, less weapons and no guns or explosions, little depth in story (not that Far Cry is known for it's stories), having a very short campaign and most of the game is essentially the side-content. With all this aside, is it a good game, is it fun, does it live up to the franchise?
Well, yes the game is good. It could have been better but it's still very good, very fun and it does live up to the franchise. In recent times, Ubisoft have been going down a very unethical and natural path where all their games share too much in common with predecessors. Gone are the days where we are able to observe technical achievements from game-to-game but in retrospect if games had three-year development cycles the games would still be fresh to the consumers. Yearly releases are bad ideas for many reasons, but Ubisoft need to tread very carefully with forthcoming releases.
Is the game value for money? Well yes. Provided you are happy putting some effort into the games side-content you can get about $1 to the hour of the on-release price and that's great value. 50 hours and completing all I want from the game, I am happy with that, as most games I don't play this long.
A lot of effort has gone into the things in the game, but all of that can be virtually un-noticeable if you can't appreciate it. It features I think three individual languages, one which has two dialects and two separate languages. There's also the work to create a world that from what professionals in the field can work out to be accurate. There has been work done into the weaponry, animal behavior, animal variety and all. The background work into this game really is solid.
Favourite moments include the master beast hunts, the beauty of the diversity of the world including the Aurora Borealis, exploring in general was far more fun than the campaign itself. The first time coming across a sabre-tooth tiger was a truly memorable battle! I also loved the fact all locations were available to the player instead of locking off certain areas like they've done in previous releases. It was quite a nice game all round.
What I didn't like, was the inconsistent performance which eventually worked itself out. There's the lackluster campaign, murdering Ull was damned easy on hard difficulty, Batari was more challenging having died a handful of times but easy nonetheless and this could be said for pretty much the whole game.
All in all, it's a great game. Unfortunately people simply aren't happy because of the really short development cycle and this is prone to destruction and a degradation of trust between the publisher and the consumers. I said it for Far Cry 4 and I'll say it again: Ubisoft need to be careful because they could potentially lose a huge quantity of their consumer-base.

They took the best parts of the Far Cry series, the hunting and crafting and exploration and environment, and built the game around those things as the primary focus. Unfortunately, the game is published by Ubisoft, who sneer at Valve's radical concept of "let people play the games that they paid for".  Far Cry Primal just recently received an update.  Work had kept me busy, but it's Saturday and I wanted to try it out and see what they've changed.  So I open Far Cry via Steam, and I get an error message saying that they couldn't sync my achievements with the Cloud.  There's a retry button, but two retries gave the same result, so I just hit "skip".  Then there was some sort of error message about sound not working, and the game exited before it could load up.  Ok, fair enough, maybe I need to update something on my end, but lemme try one more time.  This time when I try to run Far Cry Primal, I get an error saying that Ubisoft has suspended my account due to multiple login attempts.
Yes, Ubisoft has decided not to allow me to play a game that I paid for, because I had trouble launching the game that I paid for, as a result of an upgrade to the game that I paid for.  Oh, and any of their other games that I have paid for as well, since it's my entire account that is suspended.
It sucks, because I really love this game, and I've played FC3 and FC4 through twice each (well over 100 hours logged in each one according to Steam).  I pre-purchased FC Primal.  I won't make that mistake again.  Don't make the same mistake I did.  Ubisoft has a history of pulling stuff like this, but it's the first time I've experienced it firsthand. My most recent game is telling the great tale of an Irish solider known as Private First Class Bryan Murphy. He seems to be quite remarkable in the sense that he misses all his 40% - 90% shots and I can only assume that this is because he is a financially deprived alcoholic who left his kids to join XCOM and is too drunk to shoot. Although he makes incredible game changing 10%-20% chance to hit shots all the time. Needless to say, I warmed to him immediately and I literally think he has a hidden 'luck of the irish' perk or a four leaf clover stowed away somewhere.
Bryan Murphy is the only reason I am continuing to play my current playthrough and that is because of his rather magical ability to save soldiers he considers more important than him. However this is not the case. For this reason I am seriously considering spending vast amount of XCOM savings to put Bryan Murphy through officer's school. Hopefully this would boost his self esteem long enough for him to agree to a rehab program I have set up in base to help recovering substance abusers better themselves.  As a commander I am seriously concerned for his well being.
Come christmas time, I always give my soldiers a christmas bonus to raise their morale. I even take days off when the alien threat is minimal to go out and help my troops buy quality presents at excellent prices. Due to Bryan Murphy's drinking habits I personally took the liberty of visiting his loved ones and shopping on Bryan's behalf incase he was too intoxicated to remember to do so himself.
Despite a shady origin and troubled personal life, Bryan is a hardworking member of XCOM and is always ready to take on new challenges on the battlefield. He has distinguished himself amoung his peers as a good guy to watch your back. Whenever I want to test experimental weapons, armour or genetic alterations, Bryan is first in line to get to grips with the new equipment. Should the day come where Bryan wishes to leave the military and seek purpose elsewhere I give my absolute recommendation and can asure potential employers that he will receive flawless references from the XCOM project.
TL;DR XCOM: Enemy Unknown makes you care for your soldiers
10/10

Being a Saints Row 3 fan, upon looking at the trailers and previews of this game, I felt dissapointed from seeing the same exact Steelport city from the previous game. I heard plenty of rumors of it being a game that was originally designed as a DLC for Saints Row 3, but just too big to fit into one single DLC. Boy was I wrong. Even though the same city is used, Saints Row IV allows you to experience Steelport like never before, with the superpowers of jumping stories high and running faster than any car can ever go. I believe this game is the best sandbox/open world(more like open city) exploration made to date. Every moment gliding through this city brings me back to my childhood days of playing Ultimate Spider-Man on the gamecube. The game constantly references other video games in history from starfox-64, to Deus Ex Machina, to Metal Gear Solid, and so on! While taking inspiration from some of these games, the game doesn't lose it's own unique Saints Row identity. Its this very same identity that made me keep playing it for hours on end!
The game itself (on normal difficulty keep in mind) is never too difficult to handle, but also never to easy, presenting its challenges every to often. I constantly wanted to collect more and complete more quests, giving me more abilities and customization. This is one game, that I might even attempt to 100%. It just makes me want to unlock more and more, so I can experience the game when I achieve its full potential it has to offer. Having bought the "Game of the Century" Edition of the game while it was extremely cheap on the humble store, I was given all of the DLC. Having this I can say that some of the weapons and vehicles you get from the DLC, are really OP, alleviating the difficulty of the game at times when needed. Other DLC provided comical outfits and weapons, and other incredibly cool looking customizations. Even without the DLC, the humor with weapons in this game, has far surpassed its superior.
One thing that Saints 4 did much better than Saints 3, was that it referenced Saints Row 1, 2, and 3, linking the storylines together in a way that made the game flow much better. The story/plot of the game specifically, I will admit is kind of a hilariously ridiculous one, but fans of the previous game will be used to it and enjoy it immensly. My absolute favorite thing about this game is the soundtrack. From start to finish, the scripted music during the missions and parts of the story are hilarious and perfect for each situation. From a car singalong with Pierce of Paula Abdul's "Opposites Attract" to your character doing a striptease to Robert Palmer's "Simply Irresistible", this games soundtrack is one of the most enjoyable things I found about it. Literally from the very start to the ending of the game, there are hilarious moments like this.
The only thing I found to be upsetting about this game, was the irrelevant feature of Vehicle storage and customization garages. I'm guessing it was purely included for fans of the last game, but you never really use vehicles, as a means of getting around the city, once you unlock super-speed and super-jumps. In the end, I think that players and fans of Saints Row 3 will enjoy Saints 4 game 10X more than its predecessor.  Though this doesn't mean that those who have never heard of or played the series won't enjoy it. It's a blast of fun, humor and pure ridiculousness.

Bobby "Got'em" Garcia was born.
he started as a rookie within a squadron of three similar soldiers; young recruits that all showed incredible combat potential. their first mission as a squadron was to investigate a crashed ufo, downed over the coasts of japan. he was nervous, no doubt, but he was well-prepared. all of his training, the expectations of everyone, the dependance of his squadron - it was weighing heavily on his mind. but Bobby "Got'em" Garcia knew that this mission would be far from his last.
the three others laid on the cold soil, all life drained from their faces. two sectoids were hiding behind the dismantled walls of the alien spacecraft. Bobby was completely and utterly alone. he had mere seconds to react the alien's shots and movements, as they were approaching increasingly quickly. he had to think of a plan - fast. suddenly, it occured to Bobby "Got'em" Garcia that he hadn't used his fragmentation grenade. it still hung from his belt loop, pin unpulled. Garcia waited until the exact moment where the sectoids stood closest to each other, pulled the pin, and heaved it with a perfect amount of force. as the grenade exploded, the only noise audible was the dying screams of the aliens as xcom central radioed in.
"bobby, there aren't any other life forms detected. ready to head home?"
"... yes."
Bobby "Got'em" Garcia lived up to his nickname that day, but he left with the knowledge that he let his squadron down. he couldn't save his allies in the heat of battle. the odds were against him, of course - it was a 45% shot on every alien in sight. nonetheless, Bobby vowed that he wouldn't leave any more men behind.
a month passes by. To preface this, I won this on
Tower Wars is a fast paced tower defense game that pits you against other players (or bots), and you get to send waves of enemies from your own tower to defeat theirs.  As far as I can tell build order is a huge player in this and it seems like a ton of micro is what is needed to play this game at higher levels.
Aside from that, it seems the core of the game is based on the multiplayer aspects of the game.  This is a big issue as I played this close to 5 years after it came out... there isn't much of a player base anymore.  This is a tad bit upsetting as I think the game would be fun against similar skilled opponents.
I do have to profess I am terrible at the game, it mostly had to deal with time played.  If I spent more time in the game I could start to understand the build orders and such better, but there in lies my issue with the game as whole... it seemed focused on that which leaves me thinking it's core gameplay misses the mark for me.  It seems it is deterministic in play, which doesn't allow players variety that I think we all crave.
I like the concept overall and can see the potential in it.  However, I think it currently suffers from a lack of built in community and from some flaws in the core gameplay.  I would give it a 2/5, but would recommend it if you have a friend that just wants to play a Tower Defense game with you.  But it would have to be a fairly heavy discount.

I just finished playing some of the content of t his game. So far I've gotten to the third area (undead part of the game). I think that this game has the base of a really nice beatem up.
Graphics:
Characters: Visual Fidelity isn't everything in a video game. You can make a game that has a strong appeal by having your own unique visual style by using higher quality illustrations to represent your graphics. I understand that the characters were made in a way to make them easy to mix and match elements but the problem is that the graphics are being done were on the far side of easy and the end result is that the characters look very generic as a result. Had I been the one making the decisions I would have looked to characters that  are somewhat super deformed so I could do some mixing and matching with some elements and at the same time offer more quality. (think metal assault).
Animations: I would have also made the attack animations have more of a z depth. Again, I totally understand that the idea to make the animations very horizontal and verticle were by design. They were probably a cost measure as well because it would be a lot easier to create. The problem is that people buy things that look good even if they don't pay a lot of money for it. If it doesn't look awesome that's going to be a problem.
Equpment: The weapons are also hit or miss in terms of how they are illustrated. Everytime someone finds a new item it should not only make them excited by what stats are on the item, they should also be excited by how it looks. They should feel awesome when they see it. You have some weapons like the two handed sword that looks like the blade is made of stone that looks great. Then in the same breath,  you have items like the spears which look sub par.
Enemies: Like the games equpment these are hit and miss to. You have some enemies like the skeletons in the third level that look good, then you have the goblins in the first level who look subpar. I get that gobins should be diminiutive creatures but they just aren't drawn very well. The same could be said for the evil ants in the first or second level as well.
Backgrounds: The backgrounds for the levels are hit and miss but they surpisingly the better part of the games visuals. For instance, one of your screen shots has a nice looking wall with textures on it that has three alters in the middle of the room. That looks pretty good. Then you have some areas in the game(like the screen shot with the goblin tank boss) where the ball looks way to samy through the whole screen. I would recomend using larger tile sets that have "groups" of bricks togather. You should also create less division between each break in specific random areas of the wall. You should also look into discoloring the books in spots to or even have random diles where a coupble of the bricks are sticking out. This is going to have the effect of the walls to not look they are some sort of pattern, even though your using the same assets. If could also changed the lighting in different areas of the same level to create some visual interest.
Gameplay: I like the actual premise of the game. It feel like Rogue Legacy meets Castle Crashers, Having the different weapon types have a special move is a good touch. Hitting multiple enemies in one swing with some melee weapons make the game feel more enjoyable. You feel ilke a touch warrior.
Skill Tree System. If your going to have a blacksmith skill tree that focuses on melee combat there should be talents that you can select that are weapon specific. I know that it's early access it's something to keep in mind. That goes the same for the other two skill tee categories.
Finally, to say again what I said at the beginning, this game has the base of a really good beatem up. To generate some real attention the visuals need some reskinning as well as the other things I mentioned here. Good Luck.

Polished and seemingly brilliant for the first couple of plays, however , there are two types of roguelikes available to play right now, one is the skill based kind, where if you die, it's mostly your fault. These are good roguelikes.  Then there are roguelikes like FTL where luck is more important than any level of skill, these roguelikes are bad, no matter how well designed they seem on the surface.
The sheer number of random co-incidences that need to align perfectly to have any chance of successfully completing a game is rediculous, no matter how well you equip your ship and plan your strategy, one single broken encounter can ruin a hitherto flawless run.

This game is a dark fantasy RPG to it's
and I LOVE IT! Like... down to weapons actually taking up space instead of weight in your inventory. Sometimes I feel like the progression is too slow between investing in core stats (+stats and required to advance you down skill tree), passive abilities, and active skills. But that being said you can make a vast array of different builds and I've had lots of fun experimenting with what I can do. The fights are genuinely challenging at time, often forcing you to use health potions if you come in unprepared, and the dungeons are brutally long but fun.
The world is absolutely massive and while only a few select areas feel repetitive you can always find something interesting in each area. Additionally travel is easy as you use a fixed portal system, basically meaning you can teleport from anywhere to certain points on the map. I personally like the fact Grim Dawn expands on this by allowing you to return to the point you teleported from via a fixed location portal.
The loot system feels fantastic and balanced, never giving you a deluge of weapons and armor to sort through but making you feel like you've earned a lot. You will also receive a weapon/armor piece that is just blasted awesome rarely but you don't feel cheated or like it's necessary to grind. And of course half the items you receive have interesting names. I know it seems like I'm digging deep but you when come across the
(made-up example) you have a moment of "sweet!" even if it's not actually that good.
I won't say anything about the story as to avoid spoilers but it starts off strong and stay strongs through what you might consider the first 'act'. It does drop off in the second but picks right back up in the third (even eventually allowing you to pick between two factions) and I haven't gotten further than that. As for the content of the story itself: I like it. I really like the direction they took with it.
Grim Dawn really is just a refreshing RPG experience and this is coming from a guy who really doesn't care for many RPGS and definitely not MMORPG's. I'm going to give this a solid 9/10 for RPG fans and 7.5-8/10 for those who aren't. I'm also giving it the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Seal of Approval for dickish characters you relish killing and tough boss fights.

You might've seen hate about this game, but don't let that fool you. Most of that negativety are from people who wish to justify why the MMO they're playing is the best/better one instead of investing time into BDO. To each their own, but this game is a masterfully well done.
Every game has its flaws; in the case of BDO, confusion may arouse in certain aspects of the game such as NPC amity gain through conversation or how exactly 'failstacks' work. (You'll find out how important they are once you start enhancing) Despite these occasional lapses in quality, the developers, PearlAbyss, are attempting to localise Korean content as fast as possible, meaning certain parts will be missed or looked over due to the wishes of most players wanting to keep up to date with their Korean counterparts. If you can overlook these minor flawss - as there are plenty of guides readily avaliable online - BDO is by far one of the most extensive, interesting and enjoyable MMO's you can find on the market today.
Being a sandbox, there's one trait BDO emphasises: freedom. Freedom to do whatever you want whenever you want. Don't want to follow the questline? Screw it, run off to the oppposite side of the map and start grinding. Don't want to level up? Do contribution quests, earns you all the essentials of the game aside from levels. The main point I'm trying to grind home here is unlike conventional MMORPG's, where it's simple cliched 'follow this questline and receive this' or 'must do this quest before you can do this', BDO is without boundaries. (Aside from the world map, of course) The only exception I think of to this rule is reaching level 50, where PVP is enabled and you must follow a quest to advance past level 49, which I believe is quite neat as it allows you to do some research into gameplay after 50 rather than throwing you into the deepend with PVP enabled and terrible gear, and life skill quests (life skills refer to things such as cooking, gathring, alchemy etc.) which require you do a quest to gain basic knowledge of that life skill, which seems fair enough to me - nobody starts off with the knowledge of how to do everything.
Now I know, this may be controversial, but the graphics are borderline stunning. I'm running on a Rx 580 card and with everything to max... I cannot even begin to describe the visual aesthetics and appeal of this game; for an MMO, BDO has argueably the best graphics on the market. The team behind this game paid special attention to real life physics, as this sandbox tries to mimic reality as much as possible (if you look away from the magic and what not); the horses, which are mounts you can ride, don't simply accelerate from standstill and come to a halt after going at mach 1 without giving an inch, they actually take time to accelerate and if coming to a sudden halt at higher acceleration, you will see a skidding animation. This may turn some players off due to them liking instand accel and decel, but for me this only added to the visual and aesthetic appeal and it's good to know the team behind the game is trying their best to make MMO not so far-fetched that we feel completely detached from it after 3 hours of gameplay.
Now for the important part, which I'm sure many of you would like to know: the grind. How is BDO's grind? Well, it's a Korean game, and as far as I can tell, they like their grinds. Sorry, but that's the way it is. Although localised, it's based off the Korean MMO genre, which favours grinds and long hauls before achieving end game goals. Now don't get me wrong, it's not a month grind to get from level 1 to 50 (Which is where the adventure really begins, as this is when you can start PVPing in the open and 'awakening', a special second class of sorts, unlocks at 56), in all sinceriting it takes a couple hours of grinding if you know what you're doing to speed level to 50 - but i'm assuming not all of you reading this are experts in the game before playing it. Strictly following the black spirit's quests, which is the guide you get in the game, you can reach 50 in 1 week if you put in around 2-3 hours of playtime per day. Of course, this estimation can vary in length depending on how speedy you are.
Still hesitant about buying the game? Worse case scenario, you'll get a good 30 hours of entertainment out of it, and for the low price of $10 USD is a bargain, which is more than I can say for some triple A title's out there, which can only give 12 hours of campaign content at $50 or above, and they don't always entertain. If you already have it and are deciding whether or not to invest your time into it, I say give it a try. You never know what you could be missing out on, and trialling for 1 hour is literally nothing. Chances are, you'll be addicted before you know it.

So I feel I need to explain where I'm coming from before I express my views on this game. I have never liked this style of game. The third person, overhead, action RPGs where you click on enemies and the character runs over and hits them. I've always felt that PC classics like Diablo 2, Balder's Gate, and WoW completely disconnect the player from the experience. It doesn't feel like I am playing the character, it feels like I'm some guy telling the character what to do. Let me do the fight please! I always feel like these games would feel more rewarding if they controlled more like an isometric shooter, where it would afford more control over the player character. The games in this sub-genre also tend to be fairly padded, drawn out, and incredibly text-heavy. I get that some people love every single thing that I'm describing, and that's cool, I just don't get it. It's not for me.
However, Grim Dawn ended up sucking me in. I don't boast the incredible playtime of some other reviewers, but at thirty hours I definitely got my money's worth from the Humble Monthly Bundle that included this game. It's far from perfect, the story is dull the whole way through, I don't think I could name a single character, the ending sucks, it starts to get a bit repetitive unless you really change things up, and the side quests don't offer a whole lot of incentive to complete them.
The biggest issue is that the game doesn't teach you anything. There's supposed to be tutorial hints according to the options menu, but I'm not sure I ever got one. It took me until fifteen hours in to realize that the books I had no interest in gave experience if you right clicked on them in your inventory. The crafting system is an afterthought. It took asking friends for me to find out that the shift key will hold you in place while you fire a ranged weapon. Weapon and armour components are cool, but figuring out how they stack took a lot of trial and error.
Damn I have spent a whole lot of time complaining about this game considering it's a positive review. The thing is, this is a podcast game. This is a game where you open up YouTube, or Netflix, or some other internet media, and watch that on a second monitor while you play. It's a game to occupy your hands. Maybe at harder parts you can turn off My Brother My Brother and Me, turn the sound effects and music back on and focus, but mostly you're going to want to turn the sound down to zero.
This is the first time I have played a game in this genre for more than two hours, and it ended up being thirty. It's fun, it feels good to blast demons with my gun that shoots fireballs. It was a nice way to pass the time. If you like these games, this is a good one. If you don't, it might still convert you if you pick it up on sale, it's one of the better examples of the genre.

In a time of many games in the world, if I find a game that I feel worthy of playing, I will write a review.  Reccomending the game, is a funny thing.  I both like... and dislike this game for many reasons, but I will only reccomend a game to someone if I absolutely adore it.
The game itself plays and handles amazing.  There is a lot to do for the crafter, pvper, pvEr, or the person who just wants to play the auction house.  You can raise horses, build a boat, hunt whales, make your own garden, own a network of workers and traders.  But... the community is feral at best.  From the moment you log into Black Desert, expect to be bombarded with special phrases like "trans people are gay, and don't belong in my military," or my personal favorite,  "if I rub up against my dad in the shower, does that make me gay?"  If you choose to filter out the chat, the game becomes a ghost town of meandering Player characters doing their best NPC impressions, clogging up around key npcs, or adding to a general feel of lonesomeness, that I don't honestly like in an mmorpg.  From Goldsellers, to trolls, a vapid community isn't the only negative point on the list of hard notes that will be brought up.
I want to reccomend this game, since I love the mechanics so much, but they get repetative, and they do so shockingly fast.  Once you learn the base mechanics of combat, the game's combat system grows surprisingly stale.  Those who find catharsis in Dynasty Warriors type games will enjoy the grind, but it's a long grind.
New Players will either fight through the cluttered UI, find a means to remove all the clutter, or likely quit, as you are near to constantly harangued by every single thing that happens in game.  These things consist of blue whales appearing in a certain area, a war breaking out between two rival guilds, or almost always, the bombardment of players selling and listing items on the auction house.  Luckily, you can disable this, but disabled, should be the default.  Everything in Black Desert, is a grind.  From leveling up in combat skills, to leveling up a life skill like sailing, gathering, cooking, hunting, or even the component I found the most catharsis with, horse taming.  You can level up your  weight limit by carrying around a special backpack, your stamina meter by walking around,  your HP- by eating food, to which there are graphs upon graphs for how long these tasks will take.  Do you want your weight limit to be at maximum?  Set your toon to auto-loop carrying a back pack for 55 hours of non-stop online activity.  This is the same expected time frame for running a horse to level 30 (which you'll need multiple as there are multiple tiers of horses).   It's true, you can cut down on your active time playing this game if you "AFK grind"
or pay for the convenience to speed up some of the vicious grind.
The cash shop is... a strange bird at best.  On the one hand, there are several convenience items available such as inventory expansions, weight limit boosters, EXP boosters, horse death counter reset, horse breeding counter resets, underwear, house decorations, bank upgrade slots, boat, horse, and camel costumes, Pet auto-gatherers, even upgrades to a worker mini game that are otherwise unobtainable.  Most of these items are sellable via in game market, but will likely never appear or sell out immediately.  This said, there are in game costumes you can manufacture given the appropriate amount of time and materials (40 hours is the standard).
Respectively though, Black Desert is pretty to look at.  The world is well sculpted, even if they reuse the same NPC in certain towns repeatedly (sometimes 4 times in the same area).  The Worker placement mini game is fun and serves as a cyclical reminder of a reaching a certain point in game, but there are problems, that the Korean server of Black Dersert Online for example does not have.  Black Desert, is far from perfect.  Once you learn how to achieve maximum combat level there is a lot to do while you wait.  Pearl Abyss is good on adding new content regularly, and rewarding players, but expect to be reminded that you can pay to have things you want to work towards instead.
This game is one nicking cut after another.  Nickeling and Diming it's playerbase, as most FTPmmorpgs would, but Black Desert is not free to play.

Being a Saints Row 3 fan, upon looking at the trailers and previews of this game, I felt dissapointed from seeing the same exact Steelport city from the previous game. I heard plenty of rumors of it being a game that was originally designed as a DLC for Saints Row 3, but just too big to fit into one single DLC. Boy was I wrong. Even though the same city is used, Saints Row IV allows you to experience Steelport like never before, with the superpowers of jumping stories high and running faster than any car can ever go. I believe this game is the best sandbox/open world(more like open city) exploration made to date. Every moment gliding through this city brings me back to my childhood days of playing Ultimate Spider-Man on the gamecube. The game constantly references other video games in history from starfox-64, to Deus Ex Machina, to Metal Gear Solid, and so on! While taking inspiration from some of these games, the game doesn't lose it's own unique Saints Row identity. Its this very same identity that made me keep playing it for hours on end!
The game itself (on normal difficulty keep in mind) is never too difficult to handle, but also never to easy, presenting its challenges every to often. I constantly wanted to collect more and complete more quests, giving me more abilities and customization. This is one game, that I might even attempt to 100%. It just makes me want to unlock more and more, so I can experience the game when I achieve its full potential it has to offer. Having bought the "Game of the Century" Edition of the game while it was extremely cheap on the humble store, I was given all of the DLC. Having this I can say that some of the weapons and vehicles you get from the DLC, are really OP, alleviating the difficulty of the game at times when needed. Other DLC provided comical outfits and weapons, and other incredibly cool looking customizations. Even without the DLC, the humor with weapons in this game, has far surpassed its superior.
One thing that Saints 4 did much better than Saints 3, was that it referenced Saints Row 1, 2, and 3, linking the storylines together in a way that made the game flow much better. The story/plot of the game specifically, I will admit is kind of a hilariously ridiculous one, but fans of the previous game will be used to it and enjoy it immensly. My absolute favorite thing about this game is the soundtrack. From start to finish, the scripted music during the missions and parts of the story are hilarious and perfect for each situation. From a car singalong with Pierce of Paula Abdul's "Opposites Attract" to your character doing a striptease to Robert Palmer's "Simply Irresistible", this games soundtrack is one of the most enjoyable things I found about it. Literally from the very start to the ending of the game, there are hilarious moments like this.
The only thing I found to be upsetting about this game, was the irrelevant feature of Vehicle storage and customization garages. I'm guessing it was purely included for fans of the last game, but you never really use vehicles, as a means of getting around the city, once you unlock super-speed and super-jumps. In the end, I think that players and fans of Saints Row 3 will enjoy Saints 4 game 10X more than its predecessor.  Though this doesn't mean that those who have never heard of or played the series won't enjoy it. It's a blast of fun, humor and pure ridiculousness.

"Alan Wake's American Nightmare continues the thrilling story of the first game as Alan confronts his doppelganger, Mr. Scratch. The story takes place in Night Springs, Arizona, and throughout the game, you discover that the Dark Presence has followed Alan and it's up to the player to put the pieces together to save both the townspeople and himself.
Because this is not a full fledged sequel to Alan Wake, American Nightmare ends up reusing several assets throughout the campaign. This game also features an arcade mode, where Alan must face off against increasingly difficult enemy waves. Manuscript pages found in the campaign carry over as unlockable weapons this mode.
While being slightly more combat focused than the first game, American Nightmare continues Alan's struggle against the Taken and his steps into writing his perfect ending."

This game wasn't the most terrible game I ever played. However, it has a lot of glaring flaws in how it was designed.
First you aren't given enough money to begin with to really implement any real strategy. So it becomes a race between either making sure your enemy never gets a single minion through or sending as many through as possible and winning before your enemy does with minimal defenses.
The defenses also are not well designed at all. They only work well all used together meaning there are points in a match that feel slow because of this. Not only that but the defenses just feel weak overall. As opposed to the mod this game was based on, The WC3 map Tower Wars.
Everything in the game is in between either being too cheap or too expensive. Getting more income should always be devilishly expensive because it is basically their version of upgrading your tier like in most RTS. It is just too cheap in this game. Meanwhile some upgrades are either too cheap or too expensive. Which leads to totally unfair advantages during the mid point of the game. With no real way to win in a realistic amount of time for a long game.
Honestly the game would be much better if they only balanced it better as most of the problems I have with it is just the balance. The game has too much depth in areas too. The game should be a little more simple. Like there is no need to upgrade specific troops in stats, if you can already upgrade all troops in the game in a seperate menu. Instead they should have maybe had 3 levels or so, and unlock abilities instead.
The progression of tiering up your sends should be much longer too, so that weaker sends have a point to them. Towers and Sends should all be much stronger as well so it is actually fun playing the game. Towers need much more depth to them as well as having customizable tiers for defense only make sense if the sends can be. The Towers don't even feel like they are from the same game.
These are all the problems the game has and the only real upside I can give it is that it is fun to play once in a while with friends. However, once you both learn the meta of the game it can get really boring.

I'll be honest, I don't play a lot of large scale simulators.  But Tropico 4 was awesome and addicting for many reasons.
Variation of avatar: lots of different bonuses/debuffs depending on which you choose (communist, installed by USA, war hero, kleptomaniac, etc)

Lost Castle is an excellent game.  I recommend this game to anyone that likes
beat-em-ups with some RPG elements.
The gameplay is very solid at the moment, I haven't ran into any issues yet.
What makes this game great is the class system, combat, and level design.  The classes are bound to the weapons with their own skillset, for example, if you picked up a staff you are in essence a mage/wizard; you get to shoot magical energy. Or if you picked up a bow you are now an archer, or dual daggers then you are a rogue, etc..there are a lot of different weapons in the game, I haven't found them all, but am really excited to try them all out. Combat is fairly fluid, doesn't feel too "laggy" or "delay-ey".
Also each weapon has their own signature move and can vary. For example, if you picked up a great sword your special can be a earth shattering move which hits enemies in a line or it can be a charged dashed moving that pierces your opponent. And weapons have their own stats, so one might be better suited for defense while the other is better for offense..
There are different armor pieces that you can pick up that can change your character appearance and give different stats.
With this permadeath system there are some permanent features.  You have a skill tree where you can purchase passives that improve your character and these stay permanent even after you die and start over.  There is also an account/save slot level that you can gain, max is level 30.  I'm not really sure what character level does for you, but it is in the achievements.
The levels are somewhat randomized, I haven't died enough yet to see them all, but there isn't much of a variety in tilesets at the moment. Also there are different settings and enemy types which is awesome because you don't feel you're playing the same level over and over, it is refreshing. I mean if you play the game enough times then it might get to you, but as a new player it is very welcoming.
You also have item picks that you can use during your game, such as bombs and daggers.  You also have items that give passive effects such as increased damage, health, or special attacks.  Then you got your standard healing items such as an apple and banana.
The game is currently local co-op,
when the game leaves early access.  So I would wait to purchase this if you want online co-op.
I must note that the sound quality is not so great currently, sounds "watered-down" almost.  This will be updated though during early access as stated on the page.
Overall my experience has been a great one and will continue to keep playing.  I definitely see this as one of my games that I rotate through.  The current price is worth it, you will definitely get your moneys worth.  I hope this review helps you decide to purchase this game or not.
I will update my review as major updates get released.

I'm new to the Tropico series but have played other real-time simulation games like SimCity and Caesar (the latter of which appears to be the closest parallel to Tropico in my gaming experience).  I'm now eight boards into the campaign and have figured some things out.  As other reviewers have pointed out, the game is very difficult to lose, but it can be challenging for a new player to determine why their city isn't growing as fast as they'd hope or why certain problems persist (certain buildings constantly lack for workers, etc.).  The truth is that despite the slapstick banana-republic-tinpot-autocrat gloss of the game, this is actually a surprisingly deep simulation, and the game will throw a lot of information at you that is easy to lose sight of but important to keep track of.  Build-and-forget does not work.  Even the soil quality or climate of parts of the island can change, meaning that a zone that was ideal for farming a particular crop at the start of the game may not stay that way.
The most frustrating thing about the game is traffic management.  Most specifically, your tinpot dictator and his (or her) crack team of mad scientists and engineers might be able to build a nuclear program or an airport, but are congenitally incapable of building a four-lane road.  (One wonders how the planes land if Tropico's scientific community is so deep in its principled opposition to wide stretches of asphalt or concrete.)  There are also occasional graphical glitches and stability issues, but nothing too frequent or catastrophic on my 2008-vintage PC.
A solid title and worth the price, especially on a Steam sale.

Greyfox I found to be memorable in it's delivery, and stood out in it's attempt to tackle some uncomfortable subject matter not often spoken of in the day to day, never mind a game world based on real life.
Pros:
+  Encourages exploration
+  Enjoyable to play through the story at least once
+  Makes you think about stuff
+  Music is atmospheric and fits the setting
+  Characters are just developed enough to be engaging
+  The environments and people in them seemed fairly realistic, and alluded to real world issues like elder abuse, familial drama/estrangement, and...  hoarding cats, I suppose?
+  Life or Death decisions change the way the ending plays out
+  Has a wittiness at times, and more mature jokes (nothing super racy)
+  You get bang for your buck if you catch it on sale
Neutrals/Cons:
-  Linear in design, with some flexibility for trying out new things
-  Short, which doesn't leave as much room for development
-  Haven't played an RPG Maker game before, but the contrast between the "hand-drawn" and "pulled" sprites was pretty noticeable I guess? Also, the pointy-eared/elven priest dude kinda broke my immersion
-  Could have had a bit more closure on the protagonist's life following their ending
Overall:
7.5  to 8 out of 10
Greyfox I would say is a game that is more about the experience than it is about gameplay, which is a key element in point-and-click adventures. It is not pretentious like some Indie games out there, and really tries to do something different...  an aspect certain gamers may appreciate more than others.

Dark Heritage: Guardians of Hope, is a HOPA* game, developed by World Loom and published by Artifex Mundi.
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is well done.
There is some real live scenes for the most part of the game. It certainly does fit well with the non real live scenes.
The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only two difficulty game modes to choose from: Regular and Expert.
Diary Notebook it keep tracks of the story events and objectives. It isn't given automatically at the start of the game.
The inventory panel is stationary. No option for making it non stationary.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations. It's not given automatically at the start of the game.
Most of the game's hidden object scenes consists of traditional word lists, find "X" amount with some or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairy easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them.
There's a medallion that given to the individual player but not at the start of the game. But this medallion isn't fully completed. The medallion parts needed be found and place into their insets.
There are at least nine collectible scrolls in total. They're spread through out the game to find.
There are twenty-five different achievements. Only six of these achievement are a secret. But each of these achievements has certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
Since this game is a collector's edition, the bonus chapter, it's a sequel the main story; it can be accessed when the main story it's completed.
Even though this is a collector's edition doesn't have the extra contents that it usually does have. With the exception of the game's concept arts and achievements that is found under "More Info" in main splash page.
There are total of six different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Although Company of Heroes 2 is alot of fun as long as you liked vanilla CoH, you can't help but be disappointed if you are used to play with absolutely brilliant CoH1-mods. This is not the fault of the game, because going back to vanilla CoH will be almost equally as painful after playing the famous Blitzkrieg-mod (for example) literally dozens of hours. The SP-/ CoOp-content is awesome and will keep you busy quite some time, as long as you like AI Skirmishes. The devs truly deserve some credit for diversifying the overall content. Now you get CoOp-Scenarios and Defense-Missions in addition to the usual campaing and SP-missions. However so far only 1/4 additional-content bundles is free of charge, so without purchasing the other dlc, there aren't that many additional missions afterall.
To sum it up: If you liked vanilla CoH1, or are new to the series but enjoy quick and action-packed arcade-like strategy, this game is for you. However, how much you want to pay for it and if the additional content is worth a hefty price to you, is for you to decide.
Me personally, although enjoying CoH2 alot at the momenent, I will still play and go back to the CoH1 Blitzkrieg-mod from time to time. Don't compare CoH2 with modded CoH1 versions or your doomed to be disappointed.

It’s an absolutely marvelous world that I love. Its dark and of course Grim, it’s full of detail and texture. Plenty of variety as you travel through Victorian nightmare to underground caves and insect hives. Then blink in the sunlight as the second act pushes all that aside to randomly be about cowboys instead. Environmental touches are everywhere, completely selling the idea that this is a fallen land past any chance of actually saving. The abandoned villages and the crumbling walls of dungeons or the sadistic experiments in Warden's sickly green laboratory.
Exploring it is a smooth and epic-feeling experience that regularly demands long treks through enemy territory to get to the next boss or quest objective. Just about every path is scattered with both big combat engagements and dungeons to dip into for an extra boss fight and bonus loot.
Gathering loot is a cornerstone of the genre. Those junk items are worth so little compared to the cost of buying a health potion that it never feels satisfying to sell. It’s usually usable gear like swords and shields like the one you’re currently using. This makes it a real pain to sort through in search of worthwhile upgrades and gear to hold onto. Going back to town is at least painless, with a free Rift Travel spell that puts you right next to a shopkeeper and a portal back to where you just left. You can at least set the screen to only show that loot in the first place.
Magic in particular quickly steps up from a few basic sparks to screen-filling pyrotechnics, with fire-strikes turning into full explosions and what are meant to be simple lightning-based stun effects packing enough punch to not just kill enemies outright, but send them flying across the scenery as if literally dismissed as unworthy to fight for real.
Spirit or for some people Mana, is well balanced to let you cut loose with these abilities on a constant basis. Each Mastery has a powerful set to choose from, though upgrading them and unlocking new skills has to be balanced with leveling up passive increases that help provide the stats needed to wield better gear and keep up with the monster curve.
Plot is there if you want it though, in the occasional lore text and conversations with friends and villains, and I did like the slow building up of the town of Devil’s Crossing from a town of survivors basically sitting back and anticipating death to actually being a small community with a chance. The acts also unfold out to provide plenty of different scenery as you cross the huge world. Huge to the extent that even early quests to a neighboring town feel like small odysseys which are littered with bonus dungeons of every size, including special challenge ones that disable rift travel and make the only way out either victory or death.

Artifex Mundi's published games have always impressed me. What about this one? Unfortunately, not so much.
Puzzles and hidden objects scenes are fine. Graphics are great. Music is great. so what's there to complain about? For one, it's a game full of glitches and crashes constantly. As if glitches weren't enough by themselves, crashing can cause glitch in your gameplay. In turn, you must restart the entire gameplay(not just reboot) to complete it.
The real actors themselves were an interesting addition to the game, but the lack of expressions in the actors did not support the feel of the story in game which in turn only made it redundant and draggy to watch. Acting for the cutscenes were barely mediocre. However, the blending of real actors into the game scenes were fine, even if every single one of them suffered from dementia and that my arrival to the island became their panacea.
The story puzzles me, greatly. For one, it is not attention grabbing and I soon find myself losing interest of the story, only to advance through the game for the standard hidden object game mechanics. I frequently find myself lost in the attempt to understand the story as certain events that teaches you about the story triggers at an awkward time that made no sense and confused me. Sure, they all fall into place once you reach the end. The flow of events are there to guide but hardly concrete enough to form a good story. It simply feels like a mish-mash of words and pictures then characters to guide you through disorganized story sketches and the usual puzzles available in these games.
On sale, in bundles, maybe I'd recommend. Full price? Hardly. It's a half-solid game for hidden object lovers, and a decent one at least. Only half-solid because I'll never get over my frustration on the amount of crashes and bugs this game has that were not fixed nor addressed by the developer or publisher. So no, I'd not recommend it.

BDO has a lot of potential that generally falls short. The character generator is fun, but your options are limited based on your class. For example, if you play an archer you have to be female. Certain hairstyles aren't available for certain classes. The pre-generated faces are race specific (ex. Valkyrie faces are all Asian, Warrior faces are all Caucasian). Generally you can make your character look any race but it will take some work. You can also select appearances other people have made in the beauty album, which is really helpful. But I found it impossible to replicate the face of my dark knight on an archer. So you are definitely limited to some degree. There are also only about 6 different in-game clothing styles for each class and you can't mix and match the tops and pants so there isn't a lot of variety when it comes to customizing your outfit.
There's a lot to do in this game, which is great, but some of the mini games could be more fun and feel more natural. With the fishing mini game you have to push the space bar at the right time then type the letters that appear on your screen before the time runs out. It gets redundant and doesn't make much sense either. It would be more fun if you could see the types of fish you can catch in the actual water and then tug the line around and fight to reel them in. Instead, the fish you catch seems mostly random. You're basically encouraged to afk fish from what I've seen.
I'd say 80% of the playerbase is typically afk while online. They fish afk, ride horses around afk, walk around with backpacks afk to increase stats. Players also love afk clustering around the marketplace and storage, which makes it difficult to click the important npcs. The mass amounts of afkers may slow your computer down and make it take forever to load certain areas. Most frustratingly, you're forced to summon some boss monsters in these "abandoned" areas that are flooded with afk fishers.
The combat system is really fun, but I find PvE boring because the ai isn't exceptionally fantastic. I dart around and destroy everything on the screen using two combos. Tera's big♥♥♥♥♥monsters were a billion times more fun to fight. You actually had to use some tactics and effort to take those things down. Whereas BDO encourages the player to stay within their level range where the enemies die much quicker and are way less challenging. I got this game to play with friends but it honestly never feels like I need help with anything, so I'm hoping to find some other team-friendly activities if I keep playing.
Another frustrating thing is that the main quest is way too easy. Especially if you spend an hour or two grinding to test the combat. The NPCs will be sending you to swat gnats when you can destroy dragons. And you better complete those quests because they reward you with much-needed inventory space and combat exp.
All that said, it is a beautiful game with tons of promise. You can build ships and explore islands, you can catch and race horses, etc. If you get bored doing one thing, like grinding, you can easily switch over to questing, fishing, exploring, and so on. Most of the content isn't level locked, so you're not forced to grind endlessly before you can start doing other things which is really nice. So I'm still giving the game a chance because I want to try out some of these features and see what the late-game has to offer. According to most players, the game gets better with time.

People often say the price of something reflects its quality. I find that for the most part true, I mean Steam has a lot of crappy free to play games (*cough!* Spiral Knights *cough!*) but eventually you find ones worth your time. But if you want a game that will guarantee you a bit more enjoyment, premium games probably is where you will want to go. Poker Night at the Inventory is currently the first of three non-free to play games that I own and will review. So without anything else to say, let’s go!
This game has a bland plot, but it’s better than nothing. The Inventory is an illegal gambling lounge founded in 1919 Mr. Kent after a draft of the 18th Amendment. Who or what is he? We’re never told. In the opening sequence we (the guy in the game) go down an elevator into the Inventory and this short dude with an admiral’s cap (Wikipedia says it’s Reginald Van Winslow, former captain of the Screaming Narwhal)comes recognizes us a noob. He leads us downstairs to a poker table. Playing is Heavy Weapons Guy from Team Fortress 2, Tycho from Penny Arcade comics, Strong Bad from Homestar Runner and Max from the Sam & Max games. The four let you into their game of no-limit Texas Hold ‘Em with stakes of $10, 000. Since no one seems to care that they are betting 10 grand, the game starts!
Now into the game play. And...Its poker, what more is there to be said? Maybe the fact that during play characters will out of nowhere break into conversations and that are hilarious! The Heavy talking about TF2 game play and Max’s nonstop references to detective games in an innocent way. The more you go into the game, the more stuff you will unlock. There are minor differences like the cards and table icons changing to getting weapons for Team Fortress 2. At the beginning of some rounds, one of the characters will be broke and will put in a weapon to pay their fee. Knock them out and you will get their weapon. The Heavy has the Iron Curtain (minigun), Max has the Crimestopper Combo (Lugermorph – pistol and Licence to Maim - cosmetic), Strong Bad has the Dangeresque, Too? (cosmetic) and Tycho has the Enthusiast’s timepiece. After unlocking them, they will be yours to use in TF2.
Aesthetically speaking, this game is not bad in terms of visuals. There are no glaring visual problems, but Steam has a lot prettier games. The music is all right, but not catchy.
Poker Night at the Inventory is a good time in action, but is it for everyone? No. This game should be good for fans of Team Fortress 2, since playing will eventually have you starting to unlock new stuff. But for the 100 of you that don’t have Team Fortress 2, This is just another poker simulator. If you don’t care about the fancy stuff and just want to play Texas Hold ‘Em, find a poker game somewhere else because Poker Night at the Inventory simply won’t cater to you.
My final verdict is that this game is great for its price, but for people seeking a proper poker simulator, there’s nothing to see here.

A RTS game with new graphics and great cinematics, but the gameplay from XX century!
First of all, I want to admit I am a huge fan of RTS game. I have started playing them since I was a kid who was gifted with Age of Empires game. So, I found Grey Goo on the discount and bought it.
I wanted to feel new experience playing this game. While writing this review I suppose my wishes wasn't fulfilled.
Before starting the first mission I was watching a great cinematic. IT was really awesome with nice graphics and voice acting. This is the major positive part of the game. You will a cinematic between each mission. It's there a negative sides of the game come.
The gameplay is extremely boring. It feels and plays as RTS games from 20 century. Looks like the developers didn't want to change anything. You have a main base, you build some factories to gather resources, you build factories, you make a big army, you eliminate the enemy. Yeah, it was really cool in Dune in 1995 year or in Warcraft II, but in 2015 it's absolutely boring. Even in Warcraft III of 2003 years, missions has much more diversity between races and missions variety.
Each mission you start with 1000 resources, you build a refinery which takes 30 seconds. When you wait 1 minute to gather resources for another refinery, then you build it again. When you build factory, silo, tank attachment and etc. It will take up to total 10 minutes, when you do nothing expect of watching how you collect and spend resources. And it happens in the each missions. Just waste of time.
Let's speak about battle part. There are 3 playable races. Each has  ground units and 3 air units. Really? Just 10 units per race? Is it joke? OK, what are the differences? Emm... damage/attack speed/cost is changing. What's all. Absolutely. No amazing abilities, no interesting mechanics. Thy just shoot with different projectiles..I remind you the game is from 2015 year.
OK. We have poor diversity of units and.... the game balance is poor too. I passed first campaign with 7 missions just using only one unit. Just mass this unit and send the army to kill everything. New mission starts, build refinery, build 10 factories, wait 15 minutes before army of 20-30 predators come, then destroy everything. New mission, repeat again.
Ok developers. It's not a strategy game. The player doesn't find the best tactic in missions. It's a city builder game... no.. it's army builder game. Make an army and win the mission.
Pros
- Amazing cinematics between each missions with good voice acting
- Epic units are really epic
Cons
- RTS mechanic from XX century, which is pretty boring in 2017
- Very slow game with no speed up setting.
- The balance of units is bad. You can pass whole campaign using only 1 unit type.
- Expensive game. SCII has much more content whic is much more funnier and it's cheaper by half.
I can't recommend this game because it was much more pleasant for me to just watch all cinematics from the game on YouTube then actually playing the game. Tedious building  with really slow paced battle gameplay took any wishes away to play the second chapter of the campaign  from me .
If you liked old RTS games with slow and monotonous gameplay. You will probably find this game fun. Anyway, it doesn't cost a full price, buy it with at least 66% discount.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is one of the most atmospheric and immersive video games I've ever played. The story is a dark, twisted, sinister-like fantasy all wrapped up in a strong narrative by yours truly, The Champion of Light, Alan Wake.
To tell you a little bit about the developer, Remedy, they brought us the classic video games like Max Payne 1 and 2. Inventive storytelling, with a dark tonality. Alan Wake's American Nightmare might not pose any scares like the original Alan Wake, but it's such a well-polished PC port that I can't help but acknowledge Remedy for doing such a wonderful job.
The graphics feature high-resolution, and high-res textures, making the Xbox 360 version pale in comparison. I remember vividly playing the original Alan Wake on the Xbox 360 and the difference is like night and day. Although, I have no regrets about buying the original Alan Wake on the Xbox 360 because it went towards supporting such a great developer, and now we have American Nightmare. The visuals are clean and crisp. I think I took over 100 screenshots in my first 2-3 hours of gameplay. I couldn't help but stop to look at the surroundings and environments. The lighting and shadows are incredible. It's a beautiful game.
Excellent story, narrative, atmosphere, immersion, and being one of the top 10 best PC-ported video games on the planet, American Nightmare stretches to a 6-7 hour standalone game for a mere price of $5-10 on a good sale. It's totally worth that much and more.
Despite these bright features, American Nightmare is flawed by being too easy on the difficulty side. The game loses all tension on Normal mode, and it is best played on Nightmare mode instead. On Normal mode, there are ample ammo and weapons throughout the environments and fighting enemies is way too simplified and easy. Enemies do not even get close to you with the high amount of arsenal and flares at your disposal. But if you're just looking for an atmospheric experience without the challenge, then Normal mode is perfectly suitable for a playthrough.
If you thoroughly enjoyed the original Alan Wake, and you want more of pursue more of the atmospheric-story-driven game, look no further. Turn the lights off, put on your headphones, and drift away into the darkness.

American Nightmare is a fun combat focused episode set between the original game and the not-yet-if-ever-released sequel. In this chapter Alan is trying to escape from the Dark Place by writing a script of a twisted TV show, where he can alter reality and defeat his doppelganger, Mr. Scratch as he tries to take over Alan's life in the 'real world'.
The game brings some fixes of its prequel. The horrible and non-reactive controls are - fortunately - things of the past. It's a much more combat focused game, which is proven by a wast array of weapons you can find, from UZI to combat shotgun. The game introduces some - though not many - new elements and mechanics. There are new enemies like the Splitter, who splits into two when your flashlight is pointed at him. The area map and HUD are reworked, where scripts and points of interest are indicated. It's a nice addition since on the contrary of the first game, here you are encouraged to find those "damn" sheets of papers. You can get better weapons and it is fun, too.
While Alan Wake's story was controversial but well written, the same can't be said about this chapter. It sometimes feels rushed and underdeveloped. At least the ending is much more clearer now. The part where the game disappoints the most is the level design. There three only three levels non of which are large to say the least. In addition to this, each of the levels are reused 3 times. In the frame of the story it is understandable but still disappointing. To make it clear, it is not a full fledged game, but neither is a rip off DLC. It's something between, a full game with arcade length.
Alan's newest script shouldn't take longer than 4 hours to finish (6 with all the collectibles). Be aware though that normal in this game is easy compared to the prequel, so if you are up to it, try Nightmare difficulty. This can be explained by the combat focused nature of the game. You'll never have to roam trying to find ammunition and your flashlight recharges a lot faster than in the first game. There is a new game mode called Arcade Challenge. It's a simple addition where you have to survive until dawn and score as many points as you can with limited ammunition. You can squeeze a couple of extra hours out of this game mode, but don't expect dozens of hours of fun. On one side this game mode should have been in the first game, but with those horrid controls nobody would've played it.
Alan Wake's American Nightmare is not a propel sequel to Alan Wake but it's a nice side story which every fan will enjoy. The game falls short in some places to the prequel (story, level design) but bests it in other areas (controls, combat).

The hunting is very similar to Far Cry 4 (the honey badgers are back). Playing on a harder difficulty gives this game a very realistic feeling. One hit from a Saber Tooth, Bear or Elk and you're dead. The pet companions definitely add a great touch, and nothing is more satisfying than spearing an enemy off a cliff. If you enjoy the hunting, crafting, upgrading, and intense environments common to the Far Cry series, I would highly recommend buying. It's worth the full price; however, if you tend to care mostly about the storyline in this series, I would definitely recommend holding off until a price drop. The story isn't the most engaging (mainly due to the language barrier). I mostly enjoy hunting, crafting, and outposts in this series so I would recommend buying.

American Nightmare represents an epilogue to the main Alan Wake game, and as such it would be best to complete that story first.  Alan finds himself "stuck" in a new reality taunted by his evil doppleganger, whom he must eventually destroy to escape back to his wife in the "normal" world... where 2 years have passed and everyone believes Alan dead.  Again-another great idea, but the execution feels quite tedious.  The world is more open now and there is a map to guide you to your objectives.  the action mechanic of stunning and shooting the Taken is still present, although ammo and weapons are plentiful... I did not die once during the game on Normal.  There are manuscript pages, TVs, and radio shows to absorb if you have the patience to do so.  What killed it for me was the fact that you complete the same 3 maps and objectives 3 times!!  Granted, each time the tasks are attenuated a bit, but there is nothing new to discover with subsequent iterations.  Bargain bin please.

You can put four girls on the field instead of three so you can actually have all four goddesses/candidates out at the same time.
The most common problem people are having is the game choking up whenever there's a Guard Break (multiple times per battle), which destroys your framerate for 1-5 seconds. I'm expecting this to be fixed soon.

RB2 is quite easy (perhaps a bit harder than RB1) so I recommend you dont use all those broken items and plans you get right at the start. The game has been very enjoyable so far.

Although Company of Heroes 2 is alot of fun as long as you liked vanilla CoH, you can't help but be disappointed if you are used to play with absolutely brilliant CoH1-mods. This is not the fault of the game, because going back to vanilla CoH will be almost equally as painful after playing the famous Blitzkrieg-mod (for example) literally dozens of hours. So in my opinion the biggest problem CoH2 has, let aside the arguably and high-priced "ripoff" dlc-content, is that it is missing the masterpiece mods CoH1 has.
The SP-/ CoOp-content is awesome and will keep you busy quite some time, as long as you like AI Skirmishes. The devs truly deserve some credit for diversifying the overall content. Now you get CoOp-Scenarios and Defense-Missions in addition to the usual campaing and SP-missions. However so far only 1/4 additional-content bundles is free of charge, so without purchasing the other dlc, there aren't that many additional missions afterall.
To sum it up: If you liked vanilla CoH1, or are new to the series but enjoy quick and action-packed arcade-like strategy, this game is for you. However, how much you want to pay for it and if the additional content is worth a hefty price to you, is for you to decide.
Me personally, although enjoying CoH2 alot at the momenent, I will still play and go back to the CoH1 Blitzkrieg-mod from time to time. Don't compare CoH2 with modded CoH1 versions or your doomed to be disappointed.

Firsty I want to note that I experienced a game breaking bug and had to restart, around 40-60 minutes into the game. I didn't know what to do next and hints weren't helping. Thankfully (or not) other people on steam forums had had this problem and I knew what to watch out for when I restarted.
The way the story of Dark Heritage is presented is not enthralling nor exciting. I feel like they had good concepts (using real people in the cutscenes so they could convey emotion on a low budget, the society of the people on the island) but the execution...isn't there. I'm having trouble recalling what the island's backstory was because the game just wasn't very memorable. The game is about talking to lost souls so you can find elemental rocks with which to unlock a mythical magic stone! It should feel more mystic, especially because Artifex Mundi has a good reputation for conveying atmosphere. But this game wasn't developed by them.
The puzzles were often annoying. the two most memorable types were one where you press a button, or lever or what have you, and it affects other levers in the same row and you have to get them all into position, and one where you rotate rings of a circle so they align. While I'm not fond of the first type, I did them all on luck and didn't have a problem with them. The circle puzzles were worse. Often, I was feeling like the way for them to align was just a bit out of reach, thinking I was missing something. I think I used hints to get through one of them after minutes of frustrated sliding, and the solution was to slide them in a bit out of sync but enough that they aligned to the outer rim of the circle. All this did was make me feel like a fool for trying to find a perfect alignment. Another one of these puzzles (one in the bonus adventure) I skipped because the pattern was too same-looking and after many hopeful attempts I wasn't getting a solution.
Hidden object locations didn't take into account if you'd already found objects there, so while the list of things to find was new, the things you'd found previously were put back. This is a minor nitpick but it's important. Part or the satisfaction of playing a HOG is the feeling of "cleaning up" a scene; there is then more satisfaction when one goes back and has to "clean up" a scene further with a new list of things they probably remember seeing on their first time. If you go back to a scene and all those things are put back however, it's like what you did previously didn't matter, completing games doesn't matter, nothing in your life matters because you're making no impact on world. I'm exagerrating a bit, but you see my point, yes?
Also, the lipsync was off on both the only speaking human (an actor) and the bird (animated).
I don't hate this game though.

I was disappointed in this game, but I think I went into it with unrealistic expectations.
When I played 'The Walking Dead' seasons 1 and 2, it seemed like the choices I made mattered to the plot.  Things happened that were beyond my control, and I'm sure the outcomes were pre-ordained there too, but the game did a much better job of hiding that fact and maintaining the illusion of choice.
In 'Game of Thrones,' that illusion is quickly lost.  You are not the captain of your fate - you are watching a story play out, and your choices really do not matter much until the last chapter (when your final decisions lead you down one of a handful of equally unappealing paths).
That being said, as an interactive story - which, really, is the point - the game is enjoyable.  The tragedy of House Forrester unfolds like a slow-motion trainwreck... and as long as you are happy watching rather than having any meaningful impact, you will be entertained for hours.
I suppose creating a game with "true" choice would be nigh impossible - neither the writers nor the programmers nor the voice actors want to work through a hundred or more different endings based on what decisions you make.  If you can make peace with this and accept that what you're paying for is a good story, buy the game.  If you want to feel like you're in control of the story and anything can happen, your money would be better spent in tabletop role-playing games with your friends.
