It’s an absolutely marvelous world that I love. Its dark and of course Grim, it’s full of detail and texture. Plenty of variety as you travel through Victorian nightmare to underground caves and insect hives. Then blink in the sunlight as the second act pushes all that aside to randomly be about cowboys instead. Environmental touches are everywhere, completely selling the idea that this is a fallen land past any chance of actually saving. The abandoned villages and the crumbling walls of dungeons or the sadistic experiments in Warden's sickly green laboratory.
Exploring it is a smooth and epic-feeling experience that regularly demands long treks through enemy territory to get to the next boss or quest objective. Just about every path is scattered with both big combat engagements and dungeons to dip into for an extra boss fight and bonus loot.
Gathering loot is a cornerstone of the genre. Those junk items are worth so little compared to the cost of buying a health potion that it never feels satisfying to sell. It’s usually usable gear like swords and shields like the one you’re currently using. This makes it a real pain to sort through in search of worthwhile upgrades and gear to hold onto. Going back to town is at least painless, with a free Rift Travel spell that puts you right next to a shopkeeper and a portal back to where you just left. You can at least set the screen to only show that loot in the first place.
Magic in particular quickly steps up from a few basic sparks to screen-filling pyrotechnics, with fire-strikes turning into full explosions and what are meant to be simple lightning-based stun effects packing enough punch to not just kill enemies outright, but send them flying across the scenery as if literally dismissed as unworthy to fight for real.
Spirit or for some people Mana, is well balanced to let you cut loose with these abilities on a constant basis. Each Mastery has a powerful set to choose from, though upgrading them and unlocking new skills has to be balanced with leveling up passive increases that help provide the stats needed to wield better gear and keep up with the monster curve.
Plot is there if you want it though, in the occasional lore text and conversations with friends and villains, and I did like the slow building up of the town of Devil’s Crossing from a town of survivors basically sitting back and anticipating death to actually being a small community with a chance. The acts also unfold out to provide plenty of different scenery as you cross the huge world. Huge to the extent that even early quests to a neighboring town feel like small odysseys which are littered with bonus dungeons of every size, including special challenge ones that disable rift travel and make the only way out either victory or death.

If you're a die-hard hidden object fan, this game is fine.  It's not buggy, and it works, and you'll get a handful of hours of fun out of it.
However... it's one of the lowest-rent Artifex Mundi games.  There are few hidden object scenes, and the puzzles are very easy.  There are live action cut scenes likely filmed with non-English speaking actors, so their lips often don't synch with the dialogue, and most of the time they just sit there while the dialogue is spoken without even moving their mouths.  There's also a high propensity for the live-action cutscenes to go into extreme close-ups on their eyes.  Probably a tactic to solve the language issue, but it ends up being as bad as holding on a silent, non-speaking actor during dialogue.  None of this effects gameplay, it creates for an odd, amateurish feel.
The game is also thin all around.  Not many collectibles (except for a few scrolls) or achievements, and no alternatives to the hidden object scenes as with many of the Artifex Mundi games.  The game is rather short, and the story is inconsequential and nebulous.  In fact, after playing the game, I'd be hard pressed to even explain the story.  Not developed by Artifex Mundi, and one of the worst they've published... but no bugs and fine for those with low expectations who just want a competent HOG fix.

Story: Occulist and gnossis Gordon Child sends his most promising, once student a harried message concerning the Order of the Rose and the Philosopher's Stone.  He wants her to come to his city office so he can explain the details.  When she arrives, his office is in shambles and he has disappeared.  She travels (or is summoned) to the island where she discovers an immense tradegy; the inhabitants are dead and the fortunate ones have fled/escaped from the destructive and homicidal evil new master of the island who is searching for the Philosopher's Stone to gain its power.  While searching for her mentor, Gordon Child, our heroine, meets and helps various lost souls bound there, who in turn call her their "savior" and the "chosen one".  (And just to be perfectly clear, this game does NOT smack of any religious connotations, beyond good vs. evil.)
About reviews:  I decided to add this bit about reviews here after reading other reviews AFTER I played the game and wrote my own review.  1) Most reviews complain about the graphics claiming they are old.  Fine they are not exquisite pieces of art but they are highly detailed and crisp, and in many ways fitting with this supernatural and quite possibly "not in this world" island.  The artwork is consistent and stylized.  2) The cutscenes are a lot of the game, and live actors play a role in both the cutscenes and as the lost souls in the game.  One thing all the reviews seem to have missed is the heroine is "reading their mind/ emotions" with the medallion and the people are dead meaning they basically lack the outward emotion of the living.  So the live actors do not need to speak or even be lip synched properly.  I personally found the disconnect, disconcerting and baffling, and intentionally or not in my opinion it added to the surrealism and other worldly flavor (like a reminder almost) the heroine was from a different world (quite possibly literally).
Gameplay: On expert mode there are no sparkles (which in this case look like runic symbols which move sideways) and that alone makes finding the hidden object scenes, puzzles, and needed inventory items tough.  The cursor does change from an arrow to a round glass circle with a tail, but if the gamer lacks the patience to thoroughly "explore" each scene do not play on expert mode the first time.  This game requires some intuitive and a bit deductive reasoning to play.  For instance, when confronted with a half finished ladder, it is obvious the ladder needs planks for steps, nails, and a hammer.  What is not so clear is where to obtain all those items, a shed, a tool box, floating in water, against the building, laying on the ground.  This too is part of the challenge of the game, knowing what one needs, finding it somewhere on the island, and then obtaining the item once it is found.  Fortunately there is a fast travel map though it is not really needed.
The game more or less plays in a linear fashion, completing the scenerio of freeing a trapped soul before being able to move on to the next one.  There are four souls in all that need "saving".   So with the introduction, and conclusion that makes six separate but interrelated "chapters".  Plus there is a bonus chapter.
The hidden object scenes are fair, nothing outrageously hidden, but one is required to look closely for some of the finds. (One reveiwer vehemently complained about the finds stating the find clue could be several things.  This is true.  For instance, handle could an axe handle, a shovel handle, or a machine handle.  However with a bit of deductive reasoning ... say there is a shovel blade in your inventory most likely the shovel handle is what the find clue is referring to, if not click on all the handles until the correct one is found.  Simple enough.)  There are fragmented or "hidden" objects to locate which are colored in the clue list.  I do like when a clue find is found it turns red-black then dissovles into smoke.  I think it adds to whole evil/supernatural motif and different from the usual disappearing find clues.  Each hidden object scene plays twice (some possibly more) so remember where they are (especially on expert mode).  Some are played once early in the game then again much later in the game.  The same is true with some of needed inventory items, one finds the item early but may not need it or be able to get it until late in the game.
There is a variety of puzzles in this games: sliders, matching, logic, codes, rotating (the bonus chapter one is very difficult).  For the puzzles I highly recommend reading the diary.  In this game, the diary is the most helpful clue giver found in the game, and often is where the clue needed is found.  The dairy also relates the scenerio objective to the storyline, sometimes adding information to the pages after the initial reading.
There is one extra find in this game: the scrolls.  I doubt they are missable since they are obtained during game play and the entire storyline is crytically given through the visual cutscenes when the scroll is read.  Two special achievements I would like to note here are 1) watching the cutscenes and 2) examine all the notes, maps, scraps of paper.  Both are easily obtainable if one does not skip the cutscenes and actually clicks on the notes, maps, scraps of paper to read them.  I actually recommend clicking on the notes, maps, and scraps of paper because they often end up in the dairy, and once on the dairy pages often gain extra information.
Overall the game is a fair challenge on expert mode and relatively hard on casual mode depending on the gamer's experience level.

I confess to be a little startled at the amount of negative reviews on this game.  While it is not the pinnacle of the Artifex Mundi collection, I found it to be very entertaining and worth a couple hours of gameplay.  As I almost always say, I suggest getting it on sale, as I believe personally that most of these HO games are overpriced for the gametime involved.
There are certainly some odd things in the game.  Cutscenes are live-action/"acted" rather than animated and I'm not a personal fan of this style, especially as they come off like a bad foreign movie dub (lips are moving but the words aren't matching).  That said, I've also seen far worse.  The voice acting is extremely sub-par in my estimation (I've seen some varying opinions on this so your mileage may vary); everyone sounded pretty much the same and interestingly, in the credits, there is but one male and one female voice actor listed.  I have no problem with double-use (or more) of voice actors if they're able to effectively change their voices, but that's not the case here and it made me a little twitchy.
The gameplay itself, however, is just fine.  It is a pretty standard HO/pointy-clicky sort of game, typical Artifex Mundi style, with the normal mix of minigames and HO scenes, none of which were horribly difficult but they weren't pushovers either.  I didn't feel the graphics were poor at all, but I'm also not picky, having seen some of the worst of the worst over the years.
There was one bug that's been mentioned where a cutscene will occasionally not happen and prevent the game from progressing.  This did happen to me, and I did have to start over, but it's relatively close to the beginning of the game and I wasn't really bothered by the ten minutes it took to redo that early bit.
So my final recommedation is that it's worth a playthrough if gotten on sale and if things like bad voice acting and weird cutscenes aren't going to upset you.  If you're going into it without expecting something incredible, you shouldn't be too disappointed.  I, personally, am not going to have any problem replaying to clean up the last of the achievements.

A game that can't decide when it's set, with a story slightly more bare bones than the skeletons inhabiting its landscape, with FMV captured folk who either portray a single emotion (Usually little to do with the words being said or their tone), or mouth in what I'm assuming is no language known to man (I am happy to be corrected on this) overlaid on the usual Hidden Object funtimes... Except less fun, because there are important puzzle objects near exit points and the corner of the UI, hidden objects in the corners near the UI or 80% obscured by things in front of them, objects being repeated in thesame scene (Leading to "Oh, we don't want you to click *THIS* wheel), worse than usual "Nope, you can't use this on this axe on those planks, because the planks have bolts on. See?" problems, and...
...I can't recommend this. Hidden Object fans will get frustrated at the repeated objects, both HO and Adventure Game fans will hate the more-arbitrary-than-usual puzzles, and Adventure Game fans will groan at the tissue thin story. For anyone who has completed and asked "Wait, was there more to it than this Evil Master thing?" No. It's straight up bare bones Hero's Journey with a not-twist at the near-end. Find McGuffin, defeat Evil Master, Save Land.

This game for me like a blast from the past. When RTS genre was popular among people, and you always had a choice to pick any type you want. Tiberium Saga, Red Alert, Warhammer 40k Dawn of War 1 + expansions... Man, that was a really great time.
Unfortunately, theres a lot of scholboys among gamers, so a lot of games, even game genres where you need to think were drown in stupidity, simplicity and developers greed. RTS no longer so popular as some times ago. Instead a lot of people plays COD, CS, Battlefield and other stuff. Ubisoft became a joke company etc.
Anyway, speaking back about Grey Goo, I can't said nothing about its developer - Petroglyph. These are the same guys who made Dune, Tiberium Dawn and many more classic RTS games. A lot of people still playing them. Petroglyph knows how to make game interesting, with good mechanics, without such annoying bugs.
Of course, many people can say that that was before, but now it is another time, another story. But you know what? If the game is good, why shouldn't you play it then? Or at least try it?
Alright. Grey Goo is a great RTS game with four different factions & different game style. Frankly speaking, I wasn't impressed when I played it first time. I just finished half of campaign and delete the game. Because I wanted to find something unique and interesting. That was 2016. And I didn't find anything.
Things changed a few weaks ago, when I played 8-Bit serious. I like all three games, and when I noticed that Petroglyph made this series and also its a Grey Goo developer, I thought: - "Whoa, so the time has come to finish Grey Goo campaign". And I finished it.
Game is good. Probably, not everyone will like it, but for me - old RTS fan, its a great and fun time consumer.
As for you, guys and girls, I want to said - just try it. Maybe it wouldn't make you interested in, but if it would...
Then you have a chance to completely waste few of your evenings (or weekends).
Cheers :)

NOTE: I have played this far more on the Vita than i did on pc(to the point of max leveling every character and platinum trophying it.) but as it's the same game and nothing much changes it still applies here.
While the gameplay can be a slog at times and the pandering adn fanservice is always on high I can't really say I disliked this game. Sure, it's not the best game both in terms of gameplay or plot it more than makes up for it in the characters it brings to the table and replayibilty it garners as a rpg with a built in remake system. The characters( for how"token"they are) are likible and youd be hard pressed to not find at least one character you like in this game. The variety it there as well both in the sense of the character options which are high for this kind of game and the way the game has you constantly revisiting new area with a different spins added. While most backtracking is boring and repetative this game manages to make you feel invested and enjoy the trip with the remake syatem changing the way the game runs around you.
The story itself isn't really anything to write home about to be honest but thats not to say it's boring . The characters the story portrays and the self aware style of the story itself make for a enjoyable ride even disregarding the story entirely. it's incredibly meta and full of pandering and joke but thats not a bad thing as it adds to the charm of the whole thing. It doesn't try to take itself seriously and in doing so it eases itself in to a nice niche  in terms of how typical rpgs are portrayed.
Overall if your even slightly interested in an rpg thats full of variety in game and character or just enjoy a good laugh while you casually play a little you won't really be disappointed here.

Preface: I bought this game when it was 50% off, but I still think it's worth the asking price of $25. I usually say that if I can get a 1:1 ratio of dollars spent to hours played I'm happy, and I'm over that by a lot already.
I've been wanting to write a review of this game for a while but I've waited until I've gotten some more play time into it so that I can give a solid review. Right now in the game I'm on Elite difficulty on my main character which is a Witch Hunter. First I want to start off by saying that this game reminded me of how I felt when I played Diablo 2. I'm not one for hardcore characters or anything, but I still enjoy a challenge. This game definitely provides a challenge.
My first run through of this game was on normal difficulty, but if you are fairly experienced with these types of games, I would suggest going the Veteran route. It's one of those games that might kill you, but you can definitely strategize in the future to plan around getting killed again (though it does get more difficult). What I love aside from the dark atmosphere and fear of death all the time is the different types of augmentations for your character. You build it from the ground up in many different ways, and after level 50, you start getting access to Legendary items. There are attribute points (for your basic stats), mastery points (for your skills and buffs), and then shrines which give you access to devotion points which allow even more customization--something that all "classes" or masteries have access to. Depending on how you spend these, you can develop new skills or strategies or even survival methods.
I'm not one to mind grinding games too much (especially when Diablo 3 was only story mode runs...), but this game offers choices on how much you want to challenge yourself. Though at a certain point (i.e. higher difficulties) it's thrust upon you. Even still, these higher difficulties offer challenege dungeons and harder areas to play in.
It's definitely a game that I recommend using the wiki page through your playthroughs to help maximize your rewards in the game. It's a game I can play by myself which I love. I would definitely recommend getting this game if you want a hack and slash experience with great loot and skills. I'm sure others might say things against that, but it's all up to you!
One thing I would like to nitpick is that there are some buggy aspects when pointing and clicking by different levels in this game, and even things that allow you to kill enemies a little better through walls. But these bugs aren't super bad, just can be a mild inconvenience.
Thanks for reading, sorry it was so long!

I will first start off by saying: Don't buy this game at the $10+ price.  Wait for it to be really cheap, by cheap I mean past the $10.00 count.
It's sad to see a sequel to a game take a turn for the worse.  With all the advertising going into it's launch, the public discussions from developers about the mechanics and unique game play and art.  All that pales in comparision to the majority of the games main feature: Multiplayer.
This is the frist time (and hopefully last time) I've ever heard of or seen an RTS game require pay to play in it's multiplayer function.  I have never heard of such a thing.  I expect the P2P from an MMO, that's understandable for server maintenance and other specs.  But to give P2P gamers an advantage over F2P gamers is not only an unfair advantage, it's an insult to both the game and the community.
I remember when Relic made amazing RTS style titles.  The most memorable for me were Home World, Home World 2, Dawn of War, Dawn of War: Darck Crusade and Warhammer 40,000: Fire Warrior.  As well as the original Company of Heroes 1.
So it truly breaks me heart and destroys my faith in a company that would take such an approach to their fans and the community for the multiplayer approach.
Aside from the unbalance approach of P2P vs F2P.  The units lack any proper A.I. responses to the heat of battle.  This involves, tank movement away from heavy fighting, moving troops away from grenades before they're thrown and the attack response time for squads when a target is sighted.
The Campaign itself follows the Russian point of view.  Playing out as a flash back.  I won't give any spoilers, but I was hoping for a bit more time in game play.
Now while the use of a snow and ice environment is a unique and well thought out tactic for the game, such as damaging lakes of ice, areas of belwo Zero to freeze troops and so on.  These fetures don't really make up for the major problems of the game itself.  While I admire Relic's attempt too try a fresh take on the U.I. it feels more complex and difficult to master, especially when in the heat of battle when you feel RUSHED to get something built or try using a squad ability.
Again I would say DO NOT BUY unless it drops beyond the $10 price range.
Instead look for the original COH and it's expansions.  Company of Heroes 2, sadly, does not live up to its predecessor.

Long version (no story spoilers, just some game mechanic related spoilers)
This game a a hell of alot of fun.

The character classes are interesting, you don't choose a class (or classes) at the beginning, but choose as you go. You pick a single class skill tree after attaining your first level up. You can play a single class if you wish, or you can (and are actively encouraged to) delve into the skill tree of a second class as you progress. Also there are varing different build options within each class skill tree leading to a large variety of gameplay.
You can spread your points into lots of active abilities or concentrate on just adding points into passive abilities. I found 6 active abilities was more than enough for my fat fingers
In additional to these class skills, there is a 'Devotion' skill tree which can give your character unique abilities/stat increases/or augment an existing class ability. You earn points to spend on it by completing a certain type of task (i wont discuss, you will find out)
I liked the singleplayer campaign, the game creates a great atmosphere in keeping with an apocalytic setting. The music  is great, lilting at times, dark and opposive at others. Steve Pardo, the composer of the soundtrack is extremely talented. Example:
Graphically it is clean, crisp and colourful, equally as good as diablo 3 and in my opinion better/cleaner than Path of Exile.
Gameplay feels fast paced and exciting, blows have weight and feel punchy, animations are fluid, spells are beautful and look devastating, explosions create slight screen shake (optional) and knock mobs back (or just to smithereens :) ), interior locations make ranged fights feel claustrophobic and tense as you try to  avoid melee mobs closing in on your squishy mage.
I would say the mob AI is adequate, enemy ranged mobs wont  automatically round a corner into your sword and will wait for you (mexican stand off), sometimes they will shoot arrows into a wall you are behind which is a bit weird.
There are some surprises as well but i wont spoil it.... suffice to say, combat feels tight and visceral.
The loot is colour coded according to its rarity (white, yellow, green, blue, purple). Be careful when using the colour as a guide to the power of an item, there are exceptions where a commoner coloured item is infact alot better than a rarer colour, item stat weight can be extremely varied and random. Generally rarer loot drops more frequently on higher difficulties, some loot will only drop from higher difficulties.
Mechanically, Characters have 3 base stats (Physique, Cunning, and Spirit), 4 derived stats (health. energy (mana), offensive ability, defensive ability). There are also 10 different damage types, and further modifiers. As such loot can become quite complicated and as with most aRPG titles you will get a ton of loot and the bewildering array of stats on some items can be a bit overwhelming. This can  lead to situations where whether an item is better or worse than what you are wearing is unclear (perhaps this was just me?).I found after a while you will get a feel for what items are right for your character. My advise is to be ruthless when disposing of items you dont want, or stash them for use on other characters later on.
Like other titles you have item stashes: a personal stash and a larger expandable global stash for transferring items amongst characters. These are accessible from various different hubs in the game.
Each of these hubs relates to a different faction which you will encounter and you progress through the campaign.
Factions give quests for which you earn reputation which provide purchasable rewards at milestones.
There are beneficial factions and evil factions, so whilst you build reputation with a beneficial faction you are slowly becoming more despised by the opposing evil faction. At milestones in negative reputation the evil factions with start spawning additional hero and boss mobs.
There are also 2 beneficial factions which are mutually exclusive (choose one and the other becomes actively hostile, allowing you to fight them). On this point, be very careful when choosing one side over another as you will lose access to the hostile faction's rewards, and some sell blueprints that you cannot get from anywhere else except random drops, research the rewards before choosing!!
Crafting is available, and is achieved by combining components found amongst loot. Blueprints for items can also drop as loot as well as being sold by Facton vendors (if you have the appropriate reputation). Its a little clunky, idiosyncratic, and has multiple tiers (craft an item that can then be used in another recipe, and so on...a + b + c = x,  d + e + f = y, x + y = z, etc.) and as you will need to purchase / find alot of the blueprints you will not always know which components you need to keep, my advice? KEEP EVERYTHING! (if you apply components to a piece of gear you have the option of stripping it off from a particular vendor).
Also some of the components are extremely hard to come by (Ectoplasm, for example)
Campaign, progression and replayability...
The main story will progress as you kill mobs and complete quests, however,  you can exit to the main menu at any point to reset the mobs in the world if you want to run a particular dungeon or location again (farming loot or reputation).
Once you have completed the singleplayer campaign for the first time. you can go back to the main menu, up the difficulty (nomral/veteran >> Elite) and begin the campaign from scratch with the same character. You retain your level, gear and abilities, this will allow you further level the character, once completed a second time you can up the difficulty one further time (Elite >> Ultimate) and play through again. First playthrough will get you to level 50-ish, Level cap is presently 85.
There is a hardcore more (perma-death) for you masochistic types.
This is as much as i can think of for for now, might update this post later.

This may sound self-centered, especially as I know that there are a great deal of old TQ fans playing this game, and enjoying it. But there may be people out there that share my expectations and possibly, run the risk of sharing the same experience that I had. So consider this review a heads up - sometimes things aren't as expected.

This game has some of the best character customization I've ever seen, however, I will admit when it comes to costume customizations, the game is lacking. Every class is given about 1-3 unique costumes while the rest are shared with those of the same gender with subtle variances (classes are genderlocked!). You can buy them through the market so you don't have to spend the money for a costume (most of what you pay for can be bought with the in game currency on the market). Graphics are beautiful, but they can become choppy/laggy in crowded towns/cities. The level of detail put into cities and landscapes makes them feel vibrant and alive. You can almost feel that you're riding through a real world. The map is huge and there are so many quests and areas to shake up the grind.
Combat is combo based and fun. At first, you might be punching random buttons, but you learn pretty quickly which buttons are your worst and those that might save your life. Enemies are pretty easy if you keep your gear up. The sense of adventure is incredible. I've had more fun exploring exploring than anything else in the game.
There are a variety of lifeskills to choose from: gathering, fishing, processing, training, ect, to keep you earning money while you're away from the game.
As much as I enjoy this game the three biggest let downs of the game are lag/server stability, a majority of the community and enhancing.
Lag: Walk into a busy city and you risk instantly being disconnected. I get booted in the middle of nowhere even at low-pop hours. It has improved since I started but not by much. For some, the game remains unplayable.
Community: For an MMO, there very little group content or benefits to being in a group in the world. For example, XP is split between everyone (in a full group of 5 a person will only get ~50% of the XP/kill) so competition for grind spots is insanely high and the incentive to group is very low. Even when you're trying to get back to your city there are people who wait and attack you just outside the safe zone. Chat is toxic and there is very moderation.
Enhancing: Once you get to +17 (DUO) anything you do risks downgrading. Not just one level either. If you fail a TET attempt, it'll go to DUO, switch to an alt with TRI stacks and fail, well you now have a PRI. You can't repair your boss armor/weps because Memory Fragments are next to impossible to find outside of running Relic/other Scrolls. Something needs to be done about enhancing because it is insane. Good luck trying to buy your TRIs/TETs off the marketplace, they are nearly always swiped by bots and PENs are virtually non-existent. Also, many refuse to post base gear unless you gift them items from the pearl shop.
Overall, I enjoy this game. If you don't feel like grinding mobs, you can gather instead. If you don't feel like playing after a hard day, you can do life skills. There is no set goal and the end game is really what you want it to be. Want to be the best fisher in your channel? Best player in Red Battlefield? Best cook? Your choice.
Until enhancement and grouping are changed, I cannot recommend this.

Combat is fairly easy to get a hold of but harder to master, leveling is fast and the more interesting content like world boss is post lvl 56 but if you grind it hard, you can reach that in a week easy.

Nodes are complex as sht and I spent the first 100 hrs with no idea wtf to do but its a interesting management game where assign workers to gather resources for you while your off doing something else, easy to make money with.
Cash system is mostly cosmetic and convenient based, you can buy super kid friendly costumes for all your characters that dont show massive cleavage whatsoever. The game gives you plently of free inventory slots via quests so that has never been an issue and you can grind up your weight limit by carrying trade goods and just afk walking. Pets are very useful as they help pick up loots and have unique skills like faster fishing and detecting special monsters. Overall you never have to you the cash shop as you can purchase the items via the marketplace by bidding on it but you have to be lucky as tons of people will be bidding along with you.

Graphics are amazing but there are popins when you near a especially large structure sometimes. There is also a bug with the market where you will get low fps sometimes because everyone is on the same page looking at the same thing i think.
Overall I do recommend this game to fans of mmorpgs as it has some really good ideas and I really enjoy how the skill progression goes as the more you do any skill the better you get including stuff like just walking around. However I believe this game requires a certain level of dedication to become one of the best, you will have to play long hrs if you want to really get good but if your a casual like me you will just have to contend with being mediocre. I can finally tell my friends I play League.
... Oh, right. I'm writing a review. Here's my pros and cons list if you don't want to read the rest of my review.
If I was to describe Lethal League in one sentence, it would be Baseball Combat. You play as one of 6 characters, each with a different ability, and you hit the ball back and forth until it hits someone. When you get hit by the ball, you lose a life; when you lose all your lives, you've lost the match. I should note that hitting other characters directly does absolutely nothing, so you have to focus on hitting the ball such that it collides with your opponent.
Up to 4 players can play at once, and the game modes include a free-for-all deathmatch as well as a team battle mode which supports both 2vs2, 1vs2 and 1vs3 modes. Friendly fire is optional (referred in-game as ball tagging) to allow a more intense experience should you choose to play with it.
This game is very keyboard friendly if you don't have a controller (as I don't have a very good controller); controlled with the directional arrow keys for movement and the Z, X and Spacebar for other movements, you can re-map all the controls as you see fit in the options menu. My friend can confirm that this game plays great with a controller as well.
Where I think this game shines brightest is its multiplayer, especially when playing with friends. With friends, regardless of how much I was winning or losing, not a moment went by where we weren't having the time of our lives. This game is very easy to learn as the controls are limited to movement, jumping, hitting the ball and bunting the ball (hitting it lightly), and the optional replayable in-game tutorial explains things sufficiently.
Overall, this game is best played with friends, but can be played just as well solo. Definitely recommended, especially if it's on sale.

I was on the fence about getting this game for quite a while. It went on sale several times and I would look at reviews online and see it's praises and I wouldn't buy it because of the perception I had regarding the past saints row games. I'm simply not in to the gang war style video game with gratuitous profanity. Finally, over the new year the game went on sale again for a pretty good price and I finally committed to it.
I must admit, I was pleasently surprised. A lot f the online reviews point out the franchise takes a serious left turn with this iteration in the franchise, but I think it's a good thing it did because it reeled in someone like me who wasn't a fan of the other entries.
Graphically, the game is ok. It's not the most beautiful game on the planet in regards to modern graphical prowess, but the lighting and shading is incredibly good. Turn VSYNC on though.
The gameplay is incredibly fun. It spoofs so many movies and game franchises and does it so well. It's a barrel of laughs. Yes, there is a lot of swearing and profanity, but I honestly thought it was done well and wasn't gratuitous in its use. It's just plain funny to hear from the characters at just the right moments. It almost makes the scenes more realistic because, come on, who wouldn't say what the F--k?! if you're getting pulled up by an alient tractor beam.
I haven't completed the game so I can't speak for any game breaking bugs, if they're present.
Controls are tip top. I'd recommend a gamepad.
Audio wise, the sound effects and voices are well done. The gun fire effects are very throw away, but then again it's maybe because I've heard them in just about every other game in existence. The vocal work is very good though and very entertaining. The music is great, with licensed songs that help amplify the scene and the situation they're trying to spoof. I've replayed the opening scene about 8 times now just to hear the Aerosmith scene.
I don't think the campaign will be worth playing through again except in key areas, but for the price of admission, this game is well worth it.

Copy and paste the exact same mechanics as the previous games reskinned with a prehistoric vibe.  Then remove a huge chunk of variety that previous Far Cry games brought to the table with tons of weapons and gadgets.  Also remove interesting antagonists like Vaz and compelling motivation like seeing your brother killed.  Enemies will detect you from insane distances, sometimes without line of sight in classic Far Cry fashion.  To anyone who says it's not fair to judge this game by it's predecessors, I don't know what to tell you.  If a game comes out that's a copy of a previous game but worse, the comparison draws itself.
The game is very pretty.  I loved the lighting and scenery.  The few new elements like taming animals and improving your village are interesting. However the pet AI is bad and even though there are lots of different animals to tame, it is easy to get some of the best pets early on which makes the others pointless.  The village upgrading seems more like an excuse to convince you to run around and gather more resources that are scattered every five feet.  Heavies make a reappearance, but without the variety of items in previous Far Cry games the only viable way to fight them is the heavy takedown skill which removes a lot of the flexibility that made taking outposts a fun challenge instead of a timewaster.  The game takes a stab at variety with the bee bombs, berserk bombs, and fire bombs but in the end they are all useful as distractions at best against stronger enemies.  One weapon they really got right was the spear.  It is extremely fun to use melee and ranged but they break after a few uses and you will never have more than a few of them at a time.  The game will let you carry more two-handed clubs than spears for some reason.  And that basically defines this game.  The things this game does that are fun are too few and hard to come by.

Block N Load bears an interesting concept; pick a class, help your team build up your defenses, then attack the enemy when the build phase ends, making use of the minecraft build/destroy mechanics while engaging in gun fights. However, there are many issues that cripple this harshly.
First is the fact this game is a first person shooter. With characters available that have NO GUNS. I feel the need to ask: Why? I could understand a self-imposed challenge, but you are unable to switch characters, and as such, weapon loadouts, when in the middle of a match, meaning if you selected the wrong character for the match (and you have no way to know until the game is loading everyone up), you're stuck being useless to everyone on your team.
Speaking of teams, the ingame chat seems to only allow for you to speak to only your team mates, which is okay, but not okay at the same time when you want to ask the enemy team how they're doing something (so that, ya know, you might learn and get better). Instead, you can only engage in conversation with them AFTER the match has ended. End of match stats screen also lacks a block player function, meaning you could get paired up with that annoying player who either makes himself useless on your team by being the gunless hero, or stomps on you because they've been playing the game for a couple hundred more hours then you.
Matchmaking is terrible with no way to seemingly pair up players of appropriate skill level with one another, and for a 5-player team based game, only lets you invite 2 additional friends to join your party (or squad, as the game refers to it), which is pretty silly; It's a multiplayer, team-based game. Why would I want to play with strangers over my friends? Another crippling issue is the fact newer players do not start with any guaranteed Heroes to play with, instead being stuck at the mercy of the free rotation, which can include Heroes that are simply beyond their skill level to use (like the aforementioned gunless heroes).
Heroes themselves seem to lose their uniqueness when there isn't a limit on how many of a single Hero can be on the team, so games can end up having one team be completely loaded with snipers, or ninjas, or engineers, which can cause games to be very one sided with the currently state of the Matchmaking system, and without knowing what you're up against until it's too late, you're either given the option to quit the game right out the gate and get punished for it, or struggle in vain against the unbalanced match up and waste time not learning anything except maybe the map and the few blocks you have available to you.
The ingame Tutorial only covers your basic controls and objective in a game, but doesn't go beyond that with actually helpful stuff, like bots to practice against (if there are indeed bots in the game to practice against, I completely missed them, and thus renders this long sentence redundant). Current registration for Block N Load is a joke, as it's reward is a skin for a character you do not start with and need to grind the game to purchase (assuming you don't just give them actual cash to buy it). I'd rather a Hero I can play with, then a Skin I cannot use because the Hero in question wasn't in the free rotation.
In summary, the list of fixes Block N Load needs before one could consider it even worth their time: Melee-orientiated characters need better long range options for combat, better tutorial to help you practice what the basics try to show, better match making for pairing players of equal skill level together, actually starting people off with at least 1 guaranteed Hero for them to play as outside of the free rotations, lock the limit on heroes (to say, not having a full team of snipers or engineers), better chat system for engaging teammates and enemies, better post-match lobby options, and actually allow you to invite 4 friends to join you (cause clan games are just as important).

Long version (no story spoilers, just some game mechanic related spoilers)
This game a a hell of alot of fun.

The character classes are interesting, you don't choose a class (or classes) at the beginning, but choose as you go. You pick a single class skill tree after attaining your first level up. You can play a single class if you wish, or you can (and are actively encouraged to) delve into the skill tree of a second class as you progress. Also there are varing different build options within each class skill tree leading to a large variety of gameplay.
You can spread your points into lots of active abilities or concentrate on just adding points into passive abilities. I found 6 active abilities was more than enough for my fat fingers
In additional to these class skills, there is a 'Devotion' skill tree which can give your character unique abilities/stat increases/or augment an existing class ability. You earn points to spend on it by completing a certain type of task (i wont discuss, you will find out)
I liked the singleplayer campaign, the game creates a great atmosphere in keeping with an apocalytic setting. The music  is great, lilting at times, dark and opposive at others. Steve Pardo, the composer of the soundtrack is extremely talented. Example:
Graphically it is clean, crisp and colourful, equally as good as diablo 3 and in my opinion better/cleaner than Path of Exile.
Gameplay feels fast paced and exciting, blows have weight and feel punchy, animations are fluid, spells are beautful and look devastating, explosions create slight screen shake (optional) and knock mobs back (or just to smithereens :) ), interior locations make ranged fights feel claustrophobic and tense as you try to  avoid melee mobs closing in on your squishy mage.
I would say the mob AI is adequate, enemy ranged mobs wont  automatically round a corner into your sword and will wait for you (mexican stand off), sometimes they will shoot arrows into a wall you are behind which is a bit weird.
There are some surprises as well but i wont spoil it.... suffice to say, combat feels tight and visceral.
The loot is colour coded according to its rarity (white, yellow, green, blue, purple). Be careful when using the colour as a guide to the power of an item, there are exceptions where a commoner coloured item is infact alot better than a rarer colour, item stat weight can be extremely varied and random. Generally rarer loot drops more frequently on higher difficulties, some loot will only drop from higher difficulties.
Mechanically, Characters have 3 base stats (Physique, Cunning, and Spirit), 4 derived stats (health. energy (mana), offensive ability, defensive ability). There are also 10 different damage types, and further modifiers. As such loot can become quite complicated and as with most aRPG titles you will get a ton of loot and the bewildering array of stats on some items can be a bit overwhelming. This can  lead to situations where whether an item is better or worse than what you are wearing is unclear (perhaps this was just me?).I found after a while you will get a feel for what items are right for your character. My advise is to be ruthless when disposing of items you dont want, or stash them for use on other characters later on.
Like other titles you have item stashes: a personal stash and a larger expandable global stash for transferring items amongst characters. These are accessible from various different hubs in the game.
Each of these hubs relates to a different faction which you will encounter and you progress through the campaign.
Factions give quests for which you earn reputation which provide purchasable rewards at milestones.
There are beneficial factions and evil factions, so whilst you build reputation with a beneficial faction you are slowly becoming more despised by the opposing evil faction. At milestones in negative reputation the evil factions with start spawning additional hero and boss mobs.
There are also 2 beneficial factions which are mutually exclusive (choose one and the other becomes actively hostile, allowing you to fight them). On this point, be very careful when choosing one side over another as you will lose access to the hostile faction's rewards, and some sell blueprints that you cannot get from anywhere else except random drops, research the rewards before choosing!!
Crafting is available, and is achieved by combining components found amongst loot. Blueprints for items can also drop as loot as well as being sold by Facton vendors (if you have the appropriate reputation). Its a little clunky, idiosyncratic, and has multiple tiers (craft an item that can then be used in another recipe, and so on...a + b + c = x,  d + e + f = y, x + y = z, etc.) and as you will need to purchase / find alot of the blueprints you will not always know which components you need to keep, my advice? KEEP EVERYTHING! (if you apply components to a piece of gear you have the option of stripping it off from a particular vendor).
Also some of the components are extremely hard to come by (Ectoplasm, for example)
Campaign, progression and replayability...
The main story will progress as you kill mobs and complete quests, however,  you can exit to the main menu at any point to reset the mobs in the world if you want to run a particular dungeon or location again (farming loot or reputation).
Once you have completed the singleplayer campaign for the first time. you can go back to the main menu, up the difficulty (nomral/veteran >> Elite) and begin the campaign from scratch with the same character. You retain your level, gear and abilities, this will allow you further level the character, once completed a second time you can up the difficulty one further time (Elite >> Ultimate) and play through again. First playthrough will get you to level 50-ish, Level cap is presently 85.
There is a hardcore more (perma-death) for you masochistic types.
This is as much as i can think of for for now, might update this post later.

Here's my second try at a review of Grim Dawn.
I usually do not care about people who are basically fanboys and keep ranting about how the review is unfair and the reviewer is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥simply because he/she has got a different opinion other than their favourite game, which they sunk 100000 hours in, being the best game in the whole ♥♥♥♥ing world. And I imagine it could be really frustrating to admit that anything you invest that much time in is actually maybe not THAT good. This time the sheer stupidity and unwillingness to engage in an objective discussion about the review made me mad, so here it goes.
One of my points of criticism was that Grim Dawn was too similar to Titan Quest and could in some ways considered to be a reskin of it. IN SOME WAYS. But: 1) I had lots of other things I criticised and 2) it was not nearly my main point of me disliking the game. So let's focus on the stuff, which is not Titan Quest related, let's forget it ever existed.
I do not particularly like or enjoy Diablo 3 very much, but definitely not because of the combat system. Compared to D3, Torchlight 2 or Path of Exile, Grim Dawn feels like a stick up the♥♥♥♥♥
You are rarely required to do anything else but stand still, attack and occasionally pop a healing potion or start escaping for some time until you recovered some health in case you get some real damage.
The enemy variety is poor and mostly cosmetic. Doesn't matter if your foes are melee, ranged, magic - they all act the same way. They either run up to you and hit you or they get in range and shoot you from afar.
In MY OPINION that is pretty boring. Rembember: YOUR OPINION might be different, you might find that standing around and left-clicking without any thinking whatsoever is pretty exciting.
I think they did a pretty good job on the Devotion Tree, which borrows some ideas from Path of Exiles passive skill tree (which, by the way, is PERFECTLY fine, the borrowing thing) the rest of it is not that much of a highlight. You mostly invest points in leveling up your mastery which unlocks new abilities or you invest points in already unlocked abilities - so far so standard.
What bothers me though, is that none of these choices are very interesting. You get % or DPS-upgrades by investing points, other than that not much happens.
If I take two of the games above as a comparison - the rune system in D3 (which, again, I personally do not really like) is much more appealing since it offers you lots of choices and gives you some flexibility, adapting the abilities you like to the playstyle you choose. Torchlight 2 goes a more traditional way of leveling and getting abilities, but every few levels you not only get more damage or a longer lasting effect of abilities, you also get a different benefit for investing more than a few levels in a certain skill.
My two main points of criticism, and to me those are enough not to recommend the game, since pretty much all you do in GD is fight and level your char. And if the combat system is weak and leveling is run-of-the-mill (but not exactly bad), that is enough (
) to not like it and to not recommend it to other people, especially since there are several other games, which are more exciting.
I would recommend this game for anyone who is thinking it looks good because it is a great and addicting game to play even if you die it makes you want to start again and learn from your mistakes.

TL;DR:
you paid 28 euro to enter a dinosaur themed rollercoaster, the title says "jurrasic park rollercoaster", but the decor says "barnie the dinosaur". you ride the rollercoaster and the only choice you make is if you want to have your hands in the air or not, regardless the ride will go on. But the rollercoaster ends on the middle of the tracks, and instead of a satisfying drop you get a commercial for the second part of the rollercoaster.
gj telltale
you'd think telltale would try their best with an IP as enormous as GOT, but their efforts seem mediocre at best.
They first place you in a very interesting setting, and introduce you to a colorful cast of characters that YOU will be playing as or at least interact with. And this seemed obvious bc that's what ASOIAF is to most people, a character-driven story.
But soon enough the characters seem to lose their initial "character" as they all seem to think the same things. Most characters you play will have the same kind of dialogue options, regardless of where they come from or who they are. Because of this, not a single character you play as, seems alive. A self-made sellsword from essos has the same kind of tame/boring dialogue options as a squire of the north. This is probably due to the fact that telltale wants us to be able to express ourselves through the character, but this doesn't seem to work if we have to express ourselves through multiple characters. it doesn't HAVE to be like that either, look at a game like "life is strange", the choices WE make are actually choices that the mc (an introverted quiet girl) would make, it feels like we are experiencing the story through her instead of puppeteering her. Instead of getting 4 boring options that would fit any character whatsoever, why not get 4 terribly brute/rogue-ish options to choose from when we play the sellsword?
but we get things that are even worse than that, dialogue that has no point whatsoever. the plot will move on regardless of which choice you make, you basically choose WHICH character dies, but not IF a character dies. (even better would be that you made a choice, and BECAUSE of the choice, a certain character dies. Which, in the world of ASOIAF/GOT is SO FRICKING EASY!!!!! HAVE YOU EVEN WATCHED SEASON 1 OF GOT, TELLTALE??!!)
Every character that could die has a "spare", meaning that if you choose to have character A dead, character B will continue the story. (so the first critique makes sense now, because all the choices fit every character)
So it's not a game of "how can i anticipate what will happen? and how can i keep most people alive?" it's a game of: "do you like guy A or guy B?"
okay, so this 'game" is not a good "game", but is it a good story to enjoy at least?
No, and telltale has done their best to make it so, yes, i know how pretentious i sound right now, but hear me out.
Season 5 of GOT has gotten a lot of critique, because the tv show has gotten further than the books on some POVs. I won't spoil anything, but a big critique is that in ASOIAF "anything can happen" and in GOT, just like in this poorly written spin-off, "anything BAD can happen". In the books and in the early seasons all characters are on equal ground, most characters have no plot armor (i said "most") and all characters can have a say in the story. In this game however, the "bad guys" (and they are portrayed as bad guys, not as a complex antagonist we know and love like in ASOIAF)
will always have the advantage, every "blow" you manage to give them will be fully healed in the next scene, you did nothing. But they can sure as hell do a lot to you, and this further increases the frustration you get from the unimpactful "choices" you make.
The plot starts very interesting, but takes very cliché twists as a rule. And a major lesson that telltale seemed  to forget is that there is no sadness without joy. During most of the game there is a constant of depressive news and terrible events, and whenever sometimes good is about to happen, it leaves before you can do anything about it. Even the original series is not so morose as this game, you'd think i'm overexaggerating at this point. eg. i tried to cheer someone up by choosing a joke, all i got back was an angry snarl. (the amount of work put into the dialogue is astounding, i cannot stress this enough)
So they have proven that they are not the best storytellers, that's a shame for a company called "telltale", but forgivable.
Because i was on the edge of my seat while playing this! The game consists of 5 chapters and the first 4 were pretty uneventful, so i was very curious to see how they were going to knot all of the character's individual stories together in the final 5th chapter. And it's actually amazing what happened!
They just didn't do it! Nope, instead you'll need to pay for another "season" of this game to know what will happen.
This is basically where i lost my sh*t, because "the walking dead" also had a second season, but at least the first season ended with a decent conclusion! if i were to buy only the first season of the walking dead, i would have experienced a "complete game" on itself. In this game nothing ends answered or "completed", instead you get a "next time, on GOT the telltale game..."
it ends with a frickin commercial for their next game.
and this goes against all the "unspoken rules" of a commercial artwork. In most books in trilogy forms, or games that have sequels, or movies,...the first product should be able to be fully enjoyed on itself. think of hunger games, mistborn, GOT, borderlands,the walking dead telltale game... It ends as a complete work on itself and asks you if you enjoyed the work enough to proceed to the next volumes.
This is what made me think that telltale did not fully appreciate the oppurtunity they got when making this game.
They threw away GOT's atmosphere in exchange for easy-to-write dialogue and plot. They even failed to recognize what the world of GOT is all about. The walking dead-visual style was cool at first because it referenced the comics, but the graphics of this game are completely seperated from the theme or story they want to tell. They have made no decisions as to what the game and theme is all about, so the dialogue has no deeper meaning than "yes" or "no".
So in the end it wasn't the decisions that telltale made that caused this game to be so bad, but ironically the lack of choices they made.

A disappointing stand alone spin off to the superior original Alan Wake
Rating 4/10
In comparison to Alan Wake the semi-follow up/spin-off Alan Wake's American Nightmare is completely different in tone verging on parody and at times full blown comedy. Sadly it doesn't work well.
The main problem being the limited setting, gone is superbly realised setting of Bright Falls from the original and in it’s place is the desert town of Night Springs. There are only three small sections to explore and you're forced to replay through each section three times as the story repeats itself, it's a cheap trick at extending the running time.
To compound this the settings aren't that interesting, sure they look pretty but by removing Alan Wake from the cold and dark forest setting from the original it loses something. The supporting cast don't help as well, three new characters, one in each location, they are badly voiced acted and don't fit in with the Alan Wake universe.
Finally the last disappointment comes in the shape of the main antagonist, Mr Scratch. Alluded to in the original he makes his appearance and then proceeds to do very little.
There are a few positives to the single player campaign. It's short enough so it doesn't over stay it's welcome and it's nice to hear the updates on characters from the original game through the use of the radios and televisions.
They've also improved the controls and animations so the fighting and general movement isn't as clunky as before and they've added an array of new enemies to fight, some of these are nice additions.
The second part to American Nightmare is the new action mode, eight or so maps where you have to hold off waves of enemies for ten minutes or so until it is dawn. It's a survivor gametype and it plays quite nicely, however it doesn't really belong in the Alan Wake universe which was rich on story and setting. It feels tacked on and as though it belongs to another game.
So if you have the original Alan Wake and enjoyed it there isn't much to recommend here and if you haven't played the original Alan Wake avoid this follow up at all costs and play  the far superior original.

Date: 2/4/16
Review Number: 9
Game: Lethal League
From (Creator Publisher): Team Reptile
Played On: Steambox (Steam Controller)
Steam Price as of Review: $13.99
Total Time played: 45 Minutes
Review:
Admittedly, this is not a game that has come up on the randomizer.  In fact, I think I have decided that once every nine or ten days I think I am going to play a game of my own choosing, in order to balance out the reviews, and to keep me from going crazy.  So I figure the best way to start off my ‘player’s choice’ series would be Lethal League, a multiplayer smash fest from Team Reptile.  Now, I admitted earlier that I really wasn’t that big on fighting games, and in fact often just pounded the controller like I was asking for another beer at a crowded bar hoping the other guy walked into my punches.  I confess now that there was one unmentioned exception to that statement, and that was the classic Nintendo 64 version of smash brothers.  I actually spent a significant amount of time refining my skill in that game, partially because it was a fighting game I was actually fairly decent at, but more because it was oodles of fun, and a great game to play with friends.
Fast forward a decade and change, and we have Lethal League, which is a rehashing of the typical multiplayer chaos on the screen everyone pounding controllers while jumping up and down and ‘accidentally’ kicking each other while playing sort of game, only this time with the added fun of dodgeball rules added in.  See, instead of simply smashing each other directly, players instead knock a little color coded ball back and forth with the goal of hitting someone else, knocking them out until the next serve.  Difficulty is added as the ball’s speed increases every time it is hit, giving players a reward for timing over button mashing.  Each character even has their own special move, from Dice’s occasional arcing of the ball over everyone's’ heads to candyman’s wall-looping trick, each character has a way to frustrate everyone else playing.  And with both online and local multiplayer modes possible, this game will give you enough play value to make it worth any amount of money, and eventual frustration over whoever picks Latch.  Can’t recommend this one enough, folks.  Have fun!
Game’s Fate: Kept.  Also installed on the laptop.  Never know when you want another round
Buy/No Buy: Buy.  Heck, Buy a multipack and send it to all your friends.

From an audio/visual standpoint, Far Cry Primal is pretty great. To me, this is clearly the biggest strength of the game. There are so many incredible vistas/scenes, it's actually hard to find a scene in the game that isn't worth screenshotting. Combine the game's visuals with the distant echoe of primordial wildlife and you have one of the most beautifully realized prehistoric game worlds ever made. In terms of presentation, the game is actually quite stunning.
My biggest problem is that interacting with this game's vast open world feels so pointless and dull. This is an unfortunate trend in Ubisoft's open world titles. They manage to consistently create beautifully realized worlds and then fill them up with meaningless collectibles and recycled side-missions. These may be fun for you, but as someone who has spent dozens of hours in past Far Cry games - Primal is far too familiar to keep me fully engaged. There's no sense of wonder or desire to explore the world around you in Far Cry Primal because the game teaches exactly what is around every corner in the first three hours. I feel like in open world games, you should want to say " you know what, I actually think I'm gonna walk there instead of fast-traveling ". In Fallout you might find yourself in the midst of a three-way skirmish between mutants, raiders and the BoS's vertibirds. In The Witcher you might stumble upon the lair of a monster with a price on its head. This is the magic of open-world games, you lose yourself and just get sucked in by the world around you. Random events or enemy skirmishes that happen out in the world of FC: Primal are extremely predictable and overall they feel uninspired. I found myself completely ignoring them about halfway through the game. In fact, everything in the game starts to feel the same about halfway through. It almost feels there is no reason for FC: Primal to even be an open world game other than to say " Hey, look at me! I'm an open world game! Buy me!"
The sad part is that the core game is generally pretty satisfying and very fluid. I'd even say the game can be a fun way to kill an hour here and there - but I don't think it's meant to be played how other open-world games are meant to be played. The beastmaster idea is cool and ties into the Far Cry theme very well. Although, even with the best combat system, clearing out packs of enemies and animals becomes tiring after a while. The gameplay scenarios they've built around their combat system feel repetitive and poorly balanced, and if you've played a Far Cry game then you've likely seen them dozens of times before. So while riding your mammoth into a base and burning it to the ground is undeniably awesome the first time through, it gets old pretty quick.
I don't recommend Far Cry Primal at its current price (60 USD). If you've never played a Far Cry game, then you might find yourself having a good time, but in that case I would recommend maybe picking up Far Cry 3 as your first. (Far Cry 2 is great as well, but that's quite old at this point)

I was on the fence about getting this game for quite a while. It went on sale several times and I would look at reviews online and see it's praises and I wouldn't buy it because of the perception I had regarding the past saints row games. I'm simply not in to the gang war style video game with gratuitous profanity. Finally, over the new year the game went on sale again for a pretty good price and I finally committed to it.
I must admit, I was pleasently surprised. A lot f the online reviews point out the franchise takes a serious left turn with this iteration in the franchise, but I think it's a good thing it did because it reeled in someone like me who wasn't a fan of the other entries.
Graphically, the game is ok. It's not the most beautiful game on the planet in regards to modern graphical prowess, but the lighting and shading is incredibly good. Turn VSYNC on though.
The gameplay is incredibly fun. It spoofs so many movies and game franchises and does it so well. It's a barrel of laughs. Yes, there is a lot of swearing and profanity, but I honestly thought it was done well and wasn't gratuitous in its use. It's just plain funny to hear from the characters at just the right moments. It almost makes the scenes more realistic because, come on, who wouldn't say what the F--k?! if you're getting pulled up by an alient tractor beam.
I haven't completed the game so I can't speak for any game breaking bugs, if they're present.
Controls are tip top. I'd recommend a gamepad.
Audio wise, the sound effects and voices are well done. The gun fire effects are very throw away, but then again it's maybe because I've heard them in just about every other game in existence. The vocal work is very good though and very entertaining. The music is great, with licensed songs that help amplify the scene and the situation they're trying to spoof. I've replayed the opening scene about 8 times now just to hear the Aerosmith scene.
I don't think the campaign will be worth playing through again except in key areas, but for the price of admission, this game is well worth it.

The anti-USSR message shoved in the player's face during the campaign is insufferable. I play video games to be a part of epic battles, glorious tales of heroism and so on. Not to have a game tell me how to look at the world via the cheapest means possible; practically verging on Homefront levels of lazyness in the propaganda department. Except here the narrative is trying to convince you that you are the bad guy and you should feel bad, because the Soviet Union is bad okay, remember communism is bad, and Stalin is satan and... stuff...
The units aren't anything more interesting than the original's and it feels like there are a few basic roles missing, as if they couldn't be bothered to add more units. More than half the generals are "premium" aka you need to buy them. Visually it's hardly up to 2010 standards if even, and there is no shortage of Relic DLC whoring to the point of charging for faceplates.
Public custom lobbies aren't even an option, so if you liked playing Annihilation don't plan on ever playing it with anyone but someone on your friends list. After playing a few auto-matches, so far the Germans have won almost every time. Every single one of those times, their victory could be described by the two simple words: Panther & Tiger. And I've played about an equal number of times as either side, no matter what it's always the same thing. At best the USSR dominates from the start and often gets run over by tanks in the end. After six months I expect far better balance in an RTS game, never mind the lack of any multiplayer options beyond 1v1 to 4v4.
It's also plagued by performance problems, as within almost every match there is someone who is "lagging" and some matches have even frozen at 00:01 seconds into the game. There have been instances where a little message would come up saying I've been lagging and actually kicked me but given that I have a powerful gaming PC and currently a 59Mbps download, 12Mbps upload, and a ping of 11ms; this is clearly a problem on their end. Again, this is inexcusable after half a year.

So far my experience with this game has been very, very mixed.  It comes off initially as a very fun and creative, the kind of Space RPG you with you could get more of.  Sadly, the fun of the game gives way to confusion, frustration, and all around sreaming at the screen at around sector 5.  Why you might ask?  Well, the games combat is very engrosing considering it boils down to point and click cooldown abilities.  As usual, you all your attacks stand a small chance of missing, so when you rack up two or three misses in a row at a critical momen, you might just chalk it up to a once in a great while fluke.  Theres just one problem: So far this is how I have lost every game.  And not just with a run of two or three misses, but six. Seven. Eight.  IN A ROW.  Now statistics isnt my strongest suit but I still have a calculator, and according to the games own hit/miss statistics a run of bad luck like this has a .0064% chance of happening, so way less than one out of every hundred or so fights.  And as I said, this amazingly unlikely run of misses is how I have lost evey single game so far.  Not to mention that when your ship goes ka-boom you start from the very beginning.  No saves.  No retrys.  So my experince so far is building up an awesome and capable warship and crew that you have just enought time to get attached to, and this is about when you will run into a seemingly managable fight the likes of which you have done only 20 or 30 times so far.  Well, here comes your .0064%.  Five minutes later you will find yourself gawking at the screen as volley after volley sails harmlessly past the enemy vessel while they busily burn a new observation deck in yours.   I don't know if there is some flaw in the programming for the more advanced enemies or if Im just the worlds unuckiest gamer today, but so far I have played 6 games and each one ended in a statistical impossibility.  For that reason and the sake of my blood pressure I wont be touching this one again for a while, or at least until the next update.

Here's my second try at a review of Grim Dawn.
I usually do not care about people who are basically fanboys and keep ranting about how the review is unfair and the reviewer is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥simply because he/she has got a different opinion other than their favourite game, which they sunk 100000 hours in, being the best game in the whole ♥♥♥♥ing world. And I imagine it could be really frustrating to admit that anything you invest that much time in is actually maybe not THAT good. This time the sheer stupidity and unwillingness to engage in an objective discussion about the review made me mad, so here it goes.
One of my points of criticism was that Grim Dawn was too similar to Titan Quest and could in some ways considered to be a reskin of it. IN SOME WAYS. But: 1) I had lots of other things I criticised and 2) it was not nearly my main point of me disliking the game. So let's focus on the stuff, which is not Titan Quest related, let's forget it ever existed.
I do not particularly like or enjoy Diablo 3 very much, but definitely not because of the combat system. Compared to D3, Torchlight 2 or Path of Exile, Grim Dawn feels like a stick up the♥♥♥♥♥
You are rarely required to do anything else but stand still, attack and occasionally pop a healing potion or start escaping for some time until you recovered some health in case you get some real damage.
The enemy variety is poor and mostly cosmetic. Doesn't matter if your foes are melee, ranged, magic - they all act the same way. They either run up to you and hit you or they get in range and shoot you from afar.
In MY OPINION that is pretty boring. Rembember: YOUR OPINION might be different, you might find that standing around and left-clicking without any thinking whatsoever is pretty exciting.
I think they did a pretty good job on the Devotion Tree, which borrows some ideas from Path of Exiles passive skill tree (which, by the way, is PERFECTLY fine, the borrowing thing) the rest of it is not that much of a highlight. You mostly invest points in leveling up your mastery which unlocks new abilities or you invest points in already unlocked abilities - so far so standard.
What bothers me though, is that none of these choices are very interesting. You get % or DPS-upgrades by investing points, other than that not much happens.
If I take two of the games above as a comparison - the rune system in D3 (which, again, I personally do not really like) is much more appealing since it offers you lots of choices and gives you some flexibility, adapting the abilities you like to the playstyle you choose. Torchlight 2 goes a more traditional way of leveling and getting abilities, but every few levels you not only get more damage or a longer lasting effect of abilities, you also get a different benefit for investing more than a few levels in a certain skill.
My two main points of criticism, and to me those are enough not to recommend the game, since pretty much all you do in GD is fight and level your char. And if the combat system is weak and leveling is run-of-the-mill (but not exactly bad), that is enough (
) to not like it and to not recommend it to other people, especially since there are several other games, which are more exciting.

This game is fun to learn, by all means! It's an attractive, well-themed, humorously tongue-in-cheek city sim. The radio personalities, the music, and the graphics all contribute to an entertaining experience that will keep you riveted for easily ten maps.
However, once you've got the basics down - about 15 missions into the campaign, if you've bothered - there's really no reward for you to keep playing. Every island follows the exact same pattern, every playthrough is identical. The campaign missions themselves are really pathetic, with a lame plot for each mission stretched over way too many pointless and time-wasting checkpoints. The auto-generated faction and foreign power tasks are predictable and lame as well, and utterly ignorable most of the time.
The biggest challenge in the game comes from street planning - no joke. By the time your economy has matured, the layout of roads on your island is the only thing that can shut you down. If you have too many intersections, say goodbye to ever turning an export profit ever again. No one seems to be sure if these traffic management problems were entirely intentional, or an idea that snowballed into a monstrosity. I'm told the Modern Times expansion's "Metro" building helps with this, but truly, why bother?
Tropico 4 offers no reward for mastery or sustained interest, but can offer about 20 hours worth of good clean fun. It's worth picking up on sale if nowhere else, but I'd steer clear of the DLC; save yourself a few bucks.

Everybody has their tastes, and I STRONGLY suggest you at least give this game a try. You get a free two hours afterall. You can be a fisherman in this game or a trader, but you'll feel the same way doing both of those activities, although they are so diverse. so now that we have that out of the way, I will say that this is one of the best Sandbox games that I have played in ages.

For a long time, I've seen this game pop up on my recommendation list but have ignored it for one simple reason: the name. "Grey Goo" sounds like some quirky, indie game and I don't usually enjoy playing. However I recently received it as part of a HumbleBundle set which I bought for some other titles. To my surprise, this is actually a very well done and polished game. I was pleasantly surprised by the quality of the CG Cinematics. Imagine my surprise when I realized that there was a nice CG Cinematic between every mission!
And if you're wondering, parts were done by the Weta Workshop in New Zealand, which is Peter Jackson's (of Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit movie fame) FX studio. They do really great stuff. I was also surprised to see an acquaintances' name in the credits. Did not know the studio he is at (6 foot Studios) had worked on this.
I don't know what the marketing executive who approved the name "Grey Goo" was thinking, but the image that hat name implies does not reflect the nature of the game. (FYI: Grey Goo is then name of the one of the factions).
Another gripe is the huge jump in difficulty for the last mission (not bonus). Everything was manageable until that last mission where I basically had to save-scrum and (often) full-out restart the mission. I'm not the best RTS player, but I'm not terrible either.
Although it is short, it is worth a playthrough if you can get it at a decent price. Story and Visuals are wonderful and promising (though not realized to its full potential). Gameplay isn't too bad either.

The base game is amazing. The ending boss fight is the worst part about it (it's all quicktime events, when you are really expecting a full on boss battle you just get the "press A to punch" crap). But overall its a memorable experience and was in my top 5. The key word here is "was" by the way.
