As a fan of Telltale's TWD games and the ASOIAF book series, this game seemed like a no-brainer purchase.  It started off great -- You are put in charge of House Forrester, whose current situation closely mirrors that of the Starks in the tv show/novels.  You get to be present for key events from Martin's series and see some exotic locales.  The characters you play as are interesting and likeable.  The despair-heavy plot was what I expected from a game set in the ASOIAF universe and I looked forward to getting even with my enemies in later chapters.
It quickly became apparent, however, that none of the decisions really meant anything.  For example, during a dicussion with one character later in the game, every conversation option basically ends with being called a "fool" and failing in your mission.  If this 5-minute chunk of dialogue really meant nothing, then why are we forced to play it?  After I picked up on this, the feeling of powerlessness persisted through the entire game and ultimately made me regret playing it.
Pros:
1.  Viewpoint Characters - The characters are quite likeable and human.  It was refreshing to find that some characters don't fit the usualy tropes -- there are introverted characters forced into leadership roles and sellswords as honorable as they are brutal.
2.  Art - Despite what other reviewers have mentioned, I found the scenery to be engaging.  When you're in King's Landing, you can hear sea gulls and the sea breeze.  When you're across the Narrow Sea, you feel almost in another world.  This was actually one of the things I liked most about the game.
Cons:
1.  Choice System - As other reviewers have mentioned, the choice system feels rigged.  There is definitely a main "path" which is impossible to deviate from.  Prepare your defenses?  A whole bunch of enemy soldiers walk through your gates anyway.  Swallow your pride and submit to your enemies?  They still do terrible things to you.  Take pains to rescue someone?  Impossible to get them back anyway.
2.  Save Structure - There is a rewind option, so Telltale obviously wants you to be able to go back and "fix" what you perceive as mistakes, but there are only 6 save points per chapter.  At one point, I messed something up toward the end of one of these save blocks and had to replay about 10 minutes of gameplay just to correct it.  And after fixing said mistake, surprise -- The outcome was the same anyway.
3.  Unskippable Dialogue - I can understand why Telltale wants to force the story on you the first time around, but couldn't this be an option for future playthroughs?  It seems a relatively minor feature to include that would boost replayability significantly.
4.  Literary Armor - Certain characters from the novels/show are obviously bulletproof.  I found this guiding my "choices" in more than a few situations.  I found it odd that decisions could involve these characters as it narrowed my choices even further (why try to affect a character when you know exactly what they're going to do?).
5.  Unrealistic Characters - One of my biggest complaints with Telltale's TWD games was that characters were often borderline-neurotic for the sake of plot points.  This feels magnified here, almost to the point of absurdity.  The villians of the story are basically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ robots who will stop at nothing until you are humiliated and defeated, even when it serves them no purpose.  Characters in King's Landing are all obsessed with "playing the game" to the point where they behave like soap opera characters incapable of compassion and friendship.
6.  No Ending - The ending of this game disappointed me more than any game I've ever played, save Mass Effect 3.  It felt unrealistic and unrewarding.  Pretty much just a vehicle for setting up the next game.
Ultimately, I feel that Telltale went too far in invoking the "rules" of GRRM's series and in doing so took out all feeling of accomplishment necessary in a game.  The plot provides virtually no pay off for even your most well-thought out decisions and is basically, as other reviewers have said, a depression simulator.  To me, this game is essentially a visual novel with quicktime events set in the ASOIAF universe.

Purchased game at gamestop at the first available oppurtunity in April of 2014. Gamestop was the only place you could get it at the time besides directly from their website. I excited anticipated the game for over 6 months, finding out as it got closer to release that they were releasing cool weapon drop tickets for each week that you pre-ordered the game. Well as I said before I had pre-ordered the game and its season pass back in April of 2014, so I was like,"No way, I'm going to have a ton of awesome gear then since I've got roughly 8 months worth of these bonus items. Oh, and an exclusive game mode for multiplayer since I took the risk of investing so early by pre-ordering. Okay cool, thanks Techland, now I'm super stoaked. A game studio that appreciates the risk of investment that people take buying games so early.
The reality, for me, couldn't have been further from the truth. For starters, I learned while playing co-op with a friend that the steam version of the game (which wasn't available for purchase till ~September of 2014) had exclusive content that my gamestop version couldn't access, items as simple as a low-tier police baton with spikes. Furthermore I only had 5 of those special tickets for exclusive roll-of-the-stupid-dice weapons. I dug a little deeper and found that that very "promo" was only from the beginning of the month of december, forward. At this point I already felt like I had treated a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I kept my head up, cause hey I still got the exclusive game mode for pre-ordering right? WRONG:> within a month of release that status was revoked and all players could do it. Now before you write all of this off as whining or ♥♥♥♥♥ing, keep in mind the game mode "Be the Zombie" was originally intended as a rare event where a player could enter another player's game at night. It was never originally intended to be a common sighting. On top of this connections at release were very shotty and broken as well.
So, onto the actual game itself and the dlcs. All in all, a waste of space. Dishonored + State of Decay = Dying Light. Bugs were numerous for months, zombies walking through walls, players getting stuck in the ceilings of interior rooms, and so on. On top of that anyone you co-op with isn't another individual in the game or another random survivor. No, they're you, literally you go around the map like freaking clones from Kamino. The only "customizations" there are, is choosing what pair of pants your character wears/outfit and whatever weapons you find. The story started off quite well but then a major plot whole happened, and then it all just went downhill from there. I remember thinking,"okay this has to be almost over....right?" WRONG, "70% Completed" --it felt endless. And then you take a trip on acid basically, the major plot whole shows up again and then you get to the final part just to find out that "Hey it's great in co-op! Co-op is where it's at!"---"THE FINAL SCENE IS SINGLEPLAYER ONLY!"---and then you go through all this cutscene push a key to take 1 step at a time. Literally like,"press q to jump to the left, press S to take a step right, and so on..."
Mechanics and core gameplay wise, its fine...standard these days. DLC...lacking--so boring I didnt even care to finish it. The game falls flat the longer you play it. Yes I know eventually everyone burns out, but its almost like an accelerated burn.
In the end, I wanted to like this game. I really did, but I wish I could get my $90.00 and 69 hours back. Its a money scam and anymore all they care about is making their next dollar. Don't let them fool you, because it's not CDProjektRed, its Techland. I won't be buying another one of their games for a longtime due to just the sheer disappointment. I really expected more from a game that had been delayed. Granted missions and a number of things were changed between the E3 showcase and the game's actual release and the changes weren't for the better.

Grey Goo provides a slightly above average single player experience and has some interesting ideas behind it, but while the cinematics, soundtrack, and distinct factions wooed me, the lack of mission variety and final mission balancing do much against it. The straight sci-fi story also has an uninspiring conclusion with the mini-campaign, Emergence, being the only way to gain a better understanding of the true big bad.
I completely ignored the multiplayer, but it’s important to note, that there are four factions available for the online portion of the game. I believe the population is mostly dead which means you’d need to bring a friend if you wanted to see how the multiplayer matches work out.
With the single player, you’re exposed to three very different factions in this order: the Beta, the Humans, and the Grey Goo. They all have a playstyle unique to themselves with units separated into Light, Heavy, Air, and Epic categories. The Beta are the most flexible in terms of base building and can easily create forward positions or secondary bases so long as your units have vision of the area. You can expect to drop Small, Medium, and Large hubs all over the place for the expansion your territory. The Beta’s defensive structures consist of walls with the capability of housing a unit that can fire from them.
The humans, on the other hand, need to lay down power lines to expand and grow. Buildings require power to function and need an unbroken power line to keep them supplied. Depending on the tech upgrades you choose, only a couple of the turrets can power themselves and remain a threat, even if the enemy destroys your conduits. The conduit mechanics means you can only lay down lines so far before running into a no build zone in the form of a steep path, mountains, or rivers. To mine resources points beyond you reach, you need to scout with a unit to provide vision before you can drop an extractor after selecting the idle refinery. After that, it’s up to you to protect your extremely vulnerable supply lines, but keep in mind that extractors are free to build and the refineries can stay protected inside of your main base.
Beta refinery outposts are costly losses (Small Hub + Refinery at least) if resources aren’t spent to defend them. Another interesting thing to note is how both races need to spend population on defenses when it comes to building turrets or having units mount walls which prevents super turtling.
Now when it comes to the Grey Goo, they can’t turtle at all. In fact, they have no buildings to speak of or even any air units. This faction is meant to stay on the move with the HQ (Mother Goo) able to scale cliffs and create more Mother Goos, in addition to the normal army units. The anti-air and artillery units can climb cliffs too for that ever-important height advantage. Their anti-air units also appear to be the strongest in the campaign. The Mother Goo and the Proteans (formless Goo that haven’t been ordered to turn into regular units) can go around consuming enemy units and providing a movement debuff to make them easier to eat. I really enjoyed being able to move around and reposition myself when defending my location seems like a futile effort. Retreat, regroup, and recapture, the Grey Goo way. The mobile nature of this faction makes their ambushing game strong since you have the option to descend from cliffs in addition to hiding in pockets of forest. It’s too bad the unit selection sounds are a bit annoying for the most part.
There are still more aspects of this game to touch on, including the importance of scouting, the tech upgrades, and Epic units. Scouting can mean the difference between victory or watching your army crumble from hidden enemy artillery units or fast bombers. I usually don’t build scouts in the RTS’s I play, but in Grey Goo, I deliberately queued them up for production due to how vital vision is. There is a massive difference between the vision of a scout and regular units. You need them to expose enemies lying in wait, to expose units attacking you from out of visual range, and to expand your territory. Remember, if you can see it, you can build there.
There are five categories of tech upgrades available for each faction. They can how some units function by granting them different passives or additional functions. You can have buildings heal themselves over time, give ground infantry a way to shoot down air units, and even give certain scout units stealth or the ability to detect stealth. Your choice is permanent so picking the right one for the situation can help you greatly. Even a “wrong” choice will help you out still, just maybe not as much.
Finally, Epic Units. Each faction has their own. The Beta have a flying fortress, the Hand of Ruk, that you can mount units on to help defend it from enemy units that close in on it. Anything else in range can say hello to a little missile with explosive ambitions. The humans have the Alpha which fires a huge laser that melts everything in directing in front of it. The Grey Goo have the Purger which supplies Mother Goos with resources, has a ranged tentacle attack, eats units for breakfast, climbs cliffs, but all without anti-air.
Whew. So what the game do wrong? Well, the mission structure feels repetitive. You’re mostly going to different points of interest on the map, eliminating all opposition, or reaching the exit of the level. The campaign is set up in a way where it’s about 5 missions per faction (I think the humans have 6). The only real sense of difference that’s communicated to the player is the playstyle of the faction. Without interesting mission objectives or dynamically changing maps (in the sense of doing A causes B to happen), the game fails to pull itself up from the “Well, this experience is okay.” feeling. I wasn’t a big fan of the thankfully few stealth portions either.
I also didn’t care for the huge difficulty spike of the last mission. I just went ahead and watched the ending on Youtube before going onto Emergence and finishing that for the lore about the Silenct Ones. It went from being mostly pleasant ride into an overwhelming feeling of despair with an ending cutscene that just wasn’t worth it. It just expected a level of micro-management that I didn’t have when for the rest of the game, I could build up my armies and with a little finesse, conquer the map that way.
I did like the tunes though and put the songs into my music folder. They also put the same amount of effort into the gorgeous cutscenes. Do you like skin pores and robot faces? I hope you do because they do them real well here.
This game isn’t fantastic or great. Sometimes, it’s good. It’s mostly just going to be okay. I hoped to see more Red Alert come through in terms of storytelling, but hey, if they don’t want to include humor, that’s fine. Just have a proper conclusion. I'll mention that I bought the game in a $1 tier from Humble Bundle and it's definitely worth that or a sale price. I'm not too sure about the $30 regular, but I'll leave that up to you.

Do you ever just stare deep into your soul at a mirror overanalyzing your life? Deep in thought, just wondering, pondering even; over what is and once was? With all these memories flooding in, you can't help but feel lost. This happened to me and during that small silent exchange with myself, I feel like a part of me went missing. I walked into the bathroom and looked at the cornerside wall. On that wall was a mirror, and on the mirror, my hideous face. I stared deep into my own eyes. During this intense macho-man staring competition I couldn't help but feel regret. I had entered this small world within myself. It was a barren and bleak space, consisting of nothing but solemn and disdain. Deep inside my head I rocked back and forth while many faint and distant memories replayed. I couldn't help but remember all my missed opportunities; how would today be affected if I had made different choices back then? Would things really be all that different if I never held back? These were all questions I entertained silly in the back of my mind. Then it happened, I remembered Judy. How would today be if I had Judy by my side, I wondered. No matter how many years have passed, I still can't help but think about her. Her long and wavy black hair, her gorgeous blue eyes, her beautifully sweet smile. I couldn't let this go on any longer, this self torment. I had decided from that moment that I would pick up the phone and call her; I promptly left the bathroom. Now, I know what you're thinking, well, what happened?! Well, I'll tell you what happened. I ♥♥♥♥ed a dead moose.

For those wondering if the Nep franchise is for them...
Main appeal of nep franchise for me: 1. Humor 2. RPG 3. art / voice acting
Humor: Metafiction (you'll see this word a lot in the reviews) related to the culture of anime and games, and even specifically RPGs. Meaning, the more of your life you've spent with those, the funnier these games will be. The main character is also ridiculous funny, and she amounts for about 85% of my interest in the series (I'm midway through the third game and have gotten into the spinoffs too). I play Nep games because Neptune makes me laugh. I'd recommend refunding and deciding against the series if the opening scenes of this one fail to get at least a smile from you.
RPG: Crazy cluster**** game of explore all the dungeons, craft all the things. They've really gotten into the psychology of RPG players with this crafting system. I feel like I'm stuffing my face with cake nonstop while playing this.
Art / Voice Acting: The visual novel scenes are nicely done, the character images do emotes, have a subtle breathing animation, and mouth movements. The world is an inspired anime sci-fi setting. The game is filled top to bottom with voice acting, and nearly everybody on the (Japanese) cast is an anime industry regular (Horie Yui, Hanazawa Kana, for example).
Fanservice is present, it isn't why I came here but it's tolerable, usually it's at least humorous if nothing else, and the excessive fanservice is optional. I was kind of afraid of how obtrusive it would be from the steam screenshots before I played, but it's more of a sideshow than the main content.
Finally just some notes on the series. Fine to start here, but it doesn't connect to the storyline of 2 and 3 (though it establishes the main characters). 2's plotline continues to 3, but instead of Neptune, her little sister is the main character, and so the game sort of lacks...it was still a fun game but skipping to 3 wouldn't be a mistake in my opinion. I LOVE 3 so far. The TV anime adaptation from 2013 doesn't connect to the games directly but uses some characters and devices from 1-3, I enjoyed it but results may vary. 97 hours to get all achievements in Re;Birth 1, 84 to get all in Re;Birth 2... these games aren't short, but they aren't disgustingly long like Agarest, either.
10/10 best RPGs I've played in decades.

A follow-up to Alan Wake, "American Nightmare" fleshes out themes only touched on in the original. The plot is a little bit more straightforward this time around, but still leaves that feeling that you have only seen part of the bigger picture. A truly nasty antagonist, improvements to the combat engine, and an overall lighter tone, go a long way to make this game feel like a completely viable chapter in the Alan Wake storyline. Just don't be shocked when the "Groundhog's Day" structure betrays the games modest budget; or when the improvements to the combat make the game more action oriented, thus breaking some of the tension found in the previous title. If you enjoyed Alan Wake, this is a necessary chapter. If you didn't, there isn't anything here that is likely to change your misguided opinion.

People may wonder why I'm reviewing a game I've only got a little more than an hour into. The answer to that is simple. The first part of a game is crucial to the whole experience, and the start of this game didn't impress. The review they proadly wear from PC Gamer says "...it could very well rival TF2 for approachability, quirkiness, and staying power" This may be true, except the approachability isn't there.
When you start the game you only have access to one of 3 different free champions, and they may mostly be advanced or they may be starter. It's all about when you play the game, and this does work with some games. Which brings me to what I think is the source of most of the problems "It worked for League of Legends."
The "Hero" system is basically the same right down to the cycling free champions, but it's not as good because League has better assigned roles that are obvious, and 2 skill based heroes can play very differently from each other. This means that starting out can be more challenging because you're playing with things you don't understand. On a side note to this. Why can't I play the characters that look cool? I'm stuck choosing between Mr. fishbowl-head, a robot, and a pop star. All of this combines to make starting the game hard.
It may be fun to play later on, and I'm sure that high level play is awesome; but in multiplayer games players are content, and I feel like I'm being cheated becaues I want to see if I like the game before shelling out $5 for the champion I thought I'd be able  to play from the start. I know that it would be hard to get people to purchase champions if they were free, but here's an easy solution. Temporary/noob heroes. You could let players who have just started have a few free heroes for the first 5 rounds they play, and then after 5 rounds those heroes are accessed the exact same way they are now, but it would prevent a player from having to either be a boring support hero or being unable to due to choosing a cool hero that relies on advanced tactics.
If this was how the game worked it would get an resounding yes from me for being cool and unique and all the other things it does well, but if it's hard to start then it doesn't matter how good it is because not many people will reach the good part.
Side note: People say that it has a good F2P model, but it feels pay2 win to me. In my first game I was dominated by a yeti who pummeled me with infinite snowballs, and I know he either got that hero by.
A) Spending money to buy him (and as he had a skin that's what I'm guessing got him that hero)
Or.
B) Playing the game for a long time. Which makes me wonder why a noob got matched with people who have a lot of experience.

The anti-USSR message shoved in the player's face during the campaign is insufferable. I play video games to be a part of epic battles, glorious tales of heroism and so on. Not to have a game tell me how to look at the world via the cheapest means possible; practically verging on Homefront levels of lazyness in the propaganda department. Except here the narrative is trying to convince you that you are the bad guy and you should feel bad, because the Soviet Union is bad okay, remember communism is bad, and Stalin is satan and... stuff...
The units aren't anything more interesting than the original's and it feels like there are a few basic roles missing, as if they couldn't be bothered to add more units. More than half the generals are "premium" aka you need to buy them. Visually it's hardly up to 2010 standards if even, and there is no shortage of Relic DLC whoring to the point of charging for faceplates.
Public custom lobbies aren't even an option, so if you liked playing Annihilation don't plan on ever playing it with anyone but someone on your friends list. After playing a few auto-matches, so far the Germans have won almost every time. Every single one of those times, their victory could be described by the two simple words: Panther & Tiger. And I've played about an equal number of times as either side, no matter what it's always the same thing. At best the USSR dominates from the start and often gets run over by tanks in the end. After six months I expect far better balance in an RTS game, never mind the lack of any multiplayer options beyond 1v1 to 4v4.
It's also plagued by performance problems, as within almost every match there is someone who is "lagging" and some matches have even frozen at 00:01 seconds into the game. There have been instances where a little message would come up saying I've been lagging and actually kicked me but given that I have a powerful gaming PC and currently a 59Mbps download, 12Mbps upload, and a ping of 11ms; this is clearly a problem on their end. Again, this is inexcusable after half a year.

I would say that this game is neither better nor worse than the first one. It has its own pluses and minuses. Here's what I thought they were:
PROS:
+ 4 people in the party now! That was really exciting for me, cause in Re;Birth1 I always wanted to have all 4 CPUs, as well as the candidates, in one battle but that was never possible. Now it was, and I thought that was a nice addition.
+ I liked that the dungeons weren't all recycled versions of the dungeons we saw in the first game. Some look similar to those but most of them were new designs. Even the 4 cities were redesigned, and I think they look way cooler.
+ Plenty of different endings and outcomes to add to the replayability value. One of the endings in particular, the Conquest Ending, was DARK AS HELL. I mean holy crap, I've seen bad endings in video games before but this one was like, really intense. Not even Nep's humor was able to soften it for me.
+ Stella's Dungeon was a nice new feature as well. You're able to send Stella off to dungeons to find items while you continue on with the game.
+ Just like in Re;Birth1 with the sisters, you can bring in the Oracles of each city into the game to join your party. I haven't done that but I'm working on it. The requirements are pretty high, but I'm determined. They have very cool designs.
+ I guess I should put that there's a lot more boobage in the game. I mean it's not really my cuppa tea, but y'know. For all you pervs out there, I'm sure you'll be happy to know that the game wastes no time in shoving everything in your face, so to speak.
CONS:
- Besides the extra person in the party, there's really no new additions to the combat at all.
- Less customizability was something I noticed. The outfit selection in particular was a lot more limited. In Re;Birth1, there were a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of outfits in the shop. Now, though, they seem much fewer.
- Not enough Nep-Nep! I don't know about you guys, but Nepgear was such an underwhelming heroine to me. She's just so... I don't know. I mean she's likeable and all, but she doesn't have as big of a presence as Neptune did. I was gleeful when Nep-Nep finally appeared and started talking, but it wasn't enough. :c I know Nepgear was supposed to be the star of this game but she didn't feel like one at all. I just kept waiting for Nep-Nep to appear. If you're a huge fan of Neptune herself, then I'm sorry to say she's not in this game much at all.
- This is sorta tied with the not enough Nep-Nep thing. The game has much less funny moments or humor at all. Besides Neptune, Red is pretty much the only FUNNY character in my opinion. Besides that, the plot itself isn't all that engaging. Not that the first game's plot was amazing or anything, but y'know, at least it was fun to sit through due to the character interactions. In this one the characters are just meh, I think. Nepgear especially.
Overall there are many things they could've done to make this much better than the first game, as a sequel should be, but I'm still pretty happy with it and having a blast playing it so far, so I definitely recommend it despite its flaws. Plus, I saw several trailers for Re;Birth3 and it seems like they're renewing a lot of the features with that game, so I'm pretty excited!

But to be fair, Primal is missing some multiplayer interaction, despite the developers' comments about trying to make Primal as immersive as possible, you know that "immersion" is completely diminished the moment you chuck a spear into a bear's head and it doesn't die instantly :P
It would've been nice if there were was some tribal wars element, potential for teamwork, roleplaying like hunter, beastmaster, tracker etc. and affiliations like Udam, Izila, and Wenja, but actual players in a larger scale of Oros. For those who don't know what I'm talking about I mean this game could've used a large-scale, slow paced team-deathmatch system, or tribal wars, in terms of PVP (Player versus Player), if not a role playing PVE (Player versus Environment).
But I suppse this game was somewhat rushed into it's current status by hasty decisions and perhaps a conservative approach to funds by sticking to old engines and saving even more by not implementing such "unnecessary" innovations.
Either way I give this game a 9/10, and give a word of caution in that this game is an acquired taste at this point, if you LOVE hunting/stealth games with primitive weapons, and if you LOVE having savage beasts at your command, this is the game for you :)

If the other Far Cry games are as good as this, then I totally regret waiting until Primal to start playing the Far Cry games. I love lots of things about this game:
Graphics are amazing. It's definitely a game you can immerse yourself in, especially if you turn off the HUD. The grasses and leaves blow in the wind, the lighting through the canopy is the best lighting I've ever seen and there are cool ambient sounds.
Original setting: It's a refreshing setting that takes us away from the played out zombie/apocalypse/military shooter setting and places us in the Stone Age.
Weapons: It's amazing how many cool weapons they actually fit in the game, spears, arrows, bee bombs, throwing shards, etc. and most are upgradeable. And you get an owl as a scout and your tamed animals can fight with you.
Animal taming: You can tame and ride a sabretooth tiger!
Animal AI: The animals wandering around act on their own and create unique interactions. You might walk around the corner to see a fight between two brown bears (Bear Fight!) or an eagle swoop down and take the goat you were about to shoot.
Now for some of the bad:
I'm 30 hours in and the game mechanics are getting a little repetive and boring. I've tamed all the animals and upgraded all the huts. So now I've just decided to do the main quests and get it over with, haha.
Some of the mammoths kind of teleport in out of nowhere which kills the immersion a little bit.
It's pretty easy especially once you get a cave bear or sabretooth tiger to tear people apart. If you like a challenge, crank up the difficulty. Or don't use your animal companion. That ramps up the difficulty especially at night when there are more predators around.
But that's about it.

This will appeal to the SimCity people, but it has it's own merits that better itself from the SimCity games to.
The merits are:
The goal isn't just to make a constant stream of income, if you do that on SimCity you can get bored soon enough, this has challenges more meaningful than the lastest SimCity, that has cash rewards, as well as rewards such as building relationships with foreign superpowers, which improving will get you long term rewards, there's also rewards with specfic people.

So it has the building blocks of SimCity, but it's more fun in the long run because you have to work and even if you get a steady income your job isn't done there. It goes more into being a leader than just building a city. And with that it's a lot more fun.

Definitely worth the full price. I know everybody says that about a lot of different games (I bought games with reviews like that and the game turned out to be lackluster) But it is true with this game.
One life per session ups the tension, the drive to win, and to beat your last score.
Procedurally generated. Sometimes you'll get to an area and be rewarded with scraps (the game's currency) or other times you'll run into a pirate ship kitted out with a 3-burst laser guns, a combat drone, in front of a star that sets various rooms on fire at timed intervals.
There is so much to unlock and so many different combat styles to choose from. Do you place an emphasis on aggressive attack lasers? Do you tank your shields to max and rely on your starting weapons to get the job done? Do you go all out and kit your system out with 2 combat drones and a defense drone to shoot incoming lasers/ missles? Do you hire the toughest crew to board an enemy ship and tear them apart from the inside out? Do you get a mind control system and force your enemies to attack each other while you volley laser fire for good measure? Or do you mix and match these tactics and many more.
PSA: UPGRADE EVERYTHING BEFORE YOU ENTER THE LAST SECTOR. It's your last chance before you face the battlion and the enemy flagship.
So many ships to unlock. I think there is around 50. Each ship has 3 types plus a few hidden ships.
The soundtrack is great. (Google it to find a pay-what-you-want download) The songs have been stuck in my head for the last few days.

Dying Light is the greatest zombie/parkour game of all time, hands down. The amount of freedom this game provides is mind blowing. Four player co-op is beyond fun. Dropping in and out of games transferring all items and progression is a wonderful feature. The pvp is intense and is a nice feature implemented that can be turned on or off during the night cycle. If you're playing co-op with night invasion enabled, players can drop in as night hunters (mutated zombie jumper things) and the objective for the humans is to destroy the nests while the hunter must deplete human player lives. If you're in for playing solo, you not be disappointed. The campaign (main missions) provides an excellent story and gets better and better as you progress. Also, increased difficulty brings a whole new approach and realism to the zombie apocolypse. Game difficulty can be changed at anytime. On easy/normal difficulty,  you'll hack and slash your way through the game. In hard mode difficulty, you'll find yourself conserving ammo, standing on objects, running more frequently, etc. If you play on Nightmare... I'll let you find out for yourself.
With the enhanced edition, graphics were improved and have added a legend system for end-game players to further improve their character progression. There's tons of missions, different weapons, blueprints/crafting, scavengable items, and an all new expansion area called the following. The AI are smart. You'll be attacked by numerous types of different zombies and creatures, depending on the cycle of night or day. Not only are you attacked by zombies, but by other humans as well who are armed and deadly. Human enemies are much more deadly than your average zombies. They will swarm you and beat the living life out of you, block/evade your attacks, and sometimes escape if need be. That's where the almighty realism to firearms come into play. Finding a firearm for the first time is like finding a golden ticket to the chocolate factory. If another human player has a firearm, challenge accepted. What's also phenominal is the parkour and combat. The freedom to combat gives players numerous ways to fight enemies. The freedom to exploration/parkour gives players access to the entire map, with numerous ways to approach different locations. On the edge of RPG-like features, you can level up your character in four different trees, purchase skills, enhance weapons with status effects (blueprints), and outfit your character appearance.
With the enhanced edition and all the dlc, updates, end-game legend system, improved visuals, and items, this game is 9.5/10 hands down. You will not find another game like Dying Light. It's a gem and always will be. I would give a 10/10 but several of the voice actors for certain characters on side missions are horrific. That's my only complaint. I find myself skipping their skits in annoyance. Most of the excellent voice actors are found in the main story missions.

FTL is flat out amazing! I went into this game not knowing what to expect thinking, "I'll play for about an hour and see what happens." Yeah 7 hours later I'm trying a new ship with nothing but glee on my face.
FTL is a rougelike game in which you keep hurling yourself at a wall until you or the wall breaks. Is there a chance you'll beat the final boss? High is no, but you'll earn points and/or unlock a new ship. A new ship means a new way of playing and new layouts for your ship.
Instead of cinematic cutscenes it uses messages letting you know if your crew got eaten by space spiders. It's much more thoughtful making you think about your next careful step. You never know if a enemy ship will spring on you. That's when you micro manage your crew to either boost systems or repair damage to your ship as you target key points to your ship.
There were times I wanted my friend to play the game while I dress as a Star Trek captain and say, "Target their weapons! Put power into the thrusters!" And it would actually mean something. Sadly yes that statement is true lol.
Sometimes this game can show how much of a evil captain you can be. For example when I was attacked by Rock people I sealed my crew in the med bay and opened the air locks to suffocate them. Then when somebody asked me for help to get them out of an asteroid I just fired a missle and took their scrap and weapons.
Sadly you need every scrap you can get. You need scrap to upgrade your ship, purchase supplies, and even hire pirates to hold back the rebels.
This game is a much needed for any PC gamer's libary. Best $9.99 I've ever spent in my life! :D

While the game itself is fun, it has been buggy as hell and a crash-fest to boot. I feel that 'The Following' DLC is more fun than the original game, but there are plenty of bugs in both versions. Your mileage may vary, as they say, and some people DO get to play this without so much as a hickup - but it seems to be a lottery. Not even a fully patched and well performing system can guarantee a good gaming session. And the game seemed to be sabotaging itself and screwing up its own files somehow, I have lost count of how many times I had to 'verify integrity of game cache' just to download a file of two.
If you have a chance to test this game on your system before purchasing, I'd advise you to do so (I'm not even sure if Dying Light has a demo, a benchmark or something, so that might not be possible).
When you do get it to run well, it's quite fun, though some of the game mechanics are unbalanced - for instance, melee weapons break apart very soon (and can be repaired only limited amount of times) while ranged weapons have no durability stat and so function well forever, special zombies spawn almost constantly either when you make any noise (and almost everything makes a noise, even dying zombies) or just for the hell of it. The scripting is sometimes ridiculous - after plowing through an area and pretty much ridding it of zombies, new ones (and special ones at that) are instantly spawned just because you accepted a mission in the area. This makes it feel less like a living world and more of a staged drama. Some of these mechanics can be adjusted with mods, but the game doesn't seem to be all that open to modding.
The day/night mechanic is interesting but can be more or less bypassed by clever use of safe houses. I found it to be even less relevant in The Following's area.
I am on the fence about this one - when it could be coerced to work, it was more-or-less fun game (with several serious drawbacks), but more often than not, it just bugged out, failed to run or crashed. As I said, your mileage may vary, but for me, it's a thumbs down.

A game for people who want to go blind and die exclusively from ships that fly into them by accident.
Most of what's been said of the game doesn't need repeating - check just about any negative review and it'll tell you that the game is repetitive. Yes, it is. Unless you plan on buying the DLC (which I haven't), you'll play as the same ship fighting the same enemies across the same two (three if you count Chill Out) gamemodes. Which begs the question: Why do I still recommend it?
This game is not for lovers of the shoot 'em up genre. It's for people who love their music - people who can lose themselves through the majesty of the shuffle function and not need much stimulation to complement it. It's not next-level stuff. It's not going to blow your mind with what it does differently from its peers. Its experience doesn't come from the gameplay alone - Just check the first sentence of its description!
Beat Hazard, while not having as much content as one may like for a game of its caliber, doesn't cut corners. The visuals are very nice (even at 50%, which is the only way I can play), the ship handles well, hit detection performs as it should, and all in all, I have not encountered any glitches throughout my playtime. While I certainly would have liked more ships, bosses, power-ups, perks, and gamemodes (all of which are boasted in the DLC, which, again, I did not purchase), the amount I paid seems to fit the bill, and I'd personally prefer a smaller selection rather than an oversaturation of needless content. (Come on, who wants to bother memorizing boss attack patterns in a music game?)
There are certainly better games out there - better shoot 'em ups, better music games, what have you - but Beat Hazard should be treated as something meant to enhance your musical experience rather than as a standalone game. If you want to get lost in the game, certainly try something else more suited to your tastes. But if you're ready to get lost in your own music library again, don't rule it out just yet.
(This game was purchased on sale, and I have not purchased the DLC expansion. Given the amount of content there is, I would recommend that others do the same!)

Somehow, people keep coming up with new spins on the well-worn tower defense genre. Tower Wars is the tower defense genre taken to its logical conclusion, a game where you both defend with towers and attack other peoples' towers. To that end it's mainly a multiplayer game, though the last major update added ten levels of bots to lose to without anyone knowing your shame. It's a good thing too, because the odds of you getting a match against a person aren't very good these days.
Each match gives you command over a castle, a barracks, and large tracts of hex-gridded land. Everything you have is mirrored by your opponent to keep things fair, of course. Your task is to send waves of attackers to destroy your foe's castle while maintaining a field of towers to defend your own castle. The resource that fuels both of these labors is gold mined from upgradable plots in your territory, so right away you have a balance that must be struck between offense and defense. In addition, your attackers earn Battle Points for the time they spend alive in enemy territory. These points are used to unlock new units, upgrade your units, and upgrade your mines.
If all this is starting to sound complicated, it is. You need to be sending troops to attack, upgrading those troops, upgrading your mines, and managing your own towers, all based out of two resource pools. And yes, just the tower defense part is full-fledged tower defense, with the ability to place upwards of a hundred towers of eight different types and three upgrade levels on a single map. Layering further complexity over that, while an interesting idea, makes the game a huge struggle to keep up with. It's basically Build Orders: The Game so if that was your favorite part of Starcraft, there might be something here for you to latch onto.
Even so, it's hard to give a positive review to a multiplayer-focused game with no player base. None of my half-dozen attempts to find a match, ranked or unranked over several days, met with success. Poking around the forums it seems there are only a few dozen active players left, and there may be something wrong with matchmaking that the developers have not addressed. It's just as well, because the complexity pushes it up into DOTA territory, long matches and all. A single round can last thirty minutes to an hour, and a loss after all that time really hurts because it earns you nothing. There are no unlocks or points or anything to chase, just match after match. And when you can't even find one, that's a problem.

A class-based multiplayer fps that challenges players to create complex defenses and destroy their enemy's using voxel destruction and building.  Teamwork matters and there are balancing issues but it is free-to-play and not too grindy.
Block N Load (BNL) really has no story to speak of.  A diverse group of characters band together in two teams of five and square off against eachother in different arenas.  Each "hero" has a paragraph about who they are but don't expect a dossier on their life experiences.  The omnipresent announcer is the only other character in the game beyond the heroes.  No complex motivations or intriguing lore here; two teams, one winner, one loser, simple.
What is not simple about this game is how it is played.  At first glance, it appears to be a hybrid between Team Fortress 2 and Minecraft.  I consider this an apt description, but the numerous ways in which a match can be won differentiate it from other games similar to it.  While there are casual multiplayer and single player challenge modes, BNL's primary game mode is the multiplayer mode known as "Classic".  The object of this mode is to destroy the enemy's base (represented as a large cube) while simultaneously protecting your own.
At the pre-game lobby, you and your teammates each select a role, hero, perks, blocks, hero skin and vote for one of two maps.  Role can switched at will any time in game and is merely a way to let your teammates know how you intend to play.  My experience has been you need to be able change roles at a moments notice if needed.  Each match starts with a build phase where you and your team gather resources and build up defenses on your side of the arena.  Every hero has a unique "dig tool" that allows them destroy and mold voxel arenas as they see fit.  Time management is crucial here because spending too much time gathering resources can leave your base under-protected.  Once the build phase ends, the attack phase begins and both teams commence trying to destroy eachother's base.  As a defender, your job is to build health/ammo for your other defenders, kill attackers, and fortify your base with useful device blocks, such landmines and radars (allow you to see enemies if they are within the effect sphere).  Turret matrices, landmines, fake blocks that cause enemies to fall into a pit of bear traps, BNL is full of ways to creatively defend your base.  Offense is tasked with destroying the enemy cube (sometimes arenas have more than one) which requires destorying the enemy's defenses and killing enemy defenders.  This requires placing respawn pads to keep pressure on the enemy, quick arena navigation, and coordinated attacks that overwhelm the enemy defenders.
Each hero has his/her own passive and active ability that aid in combat.  Active abilities make destroying some defensive setups easier so choosing a diverse team is recommended.  Heroes have two weapons each that often have alternate fire functionalities to complement the heroes playstyle.  For example, the engineer has a shotgun for killing enemies and a caulking gun for fixing/buffing his turrets and slowing down enemies.  Perks as well as the blocks you choose to bring into a match also determine how you will pay your character.  The emphasis of BNL is teamplay so time your abilities and weapon usages well to achieve maximum effectiveness in a game.  The BNL team is actively working to address balancing issues though some may consider their progress poor considering the life of the game.
In addition to just shooting at eachother with strange weaponry, teams also fight over control of events.  During the course of a match, supply drops of 1000 bricks as well as the "blockbuster" (increases dig tool damage for your entire team) are dropped in the middle of the arena for either team to collect.  These drops usually result in heated fights for them at mid since as matches progress, respawn time increases and staying alive becomes important.   Collecting the supply drop can starve your enemy and the blockbuster can mean the difference between winning and losing.  Matches usually begin with rush tactics and end with the team that achieves a coordinated assualt.
BNL features a league system to help match players similar in skill level.  The leagues are Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Pro.  Within the metallic leagues are five subdivisions denoted with Roman numerals.  For example, players start in Bronze V and after accruing enough league points, advance to the next subdivision Bronze IV.  Acquiring league points is different in each division but no matter the divison, players can never be demoted to the previous division ( e.g. go from Bronze IV back to Bronze V or from Silver V back to Bronze I, etc.).  Advancing through leagues is not difficult until Gold where playing with a fully leveled hero is required for gaining/losing league points.  Like other games that allow you to que with your friends, higher league BNL games play host to clans and pre-made teams often (but not always) destroying teams of individuals queing.  Combine these with the usual smurfs, exploiters, stackers, and other unsavory characters you find in any multiplayer game and you may find BNL unworthy of your time.
In regard to the F2P model, BNL uses two types of currency: bricks and platinum.  Bricks, the soft currency, are earned through winning matches, losing matches, completing challenges, and leveling up your character.  You get three new challenges every 24 hours, completing all of which will earn you more than 1000 bricks.  If you don't enjoy the grind but still enjoy playing, you can pay real money for platinum, the hard currency of BNL, and things from the shop that way.  All heroes and perks (which are designed to be sidegrades, not upgrades) can be permanently bought with either soft or hard currency.  Additionally, hero skins can only be bought with hard currency.
Speaking of aesthetics, BNL has a rather unique look to it.  Heroes all have cartoonish looks and their own dialogue befitting of their personality.  The voice acting in this game is surprisingly good and some of the lines uttered by heroes are chucklye worthy.  Guns all have a nice cartoony sound to them.  Environments sport a voxel, blocky appearance that is reminiscent of Minecraft but with sharper textures and lighting.  Arenas typically feature a hot or cool color palette, while some sport a unique holiday theme or look.  Beaches, castles, and factories are all possible battle grounds ranging in size from intimate one cube maps to extremely large three cube maps.  Some arenas are relatively flat resulting in intense zerg rushes while others have surprisingly complex layouts and geography.  As matches progress, arenas become totally destroyed as explosives go off and create craters in the voxel environment.  This sandbox destruction is what makes BNL fun because no two matches playout the same in terms of how the environment is used by either team.  Aside from the main theme and menu music, BNL features no noteworthy music.  However, important events in game are preceded with a short music byte and let the player know something important is about to happen.
BNL scratches an itch for destructable envrionments and sandbox building combined with a directed multiplayer game.  Compared to experiences I've had with other games, the F2P model feels just in my mind.  It will still take a few days to grind to that character you want but the unpredictable nature of gameplay and nice looks should keep you entertained.  The league system may turn some players away so if you are not interested in competitive gameplay, stay away.  However, if you crave a multiplayer game with fun voxel destruction/building, BNL may fill that void.

Full disclosure: I bought this game at 96% off, for fifteen pence. And even at that price, I would not recommend buying this game.
This game in a word? Unrealised. The actual game has two themes -- the first being a fairly generic 'your actions have moral consequences' theme that's used extremely simplistically by giving an occasional yes/no choice, and the second being age, which is dealt with only in an exceedingly shallow capacity. While both of these themes can be compelling when written sufficiently well, the more unique and interesting one is age; most people playing videogames are fairly young or approaching middle age, so age is a topic that gets swept under the rug or only dealt with as a way to get rid of a character in most games. Given a nuanced portrayal, it could have been excellent here. It wasn't.
In terms of gameplay, it has the standard non-combat rpg maker formula -- wander around, talk to people, get information, solve puzzles. Most rpg maker games will attempt to flavour their world beyond the basic graphics by giving interesting flavour text on clickable items, a feature I adore. True, this game does have many clickable items, and a lot of flavour text... but all of it is either very bland descriptions of what you're looking at, or immature flavour text.
Actually, let's cycle back to the immature bit. Do you think naked pixelated old men are funny? Do you think it's great that a good portion of your game world is compared to poo? Because that's why some of the steam pages related to this game ask for age confirmation, and the devs never seem to get tired of it. It's pretty much worthless in terms of content, both comedically and in terms of worldbuilding. It just makes the game seem like it was made by juvenile teenagers.
The writing, outside of the themes it tries and fails to tackle, is uninspiring. NPCs are both unlikeable and boring, as, in fact, are all the player characters. There simply isn't enough dialogue given -- in a format, mind you, that really *needs* dialogue and description in order to be effective -- to characterise even one of the protagonists beyond a very simple pastiche of whatever their problem is. I feel like the dev(s?) of this game aren't really familiar with creating works of art or fiction -- although, as a plus, I only noticed one glaring grammar problem (an NPC using "were" when the correct version for the context would have been "where." There were moments of writing which, although not fantastic, was at least interesting (the
was intriguing).
Poor programming is also evident; two instances that I spotted were being able to drive directly into the wall of the Pub while in my car, and the game locking up if you gave a certain item to an NPC from below. Usually, giving the item triggers the npc to down one square out of your way, and there is no exception made for the player choosing to stand there. Even accepting that there may be technical limitations in coding npc behaviour, it would have been child's play to simply make the npc move back through the passage to a square the player couldn't occupy, or alter the map slightly to ensure the player couldn't stand below the npc but the npc could still move there.
On top of that, there is a huge lack of content in this game. It can all be seen and discovered in an hour or two, with no real problem; after that, everything else is repetition and padding.
Ultimately, it feels like somebody's first game in rpg maker -- ambitious themes, poor execution. And that's perfectly fine, but not if there's an asking price. If you want a combat-light rpg maker game with better writing, more entertaining characters, and don't mind nudity (which, to be fair, this game has as well), then go and download Embric of Wulfhammer's Castle. It's free, and a shining example of what rpg maker games can do when the effort's put in considering all the detail and jokes put into the world.
If you're considering buying this as a way to support the developer/support other rpgmaker games being on steam, don't. This game also had a small kickstarter
again, considering you'll find much, much better rpgmaker games out there for free, has already created more money than the product deserves.
To improve this game, I would advise the devs to recruit somebody with some real writing experience to draw out the potential of the themes it tries to handle, and, moreover, consider whether this is really the medium the game needs in order to shine. Very little of the good points of this game would be lost if it were in a visual novel format, due to the flavour text in the environment being mostly not worthwhile, and it would give the game chance to focus on dialogues, characterisation and story while dropping the largely redundant fetch quest gameplay. I would also advise them to do a little market research and observe what the standards are for commercial games of this type.
To clarify: I think there's potential here in the themes, and if I had just downloaded it as somebody's first rpg maker project, I would be considerably more enthusiastic about it. But Greyfox is not a good enough product to demand money for, and too basic to justify the kickstarter that was attached. With more experience, this game could have been a gem. As it is? Not worth it.

Grim Dawn is a game with a surprising depth. You start the game in a small village and get send out to do some quests. At some point you can pick your first class. Yes you did read it correct,.. FIRST class. After a couple of levels the game allows you to pick a second class. Due to being able to combine two classes there are a lot of build available for you; I even dare to say that there is a build/class for everyone’s liking.
The customisation does not stop there however. While you are devoted to conquer evil and are questing though the world you come across shrines. When you activate/repair these shrines you will be rewarded by a devotion point. These devotion points enables you to choose your blessing from the stars and unlock even more skills and buffs. Unlocking these constellations with devotion-points introduces a very effective way to complete change how your build works.
A good Action Role Playing Game leans heavily on items, and Grim Dawn does just as well. Or better said; it does it better! This game enables you to craft your own gear, apply customisations/enchantments, and enables you to buy faction gear. This faction gear gets unlocked while you are doing quests for the locals, or when you are just going berserk and  annihilate the local monster population. Killing those monsters does not only increase your reputation for the local faction, but it also increases the hatred the monsters have towards you. When the hatred gets high enough, then you will encounter even stronger hero-monsters at random (had to run with the tail between legs on several occasions).
After you have completed the game (hah,.. complete a ARPG you say!,..), you can continue on a higher difficulty level. The game supports Normal (with a Veteran option), Elite and Ultimate mode.
Graphics: 8/10 (looks good, though a bit grim at times).
Sound: 8,5/10
Gameplay: 8/10 (or 9,5/10 if you are a ARPG fan).
I bought this game while it was still in Early Acces / Beta (or however it was called back then). The game has grown a lot over the years and can now truly be considered one of the pillars of the ARPG genre. The last time I had this much fun in a ARPG was back when I played Diablo 2. If you are the least bit interested in ARPGs, then I can recommend getting this game. Even for casual player there are plenty of build which enables you the relax while cruising through Grim Dawn.
See you out there!

Grim Dawns team took back what they had promised to their backers and stated that instead, you now had to choose between the Steam copy or the DRM free copy, you didn't get both.
Prior to this drama, I was banned from their forums for modding their game, something they now encourage. However, my ban was never removed and was only done out of spite because the lead developer of the game hates me. I released some mods for the game that showed more or less weaknesses in his ideas of security. Mind you, none of this was released on the official forums. But since he can't take any form of critisim or feedback, I was banned.

I'm not a huge ARPG player. If I look at the discussions on the Steam forums I can't understand about 40% of what's being said because I don't know the lingo of the genre. I played Diablo II back in the day and enjoyed it a lot, especially the atmosphere. I also played Titan Quest, and while it's undeniably a good game, there was just something about it that didn't grab me, which is strange considering that I love Greek mythology. Without meaning to sound too harsh, it felt kind of soulless. The game of this type that I undoubtedly played the most was Ultima VIII: Pagan. People don't usually associate the Ultima series with ARPGs, and rightly so, but Ultima VIII was the odd one out because whereas the rest of the series focussed on complex story telling, Ultima VIII was all about the action. Like Diablo II it has an amazingly dark atmosphere that stays with you and it's what kept me playing despite the game's obvious technical issues.
I saw Grim Dawn on Steam one day and something told me "buy this game, you'll like it". Perhaps it was the cool title, perhaps it was the moody image of the Solomon Kane style character, or perhaps I just felt like trying to recapture some of the fun that I'd had with Diablo II and Ultima VIII. Whatever it was, it served me well, because I absolutely love Grim Dawn. I seriously love it.
I suspect that a lot of what I enjoy about Grim Dawn is not what most other people enjoy, and may perhaps be the exact opposite. You see, the reason that I'm not a huge ARPG player is that it seems to me that the focus of those who love the genre is essentially power-gaming. In other words, it's all about maxing out those all important numbers as quickly and efficiently as possible. While I can respect that, I can't "feel" it.
I'm all about relishing a game. I will painstakingly take my time to explore every nook and cranny, read every word of flavour text, and I'll happily wear inferior gear if it means keeping my character consistent with my vision of him or her (which makes the forthcoming ability to change the appearance of gear a God-send to me; Crate Entertainment know how it is). At this point you might say, "well, if exploration, immersive-storytelling, and role-playing is your thing, the ARPG genre isn't ideal for you, because it's all about the stats and the loot." Well exactly, and that makes the fact that I enjoy Grim Dawn so much just about the biggest complement I could ever pay the game.
I started on Normal difficulty, making my character choose the occultist mastery at first, and then the demolitionist mastery at level 10 when I had the option—a combo that turned him into a pyromancer. After playing for a little over eight hours, I just had to start the game again with the "Veteran" checkbox enabled. I was having such a great time developing my character and exploring the world that I felt I'd be robbing myself if I didn't experience all of these wonderful environments for the first time at their deadliest (at least at the deadliest currently available to new characters). So now I'm a level 35 pure occultist with nearly fifty hours under my belt and I have no reason to believe that I'll tire of Grim Dawn any time soon. In fact, rather annoyingly, I keep having the urge to start yet another new game with a different mastery as cool character ideas come to me. That's an urge that I must resist until I've finished the game for the first time.
You know what's rare in gaming these days? Those "oh wow, that is so cool" moments. Nineties gaming was fully of that, mainly because genres hadn't been as rigidly defined and had therefore not become as predictable as they are now, and developers were far more experimental for the most part. The fact that I'm now a jaded thirty-something probably doesn't help either. But despite that, Grim Dawn has managed to elicit an "awesooome" from me twice now. The first time was when I noticed that I could interact with and use a certain object that I had previously assumed was just part of the scenery. The second time was when I gained the ability to access blocked routes, fully expecting them to lead to a small area with some nice loot, only to find that they took me to entirely new lands, lands that I'm quite sure I have no business being in quite yet. I can't remember the last time that I experienced that good old fashioned joy of discovery in a game.
Stylistically, atmospherically, and thematically, Grim Dawn just hits all of the right notes for me. I do love my dark, depressing, and oppressive gaming worlds. I very quickly realised that if there was any game in which you could turn your Solomon Kane, Chakan the Forever Man, and Blood fantasies into an action role-playing reality, Grim Dawn is it. In fact I could swear that the developers have put some sly references to Caleb and The Chosen from the classic Blood FPS games into Grim Dawn. Or maybe I'm just interpreting certain elements to my own liking. Either way, when you're running around in a cowboy hat, wearing a trenchcoat, wielding a pistol and voodoo doll in one weapon set and a double-barrelled shotgun in the other, as well as wielding occult powers, it's hard for me not to be reminded of my beloved Blood series. The world of Grim Dawn is very much like that of Blood—a vaguelly post-apocalyptic horror setting where technology never progressed beyond the 19th century. It would also be the perfect place to recreate Garrett from the Thief series and its dark, steam-punk world. He'd be right at home. Though he would have to give up his professional thieving ways and be prepared to slaughter thousands upon thousands of foes. Oh look, another character idea that makes me want to start a new game again. You see? This is what happens when Grim Dawn makes love to my imagination—terrible and abominable things are conceived.
The gameplay of Grim Dawn is flawless from my perspective and throwing a globe of poison at a mob of enemies and watching them rush forward for a few milliseconds before scumbling to the deadly liquid just never gets old to me. The music helps tremendously in the flavouring of the game and is the perfect complement to its gritty visuals and tone. I've seen some people be a little down on the graphics, but they look great to me. Then again I'm someone who regularly and happily plays games from the eighties, so take that statement for what it's worth.
All I know is that I'm loving every minute of Grim Dawn and I'm greedily anticipating not only the upcoming expansion, but any future ones too. I really hope there will be more, because I can already tell that this is going to be one of those rare games that I return to for years to come. Grim Dawn is made by people who not only know what they're doing on a technical level, but people who clearly also have a passion for the project. The fact that the game is a work of love is obvious from just how much soul is spilling out from behind every element. The fact that I banish said soul to the abyss with an occult circle of power does nothing to change the fact that I honestly could not recommend Grim Dawn more.

This is one of those games that easily could have been a little master piece, only with a few different choices from the developers. But sadly, they didn't do it, either by choice or by other reasons (difficult to implement, for instance).
The biggest fault this game has, it is that this is a game of chance rather then a skilled based game. Doing this in a computer game is probably the biggest mistake a gaming developer can do, since you alienate two of the major groups of players (those who seek a challenge and those who play for fun). The only group this game actually appeals to, it is those players with an addiction, basically they who cannot stop playing until you beats the game.
The other problem with this game, it is that the developers actually don't want their players to win, and have made a game that is always an up hill struggle, with a final boss you only can beat if you have gotten lucky through out the game. But mostly/often you haven't gotten yourself a ship that is anywhere near of good enough to confront the final boss. And this is on easy mode.
There is also a thing that you can argue is or is not a fault with this game, and that is that you haven't the possibility to reload the game after you have been killed. I would say that it isn't a fault, but I think this game would have appealed to more people if you at least had the choice if you did want the possibility to reload or if you wanted perma death. Personally I like it, since it gives the battles a lot more risk, which increases the intensity of the battles.
But there is a lot of positive stuff in this. A lot!
Firstly, the game mechanics in the tactical mode is absolutely wonderful. No other games that I know of is anywhere near of giving you the experience of commanding a star ship in combat like FTL does. Some of the battles are absolutely fantastic, where you really fights for keeping your pixel crews alive. So this gets a 11 out of 10. Also the development of the ship is very good and you have to make compromises. Both these aspect is something you feel you get better with experience.
Also, the strategic elements in this game are decent, even though I don't like it since I prefer a more slowed paced game, where the focus is rather on exploration than just being chased across the galaxy. But this ain't something I would hold against the developers, since I believe this is something that appeals more to the people who play mainly for the challenge (I'm a person who play for fun).
But even if this game have a wonderful game in so many aspects, I cannot recommend this game. Simply because a computer game shouldn't be about random events, and that is what FTL is. The core game in FTL, it's all about randomness, and even if the tactical aspect is something that you can become very good in, the randomness can quickly outweighs all your skill. Randomness in a game should be secondary in a computer game.
But you can only dream of what FTL could have been. A "marriage" between FTL and Star Trek could been legendary game, where you have the intense battles and perma death from the FTL, and Star Trek's big universe to explore.

It would be nice if the game gave more information, for example abilities that have multiple hits could show the total damage, so you don't have to compare 3 * 173 with 5 * 53 and do the mental arithmetic by hand for 7 different multi-hit abilities to figure out which does the most health damage or guard damage. Also the games "Nepedia" does not tell you what the stats actually do (eg. what INT. and TEC. do, what they affect). Beat Hazard is an adequate twin stick shooter whose biggest strenght is the music integration. It offers up an engaging way to listen to your own tunes.
This game does have many flaws in my opinion. The blurb advertises a "unique ebb and flow based on the music". While this is technically true, even if it's unique it still feels all samey. No matter what song you're listening to, it's all the same basic experience. Sometimes, its dedication to going with the music works against it. This game is definitely more optomized for certain song structures and that makes playing through slower, quieter songs a slog. I could technically play through any song, but once I got to songs like FourFiveSeconds or Big Iron, the game kinda drudged along at an intensely slow pace.
Sometimes, the intensity of the game feels off with the music. As mentioned before, Beat Hazard really shines with a certain structure of song, most easily replicated by dubstep or any song that has a big drop as that is when the game can fluently change the intensity of the battle. However, sometimes it felt really off. Several times, when I was listening to quieter sections of songs, a big boss-like enemy comes to fight despite the calmer music and mood. At other times, when the beat drops in an electronic song, enemies are nowhere to be seen and it's just me and my super intense lasers versus some slow floating rocks.
My biggest complaint about the game, that might just be a me thing, is the visuals. When you boot up the game it warns about its use of strobing and a possibility of seizures. Now I haven't gotten a seizure from this game (yet), but the intensity of the visuals makes a drag to play for extended periods of time. Every time I've stopped playing, I've had a minor headache (nothing really serious just needed to step away from the computer for some time).
Despite all these complaints, Beat Hazard really is the best way to play a twin stick shooter on steam simply for the music integration and I would still recommend it if your looking for a way to chill out (despite the intensity of the game) and listen to some toons.
TL;DR - Beat Hazard is the ideal twin-stick shooter for its music integration despite not perfectly working with the music and its overly-involved, bright, strobing visual style.

cliffhanger that wants to lure you into buying the next season (which has already been confirmed) since basically no single plotline has been resolved in this season, unlike any other previous game from Telltale.

Where to begin... I backed this game waaaay back in the day when it was originally still being crowd-funded. During that time, if you backed the game you were promised a Steam copy of the game AND a DRM free copy of the game. Fast forward to now, that promise was broken, the website was changed to remove this and attempt to hide that promise and then the disaster of handling that promise happened on the forums. Grim Dawns team took back what they had promised to their backers and stated that instead, you now had to choose between the Steam copy or the DRM free copy, you didn't get both.
Prior to this drama, I was banned from their forums for modding their game, something they now encourage. However, my ban was never removed and was only done out of spite because the lead developer of the game hates me. I released some mods for the game that showed more or less weaknesses in his ideas of security. Mind you, none of this was released on the official forums. But since he can't take any form of critisim or feedback, I was banned.
Some reasons why I would not recommend this game:
- If you do something the developers disagree with, even off of their own site, you'll get banned.
- If you do something the developers disagree with, they'll threaten to VAC ban you. (Yes, this happened.)
- The gameplay is fairly boring, the idea to bring back an older Diablo feel works but overall it just lacks purpose.
- The story is fairly empty. You are dropped into a world with little background, some minor NPC interaction and chat, and that's basically it. Otherwise it's just get gear and level up with no real depth.
- The multiplayer is absolutely horrible and full of bugs and crashes.
The game is running on the old Titan Quest engine, so don't expect anything amazing in terms of graphics, however some would prefer it to look older and more grungy like the original Diablo's.
Ultimately I refunded my copy of the game after being lied to after backing the project. I would not recommend this game studio to anyone if they attempt to do similar crowd-funding things in the future. They are very unorganized when it comes to actually following through with their word to their backers.
