I'm not a huge ARPG player. If I look at the discussions on the Steam forums I can't understand about 40% of what's being said because I don't know the lingo of the genre. I played Diablo II back in the day and enjoyed it a lot, especially the atmosphere. I also played Titan Quest, and while it's undeniably a good game, there was just something about it that didn't grab me, which is strange considering that I love Greek mythology. Without meaning to sound too harsh, it felt kind of soulless. The game of this type that I undoubtedly played the most was Ultima VIII: Pagan. People don't usually associate the Ultima series with ARPGs, and rightly so, but Ultima VIII was the odd one out because whereas the rest of the series focussed on complex story telling, Ultima VIII was all about the action. Like Diablo II it has an amazingly dark atmosphere that stays with you and it's what kept me playing despite the game's obvious technical issues.
I saw Grim Dawn on Steam one day and something told me "buy this game, you'll like it". Perhaps it was the cool title, perhaps it was the moody image of the Solomon Kane style character, or perhaps I just felt like trying to recapture some of the fun that I'd had with Diablo II and Ultima VIII. Whatever it was, it served me well, because I absolutely love Grim Dawn. I seriously love it.
I suspect that a lot of what I enjoy about Grim Dawn is not what most other people enjoy, and may perhaps be the exact opposite. You see, the reason that I'm not a huge ARPG player is that it seems to me that the focus of those who love the genre is essentially power-gaming. In other words, it's all about maxing out those all important numbers as quickly and efficiently as possible. While I can respect that, I can't "feel" it.
I'm all about relishing a game. I will painstakingly take my time to explore every nook and cranny, read every word of flavour text, and I'll happily wear inferior gear if it means keeping my character consistent with my vision of him or her (which makes the forthcoming ability to change the appearance of gear a God-send to me; Crate Entertainment know how it is). At this point you might say, "well, if exploration, immersive-storytelling, and role-playing is your thing, the ARPG genre isn't ideal for you, because it's all about the stats and the loot." Well exactly, and that makes the fact that I enjoy Grim Dawn so much just about the biggest complement I could ever pay the game.
I started on Normal difficulty, making my character choose the occultist mastery at first, and then the demolitionist mastery at level 10 when I had the option—a combo that turned him into a pyromancer. After playing for a little over eight hours, I just had to start the game again with the "Veteran" checkbox enabled. I was having such a great time developing my character and exploring the world that I felt I'd be robbing myself if I didn't experience all of these wonderful environments for the first time at their deadliest (at least at the deadliest currently available to new characters). So now I'm a level 35 pure occultist with nearly fifty hours under my belt and I have no reason to believe that I'll tire of Grim Dawn any time soon. In fact, rather annoyingly, I keep having the urge to start yet another new game with a different mastery as cool character ideas come to me. That's an urge that I must resist until I've finished the game for the first time.
You know what's rare in gaming these days? Those "oh wow, that is so cool" moments. Nineties gaming was fully of that, mainly because genres hadn't been as rigidly defined and had therefore not become as predictable as they are now, and developers were far more experimental for the most part. The fact that I'm now a jaded thirty-something probably doesn't help either. But despite that, Grim Dawn has managed to elicit an "awesooome" from me twice now. The first time was when I noticed that I could interact with and use a certain object that I had previously assumed was just part of the scenery. The second time was when I gained the ability to access blocked routes, fully expecting them to lead to a small area with some nice loot, only to find that they took me to entirely new lands, lands that I'm quite sure I have no business being in quite yet. I can't remember the last time that I experienced that good old fashioned joy of discovery in a game.
Stylistically, atmospherically, and thematically, Grim Dawn just hits all of the right notes for me. I do love my dark, depressing, and oppressive gaming worlds. I very quickly realised that if there was any game in which you could turn your Solomon Kane, Chakan the Forever Man, and Blood fantasies into an action role-playing reality, Grim Dawn is it. In fact I could swear that the developers have put some sly references to Caleb and The Chosen from the classic Blood FPS games into Grim Dawn. Or maybe I'm just interpreting certain elements to my own liking. Either way, when you're running around in a cowboy hat, wearing a trenchcoat, wielding a pistol and voodoo doll in one weapon set and a double-barrelled shotgun in the other, as well as wielding occult powers, it's hard for me not to be reminded of my beloved Blood series. The world of Grim Dawn is very much like that of Blood—a vaguelly post-apocalyptic horror setting where technology never progressed beyond the 19th century. It would also be the perfect place to recreate Garrett from the Thief series and its dark, steam-punk world. He'd be right at home. Though he would have to give up his professional thieving ways and be prepared to slaughter thousands upon thousands of foes. Oh look, another character idea that makes me want to start a new game again. You see? This is what happens when Grim Dawn makes love to my imagination—terrible and abominable things are conceived.
The gameplay of Grim Dawn is flawless from my perspective and throwing a globe of poison at a mob of enemies and watching them rush forward for a few milliseconds before scumbling to the deadly liquid just never gets old to me. The music helps tremendously in the flavouring of the game and is the perfect complement to its gritty visuals and tone. I've seen some people be a little down on the graphics, but they look great to me. Then again I'm someone who regularly and happily plays games from the eighties, so take that statement for what it's worth.
All I know is that I'm loving every minute of Grim Dawn and I'm greedily anticipating not only the upcoming expansion, but any future ones too. I really hope there will be more, because I can already tell that this is going to be one of those rare games that I return to for years to come. Grim Dawn is made by people who not only know what they're doing on a technical level, but people who clearly also have a passion for the project. The fact that the game is a work of love is obvious from just how much soul is spilling out from behind every element. The fact that I banish said soul to the abyss with an occult circle of power does nothing to change the fact that I honestly could not recommend Grim Dawn more.

This game is all about running around a very well designed world. It's incredibly fun, especially at night. As you can see by my hours played, there's a ton of fun to be had there. But that's about it. That's fine though. It's more than enough to recommend getting it, maybe on sale.
The rest of the game is really hit or miss. Mostly miss. There's not an original character to be found, only 4 of the main characters have any kind of resolution and none of them are earned. The story itself is just beyond poor. Every single beat is frustratingly stereotypical at best, non-sensical at worst, and often both. The gameplay is balanced all out of whack and very quickly you'll be one shotting everything.
The added Hard and Nightmare modes I like, if only because I love devs who do things like that when players ask for it. Apart from that they're not a good time. They make pretty much everything tedious. Looting becomes all you do and running into every friggin house to look through cupboards is not fun, especially in a giant, pretty world like this that then disappears in the process of constantly staring at the ground. Fighting is also tedious. For example, on Normal there's a type of enemy that is tougher and meaner, but only really comes out if you're ♥♥♥♥ing around recklessly. It's a standard game trade-off. On Hard and Impossible 5 or 6 of them just show up every ten minutes no matter what you're doing, and you'll lose half of your weapons durability dealing with them. Regular enemies still outrageously resillient at endgame, even with the strongest weapons. Human enemies can take 4 point blank shotgun headshots and be fine, while you, much more realistically, die from 2 or 3 bullets at most. It's just not fun.
The expansion is more of the same, except now you have to go much further to complete short objectives on fetch quests, which is every quest. You do get to drive, if that's your thing. Same as the campaign, the endings don't fit at all because there's no reason to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about anyone or anything beyond needing to deal with them to get to the next objective. I do think they're cool ideas, but there's no weight to them, so it doesn't really matter how cool they are.
There's also one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who does nothing but stand around all day admonishing you for standing around when you're very clearly the only person in the whole goddamn city doing anything. ♥♥♥♥ that guy.

This is one of those games that easily could have been a little master piece, only with a few different choices from the developers. But sadly, they didn't do it, either by choice or by other reasons (difficult to implement, for instance).
The biggest fault this game has, it is that this is a game of chance rather then a skilled based game. Doing this in a computer game is probably the biggest mistake a gaming developer can do, since you alienate two of the major groups of players (those who seek a challenge and those who play for fun). The only group this game actually appeals to, it is those players with an addiction, basically they who cannot stop playing until you beats the game.
The other problem with this game, it is that the developers actually don't want their players to win, and have made a game that is always an up hill struggle, with a final boss you only can beat if you have gotten lucky through out the game. But mostly/often you haven't gotten yourself a ship that is anywhere near of good enough to confront the final boss. And this is on easy mode.
There is also a thing that you can argue is or is not a fault with this game, and that is that you haven't the possibility to reload the game after you have been killed. I would say that it isn't a fault, but I think this game would have appealed to more people if you at least had the choice if you did want the possibility to reload or if you wanted perma death. Personally I like it, since it gives the battles a lot more risk, which increases the intensity of the battles.
But there is a lot of positive stuff in this. A lot!
Firstly, the game mechanics in the tactical mode is absolutely wonderful. No other games that I know of is anywhere near of giving you the experience of commanding a star ship in combat like FTL does. Some of the battles are absolutely fantastic, where you really fights for keeping your pixel crews alive. So this gets a 11 out of 10. Also the development of the ship is very good and you have to make compromises. Both these aspect is something you feel you get better with experience.
Also, the strategic elements in this game are decent, even though I don't like it since I prefer a more slowed paced game, where the focus is rather on exploration than just being chased across the galaxy. But this ain't something I would hold against the developers, since I believe this is something that appeals more to the people who play mainly for the challenge (I'm a person who play for fun).
But even if this game have a wonderful game in so many aspects, I cannot recommend this game. Simply because a computer game shouldn't be about random events, and that is what FTL is. The core game in FTL, it's all about randomness, and even if the tactical aspect is something that you can become very good in, the randomness can quickly outweighs all your skill. Randomness in a game should be secondary in a computer game.
But you can only dream of what FTL could have been. A "marriage" between FTL and Star Trek could been legendary game, where you have the intense battles and perma death from the FTL, and Star Trek's big universe to explore.

Grey Goo is one of those games that could have been fantastic, but isn't. You don't have to spend long playing this to see why after just a couple years it was sold in a bundle for $1. The load times are bloody abysmal EVEN ON the LOWEST settings, and the game simply lacks charm. The entire game could just as well play at 2x or even 3x the speed since everything is insanely slow. This is not a game that's meant to be played in the standard sense; this is for players who enjoy spending a half hour building up a big army and then another five minutes just watching it trudge across to the other side of the map to blow up another army in a matter of seconds.
To make matters worse, it feels as though the devs tried to be the next Starcraft/C&C with the UI, but it ends up being frickin' obnoxious becuase the bottom middle section keeps flipping up and down for no good reason. Guys, you don't have to keep reinventing the wheel, just copy the frickin' UI from Starcraft or whatever and cut the obnoxious popup BS lmao. Or at least give your players an option to have a sensible UI, EVEN IF it occasionally features unused space, so that we don't have to contend with adware-levels of popup nonsense.
Grey Goo could have been fantastic, but it really isn't. It's a bloody shame because you can tell they spent a LOT of money on the cinematics and special effects alone, which do not automatically make the game worth playing. Not many gamers are interested in sporadic cinematic experiences with a potentially boring, uninspired story and separated by utterly lackluster gameplay. Let us hope this does not spell the end for the RTS genre, for this game is a prime example of what NOT to do.

Best dead island game with good first person parkour.
The good things:
Combat: the art of hitting stuff is pretty basic, but it feels damn good with the gore, slow motion on certain hits and zombie ragdolls.
Combat is also made much better than something like skyrim by throwable weapons, kicking, enviromental hazards and weapon crafting resulting in poisonous elemental bladed sledgehammers and double-bladed fire katanas.
Guns arent that great but also arent that important.
Movement: the games parkour system is smooth and actually stops most Fps-parkour moments feeling like James Bond ball torture.
This version of the game includes the Following expansion that adds an awesome upgradeable buggy that feels amazing but is sadly made out of paper mache, meaning repairs happen every time you exhale and inhale
Stuff you get: The games skilltrees slowly make you into amazing ninja-warrior (and later the actual spider-man) without making later fights trivial. Even later game I do sometimes have to pick my battles.
Combination of weapon-mod blueprints and these odd static upgrade blocks you find can make you some awesome weaponry, that you will still do later in game, as weapons seem to be made out of the same paper mache as the Followings buggy.
That buggy can also be turned into some sort of zombie meat grinder with lighting so thats cool too.
Side-quests: Dying light as a game can be summed up as a dead island+parkour, with you doing everyones jobs for them, investigating scary places, battling bandits and just gathering stuff.
Some of the sidequests are actually really good, and I can say at least one got me scared.
The night: The night really turns the game into a more of a survival horror experience, but most of it is skippable, and I am a giant ♥♥♥♥♥
Content: There is a ♥♥♥♥♥on, most of it is good quality.
The world: The main game has two maps: The more slummy cheapass place and the posh old town. I feel these are at times kinda gray, but places still have lots of detail and exploring around looking for bits of metal and plastic and♥♥♥♥♥♥
The expansions map is actually at times colorful, and exploring it is a real joy.
The music: this is extra subjective, but imo its good
The bad stuff:
The story: I dont actually remember much of it, there are some good moments I remember but maybe the forgettability of it tells you something.
The expansions story is quite a bit more interesting
Voice acting:Protagonist is pretty bad, and so is some other folks voiceacting
The first few hours of gameplay: I dont remember much of it, but it seems I was pretty frustrated for a long bit of it before the game tosses you some better weapons and skills
Overall opinion: If you enjoy doing quests, looting and honing your weapons into truly insane♥♥♥♥♥♥and just running around, I think you will have a blast.
HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥THERE IS ALSO MULTIPLAYER:
The game also has coop possibility and some other mode I havent touched.
Coop might make the at times frustrating start of the game better, and this is the kinda game that should be more fun with a friend.

I cannot review this game without talking about the story, so warning for those who have not played there are SPOILERS here.
With that out of the way, the game is set as a companion to the television show. Main characters from the show will apear and you can interact with them (but never play as them) and it even goes as far as to use the shows opening titles sequence. This means as such the game has spoilers from the television show in it, the game takes place through the events of series 4 of the show, so it is best to have watched series 4 before you play.
The game is seporated out into six episodes this time rather than the ususal five, which is fitting as it is a game of two halves. The first three episodes are done very well with lots of setup which leads to a great mid series finale at the end of the third episode.
The thing is thats the good parts over, from episode 4 onwards it starts to go down hill and doesn't recover. To be blunt the Forresters are the Starks. From episode 4 to the end you will watch as each Forrester is killed off one by one. The choices you make to try and save people don't matter as the bad guys will win. I realised this part way through episode 5 which made episode 6 a chore to play through. I will give them credit though, they do a good job of giving you hope that maybe you might actually succeed in something before undoing all your plans and again killing off characters.
The game has four playable characters and you switch between them as they are all in different locations, but come the end I only had one character left. The main plot point that is set up at the begining of episode 1 is meaningless and isn't resolved and has no impact on the story what so ever. You're supposed to find this 'North Grove' and you spend all five episodes searching for it and when you do find it the game ends.
This is a game where your choices are meaningless, the bad guys will ultimatly always win and deaths are just in there for shock value. This is Telltales worst output so far and I can't recommend it at all. There is a series 2 for whatever reason, everybody's dead so unless they wan't to start off with another new family there isn't much they can do.

Well... It's worth the money in a sale for a quick play but honestly... This game has nothing on the original game.  Very quickly it stands out that the main game mechanic which made this series unique has been tampered with and spoiled... The mechanic I am talking about is light.  Light is the key to defeating the darkness, and no idea lightbulbs went off in the developers heads that made this.
The First game had little weapons, and had multiple flashlight types, beyond your regular flashlight you could find a heavy duty flashlight and two lantern type lights that in a world of combating darkness was amazing... this game replaces atmosphere and light combat with dumbed down boring gun fighting, many weapons are now available such as an Uzi and M16 and to be blunt... they just dont fit.  The normal light from the flashlight no longer burns away dark... it simply does nothing, you must focus the flashlight to make it do anything... mostly it's just a case of focus light, spray uzi or M16 and repeat now this... is the ultimate sin... They basicly ruined the main combat mechanic that made this game special and replaced it with bland generic shooting.
There are only three areas in this game, and those get reused several times as a time loop plot device... the ever repeating events become dull and the newer enemys just don't make it interesting enough to make it enjoyable...  infact the other characters remembering the previous loops ahve having previous tasks already finished only highlights the boredom the developers must have realised would happen playing the same content over and over again.
The first game was dark... VERY dark and the dark fog and shimmering enemys gave me goose bumps... this game did nothing to make me feel dark was dangerous or intimidating, there was no eerie fog everywhere and no sense of dread that made you wish for teh next brightly lit area to come soon... the game just wasn't creapy, spooky, or scary... it just didn't do a good job at all.
The sandbox arcade mode where you fight till dawn is a fun addition, and it is fun to try and beat your friends scores and try to survive for the full 10 minutes untill dawn... actually that is almost the only time this game seems to remember that light is your ally...
So as I mentioned...   The game is worth a play as a sale price... it's just nowhere near as good as the first game.

First off, let me just say this: This game has no effect on the Alan Wake universe.  All the game reveals is that Mr. Scratch is a bad guy.
Now, onto the review.
This game fleshes out new ideas in case Alan Wake 2 would come out.  For example, there are some new monsters such as a spider-parasite thing, a monster that morphs into two when light is shined on it, one guy who can change from ravens to a man, and finally a guy who throws dark grenades at you.
There are also some new weapons, such as the nailgun, the machine guns, and probably some other stuff I don't remember.
For 15$, this game is not worth buying.
The story mode is unique at first, but then it gets repetitive.  In short, this game makes you repeat the exact same story three times in a row before you beat it.  Yup, that's right.  You do the same things thrice, and then you beat the story mode.  If you want to buy this game for the story mode, pass on it.
The reason anyone would want to buy this game is for the arcade mode.  It is a 10-minute fight with waves of Taken.  This is unusually easy in this version because the weapons are so much more powerful and because the flashlight recharges almost instantly, rendering batteries near useless.
TL;DR
Don't buy it if you are looking for a good story.  Buy it on sale for the arcade if that's what you want to play.

While Tower Wars puts an interesting spin on the Tower Defense genre, I really don't think it did it any great justice.
Tower Wars changes up the Tower Defense genre a bit by adding in an opponent that is actively building towers just like you are and the goal is to stop him from destroying your castle, while managing to get troops through his towers to destroy his tower.
The game has some interesting features and the Victorian/Steam-Punk era style is a nice touch, it really didn't make up for the shortcomings I saw/felt.  Tower Wars isn't an easy game.  In fact, I found it annoyingly difficult for no good reason.  I also found the tutorial to be lacking and the enormous plethora of available upgrades for towers, buildings and troops along with the equally enormous plethora of available towers and troops in the first place, much too daunting to get me to want to play in the slightest.
I would not recommend this to anyone unless you are a true Tower Defense savant and really want to give it a shot.  I don't find it fun due to the lacking tutorial, odd difficulty and overwhelming amount of options for towers and such.

Didn't think I would clock a good 44 hours into this game! I had done many things and all missions, cleared all outposts and bonfire too... tamed all tamable animals (even the elite ones) and I was getting eager to finish the game. The game mechanic is pretty much the same as established by Far Cry 3. You have skill trees to unlock during playtime. While it was an interesting mechanic brought in FC3 and used on FC4 and FCP, I hope Ubisoft will change this on their next Far Cry game.
Far Cry Primal brings you into the Stone Age! While this period of time isn't much exploited in the gaming industry, kudos to Ubisoft in trying to be original and making a fun game set in this time period. The story is pretty much lacking when compared to previous Far Cry games but hey, how spectacular can you make something groundbreaking in that aspect for a game set in the Stone Age? Anyhoo... when the game starts, you and your fellow tribe are doing some mammoth hunting... and it goes wrong, thanks to Bloodfang Sabertooth Tiger (tameable quite late in the game).
And from now on, your "job" is to build up your faction, known as the Wenja tribe (softbloods), into a formidable village by the end. The enemy factions are known as Udam (cannabalistic fellows) and the Izila (sun worshippers that loves fire!).
The gameplay is where the main focus is done here. Just walking/running in this game, hearing the sound of nature... hunting enemies with your tamed beast is quite awesome! As you progress further, you can unlock more abilities for you and also, for the beasts you can tame. You can upgrade your first beast, the owl (very useful!) into a powerful bomber and coordinate and clear a whole outpost without any intervention of your avatar.
Far Cry Primal has nothing related from previous Far Cry games, storywise and lore speaking, so you cannot be "lost" in the game in that aspect. Whether that's good or bad, it's up to you but in game sequels, I like to have some continuation, to keep me invested in the franchise but sadly, you won't find this here.
As for the characters in this game... well, as expected, their personality were quite annoying and boring. The characters are quite weak in this game, especially compared to previous Far Cry games.
I could go on and on but I'll focus the remaining information into the Pros and Cons!
PS: I had purchased the Apex Predator Edition... it adds a few buffs, new skins for select animals and early access to items. You be the judge if the extra 5$ is worth it!

Having grown up with ARPGs like Diablo, Sacred, Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights and the likes, I have really missed a decent addition to this genre in recent years. They are either somehow overproduced and not very immersive or the complete opposite and some indie production that put in admirable effort but just didn't have the means to really make it happen.... this is where Grim Dawn comes in.
The game is obviously done by a small team with limited budget and it does show here and there. Eg. not all dialogue is voiced, however GD more than makes up for it by having some kick♥♥♥♥♥♥voice acting and a very atmospherical soundtrack. The variety of game assets isn't incredible but then again they all match extremely well and make up for a very well designed world. None of that over-the-top colour explosion that online RPGs these days do just for the sake of being different. The story as far as I played it, is immersive with many windings and side tracks. The player choices that the game promises aren't extremely impactful but they leave you with few moments where you do think that you should have done that differently, so some impact on the experience is there. Lastly, the character classes and leveling system are very well done. They characters play smoothly and the options for specialization are manyfold, resulting in a lasting motivation for further leveling.
In short: GD did an excellent job at all the things that really matter, instead of doing a half-a***d job at everything. The result is a game that, although created by a small production company, was done with a lot of love and careful consideration. I enjoyed every minute of it so far and am nowhere close to being bored of it!

To preface; I will say that this is not a full review of Far Cry Primal, rather this is an overview. I am doing this because.. I feel that too many people are giving this game a negative review wihout much or any substance objectively. That and in the three or three and a half hours of plaaytime, I found this to be a very fun game, it is exciting and it is entralling. I would aactually like to see Ubisoft experrment more with different time periods, eras. And I feel that people who on the fence should know that this is worth the $60 price tag. I'll update this after I have completed the game, as some things may change. I'm sure I will develop criticisms over the course of the game, etc.. I will not mention anything about the story yet, because I have not progressed far enough into the story. The character animations and VO work that I have experienced so far is convincing and is outstanding work.
So, what makes Primal so captivating, I'll tell you. The setting in itself is one of the major reasons. The world of Oros is beautiful, full of life and is a sensory overload when it comes to the audio; a good thing. Teaming with wildlife and, yes other cavemen. Depite its beauty, this world that has been created is dangerous. You can find yourself into some serious trouble in Oros very quickly! The weapons are primitive and they do lack complex or cool looking animations, but you're a caveman, you're just trying to survive. When attacked and under stress, with your aderline pumping, and a lack of formal training, you are going to swing your club as wildly as possible, and a spear is a thrusting weapon, not a slashing weapon. You're not a highly-trained martial-artist wielding a staff or or a sword. With that said the combat is brutal and fun! That's what matters! It is satisfying to throw a spear into a mans face as it is into an animal, same thing with clubing someone to death. The hunting is great fun! I enjoy the fact how I have to track whatever game I have shot with my bow or thrown spear, because as someone who actually hunts, animals don't just drop dead on the spot most of the time. It's a nice change to see in a game. Many have complained of the partially made up language. Ubisoft did work with experts to craft a language that would be believable, though not 100% accurate. You can hear the emotions converyed through the voice actors and I appluad this apporach. The subtitles do not bother and it adds another layer of immserion to a game that very atmospheric. There is no other game, that I know of that has a wrold like Oros. It is unique in that regard, even if Ark has a world similar. In Ark you have firearms, which to me would detract from the experience overall.
I will recommend to everyone to play on "expert" difficulty and to turn most, if not all of your HUD elements off. You'll rely pretty much solely on audio cues and it'll take a while, but you will feel scared and you should feel that thrill, that anxiety. Of both being scared and exploring a land you know nothing of. Get out there and get lost, feel the experience and bask in the atmosphere! You are not at the top of the food-chain, you're far from it. I find myself, especailly at night, which is so much different from the dynamics of daytime play, always being cautious and listening very carefully to sounds. As well as hunting for animals that appear at night only. I am having as close to a caveman experience as I think we may ever get in a AAA title. And this experience feels authentic, as far as video games go. This game as is so far in my experience gets a solid recommendation.
EDIT: Having played more of the game, I feel that the story is good enough so far. It's not top tier, it is not The Witcher 3 calibre of story-telling; but it is not a bad story. What is most important that I've realized is that now that I have tamed most of the beasts, and have uncovered aa good portion of the map. The game has become highly addicting! I am about 11 percent complete with the game. My one major complaint is that night cycles should really last longer; as well as the frustration of losing a rare beast because it died. I like the mechanic on paper. It's more immersive, but it isn't fun to try to track down another rare black leopard.

This game is all about running around a very well designed world. It's incredibly fun, especially at night. As you can see by my hours played, there's a ton of fun to be had there. But that's about it. That's fine though. It's more than enough to recommend getting it, maybe on sale.
The rest of the game is really hit or miss. Mostly miss. There's not an original character to be found, only 4 of the main characters have any kind of resolution and none of them are earned. The story itself is just beyond poor. Every single beat is frustratingly stereotypical at best, non-sensical at worst, and often both. The gameplay is balanced all out of whack and very quickly you'll be one shotting everything.
The added Hard and Nightmare modes I like, if only because I love devs who do things like that when players ask for it. Apart from that they're not a good time. They make pretty much everything tedious. Looting becomes all you do and running into every friggin house to look through cupboards is not fun, especially in a giant, pretty world like this that then disappears in the process of constantly staring at the ground. Fighting is also tedious. For example, on Normal there's a type of enemy that is tougher and meaner, but only really comes out if you're ♥♥♥♥ing around recklessly. It's a standard game trade-off. On Hard and Impossible 5 or 6 of them just show up every ten minutes no matter what you're doing, and you'll lose half of your weapons durability dealing with them. Regular enemies still outrageously resillient at endgame, even with the strongest weapons. Human enemies can take 4 point blank shotgun headshots and be fine, while you, much more realistically, die from 2 or 3 bullets at most. It's just not fun.
The expansion is more of the same, except now you have to go much further to complete short objectives on fetch quests, which is every quest. You do get to drive, if that's your thing. Same as the campaign, the endings don't fit at all because there's no reason to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about anyone or anything beyond needing to deal with them to get to the next objective. I do think they're cool ideas, but there's no weight to them, so it doesn't really matter how cool they are.
There's also one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who does nothing but stand around all day admonishing you for standing around when you're very clearly the only person in the whole goddamn city doing anything. ♥♥♥♥ that guy.

I'd like to preface this by saying that Titan Quest was a good game, Grim Dawn is a good game so far, and that I do not have an issue with any resemblance between the two.  That said...
It's almost literally modern Titan Quest (TQ).  When I say "almost literally" I mean that I believe certain UI elements were straight lifted from TQ, buttons, font, default values and all.  The loot is similiar, the attack animations are similar(ly unsatisfying, generally), the entity models are a bit too close, the skill trees work exactly the same, the inventory is identical, the rewards for leveling are the same minus being able to directly increase your health and energy, and then some.  Again, I don't mean "they're in the same genre", I mean this basically feels like a modern overhaul of TQ.  At the time of writing I'm unaware if there are any previous TQ developers on board.*
While this visibly carries the entire framework of another game, the mechanics and enemies are where it differentiates.  Skills and talents are more intelligently and uniquely designed, allowing for more fun styles and customization.  Beyond that, the major differences are the enemy types and the encounters themselves.  As a whole it is good, solid execution of tried-and-true ARPG formulas.
*Edit:  A bit of looking around confirmed that Crate Entertainment is composed partially of former members of Iron Lore Entertainment, Titan Quest's developers, and that Grim Dawn is indeed running off of TQ's engine.

Best dead island game with good first person parkour.
The good things:
Combat: the art of hitting stuff is pretty basic, but it feels damn good with the gore, slow motion on certain hits and zombie ragdolls.
Combat is also made much better than something like skyrim by throwable weapons, kicking, enviromental hazards and weapon crafting resulting in poisonous elemental bladed sledgehammers and double-bladed fire katanas.
Guns arent that great but also arent that important.
Movement: the games parkour system is smooth and actually stops most Fps-parkour moments feeling like James Bond ball torture.
This version of the game includes the Following expansion that adds an awesome upgradeable buggy that feels amazing but is sadly made out of paper mache, meaning repairs happen every time you exhale and inhale
Stuff you get: The games skilltrees slowly make you into amazing ninja-warrior (and later the actual spider-man) without making later fights trivial. Even later game I do sometimes have to pick my battles.
Combination of weapon-mod blueprints and these odd static upgrade blocks you find can make you some awesome weaponry, that you will still do later in game, as weapons seem to be made out of the same paper mache as the Followings buggy.
That buggy can also be turned into some sort of zombie meat grinder with lighting so thats cool too.
Side-quests: Dying light as a game can be summed up as a dead island+parkour, with you doing everyones jobs for them, investigating scary places, battling bandits and just gathering stuff.
Some of the sidequests are actually really good, and I can say at least one got me scared.
The night: The night really turns the game into a more of a survival horror experience, but most of it is skippable, and I am a giant ♥♥♥♥♥
Content: There is a ♥♥♥♥♥on, most of it is good quality.
The world: The main game has two maps: The more slummy cheapass place and the posh old town. I feel these are at times kinda gray, but places still have lots of detail and exploring around looking for bits of metal and plastic and♥♥♥♥♥♥
The expansions map is actually at times colorful, and exploring it is a real joy.
The music: this is extra subjective, but imo its good
The bad stuff:
The story: I dont actually remember much of it, there are some good moments I remember but maybe the forgettability of it tells you something.
The expansions story is quite a bit more interesting
Voice acting:Protagonist is pretty bad, and so is some other folks voiceacting
The first few hours of gameplay: I dont remember much of it, but it seems I was pretty frustrated for a long bit of it before the game tosses you some better weapons and skills
Overall opinion: If you enjoy doing quests, looting and honing your weapons into truly insane♥♥♥♥♥♥and just running around, I think you will have a blast.

The game also has coop possibility and some other mode I havent touched.
Coop might make the at times frustrating start of the game better, and this is the kinda game that should be more fun with a friend.

I picked it up because Penny Arcade's Tycho voice Tycho for it, and he had been saying it was a lot of fun to record.  It also starred Strongbad and Heavy (Tf2) so I figured, what the hell.  Five bucks.  I easily got five dollars of entertainment out of Night at the Inventory, but that's not exactly saying much: maybe 3-5 hours of playing?  The dialogue is humorous once, maybe twice, but there isn't so much of it, so the characters repeat themselves frequently and surprisingly early in the gameplay.  While you can limit how often the characters speak, you can't eliminate it.  By default the game interrupts and slows down gameplay in favor of the dialogue, which sort of makes sense as the characters were such a huge (the only?) selling point.
Of special note are the achievements, most of which are luck based (win with a certain type of hand).  For a little while I had been trying to 100% it but I just gave up after getting bored.  Trying to land specific hands in an AI poker game just isn't fun.
So, if you're looking for maybe an hour of amusement, yeah, get it.  The dialogue is great once or twice, like I said, and I did very much enjoy the characters.  There just isn't enough dialogue to go much longer than that, and the gameplay just can't hold this one up so everything just falls flat.  Maybe if you're interested in the characters and it's up someday for 99 cents go for it, otherwise give it a pass.

BDO is advertised as a fast-paced action MMO with a unique system of leveling. And it delivers. Rapid, often seamless combos with just the right amount of curve to make a veteran MMO player catch himself messing up, while not throwing a noob into a crapstorm of death.
BDO is unique in that questing is entirely independent from leveling, as combat experience is gained through combat, rather than quests. Quests instead offer various item rewards and Contribution Points, which can be carefully planned and spent on buildings, nodes, and worksites to turn your world into a flourishing business, if you're so inclined. You could create trading routes spanning the map or buy up a whole city and the surrounding areas. The possibilities are limited only by your interests.
Gaining knowledge is another unique system. The more you know, the more you can do. Energy is used for gathering, using certain shops, hiring workers, and more, and your maximum energy is boosted by the knowledge of your characters. Some characters will offer special knowledge for a little one-time energy cost. KNowledge also makes combat easier, as the better knowledge you have of an enemy, the more damage you deal to it and the less you take from it.
The game can get a bit clunky at times, as trying to figure out the map can be a bit confusing at first. As with any action MMO, there's the problem of pay4convenience items (More inventory space or carry weight, minor bonuses for cosmetic gear).
Overall, a solid experience.

Honestly, there's parts of this game I love and others I hate.
This game has pretty good graphics for an MMO, which might be its greatest quality IMO. The combat style is different than other similar games I've played, which can be a little confusing until you learn some combos you like or find the right class for you. I didn't get into the story much, but there's plenty of tasks and quests to keep you busy.
Now, what I hate about the game.
First of all, this game is not new user friendly and has some complex features that you won't understand without proper guidance. My suggestion is just to guild up quick and learn from the vets.
This game has a price tag of $10, but really, if you want to get anywhere in the game, you're gonna have to spend more than that. I don't want to rehash to much of what other reviews have written, but there is a sort of 'buff' called the 'Value Pack' you can buy for about $15 a month. Essentially, it turns the game from a pain in the butt to playable. If you get into this game, you'll probably end up picking it up.
The amount of money you can drop into this game's alarming. One outfit for your character will cost you about $22-$34. Just for cosmetics. Clothes. Everything from the 'Pearl Shop' is frighteningly expensive, from pets that pick up loot for you to inventory expansion items.
So it's a cash grab, what game these days isn't? I can deal with micro transactions, but there's certain things about his game that ultimately made me not recommend. The game heavily rewards AFK gameplay, in fact, it almost plays itself. There's tons of tasks where you wind your character up and just watch them go for a couple hours, or overnight, or several days. I also feel like the economy in the game's a little funky as well. I play solo so I can't speak to guild life, but it took me forever to get cash together, and in the end, it just came down to hours of mindless mob grinding to keep my head above the surface.
The weapon and armor upgrade system's infuriating as well. To get a decent weapon, you're in for some frustration unless you just buy one from the Market Place, and that's only if you have the silver for it.
The final gripe that made me not recommend this game is that connecting to a server alone can be a pain. I played for over a month, and then suddenly, I couldn't join any games no matter which server I tried, even though I was playing the day before. Currently, I'm still waiting for the issue to be resolved. This seems to be a recurring problem with many people and the company's response time on the matter leaves something to be desired.
All in all, with what I've invested, I'll continue to play (as soon as I'm able). It's not a bad game, and I do enjoy it, but I'm certain there're better MMORPG's out there and I wish I'd shopped around before falling for the cheap price tag.

Tropico lets you be the dictator of your own Tropical Island. As 'el Presidente' of Tropico your will is law. Like in other city-building games you get to choose what to build, what demands shall be met, but also how to deal with unrest. The main differences with a game like Anno are that: 1) Tropico plays a bit more casual when it comes to usage of space, but does let you create roads more freely and 2) you have to deal with your population, 3) you have to deal with the international super-powers to prevent being invaded. Unique in it's setting combined with a unique sense of humour (that extends to their facebook page, example: "El Presidente takes his hat off for Kim Jong Un! Congrats to such a neatly organized and executed election. At the moment he's thinking about sending over Penultimo for a little worshop"), I can totally recomend this game.
Tropico 4 looks exactly like the third installment and if you buy the game without the expansion "Modern Times" there is really no difference. The Tropico 4 in a pack is actually quite worth your money if you enjoy city-building games and or government games.
One MAYOR negative point for this game: it comes with terribly annoying DRM. The game is completely singleplayer, there is no multiplayer element whatsoever. You buy the game here on steam, but you still need a seperate account with Kalypso. You need to log-on to Kalypso everytime you boot the game. There is no reason for this. But I'm sticking with the positive review, because I also hope they drop the DRM someday (please email them about it like I did).
When it comes to maturity of this game, when it comes to violence, repression and persecution this game tops them all. The choices you make lead to rebellions. Members of society decide to leave the city and hide in the woods on the island, pick up an AK and fight you. You need an army to quell them, and this gives some action, some firefights in the game (no strategy element) and 'el Presidente' (your customizable ingame avatar, you can even build a golden statue of your avatar!) will also join these fights.
Your will is law. If you do't like religion, dont build any churches and be prepared for angry people demanding a church. You can even 'oust' an entire faction from the island, taking away that faction's voice in sociey (be prepared for rebellions). And if you really hate religion, you can also build labor camps a jails to 're-educate' them or even let the army kill the members of that faction. + The hunting mechanic in the game is well done. Tigers, Dire wolves, Mammoths so on.

Far Cry Primal is the next game in the Far Cry series. It shies away from the previous games in the series that were mostly set in a more modern setting, and instead introduces the player to what life was like in the Far Cry universe 10,000 years before the common era. You play as Takkar and belong to the tribe known as the Wenja, which you figure out very early into the game are the punching bags of the two other dominant tribes occupying Oros... and also the animals occupying the inhospitable region. Frankly the Wenja are terrible at surviving, which is where you come in! In your epic caveman quest to become the baddest creature in Oros you will need to take on animals and humans alike by crafting better weapons, taking advantage of native plants to help adapt to new situations, and tame some of the fierce animals that inhabit Oros itself to aid you in pushing back the Wenja tribe's aggressive neighbors.
If you enjoyed the solid game mechanics from Far Cry 4 you will welcome their understandable return. Sprinting across Oros while hunting man or animal feels fluid, and once you invest some points into Takkar's caveman perk tree of... caveman skills, you will come to find sneaking, scavenging, and combat becoming much easier. There is even a simle "village growth" aspect to the game; the more Wenja you rescue from danger and the more unique characters you bring into the fold, the more the village grows. You won't have a direct influence on the growth, but it is satisfying seeing the area become full of people who can't survive on their own.
The story itself is regrttably short, but the gameplay itself more than makes up for it. If you are a completionist than the sheer amounts of quests for you to complete will be an encouragement in and of itself, even if they can become repetitive. Upgrading your gear and taming beasts is very entertaining, and I would recommend doing as much as possible early on to help you feel more like an Apex predator once the time comes for you to take on the other two tribes in their respective questlines.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation is the second instalment of the Hyperdimension Neptunia series, which has been ported over to PC from the PS consoles. Through PC ports the games themselves saw a transformation for 60 fps gameplay, achievements hunting, quick accesses to guides and possibly loss of friendships and any chances of romantic successes due to obsessions over the characters featured in game.
I picked this up on a whim back when it was on sale and I was using a really slow laptop, so I literally had no chances playing it until now in 2017 when I can properly play it and review it to a greater depth. While most people review the game when they have went over majority of the content and / or endings (for singleplayer games), I have invested just about 50 hours as of now (6/12/2017) and yet an ending is still nowhere in sight for me, but that might just be because I'm a grinder.
Pros:
- For 29.99$ AUD, you are guaranteed at least 50 hours worth of content and discovery, but might depend on how you play the game itself
- Guides are readily available and are also quite in-depth. Its up to you if you want to use a guide to help you though. Sometimes its more fun to explore for yourself.
- The game isn't taxing in terms of hardware. I was using a laptop that wasn't even made for gaming, so I had no credibility if I complained its too taxing. But once you get past a certain hardware threshold, you can enjoy a steady 60 fps with occasional fps spikes, depending on how far you passed that threshold
For information, my rig is a G4560 CPU paired with a GTX 1050ti GPU and 8GB of RAM.
-And finally, its somewhat of an improvement over the first game, with the addition of the Chirper system and Stella's dungeon, allowing you more ways to waste your time.
Gray lines:
- Graphics definitely isn't "something" (read: very dated) you expect from a game released in 2015, especially when there is Witcher III released on the same month and year. But once you get to realise that its a PC port of a console game series, you can excuse it a bit. Some might like it, some won't. I personally like it because I can't really see anime and realistic graphic going together.
- A bit too memetic: aside from watching people playing and reading a *rare* in-depth review, the entire game series doesn't see much deep coverage and reviewing so from first time buyers it is a bit of a murky choice. Therefore making decision to buy this game isn't as obvious as getting L4D2 or CSGO. Most reviews tends to make some sort of jokes and referring to the characters so thats another way to find out about the game, blocked. But once you get patient you can find out more and make a better choice to buy the game or not. I'll just cut it for you and say that its pretty good.
Cons:
- Being a PC port of a console games, you expect to see console controls layout, and indeed they are here. What makes it a con is that changing keybinds is (initially) very tough. 50 hours in and I am still not familiar with the keys at all, but what makes it a saving grace for me is the mouse, which I can use for pretty much also anything in game, from attacking to buying stuff. While a con, its not debilitating to warrant a no-recommendation as after all, PC's need a mouse, and you can play this game almost entire on the mouse.
- While the content of the game is very vast, it is sometimes so vast that you would find it hard to keep track of things, especially certain items when it comes to farming. And endings and monsters, etc... Hence why the guides are there which I designated as a pro. While the game itself is enjoyable and we all can find our own ways to enhance our own experiences with the game even further, casual players might find this game a bit daunting to cover all of it, let alone most or half.
Verdict:
While the game is pretty good, I can only recommend like so:
- As a sequel to Re;Birth 1, get it only on sale as the improvement over the first game isn't worth a thoughtless 29.99 AUD purchase save for die-hard fans.
- As a starter / introductory game to newcomers, it is recommended even at full price, but at this point, you might go for Megadimension instead.
- As a game to fill up the missing gaps of series and / or for collectors, its recommended, sale or not.

In the strategy and simulation game Tropico 4 you assume the role of a dictator, who is ruling a group of small islands. Your job is to develop each island and to accomplish various objectives given to you through the cunning use of flawed banking systems, domestic and international politics and the odd assassination. So the Russians want 500 units of spiced rum? Let’s build some sugar plantations, a distillery and upgrade it so that it produces spiced rum from the sugar! Even if this might sound a little boring to some people, please believe me when I say it’s not: Humor is an important aspect in Tropico 4 and being a dictator turns out to be surprisingly entertaining, even these days, when dictators fall left and right all over the world.
The attention to detail is amazing: You’ll spend most of your time zoomed out on the map, but if you zoom in every now and then and have a look at all the tiny animations, you’ll be impressed by everything that’s going on. Place your dictator outside an army base and he will wait for the next soldier to go on duty, give him a medal and clap his hands. The soldier will in turn salute and move on with his business. I get the feeling that the people working on Tropico 4 really have enjoyed what they have been doing and when people enjoy themselves, the result is pretty good more often than not.
Now, even though Tropico 4 is a very entertaining game, it’s more or less the same game as its predecessor, Tropico 3. The graphics are upgraded, some aspects are tweaked a bit (like the Council of Ministers and how you now always start with a garage, whereas you didn’t in Tropico 3), there are some new buildings and a few fresh edicts, but Tropico 4 feels more like an expansion to Tropico 4 than a new game. And when one of the highlights the publisher decides to focus on when comparing Tropico 4 to Tropico 3 is “Facebook and Twitter integration”, you know that they, too, are having problems justifying calling Tropico 4 a new game.
Still, something good comes out of all that: If you enjoyed Tropico 3, you’ll also enjoy Tropico 4. It’s the same game, but everything is a little better. It’s not a game you’ll sit down and play from start to finish in one go, it’s rather one you’ll play for a couple of hours, then you forget about it for a few months, before you’re back, ruling another island.

Having grown up with ARPGs like Diablo, Sacred, Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights and the likes, I have really missed a decent addition to this genre in recent years. They are either somehow overproduced and not very immersive or the complete opposite and some indie production that put in admirable effort but just didn't have the means to really make it happen.... this is where Grim Dawn comes in.
The game is obviously done by a small team with limited budget and it does show here and there. Eg. not all dialogue is voiced, however GD more than makes up for it by having some kick♥♥♥♥♥♥voice acting and a very atmospherical soundtrack. The variety of game assets isn't incredible but then again they all match extremely well and make up for a very well designed world. None of that over-the-top colour explosion that online RPGs these days do just for the sake of being different. The story as far as I played it, is immersive with many windings and side tracks. The player choices that the game promises aren't extremely impactful but they leave you with few moments where you do think that you should have done that differently, so some impact on the experience is there. Lastly, the character classes and leveling system are very well done. They characters play smoothly and the options for specialization are manyfold, resulting in a lasting motivation for further leveling.
In short: GD did an excellent job at all the things that really matter, instead of doing a half-a***d job at everything. The result is a game that, although created by a small production company, was done with a lot of love and careful consideration. I enjoyed every minute of it so far and am nowhere close to being bored of it!

I'd like to preface this by saying that Titan Quest was a good game, Grim Dawn is a good game so far, and that I do not have an issue with any resemblance between the two.  That said...
It's almost literally modern Titan Quest (TQ).  When I say "almost literally" I mean that I believe certain UI elements were straight lifted from TQ, buttons, font, default values and all.  The loot is similiar, the attack animations are similar(ly unsatisfying, generally), the entity models are a bit too close, the skill trees work exactly the same, the inventory is identical, the rewards for leveling are the same minus being able to directly increase your health and energy, and then some.  Again, I don't mean "they're in the same genre", I mean this basically feels like a modern overhaul of TQ.  At the time of writing I'm unaware if there are any previous TQ developers on board.*

The sound effects are impressive for example, and the addition of "true sight" is the one thing I would almost like to see retroactively added to the original; no longer can the enemy see me on the other side of a giant warehouse just because they happen to be in my arbitrary sight bubble.

Honestly, there's parts of this game I love and others I hate.
This game has pretty good graphics for an MMO, which might be its greatest quality IMO. The combat style is different than other similar games I've played, which can be a little confusing until you learn some combos you like or find the right class for you. I didn't get into the story much, but there's plenty of tasks and quests to keep you busy.
Now, what I hate about the game.
First of all, this game is not new user friendly and has some complex features that you won't understand without proper guidance. My suggestion is just to guild up quick and learn from the vets.
This game has a price tag of $10, but really, if you want to get anywhere in the game, you're gonna have to spend more than that. I don't want to rehash to much of what other reviews have written, but there is a sort of 'buff' called the 'Value Pack' you can buy for about $15 a month. Essentially, it turns the game from a pain in the butt to playable. If you get into this game, you'll probably end up picking it up.
The amount of money you can drop into this game's alarming. One outfit for your character will cost you about $22-$34. Just for cosmetics. Clothes. Everything from the 'Pearl Shop' is frighteningly expensive, from pets that pick up loot for you to inventory expansion items.
So it's a cash grab, what game these days isn't? I can deal with micro transactions, but there's certain things about his game that ultimately made me not recommend. The game heavily rewards AFK gameplay, in fact, it almost plays itself. There's tons of tasks where you wind your character up and just watch them go for a couple hours, or overnight, or several days. I also feel like the economy in the game's a little funky as well. I play solo so I can't speak to guild life, but it took me forever to get cash together, and in the end, it just came down to hours of mindless mob grinding to keep my head above the surface.
The weapon and armor upgrade system's infuriating as well. To get a decent weapon, you're in for some frustration unless you just buy one from the Market Place, and that's only if you have the silver for it.
The final gripe that made me not recommend this game is that connecting to a server alone can be a pain. I played for over a month, and then suddenly, I couldn't join any games no matter which server I tried, even though I was playing the day before. Currently, I'm still waiting for the issue to be resolved. This seems to be a recurring problem with many people and the company's response time on the matter leaves something to be desired.
All in all, with what I've invested, I'll continue to play (as soon as I'm able). It's not a bad game, and I do enjoy it, but I'm certain there're better MMORPG's out there and I wish I'd shopped around before falling for the cheap price tag.

Greyfox is a short RPG-Maker adventure with a modern setting and a pretty original take on storytelling: as the unnamed female protagonist you'll come to briefly experience the life of four other people and ultimately judge them.
-interesting story that doesn't shy away from adult themes (death,murder,etc)
-the "inhabiting the bodies of other people" gimmick works quite well as a storytelling medium
-the town of Greyfox, while small, has quite a bit of things and people to interact with
-as most RPG-Maker games its graphics, sounds and music are quite forgettable
-very short, can be completed in less than an hour
-the choices you're given and the endings they'll unlock seem somewhat rushed and a bit lackluster
Greyfox's choice of giving us the chance to control several characters, getting to know them and eventually decide their fate is what makes the game quite interesting: the themes you'll meet while playing give the game an overall mature feel as it surely backs away from the usual "fantasy world with elfs and orcs" games one usually gets with RPG-Maker.
Sadly the short length diminishes the strength of the story and the choices you'll make: the characters you'll control will be with you for 10/15 minutes each and it's difficult to properly connect with them in such a short time: the last dialogue and three endings also feel a bit too rushed to properly give a meaningful closure. A longer game and a bit more courage in setting up the endings would have made a better use of the good story and its characters.
I got Greyfox for 20 cents and, at that price or anything around the 1$ mark, the story alone is well worth a playthrough or two if you don't mind its short length.

What can you say about a game that is already doing your job for you. The idea is this, each specific area has it's own CPU and CPU candidate that looks over each area, unfortunately, all four of the main CPU's are trapped in the Gamindustri graveyard and it's your job to save them with the help of the CPU candidates. The plot has you going through out the world of Gamindustri collecting the mascots power to save them, while fighting your way through dungeons and "bad at there job" bad guys. You can expect a lot of references to the actual game industry, as well as poking fun at games and there tropes and anime as well, and that's kinda how this franchise thrives. It loves to reference everything it possibly can but if that's not your thing, you may find the comedy to be a bit dull, since it uses the references to make the jokes.
The whole game is very JRPG so there is little you won't be familiar with but it has one new feature and that is Stella's dungeon. You can have a character (Named Stella) who you can send to dungeons you have previously visited and she will explore them floor by floor (In real time) finding items and such. It's not that much of a gameplay improvement but hey, it allows you to get a hold of more items without putting the work in.
The dungeons themselves aren't something to be impressed about since they are fairly small with some consisting of several floors. They're pretty standard dungeons, as far as JRPG's go and don't have much in the way of exploration, just a small amount of enemies littering the area and random items and material dotted around. Many could think of this as taking the mick out of JRPG dungeons, but it doesn't really do the job if the gameplay revolves around it and it's just a small as a normal JRPG.
Moving on to the combat, it's focusing on it's strategy elements while being fast passed at the same time. Unlike the first, you can now have four characters in battle instead of three which is always better in my opinion. In each battle, each character and enemy takes there turn when it's there's (Duh) so both you and the enemy can move each of your characters around the battle arena and position them carefully to get the most out of the battle. During one characters turn, you have multiple options for what you can have her do but only specific characters can do one special thing. There's:
Attack,
EXE skills,
Defend,
SP skills,
HDD on/off,
Switch,
Item,
Flee.
Whichever one you pick (Apart from HDD) will consume the characters turn and move to the next one in line. If you choose attack (Which you'll do a lot of the time) you are given the option to choose between three attacks that are tide to one of three buttons. These allow you to do different attacks which will have different effect but once you pick one, it'll move onto the next attack tab. Break focuses on depleting the enemies guard which if you accomplish that, the enemy will take more damage till it's there turn. Power which focuses on dealing damage and rush which I'm guessing does a bit of both. It leads to you having to mix and match your attacks together to deal with an enemy faster and effectively. The rest are pretty self explanatory apart from HDD on. Characters who are CPU's or CPU candidates have the ability to transform in the middle of battle, which increases there states but use up 20% of the SP gauge. Since it doesn't have any downsides to using it, you'll more then likely use it a lot of the time.
On to my favorite part of the game and that being the art style. One things I adore about this franchise is how the environments are done, as well as how the characters are designed. Each are just so gorgeous to look at, they're colorful, bright and the way the colors blend together is fantastic.
At the end of it, I find this to be quite an enjoyable experience, it's comedy focuses on referencing things from video games and anime and poking fun at them for there tropes and problems without it getting old. It's combat is very strategy focused and fast passed which is what I enjoy, leading to you blasting through each battle one at a time. Each character is unique in there own way and have there own personalities and characteristics that suit them perfectly, but also, because of who they are it can lead to a lot of mishaps and occasional funny moments to happen.

In a World where Tower Defense games flood the Market, where one is like any other with just miniscule changes there is sometimes someone trying to switch things up a little.
technically, the principle of Tower Wars has been used in tons of WarCraft 3 Maps before. but still, this is a TD game that still manages to stand out.
Because your enemy is not a set of 20 pre-made waves.
It is a Human.
Yes, Tower Wars, as Avertised is a PvP tower Defense Game. And while it follows the "Mazing" style of TDs (you have no predetermined path enemies take. you have a patch of land and the enemies will take the shortest route towards your Fortress) it also forces you to focus on how you will attack.
You gain resources by killing enemies and having your people waddle as far as they can.
Now the Towers and Enemies are where the fun starts. You are not presented with the standart "Normal tower/ Faster but weaker tower/Splash Tower/Slow Tower" variety, but rather towers that focus on different kinds of Health as well as some supporting towers, like a wind turbine that slows enemies in its path or a huge pot that throws boiling oil to all its sides.
As far as the offensive units go, you go from the why do I worry-kind of standart waddler, faster waddlers, healing waddlers, shielding waddlers, carrying waddlers, as well as Upgrades for them. in the end I believe you stand with as many supporting units as you have actual damaging units.
Rounds may be short (if any of the players really messes up his BO) or can draw out to a 2 hour "We all send a full wave of our biggest units, all fully upgraded through each others maze and look what happens"-Stalemate. but even those are fun, because its like a snail race. In the end you only win or lose by a hairs width.
Also, Bots in 10 difficulty flavors have been implemented. So if you cant find a match (or just wanna get back in form) you can always challenge one of those to get your TD Madness on

Tower Wars is a tower defense game combined with army building. This indie title was released in August 2012, so has been around for a while coming in with about 400k owners on Steam.
As with other tower defense games, you start out with a blank battlefield, although this version of tower defense is slightly different to others, you are also fighting against an opponent, who is also building towers on their blank battlefield. The aim of the game is to get your army into the enemies base to destroy their castle before they destroy yours.  Tower Wars has two currency systems, Gold and Battle points - you are able to generate gold via the mines which are already located on your map; you can do the usual technique with tower defense games and upgrade them so that they generate more gold and are quicker at it. Battle points come through sending units to your opponent and working their way to the castle, this of course requires gold though.
You build units from your barracks with gold, there is a build queue which you can fill up however you please with different assorted units which you can train, and then push them all out in one go. Your barracks has a cool down so you can only push one wave out every 40 seconds or so. Some units are basic, some have their own special abilities, and some even increase the stats of the whole wave, regardless of whether they are near the units or not.
The tower building side of things is again, very similar to other tower defense games, you are able to position your towers pretty much anywhere you want on the map, allowing you to create all sorts of death traps, and corridors that your foe has to battle through, obviously the more ground the opponent has to cover, the more damage you can do to them with your turrets. There are plenty of the normal sort of turrets, such as cannons and arrow launchers, but there are also some really unique ones, such as a huge fan that pushes your opponents back in a certain direction, this makes for some great end of hallway traps!  All of the turrets are able to be upgraded in the usual fashion too, however I didn't really find the need to do that in the single player mode.
Tower Wars has a really nice looking graphic and art style; they are really polished and it looks like a lot of care and attention has gone into making this a beautiful steam-punk looking game.
The difficulty in Tower Wars takes a huge ramp up once you get past the tutorial. I will say though, the game's tutorial is really helpful and gets you to grips with the UI and all of the basic elements of the game. It does leave out a few bits that mean you have to go digging around and use a bit of trial and error to see what is what, but that's part of the fun of this type of game.  There are also an abundance of guides, and wiki posts out there if you really want to get into the nitty gritty of it.
Since the game is almost four years old now, the multiplayer scene seems to have died down a bit, at the time of writing this there are only  ~30 people playing the game, but thankfully the game does have the option for co-op, so that may peek the attention of some people
Technically, this game has a lot of graphical options, allowing you to cater it for your rigs power and capability, coming with plenty of resolution options too.
I have put about six hours into Tower Wars so far, and given that matches against the UI/Bots can sometimes last anywhere between 45 minutes and an hour, you can expect to get a lot of gameplay out of this even on the single player mode. If you manage to find yourself a group of friends to play this with, you are looking at a major time sink with ample amounts of fun and content.  I will definitely be carrying on playing Tower Wars after writing this review, since it also has that addicted sort of gameplay that I just cannot put down.
Thankfully, due to the price of Tower Wars being £5,59, I am going to strongly recommend this title, if it was any more I would have just said to pick it up when on sale due to the lack of multiplayer activity, but because it is already a low price as it stands, I can easily say you will get at least five or six hours of enjoyment out of it. Hardcore tower defense fans should not miss out on this game!

From the Makers of Titan Quest II, Grim Dawn is a fast paced Action RPG from Crate entertainment, and is arguably the successor to the beloved Diablo II. From Early Access to its current state (v1.0.0.9), Crate has been actively updating their game, adding more content, smoothing out bugs, balancing items and masteries, and has overall made this game an extremely pleasant experience.
It is truly a game to behold, as it is not only end game focused (Unlike Diablo 3), it provides the player with Three Difficulty settings (Albeit veteran is a modifier to the "Normal" Difficulty, so I will not count it here.), each with the same story and progression. The experience gain is adequate to provide enough levels to be able to progress at a moderately fast pace, however on Hardcore mode that is a different story (I will get to that later.) It may be linear and may get a little repetitive due to the same story-line and progression three times, however the end-game content is worth mentioning. There are three challenge dungeons, each with different types of enemies (One is Aetherial, one is Cthonic, and one is Undead), while some are harder than the others (E.G the aetherial one is harder than both the other ones combined). It provides an adequate challenge to those geared and ready to face the most difficult areas in the vanilla game, however my one gripe is that for a build to be Ultimate (Hardest Difficulty level) Viable, it is required to play a game of "How do i maximize all of my resistances so I do not get One-Shot by a boss or hero." And sadly, many builds are not top tier and therefore cannot survive through ultimate, (Unless you enjoy hurting yourself).
The game also provides a wide variety of side-quests, ranging from secret-ultra bosses (I won't spoil them for you) to finding people such as a blacksmith or an apprentice which helps you break down unnecessary gear (although these can be argued as the "necessary" side quests as they provide major benefits a player cannot go without in late-game.)
There are a number of masteries, namely Demolitionist, Shaman, Soldier, Nightblade, and Occultist (With more to come in the expansions), and you can have two of each, so it provides an extremely wide variety of gameplay and mechanics that are extremely fun to play through (There are 15 combinations. With the two masteries being added in the expansion there will be much more.) There is a "Devotion Tree" Which is much like Path of Exile's passive skill tree (Less extensive however there is much more to be added) With a specific mechanic of having to go through specific minor devotions to reach the greater "Celestial" devotions. The masteries also come with a variety of abilities that complement each other in their own unique way, some are non-viable, and others are downright overpowered. Overall, gameplay and variety is amazing.
Now, onto the aforementioned Hardcore mode: This mode is for those who enjoy some insane level of anxiety, because if you die, its game over. Hardcore mode is a single-life campaign/Co-op mode, with all the same difficulties and story progression, but you are only allotted a single life. If you die, all of your resources and gear goes with you. This provides an added level of challenge to those brave souls out there who are willing to torture themselves constantly. I, personally, am not a fan of HC (Hardcore) however there are those who stand by it. To each their own. This provides a wide variety of challenges to newcomers and players who seek something new. (Not recommended for beginners or those who are just joining the game. I myself have been on forums, the GD subreddit etc and have been playing for a while and I'm still not ready.)
Onto the Crucible DLC: Essentially a wave based survival "DLC" that provides a lot of gear and resources for the player if they are able to make it through the 150 waves. Obviously, like other wave-like game types, each wave becomes harder and harder. The hardest difficulty here is Gladiator, and if your build is a top tier ultimate viable build, this mode will put it to the ultimate test. Bombarding you with enemies, heroes, nemesises (One type of ultra-boss), Secret Bosses and End-game bosses all at once is not only a test of your tankiness but also you damage output. There are several game mechanics here that come to your aid though. There are points you may spend called "Tributes" To create towers that aid you in battle, giving you necessary buffs or damage dealers to come to your aid. A few remarks before I begin:

All that said, I'm sure you can understand why I was a little disappointed with this game. It's a sequel. If it were just a disappointing game, it would score lower.
