I found this game to be an incredibly well-balanced shooter. The controls were tight and the game design, in general, was wonderful. The visuals are borderline obscene, but fit the style of the game well. There is a decent amount of game modes to be found, each offering its own challenges.
I always appreciate the ability to customise a character/vehicle to my own tastes, so the perk system was great for me. Saving up for perks and putting together my own load-outs for each challenge I set myself, was an absolute pleasure. It was very satisfying to see myself get increasingly more powerful, but still be challenged by the game.
Having your own music be the soundtrack for 'Beat Hazard' is what makes this game truly outstanding and added may hours to my play time. It has been implemented incredibly well. Not only did every track I played offer an appropriate level of challenge but gave each song its own feel too.
With the increased difficulty levels and the addition of 'Shadow Ops' kept me coming back to this game for many hours and I would recommend it to anyone (who doesn't suffer from photosensitive epilepsy).

Recommended for those who are just getting a little tired of the original COH and want to mix things up. Personally, I still find the original to be superior as a whole. This sequal does get a few things right. The sound effects are impressive for example, and the addition of "true sight" is the one thing I would almost like to see retroactively added to the original; no longer can the enemy see me on the other side of a giant warehouse just because they happen to be in my arbitrary sight bubble.
The winter weather effects are beautifully done but are not much fun to play in. This is one of those cases in which realism trumped fun in development. I know the Eastern front was harsh (and that is depicted admirably) but sometimes it feels like I'm playing an interactive version of Jack London's "To Build a Fire." when I would rather be fighting.
Graphically there is a lot more going on, but I don't think its really a better looking game considering all the processing power it requires. It reminds me of the early Playstation games vs 16 bit era stuff. I knew 3d was the future and a lot more manipulation was happening on screen, but it still just looked like blocky polygons at the time.

'Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series' --- A spoiler-free analysis and review
First of all I have to say that in order to understand certain happenings in this game you will need to watch 'Game of Thrones', if you haven't done so already.
This game is an interesting extension of HBO's 'Game of Thrones'.
'What is it about?'
In this game you will be able to control some members of House Forrester, seated in Ironrath. House Forrester are loyal bannermen to House Stark. Throughout this game you will encounter a lot of problems that endanger the existense of House Forrester. You will have to decide how to act and respond at certain moments. Your choice matters.
'Does my choice really influence the game?'
Obviously we want to be able to influence the game as much as we can. That's the main reason why I play games produced by Telltale Games. After having finished 'Game of Thrones' by Telltale Games I can say:
Yes, your choices do influence the game. You might not realise that in the first few episodes but it is amazing how a lot of your choices can strongly change the game's story.
'What are the positives and negatives?'
In this section I will list my personal positives and negatives about this game:
Positive:
+The story is very compelling.
+The dialogues are realistic
+You start to empathise with the characters throughout the game
+The choices are often very challenging and difficult.
+Your choices influence the game
+It does have the 'Game of Thrones'-Style: Blood and violence. No sexual or erotic scenes though!
Negative:
-The graphics could be better / and some textures
-I've seen a few bugs in the game. One of the bugs specifically made me a little bit upset.
_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _  _ _ _ _
'Summarised'
In total this game is definitely a success for Telltale Games.
Not a masterpiece though!
The graphics and textures definitely need an improvement.
It is definitely worth a buy for every 'Game of Thrones' fan.
Keep it up, Telltale Games!

Some people like "clicking" games, I like this game.
I was pretty skeptical considering the high rating this game has (98%). I was really worried about the rating being cushioned by the "anime effect" that many other visual novel-esque titles have despite being really niche material. And it is true that it does benefit, but this game is fun without all the fanservice and references. Those things are fluffy little extras to a well balanced grind-fest RPG.
The grinding isn't obviously pointless (its still a game), and there are active elements of the game that evolve and change as a reward for your grind. It is simple and pleasant.
The references this game has are mostly sigh inducing eye-rollers, but they contribute to a really cheery atmosphere as they are ♥♥♥♥ing everywhere.
The cutscenes will make you laugh sometimes, but other times you will be thankful there is a skip function.
In a vacuum the story is pretty much exactly like every other generic JRPG, which in itself is just another reference.
The characters are two-dimensional in every sense of the word.
Some little things get on my nerves like reused assets; e.g., higher level monsters will have the same model as their weaker counter part with a different name(child wolf, wolf, etc), dungeons look the same with only slight path changes or extras, and some of the outfits and customizeables are just recolors.
I recommend buying this when it is on sale 100%. If you are a sucker for anime tropes and cutesy fanservice you might be interested in paying full price.

Just a little warning, this is a walking simulator in the purest sense, this isn't a bad thing on itself because they're good examples on how to do it, but for those people who don't like this genre or would want a more active gameplay then skip this one.
Otherwise if you want a game where you like to have some sort of exploration, a cute story and a lot of feels, then this game is for you and here are my points on why you should get it.
Gameplay
This being a walking simulator/first person exploration (for those who hate the name of the former) you'll do a lot of walking and very little of interaction, except when something very obvious comes out. However the charm of this game comes with the cute story and how the game handles being a blind person, for your area of vision is severely limited and you'll have to search the area in order to orient yourself and how the world reveals itself in your eyes.
There is a very crucial thing I have to mention, you'll move very slow and you'll have to do some exploration in order to see the world, this is design wise though i can understand people being bothered by (because it's very tedious) this it's made to make you feel empathy for blind people and their everyday struggles (for they have to check their world and have to be very careful if they go to unexplored territory). But because this is in the mind of a 8 year old girl the world becomes very vivid, colorful and plesant to explore, untill you reach a part when the girl feels uncomfortable.
One part that is neat is when she discovers that the sound of certain objects/animals aren't what she thinks they are. This adds up to the feeling of the game and will make you understand the struggles of blind people if they aren't keen on detecting sounds or if they confuse them.
Though if you don't get bothered by the previous point the payoff is neat, because you'll get to slowly explore how the world looks and the beautiful scenery and how she uses her other senses in order to notice where the cat went or where thigns are far away. The explored parts will stay there in case you get lost so that you'll get a sense of where to go and while it defeats the part of being blind, it's something that many appreciate because otherwise it would be a bad experience.
There are some puzzles from here and there but they're very simple to make.
The only thing i really dislike is a level where you have to go to the pier and then rain falls, this is where in a certain point the explored parts fade away and you'll have to know where you're going if you want to proceed, this took me a while because it's easy to get lost. And a part where you have to backtrack in a previous level, but other than those parts the rest are fine and worth exploring
Controls
They work, but they'll be clunky because again, you are in the role of a blind girl and thus you'll have a bit of trouble if you want to turn around.
Story
There's not much story here besides the intro, where rae losts her sight by fireworks, she's alone in her home and a cat comes out and she has to find the cat because he hasn't come to visit her in a while.
The rest of the chapters are about her experience in the adventure.
Depending if you're invested you'll either want to cheer for the girl to find the cat or want to get through the story as quickly as possible, but the story itself will make you care for her.
Graphics
They look very gorgeous and plesant to look, though a certain human might seem a bit off if you look very carefully, but the rest are something that you would like to see.
Soundtrack
The game will mostly be silent except for some parts where she discovers something or when she finds something bad. Nothing very memorable but they do impact of the feeling of the game.
Overrall
This game has some punches in the feel factor and it's a very good simulator on how it is to be blind (even if you can get the same experience by closing you eyes and walk), the worlds are interesting to explore (in the normal way, not in a surreal way) and if you can get through the clunky controls and the purposely tedious gameplay, you'll have a story that you'll appreciate in the end and maybe make you cry.
6/10 it's good, but it's simple and while I do like how it hanldes blind issues, they're games where you'll get better experience, but it's still worth checking out on it's own.

This looked like the kind of C&C-like RTS game I've been waiting for. It is made by the studio consisting of ex-Westwood developers afterall. However, it failed in the one crucial area where any RTS has to do well in order succeed as a good RTS: having interesting units with depth.
The factions are cool (except maybe Beta) as far as base building goes. The Goo is one of the most unique factions I've seen in an RTS game and it plays uniquely as well. Humans have to build power networks to be able to place buildings/turrets. If you can expand far enough without getting the network "cut" somewhere, you could do turret pushes with it. Then there's a Betas, which are all about building walls, which is why I think they are boring and tedious. You can mount the walls with your units. Since then, the new 4th faction has been added, which does everythingthrough wireless connections iirc.
Both human and Beta factions have strong walls. Too strong in fact. They take quite the punishment and as such often makes the flow of the game sluggish. In C&C the walls were only enough to hold back infantry, not tanks. In Starcraft you can build a wall using basic structures like supply depots, barracks or bunkers, but even those couldn't hold out this long. Plus you can rebuild the walls rather fast.
For that matter, this game doesn't really have infantry, tanks and aircraft as separate unit types either. It's all just "units", you build them from the same building. The humans don't even have anything that could be called "infantry". All their units are basically drones. Some can fly, but you don't really build them from a different building, like you would in Starcraft or in C&C3 and RA3. This further contributes to the units being bland and boring.
Since we're talking about units, here's the problem with them: all the units between all the factions are almost completely interchangeable. For example, every faction has an artillery unit. Nothing wrong with that right? Of course, but they all function the same way and have almost the same stats. All artillery units have the same attack, where they lob a big projectile at the enemy from a distance. The human artillery is accurate, the beta artillery is inaccurate and the goo artillery can climb onto hills. The differences between them are too small and meaningless.
Lets look at the artillery units in Red Alert 3 as comparison: the sover artilley is a V4 rocket launcher, which can be either used to decimate infantry with cluster missiles or shell turrets from afar. The cluster missiles are also good for area denal if you just have the V4s attack an area continuously. The allied artillery calls in orbital laser strikes which continuously damage anything from afar in bursts, but they can also deploy a large shield to cover a group of units - especially useful conbination in a Chronosphere attack. The Empire's artillery uses long range laser beams which take a while to charge up. The firing happens in a flash. They can 1-shot some buildings if you let them charge long enough. You can also interrupt charging at any moment to let them fire with the curent amount of charge. As such, this artillery unit is best used in ambushes to instantly delete some key units in the enemy army's composition. Or if you have good enough micro and can fire the lasers without over-charging them to destroy a lot of units faster.
NONE of the units in Grey Goo have this kind of diversity in usage between factions. They don't even have very unique voice lines, call-outs or looks. Look at all the human units in this game: white, hovering with very similar but weird shapes. Now look at the allied tank in RA2 and look at the mirage tank. It's a HUGE difference. The units in Red Alert 2/3 all had their own unique character and mood. The simple allied G.I. soldier felt so wonderful to command around because of his can-do attitude in his voice. If I write
literally every RA2 player will read this in the same voice! Hell, even if i just write
I just gave most of the readers here an org@sm.
The campaign story is somewhat interesting. It's basically humans becoming the aliend invaders (as opposed to being invaded by alines). The campaign missions are mostly just tutorials for units though. As such they are short, too.
If these devs were to create Grey Goo 2 and fix all these issues with the bland units and give the game some additional depth using upgrades and ability researches like in Starcraft, it could become an amazing RTS game. As it is now, it just falls way too short and manages to be merely average.

A game full of empty choices.
They try really hard to convince you that you had other options, but you didn't. In many seemingly pivotal decisions, every single option has the same result. For example, I reset an episode and tried everything the complete opposite. No difference. They really rub it in your face that you "chose wrong", too, even though the result is the same for every option.
There's a few characters from the TV show/books, which is cool, with one exception. Ramsay Snow. You're pitted against him multiple times, and you know full well he's narratively invincible, that nothing you do could possibly harm him, because he's protected by story canon. It was a terrible decision to make him a recurring villain. One of the key selling points of the Game of Thrones fiction is that no one feels safe. Anyone could die at any time. Good people can get beheaded, monsters can be poisoned, etc. Making a character 100% safe is a terrible idea, and pitting you against that invincible character is a game-breakingly bad idea.
This sort of magic-wand solution to plot happens quite a bit. There's obviously an expected "path" the player is supposed to follow, and if you don't choose those options they just shove you right back onto the main path as quickly and crudely as possible.
Make some tough choices to get key information about an ambush? You still get caught in the ambush.
You get the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of you just like that for the entire game, and then it's over. They seem to hint that a few choices will effect the next season, but I won't be playing it.
If you still really want to get this game, just know that you could spam click randomly through every dialog and story choice in the game and still see the same plot everyone else did.
Rating: D+

Saints Row IV is an Open World Action world, which a delightful mix of humor and drama, the game starts out playing as a third person shooter, and then switches over to feeling like you're playing a super hero game.
I've actually been putting off writing this review because I've been having so much fun playing through the game a second time. That should speak volumes for itself.
"Greetings Mr./Ms. President your immediate attention is needed regarding the problems of ruling the entire United Sates." *Zap zap zap*"
who are you?"
"Really? you just killed three of our secret agents and ruined the press conference"
*pew pew pew*
I don't want to give anything away specific about the story, simply put your crew has been abducted by aliens and it's your job to save them and bring down Zinyak to save the human race. The story is full of humor, I found myself laughing aloud at the countless references and the ways these characters interacted with each other.
As you play through the game you unlock various "super powers", from sprinting, to running, to firing ice, telekinesis, or ground stomp. The super powers flow seamlessly with the story, and genuinely make game play pleasurable to experience.
In addition to super powers, you also have various weapons that you can use, my personal favorite was the energy-sword (of course), but you had guns, hand to hand combat, laser guns, regular guns, rocket launchers, and many alien weapons that get unlocked as you play through the game.

The achievements on this game are broken down into four categories: 1) Main story achievements. 2) doing all the things, and probably missed the first time through achievements. 3) DLC achievements.
1) As the title implies most of the main story achievements you get just by playing through, you will get close to 10-15 achievements just playing through. 2) The achievements I ended up missing were a few grinding achievements that I could do at the end of the game, in addition to doing the side missions AFTER the last boss... so I need to play through the whole game again. (normally this would be immensely annoying for me, but this game is definitely fun a second time through) 3) You need to buy the DLC, and I don't own it at the moment.
I was able to successful log into my saints row account and upload a character on 09/27/15.

The standalone version without any DLC is priced at $19.99, that is a fair price based on the amount of time I've personally put into the game, and this is a game that can be replayed and enjoyed again, If you already know you like the saints row series, you should probably go for a Game of the Century Edition, or Ultimate Franchise Pack.

This game is going on my top list for favorite games I've played, I've also learned how to identify some qualities in games that I tend to really enjoy playing, from playing Saints Row IV. To quickly recap, The story was hilarious, and entertaining, the game play was excellent, The achievements were great except for the broken achievement, the price is fair.
This game appeals to most people, but especially people who enjoy open world games. I should add one comment regarding tech requirements, the game came out in 2013, so it was rough on my personal computer, I tried troubleshooting, but in the end just kept playing, even though the game crashed occasionally. ----Still love the game.

Combat: the art of hitting stuff is pretty basic, but it feels damn good with the gore, slow motion on certain hits and zombie ragdolls.

Greyfox is sort of a role playing game... in that you assume the roles of various characters throughout the game. It's basically like a point and click adventure type game, but instead of pointing and clicking you have RPG type controls and environments. The basic plot is that you, the main character, get sick of your day to day life. You decide to quit your job and move to the small town of Greyfox, which is inhabited mainly by elderly people. You quickly get into a scenario where you are forced to live a day in the life of someone in town. This happens multiple times. This is essentially all you do in the game, without going into spoiler terrirory about what happens with each character.
The gameplay, as mentioned, is basically going around, examining the environments, talking to people, getting items, and trying to use items to complete tasks within the game. Some things can be missed but others are necessary to progress. You will get to pick different options in some dialogues. The answers sometimes have consequences and sometimes don't matter. At the end of each day, you get to decide whether the character you've played as lives or dies. After all the days, there's a final cutscene and the game ends.
I liked how the game played, as opposed to actual point and click games. The RPG playstyle and art style helped me get into it more than some visual novel or point and click adventure normally would. I also like how the game gives you choices that may or may not matter. In fact, and this may be a bit of a spoiler but it doesn't really matter ultimately, in the end all of your choices have no true consequences aside from how you personally feel about them. This is a pretty cool idea, to let you feel how you want to about what you've chosen as the fate of these people. The way you play is determined by your own set of values moreso than those of the developers. It's also nice to play some depressing games now and then. It's not necessarily a happy ending, but it can be as long as you feel like it is. It's just a neat little concept.
On the downside, there's also no true goal of this game. The rather aimless nature is strung along by a few integral decidions that you have to make and actions you have to do in order to move on. You can't really lose the game. So there's no real goal here. There IS replay value to see what happens if you do different things, but there's not a lot of incentive when it goes against your own values to make such choices, especially in a game that is so fueled on such choices. Also, many times during the game certain places will be closed off to you. This doesn't feel like it's all that natural. It just seems like they didn't program interesting things in those areas for the entire game so only areas where you'd need to go are programmed in. It's okay, but feels a little lacking and as though it's trying to herd you in the right direction... in a game that's about exploring the world in other people's shoes. Also, a minor complain about the art. I like it, but it seems like a lot of it is just assests from some RPG maker. Not a big deal in terms of the story and atmosphere, but still a little lazy on some of it.
Overall? Greyfox is a fun, interesting little game. It'll probably only last you one to two hours to finish... which means you'll either want to achievement hunt or idle it to get the card drops. It's not for everyone, and I wouldn't call it an RPG, but if you like the concept of exploring the lives of old people and choosing their fate, then look into it. Is it worth the full 5 bucks? I would say no, personally. BUT, if you can get it for around 50 cents or less, it's definitely worth a shot. Maybe a dollar if you're really interested. It's just not long enough or deep enough to be worth full price. Greyfox gets a 5 out of 10 for being a fun, interesting little adventure where personal values and investment in the characters really pay off.

The not-sequel to Alan Wake, the story takes place in the fictional TV show that showed up sometimes in the original Alan Wake, Night Springs. You, the Champion of Light have to defeat your evil double, the Herald of Darkness by doing various tasks to rewrite reality and kill said evil double, who plans on taking your place in the world and ruining everything.
The combat is improved from the original. The enemies have less light health than before and your flashlight only depletes light health when you are amplifying the light like in the original. You have access to more powerful weapons sooner, and can get even better weapons collecting the manuscript pages and using them to unlock weapon cases. The game gives out ammo like candy at least on normal difficulty, so there isn't much stress about bullet levels.
It appears to run on the same base engine that Alan Wake ran on, so the graphical quality and style mostly remains the same. The voice acting never really gets cringeworthy, and the music fits the right moments.
It's pretty good overall. The combat is better, the story is different and NOT a continuation of Alan Wake, you will go through three main areas in the game. It runs pretty short at around 3 hours. It feels more like a standalone DLC to Alan Wake rather than it's own game, and for 15 dollars I feel it is worth it. It is entertaining throughout the whole time, though the ending might leave some wanting more.
If you liked Alan Wake you will probably like this, and it probably won't sell too many people who didn't like it. For 15 dollars (or cheaper through sales) it is worth it.

In short: This is an AWESOME multiplayer tower defense game, but not too many people play it, so you should convince your friends to get it. You need a few hours to master all the mechanics, but then it's great entertainment.
You and your opponent both have castles and barracks, and you need to send waves to destroy each other, while simultaneously upgrading your units and castles as well as tending to your gold mines. Gold is mainly needed for recruiting units, and as long as they are within enemy territory, they earn "battle points" for you, which you need for upgrades. This makes for some challenging gameplay, as you need gold to earn battle points, but also battle points to get upgrades to earn more gold, ...
There are many different units, each with unique attributes - speed, health, damage dealt (against opponent's castle), armor, shield. Some have special abilities, e.g. they increase other units' speed or improve their shields.
Similarly, there are lots of different towers with unique strengths and weaknesses, e.g. arrow towers, cannons, lava distributors, fans (to slow down the enemy's units) etc.
There are a few maps shipped with the game and you can download additional maps from the community. The gold mines are always placed randomly, which means that for every match, you need to come up with a new path around which to build your defense towers (although you will always be using the same basic structures).
I recommend that you buy this on sale and get additional keys for your friends, because as mentioned above, it's hard to even find opponents for multiplayer, and the matching can take ages. But I have spent way too many hours playing against buddies now and we're all hooked!
PROS:
[+] Challenging game mechanics
[+] Awesome multiplayer mode (1v1, 2v2, 3v3)
[+] Many maps to choose from and random adjustments in each round
[+] Very cool steampunk setting
CONS:
[-] Steep learning curve (although this becomes rewarding if you don't give up early)
[-] Very few people "out there" for multiplayer matches (but it's more fun with friends anyway)
[-] Boring co-op mode

Company of Heroes 2 doesn't really do anything new in the real-time-tactics genre, but it delivers more solid gameplay of the same style as the first game. With the focus shifted to the Eastern Front, gameplay has been modified to include the harsh effects of the Russian winter. While the winter maps can sometimes be aggravating to play, they capture quite well (for a game) the difficulties of fighting in the dead of winter. The German faction remains largely unchanged from their previous iteration, though German infantry feels slightly less versatile than it used to. The Russian faction captures the desperation of the Red Army well enough and the game encourages you to be profligate in spending men's lives to defeat the Fascists. The Theater of War game mode adds interesting new challenges by restricting the player to specific periods of the war and the equipment that comes with them. CoH2 ultimately does little to reinvent the wheel, but the gameplay is still fun and satisfying. 4/5 stars.

As much as I enjoy both the Game of Thrones franchise and Telltale's previous offerings, I cannot recommend this game anywhere as much as I would have liked to.
Storywise, it is
Game of Thrones: kicking the game off at the Red Wedding tells you exactly the kind of tone you should expect. There are several interactions with the events and characters from the series, and kudos to Telltale for getting members of the show's cast to provide voice acting for their characters. However, the main characters' family is a blatant House Stark clone with a bunch of Kings Landing structures (like the advisory council and the [s]Hand of the King[/s] Sentinel) weighing it down, which annoyed me. Also, with so many characters running around (five player-protagonists, each with a separate cast of NPCs), I never really developed the emotional attachments required for the obligatory Game of Thrones gut-punches to really be effective, leaving me at the end of each episode just feeling generically depressed. This is
a game you play to enjoy.
Gameplay is where it starts to fall apart. Although a necessary evil to explore the various regions shown in the show, having five player-protagonists and frequently cutting between them was something I disliked. It turned each episode into a set of loosely-related sequences instead of a more coherent single narrative. I found it difficult to keep track of each character's actions and NPC interactions, so each character failed to find a consistent 'voice' (although now that the episodes are all out, new players won't have the two-month gaps to contend with). The incresing reliance on quick-time events compared to previous Telltale titles also annoyed me, as did the ending blatantly not resolving anything in favour of leading into the upcoming second season. I do like how Telltale continues to play with and subvert their gameplay mechanisms, whether its taunting me with move commands when I
, or informing me after successfully dodging some interrogating questions that “[?] Jon Snow knows nothing”.
Graphics is another letdown. They had big problems bringing in the characters from the live-action show and rendering them in the 'Telltale style', with some of the character models just not fitting in (they did improve across the series, but Cersei's battering-ram forehead and Margaery's pixellated alabaster skin still jarred). The 'out-of-focus painting' style for the background art also failed to mesh well with the art style of the foreground and the characters. The attempt to replicate the show's title sequence was just plain clunky.
The music is pleasant but broadly unrememberable (although Talia's funeral song gave me chills). Voice acting was good, although in later episodes, conversations didn't seem to balance as well (the relative volumes and tones sounded like two people each talking at a wall, and yes I know that's how voice-recording works, but they usually hide it better). Some of the lines of dialogue were missing, particularly in the (otherwise quite well done) end of series decision recap.
Overall, if you're a really big fan of the franchise or of Telltale's work, the game may be worth considering at a discount and with a cheerful palate-cleanser on standby. Less committed fans or drive-by punters should probably steer clear.

Huge disappointment...
I am a big fan of the franchise but this watered down addition isn't worth its full price.
Campaign missions felt short and offer little to no replay value, with the exception of Tiger Hunting which I found to be the highlight of the campaign.
New multiplayer maps are dull and seem to be designed to serve the snow and blizzard mechanics; vast snowfields dotted with bonfires. It fails to compliment the original mechanic of how dynamic maps were meant to be, the beginning of your game could involve skirmishes between a maze of hedgerows and villages and end with battling out in smoldering ruins and craters. Steam workshop could redeem this with CoH 1 maps getting fan-made revivals.
The removal of the commander talent trees is what cripples the game most. No longer are the 3 distinct commander choices  that each serve their own playstyle and tactics but now DLC centered commanders that blend into eachother, the same off-map abilities and additional units rearranged and passed off as a seperate commander.The lack of commander variety will mean each game will start to feel like the last. Every game eventually leads to tanks vs tanks, grenadiers and conscripts end up serving no purpose but to rush enemy tanks, disable them with an anti-tank grenade the go capture a point while your tanks pick off the disabled enemy tank.
Theatre of War scenarios are a joke, they are simply AI skirmish matches. 1941 scenarios let you play with even FEWER units to choose from. Dont expect to see Stonewall or Panzerkrieg game modes from ToV, they'll probably be DLC down the road (hopefully steam workshop will beat them to it).
Company of Heroes 2 does not live up to its predecessor, fewer units, bland maps, mediocre campaign, and the biggest killer   is how the game is now entirely centered around DLC. I'm sad to see my favourite RTS get strangled by the DLC demon but steam workshop could be its salvation.

I'm just about wrapping up the game and I thought I'd give my two cents on it. First off, there is a dramatic difference in the "choices" you make, and having certain plotpoints happen, regardless. It was angering to see the end of episode one unavoidable-- and made me feel as though it was all pointless. Another thing that bothered me was how alike the Forresters and Starks are. I mean come on, guys. Ned dies, Gregor dies. Rodrick "dies" but becomes lord, Asher is like Jon, an outcast, and could also be paired with Gared ( not family, but like family lol ). Ethan and Bran are young little lords. Mira and Talia are pretty much "A Game of Thrones" Sansa through "A Dance With Dragons" Sansa. EVEN RYON IS DESIGNED E X A C T L Y LIKE RICKON! Only one who's missing is Arya, which could also be paired with Talia given her bravery in wanting to help and fight and stuff. But my god, it's such blatant mirroring such as this that really did bother me throughout the game. With all that being said, I have enjoyed playing it, the story, as contrived and forced as it is, really is good. The Forrester/Ironwood culture is really interesting, and something I would like to see expanded upon. The Whitehills need to stop being so ♥♥♥♥ing "menacing" because they really come off more as schoolhouse bullies than actual villains.
I wish we had played as different families, one from the North, the Reach, even Dorne for godsakes and have our choices directly screw over the other families we played as. Like imagine playing as a bannerman of the Lannisters, and choosing to go after Deepwood Motte or Riverrun? Just stuff like that, requiring a little more effort in development.
Regardless, the art is stunning, the soundtrack is based GoT music, with a little entertaining quips during fight scenes. The characters do have their own motivations that differ from one to the next, their own personalities, which is very interesting. I would recommend this game, because if you're a fan of the show ( and the books, but looking at this through my "book reader" glasses is kind of difficult ), and can look past the glaring similarities, plotholes, and lack of actual choices, it is a intense ride full of that "Game of Thrones; anyone can die at any time" nonsense. If you like that stuff, you'll like it.

At most, I think the game is okay.
I can see what its goal was to do and for what it presents, it's okay as a whole. However, the dialogue can be groan-worthy at times and the story arc for each character is too short to actually be memorable or even to have anything more than the cliches. I was able to finish this game and got all the achievements in less than two hours. The game tries to present this "depressing" and "mysterious" story and present "tough" choices for the fate of each character, but looking at it as a whole, it doesn't exactly deliver the impact that it wants to give off.
// Spoilers start here, I guess //
"A town with a sinister secret", "Uncover its mysteries".
These are two phrases that appear in the trailer, but really, I personally felt misled. There's no secret or mystery about the town; You move to a little town from the city and you feel ready to retire when some woman with the power to implant you into other peoples' bodies wants you to see that you're still too young and you aren't really ready for death. She shows you the stories of those who are, and you have the choice of whether or not you think each character should die. There's no "discovering the truth" unless you're just learning about the characters' backgrounds, and even then, they're pretty flat and to the point.
For a game that literally has the aspect of "tough choices" in its description, even the character you play as doesn't have a lot of feeling in either choice you made. She replies with short sentences that hardly show emotion, so why should the player have any emotion? Furthermore, when you can just skip to the end for some parts of an arc, it really puts all the other dialogue and event checks to waste, like in Kat's where all you have to do is get your medicine and talk to the Mysterious Woman.
One thing that bugs me is that once you finish going through the characters' stories, she tells you how many people you chose to kill and tells you that she hopes you're ready to take on the guilt of your actions for the rest of your life, but she also tells you that she's not going to tell you what's "right" or "wrong," which feels extremely contridictory to me. She brings you into these peoples' lives for you to judge them, and of course it's by your norm moral standards, so naturally you and the woman must have a sense of "right" and "wrong" when she talks about guilt for your murders (if you chose to do that), so what's her real angle here? That aspect of the story is just a nitpick for me, though.
// Spoilers end here //
Maybe I'm just more heartless than most people, but I don't really feel the impact of a depressing story like all the other positive reviewers do, because I don't feel for these characters. I do understand what the developer may have been trying to go for and it was a nice attempt. It could have been worse.
As for the visual aspect, it's not anything terrible. They're decent; Using RPG Maker's base elements plus others' isn't something that should account into this game.
/// TL;DR: I think that Greyfox is alright for a start, but is definitely only worth the $0.19 paid for it. I hope the developer will continue to try and make more content that will have a more fleshed-out story.

If you love exploring and finding collectibles with a combination of stone-age open world survival without minding story-rich content then this game is pretty much perfect to spend your time in.
Far Cry Primal is a glimpse into the past that takes the player in a hypothetical setting somewhere in the middle Europe of around 10000 BC. You play as a character who while surviving in the wild finds out that he has the ability to tame wild carnivores and use them as allies in order to achieve the only goal that mattered at that time. Survival at its best and making sure that your tribe survives.
The aim of the game is to help you emerge in a world that 3 tribes coexist, each trying to claim their own land and right to hunt, live and evolve. Your clan, the Wenja, a group of people who are spread all over the land and which you need to help survive and form a safe community. The Izila, a group of people who seem to be more evolved, are aware of how to use resources like fire and materials in order to build communities and temples and have a basic form of civilization. And the Udam, a group of people that seem to be the last remains of the kind of Homo Erectus (a species that ironically has stoped existing ever since the 70000BC but is set in the game in order to spice things up) and are at the edge of extinction.
The game offers a very interesting set of gameplay features and skills. You can craft some basic types of weapons at start and then either by evolving your crafting skills (for example finding a unique type of volcano rock to make knives out of) or by exploring(for example through the quests you will find a better type of bow) you get to have upgraded forms of these items. All your items can be crafted with materials you need to find. From gathering wood and rocks to meat and bones and special animal skins (thankfully you can set the gathering animation off). You can use nature to your benefit now and this matters a lot. You can combine strategies using your tamed animals, the element of fire, sneak attacks and your weapons in order to achieve your goals.
Graphics are amazing. I didn’t mind a few FPS drops now and then, im not going to pretend I care for a drop from 60FPS to 40FPS, things were always still smooth while set on Ultra specs. Sound and environmental design is AMAZING. Exploration is very fun and satisfying. The map size is decent, though the shape is similar to that of Far Cry 4’s but something I didn’t really mind at all because the whole design and nature settings is unique. Voice acting was nice, eventhough the languages in the game are completely made up, I find it interesting when voice actors manage to pass feelings, ideas and character to you without making any sense in words, everything was based on the perfect balance between voice and face expressions.
The game as a new release has some bugs. I missed a Uplay achievement from an action I already completed. There is a type of collectible that when found doesn’t let you interact with it. The AI of people of your clan is not so smart during missions that you have to help them. They might get on the way, get hurt, and then see you as an enemy, which is annoying since every single person you save becomes a +1 member on your growing community – a village which you will spend time and materials to help build and even upgrade.
Now many complain for this game that it is a reskin of farcry 3 and 4. That the map is the same with FC4. That is has no story. The fact is that the trailers provided and the spoiler-free opinions expressed before this was available on PC had me knowing almost exactly where I was stepping in. Hard Core Far Cry fans got something that was not what Far Cry meant to them until now. But you know what the game by itself is great. I loved this game a pretty damn lot. Only couple of things i mind is that I wish this game had a longer cmpaign and that that it's too bad it hasn’t a co-op option, like going hunting with a friend, or having a game mode with special co-op missions. That would be sweet (if done right).
All in all, I loved this game. It left me satisfied. It had enough content to leave me happy. There were some fun moments. And there were some funny moments too. I do recommend this game but I kinda wish there was a bit more into this making it worthy to spend at least 10 or 20 more hours in it. DLCs will cost money which makes me also wish this was a 50 buck title and not a 60.
It’s a 8/10 with potential of 9/10 if some fixes take place soon.

Tower Wars is a title that launched pretty successfully, and got the thumbs up from players and critics. Unfortunately, due to awful handling of multiplayer rankings and accounts, unwarranted bans and poor tutorial elements, this one started rolling down the ratings hill shortly after release, and has come to rest somewhere near the bottom.
Most of the problems of this game stem from handling of multiplayer, and while there are strong reasons not to buy it, there is also a fantastic hex-based strategic tower defence game here for the right players.
Tower Wars has a great art style and hero gimmicks, and the hex based placement atop towering maps works really well visually. The gameplay is also new and unique enough for the genre that it does stand out a little. Most importantly, the gameplay is genuinely fun and has some strategic elements, resource management, and more. There are plenty of things to think and worry about while playing each game.
* Detailed statistics, unit and damage reports at the end of the match help you understand how you're playing
* Two types of economy and battle mechanics mean that balancing elements of your battlefield is key, and changes from match to match
The vast majority of Tower Wars' problems stem from crappy handling of multiplayer. At the time of review, multiplayer is all but dead unless you play Ranked matches, and many players simply don't care about the ladder.
The landscape of multiplayer on the Ranked system is frankly a horrible mess. The nature of games means that your first few moves in a multiplayer game can determine whether you'll win or lose. In games like Starcraft, for example, you can make a decisive early move, but the seasoned enemy can overcome it with their skill. In Tower Wars this isn't the case, and you can sometimes tell you've lost a game after just a handful of moves.
Couple that with the fact that there are people abusing the ranking system by intentionally losing matches and reducing their ranking, just to play against easier opponents, for whatever reason, and you, as a new player, will encounter basically 2 types of matches:
* Your opponent is drastically better than you and will stomp you in the first few moves
* Your opponent is drastically better than you but is intentionally losing their ranking score, so will let you kill them within the first few moves
This makes the game all but pointless in multiplayer for most, and is unlikely to change in the foreseeable future. The only realistic approach, for many, is finding friends or groups who still play this game, but due to the problems mentioned above, those are now very rare.
As for single player, it has problems too:
* There's no compelling reason to keep playing single-player other than the gameplay. If you don't enjoy playing games for their own sake, there's no new units, new abilities or interesting changes to keep you playing other than a different map and a harder difficulty.
* The A.I. difficulty is extremely hard in the final single-player levels, and may be too much even for a committed player
Priced at just £5.59/7.99€/$7.99, Tower Wars clocks in at around 3-4 hours gameplay in the single-player campaign, and would be really good value for money if there were an active multiplayer. Unfortunately the public multiplayer is all but a waste of time unless you are a glutton for punishment, or you can find people to play with.
* There are some fantastic multiplayer guides and tutorials from the community which may make uneven multiplayer worth suffering through for some
* Tower Wars
, but is almost empty and can be ignored, but does offer a couple extra maps for those inclined

What can you say about a game that is already doing your job for you. The idea is this, each specific area has it's own CPU and CPU candidate that looks over each area, unfortunately, all four of the main CPU's are trapped in the Gamindustri graveyard and it's your job to save them with the help of the CPU candidates. The plot has you going through out the world of Gamindustri collecting the mascots power to save them, while fighting your way through dungeons and "bad at there job" bad guys. You can expect a lot of references to the actual game industry, as well as poking fun at games and there tropes and anime as well, and that's kinda how this franchise thrives. It loves to reference everything it possibly can but if that's not your thing, you may find the comedy to be a bit dull, since it uses the references to make the jokes.
The whole game is very JRPG so there is little you won't be familiar with but it has one new feature and that is Stella's dungeon. You can have a character (Named Stella) who you can send to dungeons you have previously visited and she will explore them floor by floor (In real time) finding items and such. It's not that much of a gameplay improvement but hey, it allows you to get a hold of more items without putting the work in.
The dungeons themselves aren't something to be impressed about since they are fairly small with some consisting of several floors. They're pretty standard dungeons, as far as JRPG's go and don't have much in the way of exploration, just a small amount of enemies littering the area and random items and material dotted around. Many could think of this as taking the mick out of JRPG dungeons, but it doesn't really do the job if the gameplay revolves around it and it's just a small as a normal JRPG.
Moving on to the combat, it's focusing on it's strategy elements while being fast passed at the same time. Unlike the first, you can now have four characters in battle instead of three which is always better in my opinion. In each battle, each character and enemy takes there turn when it's there's (Duh) so both you and the enemy can move each of your characters around the battle arena and position them carefully to get the most out of the battle. During one characters turn, you have multiple options for what you can have her do but only specific characters can do one special thing. There's:
Attack,
EXE skills,
Defend,
SP skills,
HDD on/off,
Switch,
Item,
Flee.
Whichever one you pick (Apart from HDD) will consume the characters turn and move to the next one in line. If you choose attack (Which you'll do a lot of the time) you are given the option to choose between three attacks that are tide to one of three buttons. These allow you to do different attacks which will have different effect but once you pick one, it'll move onto the next attack tab. Break focuses on depleting the enemies guard which if you accomplish that, the enemy will take more damage till it's there turn. Power which focuses on dealing damage and rush which I'm guessing does a bit of both. It leads to you having to mix and match your attacks together to deal with an enemy faster and effectively. The rest are pretty self explanatory apart from HDD on. Characters who are CPU's or CPU candidates have the ability to transform in the middle of battle, which increases there states but use up 20% of the SP gauge. Since it doesn't have any downsides to using it, you'll more then likely use it a lot of the time.
On to my favorite part of the game and that being the art style. One things I adore about this franchise is how the environments are done, as well as how the characters are designed. Each are just so gorgeous to look at, they're colorful, bright and the way the colors blend together is fantastic.
At the end of it, I find this to be quite an enjoyable experience, it's comedy focuses on referencing things from video games and anime and poking fun at them for there tropes and problems without it getting old. It's combat is very strategy focused and fast passed which is what I enjoy, leading to you blasting through each battle one at a time. Each character is unique in there own way and have there own personalities and characteristics that suit them perfectly, but also, because of who they are it can lead to a lot of mishaps and occasional funny moments to happen.

I love this game. It's got all the classic elements of a good tower defence game, and the hex-based grid is awesome.
Things I Like:
[+] Tower defense mechanics.
[+] Single Player gameplay is challenging and rewarding.
[+] Hex based grid is just fantastic.
[+] Gameplay is unique (as far as I'm aware anyway.)
[+] The art such as tower models, and characters are very nice, as well as the maps, effects, all of it. It's very sleek.
[+] Maps and the randomness created by the mines moving around each game is awesome.
[+] The audio (including character voices) is amusing and well-done.
[+] User Interface is generally well-designed, and amusing, and looks good.
[+] The camera is perfect.
Issues:
[-] User Interface and I have our disagreements. I want it to go back to a menu or let me restart right after I lose angrily and it just sits there and I hit buttons to try to make it go away, until it lets me exit the current map.
[-] When exiting a map that you just lost (or won), there is small text that must be clicked, and I haven't found a key on the keyboard to make it click through. I would like to be able to hit [ESC] or [ENTER] and have it go back to the menu at that point.
[-] I often find myself accidentally clicking and then it defaults to building a tower where I had no intention of putting a tower, and then I am sad.
[-] From what I've played it doesn't seem there's a lot of genuine strategy. You just have to balance upgrading mines, units, and global unit stats, and keep everything moving in the right direction and build a standard set of towers with as long a maze as possible. If you build some towers in large quantities, you'll lose, if you focus on one type of upgrades, you'll lose.
[-] UI doesn't agree with my pen tablet entirely. when I click to upgrade a tower it clicks constantly, and sometimes does odd things, which isn't that surprising.
[-] Hotkeys for things are not displayed. If I could hover over the send button and it would say something like "[SPACE] to Send Troops" or "[1] to queue this troop". Those keyboard shortcuts are useful but I only learned them through the tutorial or tips or guesswork. I like hovering over things for information.
[-] Hovering over units does not give any info about what unit they are or their health. I assume that's how they planned it, but I would very much like more information at my fingertips.
[-] I find it hard to build a complex maze in a hex-grid (but that said, I'd still take a hex grid any day.)
Other notes:
[~] Gameplay is exceedingly challenging, getting me stuck on one bot for quite some time in single-player, and I can only imagine it's even harder against real people, as I'm sure I'll find out soon. It's a very delicate balancing act. The fact that it is hard is not a bad thing though. It's just not for people who aren't up for a serious challenge, or those with lots of skill already in other tower defense games.
[~] Each game can be quite long, but I enjoy long games so I don't consider this bad.
[~] Full disclosure: I bought it during the summer sale, for a very low price. I do think it's worth the asking price though, for sure.
Conclusion:
I love this game, despite it's flaws. I love it's style, I love hexagon-based games, and I love it's mechanics. If you're looking for a fun, straightforward tower defense game, I highly recommend it. This game requires patience, and a willingness to learn.

I think the mistake that most people make is comparing this small-scale niche RPG to grand AAA JRPGS ( FF and the like ) so the difference in execution is something to keep in mind.
I was like that initially, but after reminding myself that it's not meant to be one ( when i was playing Re;birth 1 ) - I found myself enjoying it a lot more.
STORY
CPUs have been defeated and captured; nobody has a flipping clue about what lead to this in the past three years. Your job is to become stronger to beat up the baddies in order to restore the state of the world.
In concept, it's a parody and satire of the gaming industry and it's history. Nothing too much about ideals and higher cause -- and it constantly reminds you of it with cheeky jokes and wall-breaking interactions. Not as many jokes as Re;birth 1 so far solely due to the absence of Nep, but Red does a decent job as her replacement for a comical character.
So it's not all about the loli fantasy harem that naysayers claim it to be ( there will inevitable a bit of that, but it's within reasonable doses ;p)
GAMEPLAY
Exactly the same as Re;birth 1, but now with four characters in combat.
They've done a much better job with balancing difficulty curves early on in the game and considerably lessened the need for a grind.
Your party gets useful, but balanced skills much earlier in the game to help you out with the boss encounters without needing to outlevel them by a huge margin or coming back with overpowered gear.
e.g Red gets an AoE STR buff before level 18 , Compa gets paralysis removal and AoE heal before level 18 as well
Therefore, the pace of the game feels a lot better than the previous game - even if it feels so much easier than the first game.
GAMEPLAY PT2
This part concerns Maps and Stella's dungeon minigame
Maps aren't atrocious as the Re;birth 1 with clear-cut paths to the event sign. They now have branching paths that encourage you to go to all ends to look for that loot.
Unfortunately they made a deliberate decision to remove maps with elevation - the only sole purpose for jumping in a technical context.
it could still be a lot more complex, but it's a considerable improvement.
Stella's Dungeon is a new minigame where you send off a cute little girl into a dungeon for your own benefit (*cough* Recettear)
It works in real-time and she will go through the various floors of the dungeons you've explored in hopes of getting progressively stronger gear for herself and loot for you.
A fun mini-game to initiate while nepgear and her friends wander off into a dungeon.
SOUND
Very catchy new overworld music - better than Re;birth 1. New battle themes are also quite refreshing and in-line with the game.
One of the issues that I had was Nepgear's voice being muffled during special attacks (mirage dance, etc) and in certain cutscenes.
Another is the unbalanced audio volume. The overworld theme is overpowering everything else in the game when you're out there. It will drop in volume whenever a character idles and starts errant chatter, but in general it is still too loud

Huge disappointment...
I am a big fan of the franchise but this watered down addition isn't worth its full price.
Campaign missions felt short and offer little to no replay value, with the exception of Tiger Hunting which I found to be the highlight of the campaign.
New multiplayer maps are dull and seem to be designed to serve the snow and blizzard mechanics; vast snowfields dotted with bonfires. It fails to compliment the original mechanic of how dynamic maps were meant to be, the beginning of your game could involve skirmishes between a maze of hedgerows and villages and end with battling out in smoldering ruins and craters. Steam workshop could redeem this with CoH 1 maps getting fan-made revivals.
The removal of the commander talent trees is what cripples the game most. No longer are the 3 distinct commander choices  that each serve their own playstyle and tactics but now DLC centered commanders that blend into eachother, the same off-map abilities and additional units rearranged and passed off as a seperate commander.The lack of commander variety will mean each game will start to feel like the last. Every game eventually leads to tanks vs tanks, grenadiers and conscripts end up serving no purpose but to rush enemy tanks, disable them with an anti-tank grenade the go capture a point while your tanks pick off the disabled enemy tank.
Theatre of War scenarios are a joke, they are simply AI skirmish matches. 1941 scenarios let you play with even FEWER units to choose from. Dont expect to see Stonewall or Panzerkrieg game modes from ToV, they'll probably be DLC down the road (hopefully steam workshop will beat them to it).
Company of Heroes 2 does not live up to its predecessor, fewer units, bland maps, mediocre campaign, and the biggest killer   is how the game is now entirely centered around DLC. I'm sad to see my favourite RTS get strangled by the DLC demon but steam workshop could be its salvation.

=== No Spoiler Review ===
But for real. Its like 1/3rd visual novel (with high quality voice acting) 1/3rd kawaii final fantasy (and nothing like FF10 part 2, that was trash) and 1/3rd fan service (depending on your.. preferences of course).
I've been pleasantly surprised that the game itself is actually a challenge. You may have to grind at some points in order to beat bosses or change up your game style a bit to progress through back-to-back boss battles. Unlike most JRPGS, the grinding is actually fun and addicting in and of itself. The story and characters are all cute, funny, and well-developed (in more than 1 area... hehehe). Also, the music never gets old! Battle themes, dialogue music, the intro song... they're all very polished sounding. Legit production quality.
Honestly the only let-down I've experienced so far is a recycling of monsters and level designs. It does take away from the immersion a bit when you find there are variations of essentially the same dungeon only pathed slightly differently and with recolored monsters. There really is a lot of recycling in those regards. I'm pretty forgiving about it, but it does annoy me. To make up for it, there are a crapton of character customizability options (cosplaying outfits, weapon plan creating, changing your combos, etc) that is really nice to see in a JRPG. I really enjoy the battle mechanics because, as the game difficulty gets harder throughout the game, you really have to plan your attacks to make them count. Its also nice that the battle system isn't a linear ATB, rather akin to games like the Star Oceans and Tales series you can move around freely within a battle scene to position yourself strategically. It is a turn-based battle system, but unlike the goofy stagger system Final Fantasy 13 TRIED to utillize but failed miserably at, HDN has a guard-break mechanic that doesn't require an hour of playing just to proc once like the game-which-must-not-be-named-but-i-already-named failure title used.
Overall, its a really cute game with just as much substance as cuteness to supplement.
I got the game on sale for $7 but even at its normal price of $30 I would buy it in an instant now that I've been introduced to the HDN brand and am in love with it.
Pros:

= Whether $7 or $30 it is worth every penny
Cons:

This game is a poetic visual experience: you play as a blind girl exploring the world around her house while searching for her lost cat. The way the world is slowly revealed to you as you walk and get near things is very interesting, and even if your character is blind, your surroundings are vibrant and full of colour thanks to the girl's imagination (and get darker and darker when she's scared). The graphics are simple but very pleasant to the eye.
That was the good stuff.
Now on to the bad stuff: your character walks around very slowly. It makes sense, since she's blind and has to be careful around unknown obstacles, cars and so on, but when an area has been revealed and explored, it would make sense for her to move around it a bit faster. Slow can be atmospheric when you are exploring a new area and eliminating fog of war, but when everything is revealed and you're just wandering around to double check for achievement stuff and secrets, running would be a plus.
The girl stops completely in front of an obstacle, nevermind if that obstacle is a wall, a clothesline or swing as hard as concrete. Not very realistic, breaks the immersion a bit.
Another thing that's not very realistic: a... what, 8, 9, years old blind girl, wandering around the city for hours on end completely alone, crossing streets, walking on piers, no walking stick, no guide dog. And no one stopping her to ask "kid where the f* are your parents?".
But what made me decide for a Not recommended vote, in the end, was the ending. Had it been different, a bit brighter, a bit happier, I would've recommended the game, even with the flaws I've just mentioned. But I'm too much of a softie.
So, if you like walking simulators, slow paced poetic games, and an artistic (albeit short) experience, this game could be right for you, if you can overlook its flaws.

This is one of those games that has nearly everything a game requires to be good; simple controls, great graphics, immersive gameplay, nice soundtrack, and a large map to explore.
Combat is one of my favorite mechanics of Dying Light. Being a zombie survival game, the combat is pretty much a make-or-break mechanic; if you have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls for combat, it's not going to be a very fun zombie survival game. Thankfully, Dying Light goes above and beyond with its combat system. It's fast, easy to pick up, and adheres to the immersion of the game. For example, no matter how high your survivor rank is, you're still going to have trouble fending off a horde of zombies. The mechanics are purposely made so that going head-first into a pit of zombies will kill you pretty quickly. You have to use the environment and pick the zombies off one by one, instead of running in and swinging your machete like a maniac. The game teaches you that maniacs die during a zombie infestation, and only the ones with wit and strength survive. No matter how stupid and easy to kill the zombies appear to be, they can easily overrun you in a second. Sometimes it's better to call all combat off and run from the situation. Sometimes it's better to not approach the enemy at all, and simply maneuver your way around them without interacting with them at all. And, at the end of the day, the game still makes nighttime the scariest♥♥♥♥♥♥you will ever experience. If you don't know the ins and outs of the city, as well as have the basic common knowledge to STAY THE ♥♥♥♥ AWAY from the Volitiles, you're screwed within the first ten minutes.
The parkour element of the game is seamlessly integrated with the rest of the movement controls, and is another mechanic I really like. It's one of the few ways to "take a break" from the Biters, because they're♥♥♥♥♥♥at climbing anything. This is also when knowing the layout of the city comes into play. If you're being chased by one of the Infected that can climb things, you won't have too much time to stop and think about your next move. You have to keep going, and sometimes, when it looks like you can make the jump is when you realize you can't, and now you're either dead or left to deal with the Infected on the ground plus whatever was chasing you in the first place. The rooftops are a really good place to be when navigating the city, and not being able to get to a rooftop quickly can easily become your demise. Thankfully, there's plenty of obstacles to help you get up there. The parkour element is nearly flawless and it almost makes me think it's the one thing the developers wanted to get right first.
The storyline is unique. It's not something I would exactly expect from a zombie survival game. You're playing as a character who's from the outside world, not as someone from directly inside the quarantined area. So, you have communication with powerful people outside the infected area. I haven't seen a scenario quite like this, and so far it fits with the style of the game.
TL;DR: The mechanics of the game are great; so great, in fact, that nearly every time you die, you are solely responsible for why you died. The storyline fits with the style of the game and creates an immersive world that's fun to run, jump, and survive in. And no matter how great you think you are...
The night is always greater.

Remember Sim City? The game where you take an empty landscape, and slowly but surely transform the area, from a small town, to a gigantic Metropolis?
Picture all of that but instead of a landscape, it's a Carribean Island. Instead of turning a small town into a Metropolis, you're turning a third world Banana Republic, into a competent, capable nation, able to compete with the bigger world powers during the Cold War.
This is what Tropico is.
Tropico 4 is the fourth installment, in a line of City Management/Political Play/Strategy games, that has existed since the very early 2000s. Aside from certain notable additions, the major gameplay, and most of the models and graphics, are recycled from Tropico 3. Which, while I kinda wish they did a revamp of models, I understand the sentament. The gameplay isn't broken, and the models are just visual representations of what they are.
There are many additions to this game, some really add something to the game, others are pretty cool and add a bit, and some are just kinda meh.
One of the major gameplay mechanics is Political juggling between Seven Factions (Capitalists, Communists, Religious, Evironmentalists, Militarists, Nationalists, and Loyalists) as well as the Unites States, and The Soviet Union. The seven factions are still around, but now there are three more foreign powers, Europe, China, and The Middle East. Unlike the Soviets and Americans, who will invade you if you're relations with one or the other get's too low, these three won't invade you, as much as remove bonuses you recieve during good relations. Somtimes during your reign on the island, you'll get noticed that something bad happened between one of the nations, and you'll have to pick a side. There are also representatives for the factions. They mostly add two things. First, a face and personality to represent the faction they represent. Second, to provide side objectives during your reign to earn respect if you've lost some. The side objectives go for the Nations too, mostly in the form of sending goods that nation likes, or donating some money to that nation to earn respect.
There three more additions worth talking about, firstly, there is a story driven campaign, a first for the Tropico series. You are Presidente, being mentored by a Generalisimo Santana, in the ways of managing a nation, and growing it Economically, treating your citizens right, knowing when to "kick the dog", and overall just staying in power and not getting killed or kicked out of office.
The second is Imports. Generally speaking, if your island is a giant rock and little vegitation for food, then you're screwed and have to make the most of it. Otherwise, you can import! Say your on an island with a free Weapons Factory to build! But oh no, there is no Iron on the island at all! No worries, just have a stable economy, and import the iron from one of the foreign powers. It'll arrive on the next ship, be proccesed in the factory, and you'll earn alot of money!
Finally, there are the Disasters. In Tropico 3 you mostly had five "negative" events that could occur. A rebel attack, a coup from your own military, a hurricane, an uprising, and a faction disaster if a faction really hates you. Now there are Natural disasters to spice things up. Now you have to worry about events you can predict (via a Weather Station), but cannot control. Things like Volcanic Eruptions (if your island has a volcano), A Tornado (or several if you're really unlucky), a Tsunami, Oil Spill, fires, and droughts. Fires from volcanos and derelict buildings can be fixed by either paying for a helicopter to put it out, or by building a firestation. I personally like these disasters, because in Tropico 3 I was such a good presidente that I never had to worry about a coup or anything like that. Now, there is something I can worry about when my island is happy.
So far I really like that the game is still easy to play in general (once you know what to do that is), and the additions are very nice. But I have some cons.
Somtimes you'll get a notice about doing something and have to choose an option. You can't exit out to check your almanac to see what it could impact and how to fix it, you have to choose, and that sucks sometimes. Also some missions in the campaign are pretty tough on you. You have to make sure you've picked the right traits for President to make the island truley yours.
I don't do reviews, so I won't use a number system, and instead list the pros and cons, and then a final statement as to wether you should really grab this or not.
PROS:
-Game Mechanics are the same, with additions like imports.
-Disasters add suspense and more risk to buildings wrecked.
-Story is fun and simple
-Characters have well drawn charicature type portraits to represent them
-Some new buildings to help out with the new additions
Cons:
-AI for the Tropicans are competent, but man do they job hop around, and they'll walk through Morder itself just to get some corn.
-Sometimes a choice won't let you check statistics to really understand an impact.
-Some missions in the campaign aren't easy.
Should you buy this game? If you like Sim City, you'll love Tropico 4, if you like Sim City, but want it on a smaller scale, you'll love Tropico 4, if you want to try a "modern" Sim City game, but EA screwed it up, then You'll like Tropico 4.
But if you don't like statistics, or the recycled models and gameplay, as well as the AI, I wouldn't reccommend it.
It's $29.99 on Steam, but I'd also reccomend you grab Tropico 3 for it's cheaper price, and they're the same gameplay wise.

I would call this game a masterpiece. I would call this game one of the best turn-based strategy games of the current decade. I would call this one of my favorite games of all time.
But I can't quite bring myself to do most of those things.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a marvelous introduction to the XCOM series as a whole, and it's Expansion, Enemy Within, gives you so many delightful things to toy with that you'll have the time of your life playing it. However, to veterans of the series as a whole, or die-hard strategy experts, there's something missing. Something vital, something real. By automating and simplifying many of the extraneous or sometimes irrelevant bits, they make the game easy to pick up, and fun to play, but they remove some of the ability to truly tweak the experience. In comparison to the level of micro-managing you had with the other XCOM games, this paints in very broad strokes. WHICH ISN'T A BAD THING, NECESSARILY.
But it leaves the game sometimes feeling shallow.
However, with Enemy Within, a simple mod changes many of those concerns, and makes the game truly stupendous: The Long War mod for Enemy Within.
If you purchase this game (Which you should!) and play through the campaign a few times, and wish for a longer, more complicated, and more difficult game, Long War turns it into something that can sit on a shelf next to the other XCOM games in the series and make you go "Yeah, I see where it comes from."

Telltale truly outdid themselves with Game of Thrones. Never have I clenched my butt so much throughout an episodic story-driven game.
It helps (a lot) to be knowledgeable on the series/GoT universe, be it watching the TV show or reading the books; but you can still enjoy the game as its own story. The characters, the plot-twists, and the semi-illusion of control over the decisions one can make are all executed extremely well.
“When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die. There is no middle ground.”
Up until the release of this game, you could only watch as beloved and hated characters play this "game of thrones", but now you can truly feel like a part of it, making the decisions yourself gives you a sense of presence in the medieval dystopian fantasy world. However, this isn’t the best aspect of the game; in my opinion the best thing about this game is the writing. Like I said in the opening line, this game had me on the edge of my seat every single episode, something that I was surprised it was able to pull off. I became immersed with each character’s storyline, each character’s successes and failures, it felt so authentic.
The portrayal of the main characters in the series was excellent. Cersei, Danaerys, Ramsay, Margaery; the way each of these played into the Forrester's storyline was seamless. I hate Ramsay, love Khaleesi, and admire Margaery just as much in this game as I do in the TV show. BUT they weren’t represented well enough to steal the thunder from the true stars of the game: House Forrester. Mira, Rodrik, Asher, Gared and all the others were all incredible characters to play as. I became so engrossed with each character’s personality that I actually made decisions based on what I thought they’d choose, not what I’d choose.
With that said, I tried to keep everything under control in the game, which proved much harder than I thought. Every antagonistic character made it extremely hard for me to feel satisfied with any given situation, which I think is fairly befitting for GoT.
Each episode that I played was more unnerving than the last, ultimately leading to reactions I never thought I’d have (like screaming out of surprise, hands over mouth and genuine cringing). Right as you think something’s going well or in the direction that you planned, the game hits your with some rock hard reality and pins your back down onto the ground.
I appreciate that, because what’s the fun in playing a game where everything goes as you want it to without a challenge?
The stress, the sadness, the happiness, and every emotion in between is what you’ll go through when playing this game.
I highly recommend this game if you're already familiar with the GoT world, but I recommend it to those looking for an entry into the complicated world of A Song of Ice and Fire .
