I got this game from the GMG (Green Man Gaming) Snack Pack 2 bundle. My brother recommended me it. At first, I wasn't convinced. Even though the bundle was 5 games for 50 cents, I could've gotten some more PAYDAY 2 DLC for my pennies. As it turns out, the bundle was well worth getting. Tower Wars has been the only game I have played in the bundle. (and you can even see my icon is a unit from Tower Wars, proof of how fun this is)
Tower Wars is a classic Tower Defense type game mixed with offense. If you have played the game Toy Soldiers before, this game is like Toy Soldiers taken a step further.
Now, more in depth about Tower Wars:
Meat vs. Metal (their classic offline, "Player vs. Bot" mode)
Objective: Destroy the enemy's castle
Classic Tower Defense (also offline, and self explaintory)
Objective: Fend off as many waves as you can
Ranked Season Play (get paired with someone and play a match, tracked by leaderboards)
Objective: Destroy the enemy's castle
Unranked Play (play in a public or private lobby, nothing is scored on leaderboards)
Objective: Destroy the enemy's castle
Co-op (pretty much Tower Defense w/ a friend)
Objective: Fend off as many waves as you can
There are multiple towers, each do something different, all of them gain an advantage over one type of HP (shield, armor, or health), and gain a somewhat disadvantage over the others (not as effective).
The units are pretty interesting, there are 6 tiers. First is the guy on the logo (Mr. Moopsy).
Second you can choose from knights or speedy guys.
Third tier includes a  unit that increases DPS and speed, another giving health to units within range when killed, and last a unit that gives your units shields/increases the amount of shields.
Fourth tier you earn Stanley Cluckerbottom. He is a stong unit with lots of armor, health and shields.
Fifth tier you unlock the best by far (in my opinion) unit. The (unofficial name) Trojan Horse. The horse can be filled with more units. when the horse is destroyed, the units disembark, then the horse explodes. This gives all 1-3 tier units a protective shell, giving them a chance to get to the castle. This unit is able to be upgraded the most in the game, allowing armor upgrades, more space upgrades, and also random unit upgrades.
Sixth tier you unlock the guy on my icon; Malevolent. He has no shield, but high damage, max armor, and max health. Most of the time I can get him through or almost through the enemies defenses.
Upgrades are
important.
You can upgrade units, your barracks, or your castle.
Unit upgrades: They advance/unlock your units.
Mine upgrades are basic. All you can do is purchase more miners to increase income and upgrade your mine to purchase more.
Barrack upgrades: These upgrades give all your units an upgrade, but cost lots.
Castle upgrades are also basic. you can increase your armor and DPS (gatling guns fend off intruders). Like the mines, you can upgrade to a higher tier to increase the armor/DPS
The most basic of them all, tower upgrades: All you can do is upgrade them 3 times to increase the effectivity/range.
Gold: You earn it slowly. Purchase more miners to earn more per second. required to do anything in game besides upgrading your unit (
)
Battle Points (BP): Required to purchase any form of upgrade besides tower upgrades. Earned by units over the "TO BATTLE" line.
Cooldown: The timer before you can send another wave of troops.
Barrack Queue: Amount of units you can send in a wave
In a briefing, I would give this a 7/10.

The items you pick up and combine together to augment your gear is straight out of TitanQuest, and so is the system for picking your class and back up class. The only thing that TQ has that this game didn't is the ability to dye your gear. This game does allow you to change the story arc through the decisions you make, which is neat and adds a little unpredictability to the game. the monster mechanics and difficulty of bosses also felt a lot of like TQ (if you've ever fought a boss in TQ, you know they are 100x harder than the trash mobs around them) The story is dark and engrossing and very long. If you want to hit all of the quests, prepare to explore every inch of every map.
Overall, a great game and a gem even at full price. If ARPGs are your thing, get this now.

Three things right off the bat because I see SO many negative reviews based on such silly stuff.
1) If you're giving this game a negative review because you've played the other Far Cry games and you don't think it's up to par, I'd like to extend my deepest sympathies to you, that you tried something different and judged it on an already-existing standard. I'd like to point out that this wasn't supposed to be a direct copy of the other Far Cry games, whilst still being a Far Cry game. However out of all the reviews I see, these 'experts' are playing the game on normal and complaining about it being 'too easy'. I'm running around on expert mode having the time of my life and feeling some very REAL fear when confronted by a Sabretooth. A big part of Far Cry is immersion. Game is too easy? Up the difficulty. It's not neuroscience. If you're not feeling hunted when you're running around at night, you're not playing on a hard enough difficulty. Don't give a bad review because you didn't decide to challenge yourself.
2) People keep complaining that the melee system is flawed. Why? Because there aren't brutal melee finishers for every weapon? Last time I checked if you got into a brawl with 3 guys with a club it's not going to be a moment of finesse. It's gonna be a moment of blind rage-induced swinging hoping to hit their faces. The same is true for the spear. If I stab someone in the face or the throat it counts as a 'headshot' and is an instant fatality. That is the sort of accuracy of a spear. You're trying to tell me we should be able to swing it around like a quarterstaff? Far Cry isn't known for prompted cinematic kill moves other than silent melee kills with most weapons. Why did you expect anything other than the very basic idea of an amateur swinging a stick? You're a caveman. Not a professional assassin.
3) Complaining about the fact that they went through the trouble to include genuine proto-european dialect, or that the game is too short. I reiterate, a big part of Far Cry is immersion. If you're not paying attention to the script, the emotion in their voices, or the storyline, and then you complain about not enjoying it, it doesn't sound like a problem with the game. That sounds like a problem with you paying attention. When it comes to timeframe, I'm 33.3 hrs into the game right now, and due to difficulty level (died probably 14 times trying to kill Dah) and how I genuinely enjoy hunting in this game, I've got plenty of collectibles and side quests left, and several story and character missions.
All in all, I'm not trying to bash anyone for their review because everyone has their own opinion. However I felt that this game was very harshly judged and mostly so because of the preceding games. People either expected something completely different or relatively the same. The weird balance in between seems to have some people upset, but did any of you really expect Far Cry to evolve as a series without some trail and error? Considering this is their first foray into any other era than modern, I'd say they did pretty damn good.

I enjoy "walking simulator" games. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was one of my favorite games the year it came out, and while I found Firewatch a disappointment, that was primarily due to the story, not the actual gameplay. So when I saw that a "walking simulator" about being a blind girl was on sale, I didn't hesitate to buy it. I picked up Beyond Eyes last week when it was on sale, on Steam. It is normally $14.99, and I believe I paid around $3 or $4 for it.
After playing the game, it turns out that's $3 or $4 too much, if you ask me.
Beyond Eyes is a great example of an interesting concept held back by gameplay that desperately needs a few extra layers of polish. The concept of controlling a blind child and only being able to "see" what they hear, is an excellent concept for a slow-paced adventure game. To some extent, Beyond Eyes executed this concept very well, particularly in the earliest parts of the game. Hearing a bird in a tree, and seeing the bird pulse out of the white blindness as it chirped was a pretty neat mechanic.
At first, these sound effects acted as guides, figurative lighthouses in the white blindness. Rae, the protagonist, eventually finds a stray cat that she names Nani (Nah-nee). As stray cats tend to do, Nani runs away. The opening of the game is Rae simply walking around a pretty garden, looking for where Nani ran off too. The garden served as a good training grounds to learn how the white blindness works: it fades away based on proximity, and gradually fills-in behind Rae, as if her memory of exactly what was where is fading. It's neat at first, but as the game drags on, it becomes a major annoyance.
The problem is that the white blindness isn't consistent. In some areas you can turn around and see the trail you took to get to where you currently are, in other areas the white blindness closes very closely behind you, making it very difficult to figure out where you are in relation to anything. One of the latter levels has Rae walking through the rain and it's almost impossible to gain any sense of where she is. Her slow movement speed is understandable, since she is blind, but when you're walking around very slowly and have no idea where you're going, the charm of the game quickly wanes.
I was content with the fact that, for the sake of the experience, I was being forced to walk so slowly with such limited visibility. I dealt with the frustration of walking into countless fences or other barriers that I did not know were there until I literally bumped into them; I tolerated being strung along through the experience because I was supposed to care about a feral cat and a blind girl who should have known better than to stand mere feet away from exploding fireworks; I ignored the fact that the game features "memories" of the girl visualizing Nani doing something in an area we (the players) have never been to; or that no one (there are other humans around) even tried to help the little blind girl who was wandering around on her own. I put all of those issues aside for the sake of trying to put myself in someone else's shoes for a few short hours.
But it's rather....immersion breaking....when the game suddenly takes control of Rae and WALKS HER ACROSS ROCKS IN A RIVER. I was literally removed from the perspective of Rae, just so Beyond Eyes could give me a good view of this little blind girl walking across river rocks. There is no way she could have known those rocks was there. So she's either faking being blind or the developers just stopped caring about consistency. I'm leaning towards the latter.
That river scene was the point I decided that Beyond Eyes was one of the most poorly thought-out games that I've played in recent memory. As I said, Beyond Eyes is based on a very interesting concept to explore in a video game, but the developers absolutely floundered in their delivery of translating that concept into an entertaining experience. I literally cannot figure out why the developer thought that the inclusion of that river scene was in any way appropriate after making me walk, literally blind, through a rainstorm for the past twenty-minutes. That one scene single-handedly ruined everything that came before it, and anything that came after it. It made no sense, it invalidated the entire game.
Clearly, I am not happy with Beyond Eyes. I'd ask for a refund, but since it takes two hours just to walk out of the tutorial (hyperbolic, but you get the point), I guess I'm out $4.
[[Not Recommended]] Beyond Eyes is about a child who stood too close to fireworks, was blinded, and doesn't understand that a wild cat is probably not going to want to be her pet. The game's core mechanic is only neat for a short period of time, then it stops being fun and is quite literally a handicap to the amount of enjoyment you could have experienced in this game, had it been made with some extra consideration and care.

Beyond eyes review
This is a weird game. For starters, it's a very slow game, but not in the traditional sense of having numbers of complicated numbers to crunch or things to manage. It’s slow because your character moves slowly and information is constantly being hidden from the player. If you’re in it to beat the game, this is absolutely infuriating, but the goal of this project is not to be a game. It’s to provide an experience similar to blindness. It’s not for everyone. This is normally referred to as a walking simulator, but I wouldn’t associate it with other walking sims like Firewatch and Gone Home.
You are a little girl who went blind after an incident, and you haven’t seen your cat in a long time. You decide venturing off into the wilderness alone to look for the cat is a great idea. To find your cat, you have to walk. A lot. This is where the gameplay comes in, your basic task is to try and figure out what path your cat might have taken and follow it until you reach the end of the level. When a level starts, the entire level is completely blank. As you approach the edges of the void, paths, obstacles, and sometimes birds will pop into your radius and you use this limited information to figure out the level layout. The core gameplay revolves around exploration and discovery, which I liked once I got into the mindset of beyond eyes but for the first 20 minutes is extremely dull. The game doesn’t have giant yellow arrows pointing you where to go, that would go against the blindness experience the devs are trying to deliver. Sometimes there is a path the player is expected to follow, but when that path ends the player is expected to explore and find the path again. The lack of direction means it’s very easy to meander down the wrong path and waste a load of time doing absolutely nothing. On multiple occasions, I would just walk around in circles across areas I had already completely explored trying to figure out where I needed to go next. The first level is awful at this, as you need to visit the same spot twice at one point to trigger a cutscene. While I enjoyed the exploration aspect, giving the player less space to waste time in might have helped players not get stuck traversing areas they already know trying to find the path. At the very least I wish the walking speed was a bit faster, but again I know it might counter the core blindness experience the dev is trying to create.
As you can tell, the gameplay and story elements are barebones and that’s why I hesitate to say this is a walking simulator. It is, but normally walking simulators have a core narrative to focus on and use the gameplay to connect the player to a narrative viewpoint. In Beyond Eyes, the focus of the story is a blind girl walking through various locations, and while that can be vexing it also feels necessary, I can’t imagine a game like this being made any other way. Nothing is in the game that doesn’t work towards the core blindness experience.
The pretty visuals do a good job recreating all your senses to give you tiny bits of information. Objects that make loud sounds will be temporarily visible in the distance. That replicates hearing. The area immediately surrounding you is completely visible, that’s touch. Stuff you’ve explored stays ‘visible’, because you remember it. Everything you encounter, every area you visit is there to reinforce this lack of vision and the frustrations of exploring on imperfect information. The game is very clever, and if you’re looking for something new outside your comfort zone I’d recommend Beyond Eyes a lot.

I have mixed feelings about this game. I love playing it, i have much more fun in this game then i do in the original COH. Yes, they are starting to put most of the game in DLCs and yes the multiplayer can be a little "unfair". You either hate this game or you love it. People say they hate the campaign but i in fact loved it. The gameplay is good (not great but good) but the story is interesting. You get the see the brutality, and the horrible conditions of the eastern front. You will see Russians shooting unarmed germans and you will see the same cruelty happen towards the russians by their own commanders. I think they could have done better with Order 227. They should have had a small squad of men that was out of the way so when the men retreated, you would feel that hardship of retreating your men only to have them gunned down by the commanders they trusted. The graphics have much improved since the last game and battles feel more intense, but thats probably because i use a sound chair.
I enjoyed the theater of war add on. it gave you something else to do beside play the story and you can complete coop challenges with your friends but the overuse of the DLC's gets in the way of that due to the fact that you can only get more of these cool missions if you pay for it. One thing im getting tired of hearing is multiplayer being "unfair". War isnt fair and if you read a history book once in a while, you'll realize the russians only had the advantage due to their massive numbers. They were ill-equipped and didnt have alot to spare. Germany had a superior tank army and airforce compared to russians. My suggestion when you go into multiplayer is play as the Germans in the beginning and then as you become a better strategist, start playing as the russians. Russians are more of a challenge to use due to the germans having the technological superiorarity but like other men and i  have said before "war isnt fair."

I did not like Dead Island and it is hard to explain why but, generally speaking, it was boring to play it. This game, however, is the opposite of Dead Island. Dying Light is extremely fun to play not even in co-op (which is a shame, because in co-op it is much more fun to play, but because my friends do not have it - because they are very poor people - I am playing on my own).
The story is pretty much generic, nothing special about it; dialogues are the same. Apparently, it is not the game's strongest point, so Techland should work on that in the sequel or a spiritual successor. But the gameplay... my applause, really. Combining a very good fighting mechanics - sometimes fights are pretty challenging - with lots of different weapons (which can be broken) and their modifications and parkour are one of the best decisions ever made by developers to make the game fun. Dead Island's improved mechanics and ideas + parkour from Mirror's Edge = Dying Light.
Parkour, as I think, a good parkour mechanics, makes every game much better, because you have lots of options where to go, how to get away from zombies etc. But, maybe because I'm only in the middle of the game and did not unlock all skills, but I wish that the character was a bit faster, especially with climbing on the walls. Otherwise, everything is good.
I also really like that the game has day and night cycle because at different times of a day the gameplay is different. In the afternoon the character is basically the boss (well, most of the time), because he is faster and stronger than zombies. But at night, he isn't, he is pretty much weak against them because at night zombies are faster and stronger. And if you won't hurry to the nearest save point, if you will linger somewhere, you are dead and lots of earned points for upgrading your character's skills are gone. And to bo honest, it is a bit scary, creepy to play at night, so that is why I'm trying to avoid it.
Also, briefly about The Following expansion. I played it only to check how good is cars handling, is it good or not and I must say, it is very good. I feel that cars are not toys or log on the wheels with no physics at all. To be honest, it is better than in a majority of racing games, such as The Crew, Need for Speed (2015).
So if you enjoy good zombie games or just good action games, try Dying Light. Even if you are tired of zombies, try it, it's worth it.

This game isn't the best if you are new to the Game of Thrones world or aren't a particularly big fan, but if you are a big fan of the books and TV show, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. It is a really, really strong side story to the main overall plot of GoT that remains canon yet different enough to stay interesting. Although there is huge similarities between the Forresters and the Starks, the game itself does a very good job of making them different enough that you don't feel like you are just rewatching the show.
As much as I recognise the inclusion of certain characters such as Jon and Dany as rather weak, the representation of Cersei, Tyrion and Ramsay are all incredibly strong. So much so that I genuinely feel that I understand Cersei's character in the books even more.
Some people have complained that Telltale have simply gone for the 'everyone must die for it to be game of thrones over the top hurhurhur' but I think it is far more well constructed than that, to the extent that some of the deaths of characters are actually heart wrenching, particularily when someone has to be 'left behind' (you'll know it when you play it).
Despite people complaining that choices don't really change the story, I felt that making mundane choices that didn't really effect the story arc (with the exception of a few choices) still was good enough to make emotionally invested in the game.

I've been playing Saints Row since it was released on the Xbox 360 back in 2006. Over the years I have seen the series grow and change unlike anyother, starting as a brutal open-world sandbox "Grand Theft Auto clone" to becoming a franchise which consistantly pushes the envelope of what they can and cannot do. Back in 2006 you could compare Saints Row with GTA and debate all you want as to which did it better but today, it's simply not possible. Saints Row is as unique of a series as it gets. Not only has the series become increasingly more ridiculous  every game, it does so without losing the core story background and interpersonal relationships between the characters, many of which still hold true to their origins in prior games.
For me personally, Saints Row IV was one of, if not the, best games I had played in 2014. It was so full of throwbacks to prior games, iconic pop culture references and had a habit of consistantly poking fun at its prior games that it was a nonstop rollercoaster of emotions for me. However, I feel that these aspects of the game, particularly the references to the story of the first game, may make this game somewhat unappealing or not as engaging and fun to gamers new to the franchise and this is where this review becomes slightly more complicated for me. Being that I went into this game with full knowledge of each of the prior games makes it very difficult for me to suggest whether or not this is a game to pick up.
If you have played the other games and enjoyed them as much as I did, I see no reason why you shouldn't pick this game up now or atleast when it is on sale. If you haven't, however, here are my suggestions;
1) pick up the game, if you think this game looks fun and is something you would enjoy, don't let the IV in the title keep you from trying and enjoying the game but be prepared to have quite a few questions throughout,
2) pick up the game when it is bundled with Saints Row 2 and Saints Row 3 (unfortunatly the first Saints Row is not available on Steam), I did this so that i could have digital copies of the games but it would give you more than enough context to the Saints Row universe to thoroughly understand and appreciate the references and character conflicts throughout the game
3) skip it....for now, I don't typically suggest this to people but if you are really unsure about the game, it's story, etc. and any potential confusion, then maybe you should pass on it for now, add it you your wishlist or keep and eye out for it during sales.
I hope this was useful to some people thinking about whether or not to get this game.

What can i possibly say about this game? Well first of all, before i actually played the game i thought it was stupid how the game added super powers to Saints Row, I had played SR: The Third and was completely aware about the shenanigans that would come with SR4 but that's just one thing i didn't really like about the game. Another reason i wasn't interested in SR4 was due to the ending of SR3. When i had purchased SR4 i had went into the game with very low expectations and you'll get to see my opinion on the game.
First of all let me start with this --> You're the president of the US *The president of the United Saints* which is pretty badass.
The plot is introduced in the first few missions which compared to the other SR games i didn't really like but hey I bought this game because i'm bored of GTA this game is in no way comparable to any of the GTA games.
After revealing the plot all the things i didn't like about the game seemed to vanish, since you don't actually live in the real city of Steelport you're living in a simulation of Steelport made by the alien bad guy antagonist, which really makes me feel better about the whole idea of superpowers.
The comedy in the game is pretty hilarious, it's much better than the SR3 comedy was, it's got a lot of moments that really make me laugh.
Since i'm me there is one selling point on the game and that is: Upgrades and character progression. All of your guns have things to upgrade such as explosive ammo, fire rate, damage, recoil, RoF, it's all really cool, The penetrator remains in the game which deep down makes me happy knowing i can run around Steelport F*ing people in the face with my giant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat. Cars can also be upgraded and pimped out in the same way as previous SR games, although the reliance on vehicles is much lower due to the first two super powers you get. As you play through the game you can collect Data Clusters which allow you to upgrade your super powers, although they don't require much searching they're still really cool to collect and upgrade your powers with. And lastly you can upgrade you character himself/herself in the same way you did in SR3 collect Cache *money* and level up via missions and activities to unlock new upgrades.
Co-Op for once in a SR game Co-op is a key point to the game, without playing co-op it's impossible to achieve 100% game completion. If you're anti-social and hate people it's not the game for you. But, if you've got a friend to play it with it'll be one of the best game purchases you can make.

Since the release of Diablo 2, way back in the year 2000, basically every ARPG has been trying to be Diablo 3, yet none have truly succeeded, not even the actual Diablo 3. I'm not going to go so far as to say Grim Dawn is the 'real' Diablo 3, but its the closest an ARPG has come IMO.
For starters, Grim Dawn (GD) has just about everything you would expect. Multiple classes, the ability to mix classes, an additional alternate advancement system, lots and lots of loot in different color flavors, and hordes of various enemies and bosses to slay. You can play solo, or with up to 4 others, and you can even enable PvP if you so choose.
Perhaps its one outstanding difference is that the maps aren't randomly generated (for the main campaign, you can play custom maps, though I haven't explored that option), which initially felt odd until I just got over it and realized fully hand-crafted maps look better and are more logical than what even a good random generator can do. Will that hold up through multiple playthroughs? Not likely, but I've never been a huge fan of grinding an ARPG over and over again anyway.
The graphics are very serviceable. They won't blow you away, but they also don't feel cheap, and there are some nice lighting effects and the overall style is a slightly different take on the traditional fantasy doom world full of zombies and other creatures. Same for the sound, which includes a bit of voice acting; its not top-notch, but once you get into the game you find that it all fits and works well-enough. The game runs well and I've only seen it crash once (on my wife's computers during multiplayer).
The pace is good, and main storyline so far has been interesting (mostly told through lore text items you find), and I've liked every area I've seen so far. And since the maps aren't random, they all connect in a logical manner that gives the world of GD a more... worldly feel rather than just randomly connected zones. I think that last part is one of the major reasons I'm really like GD too; it has a better sense of progress as you uncover more of the world and the problems facing it.
I also like that you aren't bombarded with abilities. Or rather, you have that option, as its very easy to focus-in on a few abilities that sound interesting and skip others during the leveling process. You can go so far as to only unlock and upgrade your auto-attack and passives/buffs, which means less button pushing but without gimping yourself. Again perhaps more min/maxing is needed at the highest difficulty, but for an initial run, that flexibility is there.
GD is also pretty flexible in other areas too. You can undo spent skill points for a small cost, and many skills aren't exclusive to one type of weapon. So for example an auto-attack modifier will work whether you are using a 1h melee weapon or a 2h ranged weapon. That's nice and lets you switch up what gear you are using pretty easily as you find new and better drops. A constant flow of upgrades is a huge key to ARPG enjoyment, and GD nails this.
Finally, the game is very co-op friendly. It will auto-party you if you select that option, and loot can also be personal until you drop it, making 'sharing' loot much easier. Simply scoop up all the stuff you see drop, and if you find something you think might be good for your buddy, drop it and they can grab it. Easy, quick, and painless. Quests also update for everyone in the party, so it doesn't matter who landed the last hit or who talked to an NPC. It basically feels like playing the single-player in terms of pace and function, only you also have a buddy running and killing along side you.

This game will feel like Farcry but forces you to play it unlike any other. Combat is limited to primative weapons such as the bow, spear, sling, and clubs. In addition you have the animals of the wild such as bears and lions.
The Story: You are part of a tribe that has been hunted nearly to extinction. It is your role to help rebuild a once great tribe by resucing other members, and kill the tribes enemies. I personaly found it hard to really care about anyone in my tribe. This made the whole story feel bland to me.
General Gameplay: The general gameplay is really good. Nothing that should be supprising for a Farcry game. You have to hunt for matterials around the map. The game has an extensive crafting system that makes you pick how you will play the game. Unlocking new skills and crafting is done by recruiting experts to your tribe. You find them by rescuing them or recruiting them from around the map. The skills and crafting feel meaningful and is one of my favorite parts of this game. Another cool feature is the night time. During the night the predators come out to hunt. If you do not have fire to fend off the wolf packs you will die. However, some missions and prey must be hunted at night forcing you to step up to the challenge. If you have played Dying Light it reminds me of that.
Combat: Feels pretty bland in Farcry Primal. There is no dodge system in the game meaning you are running around your enemies trying to hit them with a club. However, it can be very satisfying to throw a spear into someone or shoot an arrow at someone instantly killing them, but this does get old. You can use the animals you have tammed to fight for you in combat but they can only take down several enemies before they themselves fall.
Pros:
Great crafting system
You can tame animals that each feel unique (how ever some are obviously better then others meaning only a few are viable)
Unlocking and building your village feels meaningful
The animals on the map change when its night or day
Fire spreads and feels powerful
The two hostiel factions feel unique
Cons:
Game feels bland fast
Combat is boring most of the time and boils down to you slapping someone with a club
Story is hard to get into
Few "good" animals limiting you to about 3 effective ones
TL;DR
I respect the attempt to bring something new to the table but the game does feel like a DLC for farcry 4/3 at best. Kinda like Battlefield hardline vs Battlefield 4. I would not recomend buying this game at the full 59.99$ price tag and instead find an alternate way to get it cheeper or just wait for a sale on steam. Good game but not worth the pricetag.

For those of you who played and enjoyed the first Alan Wake game, come into this one with an open mind. As far as tone goes, this game couldn't be more different, replacing the elements of a mysterious thiller with the atmosphere of a pulp supernatural action flick.
This isn't really a bad thing, though. While less of a sequel than a low-budget side-story, the series still enjoys playing with the pacing of a level, giving you brief periods of exploration before attacking you at your more vulnerable moments. This is damged somewhat by the re-use of levels in the game, but the justification for this and the different approaches taken each time you revisit an area is very well done.
Where this game shines the most, however, is the story. Alan is trapped in Night Springs, the Twiligh Zone-esque show he created early in his career. While the previous predecesor explained his ability to change reality through writing only gave him the briefest glimmers of hope, this rendition allows gamers to experience a writer's power trip, one that allows Alan to quite literally rock the heavens after some careful planning and skill.
A special mention must also be given to the game's villian, Mr. Scratch. While the idea of an evil twin is a bit of a cliche, Mr. Scratch's showboating in everything he does is consistently entertaining. Few times  has a villian been so intriguing just through sheer personality and charisma.

Within the genre of RTS WWII games, COH2 is viewed by some as merely a sequel to vCOH. Though it is similar by virture of genre and setting; It's not merely a sequel! It's a whole new interactive gameplay--from units to maps to missions. The basic game commanders as totally adequate for adding a lot of variety (which vCOH had only 3 choices) via the commanders. Buying the DLC just enhances the options though in few cases adds newer units or abilities. Personally, I like this--buy it if you want it approach.
COH2 deliveres a lot a fun, tense gameplay. Truesight, weather tech, and new infantry pathing abilities, along with a dynamically changing battlefield, really creates some great gaming. (Oh, vehicle pathing is still somewhat spastic.)
The asymetrical balance is somewhat daunting to learn (much like the Brits once nerfed), with the Wehrmacht being most similar to vCOH. Here the game made some subtle differences that makes the Wehrmacht somewhat easier to manage (without micro-managing). The Soviets, however, are fun but exasperating to play (to some degree like the Americans in vCOH). Soviet teching is not at all linear or even possible in many matches, given the massive bleeding inflicted by losses. Yet, once you've learned what combination of Soviet arms to cobble together, the Soviets really give the Wehrmacht a run for their money. Ultimately, a Soviet player has to be far more descriminating and anticipatory in what units to produce than the Wehrmact, since an early Panzer or Ostwind can ruin an otherwise good game.  Likewise, the stronger Wehrmacht tanks can't afford to get ahead of infantry support. Hence, Soviets arms typically dominate the Wehrmacht infantry, whereas the Wehrmacht tanks can outlast most Soviet armor. It's a truly asymetrical theater.
COH2 is a great game. Sequel-like but not a sequel. It's got numerous improvements (and differences....even when vCOH had some better aspects) that make COH, well, a bit old.
Cost of the buy-in is definitely higher; but the fun factor (for me) is worth it! Bigger than that, is the hardware requirements to run this graphic hog. But if you've got the gaming system that can run it, I'd recommend that you try it. It's not a FPS, but it's an awesome RTS.

Since the release of Diablo 2, way back in the year 2000, basically every ARPG has been trying to be Diablo 3, yet none have truly succeeded, not even the actual Diablo 3. I'm not going to go so far as to say Grim Dawn is the 'real' Diablo 3, but its the closest an ARPG has come IMO.
For starters, Grim Dawn (GD) has just about everything you would expect. Multiple classes, the ability to mix classes, an additional alternate advancement system, lots and lots of loot in different color flavors, and hordes of various enemies and bosses to slay. You can play solo, or with up to 4 others, and you can even enable PvP if you so choose.
Perhaps its one outstanding difference is that the maps aren't randomly generated (for the main campaign, you can play custom maps, though I haven't explored that option), which initially felt odd until I just got over it and realized fully hand-crafted maps look better and are more logical than what even a good random generator can do. Will that hold up through multiple playthroughs? Not likely, but I've never been a huge fan of grinding an ARPG over and over again anyway.
The graphics are very serviceable. They won't blow you away, but they also don't feel cheap, and there are some nice lighting effects and the overall style is a slightly different take on the traditional fantasy doom world full of zombies and other creatures. Same for the sound, which includes a bit of voice acting; its not top-notch, but once you get into the game you find that it all fits and works well-enough. The game runs well and I've only seen it crash once (on my wife's computers during multiplayer).
The pace is good, and main storyline so far has been interesting (mostly told through lore text items you find), and I've liked every area I've seen so far. And since the maps aren't random, they all connect in a logical manner that gives the world of GD a more... worldly feel rather than just randomly connected zones. I think that last part is one of the major reasons I'm really like GD too; it has a better sense of progress as you uncover more of the world and the problems facing it.
I also like that you aren't bombarded with abilities. Or rather, you have that option, as its very easy to focus-in on a few abilities that sound interesting and skip others during the leveling process. You can go so far as to only unlock and upgrade your auto-attack and passives/buffs, which means less button pushing but without gimping yourself. Again perhaps more min/maxing is needed at the highest difficulty, but for an initial run, that flexibility is there.
GD is also pretty flexible in other areas too. You can undo spent skill points for a small cost, and many skills aren't exclusive to one type of weapon. So for example an auto-attack modifier will work whether you are using a 1h melee weapon or a 2h ranged weapon. That's nice and lets you switch up what gear you are using pretty easily as you find new and better drops. A constant flow of upgrades is a huge key to ARPG enjoyment, and GD nails this.
Finally, the game is very co-op friendly. It will auto-party you if you select that option, and loot can also be personal until you drop it, making 'sharing' loot much easier. Simply scoop up all the stuff you see drop, and if you find something you think might be good for your buddy, drop it and they can grab it. Easy, quick, and painless. Quests also update for everyone in the party, so it doesn't matter who landed the last hit or who talked to an NPC. It basically feels like playing the single-player in terms of pace and function, only you also have a buddy running and killing along side you.
If you enjoy ARPGs, Grim Dawn really is a must-play.

I was looking for a tower defense game wherein I could sit and play the game for more than an hour and not get bored. I found Tower Wars on sale and immediately grabbed as I'm a fan of worlds created with hexagonal terrains put together.
The game resembles Tropical Tower Wars, a custom WarCraft III map that I used to play. Instead of having a fixed pathways and a place for your towers, you create the maze yourself. The world is made out of hexagon tiles separated into different islands. Three gold mines for each team are randomly placed in the map to create diversity for your mazing strategies.
[+] Not much to say on this as the game uses the most conventional controls for any Tower Defense game. In the time that I played I haven't felt any type of discomfort even once.
[+] As I said before, I am a fan of game terrain made out of hexagon tiles.
[+] The maps for different modes was well made allowing different kinds of strategies to be put to use.
[+] The bots are good for people who are learning the game. They start from easy and eventually gets more challenging as you defeat more of them one by one.
[+] The game gives you freedom on how you want to handle your mazes.
[+] It also has a route detector to make the game eye-friendly despite building a big amount of towers and stops you from messing up in case you get confused in your own maze.
[-] Although it gets challenging as you pick higher level of bots. The only difference you see is the rate of how fast they upgrade their towers, and mines. They keep recycling the same strategy over and over.
[+] Variety of maps to choose from.
[+] You can either play defensive, offensive, or balance depending on how you wish to control the game.
[-] Few people are playing and on that "few people" even fewer people plays Human vs. Human. Thus, expect long queues when you want to play multiplayer.

I seriously don't know why I bothered. I liked the original game; but, this game was just tedious.
Where I think it fails:
- It brings next to nothing new from the original game so there's no mystery
- Game-play is way too repetitive and offers nothing we haven't already seen
- Theme/Environment/Mood is isolated, lonely, and lacks interactivity
- As you progress in the game, nothing changes,same predictable crap, etc.
- The hidden pages don't offer much; they say a whole lot of the same exact thing
- The game is neither action, nor is a horror/thriller; rather, it seems like a feeble attempt at a mystery/adventure without enough story to make it so
- The game feels confined (which is good for horror titles) but it's just a put-off in this case
- This game makes it apparent that Alan Wake is suffering from a form of severe bi-polar dementia or schizophrenia, representing parts of his segmented life through each character, periodically relating to story lines from his previous writings (mainly 'The Hero of Light"), and that there is no Mr. Scratch at all (as opposed to the original game, which left you wondering).
- The game lacks character, no humor, nothing interesting or thought provoking (except the 'i don't wanna be good; I wanna be nasty...' part. I gotta admit that caught me off guard).
Developers: The writer is doing his job; please do something with the gameplay in the next release. I can see benefit in adding dark-themed side missions that shed light on Wake's relationships with various people in his life, facing the reality that he's demented and needs help (kind of like in "A Beautiful Mind"), or something of the sort. At present, there's no way I would consider buying a sequel to Alan Wake or this game. Perhaps a prequel...

Within the genre of RTS WWII games, COH2 is viewed by some as merely a sequel to vCOH. Though it is similar by virture of genre and setting; It's not merely a sequel! It's a whole new interactive gameplay--from units to maps to missions. The basic game commanders as totally adequate for adding a lot of variety (which vCOH had only 3 choices) via the commanders. Buying the DLC just enhances the options though in few cases adds newer units or abilities. Personally, I like this--buy it if you want it approach.
COH2 deliveres a lot a fun, tense gameplay. Truesight, weather tech, and new infantry pathing abilities, along with a dynamically changing battlefield, really creates some great gaming. (Oh, vehicle pathing is still somewhat spastic.)
The asymetrical balance is somewhat daunting to learn (much like the Brits once nerfed), with the Wehrmacht being most similar to vCOH. Here the game made some subtle differences that makes the Wehrmacht somewhat easier to manage (without micro-managing). The Soviets, however, are fun but exasperating to play (to some degree like the Americans in vCOH). Soviet teching is not at all linear or even possible in many matches, given the massive bleeding inflicted by losses. Yet, once you've learned what combination of Soviet arms to cobble together, the Soviets really give the Wehrmacht a run for their money. Ultimately, a Soviet player has to be far more descriminating and anticipatory in what units to produce than the Wehrmact, since an early Panzer or Ostwind can ruin an otherwise good game.  Likewise, the stronger Wehrmacht tanks can't afford to get ahead of infantry support. Hence, Soviets arms typically dominate the Wehrmacht infantry, whereas the Wehrmacht tanks can outlast most Soviet armor. It's a truly asymetrical theater.
COH2 is a great game. Sequel-like but not a sequel. It's got numerous improvements (and differences....even when vCOH had some better aspects) that make COH, well, a bit old.
Cost of the buy-in is definitely higher; but the fun factor (for me) is worth it! Bigger than that, is the hardware requirements to run this graphic hog. But if you've got the gaming system that can run it, I'd recommend that you try it. It's not a FPS, but it's an awesome RTS.

Hard to recommend a sequel to the highest rated metacritic rts of the 21st century, which changes (for the worse) and removes many of the original's features. From a singleplayer aspect, the ai is more intellegent this time round and provides more of a challenge. However the storyline is lacking and doesn't appear intwined very well from mission to mission. The theatre of war game modes add a nice change of pace to the standard gameplay, and lead to some nice co-operative scenarios, perhaps with inspiration from the Joint Operations mod for coh1. Again however, it isnt very well executed with some simply being skirmishes with slightly altered units depending on the timeframe.
Multiplayer matchmaking has also changed. Gone away with the lobby system, with just automatch left; this feels like such a step backwards. Removing of such core features leaves you with a small amount of customisation. You can create custom matches, but you will have to invite other players from steam to fill in the gaps. No longer can you tell whether you are competing with and against equally skilled players, with the new xp orentated level system which grants you xp for simply taking part (also accumulated in single player). No longer are there any statistics such as total online players, number of players searching as axis/soviets, how many are looking for 4v4s, 1v1s etc, leaving you feeling as though there are not many active players (percentages searching for a game jump erratically)
In game leaderboards are now gone, however have been instated in the Dec10th patch via a weblink. This feels really low effort and looks too much like an afterthought compared to the original coh1 leaderboards. I guess it is a good sign that Relic are listening to its customers as it was a highly requested feature by the community but should have been implemented into the game from release.
Gameplay wise, it hasn't been messed about with too much which is a good thing. Weather affects have been added such as blizzards which can cause your units to die from the cold, and mud which severely affects unit speed. The amount of units availiable to each army seems rather small which can limit your countering options and often leads to lack of variety on the battlefield; many players opting to use the same units because many are currently obsolete. Doctrines have been replaced with commanders which share many of the same abilities, meaning that your choice feels less centralised to one strategy; for good or bad. As with many modern games this leads to microtransactions. Commanders, skins and even faceplates are just some of the (rather overpriced) options available on the steam store. Why these are not available already to everyone, or just included in patches is poor and shows the direction in which this game is going.
To conclude; the main things that this game does well at, were already in place in the original game. Company of Heroes 2 takes away so much and yet adds so little. Adding the soviets as a playable faction in this sequel was nice, but was already done (very) well in the previous game via the Eastern Front mod. If you don't aready own the original (and its expansions) I thoroughly recommend you get that first. However if you've racked up 4digit hours playing the original like me, and you are itching for some more Company of Heroes, I can only suggest you don't pay full price. Honestly, I feel that this game is worth about a tenner, £15 max. Definitely hold out for sales on this.

Just finished all of Season 1 today.
The Good:
The game really does a good job at immersing you into the story.  The Forresters feel like they could belong in the actual TV show, and you really get the feeling that you need to fight for them.  The characters introduced are all likeable in their own way, and you really get a sense of hatred for your enemies in this game.  The combat is really well done too.
The Bad:
When you play a Telltale game, you expect your choices to make a difference.  However, this Season seems to always end exactly the same no matter what route you take.  Whether you try to be a diplomat or go all the way out in war ... the same thing seems to happen, and the ending really isn't satisfying at all.  You feel like you kind of just did all this for nothing.
The Verdict:
If you like GOT -  you will not be dissapointed (at least, not until the very end).  With Season 2 having been confirmed by Telltale Games, we can only hope that Season 2 will finally bring us the end we were waiting for.  Unlike a lot of people, I'm really anxious and excited for Season 2 to come out.
If you don't like GOT ... I doubt this game will be able to entertain you as much (unlike the Walking Dead series which did a very good job, even for people who weren't fans of the series like me).
8/10 ... hopefully Season 2 ties everything together!

There's simple stories simply told. There's complex stories simply told. There's complex stories complexly told. And then there's this game which is a simple story complexly told. The complex telling of a simple story can be a lot of things but the way this game handles the complexity of it's story has nothing to do with the telling of the story but EVERYTHING to do with the technical execution of this story. And this really brings the game down significantly. So much so that I can't recommend it.
You play as a girl looking for her cat. And that's it. That's the ENTIRE story. There's nothing REALLY to spoil until the ending but for the entire game until the final cutscene, you're basically just looking for your cat and along the way solving EXCEEDINGLY simple puzzles to figure out ways around obstacles to your path. The hook of the game is that you're a blind girl whose entire world is visually nothing represented entirely by white. You fill the world out and the details in it by walking around it and the sound from you footprints magically fills the world with a watercolor aesthetic that is seriously beautiful to look at. As a computer developer, I have to say, this portion of the game technically impressed me. There are also tricks that these sounds might play on you as they may sound like something but are in reality something else so you need to get close to these objects to figure out what they truly are.
So the mechanic of the game is that the whole world is white and you explore it to fill out the geography in your mind and move forward. Sounds simple enough and truly it is. The few puzzles that exist are very simple and usually just involve you going to another place and interacting with something else and then return to find your path opened to you.
What's wrong with the game is how this exploration plays out. See, as a blind person it stands to reason that you'd walk slowly along feeling things out and being cautious. The character here is LITERALLY THE SLOWEST MOVING THING IN GAMING HISTORY (or at least to my knowledge). This goes beyond the limits of reason and is just plain irritating. Puzzles that require you to find things are deliberately put behind barriers and walls requiring you to traverse irritatingly long distances. There's a sequence where you have to fetch a ball and that ball was behind a fence the entrance of which was almost on the other side of the ground which you have to go around in your plodding pace. Add to this the tiny range of the "sphere" around you which fills the details of the world and the stupidly large hitboxes on certain objects makes exploration UTTERLY frustrating ESPECIALLY when hitting something at even the tiniest angle COMPLETELY stops your already snail-like movement. And there's almost nothing to do as you move through the levels except for some minor secrets that are very obvious. Movement through the game is so mind-numbing you stop caring about the character and as a reason you stop really giving much of a care about her reasons for being there. Add to this the game is VERY short with only 6 chapters and the levels themselves are not that big at all which is a plus because your movement is slow and exploring anything bigger would be a PITA but this also means there's not much to "see".
If the movement speed was even 50% faster and the levels were somewhat bigger and if you there was more thought put into the puzzles, I would be recommending it. Even if the only thing that was done was fix the inane hitboxes to make exploring smoother, I'd recommend it. As it stands, at a full price of $15, it's absolutely not worth it since the story itself isn't all that great.

I am recommending this, but with the following caveat: unlike The Walking Dead, Tales from the Borderlands, or The Wolf Among us, which I would recommend to anyone looking for an interactive story with interesting characters, a good plot, and thoughtful writing- and in the case of Borderlands a whole bunch of laughs to be had- I would only recommend this episodic series to fans of the show and the A Song of Ice and Fire books (unless they're the sort of literary purists that despise even the slightest changes from material adapted from the source).
It captures the look and feel of the show fairly well (minus the nudity) and has accurate likenesses of the actors from the TV series who appear in this game. The trouble is that it feels as though the playable characters have no real agency in the world, as nothing they do can or will affect events in the HBO TV series in any significant way. Ultimately they end up dancing around in the background as events like the Red Wedding and Purple Wedding play themselves out. Characters like Ramsay Bolton, Tyrion Lannister, John Snow, and Queen Cersei are completely protected by "plot armor". The resulting experience feels more like a visit to a theme park than a proper adventure, even if the playable characters (members of House Forrester and one of their servants, a group of people I like to think of as the Starks 2.0) are put through some rather harrowing experiences.
If this is your first Telltale game, don't get suckered in by promises of your choices mattering. Most of them only change things very slightly. Play this or any other Telltale episodic series with the understanding that these are essentially interactive TV shows and not to expect wildly differing endings or multiple narrative branches.
All that being said, the voice acting is of high quality, even if some of the show's stars cameoing here such as Peter Dinklage (Tyrion Lannister) sound bored. The characters and enviroments have this rather pretty hand-painted look which I found pleasing. There are some really fun moments to be had.
Before you know it, you will be afraid to take any risks in life.

Grim Dawn has been through a lot but the devs has seen it all the way to the end and delivered a great ARPG. On the negative side i can only recall a few issues. One is animations, it gets the job done but just barely, voice acting is also very bad but there is not that much of it to begin with. In the end i find the game to be excellent and a success. Very rarely do you see the Early access program produce something so well put together, minus the few flaws i mentioned, and Crate Interactive deserves some praise for it. This game i feel is worth its asking price.

A brutally honest review of Far Cry: Primal, played on Expert difficulty, by a HUGE fan of the Far Cry series.
-----
Far Cry: Primal really makes you feel like you're a part of our ancient history. The immersion is amazing and genuinely feels like you're a terrified, tasty piece of meat, walking around carrying a stick. ..Until you become a near-god, 24~hrs into the game and find yourself thinking about all the other games available for the sticker price of $60ish.
[tl;dr] - This is a pass / wait until a discount comes out. Ignore the hype..
-----
Cons
*Missions: My biggest complaint is the lack of auto-added minimap waypoints, once you've begun a mission. Yet the game will allow you to set a way point on the other side of the map, and that shows on your minimap. But if you accept a mission and the objective is out of your viewing range, the new mission icon on your world-map, will be the exact same size shape and color as all the other missions strewn all over. Good luck finding it.
*Story: What story? Caveman loses tribe. Caveman saves idiots, grows a village. TA DA. >.>
*Enemies: Remember the drunk, Molotov tossing idiots in Far Cry 3? They're reskinned in 2 flavors. All the other enemies are exactly the same, in reguards to their mechanics, and just as repetitious and boring. /Copy Far Cry 3, retexture, change dialog, print.
*Skills/Leveling/Experience: I'm 40% in and nearly all of my Skill are maxed already. I'll be capped by 50% completion. The XP comes way too fast and far too easily. Accelerating the processes is the bonus XP to level, for completing missions and growing the population! YAY! Cap everything in 60 Hrs!
*Taming: I was hoping this would involve some mini-game, requiring skill and finesse, to eventually tame a new catagory of beasts. Nope. Might as well be point-click-tamed. And it ALWAYS succeeds. I have every beast tamed that doesn't require a special mission (and only because I'm saving them).
*Beasts: Your pet died? Mk. Open a menu and click the icon. Good as new. No wait time, and no punishment for letting your pet bleed-out.
*Crafting: The resource nodes are so abundant and easy to acquire, that you'll end up capped in the first 3 hours. You'll stay that way for the majority of the game, only dropping below cap as the Skills you select, unlock crafting options.
*Survivability/Difficulty: I am now Caveman-Superman. It took 8-12hrs to become fearless. And at 25~ I will now charge head on at any creature or enemy and poke them with a sharpened stick, knowing full well that they will collapse long before I do. Rinse-Repeat.
*FIRE: ...don't use it. Seriously. Its like turning on God-Mode and lawl-clipping your way through the game. Everything pee's their pants, panics and get's 1-shot. (metaphorically)
-----
Pros
*Survivability/Difficulty: You will die, a LOT.. for 12 hours; Until you get used to the aiming / controls and learn the sounds of animals nearby. Then, see above about the same subject. But for 12~ish hours, you will♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself every time you're charged by anything. And you WILL get eaten / mauled / trampled / gored and set on fire. Its terrifying, like Doom 3, all over again.
*Vehicles: I won't go into details, as I found out about this aspect only by immersion, but its the best feature of the game. Nothing beats hauling♥♥♥♥♥at cheetah speeds, at night, through the ancient forests.
*Language: The Tribes all speak different dialects of a Proto-Indo-European ancestor language that Linguistic Historians reconstructed and developed specifically for FC:P. The immersion it provides is heightened some-what by the lack of subtitles during open-world encounters.
-----
If you have any questions or concerns, feel free to comment. I will answer what I can in a generic form, as to not spoil your gaming experience. Nothing pisses me off more than spoilers to a game/movie I'm VERY excited about.

First off, I've only played 3 Ubisoft games including this one, so this won't be a biased opinion. I am neither a fanboy nor a hater, so I will give credit where it's due.
My first reaction to launching the story was "These graphics are beautiful, and it really suits the era they were going with" and that it runs smoothly on high settings for my out of date PC (r9 270x, AMD FX 6300 6-core processor (I think that's my processor, can't remember) and 8 gb of ram) I was always able to get 50-60 fps, with some dips to the 30's every once in a while.
So far, I've only had 1 crash and that was because I had 2 games open without noticing. Don't ask how I didn't notice.
I've always been a fan of the primal era with crude tools and this really makes me feel giddy when I play. So far, the only complaint I have is the melee system. It's really simple. Go up to someone, bash their head in, repeat. The ranged system is spot on.
Now let's talk about taming and animals in general. Taming seems too easy. To tame an animal, just walk up to the animal, throw bait, hold e. It really should be a little harder. Like the great beast taming. Those are a challenge and they feel rewarding.
Once you get a saber, you really don't need any other animal. The saber has a great mix of strength, stealth and speed. It feels rather OP. The jaguar is extremely useful for taking over bases. I use the owl (which is a great replacement for binoculars btw), tag all the enemies, drop some rot fumes on the strong guys to make them attack their own kind, and send in my jaguar to clear the guards where I can then move in and start sniping people with my longbow as the jaguar takes down anyone that notices. And if I get noticed, then I call in my saber or bear to wreak havoc.
The hitboxes for enemies are great. I never get an issue where it shows I hit them, but it doesn't do damage. I'm able to easily get headshots even with no reticle.
The story is actually pretty great. It is comical, intense, and has some emotion to it. Some games make it so you feel nothing towards the main protagonists. But this game makes you hate them with your guts, where you WANT to kill them. But then with Ull's death, you feel something for him. You kind of feel sad for him. I won't say why to avoid spoilers, but you feel like he was actually human instead of a ruthless cannibal.
The characters are great and you feel emotion towards some of them. Like when you get a mission notification from someone, I felt like saying "HELL YEAH ANOTHER MISSION FROM YOU" and some of the deaths towards the people in your tribe actually made you feel emotion towards them. They had a good buildup to a lot of characters.
Even walking around the wilderness with your minimap off is a blast. You never know what you'll expect. Whether it's a group of sabers, or a random camp or fun side mission. You never know what to expect! After I beat the story and tamed all the beasts, I turned off my minimap and just started walking around.
Yes, it used the map from Far Cry 4, but they used it as a template. The terrain is absolutely nothing alike, and this concept has been used in gaming for years, and it will be continued to be used.
All in all, I recommend this game 100%. Most of the negative reviews are just Ubisoft haters that didn't give the game a chance, or just have an error when trying to launch the game which will get fixed eventually. If you like the primal setting in games, you will love this game.
That's the end of my opinion. I will update it if I think of more to add or if my opinion of it changes.

I stayed up too late, played through my lunch hour, and generally did not much else until Kyrat was liberated. So when the next Far Cry chapter was announced, I jumped on board and pre-ordered.
I have given Primal 9 hours of my time over a week. That's not much, and decidedly less than what I gave FC3 or 4 (though unfortunately for me, it's apparently too much for Steam to give me a refund, which I requested).
The game just isn't fun. I don't feel empathy toward any of the characters - including the one I'm supposed to be - and the missions don't feel like they're working toward any long-term goal. At this point, I don't know whether I'll finish the game, or even return to it. As mentioned, I tried to get my money back from Steam, but they decided that 9 hours of playtime must mean I liked it. All it really meant is that I gave it a fair shake.

Although I have a weak spot for the Far Cry series, I find Primal to be too boring to recommend. You only have two "primary" attacks, your bow or melee; "secondary" attacks use up resources so you will likely avoid using these if you are low on resources. Some of these secondary attacks and special weapons are fun to use, but don't really add much to combat as you will be more than fine with your basic bow or club, even on the highest difficulty, specially if you have gathered the resources to level them up.
Which brings me to the most boring part of the game: Gathering resources. You have to gather resources to build up your base, to build up your tools, to upgrade your weapons. Yes, this element has been around since Far Cry 3 but Primal requires you to do this for the better part of the game, and unlike the other entries in the series, you won't be done with it until halfway through the game because most melee weapons can be used as throwing weapons, which means you will use them up, which means you will have to build more. It doesn't take long to get tedious and on the way of fun. Later on you won't have to gather as much or any at all, your village provides sufficient resources, and due to certain skills you will need less and less resources to construct weapons, but by then you have sank hours gathering and it will probably have left a bad taste in your mouth.
The game is also very easy, I had to switch to Expert difficulty for any kind of challenge and once you get your first  beast the difficulty goes down. Fast. The beasts are fun to use, but in reality you will be sticking to just a of them. The map is pretty big but uninteresting, your wanderlust is sated pretty quickly and after more of the same you will leave exploration aside and rush the game.
That said, not all is bad. The first few nights were terrifying and exiting. The first time a pack of wolves moved in my general direction I did not know if I should move and risk being spotted or stay an risk being smelled. keeping them at bay with fire while I tried to make it to a nearby bonfire was very tense and set the tone for what I hope the game was going to be like. Sadly, as I mentioned, difficulty goes down fast and I found myself sending my beast away to increase the challenge.
In short, Primal is a nice game but fluffed with uninteresting content and it doesn't takes the setting as seriously as you are lead to believe.

Es war ein regnerischer Tag als ich das erste Mal "Alan Wake´s American Nightmare" gestartet hatte. Es war dunkel und der Charakter erhob sich zum ersten Mal aus dem Dreck. Wir starten das Spiel mit einer Taschenlampe und einer Pistole. Man versteht schnell wie es funktioniert: Taschenlampe auf den Gegner, warten, schießen. Jeder Gegner in diesem Spiel lässt sich auf diese Weise ohne Probleme erledigen. Die Steuerung und die Grafik haben mir gefallen.
Kommen wir nun zum eigentlichem Problem von Alan Wake´s American Nightmare, man steht wie ich schon sagte aus dem Dreck auf, erledigt Aufgaben (Dreh das Ventil zu, mach dies, mach das) und kommt durch 4 verschiedene Level die zu einem Showdown mit sich selbst führen. Ja, man kämpft gegen sein böses Ich. Leider hat "ALAN" aber etwas vergessen, also steht er wieder am Start auf. Ich lachte  und dachte mir:" Na, was kommt jetzt". Richtig, das ganze Spiel nochmal, mit geringen Abweichungen. Als ich dann endlich wieder beim Endgegner angekommen war und das Spiel nun zwei mal gesehen hatte passierte das Unvorstellbare. Ich stand wieder am Anfang. Mir standen bereits die Haare zu Berge, da der Charakter scheinbar immer wieder Teile zu vergessen scheint. Man sieht also wieder die gleichen Leute und die gleichen Orte, mit nur geringen Abweichungen in den Aufgaben. Den Rest kennt ihr ja und ihr wacht wieder auf. Dann spielt ihr das ganze nochmal, und fertig. Spiel vorbei. Spielzeit? Unter 4 Stunden. War es die 10,00-15,00€ Wert? Nein. Für 15,00€ hätte ich auch zwei mal ins Kino gehen können, und zwar für UNTERSCHIEDLICHE Filme.

Interesting game about a blind girl searching for her cat friend.
The main mechanic of the game is that you have to walk to places to 'see' them. White is the colour that you will see the most in this game and if you are sensitive to brightness the game might be not for you. There's also the problem that you walk very slowly which adds to the atmosphere of a blind girl slowly uncovering the world around her, but makes it very tedious to backtrack. Besides those two issues the game is fun to explore and looks pretty good.
The music and sound effects are scarce, but well chosen and when something makes a noise you 'see' that part of the world for a few seconds. In two chapters of the game it is raining and while in the first of the two the world gets only slowly 'washed away' it turns into a real problem in the second of those chapters. The fact that the world turns back to white pretty quick in that chapter makes the game harder to play and without a good sense of orientation you might get lost very often.
If you can stand the very slow pace of the game, Beyond Eyes is a great experience, but I'd highly recommend getting it on sale or in a bundle as it is rather short and doesn't offer much replay value.

This is, what I thought to be, a touching experience. An accident leaves a little girl, Rae, blinded. Everyday she sits alone in the protection of her family garden, sinking further into social isolation. Unhappy and alone, her life finally improves when a friendly cat comes to visit her. Her bond with the cat strengthens until one day, the cat doesn't return. After wondering where her only friend has gone, Rae decides to venture off into an unfamiliar world. As far as gameplay goes, I wouldn't say I had fun while playing this game. You guide Rae through the world based on her perception. There are no puzzles, only the bright haze that obscures the world from you. To advance, you must navigate like Rae would - with small, deliberate steps. The slow pace can be agonizing, but ultimately adds to the experience. The goal is to place you in Rae's rain boots. The game forces you to slow down and appreciate the courage and dedication of this little girl. And it shines when portraying her feelings. There is no question when Rae is happy or afraid.  You see her hopes built up then dashed again. And with each emotional encounter, you are able to connect with her. This is its greatest strength, and it should be why you buy the game.

Beyond Eyes is a rather unique third person adventure game. You play as the blind girl Rae who is looking for her friend, the cat Nani.
The game has a great art style. The visuals are rather basic but extremely stylistic. Slowly revealing the world as you explore is a clever way to represent how a blind person might perceive the world around them.
The audio in the game is mainly ambient sounds. The various audio cues and how they can mislead the player are certainly a nice touch. The game could have used much better positional audio support, however.
Beyond Eyes does not really have any interesting gameplay. There are few hints to help you track down Nani, but most of your time is still spent wandering around aimlessly. The levels don't have many interesting details and there are way too many dead ends.
This really feels like a missed opportunity. The way the levels are slowly revealed could have easily been used for some innovative puzzles or storytelling.
There's no real difficulty, just tedium.
It's quite annoying how slowly Rae walks and turns. Furthermore, even the tiniest obstacle can block her path. A blind person certainly has to be quite careful, but this feels ridiculous.
The game has very little writing and the story is quite basic and underwhelming.
Beyond Eyes has an interesting concept and great visuals. Unfortunately the gameplay is extremely tedious and the story is rather weak. I wouldn't recommend the game.

This game is epic. Amazing. Spectacular. Just... it's really really good. The graphics can be glitchy, but I like them personally. Some people have said that they hated them and I have to admit that I didn't think highly of them at the beginning, either. But after a little while playing, I love them.
So I bought this game during the steam winter sale, for slightly less than ten euros. If I had the money, I would have definitely bought it for full price, too. The choices just... get under your skin. It makes you wonder, over and over again: 'am I doing the right thing?'. During my playthrough, I've made many wrong decissions. Many. Like, really really many. It cost me my head. Literally.
It makes you second guess yourself, over and over again. And honestly, that's probably where its greatest strength lies, but even more so its greatest weakness.
You see, replayability in this game is practically... impossible. It took me about 13 hours to beat the game, and after that I retried one of the endings. You see, you can easily 'rewind' during one of the episodes. Just go to the main menu and select one of the 'plot points' that you want to rewind from. You'll, however, have to finish the game from there. So you can't simply select a point, change something in that chapter, skip the next one since you want to keep it the same and instead go to the chapter after that. That's impossible.
But even worse, you can only do that for the episode you're at. So if you want to change one tiny little thing in episode one which I actually wanted to do, I'd have to replay the entire game.
So another 13 hours simply for a few minor changes.
I've heard some people say that, in fact, no matter what you do, the ending is always the same. I know for a fact that that's not completely true, although I'm sure that, for the most part, that might actually be the case. I've rewinded to one of the few last choices before the ending and done something different. And, in the end, the ending was mostly the same. Which, although unfortunate, I don't really care about all that much.
Some people are talking about 'Telltale's illusion of choice': no matter what you do, the ending is still the same. Which might be true. I wouldn't really know, since I haven't had the time yet for the actual other 13 hours of playing: I've replayed a little bit of episode one, but I got bored and quit. After all, I've already played it. I wish that you could AT LEAST skip some chapters and just keep them what they were the first time you played.
It's... annoying. Because the story is epic. And the choices are amazingly well thought out. I've felt anxious, and at times I was even scared of what that choice would do: would it be good in the long term but bad in the short term? Or the other way around?
However, your choices definitely DO matter. For example, in episode 1 I called Ludd Whitehill a 'craven' as Ethan (for those that don't know, 'craven' means coward). In episode 2 Ludd said: 'Your brother Ethan called me a craven'. Obviously, he remembered.
Should you attack the guard? Should you kill the traitor? Should you break your vows? These are choices that you have to make during your playthrough. And it makes you wonder: should you? It will annoy this person, but this other person will like it. Plus, I promised Talia...
The epic story, wonderful choices and just the feeling this game gives you that makes you second guess every little thing you do...
Buy it. If you like Game of Thrones (by the way, Telltale has NOT held back with gore and violence. There are no sex scenes (other than a near-naked future wife) this really does feel like the show), don't mind the graphics and like Telltale games (this is my first ever Telltale game I've played, by the way), buy it.

It took me quite a while to decide whether or not I'd recommend this game.  I like it, let's be clear on that, but I love this type of game in general, so that is certainly affecting my judgement.  But many other games do this better, and this game engages in some prime sins of bad point and click adventures.
Pros:
Gorgeous artwork
Nicely varied locations
Decent puzzles
Good music
Cons:
Counter intuitive control scheme
Repetitive Mazes
No settings access
Sins:
1.  Looking at an object should never result in the message "Nothing Happens."  Everything you look at should have a description, and if you're looking at something that was never programmed to be looked at, the message should at least say something more like "This isn't anything important."
2.  You can work yourself to points where you are stuck, but not dead.  This shouldn't happen in this type of game.  You should always be able to progress, or, if you can't, see that the game has ended.
3.  There are many items which you can pick up which serve no purpose in the game.  If they do, and I just don't see it, then I apologize, ignore this complaint, and in small doses this is okay, but during the course of the game there were more items in my inventory which I did not use than those that I did.
4.  There is not much to do compared to the amount of area you can cover.  I've gone through huge mazes that had nothing important inside them (for example, the hedge maze) and may as well have been one room.  it doesn't encourage the type of exploration a player will want to take part in.
Verdict:  If you're REALLY jonesing for a stroll through the adventure games of the 90s, get it.  it's cheap.  I got it on sale, when it was REALLY cheap, and for the price, it was worth it.  If you want a good point and click game from the 90s though, I could better recommend:
Myst
Lighthouse
Shivers
The Journeyman Project Series
Check those out first, they're all a lot more fun, if you can get your hands on them.
