Make no mistake: The Labyrinth of Time is an adventure game from 1993. Most of the puzzles are mazes and inventory fetch quests. Much of the story is told through journals. There are a few ways to get stuck. If you doesn't sound appealing, steer clear. But if that's your speed and you want an adventure game experience with a unique artistic sensibility, this is a must-play.
The world of the Labyrinth is a patchwork of surrealism, Art Deco, and classical architecture. The art direction is mesmerizing. There is simply nothing else like it in any game. Every room is with worth seeing, every useless inventory item worth examining, every dead-end worth the trek. The dark, horror-influnced soundtrack reinforces the idea that the Labyrinth is a truly alien place, and the light-sci-fi archaeological time travel story is also entertaining.
By the end, the constant backtracking and repetitive mazes can get a little tiring. But The Labyrinth of Time deserves a look for its art and atmosphere.

I decided to revisit Tropico in the form of Tropico 4. I played the original as a kid, and skipped Tropico 2 and 3. Ultimately, Tropico 4 seemed promising at first, but I quickly reached a certain point where it started to feel repetitive and too easy. I guess the crux of it is that if you plan your first steps correctly, you can make your profits grow exponentially such that by late game you have more money than you know what to do with. That means that by the the time you progress to a more developed island, the gameplay has gotten pretty boring. A lot of the main story games involve large sum payments, which just feels like a waiting game. Based on my experience, it has no replay value for me and I don't see myself playing this version again. I wish they had added a few more key aspects to the game rather than just updating the art, engine, and adding some more buildings. But it isn't completely terrible, so while I'm not recommending it, I'm not condemning it either. If you find it on sale for a few dollars, it might be worth giving it a try.

So far this game is great. The atmosphere is amazing (who would have thought zombies, otherwordly alien things, high fantasy, a sort of western vibe, and mystery went so well together?), the character building is really nice (even if i would have liked a way to customize my characters looks beyond just gender), the fact that certain quests and actions visibly impact the world around you is very enjoyable both because it makes the world seem more alive and because it makes it more fun to complete quests. The quests themselves have been pretty simplistic so far, it's a lot of fetch quests or "go to place X and kill thing Y" but the story makes the quests make sense. Also a lot of them only come with general directions (if you played Morrowind or Oblivion you're familiar with this) such as "follow the river to the delta. The stash is in a hollow tree stump." That's it. No quest marker on your map or mini-map to make things easier. Some quests do have markers but a lot of them don't which I personally find really nice.
So far my only real complaint is that the game doesn't pause when you go to your inventory screen or journal/codex screen meaning you could be reading up on what you need to do and suddenly have mobs wander in and attack you (and the game has a lot of mobs to kill) which can be quite frustrating. Also the info/tutorial blurbs fade a bit too quickly for my taste, they disappear before I've had a chance to read them.
But overall those are some minor annoyances, and once you're aware of it it's easy to anticipate and work around (basically clear out an area of mobs before you try to mess about in the inventory) and they in no way bring down the overall experience of playing this game. It may not be an AAA title, but it sure as heck plays like one (except this actually feels unique and fresh).

I actually liked this more than the regular campaign. This is kind of like a mix between the main campaign and a really basic open-world game.
It's a lot more open than the main campaign, but it's still rather linear, in that there is only ever one objective that can be done at a time, but you can roam around and explore. The areas aren't very big, and you can't freely travel between them, but this kind of gives me a taste of what the main campaign could have been like if it were designed as an open world game instead of being as utterly claustrophobic as it was.
This standalone DLC made quite a few changes from the original game, but not all of them were good. In the original Alan Wake, there were 4 weapons. In this one, there are 2 pistols, 2 rifles, 3 shotguns, 2 automatic weapons, a flaregun, and a nailgun. While choice is always good, some of the weapons are insanely overpowered, and some are just pointless. It seems like the developers took people's complaints about the main game's combat system to mean that combat was too difficult (it wasn't), and made it easier. Unfortunately, that means combat is now a cakewalk. Ammo is RIDICULOUSLY plentiful, weapons are insanely powerful, and enemies will barely ever even get close enough to hit you. Throughout the whole game, I got hit maybe 4 times, used 1 handheld flare, never fired the flaregun, and totally forgot I even HAD flashbangs.
They beefed up the flashlight as well. The enemies seem like they take less light to burn away the darkness, and the flashlight recharges CRAZY fast. From completely empty, it will charge to full in about 3 seconds, including the 1-2 second delay before it even starts charging. I was playing on Normal (there's only normal and nightmare), too, but maybe in this game that's the equivalent of easy.
The story is still rather interesting in this expansion, but the writing and voice acting are HORRIBLE. I mean absurdly stupid at times. I'm all for campy fun, but sometimes it gets so ridiculous that it really pulls you out of the experience. Speaking of acting, the little "TV" segments where your dark self talks to you go on WAY too long sometimes, and don't really play any importance in how the game unfolds (and you don't get any achievements for them or anything).
Overall I liked this. The story and acting took a step backwards from the main game, but you're not confined to the stupid outdoor tunnel sections (running through the woods), and combat doesn't get in your way as horrifically as it did in the main game either.
It's rather short, so don't pay $20 for it or anything, but I enjoyed it. Your results may vary, of course.

I do not mind elaborating: The skill-system is rather simple, allowing you to combine two out of several skill trees with each other. What sounds exciting at first is in fact less complex than the skill trees of Diablo 2. There, each class had 3 skill trees to choose from, each very different offering your character different playstyles within each class as well as a strong distinction between the classes.
In Grim Dawn, you only get two skill trees which each of themselves offer less varation as well as  less distinciton between the classes.
Having recognized that, CRATE has implemented a Star-map system which gives you smaller bonusses depending on your playstyle as you progress through the game. Everybody has access to all the Zodiacs so there is 0 distinction between the classes but rather just another progression scale that seems to be there to kill time and nothing else.
Also the setting is questionable: As there are are proper guns (using gunpowder or magic i assume- does not matter really) , there is hardly a sane reason to wear a heavy armor as you do as a melee character in the game. When the gunpowder was imported to Europe, the Knights and their notorious armors subsequently were outdated- not so in this game for some reason. This contributes to the lack of immersion which hinders everybody with a thinking mind of accepting this game as a plausible ARPG.
The playstyles also just vary between the class selections, but not between the enemies: Champions have more hitpoints and slightly more damage, bosses even more so. I have never encountered an enemy that required tactic are thinking. It comes down to button smashing.
Comparing this to Path of Exile, where you have seasoned events, the Atlas of Worlds, a great and innovative character development and a LOT more itemization, you can all answer the question, wether or not you should pay for something that has been done far better by a F2P title that has no P2W whatsoever.

An interesting follow-up to Alan Wake. Is it a sequel? No, not really. Is it a DLC? No, it is stand-alone. I guess then we can call it an expansion pack.
The story is pretty short compared to the first Alan Wake, but it is kept interesting by fast pacing and a great progression of story elements.
This time, the story is narrated as if it were an episode of Night Springs (Twilight Zone). I absolutely adore this homage, and palying through and hearing the narration in this way really made me enjoy it more.
The videos you see on the random TVs are mainly Mr. Scratch addressing Alan directly. We get to see how twisted he is, and how he delights in what he does. I think this was a great addition to the game's story elements.
Shooting, the flashlight, the HUD, and a bunch of other mechanics have been streamlined to be faster. You're more agile and nimble, and combat is much more fast due to this. This takes some of the tension of the story mode, but it is still enjoyable.
There are tons of new weapons, with some great cameos by the m14, m4, and the AA-12, as well as the MAC-10.
I'm not interested in the Arcade mode, but I've played a round and I can see it being enjoyable and challenging.
All in all, an excellent expansion to Alan Wake that clarifies some things and mystifies some even further.
Totally worth it if you loved Alan Wake.

Company of Heroes 2 is an excellent game, building upon the success of its predacessor. The game itself plays very similarly to the original, but offers enough new content to still be very exciting and entertaining. The two armies depicted in the game are very different from each other, yet the Germans even feel different from the previous game. The Russian army also has some very cool abilities, such as reinforcing in the field with squads of conscript soldiers. The game itself also offers many new features to keep it always feeling fresh, since it now supports player made maps through the Steam workshop. There is also a new mode called Theatre of War, which is constantly being updated with new campaign missions to keep playres on their toes.
Since this game plays just like the first one, there is no need to go into detail about how good this gameplay is. It is very rewarding using unit's special abilities, especially once you get a squad to veteran status, where it becomes a well-oiled, enemy dispatching machine. One note about this game is it feels easier to manage your troops, hence making coordinated offensive assaults much easier than in the first game. Likewise, it is much harder to set up good defenses to stop such assaults, leaving me still going to the first game when I'm in a mood for defense. However, if I want to play some good offense, this game does a good job of bolstering one's ability to do so.
One last note: Ignore the reviews who say this game is bad. For one thing, it is AT LEAST as good a the first one, which was an instant classic in my books. Many of the reviews point to the depicted 'brutality of the Russian army'. Well people, read your freaking history. The Russians were notoriously brutal towards even their own troops, and this game depicts that very accurately. However it also does a very nice job of showing the common Russian soldier as a simple man trying to defend his homeland, but sadly is under command of a ruthless dictator on par with Hitler. Anyone who is upset that the game depicts the Russian high command as being so harsh to their own men needs to study WWII in depth, and realize that this game does a good job of presenting things in a historically accurate context.
Overall, I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of RTS, and especially if you enjoyed the first game.

Tower wars is a tower defense game where you also need to attack, you can play against random people via matchmaking or you can play against your friends or with them vs bots.
If you're an achievement hunter don't try this game o.o one of them requires you to be #1 on the ranking of the season.

The Good part of this game is you can see where the enemy is going to walk through so you can block stairs and paths in order to make them walk the longest while your lv 3 ballistas brutally murder them.
There's 2 kinds of currency in the game , one is gold used to build troops, towers and upgrade them you get it passively via gold mines , the second is battle points which you get the longest your troops survive against the enemy towers used to get newer troops , upgrade them , and hire workers at your mines.

Same old Far Cry, just primal.
This game was likely inspired by the Shangri-la missions in Far Cry 4. The people and tech are... uncomplicated at best, so you don't get particularly fun toys (i.e. guns) and you will never see any structures more impressive than a circile of standing stones. Yes, there are relatively large villages and one tribe has managed to construct several forts, but you're most likely only going to come across a few scattered huts at a time. As pretty as it is, this left the world feeling rather empty.
...That's not quite right. Empty isn't the right word because the world is overpopulated by not-so-randomly-generated npc events, enemy tribe's hunting parties, and predators. Dispatch one hunting party and sprint away only to run into another eight seconds later. Same thing for predators, espcially at night. It is so populated that you'll easily end up in three or four way fights if you're not careful. An extreme, but not uncommon example would be Wenja and Izila hunters are exchanging arrows/spears, Udam hunters are chased into the fray by two cave lions, you join in to help your Wenja brothers, and then the nearby herd of mammoths/rhinos gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and kill everything. Remember: humans are not at the top of the food chain yet.
On toys, it is enough say you get a spear, club 1 and 2, bows 1, 2, and 3, and a throwable pot of bees. Far Cry wiki for more. It's also worth noting that balance takes precedence over realism and it may take several spears to the head to take down certain beasts. Basket-weave and bone armor on enemies keeps the majority from being killed with one hit, even if it's a carefully placed arrow/spear. Most enemies have a weak spot somewhere, but takedowns are your best bet, but you'll have to figure something else out for the animals.
I found that my beasts usually end up as a distraction/meat shield since they're more easily discovered than I am. Some do have special abilities worth keeping in mind. They look great, (though I thought they looked better in Far Cry 4 oddly enough) and they have some pretty impressive takedown animations. If nothing else, they keep away everything else lower on the food chain except for those badgers. And mammoths. And rhinos.
In Far Cry, I think it's the people that make the story. Like past entries, our protagonist Takkar is prone to getting captured, but otherwise is a reliable sort. The remaining characters are somewhat forgettable and I can't quite figure out why. They don't go on quests with you, they aren't romantically involved with you, they may only be relevant in the game short time. However, the same could be said about characters from other entries such as Sam, Noore, and Agent Willis. In the end, I can only think I find Primal's characters boring is because they are cavenmen or because they don't speak English. Superficial, I know, but that's all I've got.
If you're like me, you craft all upgrades (which are very resource-intensive without the use of skills) and get all skills before anything else. Then comes the story, Finally, you proceed to travel the map with my beast companion, taking remaining outposts and completing side missions, collecting everything. That was when I found myself immersed and having the most fun. Exploring. I'm likely going to do another playthrough soon enough, but the HUD will be completely turned off and the difficulty upped. I encourage you to do the same.
I do have to give props to Ubisoft for taking a risk on the setting. It's an interesting change of pace and a fun one, but I don't think I'd pay full price if I had to make the choice again.

Grey Goo is something of a throwback to RTS games of the past like Starcraft or Command & Conquer, and while it tries (and mostly succeeds) at blending elements from those games together with some interesting new concepts, the game ultimately comes across as slightly underdeveloped. It’s obvious that its developers really wanted elements like the game’s story to succeed, but as much as the narrative strives for being compelling, it often feels disjointed, chopped-up, and rushed instead to such a degree that portions of dialogue seem like they were placeholder text that nobody went back and edited before being recorded by a voice actor. The single player campaign starts off strong as far as game play goes, but many missions have unclear objectives and require a lot of restarts. Grey Goo often punishes the player for any sort of indecision or attempts to deviate from a strategy the mission designers intended (but did not always explicitly convey). This is extremely frustrating and, frankly, the reason why I quit playing just shy of completing the campaign.
Overall, I don’t regret purchasing Grey Goo, but I can’t recommend it either. You could certainly do a lot worse on an impulse purchase or sale, but with so many excellent games being released every year, you’re better off choosing one that’s more respectful of your time.
Positives:
- Nice graphics
- Solid, energetic soundtrack
- "talking heads" campaign mission briefings are reminiscent of the original Starcraft
- Unique game play of the Goo faction
Negatives:
- Most Human and Beta units lack personality and smaller ones tend to lack visual distinction
- RTS games shouldn’t require a web search to figure out a campaign mission objective or how to build/upgrade/repair a unit.
- Way too many campaign missions will require you to restart due to unforeseeable scripted events.
- Goo faction becomes a chore to micromanage as a battle progresses.

As of this review, I have not played any of the other Saints Row games. I came into this expecting a cool sci-fi game where I get to fly around and blow crap up. I was not disappointed. I felt that the game got a bit repetitive after 10 hours or so, but nothing ever stopped the game from being a blast. Your powers are awesome, the guns are good (the dubstep gun! Yes!!!) and running up the buildings and gliding around is just endlessly satisfying. This is a really cool game.
Oh, and the mini games. The mini game where you need to hurt yourself as much as possible in a few minutes is one of the most fun things ever. Those are possibly my favorite parts of the game.
If I have one critique, it's that there is no point in the vehicle customization aspect of the game, since after about 5 hours of gameplay, you'll be able to run faster than any vehicle and have infinite stamina. Driving around in those awesome police cars was sweet for the first few hours, but after you can run twice as fast as them and never get tired... I didn't see the point.
Also, the DLC's for this game - How the Saints Save Christmas and Enter the Dominatrix - were very short. The two together will be done in about an hour and a half, maybe two hours. They're both really good, but don't expect them to add more than one sitting of gameplay combined.
One piece of advice: fully upgrade the dubstep gun asap. Just do it. You want the fully upgraded dubstep gun.
Also, get the Game of the Century edition. The extra content is worth the extra money during a sale.

So far this game is great. The atmosphere is amazing (who would have thought zombies, otherwordly alien things, high fantasy, a sort of western vibe, and mystery went so well together?), the character building is really nice (even if i would have liked a way to customize my characters looks beyond just gender), the fact that certain quests and actions visibly impact the world around you is very enjoyable both because it makes the world seem more alive and because it makes it more fun to complete quests. The quests themselves have been pretty simplistic so far, it's a lot of fetch quests or "go to place X and kill thing Y" but the story makes the quests make sense. Also a lot of them only come with general directions (if you played Morrowind or Oblivion you're familiar with this) such as "follow the river to the delta. The stash is in a hollow tree stump." That's it. No quest marker on your map or mini-map to make things easier. Some quests do have markers but a lot of them don't which I personally find really nice.

This game lacks cheat protection, trainers are easily available and well used in online play. Besides that, it also lacks fun when compared to the competetors like Path of Exile.
I regret buying it.
I do not mind elaborating: The skill-system is rather simple, allowing you to combine two out of several skill trees with each other. What sounds exciting at first is in fact less complex than the skill trees of Diablo 2. There, each class had 3 skill trees to choose from, each very different offering your character different playstyles within each class as well as a strong distinction between the classes.
In Grim Dawn, you only get two skill trees which each of themselves offer less varation as well as  less distinciton between the classes.
Having recognized that, CRATE has implemented a Star-map system which gives you smaller bonusses depending on your playstyle as you progress through the game. Everybody has access to all the Zodiacs so there is 0 distinction between the classes but rather just another progression scale that seems to be there to kill time and nothing else.
Also the setting is questionable: As there are are proper guns (using gunpowder or magic i assume- does not matter really) , there is hardly a sane reason to wear a heavy armor as you do as a melee character in the game. When the gunpowder was imported to Europe, the Knights and their notorious armors subsequently were outdated- not so in this game for some reason. This contributes to the lack of immersion which hinders everybody with a thinking mind of accepting this game as a plausible ARPG.
The playstyles also just vary between the class selections, but not between the enemies: Champions have more hitpoints and slightly more damage, bosses even more so. I have never encountered an enemy that required tactic are thinking. It comes down to button smashing.
Comparing this to Path of Exile, where you have seasoned events, the Atlas of Worlds, a great and innovative character development and a LOT more itemization, you can all answer the question, wether or not you should pay for something that has been done far better by a F2P title that has no P2W whatsoever.
The_Mess:"It lacks cheat protection because it's designed as a primarily single player game, with co-op and to allow modding"
A: Cheaters always ruin a game - What proof do other gamers have of my legitimate achievement if all the progress could have been obtained within minutes using a trainer program?

INGREDIENTS
3/4 cup plain breadcrumbs
3/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese
Kraft Grated Cheese 100% Parmesan

8 chicken cutlets (about 1 1/2 pounds total), or 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts, halved horizontally
Salt and freshly ground pepper
1 large egg, lightly beaten
2 cups jarred tomato sauce or Easy Chunky Tomato Sauce
1/4 cup olive oil
6 ounces mozzarella cheese, preferably fresh, cut into eight 1/4-inch-thick slices
DIRECTIONS
Heat broiler. Combine breadcrumbs and Parmesan in a shallow bowl.
Season both sides of chicken with 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper.
Dip chicken in the beaten egg, then dredge in breadcrumb mixture, turning to coat both sides.
Spread tomato sauce onto the bottom of a 10-by-15-inch baking dish. Heat 2 tablespoons oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium heat.
Place 4 chicken cutlets in skillet; cook until golden, 1 to 2 minutes on each side.
Using a spatula, transfer browned cutlets to baking dish, placing them on top of sauce. Repeat with remaining oil and cutlets.
Top each cutlet with a slice of mozzarella.
Broil about 4 inches from heat source until sauce is hot and cheese is melted and lightly browned in spots, 5 to 8 minutes. Serve immediately.

A cute JRPG with a solid combat system, great humor and lovable characters.
The graphics, while not astonishing, get the job done and are stylistically sound. The character designs are great, as are the special attack animations. The only thing that bothered me here is the fact that a lot of dungeons are basically recycled over the course of the game, making it occasionally monotonous.
Sound-wise, there is not much to say. The music is okay, but hardly memorable. The voice acting is really good, though. I also liked the English translation (which is a lot sillier than its Japanese counterpart, but not in a bad way, I find).
Controls are great - if you play it with a gamepad. As it was originally a PSVITA game, this is what they are optimized for.
Gameplay-wise, it is pretty solid. It is your standard JRPG-fare with a turn-based combat system that works pretty well. While it can get slightly monotonous at times, there are generally enough characters to pick from, each of them having their own unique spells, skills and special moves, which mitigates that a bit. The game has some other out-of-combat side mechanisms as well that I won't get into here, but they do help keeping things fresh. The only real gripe I have with the game gameplay-wise is the high amount of grinding that is required, caused by sudden difficulty jumps between chapters.
Where this game truly shines, though, is the humor department. There's a lot of fourth wall breaking, cool references even to more obscure franchises, and general hilarious silliness. The main characters are all funny and endearing in their own way and are generally very memorable. The humor is what really sold me on this game!

Here is a video review on why Primal is the weakest game in the Far Cry franchise.

Pros:
- Overall a very good game, despite being well-aged.
- One of the best story-telling in a video game I've ever seen. 99.9% of the story is told through NPC interaction and dialogue, and there's basically no text boxes at all in this game.
- The game strikes a very nice balance between action-packed and tense moments  and calm, safe moments. This way, you can always take some time to relax after going through a series of action-packed moments.
- Music is excellent as well. Headphones are recommended as they also allow you to hear NPCs better.
- Puzzles are fairly challenging, but not too challenging to the point where I had to look up a walkthrough.
- Smooth and easy-to-use controls.
- You don't really need to play the first Half-Life to understand the plot, but it's still recommended.
- Can run on a toaster. No fancy-shmancy gaming rig needed.
- At time of writing, the game is going on sale for a very low price. If you haven't bought it yet, I highly recommend getting it as it is worth every penny.
Neutrals:
- The play time is kinda short. Managed to beat the game in 12 hours, but that was definitely one of the best 12 hours of my gaming experience.
- Graphics obviously aren't as good as new gen games, but IMO, it's actually pretty good for a 14 year old game.
Cons:
- Protagonist kinda relies too much on NPCs for help. Would be nice if we could open at least some of the electronic doors ourselves.
- Most of the enemies are too squishy and rely heavily on strength in numbers to even be a challenge. Also, there's nearly no variation in the way they attack.
- The NPC allies you get near the end of the game are a bit dumb. Would've been nice if they followed you more and don't get caught up in pointless fights against walkers and stuff.
Overall, I give it a 9/10. Again, if the game's on sale and you don't have it yet, definitely get it.

So with 75+ hours logged, I believe I can give you  a decent idea of this game. This is my first review so bear with me.
Far Cry Primal is a great game that brings in many aspects that gamers will love and have loved across other games. From the free roam of games like Elder Scrolls and Fallout, item crafting from games like assassins creed and again Fallout 4, and a leveling skill point system close to that of Divinity Original Sin or other RPG's, Far Cry Primal has a lot to offer. So lets break it down into Pros and Cons.
Pros
-Free roam with a wide open area, map markers, and various other tools to go where you want when you want.
-Do what you want. Gather herbs and other crafting materials, upgrade your village, level, do side quests, main quests, tame or hunt beasts or even ride a saber tooth tiger or the mighty mammoth. The range of possibilities to do what you want in the year 10000 bc is far and wide and anythign but straight linier.
-Graphics are top notch. Some of the best out there yet.
-Upgrading the quality of weapon also upgrades its visual look, which is small but nice.
-personal favorite of listening to the bones snap when your pet goes in for teh kill.
-Many more aspects of the game but would be quite a bit of spoiling.
Cons
-Combat can seem repetitive after a bit once you upgrade your weapons, and only the toughest of enemies will challenge you.
-only 1st person camera. Now this isnt necessarily a negative, but you never get to actually look at your character and see them carrying there bow, or the spears, the changes in clothes, etc etc.
-crafting system, although nice and thorough for the time period, does lack some things that could have been nice, such as, you can make a grappling hook, but not tie a rope or vine or the likes to your spear so you can pull in prey or make your own hook holds. This is an example of things in crafting that could be done. Basically it could be expanded upon.
-really graphic. DO NOT PLAY THIS INFRONT OF CHILDREN. there is casual nudity, occasional walking up on couples having sex, and language along with other things that are not suitable for children.
Conclusion
In closing, this is a great game for adults that are looking for a stone age version of fall out or similar games. It has lots of great moments and tons to do.

A mixed bag for GoT fans. On the one hand, the events of the game are deeply enough intertwined with the plot of the TV series mythos that you're bound to miss something in the coming seasons if you don't play it. On the other hand, the amount of retroactive continuity is absurd and very bad for the suspension of disbelief. Not to mention the writing is less than creative, at best.
In fairness, Telltale did a good job of repurposing the GoT narrative toolkit. The plotline follows the various members of House Forrester (a largely unmentioned house in even the book lore in a largely unmentioned stretch of The North) in the months following the Red Wedding, this is all a great setup for plenty of lore-friendly adventure and a few cameos from the big players. Unfortunately, Telltale crossed the line from borrowing the series tapestry to yanking bits wholecloth.
*There's some spoilers from here on, nothing too big, but enough to illustrate my point*
The story starts with the death of the lord of House Forrester just as the political landscape is thrown into chaos by the Red Wedding (pulling a Ned there, eh?). The firstborn of the family also dies at the Red Wedding (pulling a Rob there, eh?). So now the middle child is left to rule the house, but he's inexperienced and not respected as a ruler, especially in such hard times (pulling a Bran there, eh?). The eldest female just so happens to be at the Red Keep and now has to navigate the complex situation surrounding being connected with The North post-rebellion (pulling a Sansa there, eh?). A squire for House Forrester gets himself sent to the wall, has a hard time making friends, eventually makes friends with his tormenters, becomes a ranger, deserts the watch, and gets himself entangled in wildlings, white walkers, wargs, and magic (pulling a Jon Snow there, eh?). Meanwhile overseas, a Forrester exiled for a forbidden love gone awry (Jorah) casts aside his life of semi-renegade-merc-with-a-golden-heart swashbuckling (basically the whole Martell family and the entire damned 4th book) to rally an army to bring back to Westeros, but he gets caught up in freeing the city of Meereen somewhere along the line (Daenarys).
Alright, so the game lifts a lot of it's structure and plot from the main series, but it's still its own monolithic thing, right? Not quite... the plot goes to exhausting lengths to attempt to legitimize itself with extraneous fanservice. That character in King's Landing? A handmaiden and confidant of Lady Margaery who's had secret meetings and schemings with Tyrion, Cersei, and Margaery. That character on The Wall? Instant friends with Jon Snow and made a ranger without really much explanation at all. That character across the Narrow Sea? He finds Drogon, talks personally and at length with Daenarys, plays a large part in the taking of Meereen, and then gets his ♥♥♥♥ing uncle installed on Daenarys' coucil. Most of the cast ends up interacting with, threatening, or getting attacked by Ramsay Snow/Bolton too. None of this was cannon or even remotely hinted at, at all, until now. That's a lot of (largely unnecessary) ret-conning and it shows.
Still suffers from Telltale-syndrome too: decisions often feel pointless when you know it's all going to be tied up into the same eventual outcome anyways. That being said, the game's still well made. It's hard to expect anything less of Telltale and it is all still there. Voice casting is good, plotline is well executed (even if not very original), and it still manages to yank at the heart strings. Overall, worth it if you like GoT, as long as you have some (a lot) of tolerance for the liberties Telltale took

Beyond Eyes is a pretty little short game about a blind girl in the search for her friend, the cat named Nani. The artsyle is just lovely and I absolutely love how the developers have visualized how blind Rae sees the world. Such cleaver details they put it that put a smile on my face.
It is a simple game and it doesn't portray itself as otherwise. Many people comment on Rae's walking pace and that the game is just too slow. I can see how all of that is annoying, but this is not an action game and nor does it say that it is. This game is all about envisioning how a blind person might perceive the world and tries to simulate how it might be interacting as a blind person with the real world. Had this been a in an action game however, of course it would have bothered me quite a bit. I mean, I don't intentionally pick up tons of heavy items in Skyrim just so I can walk slowly. No, I'd rather drop that super awesome sword I just found just so I'll be able to run fast again and explore more.
This slow walk works because this is short game. Had this been 30+ hour game however, I'm not gonna lie, it would have driven me NUTS. It didn't bother me when I was discovering new roads because believe me, I wouldn’t go fast if I didn't see what I was walking into next either. But it did kind of bother me when I was backtracking roads I've already gone through. If anything, I would have liked to see Rae speed up a bit when backtracking roads she has already traversed. Kind of to simulate that she is confident in knowing the explored surroundings. But I'd understand if the developers wouldn't want to do that and I do trust them that they have playtested her speed enough times for it to be now as it is intended to be.
All in all, lovely little game with a moving story and a beautiful artstyle.

This game is INCREDABLY underrated. All I can really say about this game without going into a paragraph is that it's fun, intense, and HARD (Even on EASY). Give it a chance like I did, it may suprise you.

The game is based directly on the HBO TV-show. So the story canon is taken from there. You don't get to play as characters from the show, but instead as five different members of the House Forrester. You get to interact with some of the show's cast. For example Cersei and Tyrion, all the familiar characters are modeled and voiced by the real actors. The voice acting is ofcourse great by actors in the show, but everyone else does their job well too. Character models look decent, but there is plenty of clunky animation and blurry backgrounds. They were going after watercolored look, but didn't quite pull it off.
Just like earlier Telltale games, it's heavy on narrative and light on gameplay. You get to make choices in dialogue quite often, but rarely it seemed to have long lasting effects. Story does justice to the tv-show by being brutal, dark and full of surprises. Combat is done by quick time events and doesn't really bring anything new or refreshing to the table.
If you are fan of the show (and books) or a fan of telltale games, you might want to give the game a chance. Im fan of both, so I got enjoyment out of it. The story takes place at the end of 3rd season in the show, so there will be some spoilers. All stories in the game won't fully conclude in this first season. Second season for the game is already confirmed.

I've played RTS for a good part of my life, having played titles such as StarCraft and Supreme Commander, and Grey Goo is easily among my favorites. (If not my favorite at the moment)
While the game isn't without it's issues, it's polished in all reasonable extents. The macro can be a bit more intensive for the Goo and Shroud factions, but it's also more simple, for lack of tech attachments being involved. Beta and Humans, while having tech attachments to account for, have incredibly easy macro, with the ability to auto queue factories. (A bonus for humans is that you can teleport tech attachments, to rearrange your tech to make different units types you might need)
Outside of positioning, and some splitting, not alot of micro is required to play well, but there are cases individual unit control can make a big difference. (Largely in the early game, and especially races such as Goo, since they rely largely on the terrain to gain advantage, as well as their units regeneration) Manually targeting with artillary (Using Alt+Right click) can also make a world of difference, and isn't terribly difficult by any means. Something of note, is that having good reaction time and speed is a huge benefit, but isn't all there is to it.
Overall, I believe Grey Goo is a wonderful game, that I have been playing on and off for about a year now, and have become fairly skilled in at least a few of the races. If you have a desire to learn how to play, in a competitive sense, I am fully willing to help you learn what you need to know to at least get decent.

In a word - frustrating
Positive: Grey Goo is beautiful to look at, they clearly took their time to make both gameplay and cut scenes look incredible.
Negative: The gameplay itself is stressful.  The unit pathing and collision detection made me want to shout as my army marched repeatedly in the opposite direction I had just ordered it.  Resource gathering requires constant baby sitting. There is an incredible amount of micromanagement needed to play any of the three factions, but ESPECIALLY the Goo faction, which was very disappointing as I was most excited to play as the menacing Goo.  There is no "exit game" option from the mission menu, you must quit the mission, then go through 3 separate menus individually to get back to the home screen to close the game.  There are numerous bugs - unable to load or save if a character is talking, unable to click on mini-map any longer after alt-tabbing, graphical errors if you don't start a mission quickly enough after it finishes loading.
I managed to play the game the entire game, but on numerous instances I nearly uninstalled it out of frustration.  They tried to do something unique in the RTS genre, but ended up creating a micromanagement mess where any potential fun is overshadowed by frustrating game mechanics, poor UI, and bugs.

I do recommend this to anyone who has not played chess as it will not let you move a piece into a place it cannot go. You can also click a button and learn the history of chess. The interface is easy to navigate. Bumblebee did a nice job at making sure this can be played by as many people as possible. This makes a great addition to the chess games you already have or the perfect chess game to learn how to play. Like math, chess is a universal language. This can help you speak that language fluently. As of this review, I have not played any of the other Saints Row games. I came into this expecting a cool sci-fi game where I get to fly around and blow crap up. I was not disappointed. I felt that the game got a bit repetitive after 10 hours or so, but nothing ever stopped the game from being a blast. Your powers are awesome, the guns are good (the dubstep gun! Yes!!!) and running up the buildings and gliding around is just endlessly satisfying. This is a really cool game.
Oh, and the mini games. The mini game where you need to hurt yourself as much as possible in a few minutes is one of the most fun things ever. Those are possibly my favorite parts of the game.
If I have one critique, it's that there is no point in the vehicle customization aspect of the game, since after about 5 hours of gameplay, you'll be able to run faster than any vehicle and have infinite stamina. Driving around in those awesome police cars was sweet for the first few hours, but after you can run twice as fast as them and never get tired... I didn't see the point.
Also, the DLC's for this game - How the Saints Save Christmas and Enter the Dominatrix - were very short. The two together will be done in about an hour and a half, maybe two hours. They're both really good, but don't expect them to add more than one sitting of gameplay combined.
One piece of advice: fully upgrade the dubstep gun asap. Just do it. You want the fully upgraded dubstep gun.
Also, get the Game of the Century edition. The extra content is worth the extra money during a sale.

TL;DR I wish there was an "okay" button, because that's what 3D Chess is. Just okay. It doesn't stand out or offer much in comparison to other chess games.
As said, the visuals are great, but there's not much variety with only 4 environments.
Each environment has no music, only a sound effect which loops (Volcano-bubbling lava, Ancient Rome?- fire crackling, and Graveyard-typical spooky sounds). I was expecting the game to have some great music, hence the trailer, but there's no music at all in the game. The sound effects are stock and get so repetitive that I end up just muting it.
Gameplay is just like classic chess, and works well. You can play against the computer or another player on the same screen. Computer has 3 difficulties-easy, normal, and hard. There are also 2 other game modes- puzzles, which you have a limited amount of moves to complete 1 of 3 objectives (checking opponent's kind, avoiding check, and checkmating opponent's king), and chaos mode, where the computer plays randomly. Chaos mode is good for beginners to practice chess without repercussions.
What really irks me though is no online compatibilty. You can't play against another person, unless they're in the same room, but in that case, you may as well just play with an actual chess set.
Point being, there are other chess games on Steam that have more features and online gameplay. Only get this if you want to practice or play against the computer.

TLDR Version: Game had potential, but is extremely buggy and P2W.
This is a game that had a lot of potential, but it is extremely buggy and it took a hard turn into Pay to Win territory. The PvE combat is fun, but that is about where the good stops. There is a real money store in game where players can purchase items that give them a powerful advantage over those who choose not to spend large sums of money. Even the $30 USD costumes in the store impart ingame benefits.
Levels are practically meaningless in this game. The main way to get stronger in the game is to get better gear through enchanting or buying better items on the auction house. However this being a Korean MMO, enchanting is incredibly difficult and expensive. There is a very small chance of success when enchanting gear past the beginning levels and everytime you fail the maximum durability of your item is reduced by 5% and, for the higher levels, there is a chance of the item deleveling or being destroyed outright. To restore the lost durability you need to spend real money or vast sums of ingame money.
If you rather not mess with the ingame enchanting system and just buy enchanted gear from the auction house, good luck. Higher level gear isn't typically available on the marketplace and when it finally pops up everyone who is looking for it receives a notification. If you didn't pay the $12 USD for an item to allow you to access the marketplace from anywhere in the zone, you will need to rush over to the marketplace and hope that you have enough of your money stored at that specific location. The auction house does not work like in any other MMO. When you place "bids" on an item, you are just entering yourself for a chance to purchase the item. If you win that chance, you will still need to hit the buy button faster than every other player who also won that same chance. Even if you are trying to purchase an item where there are 10s of thousands available on the auction house, it is still a huge pain. You are only allowed buy the absolute cheapest item so if someone sets the price one silver lower than all the other listings, then every single person in the game trying to buy that item will only be able to bid on that single entry and will have to wait for it to sell to have access to any of the other items for sale.
Selling on the marketplace isn't quite as bad as buying. Every item has a minimum and maximum value you can list it at, so the price for items is fairly stable. There is a ~35% tax on every item you sell, but you can pay real money every week/month to get a reduced fee. Prospective buyers can also set a preorder for items and when an item is listed for sale there is a random chance it will be available to a random preorder buyer or go to public market. If the preorder price is set higher than the maximum price you can list for then the full amount will be taken from the buyer, but the seller will only receive up to the max price with the rest of the money being deleted.
In PvE combat you are generally fighting vast swathes of mobs that die very quickly and respawn very quickly. This leaves you very little time to loot. Instead, players are expected to buy pets from the real money shop for $9-$11 each that will automatically loot for you. As pets level up they will loot faster and you can have up to 4 pets out at a time. If you are killing very quickly, then 4 max level tier 1 pets still can't keep up with all the loot. To improve the looting you can combine two pets for a CHANCE to receive a tier 2 pet. This can be done again with two tier 2 pets for a small chance at a tier 3 pet. If it fails then you can end up with a pet of the same or possibly even a lower tier wasting all the real money spent on them.
Along with the looting, you have a limited carrying capacity and number of inventory slots. Both of which can be increased using real money in the store.
One of the absolute worst systems in the game is the PvP system. It is poorly designed, poorly balanced and you don't have the option to opt out of it. At level 50 every character can be attacked almost anywhere in the world by other players. In almost all cases that I've seen, the fights are no where near even matches. It is typically dominated by people who have spent large amounts of real money or ingame money to get overpowering gear and you have no chance of beating them, even 5-1, if you aren't similarly geared. A caveat to that is even if you are equally geared, there are some classes that are completely out of balanced and will destroy people who don't play one of the 3 or 4 meta classes.
There is a flagging system that is meant to prevent griefing, but if anything it just encourages it. When you kill an innocent person you lose karma and if your karma number goes negative you turn red and have terrible penalties for dying, such as gear breaking or deleveling. You can gain karma back by killing monsters and you can use the Pay2Win store to buy consumables that increase your karma gains. While you are red you can be attacked by other players freely and if you defend yourself, you still lose karma and sink further into the hole.
A typical PvP encounter in this game is as followes:
You show up at a PvE grind spot and use your daily 1 hour exp buff and start grinding. Another player will show up and be upset that you are killing "their" mobs and they will attack you. In nearly every PvP encounter I have had, the other player was massively overgeared and even if I was an equal or higher level, my strongest attacks would barely scratch them and their hits would devastate me. There was no skill involved in this kind of pvp. Even if you successfully dodge and block their attacks, you can't chip away their health because they can just pop a skill or consumable and heal to full.
I tried group and guild pvp and it was a joke as well. Enemies would bring healers with them that were either under level 50 so they couldn't be killed, or that just wouldn't attack so if you hit them first you would lose karma if they died. Healing other players in PvP does not flag you so they can sit back and heal with impunity. If you decide to take the karma hit to get the healer out of the fight, they will just respawn nearby and run right back up.
The quests in this game are some of the worst I've seen in any modern MMO. They are all poorly written and designed. The normal MMO go to this place and kill x number of things is a blessing when you get them compared to some of the others. The main quest line isn't quite as bad as some of the others in game, but it is something like 190 quests for the first part, is very repetitive, and if you follow along with it you'll very quickly be overleveled for what it is throwing at you. Other quests are just plain stupid. For example there are dozens of quests where you will walk 5 feet away from the quest giver to inspect an object like a fountain or wagon. This involves interacting with the object, then positioning your camera at the exact angle and distance from the object that a developer arbitrarily decided was good enough. That is the entire quest.
All of these complaints imply you can actually get in the game and play it though. There are tons and tons of bugs that make the game literally unplayable. For example anytime I log in there is a 5-15 minute delay before I take any actions and about 80% of the time I will just be disconnected from the game which forces it to close back to desktop. This isn't an isolated incident and happens to just about everyone in my 90+ member guild. Additionally there are numerous desync bugs where you can run around and fight npcs, but you can't open menus, chat, or interact with npcs or objects. Relogging might fix it, but there is a good chance that you'll just be disconnected repeatedly after logging back in.
The developers have no interest in fixing this game. Instead they will try to milk the playerbase for every penny they can.

Poker Night at the Inventory is a simple game where all you have to do is play Poker (Specifically Texas Hold-'Em) against four other NPC characters from different forms of media, ranging from online comic books, to multiplayer video games. They are Tycho from the online comic-book series "Penny Arcade", The Heavy Weapons Guy from the multiplayer FPS "Team Fortress 2", Max from the gaming series "Sam & Max", and Strong Bad from the Homestar Runner web series: "Strong Bad's Cool Game for Attractive People". The object is basically just to win the pot, like in normal Poker. However, sometimes the NPCs can buy in with items that can be used in the game "Team Fortress 2", and if you defeat the character who bought in with a weapon (A.K.A. knock them out), you get that item. There are four items, one for each character. They are the Iron Kurtain Mini-Gun, which comes from The Heavy, the Lugermorph Pistol, from Max, the Enthusiast's Time Piece, an invisible watch from Tycho, and The Dangeresque Too? Shades, a cosmetic item for the "Team Fortress 2" class Demoman, from Strong Bad. If you don't know how to play poker whatsoever, do not worry! The game very clearly explains in detail how to play Texas Hold-'Em RIGHT before you play.

I bought this game because I remember hearing some of the folks on The Co-Optional Podcast talk about how cute, inspiring and [insert compliments because it's a game about someone who disabled], etc... this game is.
Well. That was a mistake.
I am a fan of walking simulators, I enjoy almost all of them, but this one just isn't good.
It is good on the surface until you realize there is nothing new to the game after playing for 10 minutes.
The first 10-15 minutes it was kinda good, it was new, it is certainly a unique and original game.
The first minutes I spent enjoying the nice concept, the beautiful colours and other miscellaneous things I picked up on, for example if you hit a wall and start walking a-long side the wall, she, the person you play as, starts tracing the wall with one of her hands.
Just small things like that.
Once I had played for a bit and got the base concept of the game in my head I started waiting for something to happen as I was looking for this cat until I realized... this is it?
Just... walking and getting interrupted every 20 seconds because this girl is very unique and has a small panic attack every time she hears a bird or a bell in the distance?
There's more or less no story, nothing to make you care, nothing to make you attached, nothing that makes you hope to find the cat.
No dialogue, lack of of sounds.
There are a bunch of sounds until you realize that it's just the same few sounds playing on repeat.
You walk extremely slow, and yes... I get that she's blind, I get that a blind person won't really want to run around, but this is a game; you have to keep the player interested.
Walking at the speed of a snail and getting interrupted every 20 seconds and listening to the same sounds on repeat over and over and over is not a good experience, it is dull, boring and makes you long and hope and wishfully anticipate something new to happen, but that anticipated bit of something new never comes.
In conclusion...
Beyond Eyes is something that looks great on the surface, it looks beautiful, it looks like it has a great story behind it and looks like something that might make you feel emotional and last but certainly not least it looks like something new, something unique and original.
Then you play it and realize it is indeed an original game but contains nothing to carry it forward, nothing that makes you feel like this is worth it.
It is dull, boring, lacking in dialogue, soundtrack and story.

I'm rather unsure how to recommend this game. On the one hand, it matches the Game of Thrones pattern of characters dying before their arcs complete to satisfaction and of plot threads being likewise murdered before they have a chance to resolve the audience's interest in them properly. How much you dislike this here will probably be similar to how much you dislike it in Game of Thorones (the book or the show). For my part, I find it very frustrating; I'm well accustomed to books where characters I care about are treated harshly or unfairly. Where surprises occur, where characters I care about suffer harm. What I dislike more substantially is when my attention and investment and interest feels like it is wasted ... not because my favorite characters died but because the story being told about them often ends as abrubtly as their life or trails off into the distance akwardly. It is the lack of resolution, the lack of narrative focus, that frustrates me. Though, again, this seems to suit many people just fine; this is a very popular series in other mediums.
Beyond that ... normally I'm quite comfortable accepting Tell Tale's illusion of choice; I don't play these games in the belief that I can "change the story" and I don't expect Tell Tale to deliver the expereicne of a "true" branching narrative while also engaging me with a choreent authored story for a reasonable price. I expect any choisces to be more about flavor and interactive investment than actually "chaning" the path of the story. In Wolf Among Us, Walking Dead and Tales from the Borderlands (the lattermost especially) I found this plenty satisfying. Here, the authored story didn't hang together quite well enough and the illusion of choice, consequence and effect was SO fragile and transparent that even though I found myself agreeing with the familiar criticism of these types of games with respect to Game of Thrones--why am I playing this as a *game* in the first place? Why isn't it just a movie? And, unlike others I listed, I feel that it doesn't function very well at all as that "just a movie."
I'm not sure exactly why I feel that familiar reaction in response to this game, whereas I don't in response to other games in this genre and other Telltale games in particular. I didn't enjoy the experience enough to really dig into it with more useful analysis, so I'm left with a somewhat vague understanding of why I didn't like it.

Do you like walking simulators and sugar?  This is a game for people who like walking simulators and sugar.  It is an adorable story of a blind girl searching for her lost cat, that even I had to take a break from due to the metaphorical toothache.  It's a very wholesome and atmospheric experience, which I highly recommend if you want a quiet evening in the countryside that makes you feel things in a good way.
On the technical side, the sound design is amazing and the graphics are a perfect fit.  There were times I was distracted from the atmosphere thinking of the work it must have taken to create some of the effects.  I've done some programming in Unity back in college, and making the world appear around your character like that is NOT easy, particularly to make it look so effortless.  Many games try to portray blindness in a visual medium, and short of wireframes this feels like a very good implementation.  When you can't keep track of your surroundings as well in the rain it's frustrating, which may give the player a tiny bit of insight into what living with that is like.  You might also want a run mechanic due to the slow-pace, until you realize that you really
be running given how dangerous that'd be.
A lot of love was put into this game, and it shows.

The best designed faction by far are the Betas, their base building mechanics are the most profound and refined, starting with the ability to create different build layouts from one central hub, with it’s like a small puzzle and give to a lot of building variety and flexibility, and tis super weapon its by far the most useful on the whole game.

Too much goo (Ooo err misssus.)
Some general features:
-The game looks great, its really polished in its presentation, and the voice acting is top notch.
-Sound also gets the job done, even if its not hugely memorable with its theme.
-There are a bunch of unique mechanics, and design for the different species. Sadly this doesnt feel nearly as fresh as I think it could have, this could be down to poor mission design, or the annoyances that Ill go in to later robbing it of its sheen.
-I found the AI goo was amazing. It would keep probing my defences, skirting round my base, it didnt even attack me to begin with as if it was genuinely just curious. Then it would rapidly grow in force and keep adjusting where it targeted to get around whatever I built. Unfortunately it has its stupid moments later in the game, when the AI would just ignore bases because it couldnt seem to work out if Goo would be there. It could have left scouts at each location and wiped me out with ease, but never did. That kind of gives you the feeling its letting you win rather than giving a satisfying victory.
As for the gameplay:
Going through as the Beta I was having a lot of fun. Im not a great RTS player and Id get trounced once or twice, but be able to work out some new way of turtling (Something they are great at.) so I could breath and build an army, or use the terrain etc. That said their campaign ends all too quickly and you move on.
Humans, were bafflingly easier to use, so the difficuly curve seemed to go awry somewhat. They have teleportation technology that can move buildings around. Though, Its unfortunately a bit dull as I tended to stick to a particular strategy and you rarely really _needed_ to shift addons and such around. Teleporting your vehicles was fun, but made things rather easy as the AI didnt seem to cope all that well with it. Either way, all of this wraps up pretty fas as well.
Then the goo. At first its all new and interesting, lots of experimenting to do and its wildly different to the other two species, but after two or three levels the basics sink in and... its not actually that fun. At least at my skill level.
They can duplicate and spread rapidly, which is thematic but it leads to a situation where you spend ages getting everything going, get caught out by the enemy and smashed back down, then start all over again.
Several levels Id be crushed and grow, crushed and grow, over and over each time getting a little more powerful until I overwhelmed them. Again, quite thematic, but _really_ tedious. It gets so much worse when the bulk of the missions are Goo ones. I longed to play the Beta again.
and this all brings me to the miserable ending and possibly the biggest waste of game mechanics and design for a single player game Ive ever seen. The Shroud.
In the campaign the Shroud are practically non-existant, and it turns out that damn near everything has been building up to their reveal. (That shouldnt be much of a spoiler, its clear there are 4 species in the game.) It seems that Grey Goo was all about selling the multiplayer, and for people in to that it might be another story, but for me it was a huge let down to find out all that I did was leading basically nowhere.
Thats compounded by the fact that taking the Shroud for a spin turned out that they are an amazing species! They are really unique, with strange mechanics, colourful and odd design, even their structure building is very different, not only to the other species in the game but to RTSs in general. Why wasnt this a major species in the campaign!? Its a criminal waste of some fantastic design.
So the game _scrapes_ through with a recommend. Itd be a neutral if the option was available and Id definitely recommend waiting for a good sale on it. Large chunks of the game werent utilised nearly well enough, and larger chunks of the game got really grating, but there is enough thats unique and polished, and enough to keep you entertained for hours. (Even if its not as fun as it really should be.)

I do recommend this game BUT not at full price.
Pros:
-Hunting and stealth is more fun than ever.
-Beautiful world to explore with lots of collectibles and such to make you see everything.
-Tame beasts that each have special abilities (jaguars can sneak attack without alerting nearby enemies). Ride some of your tamed beasts or hitch onto a wild young mammoth.  Yes, you can do mounted combat.  You can use all your weapons while mounted and your beasts will even attack as well.
-Day and night. Packs of wolves hunting at night.  You can capture an outpost at night and eliminate your enemies while they're sleeping.
-Plenty of side missions and random events.
-Skinning and harvesting have a short animation so its quick.
-Primitive weapons and crafting!  I put these two together because for every weapon you have, you build.  Harvest materials from all over the map to build and upgrade and replenish your stock of them.
-Combat with primitive weapons is really fun. You carry every weapon in the game with you. No more weapon shops where you swap loadouts.  You can do takedowns with different weapons for different kill animations.  Ignite your weapons and arrows for deadly and interesting action (sabertooth will drop and roll when on fire).
-Fire good! Fire bad! It's so useful and deadly in this game. I remember one mission where i had to burn enemy crops; I took some high ground and kept shooting in fire arrows which burned up the entire farm and most of the enemies in it. The fire spread so much that I started to take damage from it. Good times.
-Some of your beasts do takedown/kill animations when you take them hunting!
Theres some more good things I can say about this game but these are just some highlights. Now for the (not so) bad...
Cons:
-Short story. It's not rich but it's not bad either. I enjoyed the language and the historical setting. But it was way too short that it made me regret paying a full price when I've paid way less for games I haven't even beaten yet. It should have had more story missions aside from the main plot.  If I had at least 3 or 4 more story missions with Urki, I'd cry happiness.
-No multiplayer. Games are just so much more fun when you can have a buddy join in.
-No challenge for achievements.
Even though I beat the story in a fraction of the time I played this game, I enjoyed it very much. I like the far cry games and Primal is easily my favorite of them all. The gameplay keeps me glued to it and makes me want to get 100% completion. I'd start a new game after too.
You should get this game. It's fun. But buy it at a cheaper price.

I'm still early in so far, but I can say if you are interested in JRPGs with cute characters and light hearted stories with VN style presentation you may enjoy this game. There is a big grind to collecting items however, so be advised of that.
-Pros-
*Combat system is fun, but not overly complicated
*Cute colorful characters and environments to brighten up your day
*Has some decent humor in it, so even if it's not LOL funny, there will be lots of smiles and grins (Nepgear is not the comedian that Neptune was, but she is easy to like because she is gentle and kind-hearted.)
*Sharper, higher resolution assets compared to Re:1 in many cases (Menu, in game rendering, and much of the art looks good on 1080p, where Re:1 had lots of art that was obviously scaled up to 1080p making it look soft and blurry)
*Old familiar environments have been revamped with different layouts to freshen up your grind
*While some familiar enemies return, there are new ones as well and the variety seems a tad better than Re:1
*Lots of reasons to replay after you clear because its just not possible to unlock most things on the first pass, and there are multiple endings to unlock
-Cons-
*Not all art was upgraded for 1080p, the 2D character graphics used during VN sequences are noticeably upscaled, clashing with the high resolution backdrops and interface
*Story isn't quite as interesting, feels more like a side story (not a deal breaker really)
-DLC Tips-
If you use Nepgears DLC weapons, particularly the strongest one, you will 1 hit bosses for several levels. Nepgear will 1 hit kill bosses for 40k damage when you are level 2 or 3, she will do about 40x the damage of other party members the same level.  So either don't equip them early on, or just chalk it off to her being Neptune's sister who of course is an over the top badass.
The DLC is optional, can be enabled or disabled at any time. So if you hear complaints about OP items or the controversial LVLUP plan, remember you can reserve those for when you think they fit your style. With 999 levels available(assuming you have the DLC), having something to speed that up isn't a bad thing at all.
You will be playing this for multiple playthroughs if you want to really unlock stuff. There are hundreds if not thousands of plans to unlock to access more characters, dungeons, enemies, battles and items. So I would keep this in mind.
-Performance- Tested on with Intel HD Graphics 4600 and Nvidia GTX 760 @ 1080p
*Runs @ 60fps mostly with GTX760 There are some frame drops into the 40s and a brief fps drop once you execute a guard break. Nothing game breaking and honestly easy to ignore.(Re;1 dropped to 30fps at the start of battles, and would then climb back up. This strange quirk is gone)
*Runs well enough on Intel HD Graphics 4600* So if you have a dedicated card you should have no issues
*25-30fps battles, 15fps victory poses (lots of camera movement), 40-50 fps for EXE Moves

This only gets a thumbs up because I'm still not sure where I stand on this rainbow-colored trainwreck.
Graphically & visually, aside from some hiccups (character walking speeds not matching terrain movement, namely), it's rock solid. The character models are fairly good, though design-wise I'm not terribly thrilled. Most importantly, it runs at a bedrock-solid 60FPS with very few instances of slowdown. Good on you, Idea Factory!, for that.
In terms of gameplay, things start to slip. The combat is simple enough, and the fights are usually over pretty quick unless you're fighting a boss. Unfortunately, that's either because your side smashes the enemies in a single round, or they pound you into dust. As well, while it works, there's nothing new or special about the battle system; you attack enemies, build up a gauge, and then unleash all holy hell upon them. Basic stuff for most every JRPG since Final Fantasy 7 made that the bog standard, really. There's status effects too, but those are pretty much pointless in the face of just smashing everything.
The story is where things get... weird. Beyond even "WTF Japan". I have little patience for dumb-as-a-rock characters, so having a cast full of them is an "experience". But something about it just keeps me glued, like watching a ten-car pile-up on the highway as it happens. Maybe my interest is due to some sort of morbid facination, because it certainly isn't helped by the terrible puns and rerun-them-until-they're-flat recurring "jokes". I feel like a befuddled scientist examining a specimine and musing "Well that shouldn't happen". I know with absolute certainty that I'm not the person this was made for, yet here I am...
Oh, and weirdly scynchronized boob-flopping abounds. In shots that are otherwise stills, as well as in combat. But they're so artificial that it's almost repulsive. Maybe that's part of it?
There are extras, of course: a full NG+ mode which lets you carry over levels and whatnot; all sorts of modifiers to make combat easier/harder, add new items/enemies, and so on; and a host of side-quests to perform -- most of which are of the "get/kill 'x' amount of items/enemies" variety. Other than the modifiers, though, there's little reason to repeat the game, as with most RPGs the story is dead-set linear and there are no multiple endings. I don't even think there's optional end-game/post-end-game/NG+ dungeons either, which is sort of disappointing.
Oh, and if you want the full game, you have to get the DLC. Of course. At least its better than the original version, where the DLC was the only way you could get the ability to find the "hidden" item in every map... (I actually had to research that!)
Overall, I don't *hate* HdNRB, but it's the sort of thing I'll probably shut off, uninstall, and forget about once I'm done with it. Not horrible (unless we're talking about the difficulty balance), but not exactly a shining example of the genre either. I'm still trying to decide whether I need a shower or a psychiatrist after inexplicably playing for the last 5 hours straight. I guess there must be *something* good about it, or I wouldn't be here typing this up.

Beyond Eyes is a game about a blind girl trying to find her cat. You might think there’s more to it than that, but there is not – this game is a walking simulator, and perhaps the least fun one I’ve ever played.
The core aesthetic is an interesting idea at first blush – your character is blind, so you can only see things very close to you, or things which are somewhat noisy from a distance. This latter mechanic, unfortunately, is mostly pointless – only a couple times in the game does it really give you much of a target.
So, mostly, you’re wandering around blind, trying to find your way through the levels. There’s nothing in the levels which threatens you, just a few extremely simple “bring object A to location B” “puzzles”. Indeed, there aren’t even very many of these – perhaps three in the entire game.
Given it takes several hours to beat this game, you might wonder what you do spend it doing. Do you spend it on story?
Not really; there’s no comprehensible dialogue, only three characters (you, the cat, and a random person you encounter once and help get their ball back). Mostly, the game is just walking around levels and trying to get to the end of them.
And I do mean walking – the character you control walks around very slowly, and there’s no means of going any faster. As such, getting through the levels is very tedious.
There’s a handful of achievements for doing various things in the game, but most of these are basically just “interact with some environmental object”. Yay. Worse, you must stand very close to the environmental object to interact with them, and one of the achievements is simply walking over a few patches of nondescript ground indistinguishable from everything else. What could be more fun than that?
The story, such as it is, is extremely weak and threadbare – the lack of dialogue robs it of any real characterization, and the fact of the matter is that the core of the story is pretty boring. Do I really care about this girl finding her cat? No, because I’m not really given any strong reason to care about the girl in the first place. Lack of characterization means lack of investment, and the two dozen or so story lines in the entire multiple hour long game does not endear it to me.
There is really nothing in this game to make you want to play it. The core aesthetic is a vaguely neat idea, but that’s it – and, quite frankly, it quickly becomes obvious as you play the game just how tedious it really is.

Telltale follows in the footsteps of HBO's Game of Thrones and the book series that inspired it. Not just in terms of theme and fateful moments, almost a trope of their own at this point, but also by stringing you along for as long as possible seemingly without ever reaching a conclusion. It's no surprise then that Telltale is set to release a second season of its Game of Thrones episodic game.
There is, of course, something to be said for your characters being victims in a world of more powerful and influential figures and authorities. That is fine, up to a point, but it stops being interesting once you reach Idiot Plot levels of restrictions on your actions. As Roger Ebert explained, an Idiot Plot 'is any plot that would be resolved in five minutes if everyone in the story were not an idiot'. Far too often the game offers up dumb choices that are all bad ideas under the circumstances - or leaves out the option of taking the kind of action that would resolve the situation in the character’s favour. Because the game offers no actual gameplay, its dialogue options cannot offer you the means by which to succeed outside of the narrow pre-set path defined by Telltale. Doing so would mean the conflict Telltale has sketched out would never come to pass, and that has to be prevented - even if it means turning your characters into what might well be the least clever House of Westeros. It's often hilarious because the Forresters have mastered the art of failing, but also frustrating and ultimately not very rewarding.
The graphics are limited, but more crucial in a game like this is that the facial expressions Telltale has managed to create lag far behind what LA Noire was able to accomplish years ago, making the conversations that are the game's only meaningful content unconvincing.
Not recommended.

Although I have almost no hours on this game, I can tell some few things I have noticed while playing. Black Desert Online is   pay to play action mmorpg game. The game is very noob friendly. In the start it asks if you want to have a guide or no guide. With the auto run and auto quest running, quests are made easy. I made a new character and got to level 20 in about an hour or so. With each level becoming harder to reach. I can already tell that it will be very grindy once you reach higher levels. The pvp aspect of the game is probably the only reason why most players get the game. It gives me a Blade and Soul vibe. Skills can be casted by keyboard and mouse combinations or using the numberkeys on the top of the keyboard. The graphics are actually amazing considering that the game was released a while ago. With high optimization if you have a bad pc or laptop, you might be able to play on low settings with 30 ish fps if you are okay with that. You start to learn very quickly and get used to the controls. Like I said I only have 3 or so hours so I don't know much. But for a veteran in some other popular mmorpg's I have some experience. Grinding out places in this game is almost not worth it if you are not in the end game. If you level up once or twice in an area, the next quest bonus will feel like nothing. There are a lot of other stuff that I haven't mentioned yet. I like how there is housing in this game, making it feel more unique then other grind and pvp games. I can also see that pve players won't be left alone. Now there are a few things wrong with this game. The auto run or auto quest running is a little bad, but lets be honest if you are using it then you should be able to move around objects if you get stuck. The controls are easy to learn, but they give you too much at a time. So you find yourself trying to see what does what. Or just keyboard smashing. The story is a little bland. But that is just what you expect from a mmorpg. This story feels a little more unique than others though. The start also feels very slow and you find yourself running from city to city doing quests that you haven't done yet. The last con that might be a downfall for most players, is the gender locked classes. I don't really care about that one. Wrapping it up, I do reccomend this game to anyone. With its simple gui and user friendly introduction, there is no way you can hate it. Im just a casual gamer and this game fits me.
