I'm really torn about this game.
On one hand you have a love letter to JRPGs of old. The development team designed characters and battle system that are inspired by Chrono Trigger series. The music is charming but none of the tunes stuck with me, these are not pieces you will be humming in the shower.
My biggest gripe with this game is the lack of polish. There are tons of game breaking bugs in the game. Put a monster to sleep to capture them. Game crashes. Try to record footage and exit the game. Game crashes. Fight a trivial monster after a boss fight in a specific location. Game crashes.
Then there are the minor bugs like walking through walls and getting stuck. Meeting goals for achievements that don't actually unlock the achievement. Bugs happen but what's frustrating is that the developers don't care! Look at the discussion board on Steam, a few bugs are listed with no comments from Muteki! I emailed their support email with a link to a private video of the steps to take to break the game and they never looked at the video (the view count never went up).
There's a bug where your cursor gets stuck in your menu and there's no way to get out. There's also a distinctive lack of polish in the menus. There's no way to scroll down by page and instead you must go down item per item. This gets very tedious at the end of the game when you've accumulated a ton of items! It's even worse when you go to equip something, why is it that when I go to equip a chest piece that it doesn't put me in the chest piece items and instead in the "all" category?
Why can't I reorganize my spells? The low level spells are useless at the end of the game so in each turn I have to scroll down passed all the useless spells to the bottom of my skill list (remember, no scroll by page only item per item). This makes each battle takes a lot longer than they should!
There's also questionable design decisions like a heavy reliance on RNGesus. You miss ALL THE TIME. Most modern role playing games seem to be moving away from this gimmick but Muteki seems to stick to old design patterns.
I want Muteki to succeed and I want more indie JRPGs like Dragon Fantasy but I cannot recommend this game unless you're starved for an old school RPG. I will play/buy the next chapter (as I said, I want more of these kinds of games) but I hope Muteki gets their act together.

First of all: I bought this game mainly for playing it in coop mode. In reminescence of the old days with Diablo 2 we chose this game and we certainly weren't disappointed.
The whole atmosphere is really dark, somehow you cant really believe that everything is going to be okay someday. At some points I had to stop and wanted to enjoy a flower or something beautiful because this game only gives you darkness (the music supports that).
The most outstanding feature in my opinion is the shere amount of possibilities to build your character. 6 classes from which you can choose two and freely combine the abilities. Plus the devotion system which you are simply overwhelmed by (might be seen as a contra). And you have no restrictions within the classes, there is no classical ranged combat class or a typical tank/berserker/whatever.
Unfortunately you cant always see in detail the love that was put into the monster design. You are confronted with masses of enemies and dont have the time to really look at the bosses which is kind of sad when you check the FB-page of Grim Dawn and see all the neat monster art.
The aspect with the consequences of your choices isn't really dominant. We often talk to people with quests and after a while we notice that we maybe have spoken to them in an earlier stage. Probably made some decisions but we cant remember because the NPCs arent memorable. They are somewhat interchangable and dont stick to you.
Overall:
+ great game, awesome atmosphere, gigantic character build, satisfying perks and abilities, cool concept art
- unremarkable NPCs, a little bit to few weapon designs
Recommended.

A decent game, would give a more neutral recommendation if that were possible.
In the Telltale series, you are thrust into the world of the Forresters, a house greatly shaken after the events of the Red wedding. This house (as far as i know) is not canon, so the series of events within the game are not even legitimate within the world of Ice and Fire.
Positives:
Portrays the affects of the Red Wedding on a minor house, giving a bit more depth to the George R.R. Martin world
Most of the Gameplay is quite simple, though this can also be seen as being negative
Entertaining plot throughout the game
Negatives:
The choices you make are quite limited, and often don't affect the game at all
The writers tried to make a lot of shocking deaths to emulate the TV show, but in my opinion went a bit too verboard and just seemed to want to create as much shock value as possible
A couple of the Charecters you make choices for are extemely annoying, to the point were instead of wanting the character to stay alive, you end up willingly helping them meet their demise (for me this was Ethan)
A lot of the choices you are given are the exact same as their counterparts, just rewritten differently
Not all possible choices are reflected in the dialouge choice list, and I found myself wishing I could have said what I wanted, and that often would have saved lives
All up, this is a good game if you're heavily invested in the ASOIAF lore, but otherwise I'd just give it a miss

The game itself has great depth. Unique class designs with mix and match options and a devotion system much like PoE. Gear drops that remind me of Borderlands. Enemy design that reminds me of Diablo. The Crucible DLC is not at all required, but really helps. It's like doing a Greater Rift Trial at any level that has currency and gear as a reward. The gear isn't super busted early, but I will wait to see how it is late game. As someone who likes to have a lot of characters, I want to be able to get gear without grinding 40 hours on each one.
It's just an all around great game. Cheap, well made, plenty of content, not insanely glitchy, and full of it's own flavor while also giving you tastes of all time greats. If you are wondering whether or not to get this at all, I totally would. On sale it's probably the single greatest $15 purchase I have made, and I have a lot of games.

I'm thoroughly satisfied after completing all six episodes. How much of this was predetermined and how much was due to my awful decision-making, I don't know, but the tension was consistent throughout the entire game, and that was fantastic.
You play multiple members of House Forrester in this game. I was initially put off by this, as I normally want to play the same character through an entire game, but the multiple POV characters fit Martin's writing style, and in the end it enabled me to have a wider variety of experiences (you get to play in King's Landing and beyond The Wall, for example).

:THIS IS THE PERSPECTIVE FROM SOMEONE THAT HAS NEVER PLAYED A FARCRY GAME BEFORE:
(just wanted to point it out, since i dont know whats different from the others, system wise etc)
Wanted to toss in a neutral rank on this but. it dsnt exist :P so i give it a thumbs up for the story.
GAMEPLAY:
Its a very repetative type gamestyle, its ALWAYS surrounding around "Hunt this, Skin that, Free those people" and so on, after a while it gets a bit old. There is not that much varation in those quests but altho a FEW was enjoyable. I did enjoy the Beast Master Hunt quests alot since it felt more action packed and it was a more realistic kind of a hunt.
Out in the world when hunting animals, it gets very annoying, shoot them once and they run straight to f¨¨king Africa and you have to chase them for a good 2 miles, i mean sure its realistic but considering the miles the animals runs, its just ridicoulus. If they bleeded out a bit faster i wouldnt have pointed it out that much tbh.
Out in the world i did not notice that much bugs, it was mostly the Companion AIs and interactions that was completely bugg infested.
Has a good pace on leveling up, gathering materials and its not too grindy, the ONLY problem i ever encountered with grinding for hides was to find Badgers, but i was most likely in the wrong place for it. Otherwise it was a breeze and it was exciting to find rare kinds of animals and start hunting them.
BEASTS:
First of all: Healing the Beasts seems to be VERY broken, the option to heal them doesnt pop up as it should, so you have to reposition them, yourself and wiggle it out in order to get the option, VERY ANNOYING.
There is one more MAJOR thing i want to say about them, once you get the Bloodfang Sabertooth, you will probably never switch it out. Ive let it run into camps and strongholds, let it take on 20 ppl and then the companion comes back with a big smile and still half health left. This pet is by far the best pet you can get.
The Wolfs are pretty decent companions, they reveal the area of the map, they got decent damage, speed and stealth so they are mostly all around "okay".
Bears have some kind of a Personality Disorder wich makes them think they are a wrecking ball, i dont know whats up with their AI but as quickly they see destructible fences or objects, they rush into it without a command or anything, they just go for it. So going stealth with a bear is NOT a good option, pretty decent amount of health tho and they take the attention of the enemies from you.
Did not go that much with Leopards and Lions but as the minor input i got from the Leopards atleast is that they are great at stealth, good speed but if they get seen in a camp, they are pretty much dead.
And last, probably the most OP pet there is, Sabertooths, i STRONGLY recommend to get it as early as possible, they are amazing killing machines! Fastes companion in game, they can catch up to anything in a very small amount of time, great amount of damage and decent health.
WEAPONS:
Great varation when it comes to weapons, it really felt like each weapon had a defined and specific purpose wich felt really good. no complains about them and they look awesome aswell! :O Most used weapon was the Double-Arrow Bow ;)
STORY:
Great story, written very well and was probably the ONLY thing that kept me playing this game tbh. It was good characters, the ooga booga launguage did not put me off that much, since it fits the whole idea of it being in the Stone Age:ish times.  Not many complains about it. PS: You are gonna love Urki.
BUGGS:
Companion AI is very bugged, the interaction to heal them doesnt work properly, you have to wiggle and reposition to force it out. Some pets cant jump up ledges or swim at all, Only Sabertooths can jump up ledges as i noticed and only Bears can swim.
The "Kill Command" for the companions is bugged aswell sometimes, it comes up saying "Your beast cant reach the target" even tho it stands RIGHT afront of it.
The Bears have personality disorder of a wrecking ball, and very aggressive since plenty of times it just ran off into a camp and started killing people without being provoked or harmed.
Sometimes Arrows got completely lost? For example, i shoot 3 arrows into a cannibal, retreive the arrows, i get 2 back.What happen to the 3rd? if its SUPPOSTE to break occasionally, it would be nice to know :P
When you open up the world map, could have been a personal problem with my computer, my FPS drops down to 2 or 3, so using the map to travel around gets very annoying since it takes longer than it should, was a bit un-sure to include this since it could be a problem that my PC have, and not the game itself.
IS IT WORTH BUYING?:
Well, if you love open world games where you can just run around and just do random stuff, explore with a good friend at your side, killing people in many ways, then yes. It has a good story, its interesting and it really provides with plenty of "the enemies wiew on the conflict" moments, good plot twists and good characters. I would honestly say its just a bit rough around the edges and it needs a patch or two to fix some stuff. Otherwise i did enjoy it. :)

Game of Thrones by TellTale is interactive novel that starts off in one of the most memorable moments of GoT called the Red Wedding. If you haven't watched season 3 of the show or read the third book called Storm of Swords I would highly suggest you don't read this review or play this game. With that out of the way, we start off as a lowly squire for House Forrester named Gared Tuttle. He is out fetching wine for the soldiers in celebration of The North's plan to take Casterly Rock from the Lannisters. Things do not stay cheerful for long as Fray soldiers cut down the army of The North in a vicious sneak attack and your lord is slain before your eyes. In his final words he gives Gared a sword and asks him to return it to its rightful place in the Forrester keep called Ironwrath. He also mysteriously asks of him to tell his uncle “The North Grove must not be lost” which will kick start the main goal of that character. That is a lot of names to take in, which is why those with new to GoT will likely be very lost throughout since they are entering the world near the half way mark of the overall narrative.
One of the first things you'll notice is that the graphics now have this painting like look to them instead of the comic book style of Telltales last two games. It looks alright, not really anything remotely cool looking here but it does the job. The reason I mention the graphics so early on is that you will do a lot of sitting back and just watching in this title. Even compared to Telltales last two games, you can count on a single hand just how many times you will have control of your character and there are no puzzles either which is why I called this an interactive novel in the first sentence. That may be a bad thing to some but in my eyes those were the worst parts of Telltale's games and I'm glad I no longer have to move an extremely slow character around tiny closed off environments all that often. It makes the story move along with far better flow and is much easier to get invested in. Considering you will be controlling four characters in very different situations the better pacing benefits this title a lot. Like other Telltale games they will occasionally throw in a QTE to make sure you are paying attention.
The characters you play as will be the previously mentioned squire Gared, Ethan Forrester who is the new young lord after his father’s demise, Asher the black sheep of the Forrester family and Mira Forrester who resides in King's Landing as a handmaiden for the soon to be queen Margery Tyrell. All characters want what is best for House Forrester which makes switching around to another characters perspective feel natural since they are all fighting for the same thing, though in different ways. Their House's situation is extremely dire from the get go and Telltale really captured the dark feel of the GoT universe. You never feel safe and being a small barely known House that fought on the defeated side of the war you will constantly get harassed. Most of the time the wiser choice is to just accept it and stay silent but the humiliation you go through is just so much that more likely than not you will not be able to just put up with it even if you know it can cost you everything. Not that you have much left as whenever you think things are bad they somehow get much worse. From start to finish it feels like you are drowning and there is very little hope to be found anywhere.
It is a very dark game but unlike the show or books this has zero humor in it. That ties in with the biggest flaw in this game which are the choices you make. Telltale has always offered the illusion of choice but in this title there is no illusion. Your choices are meaningless and are foiled by the dumbest reasons just to keep the story the way they are trying to tell it. For instance in one scene you are going to get murdered by a Lannister guard but a small boy defends you and is being drowned for it. You have the choice to kill the guard or run away. If you run away you later meet the boy again who is now angry with you for leaving him to his fate and said he found a nearby rock while being drowned to kill the guard with. There is just no believable way such a small skinny lad could have pulled that off against a rather high ranking guard while being drowned in the position he was. It just feels like cheap and lazy story writing to pin that murder on you either way that you choose to handle things. That insultingly improbable way of negating your choices carries on toward the whole game and some are far more unbelievable than what I choose as an example.
With the lack of humor and the already dire situation with convenient plot armor keeping you from doing anything about it, it feels like the game is screwing the player instead of a dark, dangerous world where your plans don't always work out. It's a shame too as there are quite a few important characters of the GoT universe like Ramsay Bolton, Cerci Lannister and Jon Snow all with their original actors from the show. It would have been awesome to see if you could outwit the more dangerous of characters by using what we know from the show but instead we get the choice of picking the bad choice and getting shafted by the character for it or picking the sensible choice and getting shafted by the game itself for it. If Telltale were spread thin due to all of the games they are working on I feel it would have been far better to have a few actual choices rather than a ton of poorly veiled meaningless ones. From all this criticism you may be guessing that the story is garbage but the sad part is that it is not. It is a rather interesting tale with that spans from Westeros to quite a bit of Essos. You can't help but root for the Forresters and hope they get back on their feet.
They did an excellent job with getting you to despise the villains even if they are the typical absurdly evil type. All the new characters are pretty interesting, well voiced and quite likable. None feel like they are out of place in the GoT universe and are just as likely to die as anyone else. Well other than the show's cameo characters featured here who are too important to the plot of the show to kill off in a video game. Strangely enough for the GoT universe there is no nudity anywhere in this game, though I guess in the situations are characters are in they don't feel like baby making. All in all this is a game that will only appeal to fans of the Game of Thrones looking to see their favorite characters and see some famous locations like Castle Black, King's Landing and Mareen. There is a good story here but the pretentiousness of the frequent, useless choices did negatively impact the narrative. And the ending is a very unsatisfying set up for another season that had no closure at all. This is a title you can safely skip even if you are a fan of the source material. It's not a bad game but it does feel like a rushed plothole filled mess that only the biggest of fans that can't get enough of Game of Thrones will likely enjoy.

Beyond Eyes, a game about a little blind girl that goes on a journey to find her missing feline friend, will leave the player blind through its incredibly horrible use of white space. The pleasant art style and neat moments are held back by how she discovers the world around her.
Rae, the girl who lost her sight in an accident, can only walk around. It’s a fairly slow gait she has and she doesn’t have a power walk of any sort. There are very few interactions in the game, so you can expect to become very familiar with her slow gait as you walk to and fro to reveal the environment. It’s not compelling or challenging gameplay at all and I found myself bored often in a barely two-hour experience. The game did have some neat tricks where you become accustomed to hearing a sound of one object and then having that same sound turn out to be something else when you approach the source. They even used it towards the end in a way that added to the story. On the other hand, having to walk around the town to lure seagulls to a spot only three feet away just so I could pass didn’t feel great.
The art style pleases me. It reminds me of watercolors and looks pretty good overall. I just wish that the infinite white oblivion that represents the undiscovered terrain were something else. I could even go for a light tan or a very soft blue, just not an overwhelming avalanche of white. I spent a good chunk of time frowning, squinting, closing my eyes, avoiding the screen, and swinging the camera around to have it on the revealed environment. I thought it couldn’t become any worse after playing for an hour, but once I reached the last two chapters, I had to deal with rain which reduced her “vision”. The whiteness closed in around her to make it easier to become lost as the environment would fade away instead of staying around. I was unable to enjoy the visuals and had a headache.

Telltale's Game of Thrones is more a supplement to the HBO-series than a stand-alone experience. If you are not familiar and caught up with the show, you can safely skip this one.
If you're a fan of the show (like me) however, you might find some satisfaction in this title. The important thing to note is that the whole "your choices matter" thing is really not this game's strong suit. Yes, you do get to make decisions, but usually these decisions give the same result. None of the Telltale games truly "change" all that much in the grand scheme of things depending on your choices, but they usually manage to either distract you, or conceal the illusion of choice enough to convince you that you make an impact. I rarely felt like my choices mattered in this game, with the most outrageous example being a scene where i picked a dialogue option that got me killed and had me thinking "oh my god! What have I done! How will this impact the other characters? How will i defend my house now?" only to get a game over screen and restart at the point right before i made that dialogue choice, so I could pick one of "the right ones". You, as a player, have very little impact on the story most of the time, and that is a real shame.
That being said, the game does tell a good story, with strong characters, excellent voice acting, and decent amount of variety. It also fleshes out the world of Westeros a bit (particularly Kings Landing, the north past The Wall, and to some extent Meereen), and from what I can tell the story here is actually canon with the HBO series, which is kind of neat. Characters from the show are also tastefully used. And by that I mean that they are not just shoe-horned in for some free star-power. They all have some sort of function in the grand scheme of things, and the characters all behave like they do in the TV-series. They even have the same voices, with the actors of the show reprising their roles in this game. As you may have guessed, these characters are also "plot-shielded" pretty bad, but i still think the game is stronger with them, than it would have been without them.
I would recommend this game to fellow Game of Thrones fans who are looking for more tales in Westeros while we wait for the next season of the TV-series. The choices are often meaningless and mundane, but the story told here is good enough to satisfy any fan of the show. Just make sure you get it on sale and not at full price!

FTL is the massive headache of leadership, logistics, and tactics, gracefully applied to the "wilderness" of deep space.  Your first playthrough, you'll choose whatever is aesthetically pleasing to you, and enjoy simple victories on "easy" difficulty.  But after your first tough battle, in which Rock people are running amok on your ship, which is on fire and under attack, you'll quickly become a cold-hearted pragmatist.  You have to make peace that you won't be able to save the entire crew in certain scenarios; as you vent the oxygen from half of your ship - killing a crewmember or two, but snuffing out the flames.  Despite the pixelated top-down old school look, the game takes some timing and forward thinking.  Timing laser bursts just right to coincide with a missile strike, or selectively targeting the other ship's subsystems to starve their crew of oxygen, to disabling their engine so they can't escape from you.  The gameplay and procedural nature of the campaign are the standouts of this game.  The story, is vague but believable.  The music, wow.  It reminds me of a midi version of the Mass Effect soundtrack, and is quite phenomenal on its own merits.  I use the soundtrack to help me study.  I would say, the price is right for anyone interested in space, strategy, or just punishing roguelike games.  Besides, once your inaugural is complete, you have all the Advanced Edition content to have fun with!

Oddly addictive game, with little pay to win aspects making it valid for free players.
Black desert Online is essentially sand box mmorpg with skippable storyline, set in somewhat generic fantasy world with asian flavour ( has dwarves, elves, some tiny weird loli creatures and people with horns, ogres, orcs so on), that lets you can go path of battle, focus on life skills and trading or build your own worker empires with influence and npc employees, sail sees and hunt monsters so on, even breed horses and make furniture, each taking long to master and forming a time taking path for you to follow.
Most interesting aspect of success in your craft is your "family salalry" essentially town leader npc's as well as game world pays you daily salary depending how much you have done, this also extends on guild system where guild master makes work contract with members, with salary scaling based on how much guild earns from your contribution, it's really interesting consept considering guilds get their income from attendance, guild quests and node wars, you can even own one of the major cities as guild and get set tax from it.
There's lot to do in this game, though all aspects are somewhat grindy, that is to be expected when the sole focus is to endlessly improve as the game has no level or skill caps, just exponentially increasing experience demand.
The combat system is very action ish as well though you can " wow it" if you want by setting skills to bar instead of using quick commands ( such  as Sift + right mouse for chainlightning), but there is small stamina penalty for being lazy, so comboing skills by commands is best way to go .
Money purchases are mostly cosmetic, and you can get inventory space by doing quests, weight limits by loyalty and trading and warehouse space by using influence points ( cp) to warehouses and so on.
There are some clear advantages from using money though, biggest is 30% increase in value on market change, as by default market takes 30% off item prices. this comes from value packs which are essentially sneaky way to make subscription.
You can also use money to increase storage and inventory space ( up to maximum) though this is mostly just time saver, you can get extremely large inventories by just playing the game.
Weight limit gain is most beneficial overally, as using loyalty points and working on your carry strenght gives at best 1/4th of what you get with money also the increases to worker limits can free cp and give clear advantage to buyers ( up to limit of +3 that is essentially level 2 house that costs 2-3 cp in game which is not much).
Most people just want pets and costumes though, because in game looks generally are bit dull on purpose, you can get and make costumes in game ( there are furniture and tailor workshops you can manage with workers), but it's still faster for most to buy them with rl cash, though I see no point in it.
Pets essentially are automatic looting robots, which are highly favored by people who do lot of pve, and mostly just attainable from cash store.
Besides all this there is lot of things to do in this game and gear or upgrading is not rl cash related, so free and paying players can both get to same point of power fairly easilly, payers just click less to do it.
I recommend the game, it's chaotic at first but it sucks you in once you get in to it.

Grey Goo is, first and foremost, not Starcraft. If you like the modern Starcraft-esque RTS that's fast paced, micro intensive, and largely based on twitch skill and on-the-fly adaptation mixed with scouting and mastery of build order, this may not be the game for you. Grey Goo is slow, deliberate, and methodical. The organization of your forces going into an engagement is going to be much more important than what you do in the middle of the fight, and for most of the factions, all of your production is going to be very, very centralized, leading to longer games that focus on large-scale battles. Grey Goo as an RTS is far more focused on the large-scale strategy to the small-scale tactics, and it can be jarring for a lot of people if they're familiar with more micro-intensive games.
The Good:
- Large faction diversity. Basic units are present in each faction, but infrastructure needs vary drastically and while the same general roles are filled by each class and their units (Light tank, light damage, heavy tank, heavy damage, artillery, seige, scout, air, etc.), how each race goes about those basic goals has enough variety to make playing each faction quite different, especially the unorthodox Goo of the title.
- Streamlined economy and tech management. Only the one resource to worry about, and tech, despite generally requiring certain buildings be built, isn't linked to them intrisically.
- Excellent UI and menu design. Once you get used to it, the hotkeys for building are incredibly intuitive, allowing for easier base management without having to set your infrastructure to 4-5 hotkeys just by themselves.
The Bad:
- A very slow game. The standard win-condition requires you destroy the enemy core, all of their factories, and all of their refineries. Even if they literally could not possibly recover, you've gotta whittle away their buildings if they don't feel like surrendering. Which the AI doesn't so practicing against the AI is going to be a bit of a long process.
- Buildings are very tanky and supply lines are difficult to disrupt early game, which makes harassment a non-viable option. Early-game can feel very same-y as you scout out the enemy and try and build your forces to counter theirs. The exception to this is the Goo, which...
- The Goo, despite being really cool and unique, are incredibly weak one-on-one. They're the only faction vulnerable to harassment because their health is their resource, and because they gain resources so slow early on, it's very, very easy for them to fall into a death spiral, especially on small maps.
Great Graphics, Great cutscenes, Fun Gameplay, Unique Factions. This game breathes new life into the RTS genre, introducing unique mechanics and strategies. That along with the pretyt solid story make me have no qualms recommending this to lovers of the genre.

To anyone who's though about buying this - go for it. It's some of the best money you can ever spend.
Now, here's the backstory.
I'm a latecomer to the Star Wars: Battlefront series. When it was first released, sure I heard of it, but well, I wasn't much into gaming, at least not on my PC. So, I missed out. But every time I went to the store, you know what I saw? SWBF. And I dreaded not owning it. I'm a huge SW fan, always have been. So, when I saw it go on sale, I remembered it. I would've bought it even if it wasn't on sale, but I had forgotten. There's no better SW games out there IMO, at the time of posting. If you're a SW fan, this will satisfy. Want to play as your favorite Jedi? Sure, and go ahead and try your favorite Sith and your favorite Jedi's padawan while you're at it. More of a Clone trooper fan? Sure, go ahead and play as one, each of the different classes has a special setup. Very awesome, even if you stick with the classic one. Perhaps you're more of a fan of the Empire. Play as Vader, The Emperor, or one of the many Stormtroopers. Or go back to the CW and play as a Battle Droid. Or go back and fight the Empire as a Rebel, maybe Luke? Han? Leia? Chewie? Your pick. Did I mention the vehicles? Man o man the dogfights with Star Fighters... They're awesome. I recommend getting a joystick (I used a Logitech Extreme 3D Pro, it's perfect. Not expensive and works great, it's only $30, I got mine for less) Or if you're more of a ground type of person, hop in an ATST. Blast some Rebel scum.
Now, multiplayer was stopped being officially supported by gamespy. However multiplayer is still active. You can use Game Ranger or Game Master or Tunngle. I personally use Game Ranger although I'm going to try out Game Master. There are still mods.
I will admit, the graphics are dated. But that's what you should expect, this game isn't exactly young. But IMO, they're still pretty damn good. Oh did I mention that was from playing on a craptop, with Intel Integrated? Still got more than 80FPS, no dips. (Minimal settings, 720p) But it still looks fine and is fun as heck.
TL;DR Quit reading and buy it.

Mein ursprüngliche gepostetes Review erschien unter:
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Tower-Defense Games sind immer so eine Sache. Entweder sind sie von den Farben her zu knallig, inhaltlich zu abgedreht, zu langatmig, zu schwer, zu schnell usw. usw. Für einen echten Nörgler kann die Liste nicht lang genug sein. Erfreulicherweise konnte ich mich bisher vor allen selbstgemachten Negativerfahrungen bewahren, da ich bis zum Test von „Tower Wars“ eine wahre Tower-Defense Jungfrau war. Daher kann ich vorab sagen, dass mich das Game mehr als positiv überrascht hat. Aber kommen wir doch erst einmal dazu, was die Damen und Herren von SuperVillain Studios so geschaffen haben.
TOWER WARS REVIEW – WAS IST DAS EIGENTLICH?
Nach kurzer Spielzeit wurde für mich eines sofort deutlich. Tower Wars ist ein ordentliches Tower-Defense Game, mit ordentlich Zack! Aber kommen wir doch erst mal zum Inhalt. Obwohl ich an dieser Stelle langatmig die Mechanik eines Tower-Defense Spiel erklären könnte…. ach was solls. Wie man vielleicht aus dem englischen Ableiten kann, beinhalten Tower-Defense Games Türme und Abwehr. Kombiniert man das ganze kommt man schnell auf den Trichter, dass die Türme als Mittel zum Zweck verwendet werden. Und zwar um seine eigene Basis vor den anrückenden Gegenerhorden zu verteidigen um parallel dazu, mit seinen eigenen Truppen, dass gegnerische Lager bis auf die Grundmauern niederzubrennen. Klingt das nicht schön? Nicht nur ähnlich, sondern exakt so, geht es auch in Tower Wars zu. Kommen wir daher also mal zum eigentlichen Spiel.
TOWER WARS – GAMEPLAY
Im Großen und Ganzen ist Tower Wars sehr simpel aufgebaut. Man hat neben dem Tutorial (welches verhältnismäßig lang, humorvoll ist und auf angenehme Weise die Spielmechanik erklärt) weitere Spielmodi wie z.B. den Multiplayer und der Kampf gegen die künstliche Intelligenz. Bevor man ein Spiel gegen Mensch oder KI startet, empfiehlt es sich das Tutorial zu spielen. Hier werden alle wichtigen Spielmechaniken erklärt und dies auf eine sehr humorvolle Art und Weise. Wir lassen jetzt mal unsere Fantasie spielen und stellen uns vor, wir sind im Game. Was jetzt? Im Endeffekt ist das Spielprinzip sehr einfach. Man selber (als auch der der Feind) hat eine eigene Basis, die durch das Setzen von Türmen, vor den heranrückenden Feinden beschützt werden soll. Dazu hat man eine Auswahl an unterschiedlichen Türmen. Egal ob es sich dabei um überdimensionale Armbrüste handelt, Teslaspulenartige Türme die an die Zeiten von Command & Conquer erinnern, oder riesenhafte Katapulte für Distanzangriffe. Tower Wars bietet alles! Türme haben in Tower Wars allerdings noch eine weitere Funktion. Neben der Verteidigung dienen sie auch als Möglichkeit, um die KI vor ihrer vorgegebenen Marschroute abzulenken. So laufen die Gegner immer auf einer exakt vorgegebenen Route lang, die im Spiel entweder blau oder rot markiert ist. Durch das setzen der Türme, kann diese Route entsprechend verlängert werden, was auch nötig ist. Der Feind baut im Laufe des Spiel größere und stärkere Einheiten, was ein Risiko für den Durchbruch der eigenen Verteidigungslinie immens erhöht. Neben dem Bau von Türmen ist es allerdings auch möglich eigene Einheiten zu bauen. Dies wird ermöglicht durch Gold und Battlepoints. Gold lässt sich einfach in den umliegenden Minen absammeln, während Battlepoints durch blutige Schlachten gewonnen werden können. Neben dem Einheitenbau lassen sich mit Battlepoints und Gold auch Upgrades erkaufen um die feindliche Basis noch schneller zu stürmen.
TOWER WARS – GRAFIK UND SOUND
Was lässt sich schon sagen. Ich persönlich finde die Grafik sehr gelungen. SuperVillain Studios ist ein Indie Studio welches nicht über ein Budget von mehreren Millionen Dollar verfügt, daher ist das was dem Konsumenten präsentiert wird mehr als ausreichend. Es gibt keine groben Ecken und Kanten und mir sind bisher keine groben Grafikpatzer aufgefallen. Der Sound ist allerdings erste Sahne! Neben den klangvollen Geräuschen ist insbesondere die Vertonung der Stimmen PERFEKT gelungen. Selten habe ich einen so hervorragenden, englischen Akzent in einem Videospiel erleben dürfen. Einfach nur herrlich.
FAZIT
Machen wir es kurz und schmerzlos. Tower Wars ist ein überaus gelungener Indie Titel von SuperVillain Studios, der sich nicht hinter anderen Tower-Defense Spielen zu verstecken brauch. Das Gameplay ist schnell, manchmal vielleicht etwas zu schnell. Mit etwas Übung und stimmiger Aufteilung seiner Türme ist die erste Defense Line geschaffen, wodurch erst mal brav Battlepoints gesammelt werden können. Tower Wars ist auf Steam erhältlich und dies sogar in mehreren Versionen. Während eine Kopie des Spiels schlappe 7,99 Euro kostet, ist das Tower Wars Team Pack, bestehend aus drei Kopien, für 19,90 Euro zu haben. Für Tower-Defense Fans sollte das Spiel durch die unterschiedlichen Spielmodi  lange Spaß machen. Ansonsten eignet es sich durch den Preis von 7,99 Euro auch wunderbar zu giften.
Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass Tower Wars ein spaßiges Spiel für Einsteiger ist, welches besonders durch seinen Humor und Preis beeindruckt. Daher verteile ich für Tower Wars ganze vier von fünf Sternen.

Dragon Fantasy: The Black Tome of Ice is a love letter to Squaresoft's SNES-era RPGs. It clocks in between 10-15 hours long (my played time includes some AFKing). The overall story is above-average and the game is packed with homages to games both classic and contemporary. There is a lot of tongue-in-cheek humor and goofiness, but it doesn't get in the way.
The combat is turn-based, but quick, and you can get by without much grinding if you approach the battles tactically or turn down the difficulty. I recommend turning message speed up to max. Also, there are no random battles; all monsters appear on the screen. They can be avoided and sometimes even baited away from their pack for an easy kill. They even stay dead for as long as you are in the area, often allowing you to backtrack to a campfire to recover hp/mana and save.
Graphics are so-so. There are some clipping problems here and there, lots of resused NPC sprites, and a few common special effects for skills. It has some charm of its own, but don't expect the detail of Chrono Trigger or the smoothness of Secret of Mana. There is plenty of room for improvement, but the graphics definitely aren't an eyesore.
I have a difficult time judging music, but I will say this game does it pretty well. Some of it is catchy, none of it was annoying, and most of the repeat cutovers are well-placed, if not perfect.
If you love SNES-era RPGs (Chrono Trigger, in particular), you will enjoy this game, but I would recommend it to any JRPG lover.

I had only played Civ. III before this one, so I'm not the most qualified to compare the various incarnations of the Civilization series, but I really appreciate all the features they added. Not only can you control what your civilization produces and how it interacts with surrounding nations, but now you can form your own religion and convert enemy cities. I also loved the addition of the World Congress / UN - it adds a whole new level of realism to diplomacy.
However, if I were to critique any part of it, I would have to say that the combat and expansion experience is severely lacking. Conquering the planet and destroying all opposition isn't nearly as simple, because you swiftly be branded a "warmonger," and your citizens will hate you for having too many cities.
Overall, this is yet another addicting addition to the Civilization series. It adds a slew of new ways to customize your Civilization realistically, and for the most part makes it feal like you are playing against real nations, each with their own unique personalities and reactions.

At its core, Beat Hazard is a very simple game. It's just a twin-stick shooter where you shoot at asteroids and enemies while trying to avoid touching them. The game's main advertising point is that the aesthetics and enemy generation of the game are based around the music you play, where each “stage” is a song. For example, if you’re at a loud part of the song, the game will throw a bunch of enemies at you but also increase your firepower. As a singleplayer game, it’s neat to say the least. However, I recommend Beat Hazard as a multiplayer game with a friend. That way, you get that weird joy of listening to a song with your friend while also trying to not burn through all of your shared lives. It can be rather fun chaos in the game, and my friends and I would have several systems on who got to pick the next song.
There are a few janky aspects of Beat Hazard to make that dream happen, though. First, you need both you and your friends to the same exact song files into Beat Hazard…and if you have a ton of songs, it’s a rather lengthy process where the game demands to be open. Plus, the songs are all presented in one list with limited sorting options, so if you’re looking for a specific song and you have a lot, you have to hope to not scroll past it. Furthermore, only one person can control the menus, so if your friend is the host and tends to be uncooperative, that could be an issue.
The game’s not perfect, but I think if the idea of playing multiplayer Asteroids with a friend based around songs you pick sounds like fun, it’s worth a pickup, probably on sale.

Oddly addictive game, with little pay to win aspects making it valid for free players.
Black desert Online is essentially sand box mmorpg with skippable storyline, set in somewhat generic fantasy world with asian flavour ( has dwarves, elves, some tiny weird loli creatures and people with horns, ogres, orcs so on), that lets you can go path of battle, focus on life skills and trading or build your own worker empires with influence and npc employees, sail sees and hunt monsters so on, even breed horses and make furniture, each taking long to master and forming a time taking path for you to follow.
Most interesting aspect of success in your craft is your "family salalry" essentially town leader npc's as well as game world pays you daily salary depending how much you have done, this also extends on guild system where guild master makes work contract with members, with salary scaling based on how much guild earns from your contribution, it's really interesting consept considering guilds get their income from attendance, guild quests and node wars, you can even own one of the major cities as guild and get set tax from it.
There's lot to do in this game, though all aspects are somewhat grindy, that is to be expected when the sole focus is to endlessly improve as the game has no level or skill caps, just exponentially increasing experience demand.
The combat system is very action ish as well though you can " wow it" if you want by setting skills to bar instead of using quick commands ( such  as Sift + right mouse for chainlightning), but there is small stamina penalty for being lazy, so comboing skills by commands is best way to go .
Money purchases are mostly cosmetic, and you can get inventory space by doing quests, weight limits by loyalty and trading and warehouse space by using influence points ( cp) to warehouses and so on.
There are some clear advantages from using money though, biggest is 30% increase in value on market change, as by default market takes 30% off item prices. this comes from value packs which are essentially sneaky way to make subscription.
You can also use money to increase storage and inventory space ( up to maximum) though this is mostly just time saver, you can get extremely large inventories by just playing the game.
Weight limit gain is most beneficial overally, as using loyalty points and working on your carry strenght gives at best 1/4th of what you get with money also the increases to worker limits can free cp and give clear advantage to buyers ( up to limit of +3 that is essentially level 2 house that costs 2-3 cp in game which is not much).
Most people just want pets and costumes though, because in game looks generally are bit dull on purpose, you can get and make costumes in game ( there are furniture and tailor workshops you can manage with workers), but it's still faster for most to buy them with rl cash, though I see no point in it.
Pets essentially are automatic looting robots, which are highly favored by people who do lot of pve, and mostly just attainable from cash store.
Besides all this there is lot of things to do in this game and gear or upgrading is not rl cash related, so free and paying players can both get to same point of power fairly easilly, payers just click less to do it.
I recommend the game, it's chaotic at first but it sucks you in once you get in to it.

A walking adventure where a blind girl searches the world for a stray cat that she took a liking to. Visuals and audio are nice. You start out in a mostly white empty area but as you walk around the world gets filled in around you. The story is pretty simple but you need to ignore certain things to enjoy it.
If she was my child, I'd be terrified if she randomly went out by herself for hours on a whim to find a cat. But this is a world without consequences (the devs call it a fairy tale in the store page); you're independent and can safely explore the world yourself without assistance. She walks normally without a cane or feeling around for things by hand and she doesn't bump into things and get hurt (you suddenly stop walking when you bump into an obstacle). Towns are mostly empty and the few adults that are around are stationary and she never interacts with them. However, you're free to take/steal things lying around like bread and an umbrella.
The devs try to bring out certain aspects and remove the unfun parts of being blind. The world is what the girl assumes is around her so it's not always true. Things you hear from a distance can change as you approach them and figure out what they really are. As you walk around you map out the world and fill in the empty void. It's something you might enjoy if you feel compelled to explore and like eliminating fog-of-war/filling out the map in other games. It felt nice to turn around and look at the revealed map and see how the area looked like as a whole (instead of seeing it in pieces as I revealed it).
If you want a more true-to-life experience, blindfold yourself (and get a trusted friend/family member to walk next to you and make sure you don't hurt yourself) and slowly and carefully walk around an enclosed area in a park or backyard. You can test directional hearing/sound localization, try to map out things in your mind (spatial awareness) and then take off the blindfold to see if it matches up. Walking stick recommended.
Simple controls: WASD movement, mouse for camera, and space bar to interact with unmarked objects.
I would've greatly enjoyed to have buttons to autowalk and to speedwalk/run. There is not much backtracking but if you want to revisit an old area or unveil every part of the map there'll be a lot of slow walking. I'm guessing devs don't allow fast movement in walking games because they want the player to experience the game in their way but I've played enough games that slow gameplay that you can't choose to speed up when desired is unsatisfying.
You don't walk through especially large areas but they become huge when you can't see the boundaries and have to explore every inch in case there's an exit or object in a corner you haven't explored. There are achievements for events tucked away in corners.
If you're not already appreciative of the sight you have then maybe this game can help if you take it the right way.
Maybe worth it if you can only look at it from a fairy tale perspective and are emotionally driven (and can ignore some logic). For me, I couldn't get into the story. It's not like other situations where there are problems/danger and the hero overcomes/avoids it, it's as if the problems don't exist as the hero never worried about it in the first place.
I did enjoy exploring & filling in the details of the world. If you don't want to explore the world and just want to get from cutscene to cutscene, this game might not be for you because you have to slowly and blindly wander looking for the exit.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare has pros and cons over the original game. The graphics are much better, and the mob AI is also improved substantially. To anyone who's though about buying this - go for it. It's some of the best money you can ever spend.
Now, here's the backstory.
I'm a latecomer to the Star Wars: Battlefront series. When it was first released, sure I heard of it, but well, I wasn't much into gaming, at least not on my PC. So, I missed out. But every time I went to the store, you know what I saw? SWBF. And I dreaded not owning it. I'm a huge SW fan, always have been. So, when I saw it go on sale, I remembered it. I would've bought it even if it wasn't on sale, but I had forgotten. There's no better SW games out there IMO, at the time of posting. If you're a SW fan, this will satisfy. Want to play as your favorite Jedi? Sure, and go ahead and try your favorite Sith and your favorite Jedi's padawan while you're at it. More of a Clone trooper fan? Sure, go ahead and play as one, each of the different classes has a special setup. Very awesome, even if you stick with the classic one. Perhaps you're more of a fan of the Empire. Play as Vader, The Emperor, or one of the many Stormtroopers. Or go back to the CW and play as a Battle Droid. Or go back and fight the Empire as a Rebel, maybe Luke? Han? Leia? Chewie? Your pick. Did I mention the vehicles? Man o man the dogfights with Star Fighters... They're awesome. I recommend getting a joystick (I used a Logitech Extreme 3D Pro, it's perfect. Not expensive and works great, it's only $30, I got mine for less) Or if you're more of a ground type of person, hop in an ATST. Blast some Rebel scum.
Now, multiplayer was stopped being officially supported by gamespy. However multiplayer is still active. You can use Game Ranger or Game Master or Tunngle. I personally use Game Ranger although I'm going to try out Game Master. There are still mods.
I will admit, the graphics are dated. But that's what you should expect, this game isn't exactly young. But IMO, they're still pretty damn good. Oh did I mention that was from playing on a craptop, with Intel Integrated? Still got more than 80FPS, no dips. (Minimal settings, 720p) But it still looks fine and is fun as heck.
TL;DR Quit reading and buy it.

I really didn't pay any attention to this game when I picked it up in a bundle last year. Idled for cards, made some money. My son actually played it, then challenged me to a match. I've got to say its a pretty fun game.
The jist of it is that you play tower defense against your opponent while also sending waves of units against them. There is gold from mining and battlepoints from sending units (more BP the longer they last on the map). You need both. Towers and units are bought with gold, upgrades are bought with BP, and units are unlocked with both.
What I find interesting is that you need to balance sending out lots of units to get upgrades, and you need to keep your maze strong to stop enemy units from getting BP for upgrades.
The main downside to this game is that there are some fairly predictable setups that will win matches against players that expect a regular TD game. If you find an opponent that uses a similar setup, the game can progress, but otherwise its usually quite one sided.
Overall, I think its a fun game, with some features that make it different from the rest of the TD out there.

---UPDATE----
It looks like weapons balancing has been fixed! All the weapons feel great again, and everyone gets a grenade again. Spawning has also been fixed somewhat, but though I'm no longer getting spawn killed, I'm still spawning close to war zones a bit too often. The style system is unchanged, and though I now understand that the devs were likely trying to reward slow motion solely for high flying/risky kills and such, I still don't like it. I'd rather they award 1 sec slow motion for each standard style kill (headshots, tacticool, etc), and then reward 3 seconds for riskier kills.
I am receiving another random issue. Sometimes, the game will decide to freeze up for a few seconds during gameplay. I don't know if it's because of latency or the game's performance itself. If this is only happening to me, that'd be kinda weird, because I use a top performance PC. But if it happens to other people, hopefully it can be fixed.
It's as fun to play as the beta again, and with its style system, interesting game type, and beautiful maps, there really isn't a reason to try this game again or for the first time!
---OLD REVIEW---
Though there may have been a bit of bias, since I am friends with a developer and I've been watching this game almost since its inception (and became the undisputed best player, though now there is much steeper competition giving me a huge run for my money), I was originally going to recommend this game hands-down, but after taking a bit of a look after it with the updates and the huge increase in population, I've found there are some problems with this game that make me give it the "yes" vote only slightly.
-Spawn positions need to be fixed. Especially in the newer maps, I am often spawned into the middle of a war zone and get killed within a matter of seconds without being able to even fire a shot
-Weapons need to be rebalanced. Originally, coming in with an MP5k and an M16 I was able to compete very well. Now there is a lot of favoritism towards shotguns and akimbo pistols, which have, for the most part, become the most overpowered weapons in the game. To add insult to injury, the M16 is now semi-auto instead of 3 round burst, making it a very weak weapon, even with the added style points, and both assault rifles are now mainly campers' tools, especially since the recoil makes them very hard to use while rushing.
-They need to make the slow motion system like the beta. No longer am I rewarded for tacticool kills or headshots or other such skill kills. The only shots I'm rewarded for are melee kills and dive kills, and I only get ONE SECOND of slow motion!
I really hope that the game becomes more refined and that the issues get addressed and fixed sooner than later, because from the looks of it the beta version is a better game than the final version. If things get worse, I may end up disliking the game and not playing it anymore, which would be a shame since the game really has potential and I've had many good memories playing it.

Pros:

, which the player can combine to create an entirely new profession. The different kinds of synergy produced largely impacts your gameplay experience. This only means one thing, HUGE amounts of replay value. As supposed to the more common A-RPG formula that have

* Hardcore Mode; in my opinion should be an absolute requirement for all A-RPGs/H&S RPGs. The ultimate challenge for all A-RPG addicts and natural masochists out there.
Cons:
* I am not exactly sure if this was the intended game design, or if it was the result of continues balancing/nerfs/buffs process during the beta phases of this game, but it seems to me that a  large part of game mechanics was thrown out the window. Let me elaborate by referring to the most basic RPG formula.
3 Classes:
- Warrior
- Mage
- Rogue/Assassin/Marksman
What I consider as a well-made A-RPG is a game where-in it allows players to complete its contents in Hardcore using it's inherent toolkit and employing logical gameplay tactics expected from these 3 classes to be able to succeed. Tank and Spank for Warrior based characters, Nuke and Kite gameplay gameplay for mages, Hit and Run tactics for Dex/Cun-based toons. While hybrids do exist in more modern versions of this genre, this simple formula should NEVER EVER be taken out of the game. Difficulty/Efficiency is of course varied, but nevertheless it should never be impossible.
If you ever attempt to play this game hardcore in all difficulties, using the current meta as reference, you will soon learn that every class involved in clearing the game in Ultimate with your sanity still intact involves being an unkillable walking tank versions of your class. Face-tank warrior, Face-tank marksman, Face-tank Assassins, Face-tank casters. This game has it all. The rules of the game changed to outlasting your opponents until your DPS finishes them off.
I have never seen an A-RPG that tries it's damn hardest to eliminate all possibilities and forms of kiting and hit-and-run tactics, especially during Boss Fights. It doesn't suggest you the "tank" route, it forces you to it.
Provided that it was a promising A-RPG, for this atrocity to be allowed to happen to this game; Crate should fire their whole QA team. The balancing method they used to nerf overpowered builds was to increase damage output to absurd levels that players are given no choice but to prioritize a large health pool over stat-based progression to even have a fighting chance at Ultimate non-Hardcore is such an elementary approach to "balancing." Such a sinful sinful sinful mistake, that this simple mechanic really outweighs anything positive this game has to offer.
Given it's current state, I refuse to give my recommendation to other fans of this genre, and while I will remain grinding it for achievements and just to be able to say i finished the game in all possible classes in every possible profession combination (cuz i'm a completionist like that), it does not reflect the fact that i
the game nonetheless, for wasting its potential.

Tropico 4 is a great city building sim. The time i have logged so far comes from doing the 20 campaign missions and i found them varied enough in challenge (usually centered around resources and faction/foreign requests) to keep me entertained. It feels a little more up close and personal than a lot of the other city sims due to its smaller population average, you start with 50 people in your barebones city and i rarely got over 600 total at the end of a mission. You can choose to stay on any mission and keep growing after success and while i have yet to try sandbox mode i would estimate that each island could contain a few thousand people.
The challenge comes from trying to achieve the right balance between production, keeping your population happy/suppresed and juggling relations with foreign powers. In game events add an extra challenge such as natural disasters or an economic crash which does lead to some desperate times for your populace as you struggle to rebuild or shift production.
Overall this game has enough character and playabilty to make it a worthwhile addition to the city sim franchise.

I've played Tropico a fair bit over the last couple of years and I keep coming back to it.  It's a clever sim which puts you as the president for life of a tropical island in the Caribbean.  You have to complete a series of tasks to make your island the greatest nation in all the world - and make sure that your Swiss bank account is filled to ensure that when you're finally ousted from power, that you can retire in luxury.
Controls are straightforward and the instructions through the tutorial episode are clear.  I occasionally struggled to get roads to line up precisely since you have to do it by eye - there's no visible grid pattern - but otherwise the controls worked well.  The interface is crisp and well laid-out.
The game has a charm to it, too.  The music is catchy and up-beat and after a day's play you will find it stuck in your head when you go and do something else.  The avatars which appear to advise you are never annoying, even after repeated play.  The cold-war feel is there - apparent enough to those of us who remember it but without the unremitting bleakness.
The difficulty is pitched about right, providing a real challenge on the later levels.  Trying to keep your tiny island's traffic flowing smoothly as the population grows is really tough.  Providing all the amenities while keeping exports flowing is also a challenge.  And if you find yourself getting bored then the Modern Times add-on is well worth getting.
My one gripe is with the DLC.  There are some reasonably nice addons but I found them a touch expensive at full price for what you got.  If there's a sale on, they're worth having.  And I would have liked to see a music DLC to expand the cheery music that plays throughout the game.
All in all, it's a clever game which is funny and a reasonable challenge to sim fans.

Tower wars is what one would expect from a defense/offense game. On one side of the defense you have a VARIETY of awesome towers that you can build and upgrade each with their own specific purpose (arrows, cannons, launchers, giant hammers, giant fans to slow enemies etc...). The castle is also upgradable by means of shield or ammunition effectiveness (that's as far as castle upgrades go). There are also unlock-able units as you play depending on what you want to unlock and they can also be upgraded. To go beyond upgrading simple units, the game has a upgrade system where you can add shields, armor, or even health to the units. The upgrade system (building) allows for other upgrades such as reduced wait time to send a wave of attacking units to your enemy, bigger barracks, spawn random units when deploying an assault, or upgrade battle points so you receive more. This game is also multiplayer which makes it all that much better!
I would highly recommend this game. The visuals were done right, the sounds were done right, the units were done right, the delivery on the game play was done right. Variations and modifications are always welcomed and a simple layout style (with some random obstacles) always make for an interesting game.
Warning though, one game can take 45 min to an 1 h. So don't expect to jump in and jump out. If you want a game that's not 45 minutes long I HIGHLY suggest CastleStorm which is sort of similar to this but a 2D (3D graphics) platformer.

As a veteran of the original Xcom on the Amiga, I came to the PC reboot a little sceptical - most reboots do a very bad job.
However, I was pleasantly surprised. There are features I miss from the original, such as the more in-depth research, engineering and commerce vs. space factors, but though this new X-com has "streamlined" gameplay in favour of a more arcade-style, which gives a sense of flow to a turn-based strategy game.
The graphics are excellent (Though I have some issues with the "action camera") and the music is ok.
Gameplay itself is smooth, and the difficulty trajectory is good, with a nice curve for more experienced players.
The things I miss most about the original tactical gameplay are:
1. That in the original, movement paused if you spotted an enemy - allowing you to cease your charge around a corner into a crowd of strong enemies.
2. The movement points allowed you to inch forwards and plan your route. In the new game, you frequently find your soldiers charging into poisonous clouds or fire.
3. The inventory system is completely gone, meaning you cannot loot bodies or retrieve equipment from injured soldiers.
Overall I would rate the NEW Xcom 80%- if I was new to the genre I would probably rate it higher.

This is one of my favorite games ever. You guide a starship and its crew through 8 sectors each with an assortment of points to visit. These may have enemy ships, civilian ships requesting help, stores, and environmental hazards such as nebula storms. You'll come across many decisions throughout the game as well. You'll have to decide if it's worth attacking pirates in hopes of useful loot from their ship or whether you should just avoid conflict and keep exploring. Additionally, you'll be posed with many different events. In some events, you'll need to decide whether you should save a dying crew which puts your crew in danger but can offer useful rewards. Other times you can agree to help someone only to find it was a trap. These events and their outcomes are randomized, so you can never be sure which you should choose.
You can hire new crewmembers at some stores, and sometimes you can run into people that offer to join your crew for saving them. There is a variety of crew member species, and each species offers its own advantages and disadvantages (such as having extra health or exploding upon death). Your crew can man different parts of your ship to increase systems' effectivenesses. For example, putting a crew member on engines will increase your dodge chance.
Upgrading your ship is essential. You can find or purchase augmentations that do many different things (such as long-range sensors that give you sector information or an augmentation to increase the scrap (currency) you find). As you progress, you can purchase additional systems (such as a teleporter to beam your crew aboard enemy ships). You can also purchase a drone system and drones that each have different functions such as boarding enemy ships, repairng damaged systems, destorying incoming missiles, or attacking enemy ships directly.
There are many different ship weapons in the game; there are some that only damage enemy crews and others that can blast holes in enemy ships (which will then drain oxygen from the affected rooms); there are beam weapons, missiles, bombs, and lasers. Beam weapons usually offer large damage potential, but are weakened by shields; missiles and bombs are unaffected by shields but use a missile in your inventory; lasers often fire multiple shots to drain shields, but that offers more chances for missing.
Beyond all of this, there are several ships to play, and completing achievements for each ship unlocks a secondary layout. Each ship has its own starting equipment that will determine your strategy. For example, some ships start out with a teleporter while others start out with drone systems. Each ship has its own starting weaponry as well. Some ships might have a combination of missiles and lasers while others might have formidable beam weapons.
I've thrown many hours into this game, and it's still a delight to play, and the Advanced Edition offers a great deal of new content to revitalize the game for hardened veterans such as myself. The soundtrack is beautiful as well!

Being a huge fan of the CoH series and a top tier player I aim to give a balanced review and dispell the undeserved negative user reviews. Please note this is my first proper review and any feedback is appreciated =).
Do not be fooled by the hateful meta critic user reviews that score the game incredibly low. These are all largely due to patriotic Russians who exaggerate and claim the devlopers are Nazis as the campagin portrays the Soviet Union in a bad light. One such scene they are particularly angry about is when retreating russian soldiers are being shot down by their own machine guns. Granted Relic could have portrayed these horros of war better so that they could not be misinterpreted but they didn't set out to shame an entire nation. What the campagin really shows is the the story of the war through one man's eyes, showing the great bravey of the typical russian soldier under a ruthless poltical system and an equally terrifying invading German army. Which probably took more courage to do than that of soldiers from other countries.
For those who worry about Pay to win I can assure you it's entire nonsense. None of the new content is aimed to give players an edge in multiplayer. Obviously when it is first introduced there might be some balance issues here and there but these are quickly resolved. The idea behind DLC is to give players more varitey, be that with skins or commanders it's down to your personal preference and you are no way forced to buy it to be able to compete.
I can say that although CoH2 does not possess that same unique feeling that vcoh had, it is still a remarkable and incredibly fun game that continues to get better with each passing month. I have personally played over 600 hours on the beta and current version combined and I still find new ways to play and each game is never the same. You have to remember that the orginal CoH series has had 7 years of patching and improvements whereas CoH2 has only been out for less than a year. Therefore I believe it's unfair to judge the sequel so harshly at this stage. Within that time period the developers have added a huge range of content including; Steam Workshop with user created maps and mods, offical developer created maps, new units, commanders, leaderboards, chat rooms and with plenty more on the way.
Notable improvements over the original include: Better Graphics, Bulletins, Variety in choices that makes you stand out from the crowd ie commanders, skins faceplates etc, New Features like Cold Tech and True Sight which add more tactical elements. For instance you must now keep your troops warm during a blizzard by placing them near a fire or in a house otherwise they will freeze to death.
Now on to the game's flaws. Currently I believe the developers are pre-occuiped in bringing out more dlc content then spending the most time balancing the game and improving performance. Fair enough that they have to make money but I'd much rather they focused on tweaking the current game first then adding dlc like theatre of war missions. The variety in commanders is great and all but loads of the abilities have been reused in other commanders which takes away the uniqueness of certain commanders. Theres still quite some work to do before it can be considered a proper ESport as the replay viewer still needs additional features however it is constantly improving. Compared to something like Starcraft 2, CoH2 just doesn't have the player base or the resources unlike blizzard. I honestly think that if relic promoted the game and advertised it properly it would have generated a lot more interested. As it happens the advertising around the launch date was literally non-existent.
Conclusion
Score: 8/10 Current State
Although this game has got a way to go before it can be considered to be a worthy sequel to the first, I believe that over time it will get there and even surpass it's predecessor. Relic has been listening to user feedback and many of the new features are a result of this. So if your either a fan of the old game or looking to try out a proper real time strategy then look no further. I cannot recommend this game enough.

Yes, this is how I feel about every single Telltale Game since The Walking Dead: Season 1. After a lot of joyful hours in a setting, as dark and bitter as turkish coffee, the formula can't stand up for itself anymore.
Sure. The stories are still enjoyable, but does that justify a lacking "game" in every other aspect?
I highly doubt that.
But maybe we should start at the beginning.
You play different members of house Forrester, a smaller noble familiy risiding in the very north of Westeros. You fight for influence and survival.
Like in every other Telltale game you will make decision which  determine their fates. And while the previous games allowed some freedom, or atleast made you believe it, GoT doesn't even try.
No matter which decision you make, apart from a few cosmetic changes it all turns out the same. Luckily it gets better towards the end. In a game where you concentrate on the storytelling and makes austerities everywhere else... well you see where this is going. It just doesn't work.
Now you may ask: "But what is lacking?"
And my answer would be simple: "What is not lacking!?"
Gameplay is missing completly, what was a fresh take-on in TWD, is now showing it's ugly face. Pressing W from time to time to move forward or doing tedious Quick-Time-Event, which where already boring when they saw light in the 80's with the release of
, are by no means gameplay or in any way entertaining.
Now, I grant you that, this point is a matter of personal taste, but with a growing fund and a licence as big as GoT, I expected a better looking game. The comic style is charming sure and it was fitting for games like The Wolf Amongst Us.
But somehow I didn't feel the vibes in this interactive movie. Because, lets be clear, this is not a game!
Last point of what lacking in this this self advertised adevnture game: Riddles.
Every task, riddle or whatever you can do in adventure games you have to find out by yourself. But not here. Everything has just to be clicked in no particular order and the story unfolds. There is simply no challenge.
Let's make and example.
Now that my rant is over I will give you a short list of positive and negative aspects. Imagine it as a tl:dr if you like.
+ good voice acting
+ the story stays true to the ASOIAF formula of threachery, love and war
~ plot holes (Why the fudge would someone in King's landing care about land the size of a peanut which is almost every day frozen? And a handmaiden with no skill and no political power trying to use the Queen regent or Marge the skimpy clothes? No)
~ not enough freedom in choice in a game which concentrates on that
~ no progress in graphic presentation
- a missing game
- outdated gameplay mechanics (QTE)
- clunky controls
- no localisation
A good story wrapped into an uninspiring presentation which you still can have fun with if you ignore the obvious flaws.

I've played every Telltale game since the first Walking Dead season, and loved every one of them. So I was already primed to love this game, and it pains me to say that I cannot recommend it. These are some of my issues with this game, having played all but part of the last episode, which I put down because I just couldn't stand playing any more:
*SPOILERS*
- The obvious plot railroading that results from certain choices.  It's well-known already that Telltale games ultimately always end up in the same basic place regardless of your choices -- that's not my complaint here, as it can be done well (like in Tales from the Borderlands). The problem is that depending on your choices, the consequences simply do not make sense, both in terms of character consistency and logistics. Having this happen once or twice across the series wouldn't be so bad, but it would happen multiple times in some episodes. It was distracting.
- This is related to plot railroading, but is so egregious that it deserves its own section. If you take certain actions, the traitor's motivations make no sense, and leaving you scratching your head in confusion instead of feeling betrayed.
And the writing leads you to believe that the traitor truly believes what they're saying to you, which just ends up being confusing because it contradicts what you've actually seen happening in the story.
- The use of canon characters in certain situations eliminates all tension and makes you roll your eyes instead. Oh, you have the choice to stab or not stab a significant canon character? Oh boy, I wonder what's going to happen here!
- The last minute introduction of two new characters to the story felt shoehorned, random, and like a lazy setup to season 2
I truly wanted to like this game, but it ended up really disappointing me, especially after a wondeful first episode.

An interesting take on the Game of Thrones world.
You play as members of House Forrester, who are bannermen to House Stark, and the game starts just before the red wedding. Several members of the cast of the TV show lend their voices to their characters in the game, which gives a certain amount of credibility and believability.
Your choices whilst playing the game do affect somethings, but like all Telltale games there are times when choice is just an illusion and what's going to happen will happen no matter what you do. The game follows the general feel and atmosphere of the TV show, except it sometimes takes it even a step further when it comes to killing off characters. This can be hard to accept with your choices not always mattering, and you can feel you're just along for the ride and there's nothing you could of done to save characters you've grown attached to.
Despite this, it's nice to delve back into Game of Thrones while the TV show is on break, and Telltale always do a good job of creating engaging stories and characters. There's a good balance to the game, with times when you're in a political situation trying to make shrewd, difficult decisions, and other times when the swords are swinging and you have to press action button after action button.
With all episodes of season one now released, I would recommend picking it up when it's next on sale, and if you like Game of Thrones and Telltale games in general.
