I think my copy might be broken. There doesn't seem to be any game here, I just walked for about an hour and did pretty much nothing.
No but seriously, huge props for making a child control like a tank stuck in mud. I didn't think that was possible.
No, but being actually serious, I get it. They wanted to do something different. But this is not how you do it. Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons did something like this very well. It told a story without a single word of dialogue, it built characters, it had a unique mechanic, it was beautiful, and most of all it was fun. This is basically just a walking simulator, and that's all I can say about it. But to make it worse, it's not even a good one.
Hear me out here. If you're in it for the story, there's next to none. And what few bits there are don't make any sense. For some reason when you're playing with your friends a tree explodes and blinds you (and only you). It also doesn't burn you or anything, it just somehow completely blinds you. Already that's a pretty lousy story, and it only gets worse from there. Not going to go into details in case you do decide to play the game.
But say it's not about the story, say it's about the art. Fine. It's not ugly, but it's not amazing either. There's plenty of much better looking games out there. Hell, if you just want to look at pretty things, a museum or art gallery will serve you much better. Although even if the art was stunning, you'd have to drudge through the level incredibly slowly to reveal it all before you can even see it, and even then, you can only partially reveal most of it.
And the only other thing is the gameplay, which there isn't any. You just walk slower than you've ever walked in any other game. There's no way to walk faster. And while normally walking simulators are bad enough, you can't even see where you're going. So more often than not you'll end up walking into a dead end or bumping into a bush that you haven't revealed yet. Then you have to do the walk of shame back through the area you've already discovered, and boy, is it the longest walk you've ever done, because again, you walk incredibly slow.
Some of the 'objectives' also require you to go several minutes out of your way and backtrack. The only thing that could have made walking slowly worse is walking slowly through areas you've already been through. The only reason I can think of to make the player do this is to pad out time. In some cases, it's not pretty, it's not necessary, and it's not fun. It's just a two minute walk out of your way and a two minute walk back just for the sake of making the game longer.
So should you get it? No, absolutely not. Say what you will, tell me I can't appreciate "art", tell me I only like games where you're constantly shooting things. Reality is, there is no game here, it's a chore. Even if it was all artsy fartsy, it wouldn't be any less so if you could at least walk at a decent pace. It's just a shameless way of trying to pad out the game and make it feel longer than it really is, and shame on the developer for putting length over enjoyment.
If you want a game that does this type of thing well, go play Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. It did all the things this game tries to do but better, and there's some actually gameplay there.

I love Tower Defense games so much, and this game is REALLY FUN if you enjoy TD games.
One of the greatest features of this game is you have to actively send out "creeps" against your opponent while still maintaining your own tower defense line. You also have to manage your income in the form of mines (you can upgrade them task more miners)
The upgrading is very basic, max level 3 for towers; however, there is a good amount of diversity for the macro-upgrading trees. For this, you have to spend both money AND battle points. You get battle points by sending troops out (most likely to die), so playing defensively might not be the best option if your oppnent is beating you in gold and battlepoint revenue.
You can use your towers to make mazes for the creep to pass through, and the feedback showing exactly where the creeps will travel is really helpful. Admittedly, I've taken lessons from the AI's layout.
The learning curve is pretty good despite the extra mechanics, I think the only thing people need to be aware of is how critical getting battlepoints is - balancing your income is key. There is no point of having 10000+ gold if you're waiting on your battlepoints to upgrade your stuff.
Aesthetically, the game is very nice and charming. I'm used to towers getting the most insignificant aesthetic changes in old school TD games, but all of the towers here come with their own newer, badder look. The feedback for enemy health, movement, etc is very seamless - so you can still keep track of how much damage you're doing despite 100 catapults shrouding an enemy (pretty good tactic in all TDs actually - artillery for the win!)
For the price, I would definitely recommend getting it, especially if you're a fan of tower defense games!

Straight off, let's do away with the "Choose Your Own Adventure" tag.  It's
a CYOA, as the plot doesn't appear to truly diverge except at the very end; it's just aesthetic choices which are quickly railroaded back onto the same author-set track.  That's okay, though it harshly limits replayability.  With this in mind, if Markiplier brought you here,
The speed of the text and button reveals feel appropriate to the atmosphere, but it's painfully slow when you're just trying to power through a replay.  Although mashing the space key can speed this up a bit, I think this game would benefit from a variable speed/instant reveal option.
An appropriate atmospheric soundtrack is a pivotal 'make or break' point in multimedia literature, and Buried makes it.  The Wasteland/Fallout feel of it fits well.  Markiplier claims at a few points in his playthrough that the 'calm' soundtrack doesn't fit the immediate events.  I disagree; this is a text story, and jumping to frenetic music would be distracting and would stand out like a sore thumb.  This soundtrack doesn't stand out – it looms in the background.
The writing is respectable.  I would caution author Barry Napier to "kill his darlings," however; "haul♥♥♥♥♥quot; is a phrase which should never be used more than once in a work, and then only to demonstrate what sort of person a character is.  Beyond that, there's some over-reliance on horror/action tropes, occasionally to a degree which borders on breaking suspension of disbelief (ie: Overdrawn at the Blood Bank, Ax-Crazy, Aliens are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, Science Is Bad).  Mostly, though, the writing is convincing and interesting.  I hope to see more interactive fiction like this from Mr. Napier and Bromoco Games.
And then, there's the value.  That's not exactly a Triple-A price tag.  Overall I wouldn't call this a masterpiece, but it's well-made entertainment for substantially cheaper than watching whatever trash reboot Hollywood has most recently vomited at the cinema.  Save your money and get Buried instead.

Kind of like baseball; kind of like ping pong. This game takes both concepts and amps them up to the max.
The game is pretty well-done, and keeps it simple. Where other games might expand on their work to build a bigger game, the developers here found a good middle ground and stuck to their roots.
It sometimes gets repetitive to play due to the small selection of maps and characters, but that's the main draw of this game - the simplicity. There aren't a host of power-ups or camping areas; every arena is the same size and shape, and thus every match is identical and fair.
The online community is semi-active, but don't expect quick games - sometimes takes a few minutes during peak times, or hours during dead times. It has local co-op, so it's great for couch gaming, as well as regular co-op to play with friends online.  If you have a group of friends who enjoy 4 player arcade games, this is a good fit.

Funny how people can write reviews on a game which is not finished... So, after playing the WHOLE game, here is is my little review:
After episode 6, another hard decision has to be done: recommend or not? On the one hand, the adaption from the series os great. The character's really fit in as well as the story. And as usual, Telltale was able to write a story which is able to touch you to the heart. I do not know any other games, where I hate the villains just as much!
BUT, and here it comes, the game leaves me unsatisfied. The season is not closed, all plots remain open. That was done much better in TWD or TWAU. There the main plot ended but there were still some questions to be answered in further seasons. In addition, the decision I made infuenced the story in no way and the behavior of the characters only to a minor extend. That's one thnig I critize on all TT- games. Knowing, the decisions I make have no impact is taking a lot from the experience. So I was really surprised that the decision at the end of Episode 5 made a longer lasting difference!
The last thing I have to complain about is the story itself. not the overall story line, but the small bits. There are just to many holes in there. There are just too many unlogical things that happen (Warning: Spoiler coming):
- all episode: Any decisions Maegery does and her responds to my actions are not logical.
- End of episode 5: They await an ambush and still do nothing about it?
- End of episode 6: They plan an ambush but are unable to guard the door and the victim escapes, leading to the slaugher of nearly everyone?
And these are just the ones I can remember right now (had to wait too long for episode 6).
So, in the end I cannot recommend the game, though I enjoyed it to some point (especially my hate towards Ramsey got inflamed again). But it could have been so much better! That's why it gets thumbs down: to encourage Telltale to do it better!

Telltale's game of thrones looks and feels just like the previous adaptations of R.R Martin's series and takes a more personal and smaller scale angle on one specific house and its servants whose number of living occupants shrink by the day. The game excels at making you feel powerless against the enemeis of House Forrester, all the while building up your hatred towards them for those satisfying moments where you get yours and have your moment in the sun. The story is well paced and makes you feel for the characters. While many moments feel contrived to put unnecessary pressure on you to make you squirm while making decisions (particualrly in the finale), it still takes your choices into account. My main critisism is the liniar style of the story. You do get funneled into the same situations no matter what you choose and I often found that the actions i personally would have taken were not even listed as options you could take. I still remain optomistic for the second season as the first season was more or less a checklist for who you decide the characters are. Telltale seems set on really making things matter as the endings for episode 6 are very different and will largely affect your starting point in season 2, as with The Walking Dead's season 3. Whether or not you enjoy this game hinges very much on how much you enjoy Telltale's other games and in this case, how much you enjoy Game of Thrones. I personally enjoy both of these very much. Its not for everyone but it is very enjoyable for those who do like it. If you're looking for an uplifting experience or like a firm grip on their fate, this game isn't for you. If like me you like to set aside a few hours every month to get the absoloute **** kicked out of you to get you good and furious I reccomend this far more than other game adaptations of the GoT story.

While my general outlook on FPS games is typically very cynnical, I think by now my problem is less with the genre and more with the ever more dry and overrated Call of Duty series.
That being said, this game is a very creative one indeed. It feels like on odd mixture of Team Fortress 2 and Minecraft, two games that should NOT ever be blended by any other means. However, that idea is used very well here.
The premise of Block N Load is to build up a fortress to protect your team's 'cube' in the given time. Once the clock hits zero, both teams will duke it out in an attempt to destroy the other team's cube. You can either stay back and defend your own base, or hit the offensive front and attack the enemy.
There are multiple different characters that play differently, reflecting TF2's class system. However, I feel like some of them are a little unbalanced. My personal gripe goes to the 'Sniper', my usual go-to in a shooter, as his range is not what the title entails. Also, unlike TF2, the characters in Block N Load have a very malnourished personality to go with them, which is a bit disappointing, but not a gamebreaker.
The building aspect is very interesting. Your team can build up your fort to defend your cube by using blocks and special buildings like Turrets, Glue, Caltrops and Tiki Heads, which all serve a purpose of defense. This means that you can strategize with your fellow team members to create a nest egg that will surely keep your base safe while they're on the offensive.
Overall, while my previously mentioned distaste to most FPS titles, recent installments such as this one have steered away from the overly cliche, boring and unchanging Call of Duty and Battlefield series.
If this game were to improve, I'd ask that more options for weaponry be added to the game. Each character can only use a pair of weapons. This is ok, but the problem arises when the weapons cause players to single out classes for being terrible, because their weapons are no good. More weapon options on each character (similar to TF2) would allow more customization and a bit more balancing to this game. It needs some improvement, but it has so far met my criteria for an interesting game.
Final Mark: 3/5

"Presidente, an enemy tornado penetrated our defenses!"
After the disaster, you read this: Tropican Morale: INTACT
You will find this kind of fun in this game. Tropico 4 is the perfect game for the "would-be-generalissimo", where you can always try [and make some mistakes, while] to command your own "banana republic". Have you ever wondered "what if" all people got the same [low] wages, all to expend at that decrepit pub on the corner? So this is your game.
In a comparison to Tropico 3, it's the same experience after all. Some areas were improved, it's more stable on newer computers, and we have some slight changes to game mechanics. The expansion "Modern Times" add a high-tech [for Tropican Standards] taste and more funny jokes to the main game. It's a must buy if you liked the original.
Despites the derivative sense that a player of Tropico 3 can get about Tropico 4, new challenges, choices and jokes [they are plenty and really funny if you catch the real-world references] await the veteran. For a city-buliding game, it really delivers the experience of commanding the life of each inhabitant. It's a different and welcome approach in front of games with a broad scope like SimCity and CitiesXL.
The economic sphere is simple and it's possible to make a nice profit if one follow an economic chain, from tobacco crops to cigar factories, for example. In the welfare case, Tropicans are eager than most to accept dubious services, and have an inexplicable urge to visit churches and cathedrals [don't miss the joke on the Cathedral!]
If you want a middle-range priced game that will deliver some dozens of hours at a tropical utopic/dystopic paradise, this is, I wonder, the sole competitor in genre. Players of Tropico 3 will get less of it, but it is worth the price. Newcomers will easily find themselves immersed on this atmosphere. There are plenty of DLC for when you want to revisit "las islas".

Black Desert Online is an RPG similar to both ArchAge and EVE Online, in the way that you can act as a digital civilian instead of a quest-given pawn. This makes it an excellent time-killer and gives you the opportunity to focus on becoming a fisher, farmer or even horse breeder to participate in the game’s digital economy.
Role-playing games often get boring, especially when the only thing you can do is focus on quests and combat. I used to favor the genre over all others until I got bored of the same gameplay used in so many RPGs. Black Desert Online isn’t my favorite RPG by any means, but I find the virtual life aspect of it to be exciting.
The in-game economy is probably the best feature, aside from the outstanding visuals and overall sense of virtual living. Still, there are flaws and cons in this game that I will discuss, such as the terrible heads-up display and argument that this is just another pay-to-win game.
Some games confuse complex features with a disorganized and confusing user interface. Have you ever opened a new game and felt so overwhelmed that you instantly gave up? If so, then you might not want to waste your time with this game.
Once you make it through the first few hours of gameplay and pick up on all the controls you will be fine, but it’s a lot to take in at first and the game doesn’t necessarily introduce you to the key system properly.
I don’t typically read or listen to all the NPC chats in games like this, they are often dull, or even cheesy at times. Black Desert Online is no different, and I must say the characters hardly make sense half the time. You will likely skip all the conversations possible throughout the game because they aren’t worth paying attention to.
This game is all about living that virtual life, as it gives you the chance to be an entrepreneur and sell stuff! The in-game economy is awesome, you can do everything from becoming a farmer to becoming a salesperson.
So, what’s it like to be a farmer in Black Desert? Well, it’s actually better than I first imagined. You can have multiple gardens where you plant, water and fertilize your seeds. Farming is definitely too much work for one guy, but don’t worry because you can hire workers to help!
Wheat can be sold as is, or used to make wheat by adding mineral to it. Use the dough to create exotic wine for an NPC worker, or even making meat pie (for both yourself and your customers). A funny little part of the game is how your workers require so much alcohol to stay in perfect working condition.
As you can see, there are plenty of ways to make money in Black Desert Online. It’s almost like real life, except we’re almost all too lazy to do this entrepreneurial stuff outside of the game.
Fishing is an activity features in so many games, and while my favorite fishing experiences are from classics like Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Dark Cloud 2 – the fishing in BDO is probably the most convenient. This is because your character can fish on his or her own, until you have to replace your fishing pole because it will run out of stamina. When actively fishing, you will play a quick minigame as soon as you get a bite. It’s a brief moment of excitement and I personally feel like the developer did an excellent job on the fishing element to this game. If you need to step away from the computer to eat or answer a phone call, then automated fishing is perfect.
Once you’re done fishing you can dry and sell them on the marketplace, or use them to cook food in your house.
Black Desert Online has managed to do quite a few things differently than other RPGs, and although it’s not convenient, I like how the stashes are local. Let’s say you have hired a miner in Velia to mine for iron ore, but you’re in another city. Your stash of ore is in Velia with the miner, and the quickest way for you to transport it to another location is to buy or build a wagon. To me, it’s a matter of logic, and I like how the game made our stashes local so we can’t access the same stash from all over the virtual world.
While it is a very challenging game in the beginning and some won’t make it far before giving up, the feeling of building an empire and ‘making it’ is very rewarding. It won’t be long before you’re employing a ton of drunk workers and have all the silver you need for top quality armor.
There is so much more to this game than what I have mentioned so far, but it would take hours for me to discuss everything in the game. Instead, I encourage you to give it a shot if you like what you read, as I have already covered the cons in the beginning of this article. Be prepared for a few challenging hours in the beginning as it’s possible to completely miss the tutorial and get overwhelmed.
Combat in Black Desert Online is great, but what I find more interesting is how we can actually invest in cities and farms to increase the monster drop rates. In this game you can never have too many equipment-enhancing items so it’s definitely something you will want to do as you progress throughout the game.
There is also a currency called energy which you will use every single time you cut down a tree, craft an item or mine a rock. It’s aggravating for sure, as it will limit your activity in the game and you will often run out of energy as nearly everything you do requires it, (even negotiating with other traders to get a better price).

EDIT: Definitely think twice before buying; the below review is still relevant as there (sadly) hasn't been an update since July.
REVIEW: Um...wow. Where to begin. First: Magma Chamber is a cleverly designed take on classic "don't cross your own path" game play, and features vibrant reto graphics and sound effects that are cute and servicable.
However: It's still only on "Alpha v.02" despite being over a year on Steam, with a price tag of $4.99. The entire "game," consitsting of the tutorial levels and a first 'world' took me only 10 minutes. The second world has only two levels (well...actually three, but the third level is identical to the first). On level four, this happens (presumably when the game runs out of levels):
___________________________________________
############################################################################################
FATAL ERROR in
action number 1
of  Step Event0
for object obj_level_tile:
Unexisting room number: -1
at gml_Object_obj_level_tile_Step_0
############################################################################################
Pretty much says it all. As an aside, in the ten minutes I did play, I had to restart the game three times because it crashed twice.
I don't understand this! Magma Chamber could be such a charming little puzzle game, but it feels like it's been abandoned. The level design shouldn't take this long, because all the mechanics seem to be in place. If this had Workshop support, I'd be creating my @$$ off just to get some levels out there, but it doesn't. Sadly, there is NO way anyone should pay for this in its current state.
To the developer: PLEASE! Either keep going, or add a level editor. You have the makings of a wonderful little game here. Don't let it die like this.

The store page declares that the finished game will feature 7 worlds.  After 9 months of development with sparse updates, there is still only one (~15 minutes long), despite the developer's assurance in the forum that the game would be completed by now.

The game mechanics and the concept puzzles themselves are generally simple: Rae needs to get from point A to point B and you must either use her senses to find the right path, or find an object that will allow you to remove an obstacle.
Word of warning: This game is a story about dealing with loss and it will emotionally destroy you towards the end.

For a game that is all about being blind, Beyond Eyes surprises by being one of the most visually appealing titles I've played this year. It's not just its saturated, water-color-like graphics, although those are both charming and gorgeous. It's the "fade in" effect used to represent the protagonist's inability to "see" the world until it is within hands-reach. It's a gimmick, but one that not only stresses how lucky those of we who can see /are/, but also how beautiful the world /is/. Wandering through the world, never quite sure what is ahead of you, it makes the gameworld - and the real world - seem huge, terrifying, and still worth exploring. It is a very clever effect and it couldn't help but make me emphasize with the blind and appreciate my own eyes.
Unfortunately, that is the only thing this game has going for it. This is another "narrative game", aka a walking simulator, albeit one with almost no interaction, no characters, no puzzles, and no real story. It meanders aimlessly for about two hours as you lead the protagonist an her stroll through town and country in search of her loss kitty, before coming to a sudden and pointless conclusion. The game works hard to set up the proper mood and atmosphere, but ultimately it is all wasted: the game just ends when the girl <ROT13d for spoilers>qvfpbiref ure xvggl vf qrnq. There's no metaphor to this story, no meaning; it's a shaggy-dog tale that wastes all its set-up. Worse, the journey to that point far overstays its welcome; the first half-hour of the game is the wonderful appreciation of the visual (both the in-game graphics and the ability to see) but after that the lack of variety in gameplay and setting - it's just aimless wandering - quickly takes its toll. There is no threat, and no real sense of progression. As I said, the game did make me emphasize with the blind but that happened in the first 20% of the game; the game offered nothing new beyond that. The lack of any payoff at the end was just salt in the wound.
Beyond Eyes is a game that had so much potential; with its charming graphics and appealing protagonist, it could have told a powerful story. Unfortunately, like many "indie games", its a half-realized gimmick that looks clever at first but ultimately proves to be a waste of time and money.

On top of continuity issues I've seen other people mention (I noticed this most with the bullet count. Even if you give the gun to the person that fires off a shot, the gun still only has one bullet left if you choose to spare another character) there seemed to be a disconnect with the science the game is based on.
One of the characters references the idea that there's 10 dimensions, all well and good. Backed up by current theories in physics and quantum physics.
HOWEVER. Throughout the entire game there's a severe break in the basis in real-life understanding of logic. For one, we who live in a 3D space can see things on a 2D space, but those in a 2D space (in a theoretical house drawing on a sheet of paper) cannot even comprehend us. We in the 3D cannot enter a 2D space without crushing our bodies and just dying from the compression. Basically, the laws of nature of whatever dimention you're in are the laws you're subjected to, biology be damned.
While the idea of interdimentional Lovecraftian horrors sounds like a great premise, there was a lost opportunity for character motivation by ignoring that core theory of how the different dimentions work.
They shouldn't be able to operate on their own laws from their dimention, they should be severely limited and in INCREDIBLE pain after falling into our world. If they INTENTIONALLY invaded and were stated to do so, I might buy that they had some sort of tech to help them stabalize, but the game lore admits that they AREN'T stable and glitch in and out of existence.
I'd buy that they were acting like wounded, cornered animals, especially if it were established that 3D humans fired first and didn't bother to try to make contact or misunderstood that they were in pain. Instead, the lore makes them out to be entities of pure sadistic evil. While I could maybe buy that they don't think much of 3D entities just like we wouldn't think twice about burning a stick figure drawing, that attitude drastically changes when your body has to adjust to a plane where you can no longer move in a set of directions you had before.
Had a lot of promise, but more research would have made it a better horror experience. Endings could have used more elaboration, maybe an epilogue or something for the "good" endings. Which, I'll admit the choices only affecting character relations I'm on the fence about supporting.
On one hand, it feels unsatisfying, on the other hand however it fits into the Lovecraftian theme when dealing with entities far beyond our comprehension where at best you die quickly and at worst you go insane the more you learn until you finally kill yourself upon realizing that you cannot change anything or save anyone.
I'm still recommending the game, it was a fun experience. This is more constructive criticism for the devs for any future projects dealing with the same kind of subject matter.

How the interceptors had to chase the alien ships and sometimes they got away because the were faster. Okay.. it's time I gave a review to this game. Mind you, I haven't played for a long time yet but I have played enough to get a hang of the game's mechanics and feel. So here we go. First of all, it's a FANTASTIC game. Pay no heed to haters or negative remarks about this IP. Far Cry Primal is a fresh direction by Ubisoft.
The game itself is beautiful. It runs
with my GTX 980 in ULTRA settings at 1080p, 60fps. There are a few drops in fps at certain locations with heavy foliage and shadows but the lowest it has gone for me is 55 fps. Hence, that's no big deal. The developers have used the same DUNIA engine that they used with FC4. So you can say they have recycled some of the world's resources between FC4 and Primal. However, that's common practice in the industry these days and it's really not too bad. The game is still gorgeous in lower settings. I own an older PC with a GTX 580 in there and it looks just fine in medium settings. The world of Oros is huge. So there is plenty to do here and you can pretty much spend hours in just one portion of the map.
The game's story is very simple to understand. You are a caveman/tribesman from 10,000 BC who is trying to unite a group of people (Homo sapiens) called the Wenja to fight for survival against other humanoid beings; mainly the Udam (Neanderthals) who are cannibals. Like previous Far Cry games, you start with no weapon or skills and are then given learning missions to adapt to your world, which is called Oros. After the first couple of missions, you are given free rein to run along the wild terrain of Oros; hunting, gathering, exploring, killing, befriending, taming... etc. You also light bonfires which are the equivalent of safe houses in FC3 and FC4. You can store your gear here, rest until a certain time of the day etc. That's pretty much it. It's actually fun doing all the above :).
The gameplay feels alot like FC3 and FC4 and it's no surprise Ubisoft have gone with the 'tried and tested' method in their approach to Primal. It may disappoint many fans but honestly speaking, Primal couldn't have been made any different or better, And for the most part, it makes sense as to why Ubisoft stuck with the same mechanics. There however some new elements introduced to the game as well. Like Hunter Vision, which basically highlights the flora and fauna around you. This is no new element to gaming as a whole. Many other games had introduced this years ago. But for Primal, it works to have this option because for most of the game, you will be hunting or gathering something to improve your skill and upgrade your gear.
In conclusion, Far Cry Primal is
. With its gorgeous visuals, decent gameplay mechanics, good performance etc it's definitely worth it. The only area lacking is probably the barebones story. But then again, I never played a Far Cry game for its story and so did many others. Okay I gotta go back to the world of Oros. Ciao !

Great tactical game. In some ways its quite limited here and there compared to original X-Com titles of 80s, but overall, I'm loving this game.
Things to love about XCOM:
- replayability - every new game is fun in its own way
- hella lots of fun with 2nd wave options (after you complete the game and decide to start another one, some new options unlock, randomizing your game)
- great customization (make sure you get all DLCs for this)
- interesting missions, good map variety (Enemy Within, Slingshot DLCs)
- the game sometimes gets quite brutal, wiping your team in a matter of seconds. Now try playing in Ironman mode, where you can't load! While this feels horrible, it forces you to learn your sub-optimal strategy won't work well in higher difficulties. Which is a good thing, overall.
Things to note:
- losing soldiers makes you feel bad
- enemies hitting with unrealistic odds every now and then
- your soldiers may miss 3-4 shots with 80-99% accuracy, one after another (don't worry, 100% shots always hit, although they may miss even at point-blank if its not 100%)
- some game mechanics seem weird and take time getting used to
- loading a game won't make your soldier hit instead of missing. More than that - your soldier may actually miss instead of hitting!
- skipping a DLC mission will make it never return (in Enemy Within), so don't skip it. It comes back in Enemy Unknown. Launcher treats these as separate games.
- some bugs 3 years after release. Nothing game-breaking, though.
Overall - I absolutely LOVE this game and highly recommend anyone who played Xcom of the past or any tactical shooters. Turn based tactical shooters.

So far it seems like a good game. The new setting is good step for the series, keeping things fresh.  I've spent 64.99 on the game(USD) and it feels worth it. I'll break a few things down that might be of interest and then maybe you can decide:
The map is recycled, kind of, from Far Cry 4. You'll probably only notice it when looking at the map itself(the overhead map). It's a little irritating, but with the new assets, wildlife, and gameplay style, it doesn't get in the way. Look around Oros and tell me it doesn't look have an original vista everywhere you look. If you disagree, you are blind or have been looking in different spots than me and I am wrong. That's okay, it's a big map. And if you turn off the minimap, it might seem a little less charted.
The combat is fun. Visceral, weighty. It doesn't exactly satisfy my pyschologically indicting cravings for dismemberment and brutality but until The Elder Scrolls goes the way of Fallout's gore, or Conan: Exiles arrives, I don't think anything will. It's fine, you'll probably enjoy it. I found it refreshing, watching neanderthals go flying eight feet after I speared them in the head from twenty yards away. Arrows are a little wonky if you turn off the reticule. Animals seem valuable in combat, or at least, can be, if you play on hard or expert. Don't play on Normal, or Easy. That's no fun. There's also craftables I haven't really delved into, because I guess Cavemen had bombs.
Regarding the story, or at least, its presentation, I felt fine. Unlike some of our Homo-floresiensis friends still among us on the forums, I have long since mastered the ability to read, and have little issue with the subtitles used to convey the characters speech. In fact, I liked picking apart the consistency of Ubisoft's constructed language, and their attention to the simple grammatical patterns that would seem(semi-plausibly) used by tribes of the time.
In regards to it running, it seems well done. I get sixty FPS at near max settings(turning down shadows and fog to "normal" level, everything else on High). Even maxed out it carries at sixty for most of the game, unless there's some rivers kicking up mist. For the record here is my build:
R9 280X
ASUS Mobo(the model eludes me)
i7-4650k
16 GB Ram, DDR3
500 GB Samsung SSD which is what I'm running the game off of.
Running at 1920x1080.
Did I miss anything?
My drivers are up to date at 15.30.
Oh, it sounds nice with Surround Sound too.
Anyway, those are my first impressions. It seems like a fun game. There's some more survival style mechanics, like the ability to freeze to death, that look cool but I have not yet experienced. So, take it as you will. If you read all of this you must not be a cro-magnon, or you have mastered the ability to blend into our society seamlessly without causing a problem despite your apparent illiteracy. Maybe you just don't post on the forums. It's okay, I'm not planning on hunting you to extinction.
In either case, if you're interested, take a chance, buy the game. If you're worried about compatibility with your system, search around a little, maybe make a post(but stay civil). I thought it was worth it.

FTL is a fairly tough roguelike strategy game. Roguelike in the sense that every adventure is randomized and death is not uncommon.
It is unique in the fact that it is more like a management sim than an RPG, even though it does have RPG-like elements common to roguelikes. In combat you have to manage doors, power to subsystems, weapon firing patterns, crew movement and positioning. If you're having trouble managing the chaos that is Your Ship there's a pause feature for combat which lets you command your crew and manage your ship with little stress and then unpausing to watch your actions play out. You'll be using this feature liberally.
The great thing about this game is that it allows you to deal with situations in many different ways, from fire extinguishing, combatting enemy ships and fighting boarders. You'll be learning to use simple systems to do many things. However, all of that comes with experience.
Be warned: The game is difficult on the normal difficulty. It might get frustrating later on, however if you have a good strategy you can get to the end easily even though it isn't guaranteed, as it does require both luck and experience. Luck will be a big factor in your game, but experience will allow you to make the best of what you've got (if you don't get totally screwed over, which happens in roguelike games).
The game allows a player to finish in a single playthrough, but carries high replayability.
Outside of gameplay, the graphics are charming and to the point. Sound is simple, clear and gives you a good idea of what's going on. The music is superb. And the control scheme is pretty simple.

Block N' Load is a great concept and executed well.
However, a low player-base and the inability to queue up with a full team, or seemingly anyone, completely destroys this experience. Block N' Load is a team based game where the player can choose one of a multitude of classes including Engineer, Soldier, Sniper, etc. The entire point of the game is to protect your base, represented by an energy cube, and simultaneously destroy the enemy's base. In addition to an FPS aspect, you can also mine and build defenses in block-form, as well as build things like turrets and traps, depending on your selected class. The best way to give people an idea of this game is imagine TF2 met Minecraft.
This game was fun when I first purchased it several months ago, but the low-player count led the developers to make the game Free-to-play, which I personally wouldn't mind except for that fact that it doesn't appear I got any of the "perks" they promised to the players who actually paid for the title.
In addition, the developers, likely in a desperate attempt to try to balance the game, limited the ability to queue up with your friends, allowing only 2 players to play together, as a 5-man-team would destroy any randoms with zero communication. This however doesn't even seem to work, as the last time I tried to play with a friend, solo-queueing was the only option available. This "temporary" implementation doesn't feel so temporary anymore.
Unfortunately, Block N' Load had a lot more potential than it ultimately delivered. I thoroughly enjoyed the concept and technical possibilities of mounting attacks and defenses, which few games seem to offer nowadays, but the failure to maintain an active playerbase and the rocky transition to Free-To-Play as well as the queueing limits leads to me recommending you skip this one.

Black Desert Online is an RPG similar to both ArchAge and EVE Online, in the way that you can act as a digital civilian instead of a quest-given pawn. This makes it an excellent time-killer and gives you the opportunity to focus on becoming a fisher, farmer or even horse breeder to participate in the game’s digital economy.
Role-playing games often get boring, especially when the only thing you can do is focus on quests and combat. I used to favor the genre over all others until I got bored of the same gameplay used in so many RPGs. Black Desert Online isn’t my favorite RPG by any means, but I find the virtual life aspect of it to be exciting.
The in-game economy is probably the best feature, aside from the outstanding visuals and overall sense of virtual living. Still, there are flaws and cons in this game that I will discuss, such as the terrible heads-up display and argument that this is just another pay-to-win game.
Some games confuse complex features with a disorganized and confusing user interface. Have you ever opened a new game and felt so overwhelmed that you instantly gave up? If so, then you might not want to waste your time with this game.
Once you make it through the first few hours of gameplay and pick up on all the controls you will be fine, but it’s a lot to take in at first and the game doesn’t necessarily introduce you to the key system properly.
I don’t typically read or listen to all the NPC chats in games like this, they are often dull, or even cheesy at times. Black Desert Online is no different, and I must say the characters hardly make sense half the time. You will likely skip all the conversations possible throughout the game because they aren’t worth paying attention to.
This game is all about living that virtual life, as it gives you the chance to be an entrepreneur and sell stuff! The in-game economy is awesome, you can do everything from becoming a farmer to becoming a salesperson.
So, what’s it like to be a farmer in Black Desert? Well, it’s actually better than I first imagined. You can have multiple gardens where you plant, water and fertilize your seeds. Farming is definitely too much work for one guy, but don’t worry because you can hire workers to help!
Wheat can be sold as is, or used to make wheat by adding mineral to it. Use the dough to create exotic wine for an NPC worker, or even making meat pie (for both yourself and your customers). A funny little part of the game is how your workers require so much alcohol to stay in perfect working condition.
As you can see, there are plenty of ways to make money in Black Desert Online. It’s almost like real life, except we’re almost all too lazy to do this entrepreneurial stuff outside of the game.
Fishing is an activity features in so many games, and while my favorite fishing experiences are from classics like Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Dark Cloud 2 – the fishing in BDO is probably the most convenient. This is because your character can fish on his or her own, until you have to replace your fishing pole because it will run out of stamina. When actively fishing, you will play a quick minigame as soon as you get a bite. It’s a brief moment of excitement and I personally feel like the developer did an excellent job on the fishing element to this game. If you need to step away from the computer to eat or answer a phone call, then automated fishing is perfect.
Once you’re done fishing you can dry and sell them on the marketplace, or use them to cook food in your house.
Black Desert Online has managed to do quite a few things differently than other RPGs, and although it’s not convenient, I like how the stashes are local. Let’s say you have hired a miner in Velia to mine for iron ore, but you’re in another city. Your stash of ore is in Velia with the miner, and the quickest way for you to transport it to another location is to buy or build a wagon. To me, it’s a matter of logic, and I like how the game made our stashes local so we can’t access the same stash from all over the virtual world.
While it is a very challenging game in the beginning and some won’t make it far before giving up, the feeling of building an empire and ‘making it’ is very rewarding. It won’t be long before you’re employing a ton of drunk workers and have all the silver you need for top quality armor.
There is so much more to this game than what I have mentioned so far, but it would take hours for me to discuss everything in the game. Instead, I encourage you to give it a shot if you like what you read, as I have already covered the cons in the beginning of this article. Be prepared for a few challenging hours in the beginning as it’s possible to completely miss the tutorial and get overwhelmed.
Combat in Black Desert Online is great, but what I find more interesting is how we can actually invest in cities and farms to increase the monster drop rates. In this game you can never have too many equipment-enhancing items so it’s definitely something you will want to do as you progress throughout the game.
There is also a currency called energy which you will use every single time you cut down a tree, craft an item or mine a rock. It’s aggravating for sure, as it will limit your activity in the game and you will often run out of energy as nearly everything you do requires it, (even negotiating with other traders to get a better price).

WARNING: Seizure-inducing visuals. Especially if you're a point-monger and turn the visual effects up to 200% for the bonus it gives you.
That being said, this is a lovely, simple, "I'm going to spend the next few hours blowing s*** up" game. Games like this usually see me muting the ingame music and playing my own list of songs, but rejoice! The level selection is actually a file system where you can pick your music! Remember that [..] means "go back," because they threw in a hint of DOS syntax.
The influence the song has on the gameplay is, as some negative reviews mention, pretty low. This is not a rhythm game where the beats of the music are literally what you should be pressing. Instead, the intensity of the music correlates to how fast projectiles move, how fast enemies move, and how much laser you shoot. Calm sections give you a chance to breathe, while intense sections turn the screen white and make your eye doctor cry.
There's some depth to it with the perks, upgrades, and DLC missions involving different player ships with different properties. I also enjoy the leaderboards, as low on them as I am. Adds some reason for a competitive player to stick around with the game and try to max out their scores as much as possible.
It really is a fun, small game though, and I recommend it if you want to blast your own music while shooting things with an obscene light show of lasers.

So, I was fascinated by this imperfect story and found myself really wanting to keep moving forward to see what happened. Sure, it's not a Hugo Award winner, but I'm not so cynical that I didn't enjoy it. It was a lot of fun.
However: The vast majority of choices don't seem to really have any serious consequences. I've gone back and replayed it twice, and, with a couple of exceptions, you end up in the same place no matter what you have chosen. However, there are a couple of life-and-death decisions and a decision or two that make other characters irritable for awhile.
Overall, I would have liked the game a bit more if there had been more serious consequences to the decisions made and more endings than just the 2 to 4 (depending on how you look at it). Most decisions don't really do anything and some of the decisions that the game claims are important are only acknowledged with a sentence or two later. It's almost as though the writer had intended a larger work, but then condensed everything down to where there were really no wrong turns.
Still, I enjoyed the game and the story, and I even bought a copy for my little boy to play on his account. He was convinced even the most minor decisions were monumental and really enjoyed the game as well.
Thumbs up for me.

Great tactical game. In some ways its quite limited here and there compared to original X-Com titles of 80s, but overall, I'm loving this game.
Things to love about XCOM:
- replayability - every new game is fun in its own way
- hella lots of fun with 2nd wave options (after you complete the game and decide to start another one, some new options unlock, randomizing your game)
- great customization (make sure you get all DLCs for this)
- interesting missions, good map variety (Enemy Within, Slingshot DLCs)
- the game sometimes gets quite brutal, wiping your team in a matter of seconds. Now try playing in Ironman mode, where you can't load! While this feels horrible, it forces you to learn your sub-optimal strategy won't work well in higher difficulties. Which is a good thing, overall.
Things to note:
- losing soldiers makes you feel bad
- enemies hitting with unrealistic odds every now and then
- your soldiers may miss 3-4 shots with 80-99% accuracy, one after another (don't worry, 100% shots always hit, although they may miss even at point-blank if its not 100%)
- some game mechanics seem weird and take time getting used to
- loading a game won't make your soldier hit instead of missing. More than that - your soldier may actually miss instead of hitting!
- skipping a DLC mission will make it never return (in Enemy Within), so don't skip it. It comes back in Enemy Unknown. Launcher treats these as separate games.
- some bugs 3 years after release. Nothing game-breaking, though.
Overall - I absolutely LOVE this game and highly recommend anyone who played Xcom of the past or any tactical shooters. Turn based tactical shooters.

As a guy who almost never likes fighting games due to the repetativeness from game to game I find Lethal League such a breath of fresh air and also exitment. Every match is a quick game of reflexes and quick thinking as well as honest strategy against both your opponent(s) and the ball all while still trying to simply predict and track the ball all together. The result is just a fun chaotic match that's quick and easily finished but also intense and engrosing.
I also love the urban style given to the levels and especially the characters. Each character looks unique and cool as well having a nice anime Inspired look that, while risky, paid off and is a perfect example of taking inspiration and not simply copying it.
The Controls could be slightly quicker but it's a small complaint. I only wish for more characters in the future or maybe simply a sequel. As well I'd also like to see a lot more levels to choose from as they are more just backgrounds. I would like to see some more usage of stage design and maybe the incorporation of obstacles or platforms later down the line.
All in all a terrific and tight game that, while simple and small, has succeeded in what I think it meant to set out to do. To anyone tired of the regular fighting genre or want a really nice cheap 4 person brawler to play with friends I can't think of a better game than Lethal League. Hope to see you on the battle stage.

At the surface I would recommend this game without a second thought. But that's when it all changes, when I give the game a second thought. And it is in doing that exact action which has made me say I would not recommend this game.
I'll try to keep this as spoiler free as possible. For starters, the game is nothing more than a "re-skin" of the Game Of Thrones story in relation to the Starks. Are they mentioned in this game? Yes. But the family you play as basically meets the same constant fate as the Starks time and time again. Which leads to a boring, weak and predictable story. Then you get to what SHOULD be the bread & butter for a Telltale game. Your choices and how much they matter. I laugh at that claim this time. Since 9 out of 10 times what you do makes no difference aside for maybe prolonging the predetermined outcome. The other time is the rare moment it actually results in you selecting your own path. But unfortunately those moments don't ever seem to be big choices in the end. Simply small little side stories that lead you down a different path to the same final outcome.
There also seems to be the odd technical issue here and there. Moments of framerate drops.  Unresponsive controls, I push left and the character walks forwards (either because of a bug or oddly placed invisible wall). Some of the animation is less than fluid as well. All in all, for a game that took this long to come to completion...it's just all unacceptable. I wanted to love this, I really did. I just can't.

Definetly one of the best RTS games out there, graphics are good, campaign is basically a massive multi-faction tutorial and the skirmish mode is equally as satisfying. It's quite simple compared to many others and thats what makes it great. It really is alot like the original starcraft but with a much more interesting campaign and factions that have completely different playstyles. Each faction playes differently than the other, and each faction has many different ways to play within itself, because of having such a vast selection of specialized units available. You can rush with basic infantry all the way to the end of the game if your fast enough, or play the defensive and build mega units that crush everything in their way. The GOO faction really puts a twist on how an RTS can be played and Im glad someone finally changed the genre up.
The default Hotkeys are kind of confusing and there's just too many of them, its' a good idea to play the tutorial missions and then go and re-map the hotkeys that you use the most into one spot on the keyboard.

It keeps playing while you are AFK so you can take a break, call your parents, spend time with your gf so she don't get mad at you, and you know like, live a life, go to work, get your homework done. I mean that part is optional, but you can do a lot and barely have the game open. AFK fishing is pretty cool, because you know... fishing. You can unlock a system of nodes and send workers to gather resources on job nodes. Nothing you do AFK is super lucrative until later.
AFK King
More about nodes. CP exp is the only thing you gain from questing. There is also combat Exp that you only get from killing monsters. And then every kind of skill exp. You use CP to unlock nodes, which greatly effect how you personally contribute to the game's economy. Nodes effect everything from trade, to fishing, to where you can send your SLAVES, I mean workers sorry, you really don't pay them though so guess welfare to work?
The crafting system is pretty neat. You have to buy houses and send your workers to benches in workshops within the houses you buy. Nothing you craft is going to be worthwhile to craft until you get really far into the crafting node system. Most things you are better off selling the crafting resources. Main thing you will be doing for crafting early on is making things for your own use. Some resources that your workers gather it is worth it to process just to get your skill levels up for processing, you will have diminished returns though.
The economy of the game is the real draw. It is a living breathing economy. Everything on the market has a fixed high low sell price that seems to change based on trends, not really sure about this.. There is a trading game built into it which plays a bit like port royale or patrician. I use this description loosely. I haven't used the trade system much, so I just go off of the little research I have done.
Mounts are pretty amazing. You catch your own horses in the wild. But you can buy them too. You'll also make wagons to transport goods for the trading game. Ships are new apparently. There is a boat you can fish from that looks hard to craft. All the vehicles and mounts can be equipped with items that increase stats and effect cosmetics.

Calling Grim Dawn a Diablo clone is somewhat disingenuous. It’s enough of its own beast to stand apart. That’s not to say that the game’s roots are not apparent but it’s clear enough that a lot of love and care went into creating a game that borrows the very best from other ARPGS, and brings them together into a unique and thoroughly enjoyable gaming experience.
While the debate rages as to which title owns the ARPG crown; between Diablo 3 (polished to such a point that it’s practically sterile and simplistic) and Path of Exile (nailing the mood but suffering from a clumsy interface and a bewildering skill progression tree) Grim Dawn is the dark horse that threatens to upset the cart.
In short, Grim Dawn is a real gem. The game’s multi-class skill progression is smart. The story is compelling, unpacking through exploration. And the atmosphere is compelling yet grittier than a speedo full of sea sand. Strongly recommended.

I haven't watched any of Game of Thrones in my life and am not familiar with any of it. I did enjoy it but at the same time I have felt that in recent times Telltale has really gone off the road of quality. Compared to Wolf Among Us, Borderlands and TWD seasons, this is by far the worst.
It does a good job building things up but then as you may have seen from other reviews, the finale is rushed and quite a disappointment. Any time there is a sliver of hope it's thrown away in a sloppily contrived subplot that ends with one of the main characters dead.
This season was made with the intention to be milked; and I am not a cow. The ending is literally like the beginning, setting up for the next season. If this was a show, maybe that would be acceptable, though in general I hate it when stories are not conclusive. I'm not talking about side cliff hangers but the main storyline is literally incomplete, and it has the most episodes of any of TT's games.
The choices generally don't really matter either. You can tell simply just from the dialogue and the dialogue choices that the writers took shortcuts to 2-for-1, giving the same responese regardless your dialogue choice, as well as many dialogue choices repeating the same general consent or refusal to something.
:  This was made to get customers hooked to be invested to pay into more seasons to get incomplete tales, not to tell a good story.
EDIT:  I have now seen all 5 seasons of GoT. And I can say for sure if I watched the show first, I would hate this game so much. A lot of this game is a straight parallel if not a rip off of the show. The family you follow in this game is similar to the Starks, and you go to all the same places you would in the show. Occasional main characters from the show do have their cameos or play a role to tickle the hardcore fans of the show.
There are also discrepancies with the show, like there are some characters that are supposed to be dead already at certain points in the story, according to the show, but very much alive in the game.
Lastly, the Forrester's(the family you play as) house sigil looks eerily similar to Gondor's from LotR; Blasphemy!

Tower Wars offers a unique take on the tower defense strategy genre by incorporating the standard set of towers, upgrades, and abilities, with a competetive gaming approach. Here are the Pros and Cons:
Pros:
1. Steampunk-style art offers a new take on the tower defense genre.
2. Gameplay is straightforward and easy to pick up.
3. Different levels and a hex based grid allows for a unique game each time you play.
Cons:
1. Content-wise, the game lacks diversity. There is only one set of units and the only changes in style between opposing players is color.
2. MONUMENTALLY long loading times for a small game will make you wonder if the game has frozen while spinning up a map.
3. Limited replayability as the playerbase is lacking for matchmaking/competetive play.
Summary: At its current 2.00 sale price, Tower wars is a definite buy. Even if you only get about 10 games out of it before moving on to another title, this game does offer some intense competetive play - provided you have the patience to wait through the loading times.

Overall a great addition to the series, though there is not all that much new stuff that makes it worthwile if you already own Tropico 3. I definitely recommend this game, but I'd also like to point out some weaknesses.
One of the biggest selling points for me is that they got rid of Juanito and that guerilla chick and replaced them with less annoying characters. Their lines get repetitive pretty quickly, but it's still an improvement.
I was a bit disappointed about the general difficulty of the missions: the majority of the game is way too easy.
At one point I intentionally tried to screw up and to get my people or the military to start an uprising against me - and it was almost impossible, even though I didn't provide any housing, hospitals, food and kept everyone to the minimum possible salary. People were still happy enough to give me a 40% popularity rating.
Even if you run out of money, there is usually always a way to still turn it around in the end and come out ahead.
The new disasters like tornados and volcanos are a nice gimmick, but they are not really threatening enough. You get refunded most of your loss if you have a halfway good relationship to the EU. And getting disliked by other countries is really difficult to accomplish too. Some people may die during a disaster, but you get so many new citizens with every ship that it doesn't really matter.
It's also quite easy to find a general strategy on how to manage your island which will work in every mission. You will find yourself repeating the same build patterns again and again and the scripted events during missions usually don't require you to change anything about it, since there is no time limit involved in the first tasks. So you can always establish a working economy before you even go for the actual missions.
The fact that you play 2 missions on each of the 10 islands throughout the campaign doesn't help with the replayability. Due to the general layout and placement of natural resources on each island will you probably find yourself placing structures in the same place as the first time when you get to play on the same island again.
I can't recommend the DLCs (except for Modern Times), because they add structures that ruin the gameplay balance even more and make things even easier than they already are.

An utterly gorgeous game: sheer delight.
Unfortunately, this stunning visual engine has not been used to deliver a good story. The narrative is thin and clumsy, delivering emotional subtlety with the delicacy of a sledgehammer.
We get it: for a young girl to become blind is sad and lonely. Is there really no other dimension the developer could have brought into this?
As others have commented, there is no significant gameplay -- it's pretty much a pure walking simulator -- and it's especially slow moving, though that slowness contributes to the delight of having the world unfurl gently before you like a watercolor painting.
If you're very patient and interested in a meditative experience, you will enjoy it. However, I think the premise has attracted people like me because there seemed to be potential to use technology to tell a story. And it doesn't deliver, hence the thumbs down.
Finally, thank you, devs, for supporting Linux!

I've been wanting to play this game for a while. Then, when I finally got the chance to, I didn't want to anymore.
To be totally honest, I don't like I have the liberty to rat on this game... even though I already did. I hate IGN and their so-called "reviews" of Another World and Spec Ops: The Line. So when I saw them give this game a 5.5, I felt like I wanted to give this game a high review just to spite them, but I can't do that in good conscience, because I legitimately did not enjoy this game.
Now, don't get me wrong, I don't hate Beyond Eyes. There are plenty of things I both love and hate about this game. For one, the concept is pretty unique. I haven't seen a game use draw-distance so creatively since the original Silent Hill games. I also think the watercolor graphics give the game a very storybook-y feel.
I also enjoyed how the story shifts beyween expectation and reality in Rae's head, and visualizes it well for the player to understand how this blind girl percieves the world around her. The ending also makes a strong point on understand the world you live in, and growing away from assuming you know everything from what little experience you currently have.
Now, onto the things I didn't like. First and foremost, I HATE how slow Rae walks. It's unbearable, especially when you might need to backtrack, because she barely treads across the chapters you control her in. Along with that, there is some ridiculous backtracking in Beyond Eyes. There was a dog blocking my path in Chapter IV. The solution? I had to go back to Chapter III and befriend the dog that walked be into a rock and caused me to fall over. The game didn't hint at that at all. I had to personally go find a guide that told me what I did wrong. That's more than just being unintuitive. That's being flat-out stubborn with your player.
I also didn't get past the first chapter for a little bit, because I didn't realize that a green wisp around objects meant that you could interact with said objects. The game could use at least a little more text to explain how you can interact with stuff or when a dog is actually friendly (even though everything else told me he was going to bite my f***ing face off).
If what I just said didn't faze you, then go ahead and get this game. I'm sure you'l enjoy it. It certainly is a unique title, but everything else in the gameplay just keeps me from wanting to like it more than I actually do. It's slightly similar to Journal, in that regard. I'm giving it a 6/10.

I feel pretty conflicted about this game, but I'm slightly leaning towards saying yes for recommendation.
The essential game mechanicals hasn't changed too much from Far Cry 4, but has added a few new elements to the game such as beast taming and having a beast side kick. These altered the gameplay quite a bit, it's definitely worth at least trying the game for what's new.
Because the game takes place in 10,000 BCE, classic far cry features such as vehicles and firearms are obviously not present. This is pretty bothersome for me, as you are now required to run from place to places across the maps. Although the game now has a lot of outposts/fast travel checkpoints, this is still quite tedious. You can unlock a skill that lets you ride your larger beasts, but that's not unlocked until quite a few hours into the gameplay typically.  I'm also not a huge fan of non-firearm type weapons such as spears, arrows, and clubs, but they can still work somewhat well after practicing for a bit. Although the game has tons of main missions available, the overall story and plot development is a bit lacking to me.
Overall, I'd say buy the game when it's discounted on sales. The gameplay can get quite boring pretty fast for a lot of players who aren't big on stone age weapons, but it's still definitely fun to play for a few hours at the very least. The game may seem boring at first, but it gets more fun when you've added more citizens to your village.

I have to say, this game was definately a creative pile of work. It provides a free-roaming atmosphere in a satisfyingly large map. You can choose to either fight aliens, upgrade cars and smack people on the sidewalk with them, upgrade your armoury, or simply even gear yourself out with some spanking new clothes. It is a fantastic combination of mission work and casual living in an absolutely mad simulated world. The storyline provides hours of varied gameplay, took me a week non-stop. The free-roam provided currently another week. There is a massive amount of DLC selection which costs only a £2 average, and the content increase definately makes it worth it. I would recommend this game if you like the GTA series. I would personally buy this at full price, even though I bought the GOTC edition on discount offer.

I can say there are definitely improvements to be made, and I do expect, after all of this criticism, that the choices will have more impact in the sequel to this game.  I love this game for the story and (IMO) interesting characters.  The story it is trying to tell is very obvious, it is one about characters in a desperate situation that keeps becoming more dire, with no signs of hope (or barely any) that things will improve.  The ending wasn't a rushed as many claim it was, I mean, what did you expect, another hour of footage, showing us where the characters had all ended up?  I mean, of course it had to end on a cliffhanger, all of the telltale games do.  If these developers are to continue generating profit, they need to leave open room for sequels, although this had to have been the most cliff-hangery ending that any telltale game has given us.  I am hoping the next game with conclude with a satisfying ending, a sad ending, an ending that makes us angry, multiple versions of those endings, too.  The sequel should allow us to impact the way the story moves along more than we were able to in this game.  There are moments when you realise how powerless your character was to do anything, there is either never a right dialogue option or only one "GOOD" dialogue option, that has a slightly better outcome than the other three dialogue options.  There are plenty negative things to say about this game, I'll give you that, but there is enough good to balance it out.  I will be buying the sequel to this game, and call me a fanboy, but I plan on enjoying it as best I can.

If you're an RTS buff, I definitely recommend this game.

I'd call this game a "quick" RTS - one where the matches are over pretty quickly and instead of spending a lot of time on base building, expansion, and resource gathering prior to all out war, it's one where you're generally going to build up and engage pretty quickly with the intent of obliterating your opponent. What sets this game apart, and makes it superior, is the goo itself as a faction.  It has a delightfully simple but well-designed, well-balanced, and just fun to play mechanic.  The Humans and Beta are your typical Quick style RTS fare, and play about the same as most other RTS games you've played.  The Shroud has its own set of interesting, fun mechanics as well, but imho, the goo is just awesome and fun.

I have this game through GOG and I have to say after playing it only to level 42 it is a deeply satisfying and old-school arpg. It takes the things I love about titan quest, diablo, and others and blends them seamlessly together into an addictive and highly replayable game. Like Titan Quest, you have multiple classes, one you get at level 2 and the other at level 10, which you can mix and match to create your own class. This system was deep and incredibly fun in Titan Quest but was very slow to get rolling at the start. Grim Dawn fixes this, from my first moments in the game I always felt like a badass. The devotion system allows for even deeper customization and access to devotion skills which add additional effects to your base skills such as shooting out life leeching bat fangs or summoning clouds of swirling death around your character. Overall I would recommend this game if you really liked Titan Quest as it most closely resembles that game, but any fan of ARPGs would have a good time. The only downsides I have is that if you run it in fullscreen, when you exit it's likely to blackscreen your computer. Not too much of an issue since you can just do windowed borderless, and the second is that this games seems to demand a lot of graphical power. My old 770 stuttered like crazy and just didn't work very well with the game and my 1070 kicks its fans up to a noticable speed when playing. Not too sure why that is but something to be aware of.

Half Life 2 holds a special place in my heart, it is truly the first game I bought from Valve and the first game that forced me to use another program just to run it, not the finest moments at the time considering you only had 2 - 4GB of ram to spare at the time and Steam was truly a memory hog back in those days mind you.
But the moment I laid my eyes on the trailer of Half Life 2, the graphics blew me back, the action was wild and it was something completely new and refreshing newer before seen.
I bought this game on DVD back in the olden days of Windows XP monstrousity gaming desktop PC's and IBM still owned ThinkPad.
I remember quite frankly having such a hard time to run this game smoothly on my ancient nVidia 440MX and suffered even more trying to run it on a ThinkPad T41p with only ATi Radeon Mobility 9600 having a staggering 32MB video memory.
But having it on ultra high did not matter, it was the gameplay that truly shocked me the most, the fun to be had with such a simple linear story is amazing only Valve could pull through with such and yet so simple it may have been it worked really well, the story was well told and well driven with action paced amazingly done and puzzles to solve.
The game also was fun to replay despite being linear and for its time linear games usually became boring after a few runs but Half Life 2 was different.
While Half Life 2 truly brought a new era of gaming to the board, its lenghty linear story still in the minds of men in their 20s and 30s today the game also brought something else, modding.
Never in the history of video games has there been so much creativity around Half Life 2, so many mods that puts indie games today to shame, entire new games made as mods, some combining the most unusual of elements from cowboy shooter to RTS with first person elements and fort building. Racing games, horror games, action games, new story driven linear games with amazing stories to be told there is just so much variation in Half Life 2 mods and many of those developers have gone to become successful all because of Half Life 2's Source Engine.
This engine still holds up today surprisingly with modern textures, Half Life 2 is the grandfather of indie games and we still wait for the sequel that may never come, but you know what? Half Life is still a darn fun game to play once in a while.
To make a timeless linear shooter, requires skills and dedication, and we wont see such a beast anytime soon so cheerish it while you can.

This is a very simply made game: static image backgrounds, text and music. No amazing 3D graphics, dazzling explosions or killer AI enemies... What is amazing is the terrific, immersive story you are drawn into.
The tale begins with you waking up after some kind of accident in the woods. You try to find out what has happened and are gradually drawn into lethal mystery. All the elements are top-notch. Great characters. Creepy environments. Discoveries that are both baffling and horrific. And threats that are chilling and relentless.
During the story, you regularly make decisons that will affect the narrative. You may find yourself crushed by a choice which leads to an awful death. I found there were sufficent decisions to be made to keep you deeply involved without detracting from the game's biggest strength, which is the storytelling.
The writing is gripping from start to end. For me, it felt like being trapped in a truly sinister Stephen King story - it was that good.
Negatives? Other than a few typos near the end of the story (which didn't spoil the game), none at all.
Playtime: 3-4 hours.
Overall: 10/10. I'd love to play another game like this from the same production team!

Simply put, this is a solid and reasonably intriguing horror-mystery story told in the form of an interactive novel. The visuals are minimal but effective, the sound is spooky and immersive, and the writing is simplistic and a tad underwhelming but gets the job done. No great shakes, and fairly short (a few hours, tops), but worth the three bucks if you're up for a moody and sometimes action-packed tale with a wee bit of interactivity. It won't be an earth-shattering experience for anyone who's read the odd horror/sci-fi short story - or played a certain famous video game franchise, which I won't mention the name of for spoiler reasons! - but it's an entertaining enough diversion for those of us with an unquenchable taste for the eerie and enigmatic.
Oh, and for those greatly concerned with such things: it would also appear to have some small degree of replayability due to the variety of choices on offer, even if one suspects that most if not all of the story's main mysteries are revealed in a single playthrough. But hey, what do you expect for three bucks? A blow-job AND a marriage contract?! C'mon, let's be realistic here...

This is the kind of game that you either love it or hate it. Neptune for example, you can see her as adorable or you can hate her for being so annoying and meme-like. I choose the former (owo)b I won't write a so deep review so in my opinion we have:
- Charismatic characters with different stereotypes for every taste
- A long but good enough story told as a visual novel
- Turn based combat that takes in account your position on the battlefield
- Panties (don't deny you love them)
- Many different outfits and accessories to choose for them to wear
- Many unlockables by gathering resources
- Nice music even though it can be repetitive later on
- The ability to change the game via the remake system, spawning different enemies and resources
- You can adjust the difficulty via this remake system but it has no gain or loss
- Appart of your weapon and clothes you can equip chips that increase (and most times also decrease) your stats when you go HDD letting you customize even further your battle style
- Noire <3 (or each of your favorites)
- Different endings according to chars unlocked and... well, you better discover by yourself.
- You'll need at least 3 playthroughs to get enough MB to unlock everything
- The colosseum let's you play different challenges even if still the same kind of combat
- And of course, lolis <3 You can go HDD if you prefer bigger breasts though
- The combat can end up being repetitive
- You can just use 3 chars at once even if there are 4 main ones
- It can take too long to complete everything (I'm not done yet at almost 250 current hours). That can be a pro if you want a long game
- At first it's unavoidable but later is so easy to miss events or places that you should go to unlock certain dungeons that at the same time unlock others and have items that let you unlock items
- If you don't like silly humor and/or highpitched voices you might hate a lot of this game
- The variety of enemies is quite small. Most of them will have the same model with different colors to say they are a stronger version
- Leveling takes so much grinding at first until you can beat certain monsters without being killed in the process
- Making money is the same, hard at first and later you'll be swimming in money (except if you wanna buy some chips that cost millions each)
- Once you've gone past certain level, even if you increase the difficulty, everything will be too easy
- There are a few DLC colosseum fights that are ridiculously hard compared to the rest of the game
Overall it's good even with those flaws (^_^)y
