This might feel somewhat awkward, since you'll be uncool the entire time you're playing this game!
Besides that obvious major flaw there's really not much to complain about. Think the classic asteroids where the asteroids fire back, this game is a great time waster. The style of the game is probably not for everyone. You will spend most of the game looking at absolute chaos on your screen and it's simply impossible to see everything at all times. If you're the kind of person who thinks games like snake or asteroids are harder if everything is moving too slow, this game is for you. Using your own music as a base for the 'levels' is a cool gimmick and gives you some amount of control over what kind of game you want to play. With the DLCs you do get quite a bit of extra content, including new ships that require completely different playing styles and a lot more goals to complete, which - for me - is a good way to maintain interest in a game.

This game has a serious User Interface problem. It struggles to communicate even the most basic things for the Tower Defence genre. For example: when you are going to place a tower, the menu that shows tower placement options actually gets in the way of the range indicator for the towers. Also, the tower placement menu is only visible for as long as you hold the mouse button down; and if you accidentaly misclick a tile, that counts as pressing the button (to show the menu) and releasing it (to select an action i.e. placing a tower), which means you'll built lots of towers by mistake. The buttons in the interface are way too small, there are no information tooltips for most of them (what the hell does the exclamation mark do exactly? It turns red when I click it, but that's it). The fonts are ugly and inconsitent. The creeps' HP bars are hard to read. The pathing of the creeps is smart, but it doesn't show you how it will change until you actually place your towers, so you have to think extra hard before you do anything. Even deleting units from your units queue is painfully hard, you have to double click each individual unit (also, this information is nowhere to be found, I figured it out by mistake). Seriously, the developers need to take a cold, hard look at their User Interface and User Experience. The game is frustrating before it even starts.
These interface issues were enough to make my experience (with a friend, actually) a nightmare, to the point where I ragequitted a co-op game that I was winning. Aside from that, I'd say that the game actually tries to be funny (in the tutorial and in all the tips and vocal taunts), but really it is not. And bad comedy is worse than no comedy at all.
The more I think about this game, the more I find things to hate about it. Having two different resources seems like a good idea in theory, but it sucks in game. There are loads of options everywhere and on everything, but most of them are not actually viable - they're useless clutter. You have 3 mines (where you get your resources from) and you can upgrade each one individually. Why? Why not have just one place to control your resource gathering? By the way, the "Tower Defence" aspect of this game is secondary. This is a resource-management game, pure and simple: it's about MIN/MAXING meaningless numbers on what could otherwise be an Excel sheet. Except there's a guy yelling at you trying to be a funny british king figure, and failing hard at it.
This game is not worth it.

This is the major downside to this game, but the humor completely makes it worth it nonetheless.
Another minor downside, if you can even call it that, is that the achievements are moronic. Nonetheless, game is recommended still, it is very funny and witty, and makes for a great pastime.

Too short to be a proper game, and too long to be just DLC, Far Cry Primal falls somewhere in between. Far Cry Primal is a copy and pasted Far Cry 4, some things have changed, but it's not enough to be worth the price it's being currently sold at. Being set in the stone age, the weapons that you have are vastly different and more primative from the other games in the series (obviously), but there is nothing good about this, the bows I found were too weak to be useful, I ended up throwing spears instead, and the melee weapons (there are 3, club two handed club, and spear) felt dreadful. The melee combat had not been developed at all since the past games, which isn't a good idea because in the other games you do not rely so heavily on using melee. On the standard mode, normal, this game was way too easy, I rarely used the owl to scout when I discovered I could simply charge in with a spear and spam left click.
The only language spoken in the game is a mix of made up words with a Proto-Indo-European structure, this was an issue as it meant that it was near impossible to have a real connection with any of the characters, by the end of the game I could remember basically only the main characters name as the other characters didn't mean much to me, their stories felt pointless and were there just to make the game time longer. I didn't feel like I was doing anything for a reason, I'd go to a place and kill some people and burn some stuff, with no real care as to why. The main story was also short and uneventful, spoilers but there aren't really any twists during the entire game, you go to a place, kill some person and it's gg.
The main antagonist of the game was no where near as interesting as the other Far Cry game's baddies, I felt no emotions towards him and never really wanted to kill him because he hadn't really done anything, he comes to your village in one scene and burns like a hut or two and suddenly he's the sole base of the games story.
Overall running around in 10,000 B.C was fairly enjoyable, but it felt so pointless, easy and I was never really immersed in the world, at the current price I would strongly advise against buying Far Cry Primal, if you still want it that badly then I'd just wait for it's price to drop massivley because only then would it be close to being worth a buy.

Far Cry Primal as a Far Cry game is actually rather good. You can see thatgreat care was taken to provide an authentic stone age experience, and survival actually means something in this game. For Example, wondering around in the day is much safer, as one would think, however come nightfall this changes, and suddenly the hunter can easily become the hunted.
The crafting options are in depth, and the village development adds another layer of fun, as this time you can actually see things changing as you save people, bring them together, and develop them further.
The only gripe with this game for me so far, the skills. Some of the skills are classis Far Cry, and work very well, and some skills are blatant time savers and nothing else.
The ability to tame beasts leads to interesting interactions between you and other tribes in the land of Oros. The story is not driven and shoved in your face like previous installments, however it makes sense the way the story is presented, after all this is 10 000BC, where most forms of comunication consisted of cave paintings, talking, and spear chucking.
Overall: I would say that if Far Cry Primal was the first Far Cry game in the series it would have had a much higher reception value, and would possibly have done much better, don't get me wrong, there are some mechanics here that we have seen two games ago already, but the method of implementation this time round is so much more methodical and calculated. I would easily give this game a 75%, and say even if you don't play it now, play it at some point in time, as it is definitely a good Far Cry game.

Incredibly beautiful game. Like walking through a water color painting that's being drawn.
Everything else that I would put down to poor design decisions by developers.
It's a pretty lame story, but I don't down-rate for bad stories. Basically, you play a blind girl walking around to find a cat she used to play with that has disappeared.
The world around is a blank canvas that gets colored in as you walk around. There are some cool effects where things get painted when you're further away, like if there is a sound from afar, such as a bell ringing or a babbling brook. Sometimes the girl will hear something and think it's one thing, only to find it is another as she walks closer -- like misinterpreting the sound of a lawn mower for a car.
Anyway, the primary negative aspect of the game that cannot be ignored and ruins the game:
Yeah, I get that she's blind and cannot be sprinting all over the place like Daredevil, but the pace is ridiculously slow. This is a game, not real life, so the developers could have done a better job managing the balance.
They could have given her a walking stick, which could provide justification for a faster pace. What blind girl walks around aimlessly in new territory without a walking stick? Instead, the poor thing is constantly walking into walls and fences.
The issue of pace is worsened when you need to find a path or backtrack ... the whole thing because incredibly tedious, and I exaggerate you not when I say I started to get headaches the last two times playing this.
I checked other reviews to see how long it takes to complete. A couple of reviews said it takes about two hours. If I was close, I might have finished, but I was at a point where I wanted to throw my controller through the window. I had already played one hour, and another hour may not seem like a lot, but that one hour felt like weeks. Basically, the experience of this game is the OPPOSITE of time flying.

This is a perfect example of an idea that was too big for the team that came up with it.  It's a great idea: a game from the perspective of a blind girl, where most of the world is white and is revealed as she hears noises and explores.  But the execution is extremely lacking.  The game has a small handful of interesting mechanics, but even the best of them never live up to their potential.  So much more could have been done with the idea of seeing what she's imagining, then discovering what it really is.  More could have been done with the way she interacted with the world around her; how cool would it have been if instead of just revealing the environment in a perfect orb around her by merely walking around, you had to reach out and touch things, or actively use sound?
And even when you're being pleasantly surprised by what the game does right, you're bored to tears by its most basic goal: walking around and slowly, SLOWLY revealing things at a snail's pace.  It's very obvious that the developers came up with the premise, planted a few small things to do then stretched the whole thing as far as they could.  I mean seriously, you move at an absolute crawl with no option to move faster, 90% of your time AT LEAST is spent simply walking and trying to find your way through the story path, and still the game is something like two hours long.
Overall just a disappointing experience that I can't even recommend for the tidbits that I mildly enjoyed.  The concept is a great one, but someone else with a bigger budget and/or more creativity needs to have a go at it.

In my mind, XCOM: Enemy Unknown (and more specifically, the Enemy Within expansion) create an excellent combination of old school XCOM gameplay mechanics and modern accessibility. Admittedly, I never made it very far in the original X-Com. I haven't given it a try in a long time, so I may have to pick it back up. However, in the past, my attempts to progress met with spectacular failure. Enemy Unknown/Within is extremely difficult, but not in an oppressive way. They provide just the right amount of challenge that makes you want to dust yourself off and keep playing, even after getting your butt handed to you.
Repel an alien invasion by utilizing all of the resources at the XCOM organization's disposal. Manage troops, equipment, research, upgrades, and more. Fight turn based battles against the invaders.
*Difficult decisions to be made. You can't afford everything. You can't protect every country, afford all weapons and armor, AND keep all of your troops alive. Sacrifices must be made.
*There's a lot of viable methods of upgrading your troops. Give them plasma rifles, throw them in mechanized suits, equip them with a jetpack, and more.
*Each playthrough is different. Several random elements keep you on your toes.
*The turn-based tactical combat stays fresh and exciting as new aliens emerge and your troops receive upgrades.
*The Enemy Within expansion adds a ton of extra content, including mission types, troop upgrades, an entirely new enemy force, a base defense mission, and more.
*It can be frustrating when you miss an alien when you have a 90%+ chance to hit them.
*A few of the map designs limit the number of possible tactical approaches.
Overall, this is one of my favorite strategy games. I am extremely excited for XCOM 2, and if you manage to get Enemy Unknown along with the expansion for a good price, you're going to thoroughly enjoy yourself. Just be ready to make some tough decisions and lose some troops. Good luck, commander.

“Buried: An Interactive Story”, as an interactive story has a lot going for it. But as a story it still has a way to go, and some of the issues are so integral as to likely prohibit repair. Still, for the most part not a bad way to spend three hours. (Due to offline play, I can only estimate game time at over three hours. There is a LOT of text. I found this to be both a plus and a minus, as you will see.)
The premise of “Buried: An Interactive Story” (BAIS) is that you are the boss of a logging crew who very suddenly finds that he and his crew are the victims of a mysterious and unknown disaster deep in the forest. You find your way into an underground government facility, where things really start to go bad. The story/game is broken into 5 chapters, each chapter is further broken into small segments, allowing for pauses.
The story of BAIS is pretty basic Lovecraft-like, and not particularly original. Saying that, I would also say that the mood generated is adequately creepy, with a story that feels both complete and real, in the context of this type of game. If the idea was simply to create a great story, this would fail. But since the point is to create an interactive story, it succeeds quite well, with the storyline leading not to more story so much as more decisions. The purpose is simply to drive the player to the next choice, and the choices really stand out (at least for the first three chapters.) The choices really are often quite difficult to make, as they almost always involve other characters for which you feel a genuine sense of responsibility. Some choices are simply to move the story along, and give the feeling that the response would have varied little based on the decision made, if at all. Some choices are significant, as you are notified once your choice is final. At the close of each chapter the player is notified of the statistics involving each significant choice among existing players.
UNFORTUNATELY, once the fourth of five chapters of BAIS is reached, the choices do next to nothing for the story and are rarely significant. In virtually every case it’s a simple choice of “noble choice” versus “selfish choice”, and shallow beyond belief considering the depth of many choices offered in the first three chapters. I chose “noble” (this IS fiction), so I have no knowledge of how other choices would have played out. About his point, the complexity of the game that was such a strong feature to begin…..comes crashing down. In numerous cases the story feels unconnected, and one death as related in the story was absolutely NOT the death that had occurred in “my” story. While there were many pluses to the first half of the story, I was quite happy when it finally came to a grinding halt.
Great attention was paid to the grammar in BAIS, which was much appreciated. I only found one case of a typo, one of a sentence that made little sense linguistically, and one case of “I” instead of “me”. While there were numerous cases of commas improperly used (or absent), they were by no means dealbreakers. The minor background sounds added much, as did the background stills and the choice of typeface. The feature of leaving the game with a simple ESC, then returning regardless of the position within a chapter segment was very welcome.
While I wish BAIS had either been shorter and cheaper, or long with more attention paid, it was still acceptable. Still, I would recommend waiting for a sale price of no more than $1.50 US.

Now for the positives. HOLY crap, I just can't stop playing this game. It has a movement system that I wish a game like Fallout 4 had and the combat is quick and simple, to the point ... not bogged down with too much button mashing and nonsense.
The city of Harran is amazing, feels very real and the outskirt farmlands in The Following are even better IMO.
While the story itself is a little simple, I did not mind it as the side quests seem to add a fill-element that smoothed out any disappointed about the on-rails format of the main story; even if I wished there was more player choice in what I was able to do and not do. The game would have been an AAA+ title if it just had a bit more choice for the player to make so each play-through would offer something new. Maybe in the sequel (crosses fingers).
This game is easily worth its current full price, in the Enhanced Edition The Following package. You pay cents on the hour for the game, so you for sure get your worth out of it.
On top of that, there are a few great mods available for the game ... just skip over to the Nexusmods website and there you go, some great additions to make the game even better.
Bottom line, Dying Light is worth every dollar you invest into it and sets itself a part from other zombie games with its refined gameplay and superior movement mechanics. Which, I will say, OMG gave me vertigo a little as iRL, I am not a fan of heights.

Everything Dead Island aspired to be.
-Pros-
* You can dropkick zombies into spike traps, and it actually works, and it's actually satisfying.
* There's a nifty potion system. Kind of adds a layer of gameplay to the game, and you'll definitely want to use it.
* There is kind of a stealth system during the night. Stay still and out of sight when Volatiles come close, dash as fast as you can when they're out of range. Noise attracts them, so fireworks work.
* Night is terrifiying. Make sure to stock up on those night-vision potions. Makes the experience not so nerve-wracking.
* The Volatiles will seriously put the hurt on.
* Parkour makes the maps more traversable, yet it doesn't make the game easy. Some zombies can chase you down. Volatiles WILL put the hurt on.
* The parkour allows you to pick your route across buildings instead of restricting you to the streets. More fluid motion, so to speak.
* The plot and story are kind of typical of a zombie survival game, yet this game does it quite well. Sure, there's points where the game will tell you to go here and collect this and come back. However, they lessen the blow by telling you that you're one of the few "Runners" that are venturing into the city, and manpower is spread thin. You know that you're the only one, but the game sort of apologizes for being a jerk, so it's okay.
* You're not immune, which thickens the plot a bit.
* Characters are pretty well fleshed out.
* The leveling system is pretty cool.
* You have a cool UV flashlight that keeps Volatiles at bay. Makes the playing field a little more even. They are faster and stronger than you after all.
-Cons-
* The horde DLC kind of blows. Instead of fighting off hordes of zombies in an arena for guts and glory, you're jumping through hoops, deactivating bombs, and killing targets within a time limit. Kind of disappointing, but you get some cool loot from it afterwards.
* Sometimes there's pathing issues with parkour, but with games similar to Dead Island there are no issues, only features. Will jump to a plank just to slide off into a horde of zombies again.
Oh, you can snap the neck of zombie babies. Horrible, yet satisfying. Parenting/10

Beyond Eyes tells the story of blind girl Rae and a cat named Nani.
You have to consider that the world you see in the game isn't necessarily the real world, but the one Rae pieces together in her mind from what she hears, feels and smells, and it looks absolutely stunning. It often changes in front of you as she puts more of the pieces together while progressing through the levels.
Though not very long, this game isn't for the impatient. Rae moves at a very slow pace as would be expected from a girl without her eyesight, but after hitting a dead end and having to go back the way you came it can get tedious. As long as you are willing to see it through the overall experience is worth the time.
Also take note that if you decide to play this game it would be best not to look up the ending. It may seem drawn out in parts but the levels aren't too long and only by playing through it will you have a real appreciation when you do get to the end.

(This review was written after finishing Season 1)
Only get the game if you like the ASOIAF world, and even then, you might not enjoy it fully. I'd also suggest not buying the season pass and waiting for the full game, even if it takes another year or two.
I would not recommend the game due to several issues. Apart from some optimization troubles, my biggest grief lies in how the overall story was portrayed and how little your decisions affect the end result in a game where they are hyped as the biggest feature.
It feels like the authors' hands were tied due having to write the story in an existing universe with pre-established relations and dynamics. Again, in spite of the major premise of the game being you driving the story and making meaningful decisions, this does not really happen.
I do understand that it is rather hard in this instance and that the developers would have a very difficult challenge ahead of them, especially as they plan for more seasons, but the outcomes are sometimes just ridiculous.
As for the story, it just feels the game is stacked against you. No matter how carefully you weigh your options, in most cases everything just comes back to bite you in the butt. In other situations where you receive help it sometimes feels random and undeserved, leaving next to no positive feelings of accomplishment in the player.
I do not share the idea that everything has to have a happy ending, but for some reason, everything should not just go to hell "since this takes place in Westeros and you play as a noble Northern family." Your performance has no direct perceivable result, the entire thing feels complete out of your hand. You might as well be watching a film, in which the protagonist enjoys having plot armour for some time before dying and passing his bad luck to the next of kin.
It could still make sense, but not with the build-up from all the episodes - you attempt so many plans and plots, but they all fail nonetheless.

As of this review, online mode has already been taken down, which was a big part of the game. That being said, if you manage to pick this up during a star wars sale and have never played it (or have played it, and just want to revisit it), i would definitely recommend it. If for no other reason then to just drive (walk?) around in an AT-AT. Once in the single player menu you have 2 choices, campaign (galactic conquest) and instant action.

Once you select galactic conquest, you have about 6 choices of a starting time, eg clone wars, start of the rebellion, ect. This game mode, while fun for a bit, gets boring and repetitive quite quickly once you capture a few planets. To capture a planet, you move a fleet onto that planet, if the enemy has a fleet there space combat will commence. If they do not have a fleet, you will get the much better ground combat. Space combat involves two opposing capital ships spewing fighters at each other, and each side trying to destroy 5 key points on each others command ship. You can also bring a drop ship into the other teams hanger and kill their pilots before they get to their ships, however, this is not recommended due to this game only being single player right now. Ground combat has a lot more variety (unless you keep fighting over the same planet), with different ground vehicles and occasionaly the natives will help (endor). Now, due to how this mode works, once the enemy has lost their last fleet, a new one will spawn immediately upon you ending your turn. So you end up having to block all hyperspace routes, while trying to capture the remaining planets. This wouldnt even be so bad, but they only allow you 1 move or combat per turn. And this basicly ends up with the other team engaging a fleet of yours, EVERY turn.
As for instant action, you can choose from about 20 different maps, space or ground, different victory conditions, how many AI "players" are on at a time and the era (clone wars or new republic). I would recommend mostly playing under instant action, just for variety.
With all that being said, i got about 8 hours out of it, and dont regret buying it at all. Although I do regret not playing it back when multiplayer was still up. Oh well. Heres hoping EA doesnt screw up battlefront 3!
EDIT: EA screwed up battlefront 3.

Grim Dawn is a top-down Action Role Playing Game. I would have said Isometric if the camera wasn't adjustable though. With many similar gameplay elements to THQ's Titan Quest, the game has its own distinct art style and unique flair with plenty of modern day ARPG improvements. As I mentioned, this game is a great spiritual successor to Titan Quest and although it's a little slower paced than...say...Diablo 3, I'd say the rewards and overall character progression feels much more satisfying. At the time of this review I'd still say this game and Path of Exile are the two best ARPGs out there right now and I've played them all except an obscure few. Difficulty progression is along the lines of Diablo 2. Where you start at normal difficulty, complete it and redo the whole story again in the next difficulty tier and so until a 3rd, final playthrough. You can also enable a veteran difficulty option that makes your current playthrough even tougher.
Let's get the bad out of the way first. The multiplayer can break your character if you're not careful, unless they've fixed this since this happened to me and my friend. If the host is further along in the game than the friend you invite, it will break your friends' quests and replace them with yours, making it possible to skip everything they haven't done yet and miss important NPCs and quest items with no way to return things to normal other than starting over. But as long as you stick together with fresh toons on the same quests throughout your playthrough, you'll be fine.
The story is okay, it feels like it drags on at times but it is well told and thought out. With dozens and dozens (hundreds?) of NPCs to interact with as well as a few plot altering choices along the way, Grim Dawn manages to stay fresh up until the very end. Compound that with an amazing variety of multi-class options and skill selection mixed with all types of weapons and armor to supplement your playstyle, it's a joy to play. And hey, if you screw up your skill placement there's always an NPC that can fix that....for a price. There's also an added feature called Devotion, whose points are earned from shrines scattered throughout the game and can be used to further solidify your position as a walking weapon of mass destruction.
Speaking of NPCs there are blacksmiths that will craft items from blueprints, faction based shops that will sell you items based on how friendly you are to the different factions in the area. A respec NPC, a few different types of item merchants and even a bounty system. There are tons of sidequests to be found along the path and given by NPCs.
The music, sound effects and ambient noises mix well with the game's "grim" atmosphere. Everything fits together nicely. If you're interested I suggest looking up the Grim Dawn OST on youtube at the very least.
More content is still being added, which is great. There will be an Illusionist NPC that lets you transmogrify equipment to look like other equipment you've found, much like Diablo 3's Mystic. An expansion on the way and there's already some extra dungeons and events like the Crucible that have been added over time too. Even for the full price I still think this game is worth it. I recommend it, highly. One of my all-time favorite ARPGs.

This game is exactly what it is advertised as. It is not really a game, in the traditional sense, but an interactive story. Do not go into this expecting traditional gameplay found in most titles as you're bound to be really, really annoyed. It's not even like a point and click adventure. You have no control over your character's movement, just some decisions that he makes throughout the 2-3h story.
Without ruining too much of the story, this is a sci-fi text-based adventure that takes place in the woods of Kentucky. The story is narrated on screen via text, an eerie/haunting soundtrack and evocative imagery. I highly recommend that you play this game in the dark, both literally and figuratively. Knowing anything about the story in any form would ruin the thrill completely, and for this purpose I'm not going to go into detail here.
The bottom line is - don't go into this expecting more than what you see in the title. It is just that - and it does what it does remarkably well.

Company of Heroes 2 is a nice upgrade from the original, if you don't mind compromise. It loses some of its features like a slightly more extensive (More extensive, not extensive) commander abilities list (Unless, of course, you wish to pay for them. But you still get barely any per commander). The graphics upgrade is barely notable, but strategy games don't thrive on a graphics focus, so nothing special was to be expected I think.
The winter mechanics? Well. It would be nice if we could rule them all out at once, but it seems Relic still want to only let us prevent 3 maps from loading (rather than a toggle for winter maps?).
Multiplayer. Ahh, multiplayer. Another amazing game where there's no consequence for raging. None at all. I can't even votekick unless someone lags out. Relic seem to like this idea. Not sure why. It's not the days of C&C Generals and the like anymore, Relic. Upgrade that area! I have a dropout on 60% of all my matches, and it means nothing to the system. Sometimes it's intentional dropouts and sometimes they just plain rage 7 minutes in when we didn't help their MG-mob against an ostwind.
Base building. Oh jeez. You made it nothing but bunkers, and everything is off-map. Can't infantry at least come from the bunkers? Seems odd that there isn't a single eastern battlefront with the ability to create units (If it's a realism situation, CoH1 would like to argue otherwise, where we built Panthers in the middle of Lyon).
What happened to blowing up bridges as well? Did it become hardcore, or did you just forget it?
5/10, buy it in a sale if Steam is being nice to your wallet.

Beyond Eyes is a very cutesy game about a blind girl, Rae, looking for her cat, Nani. In order to accomplish this mission, she has to stray farther from her home than she's ever been, brave the unknowns of her neighborhood, face dangerous situations and meet new people.
The game is all about the jorney, as the gameplay amounts to no more than "find your way around the level, occasionally bringing an object somewhere".
To reflect Rae's blindness, the world is hidden from the player, and is only revealed as the player walks around and finds things out. Sometimes, also to reflect Rae's blindness, she will perceive things differently than they really are, based only on how they sound or feel, and only upon further inspection will it be revealed to you what that thing truly was.
Rae will interact with other animals she meets in her jorney to find her cat, and those interactions can be very cute, which could help you better enjoy the game if you're an animal lover. However, some animals are scary, maybe even dangerous, and Rae will refuse to approach them.
The graphics are not very impressive on the technical side of things, but the game is visually beautiful, with gorgeously colorful buildings and forests, and the effects used to reveal the world as you explore it further compliment the game's artistic presentation.
Overall, it's a very short game that doesn't overstay it's welcome, it's pretty, it's cute, and it may give you warm fuzzy feelings.

Beyond Eyes is a spectacularly good walking sim. Unusually it's third-person instead of first-person, but because of the setup this actually works really well. You play a young blind girl looking for her cat. This provides a very original take on the "fog of war" mechanic, guiding the protagonist around an unknown world, sharing in her journey of discovery, her fear and delight. Each step fills a little more of the canvas; Monet in action. As well as unfolding in color and movement, the story is told through excellent sound effects, music and fragments of a pan-European pidgin that should evoke familiarity across the continent. Well-paced, beautiful, touching, inspirational... If you like walking sims, definitely pick this up.

Having seen both the Udam's and the blue people's leaders, they don't have that same vibe as the 3 and 4 main villians. The mammoth missions suck in every possible definition. I dislike the owl and its controls. The only technically innovating thing is the ability to tame the animals, and I dislike it. Having played ARK Survival Evolved, I can honestly tell you, it never gives the same satisfactory, so I just play without using the wolves and the big cats. I do wish the weapons were a little stronger especially the long bow, as I tend to love playing the sniper class and think in such a way. It does crash ALOT and it does so in such a weird way that makes my TV not register the computer sending a signal to it.
In conclusion, I do recommend this game because for all its bad, I still cannot put it down...however you might  just wait a while until it goes on sale or another patch or two.

The visualization in water colors is a cute idea and fitting to the protagonist.
